title: Causal Effect Identifiability in Causal Abstractions: A Strict Hierarchy of Criteria
description:
arXiv:2610.13520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying causal effects from observational data typically requires a fully specified causal graph, an assumption that is often unrealistic in complex or high-dimensional settings. Causal abstractions address this limitation by retaining only partial causal information, thereby defining equivalence classes of compatible causal graphs. In this paper, we study causal effect identifiability directly at the level of these graph collections, rather than at the level of individual causal diagrams. We formalize several notions of identifiability in this setting and organize them into a hierarchy that clarifies their relationships and differences. In particular, we establish that a causal effect may be identified over a collection of graphs without admitting a single causal derivation that holds uniformly across all compatible graphs. These results help reveal gaps and clarify ambiguities in the existing literature.

title: Always-on tracing for production and preview traffic
description:
With always-on tracing, you can now debug your real user requests without reproducing them.

Always-on tracing continuously collects traces from your production and preview traffic. Unlike session tracing, which only captures requests from your own browser, it samples your live traffic.

You control what's collected with sampling rules. Each rule sets a trace rate for an environment (All, Production, or Preview), optionally scoped to a path prefix like /checkout. Nothing is collected until you add a rule, so you pay only for what you choose to trace.

You can also manage sampling rules from the CLI. vercel traces config set adds a rule, or changes the rate of an existing one when you run it again with the same environment and path prefix:

Infrastructure and outbound fetch spans are captured automatically. To add framework and custom spans, instrument your app with @vercel/otel.

To view a trace, open the Logs or run vercel traces get <request-id>.

Always-on tracing is is now in beta and available to teams on all plans. Tracing is priced at $0.50 per 1M span units. Traces follow your runtime log retention: 1 hour on Hobby, 1 day on Pro and 3 days on Enterprise.

Get started by adding a rule in Settings → Tracing or from the settings icon in Logs. Learn more in the documentation.

title: React.js Best Practices: Writing Clean, Scalable, and Maintainable Components
description:
React makes it easy to build interactive user interfaces, but writing React code that remains maintainable as an application grows requires more than knowing hooks and JSX. Small decisions about component structure, state management, rendering, and side effects can significantly affect long-term development speed.

In production applications, I focus on keeping components predictable, separating responsibilities, and making data flow easy to understand. These practices help teams debug issues faster, avoid unnecessary complexity, and ship features without breaking existing functionality.

Let's explore practical React.js best practices using a runnable JavaScript example that demonstrates component separation, immutable state updates, derived values, validation, and clean event handling.

10 React.js Best Practices for Production Applications

1. Keep Components Small and Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility. Instead of building a single component that handles data fetching, validation, filtering, and rendering, split the interface into smaller components that are easier to test and reuse. Extract repeated UI patterns into shared components when doing so improves clarity.

2. Use State Only for Values That Change

React state should represent information that changes over time and affects rendering. Avoid storing values that can be calculated from existing props or state because duplicated state can become inconsistent. For example, calculate filtered products during rendering instead of maintaining a separate state variable for the filtered list.

3. Never Mutate State Directly

React works best when state updates create new objects or arrays rather than modifying existing values. Use methods such as map, filter, and the spread operator to update collections immutably. For complex nested state, consider a reducer or a dedicated state-management solution.

4. Use Effects for External Synchronization

The useEffect hook is intended for synchronizing React with external systems, such as browser APIs, subscriptions, timers, or network connections. Avoid using effects to calculate values that can be derived during rendering. Always clean up subscriptions and timers when the component unmounts or the effect reruns.

5. Handle Lists and Keys Correctly

When rendering collections, provide a stable and unique key for every item. Database IDs are generally preferable to array indexes because indexes can produce incorrect reconciliation when items are reordered, inserted, or removed. Avoid generating random keys during rendering because they force React to recreate elements unnecessarily.

6. Keep Event Handlers Predictable

Keep event handlers focused on a single action, such as adding a product or removing an item. Validate user input at the boundary and provide clear feedback when an operation cannot proceed. Functional state updates are particularly useful when the next state depends on the previous state.

7. Optimize Only When Measurement Justifies It

React provides tools such as memo, useMemo, and useCallback, but they should not be added automatically to every component. Start by writing straightforward code, profile the application, and optimize demonstrated bottlenecks. Premature memoization can increase complexity without producing a meaningful performance improvement.

8. Separate Business Logic from UI

Keep domain-specific calculations separate from rendering wherever practical. Small utility functions are easier to test independently and can be reused by different components. For larger applications, custom hooks can encapsulate reusable stateful behavior without coupling it to a particular visual layout.

9. Make Loading, Empty, and Error States Explicit

A production interface should account for more than its successful state. Display meaningful messages when data is unavailable, an operation fails, or a collection is empty. These states make the application easier to use and reduce confusion during unexpected situations.

10. Treat Accessibility and Security as Core Requirements

Use semantic HTML elements, associate labels with inputs, preserve keyboard accessibility, and communicate validation errors clearly. Never assume client-side validation provides security; validate and authorize sensitive operations on the server. Avoid rendering untrusted HTML directly, and keep secrets out of frontend bundles.

Practical Example: A Product Inventory Component

The following example uses React with modern JavaScript to implement a small inventory interface. It demonstrates component separation, controlled inputs, immutable updates, derived filtering, stable keys, and clear user feedback without requiring an additional state-management library.

import React, { useState } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

// Keep example data outside the component so it is not recreated on every render.
const initialProducts = [
  { id: 1, name: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 2499, stock: 12 },
  { id: 2, name: "Wireless Mouse", price: 999, stock: 25 },
  { id: 3, name: "USB-C Hub", price: 1499, stock: 0 },
];

// Extract reusable UI into a focused component.
function ProductCard({ product, onRemove }) {
  console.log(`Rendering product: ${product.name}`);

  return (
    <article className="product-card">
      <h3>{product.name}</h3>
      <p>Price: ₹{product.price.toLocaleString("en-IN")}</p>
      <p>Stock: {product.stock}</p>
      <button onClick={() => onRemove(product.id)}>
        Remove product
      </button>
    </article>
  );
}

function ProductInventory() {
  // State contains the source of truth for the inventory.
  const [products, setProducts] = useState(initialProducts);
  const [search, setSearch] = useState("");
  const [productName, setProductName] = useState("");
  const [productPrice, setProductPrice] = useState("");
  const [message, setMessage] = useState("");

  // Derive filtered products instead of duplicating them in state.
  const normalizedSearch = search.trim().toLowerCase();
  const filteredProducts = products.filter((product) =>
    product.name.toLowerCase().includes(normalizedSearch)
  );

  // Derive the total from current state to avoid stale totals.
  const totalProducts = products.length;
  const totalInventoryValue = products.reduce(
    (total, product) => total + product.price * product.stock,
    0
  );

  function handleAddProduct(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    console.log("Step 1: Validating product input.");

    const name = productName.trim();
    const price = Number(productPrice);

    // Validate values before updating application state.
    if (!name || !Number.isFinite(price) || price <= 0) {
      setMessage("Enter a product name and a valid positive price.");
      console.log("Step 2: Validation failed.");
      return;
    }

    console.log("Step 2: Creating the new product.");
    const newProduct = {
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      name,
      price,
      stock: 1,
    };

    // Create a new array instead of mutating the existing state.
    setProducts((currentProducts) => [
      ...currentProducts,
      newProduct,
    ]);

    console.log("Step 3: Product added successfully.");
    setProductName("");
    setProductPrice("");
    setMessage(`${name} was added to the inventory.`);
  }

  function handleRemoveProduct(productId) {
    console.log(`Removing product: ${productId}`);

    // filter returns a new array and preserves the original state.
    setProducts((currentProducts) =>
      currentProducts.filter((product) => product.id !== productId)
    );
    setMessage("Product removal requested.");
  }

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Product Inventory</h1>
      <p>Total products: {totalProducts}</p>
      <p>
        Inventory value: ₹
        {totalInventoryValue.toLocaleString("en-IN")}
      </p>

      <form onSubmit={handleAddProduct}>
        <label htmlFor="product-name">Product name</label>
        <input
          id="product-name"
          value={productName}
          onChange={(event) => setProductName(event.target.value)}
          placeholder="Enter product name"
          required
        />

        <label htmlFor="product-price">Price in rupees</label>
        <input
          id="product-price"
          type="number"
          min="0.01"
          step="0.01"
          value={productPrice}
          onChange={(event) => setProductPrice(event.target.value)}
          placeholder="Enter price"
          required
        />

        <button type="submit">Add product</button>
      </form>

      <label htmlFor="product-search">Search inventory</label>
      <input
        id="product-search"
        type="search"
        value={search}
        onChange={(event) => setSearch(event.target.value)}
        placeholder="Search by product name"
      />

      {/* Use a semantic live region to announce feedback to assistive technology. */}
      <p role="status" aria-live="polite">{message}</p>

      <section aria-label="Inventory products">
        {filteredProducts.length === 0 ? (
          <p>No matching products found.</p>
        ) : (
          filteredProducts.map((product) => (
            <ProductCard
              key={product.id}
              product={product}
              onRemove={handleRemoveProduct}
            />
          ))
        )}
      </section>
    </main>
  );
}

// Mount the application in the HTML element with id="root".
const rootElement = document.getElementById("root");

if (!rootElement) {
  throw new Error("Missing root element. Add <div id=\"root\"></div> to HTML.");
}

console.log("Starting the React inventory application.");
createRoot(rootElement).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <ProductInventory />
  </React.StrictMode>
);

// Note: This file contains JSX, so process it with a React-aware bundler
// such as Vite. Install React and React DOM before running the application.

Conclusion

React best practices are less about memorizing a collection of rules and more about building predictable systems. Small components, immutable state updates, stable keys, and clearly defined responsibilities make applications easier to maintain as requirements change.

The same principle applies to performance: keep the implementation simple first, measure actual bottlenecks, and optimize where the evidence points. A well-structured application is usually easier to profile, test, and improve than one filled with premature optimizations.

Start by reviewing one existing component in your project. Remove duplicated state, simplify its responsibilities, improve its accessibility, and make its edge cases explicit. Which React best practice has made the biggest difference in your production applications?

title: Benchmarking Embedding Geometries and Clustering Algorithms for Unsupervised Patent Claim Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.12997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior-art retrieval systems are structurally organized around classification codes, making cross-code discovery difficult. This paper asks if an unsupervised representation trained on patent text can recover relevant connections that code-restricted search cannot, and if hyperbolic space helps. We trained a hyperbolic and a matched Euclidean Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on 45,000 US patents (96 runs, 6 seeds). The hyperbolic model retrieves genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model (18.76% vs. 12.34% of top-10 results, 3,000 queries). This represents a practical gain for the motivating search problem. The hyperbolic model agrees less with official classification (NMI 0.2392 vs. 0.3206), which we explain geometrically: the two measures capture different goals, and only one aligns with prior-art search needs. In a study of 10 technology domains (50,000 more patents), we find that a domain's classification breadth--the number of distinct CPC subgroups spanned--predicts approach performance (Pearson r=-0.642, p=0.045, N=10), and that patents per subgroup is an even stronger predictor (r=0.715, p=0.020). This provides a checkable signal for practitioners to determine where the method is most valuable. We report all findings with statistical transparency and release a complete, 91-test automated implementation.

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: Fast LapSum: Exact Differentiable Top-$k$ at Million Scale
description:
arXiv:2608.06912v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Selecting the top-$k$ elements is a fundamental operation for inducing sparsity in large-scale models and optimization problems, enabling robust expert activation, token routing or attention pruning. However, hard top-$k$ is non-differentiable, while existing differentiable alternatives become increasingly expensive as the number of coordinates grows. We introduce Fast LapSum, a scalable solver for the LapSum soft top-$k$ formulation that preserves an exact selection mass of $k$, while supporting end-to-end differentiation. In Fast LapSum, we reduce sorting cost using probabilistic bracketing, which restricts sorting to a narrow band of scores around the threshold using a binomial order-statistic from kernel-noised samples. A certification pass upgrades the probabilistic localization to a verified one at the cost of one additional linear pass, with a full-sort fallback that covers the worst-case scenario. Our certified GPU implementation processes $10^6$, $10^7$, and $10^8$ scores in median times of $0.92$, $1.39$, and $7.24$ ms, respectively, making exact-budget soft top-$k$ practical within million-scale optimization loops. We demonstrate this capability in two applications: megapixel sparse adversarial examples with a small fraction of initial image pixels, where Fast LapSum achieves an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods, and 3D Gaussian splatting. In the latter, we use Fast LapSum to reduce the number of Gaussians produced by Adaptive Density Control to a substantially smaller number while retaining nearly the same rendering quality and massively reducing computation. These results demonstrate that exact-budget differentiable top-$k$ can be incorporated into practical million-scale optimization pipelines.

title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
description:
arXiv:2610.13081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.

title: LLM config repair: the syntax holds, the values move
description:
Claude Sonnet fixed every broken quote, tab and bracket in our .env, TOML and YAML files. Its misses were files that load and say something else.

The syntax, yes. The values, not reliably. We had two Claude models, Sonnet and Haiku, repair three sets of small config files: 24 in .env or INI form, 22 in TOML and 22 in YAML. Given only the request, Sonnet closed every quote left open, replaced every tab and added every missing bracket, yet just 19, 17 and 16 of its files came back right, and nearly every wrong one loaded without an error. The harm was to meaning: a value given a new type, a prefix or a key name lost, two conflicting values cut down to one in silence. With written rules for each format added to the request, Sonnet got all of them right.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/llm-config-repair-env-toml-yaml

title: TelcoAgent: A Scalable 5G Multi-KPM Forecasting With 3GPP-Grounded Explainability
description:
arXiv:2606.19821v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Key Performance Measurement (KPM) forecasting is essential for proactive network management of 5G and next-generation telecom networks. However, existing machine learning (ML) approaches face significant limitations in scalability and explainability, restricting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We propose TelcoAgent, a foundation model-based framework that enables accurate, scalable, and explainable forecasting of multiple KPMs across diverse network cells without the need for site-specific training. Specifically, the framework comprises three key components: (i) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) knowledge graph directly from specification documents, (ii) a scalable, time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline to deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasting, and finally (iii) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that provides actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluated using a 3-month, real-world, city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S.-based network operator, TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy for all 7 considered KPMs per cell across 200 cells, while delivering explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

title: Audit your UI before you redesign it: baseline first, then compare
description:
We just spent two weeks improving six dashboard pages in our research system. The tempting move was to open each page, feel what was wrong, and start fixing. That approach produces exactly what you expect: pages that each look individually fine but feel like they were designed by six different people.
Instead, we ran an audit first. Here is the method and what it caught.

The method: baseline, compare, classify

Step 1: Extract a baseline. Pick two or three pages in your system that already feel right — not because they are beautiful, but because they are consistent. Write down every convention they share: segmented controls, button styles, icon usage, font sizes, color semantics, spacing.
In our case, three pages shared a set of conventions we hadn't written down anywhere:

  • Segmented controls: gray track, pill-shaped, white floating active state
  • Back buttons: shared icon component, gray hover state
  • Icons: one shared icon library, no emoji
  • Text buttons: link-style gray-to-accent on hover
  • Loading: shared spinner component

Step 2: Compare every target page against the baseline. Not "does this look good?" but "does this match?" Each deviation gets written down as a specific, nameable difference.

Step 3: Classify each deviation. There are only two kinds:

  • The page is wrong — it should adopt the baseline convention
  • The baseline is wrong — the deviation reveals a better pattern that should be promoted to the system This classification prevents the two failure modes: inconsistency (everything is special) and rigidity (nothing can improve).

What the audit caught: 8 deviations in 6 pages

Deviation Fix
Square segmented controls Changed to gray-track pill with floating white active
Back button with red hover Changed to shared icon + gray hover
Three-line page headers Aligned to single-line pattern from reference page
Star icon in accent red Changed to neutral gray
Inline SVG chevron Changed to shared icon component
Outlined box button Changed to link-style text button
No loading indicator Added shared spinner
Inconsistent filter-clear hover Unified to same color token

None of these are dramatic individually. Together, they made six pages feel like six different products. After the audit, they feel like one system.

The color rule that fell out

One deviation taught us a principle worth keeping: a back button had red on hover. Red in UI means destructive — delete, danger, irreversible. A back button is none of those. Using red there trains users to hesitate on every red hover.
The rule we wrote down:
Accent red is reserved for numeric values and selected states. Icons and button hovers use neutral gray.

This is not a aesthetic preference. It is semantic hygiene: red should mean "pay attention to this number" or "you are here", never "this is clickable decoration".

The discipline part

After fixing, three things make it stick:

  1. Shared components only. Icons go through one file. Buttons go through one component. No page-local SVGs or ad-hoc button styles.
  2. Full verification after changes. TypeScript zero errors, all frontend tests pass, build succeeds, deployed chunk hash verified on both production ends.
  3. When a new pattern is better, promote it to the baseline. The point is not stasis — it is that changes happen at the system level, not scattered across pages.

The connection to agent governance

If you have been following this series, you will see the pattern: this is the same method as the shadow-to-gate pipeline from the previous post. In both cases:

  1. Measure before you change (shadow audit / UI baseline)
  2. Fix the mechanism, not individual instances (citation rebuild / shared components)
  3. Add a gate to prevent regression (citation gate / component-only rule) Whether you are governing agent output or UI consistency, the sequence is the same: baseline → compare → fix mechanism → gate.

Takeaway

If your multi-page application feels inconsistent, resist the urge to redesign page by page. Instead:

  1. Write down the conventions your best pages already share
  2. List every deviation in every other page
  3. Fix deviations — or promote better patterns to the baseline
  4. Enforce with shared components and full verification The audit itself took 30 minutes. The fixes took one afternoon. The result is six pages that feel like one system — something no amount of per-page tweaking had achieved.

title: Expanded search for workflow runs in Vercel Observability
description:
The runs list for Vercel Workflows in Observability now has structured search, giving you more ways to find and investigate runs.

title: Localized Generative Design of Ship Hulls with Diffusion Models and High-Fidelity Assessment
description:
arXiv:2610.12870v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Practical ship design requires localized refinement and performance evaluation. This paper presents a reward-directed diffusion framework for localized hull optimization. Parametric masking during dataset generation restricts geometric changes to selected variables, including the bulbous bow and forebody, while preserving full-hull continuity. Surrogate-assisted sequential Monte Carlo sampling targets reduced predicted calm-water resistance, with stability retained through training data and displacement matched during screening. An automated viscous free-surface CFD pipeline, validated against measurements for two benchmark container ships, evaluates a generated variant and GenHull E, a hull refined by a naval architect within the same representation. At matched KRISO Container Ship (KCS) displacement, the generated variant has comparable total resistance at $F_n=0.195$ but 45-50% higher resistance at $F_n=0.250$ and $0.260$, missed by empirical screening. GenHull E achieves 6-8% lower total resistance up to $F_n=0.240$ but higher resistance above $F_n=0.250$ as opposing friction and pressure trends reverse the gains. Aggregating resistance across this crossover can conceal tradeoffs that emerge when friction and pressure components are evaluated separately. The assessment reveals an inability to represent a faired bulbous bow and a reward lacking viscous pressure and stability terms. These findings show how high-fidelity assessment informs improved representations and objectives for physically realizable generative designs.

title: Neurograf v1: An End-to-End Romanian-First Language Model Family
description:
arXiv:2610.13134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Neurograf v1, an experimental end-to-end Romanian-first language-model pipeline developed to investigate the feasibility of training language models from scratch for a lower-resource European language. The pipeline comprises RoSfera, a 635 GB Romanian corpus containing 175.7 million documents; an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer; five decoder-only models ranging from 160M to 6B parameters, trained on 131 billion tokens; three instruction-tuned assistants; and two contrastively trained embedding models. Training and evaluation were conducted using computing infrastructure at ELI-NP/IFIN-HH.
  The model family exhibits consistent scaling of validation loss and increasing Romanian factual and cultural knowledge with model size. On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, Neurograf-6B achieves 69.89% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, while Neurograf-3.2B reaches 67.38%. Compute-optimal analysis yields a parameter-scaling exponent of approximately 0.423.
  Neurograf v1 serves as an experimental demonstrator rather than a production system. The study identifies practical challenges involving diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency, while demonstrating the feasibility of developing Romanian-first base models, instruction-following assistants, and semantic embedding models within a unified training pipeline.

title: The syntax of wh-agreement in Yemeni Ibbi Arabic
description:
arXiv:2607.04986v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This article tackles an important phenomenon in the syntax of Yemeni Ibbi Arabic (YIA), viz., wh-agreement, a phenomenon common to several languages including Greek, Indonesian, Lubukusu, Irish, etc. In YIA, wh-agreement manifests itself via agreement inflections on the Wh-Op, C, T/V, v. To account for this phenomenon, we propose an Agree across phases (AAP) approach anchored in the mechanism of Feature Inheritance (FI) in which Agree as MATCHING (AM) is a bit separated from feature valuation (FV). AM concerns Cs/vs, but FV Ts/Vs. Analyzing the agreement patterns observed between Wh-Op(erators), functional heads (precisely C, (T), v), and verbal complexes, we argue that the suffixes -eh, -uh, -nen, -um, having undergone grammaticalization process from Stannard Arabic (SA) third person pronouns, function as morphological marking of wh-agreement. Findings indicate that YIA data offer a unique empirical contribution to generative syntax, specifically concerning wh-agreement in this dialect operating via MATCHING mechanism. Our proposal straightforwardly accounts for wh-agreement cross-linguistically. This study provides further evidence that incorporating under-investigated typology provides further support for the universality of Universal Grammar (UG) by revealing how specific I-language operations reflect deeper, invariant principles of human language architecture. It concludes that the wh-agreement mechanism in YIA is more morphosyntactically robust than in languages such as Greek, Indonesian, Palauan, and Irish, providing compelling evidence for AAP as a UG approach to long-distance dependencies.

title: Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
description:
arXiv:2610.11575v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models scale parameter capacity efficiently while maintaining a fixed compute budget per token. However, traditional training paradigms enforce a static choice of top-$k$ experts, which converts a continuous routing distribution into a rigid step function. This constraint introduces a brittle boundary where highly competitive experts are arbitrarily separated into full-supervision and zero-feedback zones based on minor score fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose Elastic Expert Routing, which stochastically samples the active expert budget from a localized discrete distribution centered at $k$. Over multiple training iterations, this mechanism softens the sharp threshold into a gradual probability distribution. Because the sampling neighborhood remains symmetric, this approach matches the expected computational cost of deterministic training, while preserving the inference budget. During supervised fine-tuning, elastic routing improves downstream macro-averages on OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B by $+0.84$ and $+2.02$ points, respectively. In addition, in from-scratch pretraining, it reduces validation LM loss by up to $0.04$ and outperforms the static top-$k$ baseline by $1.6$ points on average across downstream tasks. Comparisons on Qwen3 fine-tuning and from-scratch pretraining further show higher average scores than Noisy top-$k$, expert FFN dropout, and DefaultMoE.

title: Django select_related vs prefetch_related (With Examples)
description:
Both exist to fix the same thing — the N+1 query problem — but they work on different kinds of relationships. The whole decision comes down to one question: is the relationship single-valued (a ForeignKey) or multi-valued (a ManyToMany)?

The problem they solve: N+1 queries

Say each Book has a ForeignKey to Author. This innocent loop quietly runs one query for the books, then one more per book to fetch its author:

books = Book.objects.all()
for book in books:
    print(book.author.name)   # a new DB query every iteration

100 books → 101 queries. That's the N+1 problem, and it's the single most common Django performance bug. select_related and prefetch_related both collapse those extra queries — they just do it differently.

select_related — for ForeignKey and OneToOne

select_related follows a single-valued relationship (ForeignKey, OneToOne) by doing a SQL JOIN and pulling the related object in the same query:

books = Book.objects.select_related('author')
for book in books:
    print(book.author.name)   # no extra queries — author came via the JOIN

101 queries become 1. Because it's a database join, it only works when each row has exactly one related row — that's why it's for ForeignKey and OneToOne, the "forward" single object.

prefetch_related — for ManyToMany and reverse ForeignKey

A JOIN can't efficiently fetch a multi-valued relationship (many rows per object), so prefetch_related takes a different approach: it runs a second query for all the related objects, then stitches them together in Python.

authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related('books')
for author in authors:
    for book in author.books.all():   # no extra query per author
        print(book.title)

That's 2 queries total (one for authors, one for all their books) instead of one-per-author. Use it for ManyToMany fields and for reverse ForeignKey access (the "many" side).

The rule

This is the whole thing to remember:

select_related   -> single-valued (ForeignKey, OneToOne)   -> SQL JOIN, 1 query
prefetch_related -> multi-valued  (ManyToMany, reverse FK) -> separate query, joined in Python

Put another way: if you'd follow the relationship to one object (book.author), use select_related. If you'd follow it to a set of objects (author.books.all()), use prefetch_related.

Combining them

Real queries often need both, and they chain cleanly:

# each book's author (FK) AND each book's tags (M2M), minimal queries
books = Book.objects.select_related('author').prefetch_related('tags')

You can also span relationships with __ — select_related('author__publisher') joins two levels of ForeignKey in one query, and prefetch_related('author__books') prefetches across them.

Common gotchas

  • Wrong tool, no error: using prefetch_related on a ForeignKey works but runs an extra query you didn't need — select_related is strictly better there. Using select_related on a ManyToMany raises an error, because you can't JOIN a multi-valued relation into one row.
  • Filtering after prefetch re-queries: calling .filter() on a prefetched set hits the DB again. To filter the prefetched data, use a Prefetch object with a queryset instead.
  • Only prefetch what you use: prefetching a relation you never touch just wastes a query and memory.

The N+1 problem and these two methods are a staple of Django interviews — see the full Django interview questions and the SQL questions on joins and query performance.

title: Give your eve agent a browser
description:
Your eve agent can now navigate the web like a human with agent-browser.

The @agent-browser/eve extension gives any eve agent a full set of browser tools: navigate pages, read content, click, fill forms, take screenshots, and inspect console and network activity. Everything runs inside the agent's sandbox.

Install the extension:

Then mount it under agent/extensions/:

Your agent gets namespaced tools like browser__navigate, browser__snapshot, browser__click, browser__fill, and browser__screenshot. Snapshot refs such as [ref=e12] become @e12 selectors, so the agent can inspect a page, then act on exactly what it saw.

The extension includes:

  • Sandbox isolation: Chromium and agent-browser run in the eve sandbox, not your app. Pre-install them in your sandbox template so sessions start warm, or let the extension install them on first use.

  • Domain allowlist: Restrict navigation and subresources with allowedDomains, and control output size, screenshot handling, proxy use, and session naming through extension options.

  • Credential protection: Cookie, storage, and saved-auth-state commands are never exposed to the model. Use eve extension overrides to disable tools, require approvals, or add app-specific guarded tools.

See a complete Next.js eve app with the extension mounted in the example, or read the documentation to get started.

title: How to Edit Text on a Picture Online Without Photoshop
description:
Disclosure: I work on PhoText (https://photext.ai/). This is a practical guide to editing text that is already part of a finished picture — not dropping a sticker on top, and not rebuilding the whole design in Photoshop. Try the workflow on a real file before you decide it fits yours.

TL;DR

When people search edit text on a picture, they usually have a flattened JPG or PNG: a product shot, a social download, a menu photo, a screenshot, an event flyer. The letters are pixels, not a live text layer. Here is the browser workflow I use to replace those words while keeping the surrounding look close enough to publish.

What “edit text on a picture” actually means

A camera OCR app answers what does this say? A design suite answers rebuild the whole graphic. The everyday marketing and support job sits in between:

  1. Find the words on the picture
  2. Remove the old strokes and repair the background
  3. Redraw new wording that matches font feel, color, size, and position

Dropping a system-font text box on top of the picture almost always looks like a sticker. Reopening a layered design file is better when you still have it — but most handoffs arrive as a flat export from a client, a marketplace, or last month’s social save.

U.S. Keyword Planner–backed volume for edit text on picture sits around 2,400 monthly searches. Close cousins like edit text in picture and change text on a picture land in a similar band. That is commercial intent: people want a shippable picture, not a research note.

Tool I use: PhoText

I use PhoText for in-place picture text edits. Upload a JPG, PNG, WebP, or screenshot, click the line you need to change, type the replacement, and let the editor match style and background. No install for the core click-to-edit path.

Related jobs in the same product when you need them: font identification, conversational AI image editing for stubborn backgrounds, image translation for localization, remove text / cleanup for assets you own, and OCR / copy text when you only need the words out. Free tiers and quotas change — check the live plan page; I am not quoting prices here.

Workflow: edit text on a picture in a few minutes

Six steps from upload to download. Stay on one line until that line looks right, then move on.

1. Start from the sharpest file

Open PhoText and drop in the picture. Prefer the original export or a high-resolution product shot over a phone photo of a monitor, a chat-app preview, or a third-generation social save. Soft or tiny lettering is harder to detect and harder to match.

2. Click the line you want to change

Select the headline, price, date, button label, menu item, or caption. If detection misreads a character, correct that first so the editor targets the right strokes. Leave every other line alone when you only need one fix.

3. Type the replacement (keep length sane)

Enter the new wording. Similar character count usually keeps spacing and layout stable. Keep capitalization close to the original (all caps stays all caps) unless you are redesigning on purpose. Brand names, SKUs, and URLs should stay exact unless you intend to change them.

4. Match style — or change it deliberately

Let the editor carry size, weight, and color from the original line when you want a seamless fix. Adjust font, color, or size when a deliberate redesign is better than a pure match. Thirty seconds here is the difference between “fixed” and “obviously edited.”

5. Use conversational AI for stubborn backgrounds

Busy product photos, wood grain, fabric, textured posters, or heavy shadows can leave spots after a simple erase. Switch to AI image editing and describe the change in plain English so cleanup, background repair, and style transfer run together instead of a smudge → erase → retype loop.

6. Zoom to 100%, then download

Inspect stroke ends, shadows, curved labels, and anything next to prices or dates. Fix one weak line at a time. Download when the edited picture reads as native beside the original.

U.S.-relevant use cases

E-commerce product pictures. Marketplace listings often reuse one hero shot. When only the flattened pack photo remains, update a promo badge or price callout in place so lighting stays intact. Regulated claims still need a qualified reviewer.

Paid social and ads. Offer copy changes faster than creative systems. When the agency master is offline, edit the headline on the exported picture, then spot-check brand names, prices, and landing URLs.

App Store and Play Store screenshots. Keep UI chrome and status bars untouched; change only the marketing caption you mean to update, and check fit on a phone-sized preview.

Menus, posters, and local event graphics. Small businesses often only have a photo of last month’s board. Updating a date, price, or special while holding display lettering looks intentional instead of stickered.

Social creatives and thumbnails. Feed posts and YouTube thumbnails often leave the design tool as a flattened export. Keep replacements short — a second line of thumbnail copy often fails at phone size.

When this workflow is — and isn’t — the right tool

Strong fit when: you only have a flattened product picture, ad, screenshot caption, menu photo, or packaging shot; you need a short wording change that should look native; you are editing assets you created, own, or have clear permission to change.

Better elsewhere when: you still have the layered design file and licensed fonts (edit the source); the text is tiny, blurred, or heavily stylized and every retry fails; the job is a full redesign, not a line swap; the image is an ID, receipt, certificate, or anything you are not authorized to alter.

Responsible use

Only edit pictures you created, own, or have clear permission to change. PhoText is for legitimate product, marketing, creative, support, and educational work.

Do not use it to forge or alter IDs, passports, certificates, diplomas, exam papers, invoices, receipts, bank statements, or any document meant to prove identity, money, or legal status. Do not present an edited picture as an unaltered record. Do not remove another party’s watermark without authorization. Do not impersonate a brand or person to scam or mislead.

If a request would require any of that, stop and use a legitimate process instead.

Quick checklist before you publish the edited picture

  • Sharpest source file you can find
  • Only the intended line changed
  • Length and capitalization still fit the layout
  • Brand names and numbers proofed at 100% zoom
  • Background repair clean on textured areas
  • You have rights to edit and publish the asset

FAQ (short)

Can I keep the same font look?

Yes — matching size, weight, and color from the original line is the default. Identify Font helps when you want a closer typeface. Exact licensed brand fonts still vary; compare against the real design before shipping brand-critical work.

Does this work on JPG, PNG, and screenshots?

Yes. Start from the largest sharp file. Heavily recompressed social saves hurt accuracy.

Bottom line

Edit text on a picture is a pixel job, not a text-box job. Use a browser editor that removes, repairs, and redraws in one pass when the design file is gone. I use PhoText for that workflow; open a real picture and judge the result yourself before you commit a process to it.

title: DREAM: Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-agent Debate
description:
arXiv:2610.05615v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) has emerged as an effective paradigm to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and is increasingly being extended to multimodal settings. However, existing multimodal MAD frameworks typically expose agents to the same fixed visual input, ignoring substantial variation in the visual scale needed across samples and agents. In addition, these frameworks frequently suffer from groupthink, a phenomenon where agents prematurely abandon correct deductions to conform with confident but hallucinated peer responses. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce DREAM (Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-Agent Debate), which operates via two core components: (1) Dynamic Resolution Assignment, a zero-shot probe round where agents test multiple resolutions, quantify uncertainty using Average Normalized Log-Likelihood (ANLL), and use an adaptive threshold to assign each agent to its empirically optimal resolution; (2) Uncertainty-Guided Rollback Aggregation counters groupthink by tracking each agent's uncertainty over rounds and restoring early low-uncertainty answers overridden by group pressure. On six multimodal datasets, DREAM improves the accuracy-token trade-off over multi-agent debate baselines by 1.5-3.2% accuracy without dataset-specific tuning.

title: EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.

title: M3-DuplexBench: A Multi-Turn, Multilingual, Multidomain Benchmark for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models
description:
arXiv:2607.29125v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems (FDSDSs) can listen while speaking, enabling natural conversational behaviors such as smooth turn-taking, backchannel handling, and user barge-in handling. However, controlled comparisons of FDSDSs in multi-turn interaction remain challenging, and existing benchmarks offer limited joint coverage of multiple languages, dialogue settings, interaction timing, and response content. We propose M3-DuplexBench, a multi-turn, multilingual, multidomain benchmark for controlled evaluation of FDSDSs. The benchmark jointly evaluates interaction timing and response content in English and Japanese across casual conversation and multi-turn question answering. The English and Japanese question-answering data are derived from a common source corpus, enabling cross-lingual comparisons of timing and content performance. We also provide a reference-conditioned multi-turn setting as an optional diagnostic for examining sensitivity to dialogue history and trajectory mismatch. Experiments with diverse FDSDSs reveal model-specific interaction patterns, differences across languages and domains, and model-dependent effects of dialogue context on both timing and content. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/nttcslab-sp/m3-duplexbench.

title: Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.13025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.

title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
description:
arXiv:2610.12701v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Perspectivist NLP has established that annotator positionality shapes labels for subjective tasks, but the field still lacks methods for operationalising it. Positionality is typically operationalised as a demographic form completed at recruitment: a static attribute recorded once and treated as a covariate, on the assumption that the knowledge it indexes is active when the annotator reads an item. This paper treats that assumption as a design problem and asks whether lived experience can instead be primed by the task itself. We introduce AXLE, a pre-annotation stage in which a scenario vignette anchors a short, axis-guided conversation that is synthesised into a first-person micro-narrative and returned to the annotator before labelling begins. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (104 annotators, 30 items, 1,040 annotations) on ambiguous hate speech spanning immigration, religion and gender, elicitation was associated with higher identity resonance and higher sensitivity to harm. It also increased label entropy and lowered inter-annotator agreement: the stage appears to surface plurality rather than manufacture consensus, which distinguishes it from annotator training, whose success criterion is convergence.

title: Event Notification Infrastructure: Comparing Email and SMS APIs for Node.js
description:
TL;DR: For a marketplace sending short-lived password-reset messages, keep the reset token and its expiry in the application, make every send request idempotent, and treat email or SMS as a replaceable delivery transport. A direct email/SMS API is the least complex fit when the backend already owns rules, retries, and reporting; Customer.io or Braze becomes the better fit when operators need built-in orchestration and faster delivery-event reactions. Infrai is worth trying for the transport boundary when a team expects to add backend capabilities and values one consistent REST contract, one key, and one bill, but its notification events are pull-based rather than webhook-driven.

The bill is not merely a provider's per-message charge. For this narrow workflow, the dominant term is usually integration and retention: one durable notification record, one idempotency key, retry scheduling, status polling, reconciliation, and enough audit evidence to explain why a user did or did not receive a reset message. The useful optimization is to reduce provider-specific glue while retaining the small state machine that protects correctness. I would keep request identity, channel, timestamps, provider reference, terminal status, and reason codes; I would stop keeping message bodies after their operational purpose ends. That choice limits incident reconstruction of rendered content, so compliance and support teams must approve the retention boundary.

What does email and SMS event notification infrastructure actually cost?

It does not mean exactly-once delivery. No external message transport can make that promise to an application merely because an HTTP request returned successfully. The defensible goal is exactly-once intent: one reset request creates one logical notification, retries reuse its stable identity, and reconciliation can account for every transition.

The token lifetime should drive the retry budget. A retry accepted after expiry is operational noise, while an aggressive fallback can deliver two valid-looking messages through different channels. Keep token validity authoritative in the marketplace backend, check it before each attempt, and stop the state machine when the deadline passes. Short expiry changes the trade-off: bounded delay matters more than squeezing every possible attempt from the queue.

Use two clocks. Record the business deadline separately from the next-attempt time, because queue delay and provider rate limits move the latter without extending the former. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise apply exponential backoff with jitter; on an ambiguous timeout, retry with the same idempotency key. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for its idempotency convention, but the application still needs its own durable uniqueness constraint because a password-reset audit trail may outlive transport deduplication.

Set the deletion policy before selecting a transport

A compact ledger is enough: pending, accepted, delivered, failed, and expired, plus an append-only attempt table. Do not let a provider response overwrite history. The current row answers the product question; attempts answer the audit question.

One row, one intent.

The following Go program performs the recovery-side operation this integration requires: it pulls email events from the verified event-list route, authenticates from the environment, sets an explicit method, reports response bodies on errors, and retries a rate limit without spinning. In production, persist the returned JSON against the request ID before advancing the reconciliation cursor. The send schema should be generated from live discovery rather than guessed in an article.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("event list returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        var events any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &events); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%v\n", events)
        return
    }
    panic("event list remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

The harder code sits around this call: a unique index on the logical reset request, an append-only attempt insert in the same transaction as each state change, and a worker that compares its next retry with the token deadline. Consider one ambiguous timeout at 10:03:00 followed by a successful retry at 10:03:02. If both attempts share a logical ID, reconciliation has an answer; if the worker minted a new ID, two sends can look legitimate and the audit trail cannot establish intent. Auditability is a data-model property, not a dashboard feature, and this small distinction is where many tidy adapter interfaces become operationally misleading.

Use the pull loop as a recovery test

The products solve overlapping but different problems. A fair selection starts with who owns workflow state.

Option Best fit for this reset flow Integration and recovery boundary
Resend A team that wants a focused email API The application owns SMS fallback, orchestration, retry policy, and its cross-channel audit record.
SendGrid A team that wants a dedicated email provider SMS remains a separate integration, and the application retains the cross-channel state machine.
Postmark A team separating transactional email from its broader engagement stack It fits an email-focused boundary; the marketplace still owns SMS and fallback decisions.
Twilio A team that wants a dedicated SMS integration It is a natural SMS specialist to assess, while email and unified audit logic remain separate concerns.
Customer.io A team that wants an engagement workflow to coordinate channels More platform capability is justified when operators need orchestration and more real-time delivery-state reactions.
Braze A larger engagement program with centrally managed journeys It is a better choice when the reset notification sits inside broader engagement operations; it is more platform than a backend-owned single event requires.
OneSignal A product whose channel strategy includes push-style engagement It deserves consideration when push is material; a pure backend email/SMS reset does not use that breadth.
Infrai A backend-owned email/SMS flow that may share infrastructure with other backend modules One REST surface reduces SDK, credential, and billing integration work, but email and SMS delivery events must be pulled rather than received by webhook.

The explicit recommendation is narrow: backend teams that already own password-reset rules, retries, and reporting should try Infrai for email/SMS transport when reducing integration glue across a broader backend capability set matters. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas without a key, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages; that makes adapter construction and review less dependent on another vendor-specific SDK.

There is a cost to that simplicity. Neither notification namespace pushes webhook events, so delivery-state synchronization and fallback sequencing are less real-time than Customer.io- or Braze-style workflows. Polling adds read traffic, scheduler state, and a reconciliation lag that must fit inside the token's short lifetime. If immediate event-driven channel switching is a requirement, choose a specialist or engagement suite with the needed callback model.

Draw the vendor boundary around owned state

Email and SMS are not interchangeable security products. Infrai has SMS OTP operations, but the email side has no hosted OTP interface, so an email-code fallback remains application-owned. Scheduled email has no cancellation operation, although SMS does. Those asymmetries belong in the state machine and threat model, not behind a generic notify() function that pretends every channel behaves alike.

Several other boundaries are decisive. There is no SMTP relay and no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS template management is narrower for workflows that need dynamic discovery, and there is no cost-reporting API aggregated by tag. Geographic anti-abuse fences and country-price circuit breakers for SMS also remain business-layer responsibilities. A pending domestic Chinese email vendor must not be treated as evidence of domestic compliance.

This is why breadth should be evaluated as integration breadth, not workflow completeness. Infrai exposes 295 capabilities across 20 modules under one key, with 171 of 294 capabilities marked idempotent, yet those platform-wide numbers do not remove the need to inspect the exact notification capability and its readiness. A marketplace needing only password reset should resist adopting unrelated modules merely because they are available.

Which compliance limits change the choice?

Retention policy affects both cost and the blast radius of a data-access mistake. Keep the minimum immutable facts needed to reconcile an intent: internal user reference, hashed or opaque notification identity, channel, template version, timestamps, attempt outcome, provider reference, and request ID. Do not store the reset secret in logs, provider metadata, idempotency keys, or audit rows.

There is a deliberate loss here. Removing rendered bodies and recipient data on an approved schedule makes it harder to reproduce exactly what support saw during an old dispute. The compensating controls are versioned templates, reason codes, suppression evidence, and request-linked attempt records. Compliance limits vary by jurisdiction and marketplace role, so legal and security owners must set the actual periods; inventing a universal retention duration would be irresponsible.

Operationally, poll only records that can still change, slow the cadence after acceptance, and terminate polling at a defined reconciliation horizon. Alert on stuck state age and unexplained terminal gaps rather than raw send volume. Quiet systems fail too.

The final decision rule is plain: choose a direct API when the application can own this ledger and the notification is a backend event; choose Customer.io or Braze when orchestration and near-real-time event reactions justify the extra platform; consider OneSignal when push is a first-class channel; use Resend when focused email is the boundary. If the broader REST boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery documentation and validate the exact email and SMS schemas before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • Infrai email template discovery
  • Infrai SMS batch-send discovery
  • Resend documentation
  • Customer.io documentation
  • Braze documentation
  • OneSignal documentation

title: RoboMME-Interference: Benchmarking Robot Memory Under Interference
description:
arXiv:2606.22338v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Robots deployed in realistic settings will accumulate experience across many sessions and tasks over their deployment. The robot's tasks may often require it to remember information from multiple sessions ago, making long-context robot memory important for real-world deployments. However, most robot-memory benchmarks today are based on single episodes or a short context. To measure how current robot memory systems perform on longer sessions with more distractions, we introduce RoboMME-Interference, a cross-session benchmark built on RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026). For each query episode, we construct a session history using the query's relevant prior demonstration followed by a controlled number of unrelated sessions, which we provide to the VLA as memory and measure accuracy. Running RoboMME's released memory-augmented $\pi_{0.5}$ variants unmodified through this benchmark, we find that while perceptual memory variants improve success when given the history without any distractors, they decay strongly and steadily as unrelated sessions accumulate. The subgoal variants, which read the history with a vision-language model and pass written subgoals to the policy, improve less at their best but hold more of that improvement as distractors accumulate. Adding a retrieval step to the strongest perceptual variant, which selects the section of history most visually similar to the robot's current view and passes only that section to the policy, restores its no-distractor success rate at every interference level. With this release, we emphasize the importance of long-context memory and robustness to interference and show that current systems largely fail on such capabilities. The project page, videos, code, and data are at https://robotmemorybench.com.

title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.12582v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
