title: Model-agnostic Knowledge Augmented Machine Learning for Weakly Annotated Bioimaging Data
description:
arXiv:2610.13637v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used for automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data, such as microscopy and cytomorphology images. Due to the sole dependency of automated feature extraction, existing methods yield inconsistent classification performance across weakly annotated datasets. Here, we propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that enables ML models to exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction can capture. The proposed approach improves classification performance across seven ML architectures. When integrated with masked autoencoder-based self-supervised learning, our method achieves the strongest overall performance, improving precision by 2.9% over the next-best method on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks. We perform nucleus-level classification based on mislocalization of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, a phenotype linked to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), using three independent microscopy datasets of motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Accurate quantification of this phenotype at scale remains challenging and may contribute to inconsistencies across studies. Application of the best-performing model to these microscopy datasets reveals biological interpretations related to ALS, including dose-dependent effects of the proteasomal stressor, MG132, and the oxidative stressor, sodium arsenite (SA), on TDP-43 mislocalization, variable pathology in motor neurons from sporadic and familial ALS donors, and a lack of protection of the pharmacological compounds, edaravone and niclosamide, against SA-induced TDP-43 mislocalization. Together, our pipeline enables in-vitro cellular image analysis to advance understanding of ALS-associated pathology and potential treatments.

title: How to Block AI Notetakers From Your Meetings (Zoom, Teams, Meet)
description:
You are ten minutes into a sensitive call when a name nobody recognizes appears in the participant list: Fireflies.ai Notetaker. Nobody on your side invited it. The conversation slows, and someone asks the question you hoped to avoid: who is this, and where is the recording going?

You can stop most of these bots, but not with one switch. Three layers work together: stop the invitation at its source, make the platform check who may join, and put every unknown joiner in a lobby where a person decides. A fourth step, removing a bot that got in, is the backstop.

One limit comes first. Blocking bots does not stop a person from recording with a desktop app on their own computer. Otter's desktop app and Chrome extension work without a bot in the meeting, and Fireflies, Fathom and tl;dv also offer or advertise bot-free modes. No meeting platform setting can see those. For them you need a recording policy, not a block list.

The short answer: what you can block and what you cannot

The fastest fix, about ten minutes:

  1. Hold unknown joiners in the lobby. Teams detects external bots and holds them in the lobby by default. In Zoom, turn on the waiting room. In Google Meet, set the meeting access type to Trusted or Restricted. In GoTo, lock the meeting.
  2. Require identification. Require sign-in in Zoom, or block external email domains in Webex Control Hub.
  3. Switch off auto-join at the source. Ask the person whose calendar invited the bot to turn off its auto-join. In Fireflies that is the Auto-Join setting, and its Bar Rules can exclude meetings by title or keyword.

Then give people a bot-free alternative. If you only block, some people will move to a recorder you cannot see. An approved bot-free tool keeps the notes without a tile in front of clients. CatchMeet is one: it runs on the user's computer, adds nothing to the participant list, and has a free plan.

Sections below give the exact settings per platform, the admin checklist, and the reasons blocks sometimes fail.

How notetaker bots get into a meeting

A bot reaches your meeting by one of a few routes, and each route is stopped at a different checkpoint.

Route How it works Where to stop it
Calendar auto-join The bot tries to enter at the scheduled start time of any event on a connected calendar. If a lobby is on, a host must admit it (Fireflies guide) The notetaker's own auto-join setting; the lobby
Invited address or link Someone invites the bot's address (for Fireflies, fred@fireflies.ai) or pastes the meeting link into the vendor's dashboard Sign-in and domain rules; the lobby
Marketplace integration Official apps use the Zoom Meeting SDK or Zoom RTMS, which hosts can allow or block (Zoom) Zoom's Meeting SDK Apps block list
Automation in the web client Unofficial tools drive Zoom's native or Web App. Zoom says Web App bot protection is on for all accounts and cannot be turned off (Zoom) Built in; sign-in requirement

These bots look like ordinary participants, and that is on purpose. Fireflies says its bot "is always visible in the participant list" under the name Fireflies.ai Notetaker, and Read advertises that "everyone in the meeting knows Read is there." The risk is not secrecy. It is that nobody decided to admit it.

Removing a bot once does not solve the problem. A bot that joins from calendar auto-join returns the next time the event recurs, because the invitation, not the room, is what brings it. That is why the blocks in this guide start before the meeting.

Block at the earliest checkpoint you control. The later ones catch what slips through. Sources are listed at the end.

Host settings by platform: Zoom, Teams, Meet, Webex and GoTo

Host settings work meeting by meeting and depend on someone remembering them. Use them as the first line of defense, and put the durable controls in the admin section. Where a vendor's page did not give a setting's exact path, the table says so instead of guessing.

Platform Hold joiners in a lobby Require identification Bot-specific control What the vendor page leaves open
Zoom Waiting room; guests who are not signed in can be held for host review Require sign-in to join; email-domain rules Meeting SDK Apps block list; bot blocking dashboard; Web App bot protection (always on) The block-list and dashboard articles returned no readable text when checked, so menu paths are not given
Microsoft Teams Lobby; detected bots are held there even if the meeting lets others bypass it Anonymous-join and lobby-bypass settings Bot detection with a lobby label, on by default Detection can miss bots and can flag people
Google Meet Access type: Open, Trusted or Restricted Restricted admits only invited guests None found in Google's help pages No bot detection or bot label found
Webex Lobby with Let in, Remove and Move to Lobby; site-level auto-lock in Control Hub Domain rules in Control Hub (admin) None at host level Lock and expel steps are not in the lobby guide; bots with no email address are not addressed
GoTo Locking a meeting sends latecomers to a waiting room None found None found Dismiss is documented for Classic (People pane); the current app's menu was not checked

Zoom

Zoom's waiting room article lists the controls that matter: require sign-in to join, restrict by email domain, use the waiting room, and manage which Marketplace apps may join. For a single meeting:

  1. Turn on the waiting room under Settings > Meeting > Security, then choose Edit Options under Waiting Room Options.
  2. Pick who waits. The option "Users who are not in your account and not part of your whitelisted domains" lets people from listed domains in and holds everyone else, and it is a waiting-room rule rather than a hard block (Zoom).
  3. When a name you do not recognize appears, deny it from the waiting room. If it is already in, open the participant list, choose More next to it and remove it.

Microsoft Teams

Teams labels external bots it detects and holds them in the lobby "regardless of the meeting's lobby configuration," and an organizer must admit them explicitly (Microsoft Learn). As the organizer:

  1. Limit who can admit people from the lobby to organizers and co-organizers, so a presenter cannot admit a bot by mistake. Microsoft recommends this.
  2. Treat any flagged participant as a decision, not a formality. Teams shows a risk reminder before you admit one.
  3. If a real guest is flagged, admit them and choose This is not a bot. That applies to that meeting only.

Google Meet

Meet gives hosts access types rather than a bot filter (Google Workspace help):

  1. Set the access type to Trusted (people in your organization, plus external guests invited through a Calendar link) or Restricted (only guests invited through Calendar, plus people a host invites in the meeting).
  2. Uncheck "Anyone with the meeting link can ask to join" for Trusted or Restricted meetings, so other guests are declined automatically.
  3. Turn on Host management (Calendar event > Video call options, or Host controls during the meeting) so only hosts and co-hosts can eject participants and accept knocks. Turn on "Host must join before anyone else."

Webex

Webex's article on preventing AI bots covers admin-level domain rules only (see the admin section). For hosts, Webex's lobby guide describes the practical steps. When someone is waiting, a notification appears in the meeting controls, or in the Participants panel if it is open. The list is sorted into Internal, External and Unverified, so you can act on a whole group at once. Tick the people (or choose Select all) and click Let in or Remove. To send someone who is already in back to the lobby, right-click the name and select Move to Lobby. That guide does not describe locking a meeting or expelling someone after they joined, and the lobby feature is not available in Webex Meetings for Linux.

GoTo

In GoTo, an organizer can lock the meeting. People who try to join while it is locked wait in a waiting room, and everyone waiting connects automatically when you unlock. To remove someone who is already in, the organizer right-clicks the attendee's name in the People pane, selects Dismiss and confirms with Yes; the attendee leaves and is told they were excused. That page is for GoToMeeting Classic, so check the menu in your current app. GoTo's pages do not mention bots: lock the meeting once everyone expected has arrived, and dismiss anything unfamiliar.

Admin controls and the org-wide checklist

Host settings fail the day a host forgets. Admin controls take the decision away from the host, which is why they belong in every plan. What each platform offers differs a lot.

Zoom. Zoom lets admins allow or block specific Meeting SDK apps published on its Marketplace, and says unpublished SDK apps cannot join meetings outside the developer's account. Its bot blocking dashboard in the Meetings app shows which apps are attempting to join, joining or being blocked. Waiting-room defaults can be set for the whole account under Admin Center > Settings > Meeting > Security, or per group (Zoom).

Microsoft Teams. Bot handling is a meeting-policy setting under Teams admin center > Meeting policies > Meeting Join and Lobby > Manage external bots and their access to meetings. In PowerShell it is ExternalBotAccessMode. It can be set for the whole tenant or for targeted groups (Microsoft Learn).

Admin center label PowerShell value Behavior
Do not detect bots AllowAllBots Bots are not detected or marked and appear as ordinary external participants
When detected, require approval before joining RequireApprovalWhenDetected Default. Detected bots are marked and held in the lobby until explicitly admitted

Microsoft Message Center item MC1459141 (roadmap ID 566201) describes a further policy that blocks identified external bots automatically. The listing gives its default state as Off, with worldwide general availability starting in early October 2026 and finishing by late October. The listing names no PowerShell value, and Microsoft Learn's reference still lists only the two values above, so confirm the option in your tenant's Teams admin center before scripting it. Learn's text names Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy, but its examples use Set-CsTeamsEventsPolicy, so check the cmdlet too. Microsoft says some bots will go undetected and some people will be flagged.

Google Workspace. Admins set whether Host management is on by default (Google), and can gate Gemini's "Take notes for me" by organizational unit or group. Google's documentation lists no admin setting that filters third-party notetaker bots.

Webex. In Control Hub, go to Services > Meeting > Settings and, under Meetings, choose an option next to Internal. "Block external users with selected email domains" is the option that blocks bots by domain. Enable the Site Admin feature "Request attendee email address for all sites" so the block works as intended. The article is dated 14 April 2026, applies to the Webex Suite meeting platform, and says it replaces the Site Admin "Blocked email list" (Webex). It does not say what happens to bots that join with no email address.

Webex lobby and auto-lock. Site-wide lobby behavior sits in Control Hub under Services > Meeting > Sites: choose the site, open its settings, then Security under Common Settings. When a meeting is unlocked offers three choices for guests: join directly, wait in the lobby until the host admits them, or cannot join. Automatically lock meeting locks it 0, 5, 10, 15 or 20 minutes after the start (default 10), and applies only where hosts have not set their own preference. When a meeting is locked decides whether late arrivals wait in the lobby or cannot join at all.

The org-wide checklist

  1. Inventory what is connected. List the notetaker apps people already use, and the calendar and OAuth apps your identity provider has consented to.
  2. Move from block lists to allow lists where the platform offers it. A block list only covers names you already know. Zoom's Meeting SDK allow list and Webex's approved email domains are examples.
  3. Set defaults that do not depend on hosts. Detect-and-hold in Teams, Host management on in Meet, sign-in required in Zoom.
  4. Limit who can grant calendar and OAuth access. Auto-join starts with a user connecting a calendar. Restricting that grant removes the route at its source.
  5. Publish a short internal policy. Use the template below.
  6. Monitor and review. Check Zoom's bot blocking dashboard and Teams audit logs for unusual participants, and review settings every quarter, because vendors keep changing them.

AI notetaker and recording policy (template)

  1. Approved tools: only [tool names] may record or transcribe company meetings.
  2. Announce it: the host says at the start that an AI assistant is running and waits for objections.
  3. Objection: if anyone objects, recording stops and notes are taken by hand.
  4. External meetings: external participants are held in the lobby; only the host or a co-host admits them.
  5. Unknown participants: anyone not recognized is denied admission and reported to [IT contact].
  6. Calendar access: employees may not connect third-party notetakers to their calendars without approval.
  7. Regulated content: calls covering health, legal or financial matters need [compliance owner] sign-off before any recording.
  8. Storage: recordings and transcripts are stored in [location] and deleted after [period].
  9. Review: IT reviews settings and the approved-tools list every quarter.

Why bots still join after you block them

If a bot keeps returning, one of four things is usually happening.

The invitation never stopped. A bot that follows calendar events keeps trying every time an event recurs. Removing it from the call fixes one meeting. The lasting fix is the owner's auto-join setting, or an admin limit on who can connect calendars.

The block does not match how the bot joins. A domain rule only sees the email domain of the joiner. It does nothing against a bot that joins from an account on a domain you allow, or one that is bot-free and never joins at all. Webex's article does not say how its domain block treats bots that join without an email address.

Detection has gaps. Microsoft says some external bots will go undetected and some people will be flagged as bots. Zoom says a real user flagged by its Web App protection can still sign in to join.

The tool is not a bot. Fireflies has a no-bot "Take Notes" mode in its desktop app, Fathom says you can capture notes "bot or no bot," tl;dv says "no bot required," and Otter's desktop app records without one. CatchMeet works the same way: it runs on the user's computer and adds no tile. No bot filter touches these.

Notetaker names and domains worth checking

Use this as a starting list for allow-and-block decisions, not as a finished block list. The address a bot shows can differ from its vendor's website domain, so confirm what appears in your own participant list before you block anything.

Tool What to look for Bot-free option exists
Fireflies Name Fireflies.ai Notetaker; invite address fred@fireflies.ai (guide) Yes: a no-bot "Take Notes" mode in the desktop app
Otter.ai Domain otter.ai Yes: desktop app and Chrome extension
Read.ai Domain read.ai Not stated on its home page
Fathom Domain fathom.ai (fathom.video now redirects there) Yes: "Now available bot-free"
tl;dv Domain tldv.io Yes: "No bot required"
CatchMeet Nothing to block: it captures audio on the user's computer and adds no participant tile Always: device-level capture on Mac and Windows

A starter block list. Only fireflies.ai has a bot address confirmed on the vendor's own page. The other four are the vendors' website domains, and a bot may join from a different address, so treat the list as a first pass and check it against your own participant lists.

# Starter list of notetaker domains
# Bot address confirmed on the vendor's own page
fireflies.ai     # invite address fred@fireflies.ai

# Vendor website domains; bot address not confirmed
otter.ai
read.ai
fathom.ai
tldv.io

Webex accepts a list like this under Block external users with selected email domains. Zoom's documented domain control works the other way, as an allow list that holds everyone else in the waiting room, and the Teams pages cited here have no blocked-domain field, so in both use the list as a lobby watchlist and deny a joiner whose name or address matches. A domain block cannot see a bot-free app on someone's laptop, and it also blocks real employees of those vendors.

How to find who invited a bot

  1. Note its exact display name in the participant list before you remove it.
  2. Check the calendar invite's attendee list for the bot's address.
  3. Ask the meeting's organizer which attendee's calendar is connected to the tool. The bot usually follows that person's events.
  4. Ask that person to turn off auto-join, or remove the connection from their calendar settings.
  5. If you cannot trace it, hold every external joiner in the lobby for the next occurrence and admit people by name.

False positives: blocking bots without blocking guests

The strictest setting is rarely the right one. Blocking every external participant stops bots and also stops your clients, auditors and candidates. Platforms warn about this themselves: Teams says detection can flag real people, and Zoom says a flagged user can still sign in. Pick the setting that matches the risk of the meeting.

Setting What it protects What it costs
Block all external users Maximum control; no external bot can enter Clients and partners cannot join either, so it suits internal or board meetings only
Allow approved domains only Known clients and partners join normally You maintain the list, and a new client is locked out until someone adds it
Hold every external joiner in the lobby (recommended default) Nobody unknown enters without a person deciding The host must watch the lobby and admit people by name
Detect and label only Low friction Relies on the platform's detection, which Microsoft says will miss some bots

A compromise by meeting type

Start from the lobby default and move up or down only when the risk changes.

Meeting type Setting from the table above Who admits If a bot appears anyway
Internal team call Allow only your own organization (require sign-in, or block all external users) Nobody; no external joiners are expected Trace the invite owner and turn off auto-join
Recurring client or partner call Allow approved domains only; everyone else waits in the lobby Host admits unknown names; a co-host helps Ask the client who is recording and where it goes, then agree on one record
One-off guest, candidate or vendor Hold every external joiner in the lobby Host or co-host, checking each name against the invite Deny it, message the invitee, and admit the person without the bot
Board, legal, audit or regulated call Block all external users except named invitees; no third-party notetaker Host only Remove it, pause until it is gone, and report it to the compliance owner
Large webinar or public event A lobby for everyone is rarely practical; use detect-and-label where the platform has it Co-host reviews the attendee list Remove unknown names, accept some residual risk, and state in the notice that recording is not permitted

Each row maps to a control above: Webex's four external-user options, Zoom's sign-in and domain controls, the Teams bot policy and lobby, and Meet's access types.

A few habits keep the friction low:

  1. Share the rule in the invite. One line such as "External guests wait in the lobby until the host admits them" prevents confusion and complaints.
  2. Give the host a helper. For large meetings, assign a co-host to admit people so the host can run the call.
  3. Admit by name, not by count. A lobby with three names and four people waiting is the signal to ask who the fourth is.
  4. Keep an exception path. When a real guest is flagged as a bot, admit them and record the exception. In Teams, "This is not a bot" applies to that meeting only.
  5. Approve tools deliberately. If your team does use a notetaker, put it on an allow list and say so in the policy, instead of letting each person choose. A bot-free option with a free plan, such as CatchMeet, gives people an approved choice that does not put a tile in front of clients.

A bot you decide to admit still needs the consent routine below. Admitting it is not consent.

Recording consent and the law

Blocking a bot and admitting a bot both leave the legal question open: did every person on the call agree to be recorded? This section is a summary of public legal guides, not legal advice. Laws change, and the guides cited date from 2019 to 2020, so confirm the current statute with a lawyer before you rely on it.

The baseline. U.S. federal law sets one-party consent as the national minimum for in-person, telephone and electronic conversations (18 U.S.C. §§ 2510–2511), and states may be stricter (RCFP).

All-party consent states. The Reporters Committee lists 11: California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan (at least for recordings by a third party not in the conversation), Montana, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Washington. Some states split by setting: Missouri and Oregon require all-party consent in person but not by phone, Connecticut and Nevada the reverse, and Hawaii and Maine only in particularly private places. For a call that crosses state lines, assume the stricter state's law may apply. Courts differ on whether the recorder's or the speaker's location controls.

Jurisdiction Who must consent Penalty highlights Source
California All parties to a confidential communication Criminal fine up to $2,500 or up to one year for a first offense; civil damages of $5,000 or three times actual damages RCFP: California
Washington, RCW 9.73.030 All parties to a private conversation; an announced recording notice can count as consent Gross misdemeanor; civil damages of the greatest of actual damages, $100 a day or $1,000, plus fees RCFP: Washington
Florida, Fla. Stat. § 934.03 All parties to a confidential communication Felony up to five years and $5,000; first-offense misdemeanor up to one year and $1,000 in some cases RCFP: Florida
Illinois, 720 ILCS 5/14-2 All parties to a private conversation Felony of one to three years and fines up to $25,000 RCFP: Illinois
Germany, § 201 StGB Unauthorized recording of the non-public spoken word is an offense Up to three years or a fine Statute text

A live example. In In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation, No. 5:25-cv-06911 (N.D. Cal.), a federal court ruled on 13 August 2026 on Otter's motion to dismiss. It let the federal Wiretap Act and California's CIPA section 631 claims go forward, among others. Plaintiffs argue Otter's terms, which tell account holders to make sure they have the necessary permissions, do not satisfy all-party consent states. This is a ruling on the pleadings, not a finding of liability, and Otter denies any interception.

Regulated industries. Health, legal and financial calls carry extra duties. For health information, HHS says a cloud provider that stores or processes electronic protected health information is a business associate and the covered entity must sign a HIPAA-compliant business associate agreement, even if the provider holds only encrypted data. Before a notetaker touches privileged or regulated calls, ask your counsel or compliance owner whether it is allowed at all.

A routine that works anywhere. Say at the start that an AI assistant is running. Ask for objections. Note the answer. If anyone objects, stop recording. The same routine applies to a bot you admit and to a bot-free app on your own laptop.

Taking notes without a bot: your options compared

People invite bots because they want notes. Block the bots and offer nothing else, and some will switch to a desktop app that no platform setting can see. A sanctioned bot-free option keeps the notes and keeps the decision with you.

Option How it captures What other participants see Free option
Built-in platform AI (Zoom AI Companion, Google Meet "Take notes for me") Runs inside the platform; a host or co-host starts it A visible indicator: a sparkle in Zoom, a pencil icon and banner in Meet Depends on your plan; check with your admin
Otter desktop app or Chrome extension Records on your computer or in a Google Meet tab, with no bot No participant tile Otter Basic: 300 minutes a month, 30 minutes per conversation
Fireflies desktop app, "Take Notes" Captures system audio with no bot; no speaker labels or saved audio No participant tile Check its pricing page
CatchMeet Device-level capture on Mac and Windows with Zoom, Meet, Teams and Slack Huddles No participant tile Yes: 120 minutes a month

Which one fits. If you want a bot-free notetaker with a free plan that also helps while the call is running, CatchMeet is the closest fit of the four options above. Its free plan includes live transcription, summaries, chat, mention alerts, three tracked topics, and answers and fact-checks from your own documents. Compared with Otter, it adds help during the call and runs with no bot by default. If your priority is an automatic, searchable archive with CRM sync for internal meetings, Otter is the stronger choice.

The honest limits. CatchMeet documents Mac and Windows only, its pages list no CRM integration, and it is a younger product than Otter. It also sends audio off your device: audio passes in real time through providers such as Deepgram (EU), OpenRouter and Groq (US) under zero-retention terms that are vendor claims, so ask for the data processing agreement before a regulated rollout. And a bot-free app is still recording. It needs the same consent routine as any other tool.

FAQ

Can I stop someone from running a notetaker on their own laptop?

Not with a meeting setting. A desktop app that captures system audio never joins the call, so no lobby, domain rule or bot filter sees it. The controls for that are a written policy, an approved-tools list, device management and a consent routine at the start of every call.

Does blocking a bot make my meeting compliant?

No. Blocking removes one recorder. It does not tell you whether anyone else is recording, and it does not create consent for a recording you do make. Compliance depends on notice, consent and where the data goes.

What happens to the recording a bot already made before I removed it?

The account that owns the bot keeps what it captured. Fireflies says removing its bot stops transcription but the owner still receives notes for the part already recorded. Ask the owner to delete it, and ask the vendor if the owner cannot.

Are Zoom, Teams and Meet's own AI notes the same as a third-party bot?

No. They run inside the platform, a host or co-host starts them, and they show an indicator while active. Admins can disable or gate them: Zoom AI Companion in third-party meetings, Gemini notes in Meet by organizational unit or group.

What should I say when a client brings their own notetaker?

Ask before you start: "Before we begin, who is recording, and where does it go?" Then agree on one record, or ask for a copy of theirs. If your policy does not allow it, say so and offer to take notes by hand or share yours afterwards.

Can I use a bot-free app if a client's policy bans bots?

Read the policy's wording first. Many bans name "bots" or "third-party notetakers" and would still apply to a tool that records audio. Ask for written permission, and do not assume that being invisible makes it allowed.

How often should I review my block lists and settings?

Every quarter, and after any platform announcement. Vendors keep changing this area: Teams added bot detection in 2026, Webex published its domain-block article in April 2026, and Fathom's address now redirects to fathom.ai.

Is there a free notetaker that does not join as a bot?

Yes, several. CatchMeet's free plan gives 120 minutes a month with live transcription, summaries and mention alerts, and it adds no participant tile. Otter Basic does not list in-call alerts or document-based fact-checks. Otter's desktop app on Basic gives 300 minutes a month with a 30-minute cap per conversation, and Fireflies has a no-bot "Take Notes" mode in its desktop app. All three still need the consent routine above.

Verdict and sources

Verdict. Do three things, in this order. Set your platform to hold every external joiner in a lobby and require sign-in or approved domains. Remove the route at its source by limiting calendar and OAuth grants. Publish a consent routine and a sanctioned bot-free option such as CatchMeet, which has a free plan, so people do not work around you with a tool you cannot see.

What could not be verified. Zoom's articles on the Meeting SDK Apps block list and the bot blocking dashboard returned no readable text when checked on 13 October 2026, so the admin section says what they cover but gives no menu paths; open them in your own Zoom admin session. Teams' automatic-block option rests on Message Center item MC1459141, while Microsoft Learn's policy reference lists two values only. Google's documentation lists no admin setting for third-party bots. Webex and GoTo host-level steps come from help pages for specific products and may differ in your version. Consent-law guides are summaries from 2019 to 2020 and need a lawyer's check. Product claims about CatchMeet are vendor claims.

title: Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available
description:
The Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available on all plans, giving you one place to see your security posture across every account and project.

You can access the Security Dashboard in the UI or run vercel security check in the Vercel CLI.

As teams grow and coding agents make it faster to spin up projects, small misconfigurations add up quietly. The Security Dashboard automatically flags issues like:

  • Team members without 2FA

  • Long-lived credentials that can be replaced with OIDC

  • Public preview deployments

  • Non-sensitive and stale environment variables

The Security Dashboard UI

Misconfigurations are ordered by risk with the most severe first, and each finding links to the settings that fix them.

Findings that are just noise for your team can also be muted, and all results can be exported to a CSV file for triage or reporting.

The Security Dashboard CLI

You can also run the same checks in your terminal through the new Vercel CLI vercel security check command, allowing your agents to work through the findings for you.

An agent using vercel security check --findings can read what failed, apply the fix and re-check to confirm. Fixes an agent can apply include:

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.

Get started by running your first scan from the Security Dashboard, and learn more in the Security Dashboard documentation.

title: Vercel Connect support in GitHub Tools
description:
GitHub Tools now has first-class support for Vercel Connect through the new @github-tools/sdk/connect subpath. Instead of storing a long-lived personal access token, your agent mints short-lived, scoped GitHub tokens at runtime from a connector. There is no secret to store, rotate, or leak.

Attach a GitHub connector to your project and pick a preset:

  • Scopes from presets: Presets such as code-review, issue-triage, and maintainer map to Connect scopes automatically, so tokens carry only the permissions the toolset needs.

  • Works with eve: Import from @github-tools/sdk/connect/eve and one file in agent/tools/ registers the full toolset with Connect-backed auth.

  • Multi-tenant ready: Override installationId, repositories, or scopes per call to target a specific installation or narrow access to individual repos.

  • Zero-config on Vercel: Deployments automatically authenticate with the OIDC token. For local development, run vercel link and vercel env pull.

For custom tool factories, connectGithubToken returns a lazy token provider you can pass to createGithubTools directly.

Get started by creating a GitHub connector and reading the documentation.

title: FactoryNet: A Large-Scale Dataset toward Industrial Time-Series Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2605.09081v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Industrial machines are actuated systems, yet most open time-series corpora record sensor outcomes alone; the few that do log commanded signals expose them in vendor-specific forms that differ from machine to machine, so commanded intent and measured response cannot be compared across embodiments. We introduce FactoryNet, a pretraining corpus for industrial time-series: 113M datapoints across 57k end-to-end task executions (15k real, 42k synthetic) on seven embodiments and four tasks, with 27 annotated anomaly types alongside healthy baselines and counterfactual pairs. Every signal in every source is mapped into a single control-theoretic schema, Setpoint, Effort, Feedback, Context (S-E-F-C), which expresses any actuated system in a common representational frame and makes commanded-versus-realized dynamics readable as explicit prediction residuals. Using the corpus, we find that a task-phase model trained on simulation, with no real phase labels, recovers roughly two thirds of the real-data ceiling on both robots, and that transfer holds within a robot family but rarely across manufacturers. Fault signatures behave differently: an uncalibrated simulator gives no detectable fault signal on either robot, and aligning the feature distributions does not repair it. What separation there is comes from Effort: motor current distinguishes faults where measured tool motion is close to chance, and calibrating the simulator to reproduce that one channel recovers a payload fault on the real robot. We read this as simulation capturing the stable structure of a task while fault behaviour stays diverse and fault-type specific. We release FactoryNet as a growing, multi-embodiment substrate for industrial foundation models.

title: Masked Extracts or Local Draft Models: A Debate for Agent SQL Placement
description:
A platform team watched a checkout report stall after an agent rewrote a revenue query during a release review. The statement joined three large tables and omitted a selective predicate, so the planner chose a broad scan. An engineer cancelled the statement before it held locks, then recorded the draft path rather than the model brand. The remaining decision was where the next draft should run, and which data could leave the production boundary.

That incident is a composite scenario for this debate, not a measured outage report from a named company. It still matches a pattern that shows up whenever agents draft SQL against live catalogs without a placement rule. Better language models do not, by themselves, decide whether schema text may cross a network boundary. Software controls around placement, redaction, and rehearsal still determine whether a fluent draft is acceptable to run.

Two credible positions

Position A sends a masked catalog extract to a free hosted model, then rehearses the returned SQL on a free disposable server. Position B keeps all draft generation on a local model that remains inside the team trust boundary. That position uses an external server only as an execution witness that is loaded with synthetic rows. They disagree about which artifact may move, and about which system may see real object names.

Position A argues that hosted models often draft more fluent SQL when prompts include current table names and key relationships. A masked extract can remove row samples, comments, and high-sensitivity column names before that hosted call. A free server then provides an isolated planner and a permission set that production roles do not share. The claim is that separation of draft generation from production execution reduces lock risk more than an unrehearsed local draft.

Position B argues that column names, check constraints, and relationship graphs can still reveal product structure even after row samples are removed. A local model can read the live catalog through an internal tool and never transmit that text. The free server, if used at all, should receive only synthetic identifiers and the candidate statement. The claim is that an execution witness does not require the drafting model to sit outside the boundary.

Evidence that can actually be checked

Neither position is universally cheaper, safer, or more accurate, and this article does not report a benchmark. The useful evidence is qualitative and checkable by each team against its own written catalog policy. Hosted draft quality matters only when the team is allowed to export a defined schema subset. Local draft quality matters only when the team can actually run a model beside the catalog.

Rehearsal value depends on whether the disposable server has similar indexes, not on whether the server was free. The table below compares those placement inputs without ranking any vendor, model family, or hosting plan. Availability of a free hosted model and a free server can make Position A practical for unclassified practice catalogs. That availability does not change a contractual ban, and it does not prove that masked names are harmless.

Decision input Favors masked hosted draft Favors local draft model Reject both external hops
Schema classification Names are internal but not regulated Names reveal unreleased product scope Any catalog text is barred from export
Prompt contents Row samples already stripped Catalog text never leaves the host A useful draft would require samples
Planner fidelity Synthetic server can mirror indexes Local database already mirrors indexes No safe mirror exists this week
Bad-join failure cost Rehearsal can catch it before production Local explain can catch it before review Write access cannot be prevented
Operational constraint Hosted call and server are available now Local model is maintained by the team External terms are unacceptable

A placement workflow with numbered checks

The workflow below is a concrete placement procedure for the debate, and it can be run on an unclassified catalog. Each numbered step produces an artifact that a reviewer can inspect without trusting the agent's explanation. Commands are patterns for PostgreSQL-style rehearsal, and they should be adapted to the server version in use.

  1. Classify the catalog extract before any prompt is built, and mark each table as exportable, mask-required, or local-only.
  2. Build the extract from catalog metadata only, keeping names, types, and declared keys while dropping comments and sample values.
  3. Score the extract with an automated gate that fails on missing labels, sensitive classes, or literals copied from logs.
  4. Choose hosted placement only when the gate passes and a reviewer can read the exact payload before the call.
  5. Rehearse on a disposable server with synthetic rows, a read-only role, and an explain plan captured before execution.
  6. Record the model placement, extract hash, server identity, and explain output beside the statement hash for later review.

Artifact: a gate, a role, and four checks

The following Python is a proposal for the gate in step 3, and it is not a production policy engine. It has not been executed against a private catalog for this article, so teams should treat the output as a starting check. A passing result means the payload avoided three obvious failures, not that the schema is safe to export.

import re
from hashlib import sha256

SENSITIVE = {"email", "phone", "ssn", "api_key"}
LITERAL = re.compile(r"[A-Z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Z]{2,}", re.I)

def gate(columns, payload):
    missing = [c["name"] for c in columns if "class" not in c]
    leaked = [c["name"] for c in columns if c.get("class") in SENSITIVE]
    literals = LITERAL.findall(payload)
    ok = not missing and not leaked and not literals
    digest = sha256(payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    return {"ok": ok, "missing": missing, "leaked": leaked, "digest": digest}

A passing gate is necessary but not sufficient, because the rehearsal role still needs a database-side boundary. On PostgreSQL, a reviewer can create a read-only role and inspect the plan without granting write rights. The statements below are a pattern for a disposable server, not a claim that every host uses the same defaults. Replace the dates and table names with fixtures that contain no production values before anyone runs them.

CREATE ROLE agent_reader NOLOGIN;
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE rehearsal TO agent_reader;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO agent_reader;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO agent_reader;
SET ROLE agent_reader;
EXPLAIN (FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT o.id
FROM orders AS o
JOIN payments AS p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2026-10-01';

PostgreSQL documents EXPLAIN and privilege rules in the current official reference, which is the primary source for those commands. A team should read that version's pages before copying the grants, because default privileges can differ by release. If the disposable server cannot host a faithful index set, label the plan as a syntax witness rather than a cost forecast.

Run four checks before anyone trusts the helper, and record the returned dictionary rather than a screenshot of a chat. These checks are expected behaviors for the proposal, not a transcript of an executed private run. Keep the fixture columns small enough that a reviewer can compare the dictionary with the source list by eye.

  1. Pass a payload that lists only exportable columns with classes present, and expect the ok flag to be true.
  2. Fail a payload that includes a column classed as email, and expect that column name to appear under leaked.
  3. Fail a payload that contains an email literal in the text, and expect the gate to reject that payload.
  4. Fail a column entry that omits its class field, and expect that column name to appear under missing.

Where a free practice surface fits

Some teams lack a maintained local model, yet they still need a place to practice agent SQL without touching production. In that setting, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option can serve as the practice surfaces for that gated path. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Readers should confirm current terms before relying on either surface, because this article does not treat availability as permanent.

This article does not name models, quotas, hardware, or duration, because those facts were not supplied as stable specifications. A free option can lower the cost of trying the workflow on an unclassified catalog that already passed the gate. It cannot replace the classification gate, and it should not be treated as a permanent control boundary. If the gate fails, the reviewer keeps the draft local and still uses an isolated database for the explain step.

Limitations and who should skip this

Masking column names does not anonymize a schema, because unique table names can reveal a launch, a partnership, or a fraud rule. Position A is therefore unsafe for catalogs whose names are themselves confidential, even when row samples never appear in the prompt. A free server with empty statistics will mislead cost comparisons, so its plan cost should not be treated as a production forecast. The sample gate also misses many secret shapes, including internal identifiers that do not resemble email addresses.

Teams should not use the hosted path when contracts forbid external inference or when classification labels are incomplete. They should also skip that path when the agent can obtain write credentials on any reachable database. This debate is the wrong tool if a human acceptance step cannot be staffed for every promoted statement. An automated promotion from a fluent draft to production sits outside the decision rule that follows.

Decision rule

Reviewers should choose the masked hosted draft only when three conditions hold together for that candidate statement. Every referenced object must be classified exportable before the payload is assembled for a hosted call. The gate report must show no sensitive columns and no literals, and the rehearsal server must stay isolated from production. Choose the local draft model when any object is local-only, or when the team cannot review the exact payload before the call.

Reject both external hops when write access cannot be prevented or when no faithful non-production mirror exists. The rule prefers the stricter placement whenever the evidence is mixed, incomplete, or still waiting on classification. Fluency is not evidence of safety, and a free practice surface is not evidence of an acceptable boundary. The recorded extract hash, role grant, and explain output are the acceptance package that later reviewers should trust.

If review notes already capture plans but not placement, add the extract hash before the next agent SQL change. That single field makes the debate auditable, whether the draft model ran locally or on a free hosted practice path. Teams with an export clearance can compare both placements on fixtures and keep the stricter result when the plans disagree.

title: Node.js Background Job Heartbeats: Detect Missed node-cron and BullMQ Runs
description:
TL;DR: Record a timestamp metric or increment a success counter whenever a scheduled job completes. Also write structured start, finish, and error events with a stable job ID. Those records tell you what happened after a Node.js cron or BullMQ worker ran; they cannot prove that a silent job ever started. Use an external heartbeat monitor when a missed run must wake someone up.

For a one-person e-commerce SaaS, that split is the practical answer. I want enough evidence to reconstruct a failed order-sync or abandoned-cart run without adopting a giant observability surface. I also refuse to pretend that a success counter can detect an absent process. The two jobs need two mechanisms.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the evidence side when integration time is the constraint. Its public discovery endpoint describes each capability's request schema, response schema, billing, and runnable examples, so adding logs or metrics starts with reading one endpoint rather than learning another SDK. I would try it for completion metrics and searchable job events in a small SaaS because that self-describing REST surface shortens the path to a useful result, while one credential can cover both signals. It is not the heartbeat monitor.

How should Node.js background jobs use heartbeats with node-cron or BullMQ?

Silence is ambiguous. A counter that did not increase might mean the scheduler died, the queue stalled, the worker lost credentials, the job is merely late, or nobody queried the right window. If the code never executes, it cannot report its own failure.

This matters in commerce. Suppose sync-orders should finish every 15 minutes. A successful run should update job_last_success_timestamp or increment job_run_success_total. Its logs should carry the job name, a unique run ID, start time, finish time, status, and a restrained error description. At 10:30, those facts can answer whether order ord_7821 was within the affected interval and which run handled it.

They still do not generate an alarm. The platform has no built-in heartbeat or synthetic monitor and no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route. A lightweight worker can poll metrics and logs and implement custom alerting, but then the alert depends on another scheduler that I must operate. For a solo product, that circular dependency is usually the wrong trade.

Silence needs an independent observer.

The clean design is an external deadline. Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, and Better Stack each offer purpose-built cron or heartbeat monitoring. Their exact delivery channels and plan limits change, so I would verify those on the live product pages; the durable distinction is that a separate service expects a signal and can notice its absence. Completion evidence stays in the observability store. Missed-run detection stays outside the worker.

The smallest useful evidence trail

Start with an event contract that works for node-cron, BullMQ, or a plain process timer. This runnable TypeScript example first fetches the live logs.ingest capability document, including its current schema and example, instead of guessing a request body. It then produces start, finish, and error records and emits a success metric only after the work completes. It does not put customer email, cart contents, or payment data in the log. That is deliberate data minimization, not tidiness. Install no vendor SDK; Node.js 20 or later supplies fetch.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

async function readIngestContract(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readIngestContract(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

type JobEvent = {
  event: "job.start" | "job.finish" | "job.error";
  job: string;
  runId: string;
  at: string;
  status: "running" | "ok" | "error";
  durationMs?: number;
  error?: string;
};

function emit(event: JobEvent): void {
  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(event)}\n`);
}

function reportSuccess(job: string, finishedAt: Date): void {
  process.stdout.write(
    `${JSON.stringify({
      metric: "job_last_success_timestamp",
      value: Math.floor(finishedAt.getTime() / 1000),
      labels: { job },
    })}\n`,
  );
}

async function syncOrders(): Promise<void> {
  await Promise.resolve();
}

async function run(job: string, work: () => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
  const runId = randomUUID();
  const startedAt = new Date();
  emit({ event: "job.start", job, runId, at: startedAt.toISOString(), status: "running" });

  try {
    await work();
    const finishedAt = new Date();
    emit({
      event: "job.finish",
      job,
      runId,
      at: finishedAt.toISOString(),
      status: "ok",
      durationMs: finishedAt.getTime() - startedAt.getTime(),
    });
    reportSuccess(job, finishedAt);
  } catch (cause) {
    const failedAt = new Date();
    emit({
      event: "job.error",
      job,
      runId,
      at: failedAt.toISOString(),
      status: "error",
      durationMs: failedAt.getTime() - startedAt.getTime(),
      error: cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : "unknown error",
    });
    throw cause;
  }
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const ingestContract = await readIngestContract();
  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify({ ingestContract })}\n`);
  await run("sync-orders", syncOrders);
}

void main().catch((cause: unknown) => {
  process.stderr.write(`${cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : "unknown error"}\n`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The output is intentionally boring. Route it through the log transport already used by the worker, then translate the success object into the metric reporter at that boundary. The relevant verified capabilities are logs.ingest and metrics.report; live discovery provides the current payload schema and TypeScript example. That avoids copying a payload shape into an article where it can drift. The discovery request is a read, so it needs no idempotency key; any later write should follow the capability's documented idempotency contract.

The job ID is the join key. A trace_id or span_id can also be stored on log events, but this service does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. Do not promise a tracing workflow from correlation fields alone.

What I would change as the workload grows

At one worker, one structured event per state change is easy to inspect. At 200 queues, success logs become noise. I would keep the timestamp metric for each job class, retain error events, and sample or shorten routine start/finish logs according to the incident questions the business actually asks. Signal quality wins over volume.

I would also define deadlines from business impact, not scheduler syntax. A five-minute catalog refresh and a nightly settlement export should not share an alert window. The heartbeat service owns those expected intervals. The application owns a completion ping only after durable work succeeds; acknowledging a BullMQ job before its database commit would create a reassuring lie.

For incident reconstruction, decide retention and privacy requirements before shipping customer identifiers. A limitation of this service is that its logs do not offer a per-user deletion API, bulk export, or subscription interface, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. It is not a fit when those are hard requirements; a store with explicit deletion and export controls is the better choice. Sentry is also a stronger specialist when the real problem is stack-trace grouping, source-map resolution, crash symbolication, or Session Replay rather than scheduled-job evidence. Those trade-offs outweigh a quick initial integration.

Polling can still be rational for a low-stakes internal task. Query the latest success metric on a separate process, compare it with the job deadline, and notify through infrastructure you already trust. Keep the poller outside the failure domain of the scheduled worker. Once missed revenue or settlement delays are plausible, I would outsource this undifferentiated watchdog to a heartbeat specialist and get back to the weekly release. The extra credential is cheaper than owning a second scheduler, its deployment, its notification integration, and the awkward question of who watches the watcher.

Ship the boundary.

Choosing the boundary, not a winner

Option Fastest useful result Credential and SDK surface Better fit Important boundary
Healthchecks.io Add a completion signal to a scheduled task Separate monitoring service Detecting a job that misses its expected deadline Keep richer incident evidence elsewhere
Cronitor Configure a cron or heartbeat monitor Separate monitoring service Scheduled-job monitoring as the primary problem Another vendor and credential to operate
Better Stack Add heartbeat monitoring alongside its broader tooling Separate product surface Teams that want heartbeat checks near an existing monitoring stack Validate current channels and limits before committing
Sentry Capture application errors and exceptions Dedicated SDK and project configuration Error grouping and debugging workflows Not a substitute for a missed-run heartbeat design
Infrai Read public discovery, then use REST examples for logs and metrics One API credential; no product-specific SDK required Searchable job evidence plus lightweight completion metrics No native heartbeat, alert delivery, trace tree, source maps, or replay

No row is universally best. If the only requirement is “tell me when this cron did not arrive,” choose Healthchecks.io or Cronitor and stop. If Better Stack or Sentry is already embedded, accepting their integration surface may cost less engineering attention than introducing another system. If the requirement is to retain compact metrics and searchable events across several backend concerns, the self-describing API and shared credential remove concrete setup work.

This is the decision rule I would ship: a specialist watches for absence; the observability store preserves evidence of presence and failure. It keeps the alert independent, the logs useful, and the integration small enough to maintain between product releases.

Further reading and references

  • Infrai discovery for logs.ingest
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Cronitor cron job monitoring
  • Better Stack heartbeat monitoring documentation
  • Sentry JavaScript documentation
  • GDPR Article 5: principles relating to processing personal data

If this evidence boundary fits your system, start with the live Infrai discovery document and use its current TypeScript example.

title: AI Gateway now supports team and project spend budgets
description:
AI Gateway spend budgets can now be scoped to a team or a project, in addition to individual API keys. Set a dollar limit on a scope, and the gateway meters spend against it and stops further requests once the limit is reached, until the budget resets or you raise it.

Scopes

A budget attaches to one of three scopes. A request can fall under multiple budgets and has to pass all of them: if any one is over its limit, the request is rejected, even when the others have room left.

Scope

Caps spend for

Team

Every request your team runs through the gateway

Project

All requests attributed to a single project

API key

A single API key

BYOK spend is not counted against budgets by default.

Manage budgets in the dashboard

Set and track budgets from the AI Gateway Budgets tab. The Overview breaks spend down across every scope against its limit, so you can see what is near or over before it starts rejecting requests.

Turn on email spend alerts to notify your team's usage notification recipients when usage crosses 50%, 75%, or 100% of a limit within a refresh period. Alerts are off by default and informational: they never block requests, only the budget limit does.

Set a default budget for projects or API keys, and every one without an explicit budget inherits it automatically. An explicit budget always overrides the default.

Manage budgets from the CLI

Set, inspect, and remove team and project budgets from the CLI. The refresh period is daily, weekly, monthly (default), or none for a cumulative cap.

For more information, read the budgets documentation.

title: Fear Is Not Always Fear: Variation in Emotion Label Equivalence Across Datasets
description:
arXiv:2610.12841v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emotion classifiers are routinely applied beyond their training data, on the assumption that same-named labels such as fear or surprise mean the same thing across resources. We test this assumption for five labels shared by GoEmotions, XED, and BRIGHTER, comparing models on identical inputs and under cross-corpus transfer. On the same texts, one fear classifier flags 71% as fearful and another 8%, yet the two largely agree on how the texts rank. Across 30 resource-label comparisons, training-label prevalence explains about half of this kind of scale mismatch, and a fitted intercept removes most of it. What recalibration cannot repair is larger: transferred models lose 55% of native discrimination in aggregate, agreement in ranking between classifiers is only weakly related to that loss, and for surprise the resources disagree about which texts express the emotion. The choice of training resource can therefore change conclusions: on two external tweet collections, BRIGHTER- and XED-trained classifiers give opposite answers about which shows more surprise, even after rank normalization, with intervals excluding zero in both directions. A shared emotion label name does not establish an interchangeable measurement target.

title: Why HTML, CSS, and JavaScript Aren’t Dead Yet (Even with AI Writing Code)
description:
If you spend any time on tech Twitter, LinkedIn, or YouTube lately, you’ve probably seen someone posting a 10-second video of an AI generating a fully styled dashboard from a napkin sketch.

And if you’re sitting there grinding away at CSS flexbox, debugging a weird JavaScript async/await bug, or trying to figure out why your mobile layout is breaking, a quiet little voice in your head probably asks:

“Am I learning a dying skill? Is AI going to take my frontend job tomorrow?”

Take a deep breath. Let’s talk about it.

The AI Hype vs. The Frontend Reality
Yes, AI coding assistants (like GitHub Copilot, Claude, and ChatGPT) are ridiculously powerful. They can spin up boilerplate code, write basic HTML structures in seconds, and guess what CSS properties you need.

But here is the dirty little secret that the "AI will replace all developers" crowd doesn’t tell you: Generating code and building a product are two completely different sports.

AI is an incredible copilot, not the driver. It writes code based on patterns it has seen before. But when you are building real-world applications for actual humans, you run into messy, unique problems that a pattern-matching machine struggles to navigate cleanly.

Why HTML, CSS, and JS are Still the Holy Trinity
No matter how advanced AI gets, the browser only speaks three languages natively: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Understanding how they work under the hood changes everything.

  1. HTML: More Than Just Tags
    AI can spit out

    tags all day long, but knowing semantic HTML—accessibility (a11y), SEO optimization, and proper document structure—requires human intent. If your markup is a messy soup of divs, no AI prompt is going to magically make your site accessible to screen readers or index well on Google.

  2. CSS: The Art of the Broken Layout
    Ah, CSS. The universal punchline of web development. AI can write a nice Tailwind class string, but when a client says, "Hey, can we make this hero section feel a bit more dynamic on foldable phones while keeping the typography fluid?"—that’s when you need a real human brain. Understanding specificity, layout algorithms (Grid and Flexbox), and performance rendering makes you irreplaceable.

  3. JavaScript: Logic Meets Reality
    JavaScript is where the magic (and the pain) happens. State management, edge cases, race conditions, memory leaks, and API integrations require deep architectural thinking. AI can give you a function, but when your app crashes because of an unhandled promise rejection in production at 2:00 AM, you need to know how to debug it.

How to Supercharge Your Coding with AI (Instead of Competing with It)
Stop trying to compete with AI on speed. You won't win. Instead, leverage it to become a 10x developer. Here is how you can use AI smartly in your daily workflow:

Use it as a Rubber Duck: Stuck on a tricky algorithm? Ask AI to explain alternative approaches instead of just copying and pasting the solution.

Kill the Boilerplate: Let AI handle the tedious setup—like generating mock data, standard form validations, or repetitive CSS utility classes—so you can focus on core architecture.

Write Tests: Ask AI to generate unit tests for your JavaScript functions. It's a massive time-saver and forces you to write cleaner code.

The Human Advantage
At the end of the day, software development isn’t just about typing syntax into an IDE. It’s about:

Empathy: Understanding what the user actually needs and feels when they use your app.

Problem Solving: Translating vague, messy business requirements into clean technical specifications.

Collaboration: Working with designers, backend devs, and stakeholders who change their minds every two days.

AI doesn’t care about the user experience. It doesn't feel the frustration of a clunky UI. You do.

Final Thoughts
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript aren't going anywhere. In fact, understanding them deeply makes you a better prompt engineer and a sharper developer because you actually know what to ask the AI and how to fix its mistakes when it hallucinates a broken script.

Don't fear the tech wave. Ride it. Learn the fundamentals, master your tools, and build cool things.

What’s your take? Are you leaning heavily on AI for your frontend workflow, or are you keeping it old school? Let's chat in the comments! 👇

title: The One-Word Census: Answer-Choice Conformity Across 105 Language Models
description:
arXiv:2607.12796v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When a language model must choose one answer from a large space of equally valid options, which answer does it choose, and how often is it the answer every other model chooses? Asked to "pick a word," 105 language models from more than twenty labs chose serendipity 46% of the time. We measure this convergence, and each model's share in it, with 96 single-turn prompts that each name a category with many valid one-word answers ("Name a tree."), asked eight times per model and scored by exact match, with no embeddings and no judge. A model's answer-choice surprisal is the average -log2 probability of its answers under the pooled answers of all other models. In 28 of 96 categories a single answer takes at least 80% of all answers. The concentration does not depend on small or persona-tuned models: the 87 major-lab models are at least as concentrated as the full field. Lightly post-trained and persona-tuned models are the most divergent; heavily post-trained assistants from the major labs are the most conformist. Models that avoid the modal answer mostly land on the same runner-up. Within the major providers' lineages, release order shows no panel-wide trend once model tier is controlled; GPT, Gemini, Grok and Qwen become more conformist across releases, and Claude's generation-5 releases reverse. On open checkpoints of three post-training pipelines, supervised fine-tuning is the largest step toward the field's answers. Against human category-production norms, the field is more concentrated than people in 18 of 20 shared categories. All prompts, transcripts, and code are public.

title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.12917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model.
  Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%.
  Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow
description:
arXiv:2610.13253v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.

title: ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation
description:
arXiv:2602.01709v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Current test-time scaling (TTS) techniques enhance large language model (LLM) performance by allocating additional computation at inference time, yet they remain insufficient for agentic settings, where actions directly interact with external environments and their effects can be irreversible and costly. We propose ARTIS, Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation, a framework that decouples exploration from commitment by enabling test-time exploration through simulated interactions prior to real-world execution. This design allows extending inference-time computation to improve action-level reliability and robustness without incurring environmental risk. We further show that naive LLM-based simulators struggle to capture rare but high-impact failure modes, substantially limiting their effectiveness for agentic decision making. To address this limitation, we introduce a risk-aware tool simulator that emphasizes fidelity on failure-inducing actions via targeted data generation and rebalanced training. Experiments on multi-turn and multi-step agentic benchmarks demonstrate that iterative simulation substantially improves agent reliability, and that risk-aware simulation is essential for consistently realizing these gains across models and tasks.

title: What Really Happens Behind a Website? My First Look at the Backend
description:
I can build a website that looks good and feels alive. A form takes my input, I press submit, and the data vanishes.

But where does it go?

"The backend," you might say. Fair, but how does it get there? A week ago, I couldn't have told you. So I ran my first Node.js server to find out. This post is what I learned, including the mistakes.

Frontend vs. Backend

The frontend is everything you can see: the sign-in form, the buttons, the layout. The backend is everything else, working out of sight: the server, the API, the database, and the rules that connect them.

Whenever you open a website, your browser (the client) sends a request to a server. The server does its work and sends a response back. That's the client-server model, and nearly everything on the web follows it.

Take logging in. You type your details and press the button. The backend checks them against records in the database and replies with either "Welcome!" or "Wrong password."

Do you always need a database? No. Only when the backend has something to save.

Why Node.js and Not Just JavaScript?

JavaScript was originally built to run inside the browser. Node.js is a runtime built on Google's V8 engine that lets JavaScript run outside the browser. It's not a new language, just another place JavaScript can run.

I chose it because I can use one language for both frontend and backend. Node.js also comes with npm, a huge library of free code shared by developers, so you install what you need instead of writing everything yourself.

Building My First Node.js Server

Step 1: Install Node.js

Download the LTS version from nodejs.org, then check it worked:

node -v
npm -v

If both show version numbers, you're ready.

Step 2: Create a project 

mkdir my-first-backend
cd my-first-backend
npm init -y

This makes a folder and a package.json file, which stores your project's details and dependencies.

Step 3: Write the server

Create a file named server.js:

const http = require('http');

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from my first Node.js server!');
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log('Server running at http://localhost:3000');
});
  • http is a built-in Node.js module.
  • createServer() makes a server that runs your function for every request.
  • req is the request, and res is what you send back.
  • res.end() sends the message and finishes the response.
  • listen(3000) waits for visitors on port 3000. A port is like a numbered door on your computer.

Step 4: Run it 

node server.js

The terminal keeps running. That's normal, because the server is waiting for requests. Press Ctrl + C to stop it.

Step 5: Open your browser

Visit http://localhost:3000. You should see:

Hello from my first Node.js server!

Seeing my own server answer my browser made everything click.

What actually happened?

  1. The browser sent an HTTP request to my server.
  2. Node.js ran my function.
  3. The server sent back a response, and the browser showed it.

localhost means my own computer, so only I can open it. A deployed server runs on a remote machine so anyone can reach it.

5 Common Problems I Faced (and How I Fixed Them)

1. EADDRINUSE: port already in use

I ran node server.js and got an error saying port 3000 was already in use. I had forgotten that my old server was still running in another terminal. I stopped it with Ctrl + C and ran the command again.

If you can't find the old terminal, kill the process:

# Windows
netstat -ano | findstr :3000
taskkill /PID <number> /F


You can also just use a different port, like `3001`.

### 2. `Cannot find module`

Node told me it couldn't find my file. The cause was a small typo in the file name, and I was also in the wrong folder.


bash
node sever.js # wrong
node server.js # right
npm install express # install packages before using them


Now I check the spelling and run `ls` (or `dir` on Windows) to confirm I'm in the right folder.

### 3. Connection refused

My browser showed "This site can't be reached." The server wasn't running, so nothing was listening. I started it again and the page loaded.


bash
node server.js


Also make sure the port in the browser (`localhost:3000`) matches the port in your code.

### 4. No error handling

I didn't think about this at first, because my server only returned one message. But one bad request can crash the whole server, so I now wrap risky code in `try/catch`.


js
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
try {
const data = JSON.parse('not valid json');
res.end('ok');
} catch (err) {
res.writeHead(500);
res.end('Something went wrong.');
}
});


Now the user gets a clear message and the server keeps running.

### 5. Hardcoding the port and secrets

I wrote `3000` directly in my code. That works on my laptop, but hosting services choose the port for you, and secrets like passwords should never sit in your code.


js
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;
server.listen(PORT);


Secrets go in a `.env` file, and I add that file to `.gitignore` so it never reaches GitHub.


## Where Does Express Come In?

As apps grow, handling every request by hand gets repetitive. **Express** is a framework that makes building servers and APIs easier. It isn't built in, so install it first:


bash
npm install express


js
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
res.send('Welcome to the homepage!');
});

app.listen(3000);




`app.get('/')` means "when someone visits the homepage, run this function."

## What I Learned
I started this journey with one question: where does my data go?

Now I know. It goes to a server, a program that waits for requests and answers them. My first one only said “Hello,” but it was mine, and it was running on my own laptop.

Next stop: REST APIs and MongoDB. I’m not afraid of the backend anymore. I’m curious about it.
