title: SharP: Soft and Hard Prompt-Guided Augmentation with LLM for Low Resource Fake News Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.13207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fake news detection under low resource conditions is challenged by the scarcity of labeled data and the difficulty of capturing subtle deceptive patterns. In this work, we focus on low resource fake news detection, where only a small labeled set is available for training, while evaluation is performed under a fixed and unchanged test protocol. This setting is motivated by costly, ambiguous fact-checking and emerging topics and domains that are poorly covered by existing benchmarks. Existing data augmentation methods, such as synonym substitution, generative adversarial networks, and large language model (LLM)-based generation, often produce fluent but overly generic content, lacking the task-specific relevance needed for accurate detection. To address this, we propose SharP, a boundary-aware text generation framework guided by soft and hard prompts, which leverages LLMs as tools adapted to produce task-specific synthetic samples. SharP employs a dual prompt mechanism: hard prompts provide structured guidance and factual constraints, while soft prompts introduce learned semantic patterns from the data. These two types of prompts are combined to guide the generation process, enabling the model to produce samples that closely align with the characteristics of news. To further enhance detection performance, we incorporate a boundary-aware strategy that steers generation toward areas where the classifier is less confident, helping to clarify subtle distinctions between real and fake content. In addition, we adopt a dual objective optimization that balances semantic alignment with the source data and classifier feedback. This encourages the generation of samples that are both domain-consistent and helpful for refining decision boundaries, ultimately improving model robustness and generalization in low resource fake news detection.

title: Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
description:
arXiv:2610.13810v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard source of query expansion terms but they hallucinate. They inject non existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise and can hurt strong retrievers. Existing remedies such as corpus grounding, mutual verification and preference alignment treat hallucinated terms as an undifferentiated nuisance to be filtered by agreement heuristics, without a mechanistic account of why a given term appears or a principled criterion for how many terms to keep. We propose Subsequence-Association Filtered, breadth-aware query expansion (SAFE-QE), a training-free, retriever agnostic method that draws on the subsequence-association account of hallucination. We score each candidate expansion term by its corpus conditioned cross-context reproducibility, terms that reappear under randomised query contexts yet lack support in the pseudo-relevant set are flagged as products of dominant hallucinatory associations and down-weighted. Drawing on the characterisation of language generation as a trade-off between consistency (no hallucination) and breadth (coverage), we cast term selection as constrained coverage maximisation over the pseudo-relevant set, keeping a set that is approximately broad but consistent and stable across resampling. We also introduce the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate, a query side faithfulness metric that counts injected expansion terms no relevant document supports. We evaluate our approach on benchmarked TREC and BEIR collections. Our SAFE-QE is statistically indistinguishable from generative and corpus-steered expansion on nDCG@10 while injecting fewer unsupported terms 4.3 per query against 27.8 for Query2doc and 57.5 for HyDE and on a strong learned sparse retriever, where every expansion method regresses. Faithfulness is therefore available at no measurable cost in ranking quality.

title: Building Your First PC: A Practical Roadmap
description:
Introduction
For a hobby made of parts that mostly fit only one way, building a PC has an outsized reputation for difficulty. The reality is closer to adult construction blocks with better cables: seven or eight components, each with a home, assembled in an order that almost suggests itself. Millions of people who have never held a screwdriver for electronics manage it every year.
What first-time builders actually need is not talent but sequence — knowing what to decide before you buy, what to check before you assemble, and what to do when the finished machine refuses to start. That is what this roadmap provides: the practical path from an empty desk to a running computer.
Quick Summary
• Planning is most of the build: define the purpose, pick a processor platform, and let every other part follow from those two choices.
• Compatibility checking before purchase prevents nearly all first-build disasters.
• Assembly itself takes one to three unhurried hours and requires no special skills, only patience and a screwdriver.
• If the finished PC does not start, the cause is usually a loose cable or a forgotten setting, not a dead part.
What Does Building a PC Involve?
To build a PC is to select and assemble the components of a desktop computer yourself instead of buying one preassembled. The cast is short: a processor (CPU) that does the calculating, a motherboard that connects everything, memory (RAM) for the working space, storage for files, a power supply unit (PSU) that feeds the system, a case that houses it all, a cooler that keeps the processor safe, and usually a graphics card (GPU) for demanding visuals.
What you are really doing is making trade-offs with your own hands. Every prebuilt computer balances those parts for an imagined average buyer; when you build, the balance is yours. You decide where to spend, where to save, and what the machine will be for.
Be clear-eyed about what it is not. It is not always cheaper than a sale-priced prebuilt, since large makers buy parts in bulk. The gains are control, upgradeability, no bundled software you never asked for, and the knowledge of your own machine.
How to Build a PC
Start before any shopping. Write down what the computer is for — games, office work, video editing, a home server — and a budget range. The purpose decides the priorities: games lean on the graphics card, editing leans on memory and storage, office work barely cares.
Then choose in this order. First the processor, because it sets the platform and, with it, which motherboards and memory generations are compatible. Second the motherboard, matched to that socket with the ports and slots you actually need. Third, memory and storage — sixteen gigabytes of RAM and a solid-state drive are sensible baselines for most purposes. Fourth the graphics card, sized to your purpose and usually the largest line in a gaming budget. Finally the power supply with comfortable headroom, a case that fits the board and cooler, and the cooler itself.
Before buying anything, run a compatibility check. Free online tools and retailer websites verify that the CPU fits the board's socket, that memory matches the board, that the case fits everything, and that the power supply has the right connectors and wattage. Ten minutes here prevents nearly every catastrophic mistake.
Assembly follows a calm order, and this summary is deliberately simplified — follow a current video guide alongside it. Touch the case occasionally to discharge static. Fit the processor into its socket gently, with no force. Attach the cooler, following its instructions exactly, including the paste. Seat the memory until both clips click. Install storage, screw the board into the case's standoffs, connect the power supply cables, then the small front-panel wires for the power button — the fiddliest step in any build. Add the graphics card last, where access is easiest.
On first boot, the machine should power on and the firmware screen should appear; if it does, install an operating system from a USB stick and let it fetch drivers. If it does not, see the troubleshooting questions below. Finally, run a demanding task and watch temperatures settle into the normal range.
Key Features
• A written purpose first. Builds drift when shopping starts before the plan does; one sentence about the machine's job keeps the budget honest.
• Platform thinking. The processor choice quietly decides the board, memory, and upgrade path, so it deserves the most deliberation per dollar.
• Compatibility checks. The single habit that separates smooth builds from returns and refunds.
• A patient workspace. Good light, a clear table, and a small tray for screws prevent most self-inflicted damage.
• Testing before closing up. Confirming the machine starts with the case open makes the inevitable loose-cable fix painless.
Real-World Applications
The classic case is the gaming desktop: a student or young professional spreads a budget across a graphics card and a capable processor, building a machine that can be upgraded piece by piece for years.
Home offices are a quieter use case. A remote worker builds a compact, silent machine for document work and video calls, spending little. Home-lab hobbyists build machines to run file storage, media servers, or practice networks — the build itself is the education. Schools and maker clubs increasingly use first builds as coursework, since assembling a computer teaches what every component does better than any diagram.
Benefits
• Control over every dollar. Money goes to the parts your workload values, not to a prebuilt's marketing budget or a padded parts list.
• Upgradeability by design. A standard board and case with room to spare turn future upgrades into swaps instead of replacements.
• Real knowledge. After one build, hardware stops being mysterious; troubleshooting and buying decisions all get easier.
• Repair confidence. When something fails in year four, you will open the case rather than replace the computer.
Challenges and Limitations
Honesty first: there is no single warranty. If a part fails, you deal with that manufacturer individually, and diagnosing which part failed is your job. Prebuilts handle this with one phone call.
Costs swing with the market. Component prices rise and fall with supply, so a build that looked economical in one season may not in the next. Time is a real cost too: research, assembly, setup, and troubleshooting can fill a weekend. And some first-boot problems are genuinely tedious; a board that needs a firmware update to accept a new processor can send a beginner into a loop until they learn the right trick.
Security and Privacy
A new build is a fresh start for security, and a few early choices set the tone. Update the motherboard's firmware soon after the first boot — early firmware sometimes carries fixes for known vulnerabilities — and leave Secure Boot enabled, since it verifies that the code starting your operating system is trusted. Install the operating system from an official source; pirated copies are a classic malware delivery route.
Turn on the operating system's full-disk encryption and back up the recovery key somewhere safe. Privacy-wise, a self-built PC contains no vendor telemetry beyond what the operating system and drivers include, and setup prompts let you decline optional data sharing. Be cautious with used parts, too: a secondhand power supply has a past you cannot inspect.
Examples
A university student assembles a budget gaming rig before the fall term, choosing a mid-range graphics card and a modest processor.
A wedding photographer builds a quiet tower for photo editing, spending generously on memory, a solid-state drive, and a quality screen, and relying on the processor's built-in graphics because her work never touches 3D.
A retiree who wants a project builds a compact home-theater computer in a small case with quiet cooling, and finds the assembly takes an unhurried afternoon.
Impact on Businesses and Society
The ability to build and repair PCs quietly underpins the right-to-repair conversation: every person who has swapped a drive or upgraded memory is a customer the disposable-computer model has to convince otherwise. Builder knowledge also feeds the IT workforce, since technicians and support staff overwhelmingly learned hardware by opening cases.
For the market, the do-it-yourself segment keeps manufacturers honest on standards, pricing, and documentation. For society, longer-lived and repairable computers reduce electronic waste. Building a PC will never be a mass necessity, but as a skill it compounds: one afternoon of assembly buys years of cheaper, better-understood computing.
Future of Building a PC
The craft is likely to get easier before it changes. Toolless cases, clearer labeling, and manufacturer setup apps already shave friction each generation, and firmware processes that once required technical tricks are increasingly automated.
Further out, two forces may reshape the hobby. More integrated designs — where memory or even processing lives on the board — could narrow what a builder swaps. And AI assistants that help choose compatible parts and diagnose a silent first boot may compress the research and troubleshooting hours that intimidate newcomers. The realistic picture is a smaller, friendlier version of today's hobby: still the best way to learn what a computer is.
Editor's note: Product capabilities, laws, and market conditions change quickly. Verify current specifics against official sources or recent coverage before relying on them.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is it cheaper to build a PC than buy one?
Sometimes, but not reliably — large makers get bulk discounts. The surer advantage is control: better parts for the same money and no unwanted software, not a guaranteed discount.
What tools do I need to build a PC?
One Phillips screwdriver covers nearly everything. A clear table, good light, and the boxes the parts came in finish the list; anti-static wristbands are optional for careful home builds.
How long does a first PC build take?
Expect one to three hours for assembly at an unhurried pace, plus operating system setup.
What if my new PC turns on but shows nothing?
Start with the basics almost every builder meets once: reseat the memory, recheck the monitor cable, confirm the screen input, and consult the motherboard manual's diagnostic lights before suspecting any part.
Can I reuse parts from an old computer?
Often yes — cases, storage, and sometimes memory carry over well. Check compatibility, and be more skeptical of old power supplies than of old cases.
Do I need to be good with electronics?
No. Assembly is fitting shaped connectors into shaped slots and tightening screws. Nothing is soldered, and force is almost always a sign something is misaligned.
Conclusion
Building a PC is a weekend-sized project with decade-sized payoffs. The plan matters more than the assembly: decide the machine's purpose, choose the platform, verify compatibility, then follow a calm order with a screwdriver. The first boot comes with a moment of held breath, and the troubleshooting will teach more than the assembly did.
The people who benefit most are not necessarily gamers or engineers — they are anyone who would rather understand their computer than rent one. If that curiosity is there, the roadmap is short: plan, check, assemble, boot.

title: Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence
description:
arXiv:2606.19386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. A scriptable gpt-5.4-mini agent loop measures latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s), inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.

title: Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
description:
arXiv:2610.13416v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents. Nevertheless, as users expect agents to complete long-horizon, end-to-end tasks, they increasingly need to conduct broad information gathering, perform browser actions, and revisit acquired evidence within a single trajectory. Yet our preliminary analyses reveal that existing access models struggle to meet these demands. They primarily support either information gathering or browser interaction, while combining their capabilities can involve substantial costs or performance trade-offs. To this end, we present Web\$hell, an interface that unifies web access under a single access model. Using a common schema defined by WebContract, WebCompiler compiles live webpages into addressable information and action objects. These objects are maintained in WebCache and handled through a shared set of operations, providing agents with consistent, operable, and persistent web access. Through extensive experiments across web search, web navigation, and deep research benchmarks, we show that Web\$hell achieves strong task performance at lower cost. Our results further indicate the importance of interface design for effective web access, with Web\$hell opening new possibilities for more capable and efficient LLM agents on the web.

title: Looking Ahead and Back: Anticipatory Generative Modeling for Road-Network Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2610.13131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trajectory generation underpins urban applications such as traffic management and urban planning. Within road networks, vehicle movement along road segments is largely deterministic, whereas transitions at intersections are critical--multiple outgoing paths may appear equally plausible, yet they can lead to substantially different downstream routes. Existing generative methods such as diffusion models simulate location sequences and fail short of next transition selection, even producing trajectories that drift off the road network. To fill this gap, we advocate a fundamental shift: moving beyond location simulation toward behavior modeling on the road network. In this paper, we revisit trajectory generation through the lens of generative route planning, and introduce a new graph-constrained generative paradigm, Anticipatory Generative Modeling, which resolves next transition selection by incorporating the Anticipation of how the future route may unfold toward the destination. Concretely, we propose a novel generative model named Foresight that formulates a probabilistic model for an "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop that enables longer-term foresight while continuing sequential generation along the historical trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight wins state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Vercel WAF for Blob is now in beta
description:
The Vercel WAF can now protect a Vercel Blob store. The same rules that guard your deployments (deny, challenge, rate limit) now apply to blob traffic with no changes to your code, blob URLs, or @vercel/blob.

Every blob is already served through Vercel's CDN, so protection is a switch on the store, not a new proxy. Stop scrapers, geo-restrict downloads, rate limit expensive assets, or block abusive IPs before a byte is served.

Rules evaluate at the edge, matching on IP, country, path, and more:

  • Deny returns a 403 and stops the request early, so no data transfer is incurred.

  • Challenge serves the standard browser challenge, and a request that fails it is blocked.

  • Rate limit returns a 429 when a client exceeds your limit.

  • Redirect and log behave as they do for deployment traffic.

The OWASP Core Ruleset is not supported, since it targets dynamic application traffic, not object delivery.

Protecting a store

Setup is a single switch in the dashboard:

  • Open your Blob store, select Settings, then Protect your store.

  • Vercel connects it to a shared vercel-blob-default-project on your team. You author its rules with the standard rule builder, and they take effect immediately.

  • One rule set covers every protected store, so rules can't be scoped per store.

During the beta, setup is dashboard-only, and challenges need a browser to solve, so server-side @vercel/blob requests matching a challenge rule are blocked. Use challenge rules for browser traffic.

Vercel WAF for Blob is available in beta on all plans. See the documentation for the full setup.

title: System design for physical AI: catching flatlined and swapped radar tank gauge readings
description:
This is the engineering summary of an open reference architecture. The paper, its object model as JSON and the model register are free to reuse under CC BY 4.0: https://codeatoms.ai/tank-gauge-integrity-pakistan/. The operator is described by class, never by name.

A fuel terminal in Pakistan gauges thirteen tanks with radar tank gauges wired on three serial Modbus RTU loops into one centralized gauging host. A flatlined gauge reads as a plausible low level. A swapped gauge makes two tanks trade identities. Both surface only when the central inventory picture disagrees with physical stock, long after the signal failed.

Here is how that turns into readings that fail loudly.

1. Survey the signal before buying anything

The loops' signal health is invisible today. The design measures it first, then engineers three booster installations from the survey, each inside an explosion proof junction box with its own field power supply, under the gauging host manufacturer's written authorization. The survey sets the count, not the paper.

2. Model the loop, not just the tank

Fifteen typed objects: fuel tank, radar tank gauge, communication loop, Modbus booster, junction box, gauge reading, data quality event, central inventory picture, loop wiring as-built, service order, warranty record, OEM authorization letter, HSE work permit, instrumentation technician and location engineer. From a distorted level at one tank, one query reaches the loop, the booster that serves it, the as-built that documents it, the technician assigned to it and the permit that covers the work.

3. Deterministic checks, no learned model 

freshness        a gauge that stops answering its polls
flatline         a stuck value that keeps arriving looking valid
address binding  a reading attributed to the wrong tank, the signature of a swap

Every check is a rule an instrument engineer can read, so the model register is empty by design. The ontology service and the integrity monitor run as two containers on the operator's own site application server, inside its OT boundary, projecting a central inventory picture over the gauging host without replacing it.

4. A named person closes every event

Each data quality event moves from open to acknowledged to resolved, and every transition names the person who made it. The location engineer signs acceptance; no phase closes without a signature.

5. What it costs

No compute to buy. The field equipment sits inside the requirement's own supply scope and is priced by OEM quotation against the survey, so the paper prints no list prices.

Full design, figures and the object model: the paper. Cite it as DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23157967.

Designed on CodeNinja Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for designing physical AI systems. The object model imports into Hyper Ontology, which turns it into a living system. Load it yourself with the open hyper-ontology loader.

title: AutoControl Arena: Synthesizing Executable Test Environments for Frontier AI Risk Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2603.07427v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents, existing safety evaluations face a fundamental trade-off: manual benchmarks are costly, while LLM-based simulators are scalable but suffer from logic hallucination. We present AutoControl Arena, an automated framework for frontier AI risk evaluation built on the principle of logic-narrative decoupling. By grounding deterministic state in executable code while delegating generative dynamics to LLMs, we mitigate hallucination while maintaining flexibility. This principle, instantiated through a three-agent framework, achieves over 98% end-to-end success and 60% human preference over existing simulators. To elicit latent risks, we vary environmental Stress and Temptation across X-Bench (70 scenarios, 7 risk categories). Evaluating 9 frontier models reveals: (1) Alignment Illusion: risk rates surge from 21.7% to 54.5% under pressure, with capable models showing disproportionately larger increases; (2) Scenario-Specific Safety Scaling: advanced reasoning improves robustness for direct harms but worsens it for gaming scenarios; and (3) Divergent Misalignment Patterns: weaker models cause non-malicious harm while stronger models develop strategic concealment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CosmosYi/AutoControl-Arena.

title: Commercial Property in Delhi NCR: Green Ratings Decoded published: false
description:
If your company is shortlisting commercial property in Delhi NCR, the brochures will show green badges. LEED Platinum. IGBC Platinum. GRESB 5-Star. They look alike. They answer three different questions.

LEED rates a single building's design and, in some versions, its operations. IGBC is India's own system and often appears as a "pre-certification" at the design stage. GRESB rates the company and its portfolio, not your floor.

If you are the engineer or facilities person asked to "check the sustainability stuff," this is the short version, plus a small script to test whether a building's air data backs up its badge.

LEED: a points table for one building

LEED comes from the U.S. Green Building Council. A project earns points across energy, water, materials, indoor air and site. Under LEED v4, the tiers are Certified (40-49 points), Silver (50-59), Gold (60-79) and Platinum (80+).

Think of it as a scorecard at a point in time. A building certified under a design and construction track tells you how it was built. It does not, by itself, tell you how it runs today.

Max Towers in Sector 16B, Noida, holds LEED Platinum. That is a strong design signal. The follow-up question for any LEED building, this one included, is simple: which rating system, which year, and is there recent operational data?

IGBC: pre-certified is a promise

The Indian Green Building Council, part of CII, runs India's main rating system. Its tiers mirror LEED's: Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum.

The word to watch is "pre-certified." Pre-certification is granted on design documents before or during construction. Full certification comes after the building is complete and verified.

Max Square in Noida carries IGBC Platinum pre-certification. That tells you the design targets are high. It is fair, and normal, to ask the landlord when final certification is expected.

GRESB: the company, not the floor

GRESB assesses real estate companies and funds every year on ESG management and performance. Star ratings (1 to 5) compare a participant against its peers in that cycle.

Max Estates holds a dual GRESB 5-Star rating. What that means for a tenant: the landlord reports ESG data in a structured, audited way. If your own company files Scope 3 emissions, a GRESB-reporting landlord is usually easier to get numbers from.

What it does not mean: that your specific floor has better air than the next building. That needs its own check.

Questions a tech team should ask

Badges are inputs. Data is the answer. Ask for these before you sign.

Indoor air data

Ask whether the building measures PM2.5 and CO2 at the floor level, and whether tenants can see the feed. A dashboard screenshot is a start. An export or an API is better.

Ask what CO2 level triggers more fresh air, and who sets that threshold.

Energy and meters

Ask for sub-metering per tenant area. Without it, your energy share is an estimate. Your sustainability team will need real numbers for annual reports.

Certificate dates

Ratings carry dates and versions. Ask for the certificate, the rating system version, and any recertification plans. An old certificate on a busy building is worth a follow-up question.

A small script for an air feed

Say the landlord shares an hourly CO2 export as JSON. You can test it in ten lines.

import json

THRESHOLD_PPM = 1000   # set this to your own policy

with open("co2_hourly.json") as f:
    rows = json.load(f)   # [{"ts": "...", "floor": "7", "co2": 640}, ...]

office_hours = [r for r in rows if 9 <= int(r["ts"][11:13]) < 19]
over = [r for r in office_hours if r["co2"] > THRESHOLD_PPM]

share = 100 * len(over) / max(len(office_hours), 1)
print(f"{len(office_hours)} office-hour readings")
print(f"{share:.1f}% above {THRESHOLD_PPM} ppm")

The threshold here is a policy choice, not a rule. Pick one with your facilities team and keep it fixed across every building you compare. A number that changes between buildings makes the test useless.

Also check for gaps. A feed missing three days a week is telling you something too.

Where the badges stop

Green ratings say nothing about rent, lift wait times, fit-out timelines, or your team's commute. A Platinum building two hours from your hiring pool is still two hours away.

Use the badges to narrow the list. Use data and site visits to decide.

Further reading

The Max Towers project page lists its certification, and the Max Estates sustainability page covers the portfolio-level ESG reporting. For a wider view of office options across the region, the Delhi NCR Properties guide is a decent starting map.

title: From 2.1M Hours of Raw Broadcast Audio to Finnish Speech SSL: Confidence Filtering and Architectural Analysis at Scale
description:
arXiv:2610.13102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Broadcast archives offer scale and diversity for self-supervised learning (SSL) but contain substantial noisy, non-speech, and multilingual content. Prior work typically relies on voice activity detection or language identification (LID) to extract speech, ensuring presence rather than quality. Whether and how to filter unlabeled speech by quality for SSL, particularly from noisy broadcasts, remains underexplored. We present a large-scale Finnish SSL study starting from 2.1M hours of unconstrained broadcast audio. We propose automatic speech recognition (ASR) confidence as a proxy for pretraining data quality and show 3-7% relative WER improvements over LID-based filtering despite a smaller training set. We further address the lack of controlled architectural comparisons in speech SSL by evaluating Transformer, Macaron-Net, Conformer, and E-Branchformer at matched parameter budgets. Our models improve upon prior Finnish SSL baselines, particularly at Base scale and out-of-domain.

title: RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. Weight-and-activation quantization offers a natural way to accelerate this computation through lower-precision arithmetic, yet repeatedly applying quantized computation introduces numerical perturbations that accumulate along the recurrent trajectory. We systematically analyze how such errors propagate across recurrent depth and show that quantization errors introduced earlier are attenuated by more subsequent recurrent steps and therefore have a smaller effect on the final representation. Matched-budget experiments strongly support this prediction, showing that placing quantized computation earlier in recurrent depth consistently yields the best fidelity. Based on this insight, we introduce RAMP (Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision), which performs early recurrent refinement using low-precision weight-and-activation computation and restores high precision for terminal refinement. Across context lengths up to 4K, RAMP preserves near-full-precision prefill quality while achieving up to 1.16x end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100, corresponding to a 13.9% latency reduction.

title: WebSocket support for OpenAI Responses API live on AI Gateway
description:
AI Gateway now supports WebSocket mode for the OpenAI Responses API. You can keep a persistent connection open and continue each turn by sending only new input items plus previous_response_id, instead of re-sending the full context over a fresh HTTP request every turn.

OpenAI reports up to ~40% faster end-to-end execution on WebSockets for agentic rollouts with 20 or more tool calls.

Route Responses API traffic over WebSocket

The Responses route opens at GET /v1/responses and accepts raw response.create frames over a persistent WebSocket connection. The mode is compatible with store=false and Zero Data Retention, and follows OpenAI's WebSocket mode specification upstream.

See the AI Gateway documentation for setup and the full route list.

title: How Sandstone grew 40x in 147 days on Vercel
description:
Sandstone on Vercel

  • 1,000+ legal requests managed daily across customer teams

  • 7-app turborepo monorepo deployed seamlessly to multiple Vercel projects

  • Multi-step agentic legal workflows built end-to-end with AI SDK

When in-house legal teams get a request from their business, it kicks off a manual process of pulling data from multiple systems. In a typical workflow, lawyers will pull deal details from Salesforce, review past contracts, and chase account teams for missing context, all before they start the legal work itself.

Sandstone automates this data gathering process, and centralizes requests into a single platform. When a request is created, Sandstone automatically ingests context from every system, including messaging and email tools. By the time the lawyer sees it, they have all of the information they need to get to work.

The founding team includes a McKinsey legal tech veteran, a lawyer-turned-engineer, and cybersecurity founder. At Sandstone, that mix shows up directly in the product: legal professionals work alongside engineers, catching the workflow details and legal nuances that only someone who has practiced law would notice. That is how Sandstone ships fast and correctly for one of the most demanding buyers in enterprise software.

That attention to detail has paid off: in less than 6 months after their launch, their revenue grew 40x. Three things made their growth possible on Vercel:

  • Preview deployments fast enough to win enterprise trust

  • An AI layer flexible enough to ship agentic workflows in minutes

  • Secure Compute that makes security a one-sentence answer

Vercel deployments turned a Sunday request into a five-minute fix

For Sandstone's customers, trust is built on responsiveness, and lawyers are trained to notice small details. Liam Germain, Co-Founder and CTO, puts it simply: when a customer asked for a scrollbar accessibility change on a Sunday, he had it live in production in five minutes. On any other platform, he said that same change would have taken five or ten times longer.

Vercel deployments help with more than just fixes. Preview branches with inline commenting mean Sandstone's head of marketing can leave a note on a live landing page with Vercel Toolbar, which is configured to automatically creates a Linear issue and assigns it to engineering. What used to take an afternoon happens in a single comment.

Vercel Flags runs feature flags across all applications, giving the team dynamic control over what is live, what is demoed, and what is still in progress, without touching a deployment.

Sandstone runs a monorepo of over seven applications across multiple Vercel projects with clean environment variable linking and a custom CLI built on top of Vercel's API layer, and every push on every repo generates a preview of production.

Without the right foundation, complexity kills velocity

Sandstone's product started as smart triage, routing requests to the right lawyer. But the bigger opportunity was what happened when a request landed: every lawyer was still manually gathering context before they could act, pulling relevant details from a handful of separate systems, every time, for every request. Shipping a system that could handle that automatically required infrastructure capable of keeping pace with the product vision.

AI SDK unlocks faster agentic workflows

Sandstone has evolved into an AI system that executes complex, multi-step legal workflows end-to-end, searching through thousands of procurement agreements, surfacing the most at-risk agreements, alerting owners via Slack, and notifying legal when responses come in.

Vercel's AI SDK is what makes those workflows composable enough for a small team to keep pace with a rapidly expanding product surface.

The composability shows up across the entire stack. Chat SDK powers the Teams integration. Emulate SDK handles integration testing for Slack and Okta. Agent Browser SDK runs agentic testing locally. Flags SDK drives the toolbar integration. One SDK, four workflows, zero separate infrastructure.

Vercel Secure Compute makes security a one-sentence answer

Sandstone uses Vercel Secure Compute to establish private communication between Vercel and its data layer. The setup was straightforward to implement and well-architected enough that it became a point of confidence rather than friction in every enterprise conversation. When the security question comes up with customers and prospects, and it always does, the answer is simple: all communication between Vercel and Sandstone's data layer is private and never touches the public internet.

Sandstone chooses platforms they believe will be ahead of the market in three to five years, a vendor evaluation framework they apply to both frontier model providers and core infrastructure.

Sandstone connected with the Vercel team through the Sequoia startup partnership. Within ten days of starting the company, the program gave them a shared Slack channel and access to engineers who could help think through architecture decisions in real time.

What’s next

Less than 6 months after launch, Sandstone had grown revenue 40x and landed customers across technology, manufacturing, and ecommerce, leading to a $30M Series A led by Lightspeed. The team is already shipping fast, so the goal for using that capital is straightforward: get Sandstone into more legal departments.

The vision they are building toward is a Legal Relationship Management platform that not only manages intake but also connects every workflow to the business context behind it, flags issues before they surface, and operationalizes legal knowledge through supervised agents. Sandstone describes this as a system of action for the legal department of the future.

For a team shipping with speed toward that ambition, the infrastructure underneath the product has be a competitive advantage, not a burden, and that's why Sandstone runs on Vercel.

About Sandstone: Sandstone was born out of the acute frustration experienced by in-house legal teams who spend more time on process than progress due to fragmentation across disparate business systems. The platform provides a comprehensive solution for intake, triage, execution, fulfillment, and measurement of legal work, designed to run across email, messaging, and the business tools teams already use.

title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: U4RASD at KnowledgeGraphEval-2026: Ontology-Constrained Encoder and LLM Systems for Arabic Relation Extraction
description:
arXiv:2610.12742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper details our submission to KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Subtask 2 on directed Arabic relation extraction. We explored encoder-based and large language model approaches for predicting one of 40 relations or no_relation from an Arabic sentence and a subject-object pair. Our encoder systems use typed entity markers and separate relation-existence and relation-classification heads, while our LLM systems fine-tune Yehia and Qwen3.5 with QLoRA and ontology-constrained prediction. Our best system, an ensemble of Yehia-RE, Qwen-RE, and TypedPair, achieved a micro-F1 score of 94.06 and ranked 1st in Subtask 2. Yehia-RE (full-vocabulary) achieved 92.98, while the best encoder and Qwen-RE achieved 92.69 and 91.94 respectively. Our results highlight the importance of constrained prediction and complementary modeling approaches for Arabic relation extraction.

title: I Put My App on Fiverr. The First 'Order' Was a Scam.
description:
On October 10, 2026 I published my first Fiverr gig. Almost immediately a message came in: an order had been placed, please review the file.

It wasn't an order. It was a scam aimed at brand new sellers, and the timing was not a coincidence. This post is about why I tried Fiverr for a developer tool in the first place, the two surprises I hit on day one, and what I'd tell anyone listing their own product there.

Why a developer tool ends up on Fiverr
PeerPlay is a Flutter and Firebase app I build and run on my own. It helps developers get through Google Play's closed-testing requirement for new personal accounts, 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days, by having developers test each other's apps in tracked rounds. There are also paid campaigns: Starter Pro is $24.99 for 15 verified testers and Production Pass is $34.99 for 20.

I had been doing outreach by hand, one developer at a time, replying to people who posted on itch.io and other forums that they needed testers. It works, but it does not scale. When I looked at how other testing services find customers, marketplaces kept coming up. Developers who are stuck on the 12-tester rule already search Fiverr for help, so the idea was simple: be where they are already looking, and fulfil each order with a PeerPlay campaign.

The same day, I also rewrote PeerPlay's Play Store listing around the problem people actually search for. The title is now "PeerPlay: 12 Testers, 14 Days". Fiverr was the second half of the same bet.

Surprise one: a $100 minimum
The first category I picked for the gig required at least $100 per package. That breaks the whole idea. From what I saw, comparable single-app closed-testing gigs sell for around $20 to $30, and my own in-app packages sit in that range too. A $100 entry price for one app's 14-day test would just sit there.

The fix is either a different subcategory with a lower minimum, or bundles aimed at studios and agencies that ship several apps. If you are listing a product rather than an hourly service, check the price floor of a category before you write a single line of the gig. Fiverr's category choice is not only about search, it can quietly decide your pricing.

Surprise two: the order that wasn't
Then came the message. An order was placed, please review the file. It looks harmless if you have never sold on Fiverr, and that is the point. A new seller is excited, has no idea what a real order looks like yet, and wants to respond fast.

Here is what gives it away. A real order shows up on your Orders page with payment already handled by Fiverr and the buyer's requirements attached there. Nobody needs you to open a file from a chat to start an order. And a brand new gig with zero reviews getting an "order" within moments of going live is far more likely to be someone watching for new sellers than a buyer who found you.

The boring response is the right one: do not open the file, do not click links in the message, check the Orders page, and report the account to Fiverr. If the Orders page is empty, there is no order.

Fiverr rules that shape a dev tool gig
A few platform rules changed how the gig had to work. Fiverr does not allow links or contact outside the platform in the gig or in chat before an order, so the gig cannot point to PeerPlay's website or Play Store page. Progress has to be shared inside Fiverr messages. Fiverr also keeps 20% of each order, which matters when your packages are priced close to your in-app prices.

There is one promise I would not make: that Google will approve production access. Nobody can guarantee that, because Google decides. What a testing service can honestly promise is the testing part: enough real testers, opted in, active for the full 14 days.

What I'd tell another solo developer
It is too early to say whether Fiverr will work for PeerPlay. What I can say is that day one taught me more about the platform than any guide did. Check the category's price floor before you write the gig. Expect a fake order within your first hours and know what a real one looks like. Keep your offer honest about what you control. And treat any file from a stranger as hostile until an actual order exists.

title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.

title: I Built AIVideoCaption Because Hindi and Hinglish Kept Breaking English-First Caption Tools
description:
A sentence like this looks completely normal to an Indian creator:

Aaj reel export karni hai, but captions sync nahi ho rahe.

It contains Hindi, English, and Roman script in a single sentence.

However, many captioning tools do not treat it as a normal sentence. They may skip the Hindi words, convert everything into the wrong script, misinterpret the English terms, or produce a reasonable transcript with captions that appear noticeably late.

I kept encountering variations of this problem while working with short-form Indian videos.

That is why I built AIVideoCaption, a browser-based caption editor designed around Hindi, Hinglish, and other Indian-language videos.

The problem was not just transcription

At first, I thought the main challenge would be speech recognition.

If the system could understand the words correctly, generating captions should be straightforward.

That assumption was wrong.

A useful captioning system has to solve two different problems:

  1. Determine what was said.
  2. Determine exactly when each word was spoken.

A transcript can be almost perfect while the captions still feel unusable.

If one word stays on screen too long, every word after it can start drifting. Fast speech makes this more visible. Chunking a long audio file can also cut through words or produce duplicates at the boundary between two chunks.

For short-form video, timing is part of the product—not a small finishing detail.

Separating transcription from alignment

The pipeline now treats transcription and timing as separate stages.

I use Sarvam AI for speech-to-text, which provides the initial transcript for Indian-language audio.

For more precise word timings, I run a local alignment stage using an ONNX version of an AI4Bharat IndicConformer model.

The simplified pipeline looks like this:

Video upload
    ↓
Audio extraction
    ↓
Speech-to-text transcription
    ↓
Text and audio normalization
    ↓
Local forced alignment
    ↓
Word-level timestamps
    ↓
Caption editor
    ↓
MP4 or SRT export

For alignment, supported Indic scripts are converted into a shared phonetic representation. This lets the alignment model listen for how the words sound instead of relying only on the script in which they are written.

That distinction is particularly useful for code-switched speech, where Hindi and English may appear in the same sentence.

The chunk-boundary problem

Long audio cannot always be processed as one continuous request, so it needs to be divided into chunks.

The obvious implementation is:

  • split the audio;
  • transcribe every chunk;
  • combine the results.

In practice, that can introduce missing or duplicated words around each boundary.

I changed the pipeline to use padded chunks with overlapping context. After transcription, it checks the overlap and removes likely duplicates before calculating the final timestamps.

I also added checks for suspicious timing patterns—for example, one word absorbing a large section of audio while several following words are squeezed into a tiny interval.

These repairs do not make imperfect audio magically perfect, but they produce a much more usable starting point for the editor.

Preview and export must match

Another unexpectedly difficult part was keeping the browser preview consistent with the exported video.

A creator may carefully adjust:

  • font size;
  • line breaks;
  • word highlighting;
  • caption position;
  • outline and shadow;
  • words per caption.

If the downloaded video looks different from the preview, the editor immediately loses the creator’s trust.

To prevent that, the browser and server use the same preset definitions and layout rules. I also created 166 frozen rendering cases that check different fonts, scripts, sizes, positions, and caption styles.

When the renderer changes, these tests help catch small visual differences before they reach the exported video.

The current stack

The application currently uses:

  • FastAPI for the API;
  • PostgreSQL and Alembic for data and migrations;
  • a PostgreSQL-backed job queue;
  • Sarvam AI for transcription;
  • AI4Bharat IndicConformer with ONNX Runtime for local alignment;
  • FFmpeg for audio and video processing;
  • Pillow and FontTools for caption rendering;
  • plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the studio interface.

I intentionally kept the infrastructure fairly small. At this stage, predictable rendering and reliable jobs matter more to me than adding more services.

What AIVideoCaption can do today

The current version supports:

  • Hindi and Hinglish;
  • English;
  • Gujarati;
  • Marathi;
  • Bengali;
  • Tamil;
  • Telugu;
  • Kannada;
  • Malayalam;
  • Punjabi;
  • Odia.

Creators can choose Roman or native script where supported, correct individual words, split or merge caption lines, reposition captions, and select from 17 caption styles.

The result can be exported as a captioned MP4 or an SRT file.

What it does not solve yet

I do not want to present it as perfect.

Clear, single-speaker audio still produces the best result. Background music, overlapping speakers, uncommon names, strong regional accents, and very fast speech can require manual correction.

AIVideoCaption also transcribes what is spoken; it is not intended to be a general-purpose translation tool.

Some regional-language workflows are still in beta, and I am continuing to improve alignment and font handling based on real videos.

What I learned while building it

The biggest lesson was that “supports Hindi” cannot be treated as a checkbox.

Real Indian speech involves:

  • code-switching;
  • multiple writing systems;
  • Romanized Indian languages;
  • English brand names inside regional sentences;
  • different caption-reading habits.

The second lesson was that transcription accuracy and caption quality are not the same metric. A correct sentence with poor timing still feels broken.

The third lesson was that the preview is a promise. If the export does not match it, even a technically accurate transcription is not enough.

I would value feedback from Indian-language creators

There is a free plan with three transcription minutes, no card required, and MP4 and SRT export:

👉 Try AIVideoCaption

If you test it, I would especially like to know:

  1. Which language or code-switching combination did you try?
  2. Did the captions remain synchronized during fast speech?
  3. Was choosing between Roman and native script clear?
  4. Did the exported video match the editor preview?

I built AIVideoCaption, so this post is naturally biased. My goal in sharing it here is to get practical feedback from developers and creators working with the kinds of videos that English-first tools often overlook.
