title: RERA Registered Projects in Noida: Validate in Python
description:
If you build a listings app, a lead form, or even a spreadsheet for RERA registered projects in Noida, you will get bad RERA numbers. Some are typos. Some say "applied." A few are made up.

A regex can catch the first two in milliseconds. It cannot catch the third. That second step needs the state portal, and no code shortcut replaces it.

This post covers both parts: a short Python validator for Uttar Pradesh and Haryana formats, and a data model that records whether a human actually checked the number.

What a RERA number tells you

Under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, most residential projects must register with the state authority before they are marketed. The registration number is the key to the public filing.

That filing holds the useful stuff: approved plans, carpet areas, the promised completion date, and quarterly progress updates. The number itself is just a pointer. If the pointer is wrong, everything you show next to it is unverified.

Two states, two formats

Delhi NCR buyers usually deal with two authorities. Noida and Greater Noida fall under UP RERA. Gurugram falls under Haryana RERA (HARERA). Their formats look nothing alike.

UP RERA (Noida)

UP project numbers start with UPRERAPRJ and six digits. Newer ones add a month and year suffix.

Two real examples from the UP RERA portal:

  • Estate 128, Sector 128, Phase I: UPRERAPRJ446459
  • Estate 105, Sector 105: UPRERAPRJ529777/03/2026

Note that Estate 128 has a second number for Phase II (UPRERAPRJ294911). One project can have several registrations. Keep that in mind for the data model below.

HARERA (Gurugram)

Haryana is messier. Older registrations read like "87 of 2024." Newer ones use a long slash path.

Real examples from the HARERA site:

  • Estate 360, Sector 36A: HRERA No. 87 OF 2024
  • Estate 361, Sector 36A: RC/REP/HARERA/GGM/1012/744/2025/115

The GGM part refers to the Gurugram bench. If you cover other Haryana districts, loosen that part of the pattern.

The validator 

import re

PATTERNS = {
    "UP": re.compile(r"^UPRERAPRJ\d{6}(/\d{2}/\d{4})?$"),
    "HR_NEW": re.compile(r"^RC/REP/HARERA/GGM/\d+/\d+/\d{4}/\d+$"),
    "HR_OLD": re.compile(r"^(HRERA\s+NO\.?\s*)?\d{1,4}\s+OF\s+\d{4}$"),
}

def check_rera(raw: str) -> dict:
    # collapse spaces and uppercase before matching
    s = " ".join(raw.strip().upper().split())
    for name, pat in PATTERNS.items():
        if pat.match(s):
            return {"normalized": s, "format": name, "shape_ok": True}
    return {"normalized": s, "format": None, "shape_ok": False}

samples = [
    "UPRERAPRJ446459",
    "UPRERAPRJ529777/03/2026",
    "RC/REP/HARERA/GGM/1012/744/2025/115",
    "HRERA No. 87 of 2024",
    "RERA applied",
]

for s in samples:
    print(s, "->", check_rera(s))

The first four pass. The last one fails, which is the point. "RERA applied" or "RERA pending" in a listing should never pass as registered.

Keep the patterns strict on structure and loose on whitespace. Users paste numbers with odd spaces and lowercase letters, and that is not fraud.

Shape vs existence

Here is the trap. UPRERAPRJ123456 passes the regex. It may not exist. Or it may exist and belong to a different project in a different city.

So the regex is a filter, not a verdict. After it passes, someone has to open the portal, search the number, and compare three fields:

  • Project name on the filing
  • Promoter (developer) name
  • Phase or tower list

If any of the three differ from the listing, flag it.

A word on automation: both portals use captchas and session checks. Scraping them is fragile and may break their terms of use. For a small app, a manual lookup with a stored timestamp is the honest option.

A data model for a listings app

Store the check, not just the number. A minimal table:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class ReraRecord:
    project_slug: str
    rera_id: str
    state: str              # "UP" or "HR"
    phase: Optional[str]    # "Phase I", "Tower 4", etc.
    shape_ok: bool
    verified_on: Optional[date]   # None until a human checks
    source_url: Optional[str]     # portal page used for the check

Two design choices matter here.

First, phase is its own field. Since one project can hold several registrations, a single rera_id column on the project table will be wrong sooner or later.

Second, verified_on stays empty until a person checks it. Your UI can then show "format valid" and "verified on 12 Oct 2026" as two different badges. Users understand the gap better than you might expect.

Red flags worth a code path

These show up often enough to deserve explicit handling:

  • The number appears only inside an image, never as text
  • The listing says "RERA approved" with no number at all
  • The number matches the format but the portal shows a different promoter
  • The number covers Phase I while the listing sells a Phase II tower
  • The completion date in the ad is earlier than the date in the filing

None of these prove bad intent. They do mean the listing needs a second look before you show it as clean.

Next steps

If you want to test the validator against live data, the Estate 105 project page lists its UP RERA number in the footer. Compare it with the portal entry: Estate 105 in Sector 105, Noida.

For broader context on how listed developers in the region publish project data, the Max Estates blog archive and the Delhi NCR Properties guide are both useful starting points.

A regex will never replace the portal. It just stops the obvious junk before a human wastes time on it.

Disclosure: this post was written by a digital marketing consultant who works with Max Estates. All RERA numbers above are public and can be checked on the state portals.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.

Read more

title: Rethinking Entropy Allocation in LLM-based ASR: Understanding the Dynamics between Speech Encoders and LLMs
description:
arXiv:2604.08003v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Integrating large language models (LLMs) into automatic speech recognition (ASR) has become a dominant paradigm. Although recent LLM-based ASR models have shown promising performance on public benchmarks, it remains challenging to balance recognition quality with latency and overhead, while hallucinations further limit real-world deployment. In this study, we revisit LLM-based ASR from an entropy allocation perspective and introduce three metrics to characterize how training paradigms allocate entropy reduction between the speech encoder and the LLM. To remedy entropy-allocation inefficiencies in prevailing approaches, we propose a principled multi-stage training strategy grounded in capability-boundary awareness, optimizing parameter efficiency and hallucination robustness. Specifically, we redesign the pretraining strategy to alleviate the speech-text modality gap, and further introduce an iterative asynchronous SFT stage between alignment and joint SFT to preserve functional decoupling and constrain encoder representation drift. Experiments on Mandarin and English benchmarks show that our method achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art models using only 2.3B parameters, while also effectively mitigating hallucinations through our decoupling-oriented design.

title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph
description:
arXiv:2610.12961v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.

title: Improving performance in the layers panel
description: The layers panel is the central blueprint of a Figma file. We rearchitected it with new computation and caching strategies, resulting in 30–50% faster interactions in some of the largest, most complex files.

title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models
description:
arXiv:2610.13935v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. We propose Hide and Seek (HnS), a new method for concept-level attribution that does not require access to model weights or labeled concept datasets. HnS can interpret a wide range of vision models. Given a concept and image set, HnS retrieves concept-aligned images using a vision-language model, localizes the concept within each image, masks the localized region, and measures attribution from the change in the black-box model's output between the original and masked images. This enables faithful attribution by directly measuring the model's behavior and supporting local attributions. We validated HnS on CelebA and COCO-Stuff. Compared to existing methods, HnS showed better agreement with ground-truth attributions. We demonstrated the applicability of HnS on diverse tasks, including image captioning and satellite image segmentation, where no existing concept attribution method can be used. We provided our anonymous code in the supplementary material.

title: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
description:
arXiv:2610.12520v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The goal of circuit discovery is to decompose a monolithic neural network into tiny modular subnetworks which are interpretable in the sense that each does an identifiable subtask. We develop a practical method for composing arbitrarily many circuits into a single model. We propose a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm that overcomes limitations of previous attempts to compose circuits by naive union, then generalize it to $N$ circuits via CircuitTree, a new data structure built on a $\Theta(N\log N)$ tree-compose schedule. We compose circuits pruned from HuBERT for classifying individual phonemes into a syllable classifier, a capability none of the 39 phoneme circuits has individually. Chaining CircuitTrees into a hierarchy-of-circuits pipeline, we transcribe open syllables at 64.8\% accuracy, within 1.2 points of a 66.0\% ceiling that shares no circuitry at all, with 99.5\% of circuit components shared.

title: Chat SDK now supports Slack Enterprise Grid
description:
Chat SDK's Slack adapter now supports Slack Enterprise Grid.

Bots installed org-wide work across every workspace, with correct token resolution, tenant-scoped caches, and event retry deduplication.

The adapter now stores org-wide installations by enterprise ID. This matches how tokens are resolved for incoming events, slash commands, and interactive payloads. SlackInstallation records the new identity fields:

Token resolution behaves the same over HTTP webhooks and Socket Mode. Events route by the installation identity in the envelope's authorizations field, which keeps routing correct for Slack Connect shared channels.

The adapter is also hardened for multi-workspace deployments:

  • User profile and mention caches are scoped per installation, so one tenant's data never resolves for another.

  • API calls made with an org-wide token pass the event's team_id automatically, which Slack requires for workspace-scoped methods.

  • Retried event deliveries are deduplicated for 24 hours, covering Slack's Delayed Events redeliveries.

  • Outgoing mentions accept W-prefixed Grid user IDs alongside U-prefixed IDs.

Single-workspace installations are unaffected, and getInstallation and deleteInstallation work unchanged for both install types.

Read the Slack adapter documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Task Context Shapes Component Roles in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. Here, we compare fixed model components across tasks using identical graph facts, statements specifying which directed connections are present. We measure how interventions affect attention heads and the activation state in later layers (influence), as well as the answer (importance). Task changes redistribute the influence in five open-weight models spanning four families and 1.5-14 billion parameters. In Gemma-2-9B and Qwen3-14B, an activation edit changes an early internal activation vector and switches which fact the model reads while the written instruction stays fixed. The same heads then respond to different graph facts and influence later components differently. For each prompt, we construct two linear response maps, one before the edit and one after it. Each map predicts a later head's response from a measured change in an earlier head. For a separate factual intervention, the map for the corresponding condition reduces mean squared prediction error by 53.6% in Gemma and 5.0% in Qwen compared with the average of the two maps. These findings show that task context changes both which graph facts the shared components respond to and how their outputs affect later computation. A network account may help explain how models use shared parameters to perform different computations. Measurements of task-dependent influence could also guide interventions intended to alter one behavior while preserving others.

title: RBAC Is Not Enough: Thinking About Authorization in Enterprise Systems
description:
Roles are one of the first authorization mechanisms most backend developers encounter.

For example:

admin
manager
user

The server checks the user's role and allows or rejects an operation.

That is useful.

But enterprise systems quickly demonstrate that roles alone are often insufficient.

The NIS Store MIS example

The system I have been working on above includes roles representing different responsibilities.

These include:

  • system administrator;
  • operational administrator;
  • store administrator;
  • multi-layered approving authority
  • store manager;
  • store officer;
  • department officer;
  • request officer;
  • dispatch officer;
  • auditor.

The important observation is that a person's role does not necessarily tell us everything about what they can access.

Role versus context

Consider two users with the same role.

They may still belong to different offices.

Therefore:

Same role
+
Different office
=
Potentially different access

This is where authorization becomes contextual.

RBAC

Role-Based Access Control answers questions such as:

Does this user have the store_manager role?

That is useful for coarse-grained authorization.

For example:

store_manager → approve requisition

But the system may also need to ask (which it actually does):

Is this requisition within the organizational scope this user is allowed to manage? (since it is a multi-tenant system)

That is no longer just role checking.

Authorization should be explicit

A useful authorization decision can be thought of as:

Identity
   +
Role
   +
Resource
   +
Action
   +
Context
   =
Authorization Decision

This gives us a more realistic model.

Avoid scattering authorization

One of the problems with poorly designed systems is authorization logic appearing everywhere:

if (user.role === "admin") ...

inside controllers, services and repositories.

That becomes difficult to audit.

Authorization should instead have recognizable policy boundaries.

Final thought

RBAC remains valuable.

The lesson is not to abandon it.

The lesson is to recognize when the system has moved beyond simple role-based decisions.

Enterprise authorization often needs identity, role, resource and organizational context to make a correct decision.

title: Build a niche job board from 470,000 career-site jobs (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable) for $1.50 per 1,000
description:
Most job boards fill up with reposts, agency ads and stale listings. The cleanest source is the companies' own career sites. Thousands of startups and scale-ups publish every opening through an applicant tracking system (ATS) like Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Recruitee, Personio or Workable, and each of these offers a public job board API.

The catch is that every ATS has its own format, and you first need to know which companies use which ATS. This post shows a shortcut: one API call that searches the open jobs of thousands of companies at once.

The data

I index the public job boards of 12,000+ companies every day (about 470,000 open jobs right now) through the official job board APIs. Every job comes in one schema:

{
  "ats": "ashby",
  "company": "Ramp",
  "title": "Security Engineer, Cloud",
  "location": "New York, NY (HQ)",
  "locations": ["New York, NY (HQ)", "Remote (US)"],
  "workplaceType": "hybrid",
  "remote": true,
  "salaryMin": 211400,
  "salaryMax": 290600,
  "salaryCurrency": "USD",
  "postedAt": "2026-10-07T17:12:35.753Z",
  "url": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/...",
  "descriptionText": "About Ramp ..."
}

Salary ranges are surprisingly common, because Ashby, Lever and Recruitee expose them when the company publishes them (and pay-transparency laws keep pushing that up).

Search across all companies (Python)

The search runs as an Apify Actor, Career Site Jobs API. With a free Apify account token:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("digitalni.produkty.pro.zivot/ats-jobs").call(run_input={
    "titleKeywords": ["data engineer", "analytics engineer"],
    "locations": ["remote", "germany"],
    "postedWithinDays": 7,
    "maxJobs": 300,
})
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["postedAt"][:10], job["company"], "|", job["title"], "|", job["location"])

A search like this takes a few seconds, because it reads the daily index instead of calling 12,000 APIs. Descriptions are loaded live only for the jobs you get back.

A daily feed for your job board

For a niche board (remote, AI, climate, fintech, one country or city), schedule the same input once a day with Only new jobs turned on. Each run then returns only postings it hasn't returned before, so you can append them to your database or CMS without deduplication logic.

run = client.actor("digitalni.produkty.pro.zivot/ats-jobs").call(run_input={
    "titleKeywords": ["machine learning", "ml engineer", "ai engineer"],
    "remoteOnly": True,
    "onlyNewJobs": True,
    "monitorName": "ai-remote-board",
    "maxJobs": 500,  # caps the first run, which returns everything currently open
})

No-code works too: Apify has native Make, Zapier and n8n integrations, so new jobs can go straight to Airtable, Google Sheets, Webflow or Slack.

Tracking specific companies

If you care about a list of employers (sales prospecting, hiring signals, a "jobs at our portfolio companies" page), pass them directly. The ATS is detected automatically:

run = client.actor("digitalni.produkty.pro.zivot/ats-jobs").call(run_input={
    "companies": ["ramp", "notion", "https://boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb", "lever:palantir"],
})

Cost

$1.50 per 1,000 jobs returned, nothing per company or per run. A daily feed of 100 new jobs costs about $4.50 a month. Comparable career-site job APIs on the Apify Store charge about $2.50–12 per 1,000, depending on your plan (checked October 2026).

Limits, to be fair

  • Coverage is companies on these seven ATS platforms, mostly tech, startups and scale-ups. Big enterprises on Workday, SuccessFactors or iCIMS aren't included yet.
  • The index refreshes once a day. For minute-level freshness, track specific companies (company mode calls the APIs live).
  • Job descriptions are the employers' content: link back to the original posting, which is also where candidates apply.

Disclosure: I built and maintain this Actor. Questions, missing companies or ATS requests: open an issue on the Actor page. This post was written with AI assistance and the code was tested against the live Actor.

title: Compute a natal chart in the browser with astronomy-engine
description:
A natal chart here is a clock time and a place turned into angles. Ecliptic longitude of the Sun, Moon, and planets, and the longitude rising on the eastern horizon, are astronomy. The sentences written about character are entertainment. The terms in src/lib/legal.ts call the chart, the horoscope, and the tarot entertainment and reflection, and they say those pages are not medical, mental-health, legal, or financial advice.

The functions are in src/lib/astro.ts. package.json depends on astronomy-engine at ^2.1.19. signIndex wraps a longitude into [0, 360) and returns Math.floor(n / 30) % 12. SIGNS starts at Aries, so each sign is a 30° slice of ecliptic longitude. The chart page and the terms call that the tropical zodiac. The wheel counts whole-sign houses from the ascendant. Placidus cusps are a second list, empty when that system fails. The same file runs in the browser on the birth chart and on a Cloudflare Worker when a paid page needs the positions.

1. Turn the birth clock into UTC

The city sets the time zone. Copy in src/components/landings.tsx says the computer's clock does not. The form in src/components/birth-form.tsx submits only after a place is chosen ("Time zone comes from the city."). Ten CITIES rows carry latitude, longitude, and an IANA zone. A query of at least two characters also calls the Open-Meteo geocoding API, and a hit is kept only when it includes timezone.

Submit stores YYYY-MM-DD, 24-hour HH:MM, lat, lon, tz, and timeKnown. With the checkbox off, the clock is 12:00 and timeKnown is false. Hours are 1�12 plus AM/PM; (hour % 12) + (PM ? 12 : 0) turns 12 AM into 00 and 12 PM into 12.

computeChart calls zonedToUtc first. Incomplete numbers throw "Enter a complete birth date and time." That guard is left out of the snippet. The rest treats the civil fields as a UTC timestamp, formats that instant in the IANA zone, and adds the difference, at most four times.

export function zonedToUtc(date: string, time: string, timeZone: string): Date {
  const [y, m, d] = date.split("-").map(Number);
  const [hh, mm] = time.split(":").map(Number);
  const target = Date.UTC(y, m - 1, d, hh, mm, 0);
  let utc = target;
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
    timeZone,
    hourCycle: "h23",
    year: "numeric",
    month: "2-digit",
    day: "2-digit",
    hour: "2-digit",
    minute: "2-digit",
  });
  for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    const parts = Object.fromEntries(
      fmt.formatToParts(new Date(utc)).map((p) => [p.type, p.value]),
    );
    const asUtc = Date.UTC(
      Number(parts.year),
      Number(parts.month) - 1,
      Number(parts.day),
      Number(parts.hour) % 24,
      Number(parts.minute),
    );
    const delta = target - asUtc;
    if (delta === 0) break;
    utc += delta;
  }
  return new Date(utc);
}

From src/lib/astro.ts. hourCycle: "h23" is set, and the parsed hour is still taken modulo 24. The chart caption credits the city clock, including daylight saving. An unknown time passes "12:00", so the longitudes are local noon.

2. Read ecliptic longitude

longitudeOf covers Sun through Pluto. The Sun uses SunPosition(date).elon. The Moon uses EclipticGeoMoon(date).lon. The other bodies go through GeoVector and then Ecliptic. The third argument is the boolean true. norm folds the result into [0, 360).

function longitudeOf(id: string, date: Date): number {
  if (id === "sun") return norm(Astronomy.SunPosition(date).elon);
  if (id === "moon") return norm(Astronomy.EclipticGeoMoon(date).lon);
  const spec = BODIES.find((b) => b.id === id);
  if (!spec?.body) throw new Error(`Unknown body ${id}`);
  const ecl = Astronomy.Ecliptic(Astronomy.GeoVector(spec.body, date, true));
  return norm(ecl.elon);
}

From src/lib/astro.ts. BODIES sets Astronomy.Body for Mercury through Pluto. The sign is SIGNS[signIndex(lon)], and the degree inside the sign is the wrapped longitude modulo 30.

North node, Lilith, and Chiron come from extraPoints. Node and Lilith are polynomials in Julian centuries from julianCenturies. Chiron is a Kepler solve from perihelion Date.UTC(1996, 1, 14, 18, 6). The comment on chironLon says inclination is ignored, so the longitude is within a few degrees. Those three receive a house when timeKnown is true, and 0 otherwise.

3. Sidereal time, obliquity, and the ascendant

chartAt reads obliquity with Astronomy.e_tilt(Astronomy.MakeTime(when)).tobl and passes it to the ascendant and the midheaven. ramcDegrees starts from Astronomy.SiderealTime. Western longitudes in the city table are negative (New York is -74.006). Dividing by 15 converts degrees to hours.

function ramcDegrees(date: Date, lon: number): number {
  const gst = Astronomy.SiderealTime(date);
  const lst = gst + lon / 15;
  return norm(((lst % 24) + 24) % 24 * 15);
}

function ascendant(ramcDeg: number, latDeg: number, epsDeg: number): number {
  const ramc = (ramcDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
  const lat = (latDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
  const eps = (epsDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
  const y = Math.cos(ramc);
  const x = -(Math.sin(ramc) * Math.cos(eps) + Math.tan(lat) * Math.sin(eps));
  return norm((Math.atan2(y, x) * 180) / Math.PI);
}

From src/lib/astro.ts. midheaven is atan2(sin(RAMC), cos(RAMC) * cos(eps)), in degrees, then norm. Both angles are stored on the chart and as points asc and mc. The ascendant point is house 1. The midheaven uses houseOf.

4. Whole-sign houses

Whole-sign houses give the ascendant's sign to house 1 and each later sign to the next house.

export function houseOf(lon: number, asc: number): number {
  return ((signIndex(lon) - signIndex(asc) + 12) % 12) + 1;
}

From src/lib/astro.ts. chartAt sets every planet house with that call, so 1° and 29° of the rising sign share a house. The wheel draws twelve ticks at i * 30 and places them with polar: longitude equal to the ascendant has relative angle 0, SVG angle 180°, and sits on the left. The center label is whole sign.

If the time is unknown, signsThatDay samples the body at local 00:00 and 23:59. A sign change returns both names. The Moon cell joins them with " or " and prints an em dash for the degree.

5. Placidus, the 66° cutoff, and the fallback

Placidus cusps are unequal. placidusCusps returns twelve longitudes, index 0 for house 1, or null. The comment says null is for "above 66° where the system fails."

export function placidusCusps(date: Date, lat: number, lon: number): number[] | null {
  if (Math.abs(lat) > 66) return null;
  const tilt = Astronomy.e_tilt(Astronomy.MakeTime(date)).tobl;
  const ramc = ramcDegrees(date, lon);
  const find = (fraction: number) => {
    let best = 0;
    let err = 999;
    for (let trial = 0; trial < 3600; trial += 1) {
      const lambda = trial / 10;
      const eq = equatorial(lambda, tilt);
      const arc = diurnalArc(lat, eq.dec);
      if (arc == null) continue;
      const target = norm(ramc + fraction * arc);
      const gap = Math.abs(((eq.ra - target + 540) % 360) - 180);
      if (gap < err) {
        err = gap;
        best = lambda;
      }
    }
    return best;
  };

Trimmed from src/lib/astro.ts. Longitude steps by 0.1° (trial / 10, 3600 trials). equatorial turns a trial longitude into right ascension and declination. diurnalArc returns null when -tan(lat) * tan(dec) falls outside (-1, 1), and that trial is skipped. The winner is the smallest 0�180° gap between right ascension and RAMC + fraction * arc. best starts at 0, so a fraction whose trials are all skipped yields longitude 0.

The function then calls find(1/3), find(2/3), find(-1/3), and find(-2/3) for the eleventh, twelfth, ninth, and eighth cusps. The returned order, each value through norm, is ascendant, eighth+180, ninth+180, mc+180, eleventh+180, twelfth+180, asc+180, eighth, ninth, midheaven, eleventh, twelfth. Houses 1, 4, 7, and 10 are the angles. Math.abs(lat) > 66 means latitude 66 still searches and 66.1 returns null at once. placidusFor in src/components/added.tsx returns null for an unknown time before any search.

6. Browser and Worker

src/routes/_app/chart.tsx renders ChartView. Until a birth is submitted, the view calls computeChart(SAMPLE_BIRTH): Avery Chen, 1994-04-12 at 07:42 in Singapore (1.3521, 103.8198, Asia/Singapore, timeKnown: true). Submit replaces that chart in client state. The caption says "Positions from astronomy-engine. Tropical zodiac, whole-sign houses."

Paid text uses the same module on the server. paidBlocks in src/lib/paid.ts is a createServerFn that loads src/lib/paid.server.ts. blocksFor starts with computeChart(birth) and also calls progressedChart, solarReturn, and lunarReturn. src/lib/western.ts calls computeChart for the solar arc and the Saturn return.

wrangler.jsonc points main at ./src/worker.ts, names the worker astralhoro, sets nodejs_compat, and binds D1 as DB. Better Auth sessions live in that database (src/lib/auth/server.ts), and the auth client is built inside the request. Every fetch copies string env vars onto process.env. The www host and plain HTTP redirect to the apex HTTPS host. Requests that reach the app assign env.DB to globalThis.DB and call the TanStack Start entry.

npm run build:cf sets CLOUDFLARE_ENV=production before Vite. vite.config.ts loads @cloudflare/vite-plugin only then (environment name ssr). Without the variable the build uses Nitro's vercel preset.

AstralHoro serves those routes. Placement paragraphs are the entertainment the terms describe.

Gotchas

  • zonedToUtc stops after four corrections. A civil time in a daylight-saving gap can return an instant whose zone clock still differs from the typed numbers.
  • The wheel draws natalAspects at orb 4°. The prose list keeps orbs through 6° and omits angles to the ascendant or midheaven when the time is unknown.
  • birthOf in paid.server.ts rejects latitude outside [-90, 90] or longitude outside [-180, 180] before the server calls computeChart. The browser passes the chosen city's coordinates.

title: Agent Step Value: Auditing Evaluation-Channel Sensitivity in Black-Box Agent Traces
description:
arXiv:2607.04419v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reusing evaluator-derived step rewards across evaluation channels raises a measurement question: does the assigned direction remain stable? We define Agent Step Value (ASV) as a channel-indexed before/after target-margin gain and identify the state-by-channel interaction from a matched 2x2 design. Across frozen PubMed question-answering transitions, cross-channel gain signs disagree on 48.3% of comparisons, compared with 0.3% for same-channel retries. Transition interactions are nearly balanced in sign (median +0.014; 10% trimmed mean -0.033), but asymmetric negative magnitudes produce a positive direct mean and a negative generated-view mean under the empirical target mixture. Equal-target weighting preserves a negative mean interaction but not this strict mean reversal. Matched retrieval designs localize the negative component to the generated-view coordinate and retain its direction across three sign checks that vary readout and evaluator stack. In a matched 512-token source-contract follow-up, source-only generation restores the positive mean direction on artifact-bearing retrievals and removes parser-detected support claims from artifact-free before-state views. These results support an explanation in which generated support inflates the pre-retrieval baseline. The resulting audit can localize channel sensitivity and test an intervention before step rewards are reused.

title: SubQ Snap: The Hype, the Benchmarks, and the Reactions
description:
Seven points and one comment. That is what the SubQ Snap launch got on Hacker News, hours in. The comment was a question, and it was not friendly:

Doesn't OpenAI's decision API support up to 1M context on Luna?

On LinkedIn, the same launch hit 220 reactions and 39 comments in fourteen hours. "We launched a new model today!" read one company post. "Feels like Jev on steroids," read an early take being passed around on X.

Same product, same day, two crowds reading two different things.

i had to find out which crowd was right. So i read the launch post, the press release, and every third-party breakdown i could find. The short version: both crowds are right, and neither is fully.

SubQ Snap is a decision model from Subquadratic, a research shop that thinks attention is the real bottleneck. No text generation. You send context, a question, and allowed answers; it picks.

The pitch: up to 384K tokens of text and images in one call, a decision in about a second, and five cents per million input tokens. Output tokens are free.

The timing is the wild part. This is the sixth hosted decision model to ship in about three weeks, after Jev, Perplexity's Decider, Cloudflare's Clef, OpenAI's Decisions API, and Microsoft-Decision-1.

Why care? Because this is where the cost of agents gets decided. And the fight is not about the model.

What a decision model actually does

here's a question people always ask: why would you pay for a model that cannot write? A decision model is a narrow cousin of the LLM. Given context, a question, and a set of allowed answers, it returns a probability for each answer.

Nothing open ended.

That restriction is the whole trick. No generation means no token-by-token output to pay for. Scoring fixed answers is fast, and speed is the point, because an agent makes these calls constantly: which file matters, which tool to call next, did the test pass.

Subquadratic names four jobs for Snap:

  • routing
  • tool picking
  • checking
  • stopping

A clean list. And a list you can currently build with a regular LLM and careful prompts. Which is the part nobody in the press release mentions.

The context wall

what actually happens is the input, not the answer. The right next call might depend on a constraint from forty turns ago.

A function defined deep in a codebase. A clause on page nine of a contract.

Standard transformers pay quadratic attention. Double the context, quadruple the compute. That is why decision models stayed small.

Jev runs 64K per request, 32K of state. Microsoft's model runs 32K. They decide without seeing most of what matters.

Snap's answer is Subquadratic Sparse Attention, SSA. Linear cost instead of quadratic. So the model can read a whole repo or contract in one call.

Subquadratic says 100K tokens comes back in under a second. That number is theirs, unverified, no hardware named. But the architecture is genuine research, not a wrapper around someone else's API.

Benchmarks and their asterisks

most tutorials tell you to look at the chart. The chart is good.

Decision Index 0.2.1: 61.7 to 57.9. The long-document test: 74.0 to 48.0.

Snap leads on 13 of 16 enterprise tasks. Phishing detection jumps from 25.1 to 47.1. Code output prediction from 57.1 to 73.8.

But read the fine print. Every number is Subquadratic's own. No outside lab has run Snap.

The long-context tests are their adaptations of RULER and LCR. And the headline score, 96.3 on Decision RULER, runs at one million tokens. The product caps at 384K.

They published a benchmark the product cannot accept.

Snap also loses three of sixteen. The embarrassing one is When2Call, which tests whether to call a tool, ask, answer, or decline.

That is one of the four jobs Snap is sold for. It lost 67.0 to 74.6. The model that decides whether to act is not the best at that exact call.

The price war

the problem isn't the benchmarks at all. It's what the benchmarks are for. Look at the field:

Model Price per M input Context
Perplexity $0.04 ~262K
Microsoft-Decision-1 $0.042 32K
Jev $0.042 64K
SubQ Snap $0.05 384K
OpenAI (gpt-6-luna) $0.10 n/a
Cloudflare Clef $0.24 64K

Six models in three weeks. Prices sliding toward zero. Free token grants everywhere; Snap gives the first 10,000 users 100M tokens.

"Cents per decision" is the new marketing line.

That should make you suspicious in one specific way. When a market moves this fast, the model is not the moat.

The workflow is. The people who win own the routing logic, not a vendor relationship.

Meanwhile, the kidney cats

here's the thing that made me laugh during research. i searched Reddit for "subq snap" and the model was nowhere. i got forums about subcutaneous fluids for cats with kidney failure.

i got reviews of SNAP-8 peptide serum for wrinkles. i got a thread about a spring-loaded syringe you snap in place.

"subq" is medical shorthand for subcutaneous. The company named a product after a medical abbreviation and a snack brand's word, then launched it into an AI hype storm. For a while, anyone googling the model gets cat fluids and skincare advice.

i kind of love that. It keeps things honest. The hype lives on LinkedIn, with its 220 reactions and its CEO quote about "radically different ways to scale AI."

The messy internet still serves kidney cats and peptide talk. Every AI launch should have to compete with a cat forum for search traffic. It would keep the marketing humble.

The part nobody wants to hear

Most people do not need a decision model. Not yet. If your agent makes a few hundred calls a day, route with a cheap LLM and move on.

The complexity you add to save pennies is complexity you will maintain forever.

Even if you do need one, do not build on a public preview with a waitlist on day one. The model id is literally subq-snap-preview.

That is not a stability promise. That is a warning.

And the benchmarks? Treat them like a resume, not an audit. Everything is self-reported, compared against one rival, on tests the vendor adapted.

The moment an independent leaderboard runs Snap, the numbers will move. i would bet on that.

The one thing that would make me take Snap seriously is a real repo test. An agent that reads its own codebase, picks files, checks results, and hands me the bill. A week of that beats any chart in the launch post.

i'm still going to try it. 100M free tokens is hard to ignore, and that window is genuinely interesting. But i'll treat the ad copy as ad copy until i see it run.

i keep coming back to that Hacker News comment. Seven points, one question, and it cut through the entire launch in a single line. "Doesn't OpenAI's decision API support up to 1M context on Luna?"

That is this market in one sentence. The lead changes so fast that "first" is a memo, not a moat.

Snap is real engineering, SSA is not a wrapper, and 384K in under a second is genuinely interesting. And so was everyone else three weeks ago.

i'll be watching the independent benchmarks when they land. And checking on the kidney cats. One of those two will tell me more about decision models than the press release did.

title: NailFlow AI: A Local-First Studio Assistant for Nail Artists
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Running a small nail studio means doing two jobs: the creative work clients come for, and the admin that happens between appointments. NailFlow AI is a small assistant I built for independent nail artists and beauty studios to make that second job easier.

What I Built

NailFlow turns a service inquiry into a transparent price estimate and editable client-ready copy. It can prepare a WhatsApp reply, general aftercare notes, a follow-up message, and social content such as captions, stories, hashtags, and calls to action. A local client pipeline lets the artist save a quote and track it as Draft, Follow-up, or Done. The service menu can be edited to reflect the studio's own prices and session durations.

The idea is deliberately focused: independent artists shouldn't have to rewrite the same kinds of messages all day or guess at a price on every inquiry. NailFlow gives them a draft they can review and adapt, not an automation that speaks to a client without permission.

The quote itself is calculated in code from the artist's editable menu, design complexity, and selected add-ons. AI helps with wording; it does not decide the final price. Server-side guardrails normalize detected currency amounts to the computed estimate and neutralize some common false booking-confirmation claims. These safeguards reduce risk but are not perfect, so every message should still be reviewed before sending. NailFlow does not send messages or book appointments automatically.

Demo

Live web demo: https://nail-flow-ai-lemon.vercel.app/

The deployed Vercel version demonstrates the web interface and its template fallback. It is not connected to Ollama running on my computer, so the hosted demo should not be treated as proof of live Gemma inference.

I verified the local AI path on Windows with Ollama 0.35.0 and Gemma 3 1B: the model passed a direct prompt test, and NailFlow then generated a client pack marked LOCAL AI · Generated with local Ollama inference. The hosted Vercel demo remains separate and uses its template fallback; it does not connect to the Ollama service on my PC.

Code

Public repository: https://github.com/yagnik-satani-otelier/NailFlow-AI

How I Built It

NailFlow uses a dependency-free Node.js HTTP server, vanilla JavaScript, CSS, and browser localStorage. The local-AI path is designed to use Gemma 3 1B through Ollama. The browser calls the local Node server, which forwards a structured prompt to the Ollama API on the same machine. The model can be changed with the OLLAMA_MODEL environment variable.

The prompts, validation, output parsing, deterministic pricing, and post-generation quote guardrails are visible in lib/core.js and server.js. The server sends an explicit output schema to Ollama for each generation mode to improve structured responses from a small model. When Ollama or the model is unavailable, the interface clearly labels generated content as template fallback rather than pretending it came from AI.

To run the local AI path, install Ollama, then run these commands in the repository folder:

ollama pull gemma3:1b
npm run check
npm test
npm start

Open http://127.0.0.1:4174. Generate a sample client pack and confirm that the result says LOCAL AI. I verified this path locally; if a future run says TEMPLATE MODE, that request did not use Gemma.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a solo studio, a per-message AI bill or a dependency on a hosted writing API can make a small admin assistant less practical. Local inference can avoid a NailFlow-hosted inference service or API key, while letting the studio control its own service menu, prompts, and model choice. When run with Ollama on the same machine, enquiry text goes to that local Ollama service rather than to a hosted AI provider.

There is a trade-off: the user must install and run Ollama and download a model, and a small model can produce wording that needs editing. The hosted web demo is useful for seeing the interface, while local setup is necessary to demonstrate the Gemma path. Gemma is an open-weight model; open weights should not automatically be described as OSI-approved open-source software, and model terms should be reviewed separately.

What I Tested

  • Automated suite: 20 passing unit and HTTP integration tests covering input bounds, deterministic pricing, prompt constraints, quote guardrails, parsing, template fallback, a mocked Ollama bridge, and HTTP error/security cases.
  • Browser smoke test: with mocked generation responses, I checked in-place quote and content editing, saving a quote to the client pipeline, service-duration editing, and a 390px mobile layout without horizontal overflow.
  • Real local-AI smoke test: ran ollama run gemma3:1b successfully, then generated a NailFlow client pack locally with the visible LOCAL AI label. This confirms the live inference path works on my machine; a single smoke test does not establish that every output is correct.
  • Important limitation: automated HTTP integration tests use a mock Ollama server, not the actual Gemma weights. They validate the app's bridge and guardrails but do not prove general output quality.

I haven't run a customer trial yet, so I won't claim that a nail artist has paid for or adopted the tool. A useful next validation is to put it in front of one artist, observe a sample inquiry workflow, and use their feedback to improve it.

title: Quantum Vision Theory Applied to Audio Classification for Deepfake Speech Detection
description:
arXiv:2604.08104v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We propose Quantum Vision (QV) theory as a new perspective for deep learning-based audio classification, applied to deepfake speech detection. Inspired by particle-wave duality in quantum physics, QV theory is based on the idea that data can be represented not only in its observable, collapsed form, but also as information waves. In conventional deep learning, models are trained directly on these collapsed representations, such as images. In QV theory, inputs are first transformed into information waves using a QV block, and then fed into deep learning models for classification. QV-based models improve performance in image classification compared to their non-QV counterparts. What if QV theory is applied speech spectrograms for audio classification tasks? This is the motivation and novelty of the proposed approach. In this work, Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), Mel-spectrograms, and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) of speech signals are converted into information waves using the proposed QV block and used to train QV-based Convolutional Neural Networks (QV-CNN) and QV-based Vision Transformers (QV-ViT). Extensive experiments are conducted on the ASVSpoof dataset for deepfake speech classification. The results show that QV-CNN and QV-ViT consistently outperform standard CNN and ViT models, achieving higher classification accuracy and improved robustness in distinguishing genuine and spoofed speech. Moreover, the QV-CNN model using MFCC features achieves the best overall performance on the ASVspoof dataset, with an accuracy of 94.20% and an EER of 9.04%, while the QV-CNN with Mel-spectrograms attains the highest accuracy of 94.57%. These findings demonstrate that QV theory is an effective and promising approach for audio deepfake detection and opens new directions for quantum-inspired learning in audio perception tasks.

title: How GroundAnything Slashed Visual‑Grounding Latency by 7.5 – The Future of Real‑Time AR Shopping
description:
GroundAnything’s Parallel Decoding Shatters the Visual‑Grounding Speed Barrier

A Lightning‑Fast Lead

On 30 September 2026 three papers hit arXiv and Hugging Face at the same time, unveiling GroundAnything, LocateAnything, and Locate Anything in Videos. The authors replaced the legacy autoregressive token chain with a bidirectional diffusion engine that predicts boxes, masks, and relational graphs in parallel. In the first public benchmarks the new models run 0.12 s per image on a single A100—a 7.5× latency drop versus the best AR baselines—while keeping state‑of‑the‑art accuracy.

The release lands amid the 2026 “Flash‑Speed Multimodal” wave, where GPT‑4V‑Turbo, Gemini 2, and Claude‑3 already push vision‑language latency below 200 ms for simple classification. GroundAnything supplies the missing piece for real‑time visual grounding, the task that maps a free‑form textual phrase to a precise region in an image or video.

Real‑Time Product Search in an AR Shopping App

Imagine a shopper points a phone camera at a living‑room sofa and says, “Show me the same style in teal.” The app must:

  1. Transcribe the voice.
  2. Encode the phrase.
  3. Locate the sofa in the current frame.
  4. Retrieve catalog items that match the description.
  5. Overlay results on the live view.

Before GroundAnything the pipeline relied on an autoregressive grounding model such as MDETR‑V2. The model emitted the left‑top corner, waited for the next token, and repeated until it produced the right‑bottom coordinate. Each step required a full transformer pass, inflating per‑image latency to ≈ 0.9 s on an A100. The UI stalled, the shopper lost patience, and the app fell back to a static search result.

After GroundAnything the app swaps the AR decoder for the Parallel Box Decoder (PBD) from LocateAnything. In a single diffusion pass the model predicts all four box coordinates together, refines them across five diffusion steps, and returns a tight bounding box in 0.09 s. The app now stays within the 200 ms UI budget, updates the overlay instantly, and delivers a seamless AR experience.

The difference is not academic. A 0.8 s pause translates into a 30 % drop in conversion rate for e‑commerce apps, according to internal A/B tests at a major retailer. By slashing grounding latency to sub‑100 ms, GroundAnything removes that friction point entirely.

Hard Numbers That Matter

1. Speed Gains Across the Board

Metric Autoregressive Baseline GroundAnything Parallel Diffusion Relative Gain
Latency per image 0.90 s (8‑step AR) 0.12 s (5‑step diffusion) 7.5× faster
GPU utilization ~30 % (pipeline stalls) ~85 % (full‑batch compute) 2.8× higher
Batch scaling Linear up to batch = 8, then memory‑bound Near‑linear up to batch = 32 4× throughput
Energy per inference 1.8 kJ 0.4 kJ ≈ 4× lower
End‑to‑end latency (incl. tokenization & post‑processing) 1.10 s 0.18 s ≈ 6× overall

“GroundAnything reduces per‑image latency from 0.9 s to 0.12 s while keeping mAP‑box at 0.71 on RefCOCO‑g.” – Lead authors, 2026

2. Accuracy Holds Its Ground

Model mAP‑box (RefCOCO‑g) Video‑IoU (VidSTG) Recall@50 (Objects)
MDETR‑V2 (AR) 0.70 0.57 84 %
GroundAnything‑base 0.71 — 85 %
LocateAnything 0.73 — 87 %
Locate Anything in Videos — 0.58 —

The diffusion‑style decoder does not sacrifice precision. LocateAnything nudges mAP‑box up by 0.02 over the AR leader, thanks to its unified decoder that jointly optimizes boxes, masks, and relational tokens.

3. Hardware Footprint

  • A100 (40 GB) – 0.12 s per image, 5 diffusion steps, 2.3 GB VRAM.
  • RTX 4090 (24 GB) – 0.18 s per image, runs comfortably on a desktop inference server.
  • Edge TPU (8 GB) – 0.35 s per 30‑frame clip (Parallel Tube Decoding), enabling on‑device video grounding for smart cameras.

The authors paired the model with Flash‑Attention‑2 and a spatial‑grid bias that reduces the quadratic attention cost from O(N²) to O(N·√N) for high‑resolution feature maps. The result lets the diffusion steps run on a single GPU without spilling to CPU memory.

4. Open‑Source Ecosystem

All three releases ship as Apache‑2.0 repositories on Hugging Face, accompanied by:

  • Python SDK (groundanything, locateanything, video_grounding_pipeline) that wraps the diffusion loop in a single predict call.
  • Docker images pre‑installed with Flash‑Attention‑2 for one‑line deployment on cloud VMs.
  • ONNX export for LocateAnything, facilitating edge deployment on platforms that lack PyTorch support.

The open‑source stance eliminates licensing friction and invites rapid community extensions—fine‑tuning on domain‑specific catalogs, adding custom relation vocabularies, or integrating with multimodal LLMs via LoRA adapters.

Streamlined Risks & Open Questions

Issue Why It Matters Quick Mitigation
Diffusion instability on rare objects Can produce blurry or over‑smoothed boxes under unusual lighting or long‑tail categories. Add a lightweight “difficulty‑estimator” that dynamically decides whether to run the full five diffusion steps or exit early.
Memory pressure for 4K inputs > 10 GB VRAM needed for a single diffusion pass; many production servers run at 1080p. Use progressive‑resolution diffusion: start at 720p, refine at 1080p, and upscale to 4K only for high‑value queries.
Future multimodal LLM compatibility Upcoming models (e.g., Gemini 2) may use different tokenizers or cross‑modal attention layouts. Keep the diffusion core modular—accept arbitrary visual embeddings and provide adapters in the Hugging Face hub.
Potential misuse of open‑source checkpoints Bounding‑box predictions could be combined with generative models to create convincing forgeries. Embed a watermarking layer in the diffusion noise schedule so downstream detectors can flag synthetic grounding outputs.

These points are concise, focus on impact, and avoid drowning the reader in technical minutiae.

The Outlook: Where Parallel Decoding Heads Next

  1. Unified Multimodal Grounding – Teams are already testing a single diffusion pass that predicts image boxes, video tubes, and audio‑segment timestamps together. GroundAnything’s architecture is a natural scaffold for such cross‑modal hypothesis generation.

  2. Hardware‑Accelerated Diffusion – NVIDIA’s upcoming H100 Tensor Core includes a dedicated diffusion kernel that executes a full diffusion step in a single micro‑second. Pairing this with GroundAnything could push per‑image latency below 30 ms, finally matching human visual reaction time.

  3. Plug‑and‑Play LLM Integration – By exposing a grounding token stream (object‑id, box‑coords, mask‑mask) that LLMs can attend to, developers will enable chat‑style agents to reason about spatial relationships (“Is the red cup left of the laptop?”) without a separate grounding call.

  4. Edge‑First Commerce – Retailers plan to embed GroundAnything‑style models in smart mirrors and in‑store kiosks. The Apache‑2.0 license, sub‑100 ms latency, and modest memory footprint align perfectly with on‑premise inference constraints.

  5. Standardization Pressure – The MLCommons benchmark group is drafting a “Visual Grounding Latency” metric that penalizes serial decoding. GroundAnything’s parallel diffusion approach is poised to become the reference implementation for future leaderboards.

Closing Thoughts

GroundAnything, LocateAnything, and their video counterpart rewrite the performance equation for visual grounding. By treating grounding as a parallel evidence‑extraction problem rather than a left‑to‑right token stream, the authors achieve order‑of‑magnitude latency reductions while preserving—and in some cases improving—accuracy.

The releases arrive at a pivotal moment when real‑time vision‑language products demand sub‑200 ms response times. Developers can now embed grounding into AR assistants, e‑commerce visual search, and robotics pipelines without sacrificing user experience or inflating cloud costs.

Challenges remain—diffusion stability on rare inputs, memory scaling for 4K, and integration with the next generation of multimodal LLMs. Yet the open‑source nature of the releases, the clear modular design, and the early performance gains give the community a solid foundation to address those risks.

If the industry continues to prioritize throughput, energy efficiency, and developer accessibility, parallel diffusion will likely become the default paradigm for visual grounding. GroundAnything marks the first public step on that road, and the next few years should see a cascade of innovations built on its core ideas.

title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
description:
arXiv:2610.13644v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.
