title: Como consultar CPF via API em Node.js e Python
description:
Transparência: sou fundador da CPFHub, a API usada nos exemplos. Os conceitos (validação local, tratamento de erros, LGPD) valem para qualquer API de consulta de CPF.

Se você tem um formulário de cadastro, um checkout ou um backoffice no Brasil, cedo ou tarde precisa conferir se o CPF digitado existe e bate com o nome informado. Neste tutorial mostro como usar uma API de consulta de CPF em Node.js e Python: validar os dígitos localmente, fazer a consulta, tratar erros e decidir quando vale a pena consultar a Receita Federal em tempo real.

O que uma API de consulta de CPF retorna

Na consulta simples você envia o CPF e recebe os dados cadastrais básicos do titular:

  • nome completo (name e nameUpper, em maiúsculas, bom para comparar);
  • gênero (gender: "M", "F" ou null quando a base não tem a informação);
  • data de nascimento (birthDate no formato DD/MM/AAAA, mais day, month e year separados, úteis para calcular idade).

Exemplo de resposta (dados fictícios):

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "cpf": "12345678909",
    "name": "Fulano de Tal",
    "nameUpper": "FULANO DE TAL",
    "gender": "M",
    "birthDate": "15/06/1990",
    "day": 15,
    "month": 6,
    "year": 1990
  }
}

Passo 1: valide os dígitos antes de chamar a API

Todo CPF tem dois dígitos verificadores calculados pelo módulo 11. Validar isso localmente é gratuito, instantâneo e evita requisições inúteis (CPF digitado errado, tudo repetido como 111.111.111-11 etc.).

Node.js:

function cpfValido(entrada) {
  const cpf = String(entrada).replace(/\D/g, "");
  if (cpf.length !== 11 || /^(\d)\1{10}$/.test(cpf)) return false;

  const digito = (base) => {
    let soma = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < base.length; i++) {
      soma += Number(base[i]) * (base.length + 1 - i);
    }
    const resto = (soma * 10) % 11;
    return resto === 10 ? 0 : resto;
  };

  const d1 = digito(cpf.slice(0, 9));
  const d2 = digito(cpf.slice(0, 10));
  return d1 === Number(cpf[9]) && d2 === Number(cpf[10]);
}

Python:

import re

def cpf_valido(entrada: str) -> bool:
    cpf = re.sub(r"\D", "", str(entrada))
    if len(cpf) != 11 or cpf == cpf[0] * 11:
        return False

    def digito(base: str) -> int:
        soma = sum(int(n) * (len(base) + 1 - i) for i, n in enumerate(base))
        resto = (soma * 10) % 11
        return 0 if resto == 10 else resto

    return digito(cpf[:9]) == int(cpf[9]) and digito(cpf[:10]) == int(cpf[10])

Atenção: dígito válido não significa que o CPF existe ou pertence a quem digitou. Para isso serve a consulta.

Passo 2: consulta simples (GET)

Na CPFHub, a consulta simples é GET https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/{cpf}, autenticada pelo header x-api-key. O CPF pode ir com ou sem máscara. Custa 1 crédito por CPF encontrado; CPF não encontrado (404) não consome crédito. O tempo típico é de ~150 ms (tempo típico, não SLA), e a documentação recomenda timeout de cerca de 10 s.

Os erros que você deve tratar:

Status Significado O que fazer
400 CPF sem 11 dígitos Corrigir, não repetir
401 API Key ausente ou inválida Conferir o header x-api-key
403 Créditos esgotados ou conta bloqueada Recarregar créditos, não repetir
404 CPF não encontrado na base Resultado normal
422 Dígito verificador inválido Corrigir, não repetir
429 Limite por minuto (30/min no padrão) Esperar o header Retry-After
500/503 Falha passageira Repetir com espera crescente

Um detalhe: em erros de autenticação o campo error vem como string; nos demais, como objeto com message. Leia os dois formatos.

Node.js (18+, fetch nativo):

const API_KEY = process.env.CPFHUB_API_KEY; // nunca no front-end

async function consultarCpf(cpf) {
  if (!cpfValido(cpf)) throw new Error("CPF inválido (dígitos)");

  const res = await fetch(`https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/${cpf.replace(/\D/g, "")}`, {
    headers: { "x-api-key": API_KEY },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
  });
  const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
  const msg = typeof body.error === "string" ? body.error : body.error?.message;

  if (res.ok) return body.data;
  if (res.status === 404) return null; // não encontrado, sem custo
  if (res.status === 429) {
    throw new Error(`Limite por minuto; tente em ${res.headers.get("retry-after")} s`);
  }
  if (res.status === 403) throw new Error(`Sem créditos ou conta bloqueada: ${msg}`);
  throw new Error(`Erro ${res.status}: ${msg}`);
}

const dados = await consultarCpf("123.456.789-09");
console.log(dados?.name, dados?.gender, dados?.birthDate);

Python (requests):

import os
import requests

API_KEY = os.environ["CPFHUB_API_KEY"]

def consultar_cpf(cpf: str):
    if not cpf_valido(cpf):
        raise ValueError("CPF inválido (dígitos)")

    numero = "".join(c for c in cpf if c.isdigit())
    r = requests.get(
        f"https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/{numero}",
        headers={"x-api-key": API_KEY},
        timeout=10,
    )
    try:
        body = r.json()
    except ValueError:
        body = {}
    err = body.get("error")
    msg = err if isinstance(err, str) else (err or {}).get("message")

    if r.ok:
        return body["data"]
    if r.status_code == 404:
        return None  # não encontrado, sem custo
    if r.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Limite por minuto; tente em {r.headers.get('Retry-After')} s")
    if r.status_code == 403:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Sem créditos ou conta bloqueada: {msg}")
    raise RuntimeError(f"Erro {r.status_code}: {msg}")

dados = consultar_cpf("123.456.789-09")
if dados:
    print(dados["name"], dados["gender"], dados["birthDate"])

Se o timeout estourar do seu lado, lembre que a consulta pode ter sido concluída e cobrada no servidor; repetir cobra de novo.

Passo 3: consulta em tempo real na Receita Federal (POST)

Quando você precisa da situação cadastral ou de um comprovante, use POST https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/realtime. Ela consulta a Receita Federal no momento da chamada e exige CPF + data de nascimento (DD/MM/AAAA ou DDMMAAAA). Custa 1,5 crédito por consulta bem-sucedida, em qualquer situação cadastral. O tempo típico é de cerca de 1 segundo (não é SLA), mas a documentação pede timeout de pelo menos 60 s.

A resposta traz name, birthDate, situation (REGULAR, PENDENTE DE REGULARIZAÇÃO, SUSPENSA, CANCELADA, NULA ou TITULAR FALECIDO), deathYear e, quando disponíveis, controlCode, emissionDate, emissionTime, validationUrl (conferência no site da Receita) e validationHtmlUrl (comprovante).

Sobre deathYear: o campo sempre vem, como inteiro ou null. null significa que não há óbito registrado (ou o valor recebido era inválido). Não trate null como prova de que a pessoa está viva. E só REGULAR indica CPF sem pendências.

Node.js:

async function consultarReceita(cpf, dataNascimento) {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/realtime", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-api-key": API_KEY, "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ cpf, birthDate: dataNascimento }),
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(60_000),
  });
  const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
  if (res.ok) return body.data; // { situation, deathYear, controlCode, ... }
  // 422: dígito inválido ou a Receita recusou (ex.: data divergente) — sem custo
  // 429: 5/min no padrão; 502/503: repetir com espera crescente — sem custo
  const msg = typeof body.error === "string" ? body.error : body.error?.message;
  throw new Error(`Erro ${res.status}: ${msg}`);
}

Python:

def consultar_receita(cpf: str, data_nascimento: str):
    r = requests.post(
        "https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/realtime",
        headers={"x-api-key": API_KEY},
        json={"cpf": cpf, "birthDate": data_nascimento},
        timeout=60,
    )
    body = r.json() if r.content else {}
    if r.ok:
        return body["data"]
    err = body.get("error")
    msg = err if isinstance(err, str) else (err or {}).get("message")
    raise RuntimeError(f"Erro {r.status_code}: {msg}")

d = consultar_receita("12345678909", "15/06/1990")
print(d["situation"], d["deathYear"])

Duas cautelas: o POST não é idempotente, então depois de um timeout local confira o saldo em GET /quota antes de repetir; e o link validationHtmlUrl é público (abre nome, CPF e situação), então guarde-o só no back-end e fora dos logs.

Quando usar cada consulta

  • Simples (1 crédito): confirmar nome, gênero e idade no cadastro ou checkout. Rápida e barata.
  • Tempo real (1,5 crédito): quando você precisa da situação cadastral na Receita ou de um comprovante (crédito, contratos, cadastro regulado).
  • Lote (POST /cpf/bulk, 1 crédito por CPF encontrado): listas de até 10.000 CPFs, processadas em segundo plano — por exemplo, higienizar uma base antiga.

O plano gratuito inclui 50 créditos por mês, sem cartão, o que dá para testar tudo isso. Detalhes de cada endpoint estão na documentação da CPFHub.

LGPD: consulte com finalidade

CPF e data de nascimento são dados pessoais. Antes de integrar qualquer API de consulta de CPF:

  • tenha uma finalidade legítima e uma base legal (ex.: execução de contrato, prevenção a fraude no cadastro);
  • não guarde mais do que precisa: se só precisa saber se o nome confere, guarde o resultado da checagem, não a resposta inteira;
  • mantenha a API Key e as respostas no back-end, e não registre CPFs completos em logs.

Bônus: consulta de CPF por agentes de IA (MCP)

Se você usa Claude, Cursor ou outro cliente MCP, a CPFHub tem um servidor MCP remoto em https://api.cpfhub.io/mcp (autenticado pelo mesmo x-api-key), com as tools lookup_cpf, lookup_cpf_realtime e get_quota_info. Para clientes sem suporte a HTTP existe o pacote local @cpfhub/mcp (via npx), que hoje só tem lookup_cpf funcionando.

Resumo

  1. Valide os dígitos localmente.
  2. Use a consulta simples para nome, gênero e data de nascimento.
  3. Use a consulta em tempo real quando precisar da situação cadastral na Receita.
  4. Trate 404 como resultado normal, respeite 429 e não repita POST depois de timeout.
  5. Colete e guarde só o necessário.

Para testar, crie uma conta gratuita em cpfhub.io e gere sua chave. Dúvidas sobre a consulta CPF via API? Deixe nos comentários.

title: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents can execute increasingly complex tasks, but effective assistance also requires aligning their actions with goals and constraints that users may leave unstated. We study this problem as interactive intent alignment through clarification. Yet clarification is useful only when the agent can turn the answer into better decisions. As training changes how the agent handles incomplete information and uses additional answers, the same clarification can become more or less useful. We introduce CLEAT (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training), a framework that co-trains a clarification-value controller and the task policy from shared interaction outcomes. We formulate residual query value to measure the task utility gained by asking rather than proceeding under the current policy, and estimate it through paired rollouts from the same interaction history. These paired returns train the controller to predict clarification value and the task policy to select useful questions and act on the answers. The controller guides subsequent rollout collection, while outcomes from the updated agent provide new value labels that allow clarification guidance to adapt as the agent learns. With Qwen3-4B, CLEAT achieves the highest mean score in all ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks. Gains over the strongest baseline reach 13.2 and 6.5 percentage points on UserGym Travel and IN3 underspecification judgment accuracy, respectively. Ablations show that co-training improves the task policy even when the controller is removed at inference, while adapting clarification guidance to the evolving policy yields further gains.

title: CRM: Retrieval Model with Controllable Condition
description:
arXiv:2412.13844v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Retrieval models for recommendation need to account for outcomes such as watch time while searching large item corpora efficiently. We present the Controllable Retrieval Model (CRM), an outcome-conditioned retrieval framework that adds watch time as an input to the user tower. During training, CRM learns to predict the next item given its observed watch time; at inference, we supply a desired watch time to steer retrieval without retraining. The item tower is independent of the condition, so item embeddings can still be precomputed and indexed for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. We implement CRM as both a DNN-based two-tower model and a Decision Transformer. The Transformer interleaves item tokens with watch-time-to-go condition tokens, using the target watch time as a numerical prompt for next-item prediction. For each online request, we choose between the average and maximum watch times in the user's recent history as the condition. CRM is deployed in Kuaishou's short-video recommendation system, which serves over 400 million users. Online A/B tests show video watch time improvements of 0.372% in Kuaishou and 0.457% in Kuaishou Lite.

title: TanStack Start + TanStack Query: Sharing Data Between Loaders and Components
description:
TanStack Start + TanStack Query: Sharing Data Between Loaders and Components

One thing I like about TanStack Start is how naturally TanStack Router and TanStack Query fit together.

A route loader can fetch data before rendering. A component can read that data through useQuery. With shared query options, both can use the same cache instead of maintaining separate data-fetching logic.

But there is another piece to consider: the HTTP client.

How do you handle typed responses, authentication, request cancellation, SSR headers, and errors without duplicating the same logic across loaders and components?

That's where I use tanstack-fetch, an independent HTTP client designed to work with the TanStack Query mental model.

In this guide, we'll connect TanStack Router, TanStack Query, and tanstack-fetch, then look at SSR, mutations, SSE, tRPC, and migration.

The core idea

Keep three responsibilities separate:

  • TanStack Router: navigation and route-level loading.
  • TanStack Query: server-state caching, synchronization, and invalidation.
  • tanstack-fetch: HTTP requests, typed responses, errors, and request-level behavior.

The goal is simple: don't create one fetching strategy for loaders and another for components.

1. Install the dependencies 

npm install tanstack-fetch @tanstack/react-query @tanstack/react-router

2. Define reusable query options

Start by defining the query once. Both the loader and the component can reuse it.

// queries/users.ts
import { queryOptions } from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { api } from '~/lib/api'

export const usersQueryOptions = queryOptions({
  queryKey: ['users'],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
    api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal }),
})

Notice the signal parameter.

TanStack Query provides an AbortSignal to the query function. Passing it to the HTTP client allows the request to be cancelled when appropriate.

This is one small detail that is easy to miss when implementing data fetching manually.

3. Put QueryClient in router context

The router needs access to the same QueryClient used by your React application.

// router.tsx
import {
  createRouter,
} from '@tanstack/react-router'
import {
  QueryClient,
  QueryClientProvider,
} from '@tanstack/react-query'

export const queryClient = new QueryClient()

export const router = createRouter({
  routeTree,
  context: {
    queryClient,
  },
  Wrap: ({ children }) => (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      {children}
    </QueryClientProvider>
  ),
})

This illustrates the wiring. In a production TanStack Start application, follow the framework's SSR setup and create request-scoped server state where required rather than sharing a mutable server-side QueryClient between users.

4. Load data before rendering

Now the route loader can populate the Query cache.

// routes/users.tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router'
import { usersQueryOptions } from '~/queries/users'

export const Route = createFileRoute('/users')({
  loader: ({ context }) =>
    context.queryClient.ensureQueryData(
      usersQueryOptions,
    ),

  component: UsersPage,
})

function UsersPage() {
  const { data } = useQuery(usersQueryOptions)

  return (
    <ul>
      {data?.map((user) => (
        <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

The loader and component share the same query definition.

ensureQueryData ensures that cached data is available, fetching it when the query has no cached result. If you also need to revalidate stale data before continuing, consider ensureQueryData with revalidateIfStale or an appropriate prefetch strategy, depending on your desired navigation behavior.

This gives you a clear separation of responsibilities: the router coordinates loading, Query owns the cache, and the component subscribes to it.

5. Configure the HTTP client for SSR

Server-side rendering introduces another concern: requests may need headers or cookies from the incoming request.

Here's a simplified client configuration:

// lib/api.ts
import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'

export const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl:
    typeof window === 'undefined'
      ? `${process.env.SSR_ORIGIN ?? ''}/api`
      : '/api',

  source:
    typeof window === 'undefined'
      ? 'ssr'
      : 'browser',

  plugins:
    typeof window === 'undefined'
      ? ['ssr-forward']
      : [],
})

This is an illustrative configuration. Verify the ssr-forward plugin's setup against your version of tanstack-fetch and the headers available in your server request context. Forward only the headers your application needs.

For nested routes, the same pattern applies:

userQueryOptions(params.userId)

Use the resulting options in both the loader and the component. When routes have dependent data requirements, use route-level prefetching and carefully designed query dependencies to avoid unnecessary waterfalls.

6. Handle mutations with the same cache

Mutations should invalidate the same Query cache that loaders and components use.

const mutation = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (input: CreateUserInput) =>
    api.post<User>('/users', {
      body: input,
    }),

  onSuccess: () =>
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({
      queryKey: ['users'],
    }),
})

After a successful mutation, Query can refetch the affected data according to its invalidation and observer behavior.

You don't need a separate cache invalidation mechanism just because the initial request happened in a route loader.

7. Authentication and token refresh

Authentication is another place where HTTP logic tends to get duplicated.

An HTTP client can centralize token retrieval and refresh behavior rather than implementing it separately in every query function.

For example, tanstack-fetch provides a refresh-token interceptor:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'
import {
  createRefreshTokenInterceptor,
} from 'tanstack-fetch/plugins'

const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: '/api',
  getToken: () =>
    localStorage.getItem('access_token'),
})

api.use(
  'refresh-token',
  createRefreshTokenInterceptor({
    refresh: async () => {
      // Refresh the access token using your
      // application's refresh endpoint.
    },
  }),
)

The refresh implementation depends on your authentication flow and the installed package version. Configure the interceptor using the documented options for your version.

For production applications, consider concurrent refreshes, retry limits, refresh-token rotation, and what should happen when refreshing fails. Avoid using localStorage for credentials if your security model requires an HttpOnly cookie-based session.

The benefit of centralizing this behavior is that individual query functions can focus on retrieving data instead of repeating authentication logic.

8. Add live updates with Server-Sent Events

Not every screen is a good fit for request-and-response fetching.

Dashboards, notifications, and live status pages may need server-pushed updates. Browser EventSource does not support arbitrary Authorization headers, which can complicate authenticated SSE connections.

The tanstack-fetch/sse entry point provides a fetch-based alternative.

import { useSse } from 'tanstack-fetch/sse'

Use the documented useSse API in a client-side route component for the stream, while keeping initial data loading in your normal Query-based loader.

A practical division is:

  • Load the initial state through a REST or tRPC query.
  • Subscribe to updates through SSE.
  • Update the relevant Query cache or invalidate queries when events arrive.
  • Close the stream when the component no longer needs it.

A reconnect alone doesn't guarantee that no events were missed. If your application needs reliable resumption, design the server protocol around event IDs, replay, and recovery.

9. What about tRPC?

If your application already uses tRPC, you don't necessarily need a separate HTTP transport strategy for every feature.

TanStack Start has established integration patterns using createTRPCOptionsProxy and router context.

See the tanstack-fetch TanStack Start tRPC guide for the integration details.

The important architectural principle remains the same: keep transport concerns separate from query caching and route orchestration.

10. What does tanstack-fetch actually simplify?

The benefit isn't that raw fetch is bad. For a small application with a few requests, it may be all you need.

The difference becomes more relevant as an application grows.

Concern Raw fetch tanstack-fetch
HTTP requests Built in Built-in
Typed application responses Define your own conventions Typed client API
HTTP error handling Implement your own checks FetchError-based handling
Query cancellation Pass the signal manually Integrate through the query function
Token refresh Implement your own flow Refresh interceptor available
SSE Build your own integration Dedicated SSE entry point
Router and Query integration Compose the pieces yourself Reuse the same client in query options

These are architectural trade-offs, not benchmark results. Your application's actual complexity will depend on the features you need and how consistently your existing code handles them.

11. Migrate incrementally

You don't have to rewrite every request to adopt this approach.

Start with one route that currently fetches data in its loader.

  1. Move the request into a reusable queryOptions definition.
  2. Replace the loader request with ensureQueryData.
  3. Read the same query through useQuery.
  4. Pass Query's signal to the HTTP request.
  5. Move repeated HTTP behavior into your client configuration.

You can also explore the migration CLI:

npx tanstack-fetch migrate \
  --from fetch \
  --framework react \
  --write

npx tanstack-fetch doctor --dir ./src

Review generated changes before committing them, especially around authentication, error handling, and SSR behavior.

12. Suggested project structure

A simple structure can keep the boundaries clear:

src/
  lib/
    api.ts
  queries/
    users.ts
  router.tsx
  routes/
    users.tsx
    users.$id.tsx

You can introduce additional modules for authentication, mutations, and live subscriptions as the application grows. There's no need to add abstractions before the codebase needs them.

Final thoughts

TanStack Start, TanStack Router, and TanStack Query already provide a strong foundation for server-rendered React applications.

The pattern I find most useful is to let each layer do one job:

  • Router coordinates when route data is needed.
  • Query manages cached server state.
  • The HTTP client centralizes transport behavior.

tanstack-fetch is an independent open-source project built around that approach. It isn't an official TanStack package, and you don't need it to use TanStack Start. It is an option worth evaluating when typed HTTP requests, shared transport behavior, authentication, or SSE become recurring concerns in your application.

Explore the documentation: tanstack-fetch.

If you're using TanStack Start in production, I'd be interested to hear how you handle request-scoped Query clients, SSR authentication, and cache reuse between loaders and components.

title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
description:
arXiv:2610.13247v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. The correlation does not show what the judge responds to: the music, the text prompt, or the way the question is asked. We propose four probes that test each of these, three of them read against a control computed from the human ratings: removing the audio, replacing the clip with another model's clip for the same prompt, swapping the order of two clips in pairwise judging, and rewording the instruction. We apply them to five open judges on all 2,748 clips of MusicEval, and the last two to the SongEval songs. Without audio, no judge exceeds what the prompt alone predicts from the human ratings, and for prompt alignment every judge falls below it. With audio, every judge follows the clip it hears when rating prompt alignment, two do when rating musical quality, and the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts' alignment rating more than their quality rating. The pairwise verdicts of the four smaller judges follow the position of a clip in the pair (its slot) rather than its quality on both rating sets. For musical quality, rewording the instruction moves the correlation of most judges as much as changing the judge. MusicEval's prompt assignment bounds any prompt-only judge at the model level. We recommend reporting the four probes with every music judge.

title: Towards the Roof of the World: NLP Progress in Tibetan Languages
description:
arXiv:2610.13398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tibetan, spoken by some seven million people on and around the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, remains underrepresented in natural language processing (NLP). We present, to our knowledge, the first peer-reviewed systematic bibliometric survey of Tibetan NLP: 140 publications from 2004 to 2026 in the ACL Anthology and DBLP, annotated for venue type, research area, first-affiliation country, and resource release. Output has grown rapidly, with 84% of the publications appearing since 2018, and has expanded bottom-up along the NLP pipeline, from corpora and word segmentation through script, speech, and applications to large language models (LLMs). Researchers based in China first-authored 87% of the publications, which span all 25 represented research areas, whereas work from other countries concentrates on Classical Tibetan. We argue that this full-pipeline paradigm, realized under the compounded constraints of a complex script, dialectal diversity, and geographic remoteness, offers a reference model for other low-resource languages of the Global South. We also identify gaps in dialect coverage, responsible NLP, native and comparable evaluation, cross-community visibility, and resource release (only 29% of the publications release data, code, or models), and recommend open science, shared standards, and community participation for the LLM era.

title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL?
description:
arXiv:2610.13197v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP

title: Specify interactive explanations as inputs, state and checks
description:
An interactive explanation needs a small behavioral specification. Naming the inputs, the state and a few checks gives a developer something more precise to build or review than a request for an attractive interface.

This article was generated with AI assistance and source verification. The code below is an original, deterministic example. It does not claim that a particular ChatGPT account produced or supports a particular interface.

Start with one task

Consider a study planner that offers 25, 45 or 90 minutes. Its job is to divide the chosen time into warmup, practice and recall, while keeping completion marks separate from the time allocation. The independent Intelligent UI field guide provides prompt ideas and an original browser demo as reference points. Its own demo is labelled as a site demo, rather than a verified ChatGPT output.

For an original example, keep warmup at five minutes and recall at ten. Practice gets the remaining minutes. These are design choices for this example, not an experimentally established learning schedule.

export function allocate(minutes) {
  if (![25, 45, 90].includes(minutes)) {
    throw new RangeError('Choose 25, 45 or 90 minutes.');
  }
  return { warmup: 5, practice: minutes - 15, recall: 10 };
}

Separate input state from completion state

The selected duration determines the allocation. A checked task records an action by the user. Checking a box should not silently change the duration or claim that the topic has been learned. Resetting completion marks should not erase the selected duration unless the reset action says it does.

Keeping those relationships explicit makes a generated interface easier to evaluate. A slider, radio group or select box can represent the same input; the behavior matters before the visual treatment.

Check totals, boundaries and rejected inputs

For each permitted duration, all three blocks must be nonnegative and their sum must equal the selected duration. Check the smallest and largest values, then an unsupported value. Do not silently accept 40 minutes when the specification offers only three choices.

for (const minutes of [25, 45, 90]) {
  const plan = allocate(minutes);
  const total = Object.values(plan).reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0);
  if (total !== minutes) throw new Error('Incorrect time total');
  if (Object.values(plan).some(value => value < 0)) {
    throw new Error('Negative time block');
  }
}

These checks verify this allocation function. They do not test an entire browser interface, a model response or the learning outcome of the schedule. Add separate checks for labels, controls, completion marks and reset behavior when implementing an actual interface.

State the expected feedback in the prompt

An original prompt could ask for a planner that uses only the three durations, explains the allocation formula and shows the total beside the controls. Ask it to keep unknowns explicit and to avoid treating task completion as proof of understanding.

OpenAI's prompt-engineering documentation explains that generated content can vary. Inspect the response you receive against the behavior you specified. An interface sketch is a starting point for that review, rather than evidence that the checks passed.

Published under Carl Sagen's authorization for IntelligentUI. Source information checked October 11, 2026. No account-specific feature availability or firsthand model-output experiment is claimed.

title: Building a High-Throughput Cashless Payment & RFID Ticketing System for Saudi Mega-Events
description:
When engineering the infrastructure for an event ticketing and management system in Saudi Arabia, the physical reality of the venue dictates the software architecture.

Under the Saudi Vision 2030 events strategy, mega-summits in Riyadh and Jeddah frequently process upwards of 10,000 delegates. These environments are hostile to standard cloud-dependent web applications:

  1. Network Saturation: Cellular towers congest and venue Wi-Fi degrades under massive attendee density.
  2. Fragmented Stacks: Venues traditionally run three isolated systems—one API for ticketing, a separate local database for gate turnstiles, and independent POS terminals for food/merchandise.
  3. High Concurrency Peaks: 80% of gate entries and 60% of F&B purchases happen in tight 30-to-45-minute windows (e.g., morning ingress and keynote breaks).

To eliminate venue queues and financial reconciliation errors, we built a unified, edge-resilient architecture that merges secure ticketing, RFID attendee tracking, and cashless event payments into a single cryptographic smart credential.

Here is how we architected the system to guarantee sub-second gate scans and offline-resilient financial transactions.

1. The Unified Credential: UHF RFID + NFC

Instead of relying on fragile optical QR codes that require line-of-sight scanning, the foundation of the system is a physical smart badge or RFID wristband.

When a delegate arrives, their digital ticket triggers an on-demand thermal print cycle (sub-3 seconds). Simultaneously, an integrated encoder writes an encrypted payload to a dual-frequency inlay:

  • UHF EPC Gen 2 (865–868 MHz): Used for passive, zero-contact spatial tracking. Overhead portals read these tags at distances up to 8 meters to monitor civil defense hall capacities and VIP dwell times without requiring the user to stop.
  • HF NFC (13.56 MHz / ISO 14443): Used for deliberate, secure intent actions—specifically, tapping to pay at a vendor terminal or tapping to open a restricted ministerial lounge door.

2. Edge-First Gate & POS Architecture (SQLite WAL)

If a vendor's Point-of-Sale (POS) terminal requires a round-trip HTTP request to a cloud server to verify a wristband's wallet balance, the transaction will inevitably fail when venue Wi-Fi drops.

To achieve guaranteed sub-second tap-to-pay transactions, we decoupled the physical read layer from the wide-area network. Both our gate controllers and vendor POS devices act as autonomous edge nodes.

Local Persistence with Write-Ahead Logging

Each edge terminal runs an embedded SQLite database configured for high-concurrency appends:


sql
-- POS Edge Node Initialization
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS local_transactions (
    txn_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    wallet_uid TEXT NOT NULL,
    vendor_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount INTEGER NOT NULL, -- Stored in base currency units (Halalas)
    epoch_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
    sync_state INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);
When an attendee taps their wristband to purchase a coffee, the NFC reader validates the cryptographically signed wallet balance directly from the chip's secure memory sector. 

The ledger deduction is written to the local SQLite WAL companion file in under 4 milliseconds.

A background Go daemon continuously monitors network health and asynchronously flushes committed transactions to the central cloud API when connectivity permits.

3. High-Throughput Ingestion Pipeline (Go & Redis)When network connectivity is stable, hundreds of edge portals and POS terminals continuously stream telemetry and financial ledgers to the central cloud.

To prevent our primary PostgreSQL relational database from locking under heavy concurrent writes, we use Redis Streams as a high-speed ingestion buffer.   Our Go ingestion gateway handles incoming TCP payloads and pushes them to Redis in memory:Gopackage main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "[github.com/redis/go-redis/v9](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/v9)"
)

var ctx = context.Background()
var rdb *redis.Client

type CashlessTxn struct {
    TxnID    string `json:"txn_id"`
    Wallet   string `json:"wallet"`
    Amount   int    `json:"amount"` // Halalas
    VendorID string `json:"vendor_id"`
    EpochMS  int64  `json:"epoch"`
}

func ingestTransaction(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var txn CashlessTxn
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&txn); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    // Push to in-memory Redis Stream buffer
    err := rdb.XAdd(ctx, &redis.XAddArgs{
        Stream: "stream:cashless_transactions",
        Values: map[string]interface{}{
            "txn_id": txn.TxnID,
            "wallet": txn.Wallet,
            "amount": txn.Amount,
            "vendor": txn.VendorID,
            "epoch":  txn.EpochMS,
        },
    }).Err()

    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "Ingestion Failed", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
}
4. Live Financial & Spatial Command DashboardsA worker pool consumes the Redis Streams, applying deduplication (based on TxnID) and writing the settled records to TimescaleDB for permanent storage.

Simultaneously, the workers compute rolling 60-second aggregations and broadcast them via WebSockets to our KSA custom reporting dashboards.

This provides event operations teams with real-time, actionable intelligence:Live Vendor Settlements: Financial controllers can monitor live POS revenue across the entire exhibition floor, tracking exact spending velocity without waiting for end-of-day batch processing.

Civil Defense Density Adherence: Security teams receive immediate alerts if passive UHF portals detect that a specific keynote hall is nearing its municipal capacity limit.

Architecting for Scale in the GCCBy unifying ticketing, spatial tracking, and digital wallets into a single edge-resilient architecture, we eliminate the physical queues and data silos that plague legacy event operations.

If you are developing solutions for physical venues or exploring hardware-integrated fintech, review the deployment models powering StampIQ's cashless payments for events and their enterprise event registration platform

title: Orientation Slots Are the Only Writable Region on a Reference Page
description:
Reference documentation stays trustworthy when interface facts are extracted and locked before any model writes orientation prose around them. A block-role manifest records that split before drafting starts, so review does not depend on catching invented flags by eye. Deterministic extraction owns signatures, flags, environment variables, and error codes, while the model may fill only marked orientation slots. The checker later in this article fails the page when drafted prose names an interface token that the locked inventory does not contain.

Models that draft reference pages often smooth over a missing row by inventing a plausible flag, status, or default value. That failure is different from a weak explanation, because the sentence looks fluent while the contract itself is false. Full-page review does not scale once several endpoints share one pull request and each page mixes tables with narrative. A role tag on every block makes the allowed draft surface small enough for a script to check without rereading tables.

Heading-level ownership is not enough when one heading contains both a generated flag table and a paragraph of advice. The unit of control here is the block, not the file and not the heading, because those larger units hide mixed authority. A style promise about tone also does not stop a model from adding a flag that no release ever shipped. The manifest therefore names concrete tokens, and the checker compares drafted sentences against that closed token set.

What the model may draft

The model may draft orientation slots that explain sequencing, prerequisites in plain language, and common misreadings of a locked row. Those slots may compare two documented flags only when both flags already appear in the inventory for that page. The model may also propose a short note about when not to call the operation, if every concrete token is already listed. Generic words such as request, client, and retry stay allowed, while product-specific tokens must be listed before any draft.

Orientation text should use a surface from the locked row rather than restating the default, the type, or the status code. Restating those fields creates a second source of truth that will drift on the next release even if the first draft was careful. If a sentence needs a default, the page should render that default from the inventory, not from the drafted paragraph. The drafting prompt should receive slot ids and allowed surfaces, not the unfinished page as a free-form writing canvas.

What a human must own

A human must own the inventory source, whether that source is an OpenAPI document, a captured help file, or an error catalog. A human must own status mappings, default values, deprecation markers, and the decision that a given token is public. A human must approve each orientation slot before it exists, because an extra slot is an extra place to invent scope. A human must also merge extracted tables into the page, so a model cannot rewrite a locked block while polishing nearby prose.

Ownership is not the same thing as typing every sentence that a reader eventually sees on the published page. A human can delegate extraction to a script, then review the inventory diff before any prose job is allowed to run. What cannot be delegated is the judgment that a token is safe to document, stable enough to name, and correctly scoped. If that judgment is missing, a drafting pass will not create it, and the checker will only confirm that the invention was consistent.

Step-by-step workflow

Follow the six steps in order, and treat each artifact as an input to the next rather than as optional notes. Skipping the lock file and asking for a full page is how invented flags re-enter an otherwise careful repository. The commands and files below are a proposed workflow, not a record of a run against a production documentation set. Replace the sample command name with the binary or spec that the team already treats as the interface source.

1. Capture the interface inventory

Store one inventory file per reference page, and treat that file as the only list of public tokens the page may name. Capture help text or spec excerpts with a deterministic command, then convert the capture into a token file a human reviews. Do not ask a model to transcribe a specification into the inventory, even when the specification is long or awkwardly formatted. A transcription pass can drop a required field and still look complete to a reviewer who did not open the source.

mkdir -p docs/inventory docs/pages docs/slots docs/fixtures tools
# Proposed capture. Replace mycli with the binary the team actually ships.
mycli --help > docs/inventory/mycli-help.txt

{
  "page_id": "export-job",
  "source_capture": "docs/inventory/mycli-help.txt",
  "note": "Proposed inventory. Defaults are null because this file is not a captured product.",
  "tokens": [
    {"id": "flag.out", "kind": "flag", "public": true, "default": null},
    {"id": "flag.since", "kind": "flag", "public": true, "default": null},
    {"id": "err.partial", "kind": "error", "public": true, "default": null}
  ]
}

If the source is OpenAPI, extract operation ids, parameters, and response codes with a parser the team already trusts. Keep the raw capture next to the token file so a reviewer can see what the parser dropped or renamed. Commit the raw capture and the token file in the same change, and reject token files that have no matching capture. This step is finished only when a human has marked each token public, internal, or omitted from the page.

2. Write the block-role manifest

The manifest is the contract between extraction and drafting, and it should be reviewed like a schema change rather than like prose. Each block has a role of extract or orient, plus the token ids that the role is allowed to mention. Extract blocks are rendered from the token file and are not sent to the model as writable text. Orient blocks are the only regions a drafting job may replace, and each one carries a word cap.

# docs/inventory/export-job.manifest.yaml
# Proposed example. Not a captured production file.
page_id: export-job
inventory_sha256: "<fill-after-step-3>"
blocks:
  - id: flags
    role: extract
    source: docs/inventory/export-job.tokens.json
  - id: sequencing
    role: orient
    max_words: 120
    allowed_token_ids: [flag.out, flag.since, err.partial]
  - id: skip-when
    role: orient
    max_words: 80
    allowed_token_ids: [flag.since, err.partial]
tokens:
  - id: flag.out
    surface: ["--out"]
  - id: flag.since
    surface: ["--since"]
  - id: err.partial
    surface: ["EXPORT_PARTIAL", "partial export"]

The surface list is the set of spellings a sentence may use for a token, and the sample keeps those spellings distinctive. A multi-word surface, such as a named error phrase, belongs in that list so the checker can allow the phrase without allowing nearby inventions. Keep allowed_token_ids narrow, because a slot that may name every token on the page is almost as loose as a full-page prompt. If two slots need the same flag, list that flag in both, rather than creating one large slot that covers the whole page.

3. Lock the inventory hash

Compute a hash after a human accepts the token file, and store that hash in the manifest before any slot is drafted. The hash binds the prose job to a specific inventory, so a quiet edit cannot change the contract under an old draft. If the token file changes, the hash check fails until a human updates the manifest in the same commit on purpose. That failure is useful, because orientation jobs should stop when the interface moves instead of rewriting themselves around the change.

python3 - <<'PY'
import hashlib
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("docs/inventory/export-job.tokens.json")
print(hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest())
PY

Paste the printed digest into inventory_sha256, and do not let a drafting script update that field automatically. An automatic hash update would hide the very edit the lock is meant to surface during review. Reviewers should look at the token diff first, then accept or reject the new digest as a separate decision. Only after that decision should anyone schedule a new orientation draft for the slots whose allowed tokens changed.

4. Draft only the orientation slots

Send the model the slot id, the word cap, and the allowed surfaces, and ask for that slot alone. Do not send a request that says to write the reference page, the introduction, and the examples in one pass. A narrow prompt reduces the chance that the model adds a sibling flag that merely sounds consistent with the table. Save the result under a slot file named for the block id, and leave every extract block untouched by that job.

Draft slot sequencing only.
Allowed surfaces: --out, --since, EXPORT_PARTIAL, partial export.
Do not name any other flag, environment variable, status, or error code.
Do not restate defaults, types, or status codes.
Maximum 120 words.

When a drafting tool is useful for this step, keep it on slot text only, after the inventory hash is already committed. MonkeyCode's free model access can draft an approved orientation slot, and the free server option can run the hash step and the checker.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

This article does not claim particular model names, quotas, hardware sizes, time limits, or benchmark results for that setup. The page remains useful without those options, because the manifest, the hash, and the checker are ordinary repository files. A local Python install is enough to rehearse the gate before any hosted runner is involved. The hosted option is a placement choice for steps that are already specified, not a source of interface facts.

5. Render the page from roles

A renderer should concatenate extracted tables and orientation files in manifest order, without asking a model to assemble the page. It should refuse to read a slot file for an extract block, because that file is evidence that a draft overwrote a locked region. It should also refuse to render an orient block whose slot file is missing, rather than filling the gap with generated prose. Missing prose is a visible gap a human can fill, while silent generation hides the fact that no approved slot text existed.

6. Run the token checker

The checker loads allowed surfaces, rejects unknown interface-like tokens in orientation files, and verifies the inventory hash before it reads prose. It is a proposed, unexecuted example, so treat the results as a specification for the gate rather than as measured outcomes. The script depends on PyYAML, uses only the standard library otherwise, and never contacts a model or a network service. Run it in the same job that builds the page, and block publication when the exit code is nonzero.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Proposed, unexecuted checker for orientation slots.

Compares slot files with a locked manifest. It does not call a model.
Requires PyYAML.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

FLAG_HINT = re.compile(r"--[a-z0-9][-a-z0-9]*")
CONST_HINT = re.compile(r"\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{2,}\b")
HTTP_HINT = re.compile(r"\bHTTP\s+\d{3}\b")


def load_manifest(path: Path) -> dict:
    data = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise SystemExit("manifest must be a mapping")
    return data


def assert_hash(manifest: dict, token_path: Path) -> None:
    expected = str(manifest.get("inventory_sha256", ""))
    actual = hashlib.sha256(token_path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    if expected != actual:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"inventory hash mismatch: manifest={expected} file={actual}"
        )


def assert_ids(manifest: dict, token_path: Path) -> None:
    payload = json.loads(token_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    ids = {row["id"] for row in payload["tokens"]}
    for row in manifest["tokens"]:
        if row["id"] not in ids:
            raise SystemExit(
                f"manifest token missing from inventory: {row['id']}"
            )


def surfaces(manifest: dict, allowed_ids: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    by_id = {row["id"]: row["surface"] for row in manifest["tokens"]}
    found: list[str] = []
    for token_id in allowed_ids:
        if token_id not in by_id:
            raise SystemExit(f"unknown token id in slot: {token_id}")
        found.extend(by_id[token_id])
    return found


def strip_allowed(text: str, allowed: list[str]) -> str:
    cleaned = text
    for phrase in sorted(set(allowed), key=len, reverse=True):
        if phrase.startswith("--"):
            pattern = re.escape(phrase) + r"(?![A-Za-z0-9-])"
        elif " " in phrase:
            pattern = re.escape(phrase)
        else:
            pattern = r"\b" + re.escape(phrase) + r"\b"
        cleaned = re.sub(pattern, " ", cleaned, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    return cleaned


def unknown_hints(text: str, allowed: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    leftovers = strip_allowed(text, allowed)
    found: list[str] = []
    found.extend(FLAG_HINT.findall(leftovers))
    found.extend(CONST_HINT.findall(leftovers))
    found.extend(HTTP_HINT.findall(leftovers))
    return found


def main() -> None:
    if len(sys.argv) != 4:
        raise SystemExit(
            "usage: check_orientation_slots.py MANIFEST TOKENS SLOT_DIR"
        )
    manifest = load_manifest(Path(sys.argv[1]))
    token_path = Path(sys.argv[2])
    slot_dir = Path(sys.argv[3])
    assert_hash(manifest, token_path)
    assert_ids(manifest, token_path)
    failures: list[str] = []
    for block in manifest["blocks"]:
        slot_file = slot_dir / f"{block['id']}.md"
        if block["role"] != "orient":
            if slot_file.exists():
                failures.append(f"extract block has a draft file: {slot_file}")
            continue
        if not slot_file.exists():
            failures.append(f"missing orientation slot: {slot_file}")
            continue
        text = slot_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        words = text.split()
        if len(words) > int(block["max_words"]):
            failures.append(
                f"{block['id']} has {len(words)} words; cap is {block['max_words']}"
            )
        allowed = surfaces(manifest, block["allowed_token_ids"])
        for hint in unknown_hints(text, allowed):
            failures.append(
                f"{block['id']} names unlisted interface-like token: {hint}"
            )
    if failures:
        print("\n".join(failures))
        raise SystemExit(1)
    print("orientation slots match the locked inventory")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A passing slot uses only allowed surfaces and stays under the word cap recorded for that block in the manifest. A failing slot names a flag or an error constant that never appears in the surface list for that slot. The sample failure below uses a gzip flag and an export timeout constant, neither of which is present in the sample inventory. Against that failing fixture, the checker is specified to exit nonzero and to print each unlisted flag or constant.

Write the archive with --out, then narrow the window with --since.
If the job reports EXPORT_PARTIAL, rerun only after the source is complete.
Do not treat a partial export as a finished archive.

<!-- Proposed failing fixture. Keep it outside docs/slots until you want a red build. -->
Pass --gzip when the archive is large, and set EXPORT_TIMEOUT if the network is slow.

python3 tools/check_orientation_slots.py \
  docs/inventory/export-job.manifest.yaml \
  docs/inventory/export-job.tokens.json \
  docs/slots

How to read a checker failure

Read a failure as a routing decision, not as a suggestion to regenerate the whole page and hope the next draft is cleaner. The table below maps common signals to the role that must change and to the person or tool that should act. Use it during review so a model is not asked to repair a row that a human still has to own. If the table and the checker disagree, trust the inventory and fix the checker, rather than widening the prompt to silence the gate.

Signal Role that owns the fix Required action
Unlisted flag or error constant in a slot orient Reject the slot and redraft with the same allowed surfaces
Default, type, or status restated in prose orient Delete the restatement and render the field from the inventory
Sequencing advice that uses only allowed surfaces orient Human edit for clarity, then accept
Missing deprecation marker or wrong default extract Human updates the token file, then rehashes
New public error code extract Human adds the token, rehashes, then refreshes affected slots
Extract block has a slot file extract Delete the slot file and investigate how it was written
Hash mismatch inventory Stop drafts until a human accepts the new digest

Limitations of the gate

Word-boundary and hint matching miss inventions that avoid tokens, such as a sentence that adds an optional path argument without naming it. A human still needs to read every orientation slot, because a real flag can be described incorrectly without introducing a new token. Phrase search can false-positive when a surface is a common word, so prefer a distinctive spelling whenever the interface gives you one. The checker does not review security claims, legal wording, support promises, or whether a public token should have been public.

Hash locking detects inventory drift, but it does not tell you whether the accepted inventory matched the binary shipped last week. You still need a release process that ties the capture command to a version, a commit, or another source you can reopen. The hint pattern is intentionally narrow, and a team with different token shapes should extend the tests before extending the regular expression. Widening the pattern without fixtures will create noise, and reviewers will start ignoring the gate that this workflow depends on.

Who should not use this approach

Teams with no specification, help capture, or other inventory source should not adopt this workflow yet. The checker would then bless a hand-typed list that nobody tied to a shipping interface, which recreates the original risk under a new filename. Marketing pages, incident narratives, and conceptual essays without stable tokens are a poor fit for extract and orient roles. Anyone who wants a model to discover the interface should stop, because discovery is an ownership task rather than a drafting task.

Large generated references that are already rendered entirely from a specification may not need orientation slots at all. Adding slots there only creates prose that can drift from the generator, so prefer improving the generator over adding a second writer. Solo maintainers who cannot review slot text should also skip the drafting step and keep the page fully extracted. A gate that nobody reads is worse than a short page, because it suggests a control that the repository does not actually practice.

Put the gate in the build

The practical split is small and strict: tools and humans own interface rows, and a model may write only inside preapproved orientation slots. Lock the inventory hash, render extract blocks without a model, and reject any slot that names an unlisted surface. If MonkeyCode's free server is already available to the team, run the hash step and the checker there before merging any free-model slot draft. That order keeps drafting convenience from becoming the source of the interface the page claims to document.

title: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
description:
arXiv:2610.13461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench, a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function $f(n)$ whose values are known only for small $n$, and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds $f$. A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds $f$, that it is no worse than the current record at any $n$, and that it is strictly better at some $n$. Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single $n$ or its growth rate. At every $n$, the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining $f(n)$. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes $f$ by exhaustive search at small $n$, and a maintainer only reads the submitter's report and looks for such a search at larger $n$. We release ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty proved initial records and the admission tools. As a baseline, agents based on a frontier language model, with at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, without going beyond the published literature. Agents based on two newer models then started from these records, had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.

title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.13693v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Neural networks (NNs), while highly flexible and versatile, are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration methods adjust the outputs of an already trained model using a separate calibration dataset and additional calibration parameters. This process adds overhead that requires separate optimization of the calibrator and subsequent model selection. In this paper, we show that standard (post-hoc) calibrators can be trained end-to-end with the backbone via a bilevel Stackelberg formulation. This formulation eliminates the need for a separate calibration set or a dedicated calibration loss by jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration using cross-entropy, introducing only one additional hyperparameter: the calibrator learning rate. Although our framework supports calibrators ranging from temperature and matrix scaling to NN layers, our results show that using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no additional parameters. Our approach outperforms SOTA calibrators with minimal added complexity, while also avoiding the multiplicative overhead of separate calibration components in settings such as multi-task learning.

title: Decoupling the Declarative from the Procedural in Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2606.21496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deploying generalist robotic agents in the real world requires transferable skills. Specifically, a policy trained to clone a behavior from object-specific demonstrations must generalize beyond that object, otherwise data collection requirements become intractable. Recently, fine-tuning of pre-trained billion-parameter Vision-Language Models (VLMs), initially on large-scale robot datasets and then on fewer scenario-specific demonstrations, has emerged as the predominant paradigm for designing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. While these policies achieve state-of-the-art manipulation performance in-distribution, they remain brittle to minor spatial, semantic, and task variations. In this work, we address the inability of current models to decouple the declarative (i.e., concepts and entity semantics) from the procedural knowledge (i.e., how to do something) encoded in their parameters, which is a fundamental bottleneck for zero-shot skill transfer to novel objects. To address this, we propose w$^{2}$VLA, a new VLA model with restructured information flow. Rather than feeding all multimodal tokens from the VLM encoder into a large, opaque transformer-based action expert, our approach modulates the robot state sequence with visual, spatial, and skill information in a compositional and interpretable manner. Unlike popular, state-of-the-art VLAs, we show that our modular approach successfully decouples knowledge representations, enabling robust behavior cloning and unprecedented zero-shot skill transfer capabilities across dissimilar, unseen objects.

title: A task feed should distinguish a reference from a result
description:
When a task library exposes an API, downstream readers can lose qualifications that were obvious on the original page. A title such as “Prepare a school supply cart” can become a capability claim if the consuming application drops the source and evidence label.

I maintain Muse Task Hub, an independent, unofficial guide. Its public feed is at the /api/tasks path on the guide’s domain. The records include taskId, title, summary, category, evidenceType, url, sources, version, contentVersion, publishedAt, modifiedAt and withdrawn. The response envelope includes the snapshot identifier and pagination cursor.

Those fields do different jobs. The task ID identifies a record. The page URL points to the fuller explanation. The source URLs identify the material behind it. The evidence type distinguishes a community report from a product-maker example. Version and modification metadata help a consumer recognize updates. The withdrawn flag should not be discarded merely because an old title remains recognizable.

A reader interface should keep the title, source class and qualification together. It should link to the guide page for context and to the original source for verification. It should never relabel an official example as an independently verified outcome.

The October 10 snapshot contains 279 unique records collected across 14 paginated responses. Four records are labeled official and 275 are user reports. This distribution says something about the collection's provenance. It says nothing about how often an assistant succeeds or which task category is most popular among all users.

For a local consumer, a useful starting point is to filter withdrawn records, show the source class, and make the task-page link available:

import json
from pathlib import Path

snapshot = json.loads(Path("tasks.json").read_text())
for task in snapshot["items"]:
    if task.get("withdrawn"):
        continue
    print(task["title"])
    print("Evidence:", task["evidenceType"])
    print("Context:", task["url"])
    print("Sources:", task["sources"])

The dated export is available at https://github.com/1021ju/muse-task-hub. It is reference metadata, not a benchmark dataset. The guide has not independently reproduced the examples and is not affiliated with Meta. Third-party source rights remain with their owners; the repository does not assert a blanket license over them.

title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
description:
arXiv:2610.13778v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
