title: Can escalation channels redirect reward hacking toward defect disclosure?
description:
arXiv:2608.29460v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When coding agents encounter defective test infrastructure they may reward-hack: hardcoding outputs or editing test files to pass tests they cannot legitimately satisfy, a pattern that has now appeared outside benchmarks, in a coordinated multi-agent intrusion of a major AI platform's production infrastructure. The same capability that lets an agent detect and exploit a defect could let it report one, given the right decision environment. We evaluate escalation channels, structured reporting tools available to the agent at the point of conflict, as a decision-environment intervention that both reduces reward hacking and surfaces the infrastructure defects that trigger it. A $2 \times 2$ factorial separates the contributions of an escalation tool, a standalone anti-reward-hacking policy, and their combination. Across 8 frontier models spanning 5 families, the combined intervention reduces reward hacking from 23.6% to 5.3% (mixed-effects logistic OR = 9.2, 95% CI 5.0--16.8, $p < 10^{-12}$) with no detectable cost or performance overhead, eliminating it entirely for 6 of 8 models. Escalation and hacking are near-perfectly mutually exclusive, with 98.7% of escalations involving no hacking (100% under the combined intervention). Beyond reduction, escalation channels function as diagnostic infrastructure: on top of monitoring, escalation adds +10.1 percentage points of defect detection coverage and is more accurate once it fires (99.4% vs 85.8%). Unlike containment-based approaches that risk outpacing growing model capabilities, escalation channels redirect capability toward disclosure rather than exploitation.

title: Building with eBay Data in 2026 — 6 Endpoints, 10 Markets, and the Billing Trap Nobody Warns You About
description:
I want to start this post with the single most important thing to understand about eBay data APIs before you write a line of code.

A search request and a product record are not the same thing.

This sounds obvious, but it's responsible for more eBay API budget surprises than almost any other mistake. I'll explain the distinction, then show you how to use each of the six operations Serpent API's eBay endpoint exposes — with real code for each one.

The Data Model

eBay's public data has a natural hierarchy:

Search query
  └── Listing page (contains N listing cards)
        └── Listing card (title, price, condition, seller, item link)
              └── Item detail (images, specifics, availability, description)
                    └── Seller profile (identity, feedback score, positive rate)
                          └── Seller listings (inventory, page by page)
                          └── Seller feedback (buyer comments, ratings)
                          └── Product reviews (review text, rating, author)

Each layer is a separate API call. Each has its own rate. The mistake teams make is assuming that a "search" returns all of this. It doesn't — search returns the top level only. Enrichment requires additional calls per item.

This isn't a flaw — it's correct data architecture. You shouldn't pay for description data on items you're not interested in. But it means your cost model needs to account for every layer your application touches.

Setup 

pip install requests python-dotenv

# .env
SERPENT_API_KEY=your_key_here

# ebay_client.py
import requests
import os

API_KEY = os.getenv("SERPENT_API_KEY")
BASE = "https://apiserpent.com/api/ebay"

HEADERS = {"X-API-Key": API_KEY}

def get(endpoint, params):
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}{endpoint}", params=params, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

Operation 1 — Search Listings

GET /api/ebay/search returns a page of listings for a keyword on a specified marketplace.

def search_listings(query, marketplace="EBAY_US", locale="en-US", page=1):
    """
    Returns listing cards: title, price, condition,
    shipping, seller identity, item link.

    10 supported marketplace/locale pairs:
    EBAY_US/en-US  EBAY_GB/en-GB  EBAY_DE/de-DE
    EBAY_AU/en-AU  EBAY_IT/it-IT  EBAY_FR/fr-FR
    EBAY_CA/en-CA  EBAY_ES/es-ES  EBAY_NL/nl-NL
    EBAY_PL/pl-PL

    Rate: $0.40/1K calls at Default tier
    """
    return get("/search", {
        "q": query,
        "marketplace_id": marketplace,
        "locale": locale,
        "page": page
    })

# Example
results = search_listings("vintage camera", "EBAY_DE", "de-DE")
for listing in results.get("listings", []):
    print(listing["title"], listing["price"], listing["currency"])

What the response contains:

  • title — listing title as displayed
  • price / currency — displayed price in the marketplace's currency
  • condition — New, Used, Refurbished, For parts, etc.
  • shipping — shipping cost and type if displayed
  • seller — seller username
  • item_url — full item URL (use as item ID for subsequent calls)
  • item_id — eBay item ID

The page trap: a search returns one page. If eBay shows 48 listings on page 1, you get 48 rows. If 12 are sponsored/promoted and you filter them, you have 36. Cost is per page request, not per usable listing. Always measure yield on your actual keywords before budgeting at scale.

Operation 2 — Item Details

GET /api/ebay/item returns structured data for a specific item by ID or URL.

def get_item(item_id, include_description=False):
    """
    Returns price, images, item specifics, availability, seller.

    Add include_description=1 to get the full seller HTML description.
    Description calls: $1.50/1K (3.75x the standard rate).
    If description unavailable but core item exists, standard rate applies.

    Use include_description only when your pipeline needs it —
    most price monitoring workflows don't.
    """
    params = {"item_id": item_id}
    if include_description:
        params["include_description"] = 1
    return get("/item", params)

# Price check without description (standard rate)
item = get_item("v1|123456789012|0")
print(item["price"], item["currency"], item["condition"])

# With full description (description rate)
item_full = get_item("v1|123456789012|0", include_description=True)
print(item_full.get("description", "")[:200])

When to use include_description:

  • Product detail pages that show the seller's own copy
  • Condition verification that requires reading the description text
  • Content analysis pipelines

When NOT to use it:

  • Price monitoring (price is in the core item)
  • Stock tracking (availability is in the core item)
  • Search enrichment loops (you'd pay 3.75× for data you don't use)
  • Operation 3 — Seller Profile

GET /api/ebay/seller returns identity and reputation data for a seller username.

def get_seller_profile(seller_username):
    """
    Returns: seller identity, feedback score,
    positive feedback rate, profile link.

    Useful for: trust scoring, seller monitoring,
    marketplace research, fraud detection signals.
    Rate: $0.40/1K calls
    """
    return get("/seller", {"seller": seller_username})

profile = get_seller_profile("vintage_camera_shop")
print(
    profile["feedback_score"],
    profile["positive_feedback_rate"],
    profile["member_since"]
)

Operation 4 — Seller Inventory

GET /api/ebay/seller/items reads a seller's public listings, one page at a time.

def get_seller_inventory(seller_username, page=1):
    """
    Returns structured item cards from a seller's active listings.
    Paginate to collect the full inventory.

    For large inventories (100+ pages), use a background job
    when listed in the API catalog — only served pages are charged.
    Rate: $0.40/1K calls or served pages
    """
    return get("/seller/items", {
        "seller": seller_username,
        "page": page
    })

def collect_all_seller_items(seller_username, max_pages=10):
    """Collect a seller's full inventory page by page."""
    items = []
    for page in range(1, max_pages + 1):
        data = get_seller_inventory(seller_username, page)
        page_items = data.get("items", [])
        if not page_items:
            break
        items.extend(page_items)
        print(f"Page {page}: {len(page_items)} items")
    return items

Direct calls vs. background jobs: For a seller with 400 listings across 16 pages, a direct loop makes 16 synchronous calls. A background job submits once, handles retries internally, and charges only for pages that complete. If pages 15–16 don't complete, you're not charged for them. For large inventories, background jobs are both cheaper and more reliable.

Operation 5 — Product Reviews

GET /api/ebay/product/reviews returns buyer reviews for an eBay catalog product ID.

def get_product_reviews(product_id):
    """
    Returns: review text, star rating, author username, date.
    Note: requires an eBay catalog product_id (e-pid),
    not a listing item_id. These are different identifiers.

    Rate: $0.40/1K calls
    """
    return get("/product/reviews", {"product_id": product_id})

reviews = get_product_reviews("235190997")
for review in reviews.get("reviews", []):
    print(review["rating"], review["title"], review["date"])

The product_id vs item_id distinction: eBay has two identifier systems. An item_id identifies a specific listing from a specific seller. A catalog product ID (often called e-pid or epid) identifies a standardized product in eBay's catalog — the same physical product sold by many sellers. Reviews are attached to the catalog product, not to individual listings. If your workflow starts from search results, you'll need to extract the product ID from the item detail before calling reviews.

Operation 6 — Seller Feedback

GET /api/ebay/seller/feedback returns feedback entries left by buyers.

def get_seller_feedback(seller_username, page=1):
    """
    Returns: feedback entries with buyer username,
    positive/negative/neutral rating, comment text, date.

    Useful for: sentiment analysis, seller trust scoring,
    fraud signals, marketplace research.
    Rate: $0.40/1K calls
    """
    return get("/seller/feedback", {
        "seller": seller_username,
        "page": page
    })

feedback = get_seller_feedback("vintage_camera_shop")
for entry in feedback.get("feedback", []):
    print(entry["rating"], entry["comment"][:80])

A Complete Price Monitoring Pipeline

Here's how the operations compose into a real workflow:

import time
from datetime import datetime

def run_price_monitor(keywords, marketplaces, output_file="prices.jsonl"):
    """
    For each keyword × marketplace pair:
    1. Search listings (discovery)
    2. Get item detail for top N results (enrichment)
    3. Log price, condition, seller, timestamp

    Cost at Default tier ($0.40/1K):
    - 1 search call + N item calls per keyword/market pair
    - For 10 keywords × 3 markets × top-5 items:
      30 search calls + 150 item calls = 180 calls total
      180 / 1000 × $0.40 = $0.072 per run
    """
    import json

    results = []

    for keyword in keywords:
        for marketplace_id, locale in marketplaces:
            # Layer 1: Search
            search_data = search_listings(keyword, marketplace_id, locale)
            listings = search_data.get("listings", [])[:5]  # top 5 only

            for listing in listings:
                item_id = listing.get("item_id")
                if not item_id:
                    continue

                # Layer 2: Item detail (no description — not needed for price monitoring)
                try:
                    item = get_item(item_id)
                    record = {
                        "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
                        "keyword": keyword,
                        "marketplace": marketplace_id,
                        "item_id": item_id,
                        "title": listing["title"],
                        "search_price": listing.get("price"),
                        "item_price": item.get("price"),
                        "currency": item.get("currency"),
                        "condition": item.get("condition"),
                        "seller": listing.get("seller"),
                        "availability": item.get("availability"),
                    }
                    results.append(record)

                    # Write incrementally so partial runs aren't lost
                    with open(output_file, "a") as f:
                        f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")

                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"Item {item_id} failed: {e}")

                time.sleep(0.1)  # gentle rate limiting

    return results

# Run it
KEYWORDS = ["vintage camera", "film camera", "polaroid camera"]
MARKETS = [
    ("EBAY_US", "en-US"),
    ("EBAY_GB", "en-GB"),
    ("EBAY_DE", "de-DE"),
]

data = run_price_monitor(KEYWORDS, MARKETS)
print(f"Collected {len(data)} price records")

Cost Reality Check

At the Default tier ($0.40/1K calls):


For price monitoring at meaningful scale — 100 keywords × 10 markets × 20 items daily — that's roughly 21,000 calls/day, $8.40/day at Default tier, $0.84/day at Scale tier ($0.03/1K after the $500 one-time deposit).

Start free: apiserpent.com/ebay-api — 10 calls, no card, covers the search + item workflow for initial testing.

Full endpoint reference: apiserpent.com/docs#ebay-api

title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.13092v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.

title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
description:
arXiv:2610.02626v2 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
description:
arXiv:2609.26550v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge scales evaluation, but reasoning judges are slow and costly. We study JEV-as-a-Judge: evaluation with JEV, a decision-only judge that returns label probabilities instead of text, and whose confidence decides whether to accept its verdict or escalate to a reasoning judge. Against sixteen generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, JEV comes within three points of GPT-6 wherever a verdict can be read off the text, at 0.36% of its fee and a 0.15-second median latency, and falls behind where the verdict must be derived, as in math, code, and logic. Its confidence marks this boundary. With a threshold frozen in advance, accepting confident verdicts and escalating the rest is 0.9 points more accurate than GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of its fee, and in a pre-specified live test on two new workloads the cascade matches GPT-6's accuracy exactly. Confidence routing weakens on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose; we close with a simple recipe for validating thresholds locally.

title: When to off-road the product roadmap
description: The product landscape has changed. It’s time our product development process changes with it.

title: MENTOR: Learning from Failure with On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention
description:
arXiv:2610.13594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a key driver for Large Reasoning Models, but it is vulnerable to "zero-reward collapse", a training failure where a sudden increase in task difficulty causes the learning signal to vanish. We argue that the conventional approach of discarding these failed trajectories is wasteful, as they contain valuable diagnostic information about the model's cognitive gaps, a bright side that can be leveraged for recovery. Existing solutions, however, often regress to static, "off-policy-style" interventions like pre-defined hint libraries or perform post-hoc refinement, failing to provide the adaptive, forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift towards on-policy pedagogical intervention and introduce MENTOR, a multi-agent framework that acts as a live mentor. MENTOR diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and dynamically generates targeted, instructional prompts to guide the learning agent's next attempt. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR integrates seamlessly into existing policy optimization pipelines like GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Extensive experiments on math and code generation show that MENTOR effectively mitigates zero-reward collapse, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it achieves massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.

title: Edge Config is now Global Config
description:
Edge Config is now Global Config. This rename better reflects that it is a globally replicated data store with ~1ms reads in every region, built for the configuration that applications read at runtime, such as feature flags, redirects, and experimentation settings.

Global Config stores can now hold up to 1 MB on every plan, and Pro and Enterprise teams can create unlimited stores with more writes per day. The rename also ships with a new server-side SDK, @vercel/global-config, and a new environment variable.

What changed

  • Name: Global Config is the new name for Edge Config. The store itself is unchanged.

  • Package: @vercel/global-config replaces @vercel/edge-config as a drop-in replacement.

  • Environment variable: Connecting a Global Config store to a project creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable instead of EDGE_CONFIG.

  • Limits: Raised on every plan. Pricing is unchanged.

What you need to do

  • Existing projects: no action required. Deployments, connected stores, and the EDGE_CONFIG environment variable continue to work.

  • Upgrading proactively is safe. The new SDK reads GLOBAL_CONFIG by default and falls back to EDGE_CONFIG, so it works with stores connected before and after the rename. You can switch packages today without touching your stores.

  • Creating stores and pushing new config values work without upgrading. Neither depends on which SDK version your project uses.

  • Upgrade before connecting new stores to a project. Connecting a store now creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable, and the legacy SDK only reads EDGE_CONFIG by default. A project still on @vercel/edge-config cannot read a newly connected store.

title: Towards Enriching Design-Time Models with Evidence from Simulation and Operational Activities
description:
arXiv:2610.13456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems are developed through multiple model based activities, comprising several stages of development. As the development progresses through simulation, experimentation, and operation, observations of system execution may reveal missing, uncertain, or invalid design knowledge. The path from execution results to persistent design-time enrichment, however, is often implicit. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing an evidence driven workflow for systematically transferring knowledge produced during simulation and operation back into design-time models. We demonstrate the workflow using an Influence Model, a design-time artefact used to represent how design artefacts and environmental factors jointly affect system response properties, using a sign-following robot use case. We show how simulation evidence can enrich Influence Models by supporting participant pruning decisions, interaction characterisation, influence-function abstraction, and validity-scope information. The application demonstrates the feasibility of the workflow for simulation-based evidence and its potential benefits to improve design-time reasoning and feedback in subsequent development iterations.

title: Latent Reward Steering: An Adaptive Inference-Time Framework that Implicitly Promotes Cognitive Behaviors in Reasoning LLMs
description:
arXiv:2606.00726v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Strong reasoning depends not only on model knowledge but also on how effectively cognitive behaviors are deployed during generation. Existing methods often rely on explicit behavior-level control, making them insufficiently adaptive when failures and required corrections vary across reasoning states, tasks, and models. To this end, we propose Latent Reward Steering (LRS), an adaptive inference-time framework that promotes cognitive behaviors by optimizing the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) latent states that implicitly carry them. Rather than relying on predefined cognitive behaviors or steering directions derived from them, LRS trains a latent reward model on reasoning traces by final answer correctness to estimate the quality of intermediate latent states. During inference, reward gradients provide state-specific correction directions for fragile latent states, while a reward and confidence gate restricts intervention to states the reward signal flags as fragile. Experiments on multiple reasoning LLM backbones and benchmarks show that \ours consistently improves performance over various baselines, and post-hoc analyses further indicate that \ours implicitly promotes good cognitive behaviors that fix the original reasoning errors. Code is available at: https://github.com/jiakanglee/Latent-Reward-Steering.

title: The Invisible Hand of Physics: When Video Diffusion Models Know More Than They Show
description:
arXiv:2606.05328v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern video diffusion models generate increasingly realistic and temporally coherent videos, motivating their use as candidate world simulators. Yet it remains unclear whether these models internally encode physical structure, or merely reproduce motion patterns seen during training. We study this question by probing video diffusion models along latent trajectories corresponding to real videos with known physical plausibility. To obtain such trajectories, we approximately invert the deterministic sampling process by integrating the learned velocity field backward from a clean video latent to noise, giving access to the model's intermediate states and attention maps. Using these recovered trajectories, we show that physical plausibility is linearly decodable from diffusion transformer states across IntPhys and InfLevel, reaching around 81.27% average accuracy and outperforming dedicated representation-learning baselines such as V-JEPA and VideoMAE. Surprisingly, this signal is absent from the VAE latent input and emerges inside the denoising transformer itself, despite the model not being trained with a self-supervised predictive objective. These findings suggest that physically meaningful representations can arise as a byproduct of generative denoising.

title: Building a Document Pipeline for International Job Applications (OCR, Validation, and Translation Tracking)
description:
If you've ever helped a friend, partner, or yourself apply for a job abroad, you know the paperwork problem isn't really about translation quality. It's about tracking a pile of documents (employer letters, work certificates, reference letters) through multiple states: original → scanned → translated → certified → apostilled → submitted.

This is a document pipeline problem, and it's one developers are well equipped to solve, even with simple tooling. The legal and procedural side of certified translation for employment documents is covered well in this article on certified translation of employment experience letters. This post covers the technical side: how to build a lightweight system to manage the process instead of tracking it in your email inbox.

Why this is harder than it looks

A single international application can involve:

  • 3-5 source documents (employer letters, certificates, performance reviews)
  • Each needing OCR-quality verification before translation
  • A certification step (lawyer or notary signature, in Portugal's case)
  • Possibly an apostille from a separate government body
  • Cross-referencing names and dates against a CV

Miss a stamp during scanning, or let one document's dates drift from your CV, and the whole application can bounce. This is exactly the kind of multi-step, stateful process that benefits from being modeled explicitly rather than tracked ad hoc.

Step 1: Validate scans before they go anywhere

The source article notes that "faint stamps or signatures cut off during scanning slow down certification." This is a solvable problem with basic image processing before you ever send a document to a translator.

A simple pre-check script using OpenCV and Tesseract can flag likely problem scans:

import cv2
import pytesseract

def check_scan_quality(image_path, min_text_confidence=60):
    img = cv2.imread(image_path)
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

    # Flag low contrast (common cause of faint stamps)
    contrast = gray.std()
    if contrast < 40:
        print(f"WARNING: low contrast ({contrast:.1f}) — stamps may be unreadable")

    # Run OCR confidence check
    data = pytesseract.image_to_data(gray, output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
    confidences = [int(c) for c in data['conf'] if c != '-1']
    avg_conf = sum(confidences) / len(confidences) if confidences else 0

    if avg_conf < min_text_confidence:
        print(f"WARNING: OCR confidence {avg_conf:.1f}% — rescan recommended")

    return {"contrast": contrast, "ocr_confidence": avg_conf}

This won't replace a human translator checking the document, but it catches the obvious failures (cut-off edges, washed-out stamps) before you waste a certification cycle on a bad scan.

Step 2: Build a document state machine

Each document in the application needs to move through a defined set of states. Modeling this explicitly, even in a spreadsheet or a small SQLite table, prevents the "did I already send this one" problem.

from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date

class DocState(Enum):
    COLLECTED = "collected"
    SCANNED = "scanned"
    SENT_FOR_TRANSLATION = "sent_for_translation"
    TRANSLATED = "translated"
    CERTIFIED = "certified"
    APOSTILLED = "apostilled"
    SUBMITTED = "submitted"

@dataclass
class Document:
    name: str
    doc_type: str  # employer_letter, reference_letter, certificate
    state: DocState = DocState.COLLECTED
    requires_apostille: bool = False
    dates_mentioned: list = field(default_factory=list)
    names_mentioned: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def can_submit(self):
        if self.requires_apostille:
            return self.state == DocState.APOSTILLED
        return self.state in (DocState.CERTIFIED, DocState.APOSTILLED)

The can_submit() check matters because it encodes exactly the rule the source article flags as a common mistake: documents go out without the apostille they actually needed, because someone assumed certification alone was enough.

Step 3: Cross-reference dates and names automatically

One of the stated reasons applications get rejected is inconsistent names and dates across documents. This is a text-matching problem you can partially automate.

import re
from datetime import datetime

def extract_dates(text):
    # crude pattern, adjust for your document formats
    pattern = r'\b(\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4})\b'
    return re.findall(pattern, text)

def cross_check_documents(documents_text: dict, cv_text: str):
    cv_dates = set(extract_dates(cv_text))
    mismatches = {}

    for doc_name, text in documents_text.items():
        doc_dates = set(extract_dates(text))
        missing_in_cv = doc_dates - cv_dates
        if missing_in_cv:
            mismatches[doc_name] = missing_in_cv

    return mismatches

This isn't a substitute for careful proofreading, but running every document and your CV through a script like this before sending anything for certification catches the kind of typo that otherwise surfaces three weeks later when a qualifications body sends a rejection email.

Step 4: Track the certification and apostille chain

The source article explains that Portugal's certification model routes through a lawyer or notary, and the apostille is a separate step through the PGR. These are two different authorities with two different turnaround times, and conflating them in your tracking is how deadlines get missed.

If you're coordinating this for multiple documents or multiple family members' applications, a simple status table beats a scattered email thread:

Document Certification status Apostille needed Apostille status Submission deadline
Employer letter Certified 03/14 Yes Pending 04/01
Reference letter Pending No N/A 04/01

Even a Google Sheet with conditional formatting on the deadline column solves 80% of the coordination problem. If you want something more durable, this maps cleanly onto a small Airtable base or a few tables in Postgres with a status enum matching the DocState above.

Where this pipeline actually ends

None of this replaces the legal step. A script can flag a blurry stamp, but it can't certify a translation, and it definitely can't decide whether your destination country needs an apostille or consular legalisation. That part is a legal and procedural question, covered in detail in the source article on certified translation for employment experience letters.

What this pipeline does is remove the operational noise: bad scans, missed apostille steps, and inconsistent dates, so that by the time a document reaches a certified translator or a notary, it's actually ready to be processed correctly the first time.

If you're building something similar for your own relocation or for a team handling multiple applicants, start with the state machine. Everything else (OCR checks, date matching, deadline tracking) can be added incrementally once you have a clear model of what state each document is actually in.

title: Breaking the Cloak! Unveiling Chinese Cloaked Toxicity with Homophone Graph and Toxic Lexicon
description:
arXiv:2505.22184v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Social media platforms have experienced a significant rise in toxic content, including abusive language and discriminatory remarks, presenting growing challenges for content moderation. Some users evade censorship by deliberately disguising toxic words through homophonic cloak, which necessitates the task of unveiling cloaked toxicity. Existing methods are mostly designed for English texts, while Chinese cloaked toxicity unveiling has not been solved yet. To tackle the issue, we propose C$^2$TU, a novel training-free and prompt-free method for Chinese cloaked toxic content unveiling. It first employs substring matching to identify candidate toxic words based on Chinese homophone graph and toxic lexicon. Then it filters those candidates that are non-toxic and corrects cloaks to be their corresponding toxicities. Specifically, we develop two model variants for filtering, which are based on BERT and LLMs, respectively. For LLMs, we address the auto-regressive limitation in computing word occurrence probability and utilize the full semantic contexts of a text sequence to reveal cloaked toxic words. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C$^2$TU can achieve superior performance on two Chinese toxic datasets. In particular, our method outperforms the best competitor by up to 71% on the F1 score and 35% on accuracy, respectively. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/XDxc-cuber/C2TU-Chinese-cloaked-toxicity-unveiling.

title: Introducing Run SDK: secure eval for your agents
description:
Agents increasingly write TypeScript programs to coordinate tools and process their results. Once those programs touch real applications, some steps require authentication, while others need human approval.

Executing that code with eval gives it the same access as the application around it, including its secrets and internal services, and leaves no durable way to pause at those boundaries.

Today, we're releasing the Run SDK, a package for executing untrusted JavaScript and TypeScript without giving it direct access to your application or system. Applications expose narrow host functions and can interrupt execution for authentication or human-in-the-loop approval. The program resumes after a decision without repeating completed work.

A small interface to the host

The Run SDK evaluates JavaScript or type-stripped TypeScript in a fresh QuickJS context inside a worker thread, with no direct route to Node.js or the network.

The application exposes selected operations through hostFunctions. These are regular functions that become callable globals inside the sandbox:

Here, the generated program knows about store.listOrders(). The database client and its credentials remain in the application.

Calls cross the sandbox boundary through serialization. A host function may return a promise, so existing service clients can sit behind this interface without being passed into the sandbox.

You can try this in the playground. Code you run there can only reach the host functions on the page.

Code mode in practice

The Run SDK is the internal module powering code mode tool execution in the AI SDK. Giving an agent a program changes the unit of work. One model response can describe the calls and the logic connecting them:

The two requests happen concurrently, and invoice filtering stays local to the program. Only the useful result returns to the application.

This is a good fit for agents that work across several internal services. A research agent can combine search results before answering. A support agent can inspect an account without putting an entire billing response back into its context.

The same package can power a code interpreter or a product feature that accepts customer-defined transformations. In both cases, the application chooses the available data and operations.

Host functions work best when they map to actions in your product, like refunding an order. Exposing orders.refund(id) gives the application a clear place to check the user and the order. A generic request function would make that authority much harder to reason about.

Native support for human-in-the-loop and auth

Reading invoices is different from issuing a refund. When generated code reaches a sensitive operation, the host function can interrupt execution:

When the run is interrupted, the result includes a signed token the application can save with an approval request and use to resume the run when a decision arrives.

Resuming replays the program, but settled host function calls use their recorded results. Host function work completed before the interruption does not run again. The interrupted function receives the approval and continues from there.

This mechanism also works when a workflow must wait for authentication. The application owns the waiting period; the worker does not need to remain alive.

Running within limits

A sandbox still needs to account for code that loops forever or produces an oversized result. createRunner() sets shared limits:

Limits can also be set per run. The defaults cover the QuickJS heap and the values crossing the host boundary; applications can tighten them for their workload.

Each invocation receives a new QuickJS context. Dynamic evaluation is disabled and built-in prototypes are hardened. This boundary applies to the generated program, while host functions remain trusted application code and must perform their normal authorization checks.

The Run SDK is intended for JavaScript computation inside an application. Workloads that require an operating system, package installation, or process-level isolation should use Vercel Sandbox instead.

Extracting the execution layer

The first version of this runtime lived inside just-bash as js-exec, backed by QuickJS. It let agents write TypeScript against the shell's virtual filesystem and command set.

We extracted that layer into the Run SDK and replaced the Node-shaped environment with application-defined host functions. We tested the underlying mechanism in eve, using it to run agent-generated TypeScript against real tools. It now powers code mode in the AI SDK where existing AI SDK tools are mapped to host functions, while the Run SDK handles their sandboxed execution.

Getting started

The Run SDK supports Node.js 22.13+ and Bun. You will need pnpm or another package manager installed on your local development machine.

Check out the documentation and API reference.

title: Next.js 16 Image: priority Deprecated, quality Now Allowlisted
description:
Your team ships a product page with a hero image: <Image src={photo} quality={90} priority fill />. It looked right in Next.js 15. You upgrade to 16, run a visual regression pass out of habit, and the hero image is... a little softer. Nothing crashed. No error in the terminal. No red line in CI. The quality={90} prop is still sitting right there in the JSX, doing nothing, and you'd have no way to know unless you happened to run the dev server and read a console warning that most people's eyes skip past.

That's the real story behind two changes Next.js 16 made to next/image: the quality prop is now checked against an allowlist (images.qualities, defaulting to [75]), and the priority prop is deprecated in favor of a new preload prop. Neither one is flashy enough to make a release-notes headline, and neither one throws a build error, which is exactly why they're worth a proper look: this article is written against Next.js 16.4 (verified against the framework's own next/image and next.config.js reference docs, and its source in packages/next/src/shared/lib, in October 2026), and by the end you'll know precisely what changed, why, and how to fix it on purpose instead of by accident.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain what images.qualities does, why it defaults to [75] in Next.js 16, and what happens to a quality value that isn't on the list
  • Predict whether a given quality prop gets silently coerced or causes a hard 400, and why those are two different code paths
  • Migrate priority to preload correctly, and understand why Next.js changed the name rather than the behavior
  • Read the Version History table at the bottom of a Next.js docs page and use it the way this article does
  • Configure images.qualities and preload/loading/fetchPriority together without fighting the framework's own validation

Who this is for

You've used next/image in an App Router project — at minimum, you've written <Image src={...} width={...} height={...} /> and set priority on a hero image at some point. You don't need prior knowledge of the Image Optimization API internals; we build the model from the prop down to the request.

Table of contents

  • The problem: a prop that still compiles but silently does less
  • The mental model: your props pass through a config-aware layer first
  • Walkthrough: the quality allowlist
  • Walkthrough: priority to preload
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: a prop that still compiles but silently does less

Here's the Next.js 15 component from the intro, completely ordinary code:

// Works exactly as written on Next.js 15
<Image
  src={photo}
  alt="Studio monitor on a desk"
  fill
  quality={90}
  priority
/>

Upgrade to Next.js 16 with no other changes and two things happen, neither of which raises an error:

  1. quality={90} stops meaning 90. Next.js 16 ships a default images.qualities: [75]. Since 90 isn't on that list, the component silently requests the closest allowed value instead — which, with the default config, is 75. In development you get a console warning. In a production build, there is no warning at all; the image is just a little softer than the designer approved.
  2. priority is marked @deprecated in the type definitions, and the official docs now describe preload as the prop to reach for. Nothing breaks. Nothing tells you at runtime, either — unlike some other deprecated Image props (onLoadingComplete, for instance, logs a warning telling you to switch to onLoad), priority just keeps working, silently, for as long as you keep writing it.

Both changes share the same shape: a prop you set still "works," in the sense that your code compiles and the page renders, while quietly doing something other than what the Next.js 15-era mental model says it does. That's the gap this article closes.

The mental model: your props pass through a config-aware layer first

It's tempting to think of <Image quality={90} priority /> as "pass these two numbers/flags to the <img> tag." It never was that simple, and in Next.js 16 it's explicit: both props go through a validation and normalization layer that consults your next.config.js before anything is requested over the network.

The mental model: <Image>'s props aren't a direct line to the browser. They're inputs to a decision Next.js makes on your behalf, and that decision depends on config you may not have touched. Quality gets snapped to the nearest value your config allows; priority-style loading urgency gets normalized into one signal. In both cases, the component decides what actually leaves your server — your prop is a request, not a guarantee.

Two separate decisions fall out of that model, and they're the two things that changed in 16:

  • What quality number actually gets requested — governed by images.qualities.
  • Whether the image loads eagerly and gets a <link rel="preload"> — governed by priority/preload/loading.

Walkthrough: the quality allowlist

Stage 1 — the default, unconfigured app

With no images config at all, Next.js 16's effective default is:

// next.config.js — this is the IMPLICIT default in Next.js 16, you don't have to write it
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [75],
  },
}

Key concept: every <Image quality={N}> in your app is now checked against this array. If N isn't in it, Next.js doesn't throw — it picks whichever configured value is numerically closest to N and uses that instead.

Stage 2 — what "closest" actually means

This isn't a vague "rounds to a nice number" — it's a specific, small algorithm, and you can reason about it exactly:

// This is Next.js's own logic (shared/lib/find-closest-quality.ts), reproduced for clarity
function findClosestQuality(quality, configuredQualities) {
  const q = quality || 75
  if (!configuredQualities?.length) return q
  return configuredQualities.reduce(
    (prev, cur) => (Math.abs(cur - q) < Math.abs(prev - q) ? cur : prev),
    configuredQualities[0]
  )
}

findClosestQuality(90, [75])           // → 75 (only option)
findClosestQuality(82, [50, 75, 100])  // → 75 (|82-75|=7 beats |82-100|=18)
findClosestQuality(90, [50, 75, 100])  // → 100 (|90-100|=10 beats |90-75|=15)

Try the exact same function with your own numbers in the playground below — it runs this reduction live, not a simplified stand-in.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stage 3 — configuring it on purpose

If 75 is too aggressive for a photography-heavy site, widen the allowlist explicitly:

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [40, 60, 75, 90, 100],
  },
}

Now quality={90} on a component is requested as 90, exactly, because 90 is on the list. The fix for the regression in the intro isn't "add quality back" — it was never removed — it's "put 90 in images.qualities."

Stage 4 — the two different failure modes

This is the part that trips people up, because there are genuinely two code paths, not one:

  • Through <Image> (the normal path): a disallowed quality is coerced to the closest allowed value. No error, no 4xx — your visitor gets a real image, just at a different quality than you asked for. Development logs a console warning naming the exact value to add to your config; production does not.
  • Through the raw optimization endpoint (GET /_next/image?url=...&w=...&q=90, the kind of URL you'd get by copying a src out of dev tools, or by hand-building a request): the server validates q against the same allowlist and, if it isn't an exact match, returns a 400 Bad Request. There's no "closest value" leniency here, because this endpoint isn't going through your component's props at all — it's a public HTTP surface, and Next.js treats an unlisted quality value the same way it treats a malformed width: a bad request.

So "what happens if the quality isn't allowed" has two honest answers depending on which door you walked through, and both are intentional: the component degrades gracefully for real visitors; the raw endpoint stays strict so the allowlist can't be bypassed by hitting the optimizer directly.

Walkthrough: priority to preload

Stage 1 — what priority always did

priority on <Image> has always done two things together: it stops the image from being treated as lazy-loaded (so the browser doesn't wait to discover it near the viewport), and it has Next.js insert a <link rel="preload"> for it, so the browser's preload scanner can start fetching it before React even renders the <img> tag. That combination is exactly what you want for a Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) candidate — your hero image, the above-the-fold product photo.

Stage 2 — the rename, and why it's a rename and not a behavior change 

// Next.js 15 — still compiles on 16, still works, but the type is now @deprecated
<Image src={hero} alt="…" priority fill />

// Next.js 16 — the documented way forward
<Image src={hero} alt="…" preload fill />

Key concept: for the common case — "this is my LCP image, load it with urgency" — preload is a straight swap for priority. Both disable lazy-loading and both trigger the same preload <link> insertion; Next.js didn't change what the prop does here, it changed what it's called, specifically so the name describes the mechanism (a resource preload) instead of a vague notion of importance. You're not supposed to set both: the component throws "Only preload should be used" if a single <Image> has priority and preload together — but, like the quality-coercion warning, that check only runs while NODE_ENV !== 'production', so it surfaces in next dev, not in a next build/next start production run.

Stage 3 — reaching past preload when you need more control

The docs are explicit that preload isn't always the right tool, even for an above-the-fold image: "In most cases, you should use loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" instead of preload." Reach for those two directly when:

// Multiple images could plausibly be the LCP element depending on viewport size —
// don't blanket them all with preload (that fights the browser's own prioritization)
<Image src={hero} alt="…" loading="eager" fetchPriority="high" fill />

preload is a blunt, singular signal — "fetch this one early, with a <link> tag." loading/fetchPriority let the browser's own scheduler make the call across several candidates, which matters once a layout has more than one image that could end up being the LCP element on different screen sizes.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • Nothing warns you to migrate priority. It's @deprecated in the types (your editor may gray it out or flag it with a linter that reads JSDoc), but there is no runtime console message pointing you to preload, so code that never gets a type-check pass can carry priority indefinitely without anyone noticing it's the old name.
  • The production quality warning doesn't exist. The images.qualities mismatch warning only fires in development (NODE_ENV !== 'production'). A staging environment running a production build will not tell you a quality prop is being coerced — only next dev will.
  • A static import's quality is checked too. quality behaves identically whether src is a remote URL, a path under public/, or a statically imported image — the allowlist check doesn't care how the src arrived.
  • Raising the allowlist raises optimizer work. Every quality value you add to images.qualities is a value the Image Optimization API may actually have to render on demand. A wide allowlist (say, every integer 1–100) defeats the point of having one at all — the docs frame the default narrow list as a deliberate guard against letting "malicious actors... optimize more qualities than you intended," since each distinct quality is a distinct image variant your server (or your hosting provider's optimizer) has to produce and cache.
  • priority/preload and loading="lazy" are mutually exclusive, and so are priority and preload together. The component throws for either combination rather than silently picking one — but that throw lives in the same NODE_ENV !== 'production'-gated code as the quality warning, so it's a next dev error, not a guarantee your next build/CI pipeline will catch it. If you only ever test with a production build, an invalid combination can ship unnoticed.

Best practices

  • Set images.qualities once, deliberately, in next.config.js, based on the quality values your designs actually use — don't leave it at the 16 default if your app already standardizes on, say, 85 for photography.
  • Reserve preload for the one true LCP candidate on a given page. If more than one image could be it depending on viewport, use loading="eager"/fetchPriority="high" on the candidates instead and let the browser's scanner decide.
  • Run next dev at least once after a major upgrade, specifically to read the console for images.qualities warnings — they don't appear in a production build, and they're the only signal this change produces.
  • Grep for priority across .tsx files during a 15→16 upgrade and rename to preload as a mechanical pass; it's a safe, behavior-preserving rename for the common usage described above.
  • Don't widen images.qualities to "everything" as a reflexive fix — pick the two or three values your design system actually ships, the same way you'd pick deviceSizes.

FAQ

Does quality={90} throw an error in Next.js 16?

No. If 90 isn't in your images.qualities allowlist, the component silently requests the closest allowed value instead (75, with the default config). No exception, no build failure — just a different number than the one in your JSX. The console warning for this only appears in development.

Why does hitting /_next/image?...&q=90 directly return a 400 but the component doesn't error?

Because they're different code paths. The <Image> component coerces an out-of-range quality to the closest allowed value before building the request — it never sends an invalid q. The raw optimizer endpoint validates q as a strict allowlist with no coercion, because it's a public HTTP surface that has to reject bad input rather than guess what you meant.

Is priority removed in Next.js 16?

No, it's deprecated, not removed. It still compiles and still behaves the same as preload for the eager-load-plus-preload-link use case. The Version History table in the official <Image> reference records it as deprecated starting in v16.0.0.

Do I need to migrate priority to preload immediately?

Not urgently — there's no runtime warning pushing you to, and the behavior hasn't changed. Treat it like any other mechanical rename: do it the next time you're already touching a file, or as a dedicated sweep during a major-version upgrade, rather than a hotfix.

Does images.qualities affect images served through a custom loader?

Only partly. The dev-only console warning for an out-of-allowlist quality fires regardless of which loader you use. But the actual snap-to-closest-value coercion (findClosestQuality) is implemented inside Next.js's own default loader, not in a shared layer every loader passes through — a custom loader function or images.loaderFile receives the raw quality prop exactly as written and is responsible for applying (or ignoring) images.qualities itself. It also isn't going through the /_next/image endpoint in the typical case, so the strict-400 behavior doesn't apply there either.

Cheat sheet 

// next.config.js — the Next.js 16 defaults, written out explicitly
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [75],        // REQUIRED allowlist since v16.0.0; unlisted quality → closest match
  },
}
Task Code What actually happens
Request a quality on the allowlist <Image quality={75} /> Requested exactly as given
Request a quality NOT on the allowlist <Image quality={90} /> (allowlist [75]) Silently coerced to 75 (closest match); dev-only console warning
Widen what's allowed images: { qualities: [50, 75, 100] } quality={90} now resolves to 100 (closest), not 75
Hit the optimizer directly with a bad quality GET /_next/image?url=...&w=640&q=90 (not on allowlist) 400 Bad Request — no coercion on this path
Mark the LCP / hero image (current) <Image preload fill /> Eager load + <link rel="preload"> inserted
Mark the LCP / hero image (deprecated, still works) <Image priority fill /> Identical to preload — no runtime warning to switch
Multiple possible LCP candidates <Image loading="eager" fetchPriority="high" /> Finer-grained signal than preload; lets the browser's scanner weigh several images
Invalid combination (next dev-only error) <Image priority preload /> or <Image priority loading="lazy" /> Throws: "Only preload should be used" / "Only one should be used" — only while NODE_ENV !== 'production'

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Key takeaways

  • images.qualities defaults to [75] in Next.js 16. Any quality prop not on your configured allowlist is silently snapped to the closest value that is — gracefully through <Image>, strictly (400) through the raw optimizer endpoint.
  • The coercion warning is development-only. A production build will not tell you a quality value got rewritten; the only way to catch it is to run next dev and read the console, or to simply set the allowlist to match your design system up front.
  • priority isn't gone, it's renamed to preload, and for the one thing almost everyone uses it for — flagging the LCP image — the swap is behavior-preserving. Nothing nags you to make it, so plan it as a deliberate pass rather than waiting for a warning that will never come.
  • loading="eager" + fetchPriority="high" is the more precise tool when a page has more than one plausible LCP candidate; preload is for the single, known one.

You upgrade, the build succeeds, the page looks almost right — and that gap between "compiles" and "renders exactly as specified" is where both of these changes live. Now that you've seen the allowlist and the rename from the inside, a soft hero image or a silently-working priority prop stops being a mystery and starts being a one-line fix in next.config.js or a safe find-and-replace.

If you've been caught by either of these since upgrading to Next.js 16, or found a case the allowlist handles differently than described here, say so in the comments — these are the two next/image changes with the fewest search results and the most "wait, why did my image get softer" GitHub issues.

This episode builds on two earlier ones in this series: Next.js Cache Components Explained covers the broader caching model next/image sits alongside, and Next.js Route Handlers: GET Stopped Caching in 15 is the same "quiet default change with no error message" pattern applied to Route Handlers instead of <Image>.

title: React JS Course for Beginners: Learn to Build Modern Web Applications
description:
Modern websites need interactive interfaces that respond quickly to user actions. React JS is a JavaScript library that helps developers build these interfaces using reusable components.

If you are learning frontend development, understanding React can help you move from building static web pages to creating interactive applications.

What Is React JS?

React JS is an open-source JavaScript library used to build user interfaces. Instead of writing an entire interface as one large block of code, developers divide it into smaller, reusable components.

For example, an e-commerce website may have separate components for the navigation bar, product cards, search box, shopping cart, and checkout form.

Each component can be developed and maintained separately, making larger applications easier to organize.

What Should Beginners Learn Before React?

Before starting React, build a foundation in these technologies:

  • HTML: Structure web pages using elements and forms.
  • CSS: Control layouts, colours, spacing, and responsive design.
  • JavaScript: Learn variables, functions, arrays, objects, events, and modern ES6 syntax.
  • DOM basics: Understand how web pages respond to user interactions.

Once you understand these fundamentals, React concepts become easier to follow.

5 Important React JS Concepts

1. Components

Components are reusable parts of a user interface. You can create a button, header, product card, or complete page section as a component.

function Welcome() {
  return <h1>Welcome to React!</h1>;
}

export default Welcome;

2. JSX

JSX lets developers write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. It helps keep interface structure and component logic together.

3. Props

Props pass information from one component to another. For example, a product card can receive its name and price through props.

4. State

State stores information that can change while an application runs. A counter, shopping cart, or expandable menu can use state to update the interface.

5. React Hooks

Hooks such as useState and useEffect help functional components manage state and handle side effects.

Build Projects While Learning

Reading documentation is useful, but building projects helps you understand how the concepts work together.

Try these beginner projects:

  1. A counter with increment and reset buttons.
  2. A to-do list with add and delete features.
  3. A product listing page with search and filtering.
  4. A form with input validation.
  5. A weather application that fetches data from an API.

As you progress, explore React Router, API integration, reusable components, and state management. Use Git and GitHub to track your code and share your projects.

How Does Graphic Design Connect With Web Development?

Frontend developers often work with designers to turn visual concepts into working websites. Understanding layout, typography, colours, and image formats can make this collaboration easier.

If you want to understand the visual side of digital work, explore the Graphic Design Course in Surat.

For vector illustrations, logos, and scalable artwork, tools such as CorelDRAW are also useful. You can learn more through the CorelDRAW Training Course in Surat.

Choosing a React JS Learning Path

A practical learning path starts with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, then moves to React components, props, state, hooks, routing, and API integration.

You can review the topics covered in the React JS Training Course in Surat to understand how structured training can fit into your learning plan.

When comparing courses, check the curriculum, practical projects, trainer experience, and opportunities to build a portfolio. Choose a programme that matches your current knowledge and career goals.

Final Thoughts

Learning React JS takes regular practice. Start with small components, build complete projects, and learn to debug your own code. A strong understanding of JavaScript and consistent project work will help you develop the skills needed for modern frontend development.

What React project are you building right now? Share your experience or a beginner-friendly project idea in the comments.

title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation for Robust Conversational Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12757v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under realistic conditions, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior. Existing function-calling benchmarks underrepresent adversarial conversation trajectories, thereby limiting the training resources available for developing robust agents. We present MADS (Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation), a synthetic data generation pipeline that produces structured, diverse dialogue trajectories. We inject adversarial conversation, producing validated conversation trajectories that capture realistic, unhappy paths. Using MADS, we construct MADS-Bench: a benchmark spanning six domains, 55 personas, and 1095 conversations, with approximately 66% of conversations containing failure-prone conversation scenarios. We evaluate the robustness of the trained models using a two-stage training approach that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

title: IBBench-Light: A Paired Evaluation of Task-Conditioned Responses to External Directives
description:
arXiv:2609.13725v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: An external record may contain a procedure to apply or text to read, depending on the user's request. IBBench-Light tests both uses against the same record. Twelve semantic bases yield 144 matched pairs per model; four quantized instruction models produced 1,152 archived greedy responses. Paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA) requires both members to satisfy their output contracts. Qwen succeeds on 132 execute and 109 process prompts, but only 97 complete pairs, showing what marginal averages omit. We audit literal-target exposure and case normalization, then add 1,722 logged CPU generations to test directive-absent controls, twelve additional semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping. In the pinned Phi rerun, changing the end-of-sequence (EOS) set changes exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. A bounded IHEval comparison uses the same SmolLM2 checkpoint and output budget while preserving its published instruction roles and scorer. The benchmark measures conditional task and output-contract success. Its task margins and paired count need to be read together with the stopping policy.
