title: Distributed Task Scheduler System Design: Jobs, Retries, Leases, and Failures
description:
Distributed Task Scheduler System Design: What Happens When a Job Is Due?

A user schedules a payment for 9:00 AM. At 9:00, the scheduler finds the job and hands it to a worker. The worker calls the payment provider, the charge succeeds, and then the worker crashes before recording success.

What should happen next?

The scheduler cannot simply forget the job: it has no durable confirmation that execution finished. But blindly running it again might charge the customer twice.

That tension is central to distributed task scheduler system design. Finding work at the right time is only the beginning. A production scheduler must preserve jobs across failures, coordinate concurrent schedulers, handle retries without inventing exactly-once guarantees, and make recovery safe even when the outcome of an earlier attempt is unknown.

This article designs a distributed job scheduler for one-time and recurring tasks, with the focus on the correctness boundaries that matter in production.

First, define what the scheduler promises

A task scheduler answers when work becomes eligible to run. It does not inherently guarantee that a worker starts at an exact wall-clock instant, that a remote API succeeds, or that an external side effect happens exactly once.

A useful contract separates four timestamps:

  • due_at: the earliest instant a job is eligible to run.
  • dispatched_at: when the system hands an execution request to its delivery mechanism.
  • started_at: when a worker begins the attempt.
  • completed_at: when the system durably records a terminal outcome.

A 9:00 AM job may begin after 9:00 because of polling, queueing, worker capacity, or an outage. The product should define an acceptable scheduling lag and whether a late job should still execute. For workloads with hard deadlines, expiry is a separate policy: running a stale trade or promotion after its validity window may be worse than skipping it.

We'll assume jobs can be scheduled once or on a recurrence, cancelled or rescheduled before execution, retried for eligible failures, and queried for status. We will not assume every job is safe to repeat.

The basic architecture 

Client / API
     |
     v
Durable Job Database  <----- Recurrence Generator
     |                       (creates occurrences)
     v
Due-Job Discovery / Claimers
     |
     | atomic DB transaction:
     | claim + dispatch-outbox record
     v
Transactional Outbox
     |
     v
Outbox Relay -----> Durable Queue -----> Workers
                                           |
                                           v
                                    Business Side Effect
                                           |
                                           v
                                  Status / Attempt Store

Lease Reaper ------> expired attempts / safe retry decisions

The database owns the authoritative job state. The queue transports work to workers; it does not replace the scheduler's lifecycle record in this design. The outbox bridges the database-to-queue failure gap. A lease reaper finds attempts that stopped making progress.

This is one reasonable architecture, not a mandatory stack. A smaller scheduler can begin with indexed database polling and workers claiming rows directly. Some workloads use broker-native delayed delivery; others add Redis sorted sets or timing wheels for due-time discovery. Each alternative has different limits and failure semantics.

1. Store jobs durably before promising acceptance

A minimal model might look like this:

jobs
  job_id
  tenant_id
  payload_ref
  due_at
  status
  version
  creation_idempotency_key
  deadline_at

attempts
  attempt_id
  job_id
  generation
  status
  lease_expires_at
  started_at
  completed_at
  error_category

outbox
  event_id
  attempt_id
  payload
  published_at

For recurring work, add a schedule definition containing the recurrence rule, IANA timezone, misfire policy, overlap policy, and the next occurrence to generate. Each generated occurrence gets its own job identity.

The creation API should make a durable write before returning an unqualified success response. If a client times out after the commit, a stable creation idempotency key and a uniqueness constraint let it retry without creating a second logical job.

Job status is not the same as an attempt's status. A job may have multiple attempts; one attempt can fail transiently while the logical job remains eligible for retry. Keep enough attempt history to explain what happened without treating an old attempt's completion as permission to overwrite newer state.

2. Discover due jobs without scanning everything

The simplest viable due-work detector is a database index supporting a query shaped like:

SELECT job_id
FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'SCHEDULED'
  AND due_at <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
ORDER BY due_at, job_id
LIMIT 500;

The relevant index, bounded batch size, and query plan matter more than the particular batch size shown here. In a multi-scheduler design, merely selecting rows is not sufficient: two instances could read the same jobs. A claim must be atomic and conditional on current state, commonly using row locks such as FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction or an equivalent compare-and-swap transition.

SKIP LOCKED is a useful mechanism, not a universal requirement. Another design gives one elected leader ownership of due-time discovery. At higher scale, ownership can be sharded so independent schedulers process different partitions. Leader-based systems need fencing: a leader whose lease expired may resume after a pause and must not be allowed to make stale authoritative writes.

A Redis sorted set can speed up discovery when database due-time queries become a measured bottleneck. But if Redis is only an index, its loss must not erase jobs: rebuild it from the durable store, validate candidate jobs against authoritative state, and reconcile missing entries. A timing wheel similarly needs a durable backstop if its in-memory state can disappear.

3. The database-to-queue dual-write trap

Consider this dispatch sequence:

  1. Update a job to QUEUED in the database.
  2. Publish an execution message to Kafka, SQS, or another broker.

If the process crashes between steps, the database says the job was dispatched, but the broker never received it. Reversing the order creates the mirror failure: the broker receives a message, but the database update fails, so a retry may publish it again.

A transactional outbox handles the first problem without pretending the database and broker share one atomic transaction. In one database transaction, the scheduler records the job/attempt transition and inserts an outbox event. A relay later publishes that event to the broker and records publication progress.

The relay itself can crash after publishing but before marking the event published. It may then publish the same event again. Thus the outbox supports eventual, at-least-once publication, assuming the relay and broker recover and retry successfully; it does not make downstream execution exactly once.

Messages need stable identities. Repeated delivery of the same dispatch event should not create an unrelated business operation. The worker checks authoritative job and attempt state before claiming execution, and downstream effects still require their own idempotency protections.

4. Worker leases handle crashes, not exactly-once effects

A worker claims an attempt with a lease. While running, it renews the lease if the design supports long-running work. If the worker dies, a separate reaper can detect the expired lease and make the job eligible for another attempt.

But lease expiry is not proof that the old worker stopped. A long garbage-collection pause, lost heartbeat, or network partition can cause a live worker to lose its lease while it continues processing. Another worker may start at the same time.

To protect scheduler state, attach an increasing attempt generation or fencing token to conditional writes. A stale worker must not be able to mark a superseded attempt successful or overwrite the current state. Fencing protects only resources that actually validate it; it cannot retroactively undo a payment sent to an external provider.

The lease duration and heartbeat cadence must be chosen against real pause times, execution durations, and acceptable recovery latency. There is no universally correct TTL or heartbeat ratio.

5. Retry correctness depends on where the side effect happens

Return to the payment example. Worker A successfully charges the customer but crashes before saving the result. Worker B eventually receives a retry. From the scheduler's local records, the outcome is ambiguous.

A database flag saying started is not enough. If a worker writes that flag and crashes before the charge, treating the flag as proof of completion silently loses the payment. A completion marker written before an external effect has the same flaw.

There are three importantly different cases:

Local database mutation. If the business change and completion record live in the same database, commit them in one transaction, with appropriate uniqueness or conditional constraints. Either both commit or neither does.

External API supporting idempotency. Send a stable business-operation idempotency key that survives retries and worker replacement. The provider's documented deduplication semantics and retention window determine what guarantee this actually gives. An internal attempt ID is usually the wrong key because it changes across attempts.

External API without reliable idempotency. A timeout cannot reveal whether the operation happened. Durable pending state, provider-side lookup where available, and reconciliation may resolve uncertainty. If the provider offers neither deduplication nor reliable outcome lookup, the scheduler cannot promise exactly-once external effects. The product must explicitly choose how to handle that residual risk.

This is why at-least-once execution attempts and exactly-once business effects are not interchangeable claims.

6. Retry policy is more than exponential backoff

Retries begin with failure classification:

  • Transient failures, such as some timeouts or temporary service unavailability, may be retried if the operation is safe to retry.
  • Rate-limit responses require respecting the provider's applicable retry guidance and quotas; an HTTP 429 is not permission to retry immediately.
  • Permanent validation or business-rule failures generally should not be retried unchanged.
  • Ambiguous outcomes require idempotency or reconciliation, not optimistic assumptions.

Use bounded attempts, capped exponential backoff with jitter, execution deadlines, and a dead-letter or terminal-failure path. Backoff spreads attempts over time, but does not by itself cap aggregate load on a struggling dependency. A dependency-scoped rate limit or retry budget, and circuit breaking when appropriate, prevent thousands of independently reasonable retries from combining into a retry storm.

A dead-letter queue is not a garbage bin. Preserve job identity, failure reason, and attempt history. Replays should be authorized, observable, rate-limited, and idempotent. A replay may create a new attempt, but it must not invent a new business operation identity.

7. Recurring schedules need separate occurrence identities

“Every day at 9:00 AM” is a schedule definition, not one job repeatedly moved back to SCHEDULED.

Generate individual occurrences, each with a deterministic identity based on the schedule and nominal occurrence. A unique constraint ensures two generators recovering from a failover do not create duplicate logical occurrences.

For a recurring schedule, store the recurrence rule and an IANA timezone, such as Asia/Kolkata or America/New_York. A fixed UTC offset is not sufficient for local-time recurrences across daylight-saving changes. Every occurrence must be resolved using the timezone rules applicable to that date.

Two edge cases need explicit product decisions: during spring-forward, a configured local time might not exist; during fall-back, it might occur twice. Decide whether to skip, shift, or select a particular occurrence rather than relying silently on a date library's default.

After downtime, decide whether to skip missed runs, catch up all valid runs, or coalesce missed runs. For billing, every period might matter; for a transient reminder, replaying all missed notifications could be actively harmful. Also specify whether successive occurrences may overlap, should queue behind one another, or should skip while an earlier occurrence is still running.

8. Cancellation is a race, not just a status update

Cancelling a scheduled job before it is claimed is relatively straightforward. Cancelling a queued job is harder because its message may already be in transit. A worker should check authoritative state and the dispatched version before beginning work; a stale message must not bypass a recorded cancellation.

That check still does not make cancellation of running external work instantaneous or reversible. Cancellation may be cooperative, and there can be a race after the final pre-execution check. A precise API distinguishes cancellation requested, cancelled before execution, and already running or completed. Never promise that a successfully returned cancellation can undo an email already sent or a charge already made.

Rescheduling also changes job version and due time; old queued messages must not cause execution against an obsolete schedule.

9. What happens at the 9:00 AM burst?

Imagine millions of jobs become due at the same moment. It is tempting to prescribe Redis or a bigger queue immediately. Neither is a universal answer.

The first bottleneck might be the due-time index, claim contention, outbox relay, broker ingress, worker concurrency, network egress, or a third-party API's quota. Measure due-to-dispatch lag, queue waiting time, worker start lag, oldest overdue job age, retry rate, and downstream throttling to identify where capacity is actually exhausted.

Bound due-job scans, partition hot scheduling ranges when needed, enforce per-tenant quotas and fairness, and pace dispatch to sustainable downstream throughput. Predictable bursts may justify pre-scaling workers.

Pre-staging work before its due time can help only if execution is still gated by eligible_at. Starting a 9:00 AM payment at 8:59 merely to flatten the graph is a correctness regression unless early execution is explicitly allowed.

A backlog is not necessarily data loss. But a scheduler that keeps accepting jobs faster than they can execute needs an explicit lateness and admission-control policy; a queue cannot manufacture downstream capacity.

10. Recovery paths worth designing before production

Scheduler crashes. Durable due jobs remain discoverable. Another claimer or a fenced new leader takes over, then performs a bounded catch-up scan rather than dispatching every overdue job at once.

Database primary fails. Job creation and authoritative transitions may become unavailable. Reject uncommitted new requests explicitly instead of pretending an in-memory buffer is durable. Replica promotion's data-loss exposure depends on replication acknowledgments and actual lag, not a universal recovery number.

Broker is unavailable. Outbox events remain durable and publication lag rises. Once the broker returns, drain the outbox at a controlled rate.

Worker crashes or an ACK is lost. A lease expiry or broker redelivery may cause another attempt. That is expected at-least-once behavior; side-effect idempotency or reconciliation is the safety boundary.

A leader resumes after losing ownership. Conditional state transitions and fencing reject stale authoritative writes. Merely holding a time-limited lock is insufficient.

A region fails. A standby region can take over only under a defined ownership and fencing protocol, using whatever state was durably replicated. Recovery time and potential data loss are properties of the chosen replication and failover design, not free guarantees of “multi-region.”

11. The trade-offs that change the design

Decision Simpler starting point When a different approach earns its cost
Due-time discovery Indexed database polling Redis index, timing wheel, or sharding when measured due-discovery limits justify them
Scheduler coordination Atomic competing DB claimers Leader election or shard ownership for particular contention and operational requirements
Dispatch Direct database-backed worker claims for a small design Queue + transactional outbox for decoupled, durable, high-throughput handoff
Worker recovery Fixed leases for bounded short jobs Renewable leases and checkpoints for long or variable-duration jobs
Missed recurrences Explicit per-schedule misfire policy Different catch-up behavior by workload, not a universal replay-all rule
Regional topology One authoritative region with standby More complex cross-region ownership only when availability needs justify it

The goal is not to collect the most distributed components. It is to add mechanisms that solve a demonstrated bottleneck or close a specific correctness gap.

A practical way to reason through the interview

Start by asking what “run at 9:00” means, how late jobs may be, whether retries and overlap are acceptable, and which external side effects cannot safely repeat. Establish peak due-job rate and burstiness as assumptions, not universal scale thresholds.

Then evolve the design in order: durable jobs; indexed due discovery and atomic claiming; a dispatch boundary; worker leases; retry classification; idempotency at the business-effect boundary; and failure recovery. Add an outbox when dispatch crosses a database/broker boundary. Add a fast due-time index or sharded ownership only when its benefits outweigh the consistency and operational costs.

A strong system design explanation follows one job through an actual failure. The most revealing question is often not “how do you schedule a million jobs?” but “what do you do when the external effect succeeded and your worker cannot prove it?”

The essential takeaway

A distributed task scheduler is a durable coordination system under uncertain execution outcomes. Its clock determines eligibility, its store preserves intent, its dispatcher delivers work, and its workers perform effects. Those boundaries can fail independently.

Reliable scheduling therefore comes from a combination of atomic claims, durable dispatch, leases and fencing, bounded retries, explicit recurrence semantics, and idempotency or reconciliation at the point where the business effect actually occurs. None of these alone provides a universal exactly-once guarantee.

For the full visual and production-oriented treatment, explore Distributed Task Scheduler — Complete Design, Architecture Deep Dive, Trade-offs & Decisions, and Failure & Scale Scenarios on SeeItFlow. The Visual Design Journey walks through the design's evolution interactively.

title: Generating Edit-Inducing Questions for AI Research Manuscripts
description:
arXiv:2609.36617v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study the ability of LLMs to generate edit-inducing questions whose answer will improve a paper draft. On a dataset of paired submission and camera-ready papers from ICLR and NeurIPS, we compare the helpfulness of questions from GPT models with or without full paper context to that of human reviewers. GPT produces more edit-inducing questions and its questions are associated with more extensive edits and cover a broader range of edited content compared to questions from reviewers. However, a much smaller percentage of the GPT questions are edit-inducing. Our analyses confirm that automated questions can be beneficial to authors and highlight an example task where proper attending to long context deteriorates reasoning model ability to produce helpful output.

title: Training User Simulators with Latent Intrinsic Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.13617v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User simulators are gaining attention as environments to train LLM assistants that can better cope with the nuances of multi-turn conversations with real users. Prior work on user simulation has emphasized generating realistic user utterances, leaving unexplored their potential as a source of direct feedback on the assistant's responses. Such evaluation signals may not be explicitly communicated in language, but can instead reside in the latent reasoning of users. In this work, we introduce user simulators with intrinsic feedback, namely, models equipped with latent evaluation states: internal thoughts, reactions, and scalar ratings that evaluate the assistant from a first-person user perspective at each conversation turn. We train LLM-based simulators using interaction logs between real users and assistants and demonstrate that intrinsic feedback improves simulation realism and critiquing behaviors versus prompted simulator baselines, while also providing turn-level evaluations that existing fine-tuned simulators lack. Further, evaluations generated by our trained simulators correlate better with human judgments than those of prompted simulators of the same size. Lastly, our experiments reveal that simulators with intrinsic feedback provide effective reward signals for multi-turn RL training, matching setups that rely on external judge LLMs for rewards while cutting RL compute by more than half.

title: Mesh-Native Tokenisation: Retrofitting Foundation Models to Unstructured Data
description:
arXiv:2610.12618v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Physics foundation models are an increasingly popular approach for building versatile emulators for spatiotemporal systems. They require tokenisation layers that lift physical field data into a latent representation suitable for dynamic processing. A typical choice for this layer is a convolutional encoder, which lifts field information in a locality-aware way and can be trained very efficiently. However, this choice cannot be applied to a large class of scientific computing problems where data are represented on unstructured meshes, for example simulations on domains with curved boundaries. Such data typically require graph neural network architectures, which are more expensive to train and, in the form currently used, encode information differently from their CNN counterparts, thus limiting the portability of physics emulators between these data regimes. In this work we introduce Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC), a locality-aware tokenisation layer that encodes unstructured mesh-based data in a way that is analogous to CNNs. This approach leads to models that can be trained once on mesh data and then deployed to arbitrary unstructured meshes, even if these are irregular, with minimal retraining. We show that this tokenisation approach can be used to retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models efficiently on unstructured meshes and provide theoretical results to confirm the consistency of this approach with classical CNN encoders. We demonstrate the favourable performance of this retrofitting approach, which in many cases reaches acceptable accuracy even in zero-shot deployment, and outperforms existing baselines after only a few epochs of fine-tuning, thus providing an efficient bridge between the two data regimes.

title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.13600v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.

title: MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution
description:
arXiv:2609.35664v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Gated Linear Attention (GLA) Transformers advance linear recurrent models through data-dependent gating, but face a core limitation: the fixed-capacity memory matrices across all heads operate at a single temporal resolution, where each token is processed individually, forcing them to simultaneously encode local syntactic patterns and long-range semantic structure, creating a representational bottleneck that gating alone is insufficient to resolve. We introduce Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention (MS-GLA), which addresses this by distributing attention heads across multiple temporal resolutions. Coarser resolutions pool longer token spans naturally specializing toward long-range dependencies, while finer head groups retain sensitivity to local syntactic structure. A learnable, input-dependent fusion layer dynamically recombines head group outputs at each timestep, expanding effective memory capacity without increasing per-head state size. This multi-resolution decomposition draws on principles from Multi-Scale State-Space Models (MS-SSM), adapting them to the gated linear attention setting. We evaluate MS-GLA on language modeling, recall-intensive tasks, and long-context generalization. Across all settings, MS-GLA consistently achieves higher accuracy and lower perplexity than GLA at matched parameter counts, with up to 18.9% improvement on recall-intensive tasks and 9.5% lower average perplexity on language modeling benchmarks, validating multi-temporal resolution decomposition as a principled and effective extension of Gated Linear Attention.

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: Co-Modifying Application Code and Deployment Infrastructure: A Causal Study of AI Agent Pull Requests
description:
arXiv:2610.12849v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Current software engineering agents are evaluated predominantly inside isolated sandboxes against synchronous local tests. However, deploying features in collaborative repositories requires modifying continuous integration (CI/CD) pipelines, containers, and provisioning manifests alongside application logic. Because agents lack deployment awareness, attempting cross-domain modifications introduces unverified dependencies into asynchronous integration pipelines. To isolate the causal integration overhead of dual-scope pull requests (PRs)-modifying both application code and deployment infrastructure-we evaluated 26,999 PRs across two large datasets (AIDev v5 and MOSAIC-3M) encompassing six agent architectures and an aligned human baseline. Using a deterministic four-tier file taxonomy and an exact 4D strata-matching framework, we isolated integration metrics under conditional exchangeability while controlling for application volume. We find agents operate primarily as application coders or chore workers, with maintenance tasks capturing 17.70% to 25.41% of agent PRs. Dual-scope modifications represent only 4.48% to 4.55% of agentic PRs, yet trigger bimodal integration outcomes. In the first mode, explicitly reviewed contributions experience protracted delays, adding a median penalty of +13.13 hours and multiplying time-to-merge by 3.24x, driven mechanically by CI/CD and provisioning manifests. In the second mode, maintainer gatekeeping exhibits a structural bypass: even for external contributors lacking repository write access, agent identity reduces the odds of human review by 63.7% compared to human peers. Consequently, 43.1% to 56.2% of dual-scope PRs bypass inspection to merge silently in a median of under 31 minutes. These uninspected modifications compromise build verification, demonstrating the need for deployment-aware benchmarks and strict path-based access controls.

title: Les Mis\'erables Dialogue: A film-based network representation of social communication
description:
arXiv:2610.13148v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In this work, we revisit the classic Les Mis\'erables benchmark network from the perspective of social communication. Using the 1998 film adaptation of the novel, we construct the publicly available Les Mis\'erables Dialogue temporal text network, which explicitly distinguishes speakers, addressees, and other recipients of each utterance, along with its content and timing. Using the ten social dimensions model, we also derive multilayer network representations of the network, in which layers correspond to distinct relational dimensions. Beyond the network dataset, this work offers a general methodology for building similarly rich communication datasets from similar narrative sources.

title: When Edge Independence Fails: Joint Graph Diffusion with Latent Sociability Priors
description:
arXiv:2610.13765v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Discrete graph diffusion models corrupt graph structure through independent edge updates with a Markovian noise model. Combined with the exchangeability requirement on the output distribution, the terminal prior is necessarily an Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi (E-R) random graph. This has a fundamental consequence for unconditional graph generation without node features: in the large graph limit, any GNN denoiser applied to an E-R graph approximately outputs an E-R graph, making effective denoising difficult. In practice, generated graphs fail to recover meaningful node heterogeneity and higher-order structure. Previous models introduced specialized node features to compensate, framing this as an expressivity problem, while the role of the prior remained unexamined. We instead address the root cause by introducing the Latent Sociability Prior (LSP) and a join} diffusion process that co-evolves latent node sociability variables and graph structure, removing edge independence while preserving exchangeability. Unlike existing latent graph diffusion methods, the sociability mechanism requires no complex encoder: its sole role is to guide edge updates and preserve node heterogeneity throughout the trajectory. We validate our approach on multiple graph generation datasets and show that the proposed framework more accurately captures graph distributions than baseline methods without node features.

title: Nexus Repository Manager: 112,040 title matches against 185 fingerprints
description:
Nexus Repository Manager: 112,040 title matches against 185 fingerprints

The artefact store that every build trusts

A repository manager sits in the build path. Every continuous integration job pulls dependencies through it, every release is published to it, and in many organisations it is also the only place where some internal artefacts exist at all. Compromise of a repository manager is a supply-chain event, not a single-host incident.
That makes its external footprint a legitimate question, and the difference between the available queries is instructive.

What was queried

Two queries against ZoomEye on 2026-09-26 (UTC), Python SDK, sub_type=all, page size one:

  • title="Nexus Repository": 112,040
  • app="Sonatype Nexus": 185

Interpreting the spread

The title query returns a large count because the phrase appears on login pages, in documentation, and on instances that render the product name in the page title. It is an upper estimate of pages that mention the product.
The fingerprint returns 185. Repository managers are frequently deployed on an internal network behind a proxy that handles authentication, and the externally visible portion may be only a redirect or a proxy error page that carries no distinctive signature. As with other administrative systems, the fingerprint measures the recognisable population rather than the deployed population.
The two numbers are not in conflict. They describe different questions, and the honest answer to how many repository managers are exposed cannot be produced by either query alone.

Operational priorities

  1. Treat the repository manager as an identity system. Its administrative accounts should not be the same as the build accounts, and anonymous read access is a decision that should be made explicitly rather than inherited from a default.
  2. Protect the publish path. Ability to write to a repository that builds consume is equivalent to the ability to inject code into every product that depends on it. Restrict write credentials to named pipelines and monitor publish events.
  3. Review the components that proxy to public registries. A group repository that fetches from the internet on demand imports whatever the upstream serves, and that path should have its own review.
  4. Separate administrative access from developer access, and place the administrative interface behind the same network controls as other management planes. Vendor guidance covers repository management configuration, and the underlying access model is described in the product's own documentation.

Limitations

These figures do not indicate the version, the repository formats configured, or whether anonymous access is enabled. They do not establish that any instance is vulnerable. Where the question is whether a specific deployment is exposed, the answer comes from the operator's own inventory.

References

  • Sonatype Nexus Repository Manager — https://help.sonatype.com/en/nexus-repository-manager-3.html
  • Sonatype security guidance — https://help.sonatype.com/en/security.html
  • Sonatype Nexus Repository 3 security — https://help.sonatype.com/en/sonatype-nexus-repository-3-security.html
  • ZoomEye documentation — https://www.zoomeye.ai/doc

title: Service tiers now available on AI Gateway
description:
AI Gateway now supports service tiering. Service tiers let you optimize for latency, throughput, and cost per request to match your use case. Pick a faster tier for interactive workloads (less queueing, higher token throughput), or a lower cost tier for background jobs that can tolerate more latency.

At launch, service tiering is available for OpenAI and Gemini models.

Service tiers work across every AI Gateway API format: AI SDK, Chat Completions API, Anthropic Messages API, OpenAI Responses API, and OpenResponses API. AI Gateway adjusts billing based on the tier each request used.

Tiers

  • default: Standard processing

  • priority: Faster processing at increased cost

  • flex: Lower cost with potentially higher latency

If a service tier is not specified, requests run on the default tier.

Basic usage

Set serviceTier under providerOptions.gateway. The same option works across all models and providers that support service tiers, so you can swap the model without restructuring provider-specific options:

The applied tier is returned in the provider metadata so you can confirm which tier served the request. This is useful when a priority request falls back to default capacity, or when comparing observed latency across tiers.

Service tier is serviced on a best-effort basis: if a tier can't be applied, the request runs on the default tier at the default rate, and only an invalid service tier value fails the request.

Per-provider control

If a model can be served by multiple providers and you only want a service tier on some of them or to configure different service tiers across each, set the tier on the provider's own namespace instead.

Pricing

AI Gateway applies per-tier rates automatically based on the tier each request actually used. If a priority request gets downgraded to default capacity, billing reflects the default rate, not the priority rate.

title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12569v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

title: From Mastery Profile to Simulated Response: Stochastic Student Knowledge Graphs (SSKG) for Faithful LLM Student Simulation
description:
arXiv:2608.21668v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate students at different mastery levels to generate synthetic training data and stress-test tutoring systems. Existing approaches primarily leverage an LLM to answer questions or perform tests while instructing it to simulate various skill levels. However, LLMs tend to execute at their full built-in capability regardless of target skill levels. We demonstrate this limitation on SAT questions across five mastery levels, where three LLMs consistently achieve 96.8-100\% accuracy. To faithfully simulate student behavior, we propose a Stochastic Student Knowledge Graph (SSKG)-based approach that leverages the strengths of LLM in different ways. Using human-in-the-loop workflows, LLMs extract a Curriculum Knowledge Graph (CKG) from course materials, decompose solution paths into CKG triples, and map incorrect distractors. A student's mastery profile is represented as an SSKG, assigning mastery probabilities to CKG triples. When solving a problem, the SSKG is sampled to determine the outcome, after which an LLM generates a rationale consistent with the sampled result. Compared to seven baselines which fail to separate profiles and maintain 86.5-100\% accuracy, our SSKG-based approach achieves 44.1-85.2\% accuracy from low to high-mastery profiles, creating a clear monotonic gradient. An ablation study demonstrates that taxonomy awareness contributes most significantly to these fidelity gains, particularly for lower-mastery profiles.

title: Heterogeneity-Aware Client Sampling for Optimal and Efficient Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2505.11304v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Federated learning (FL) commonly involves clients with diverse communication and computational capabilities. Such heterogeneity can significantly distort the optimization dynamics and lead to objective inconsistency, where the global model converges to an incorrect stationary point potentially far from the pursued optimum. Despite its critical impact, the joint effect of communication and computation heterogeneity has remained largely unexplored, due to the intrinsic complexity of their interaction. In this paper, we reveal the fundamentally distinct mechanisms through which heterogeneous communication and computation drive inconsistency in FL. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified theoretical analysis of general heterogeneous FL, offering a principled understanding of how these two forms of heterogeneity jointly distort the optimization trajectory under arbitrary choices of local solvers. Motivated by these insights, we propose Federated Heterogeneity-Aware Client Sampling, FedACS, a universal method to eliminate all types of objective inconsistency. We theoretically prove that FedACS converges to the correct optimum at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{R})$, even in dynamic heterogeneous environments. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets show that FedACS outperforms state-of-the-art and category-specific baselines by 4.3%-36%, while reducing communication costs by 22%-89% and computation loads by 14%-105%, respectively.

title: Robustness of Reinforcement Learning-Based Congestion Management in Low-Voltage Grids
description:
arXiv:2607.16004v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Increases in photovoltaic generation, charging of electric vehicles and heat-pump demand challenge operating limits in low-voltage distribution grids. This requires curative curtailment methods that can operate under sparse observability, noisy measurements, and imperfect grid models. Unlike prior end-to-end reinforcement-learning approaches for partially observable curtailment, this work decouples congestion detection and control by combining a random-forest violation pre-classifier with an actor-critic controller, and evaluates its robustness to measurement noise and grid-parameter mismatch. The framework is tested on a real low-voltage grid using synthetic future operating scenarios with low observability and controllability. With accurate grid parameters, the controller reduces total violation magnitude by 98.9%, and this performance remains nearly unchanged under the tested measurement-noise settings. Grid-model mismatch proves to be more challenging, but the controller still mitigates most violations under the tested mismatch assumptions.

title: Provably Accurate Shapley Value Estimation via Leverage Score Sampling
description:
arXiv:2410.01917v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Originally introduced in game theory, Shapley values have emerged as a central tool in explainable machine learning, where they are used to attribute model predictions to specific input features. However, computing Shapley values exactly is expensive: for a general model with $n$ features, $O(2^n)$ model evaluations are necessary. To address this issue, approximation algorithms are widely used. One of the most popular is the Kernel SHAP algorithm, which is model agnostic and remarkably effective in practice. At the time of our original submission, no strong non-asymptotic complexity guarantees were known for Kernel SHAP. We address this issue by introducing Leverage SHAP, a lightweight modification of Kernel SHAP that provides provably accurate Shapley value estimates with just $O(n\log n)$ model evaluations. Our approach takes advantage of a connection between Shapley value estimation and agnostic active learning by employing leverage score sampling, a powerful regression tool. Beyond theoretical guarantees, we find that Leverage SHAP achieves an approximately $50\%$ reduction in error compared to the highly optimized implementation of Kernel SHAP in the widely used SHAP library [Lundberg & Lee, 2017].

title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.13059v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.

title: Grade A Office Space in Noida: A Tech Lead’s Checklist
description:
At some point a tech lead gets pulled into an office search. Usually with a week's notice. Usually after the shortlist is already made.

If that shortlist is Grade A office space in Noida, here is what to check. Power and network first, because outages cost money. Then floor plate, air, commute, and the lease clauses that hurt in year three.

None of this needs a broker's vocabulary. It needs the same habits you use in a design review: ask for evidence, test the failure modes, and write down the answers.

What Grade A means in practice

There is no legal definition of "Grade A" in India. It is a market label. Property consultants use it, and each one draws the line a little differently.

In practice it usually means large, regular floor plates, central air handling, full power backup, professional facility management, and often a green certification. Treat the label as a claim, then check each part.

Power and uptime

Backup at the building level

Ask what share of your load the building's generators cover, and how long switchover takes. Then ask who owns the UPS. In most leases the tenant buys and maintains UPS for its own racks and desks.

Ask for the last outage log if they have one. A team that keeps one is usually a team that runs a tight building.

Two separate fiber paths

"Multiple ISPs available" is not the same as two physical paths. Ask where fiber enters the building and whether two providers use different entry points and risers.

If both lines share one trench, one backhoe takes them both out. Ask for the riser plan and look at it yourself.

Floor plate and efficiency

You pay rent on chargeable area. Your people sit in carpet area. The ratio between them is the efficiency.

efficiency = carpet_area / chargeable_area

Two buildings at the same rent per sq ft can differ by a lot in real cost per desk because of this ratio. Ask for both numbers in writing.

Also look at the column grid. Odd column spacing breaks desk layouts and wastes space that you still pay for.

Air, light and noise

Ask whether the building tracks CO2 and PM2.5 per floor, and whether you can see that data. Delhi NCR winters make outdoor air a real issue, so filtration matters here more than in many cities.

Check daylight depth. Floors that are very deep leave the middle dark. Then sit in the space at 4 pm and listen. Road noise and HVAC hum show up on a site visit, not in a PDF.

Commute math

This is where a dev can add real value. Most teams guess the commute. You can measure it.

Collect home pin codes from your team (anonymized, with consent), then compute travel times to each shortlisted site with an open routing engine such as OSRM or OpenRouteService.

# sketch: median drive time from team pin codes to each site
import statistics

def median_minutes(times_by_person: list[float]) -> float:
    return round(statistics.median(times_by_person), 1)

sites = {
    "site_a": [42, 35, 58, 61, 29],   # minutes, from your routing calls
    "site_b": [38, 47, 33, 52, 40],
}

for name, times in sites.items():
    print(name, "median:", median_minutes(times), "min")

Use the median, not the mean. One person living in Faridabad should not swing the result.

Add metro access as a second column. Noida is served by the Delhi Metro Blue Line and the NMRC Aqua Line, so walking distance to a station changes the picture for many staff.

Lease terms that bite later

These clauses look small in year one:

  • Lock-in period and what exit costs after it
  • Rent escalation rate and how often it applies
  • Rent-free fit-out period, and whether it covers your real build time
  • Reinstatement: do you have to restore the floor to bare shell on exit?
  • Right of first refusal on adjacent space if the team grows

Get your finance and legal teams on these early. A tech lead's job is to make sure the expansion clause matches the hiring plan.

One reference point

Max Square in Noida is an example of the profile above. It carries IGBC Platinum pre-certification, and Adobe leased about 1.58 lakh sq ft there. A large tenant of that kind has usually done its own technical checks.

Still, run your checklist anyway. Another company's needs are not yours. The Max Square project page has the basics to start from.

For more on the region's office market, the Max Estates blog and the Delhi NCR Properties guide cover Noida and Gurugram options side by side.

title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
description:
arXiv:2610.13909v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression.

title: Agentic Peer-to-Peer Networks: From Content Distribution to Capability and Action Sharing
description:
arXiv:2603.03753v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The ongoing shift of Artificial Intelligence (AI) from centralized cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) to local inference on edge devices is enabling Client-Side Autonomous Agents (CSAAs) - persistent personal agents that can plan, access local context, and invoke tools on behalf of users. As these agents collaborate directly, they form Agentic Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Networks. Unlike classic overlays exchanging static, hash-indexed content (e.g., BitTorrent), agentic P2P exchanges dynamic, heterogeneous capabilities that are potentially unsafe, requiring semantic discovery, drift management, and risk-aware execution. We outline the networking foundations for such collaboration. To organize this design space, we propose a plane-based reference architecture decoupling connectivity, semantic discovery, and execution. To support discovery under drift, we introduce signed, soft-state capability descriptors to support intent-aware routing. Finally, to cope with adversarial settings, we present a tiered verification spectrum - ranging from reputation signals (Tier 1) and canary probes (Tier 2) to cryptographic evidence (Tier 3) - that aligns trust costs with task risks. Results from a proxy-level discrete-event simulation suggest improved workflow success under poisoning and drift with modest control-plane overhead.

title: Scalable Circuit Learning for Interpreting Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2606.16939v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A prominent research direction in mechanistic interpretability is learning sparse circuits over LLM components to reveal how they jointly produce model behavior. However, raw neurons are polysemantic, making learned circuits hard to interpret. Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features alleviate this, but their high dimensionality makes existing intervention-based circuit learning methods computationally prohibitive. We propose CircuitLasso, a scalable circuit learning approach based on sparse linear regression. CircuitLasso recovers circuits whose structural accuracy matches that of state-of-the-art intervention-based methods on the benchmark data, at a fraction of the computational cost. For interpretability, CircuitLasso efficiently uncovers relationships among SAE features, showing how human-interpretable semantic features propagate through the model and influence its predictions. Finally, we validate the utility of our learned circuits by leveraging their insights to achieve comparable performance at substantially lower cost on a domain-generalization task.

title: Quality, Not Just Outcome: A Structural Scoring Framework for Selecting Coding-Agent Trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2610.13152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open coding agents are commonly trained through supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories whose final patches pass the benchmark test suite. However, this outcome-level filtering criterion ignores process quality: trajectories that eventually succeed may still contain inefficient interaction patterns such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification behavior, all of which become part of the imitation target. We propose TQS (Trajectory Quality Score), a structural scoring framework for coding-agent trajectories that operates directly on trajectory structure, requires no LLM judge, and runs in linear time. TQS characterizes trajectory quality through structural signals organized around structured convergence: information focus, intent--action alignment, and policy dynamics. Using 155,144 successful trajectories from a public open-license corpus, we rank trajectories by TQS and fine-tune coding agents on filtered subsets. Models trained on top-ranked trajectories consistently outperform those trained on random or bottom-ranked subsets on SWE-Bench-Verified. Our results suggest that process-level trajectory quality is an important factor in coding-agent supervision and that structural trajectory filtering provides an effective and scalable alternative to LLM-based data selection.

title: How Speechify serves 500,000 dynamic pages to 60 million users on Vercel
description:
Speechify on Vercel

  • 500,000+ pages served across 40+ languages

  • Cut costs 50% by auto-scaling with Fluid compute

  • Zero user impact on bad deploys with Instant Rollbacks

Speechify started as a tool for people with dyslexia. Cliff Weitzman, Founder & CEO, built it because reading was challenging and audio made it much easier. That initial use case led Speechify to tens of millions of users and an Apple Design Award for inclusion.

The product has since grown into something much larger: an AI work platform where 60 million people listen to documents, delegate tasks to agents, and complete work entirely through voice.

But the journey wasn't easy. Early on, they got hacked, and for half a day, every visitor was redirected to a casino website. After that, Denis Chernobai, Head of Growth Engineering, knew it was time to re-evaluate their infrastructure stack.

He decided to rebuild from scratch on Next.js and Vercel, and they ended up serving 40 times more pages, reaching a global audience three times larger, and achieving a 50% cost reduction. Since migrating to Vercel, Speechify has maintained 99.99% uptime and hasn't had a single security incident.

The cost of serving 500,000 dynamic pages

Speechify's website is its primary growth engine, with 10,000 base pages translated into 40+ languages across onboarding funnels, localized landing pages, and pricing experiments that change constantly. Static generation isn't an option because the content changes too frequently. But serving everything dynamically means every visitor is a potential database read, which compounds fast at hundreds of thousands of visits every day.

Vercel's Data Cache, ISR, and Next.js Cache Components resolve both problems at once. Pages render dynamically on first visit, cache immediately, and serve from the closest point of presence until something changes. The result is a global growth engine that scales without the infrastructure costs scaling with it.

The risk of shipping to 60 million users

Instant Rollbacks: ship fast, fix faster

Speechify's growth team ships constantly. New funnels and A/B experiments are deployed every few days to a user base of millions who expect everything to work. At that scale, a bad release isn't a bug for developers to fix. It's a revenue problem that can show up before anyone has time to react.

Before Vercel, a bad release meant scrambling to patch it before it became an incident. That shift from deploying with dread to deploying with confidence is what enables a small growth team to operate at a speed that would otherwise require a much larger team.

The cost of moving slower than the market

Next.js on Vercel: from code to global delivery

When AI moves this fast, you need to constantly ship to stay competitive, and capabilities evolve rapidly, often every few weeks. "We see new voice functionality and agents emerging that didn't exist just last month," said Rohan Pavuluri, Speechify's Chief Business Officer. Each week that an idea remains unimplemented is a week someone else might bring it to life first. With Next.js on Vercel, the only hurdle to turning an idea into reality is the code itself.

Speechify ships on Next.js with continuous deployments. The growth team doesn't have a dedicated platform engineering function and doesn't need one. Security patches apply automatically, infrastructure scales to demand with Fluid compute, and there's no deployment pipeline to maintain.

What's next

Speechify is expanding into new international markets and shipping new AI capabilities to millions of users.
