title: S$^3$R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.13202v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution. Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.

title: research-ledger: a skill that helps one person and several AI models not fool themselves
description:
I am not a professional researcher. I work in IT support, and in the evenings I explore ideas with several AI models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok. Over a few months, that work produced a lot of ideas and very few results. It also showed me a pattern: the main risk was never a lack of ideas, it was fooling myself.

Out of that experience came research-ledger, an MIT-licensed skill (a SKILL.md folder) that turns any assistant that reads skills into a disciplined research partner. This post explains what it does, where it came from, and what it has caught so far.

The problem: four ways to fool yourself with AI

  1. Models agree with each other. Three models saying "yes, this is a real connection" feels like evidence. It isn't. They share much of their training data, so agreement is a reason to check the algebra, not a result.
  2. Metaphors dress up as mechanisms. "X in physics is like Y in learning" sounds deep. Usually nobody can write the step that actually transfers.
  3. Thresholds move after the result. A 0.62 becomes "promising" because you wanted it to be.
  4. "I didn't find it in the literature" becomes "it's new." That sentence is a statement about your search, not about the world.

What the skill does 

idea ──► sieve (5 min) ──► translation ──► prior art ──► preregistration
                                             │
                     LANDED ◄────────────────┤
                                             ▼
                       pilot ──► confirmatory test ──► blind round (milestones)
                                             │
                                             ▼
            DEAD · LANDED · BRIDGE CANDIDATE · BRIDGE · EXPLANATION ──► ledger
  • Sieve first. Most ideas die in five minutes against a short checklist. They get no paperwork.
  • Translation. Every metaphor must become a measurable test or a precise statement with a proof goal. For each analogy, the skill asks one question: mechanism or theme? If you can't write the equation or step that transfers, it's a theme. It goes into the ledger, not into an experiment.
  • Prior art with scope. "Not found" is recorded together with the date, the search terms and the nearest source, never as novelty.
  • Preregistration. Predictions, thresholds, controls and statistical power are frozen before the run. In a Git ledger, a separate PREREG commit pushed before the run is the proof.
  • Pilot ≠ confirmatory test. A pilot may tune settings, but it never gives a PASS.
  • Blind rounds. At milestones, the same seed goes to two or three models from different labs, in clean conversations, with no project context.
  • Five verdicts.
    • DEAD: wrong, a tautology, or killed by a control.
    • LANDED: you rediscovered a known bridge. That's calibration, not defeat.
    • BRIDGE CANDIDATE: known pieces, connection not found, and a new prediction.
    • BRIDGE: only after a confirmatory test, a blind round and an independent check.
    • EXPLANATION: a known mechanism explains the pattern.
  • Append-only ledger. Every "no" is kept, together with what it shows and the regime where its lesson holds.
  • Glossary. Every new term gets its standard name and a reference, or an explicit "no standard term known". A new name is not a new idea.

On first use the skill asks six to eight setup questions and writes a small config: your field, where the ledger lives, which models you have for blind rounds, and how strict to be. It also asks which of your own favourite hypotheses must never be used as premises.

Where the idea came from

It grew out of my own log of tests, roughly forty numbered experiments so far, in toy quantum models, combinatorics, small neural networks and numerology of physical constants. Every rule in the skill is a scar from one of them. A few examples:

  • "Zero error" can mean nothing. One model reproduced a set of measured ratios with error 0.0000. Then we ran the forgery control: random "fake" target ratios. About 3,700 formula "keys" fit the real numbers, and just as many fit the fakes. The fit was empty. That became the lock-leakage check: count how many keys fit the real lock and how many fit forged ones, before celebrating.
  • The translator inserts what it already knows. I fed fringe and amateur texts through models to look for ideas the mainstream had missed. Most "insights" turned out to be the model translating the text into a known concept. Of the leftovers that survived translation, 6 of 8 were known science that the amateur had rediscovered. Hence the rule: check every leftover against the literature before combining it with anything.
  • A control that can't differ from the treatment proves nothing. In a continual-learning test, the "noise control" turned out to be algebraically identical to the treatment, so the test had no power at all. The rule now: write down, before freezing, why control and treatment cannot coincide by construction.
  • Equal strengths hide everything. Several effects worked only when all components had the same weight and vanished with heavy-tailed weights. The rule now: always retest with heavy tails.

The seed style for blind rounds was added this month, after I studied the published problem prompts in openai/math. Their prompts say prove **or* refute* (never "show that"). They fix the conventions explicitly, list what is not in the setting, give no method hints and use no analogies. I adopted all of that.

What it has caught (honest results)

Most ideas die, and that is the method working. The ledger is mostly DEAD and LANDED entries. A pile of LANDED verdicts is useful in its own way: it measures what the translator already knows, not progress toward something new.

An example of a clean kill. One idea combined local learning rules (no backpropagation) with "selectivity": only units that match the input get updated. We preregistered kill criteria and a strong control: a fly-olfaction-style model with fixed random features. The result:

  • the selective rule made units go silent and starve, so it learned worse than updating random units;
  • learned features beat the fixed random ones by a lot, and even a 16× wider random model stayed behind;
  • plain feedback alignment without any gating did just as well as the gated version.

So the idea is not refuted in general, but it brings nothing in that setting. Written down, with the regime, so nobody tests it again.

Cross-lab review catches different things, and sometimes catches the reviewer. This week I used the method on a side project: a machine-readable atlas of proof techniques extracted from the 719 manuscripts in openai/math. Forty extracted "signatures" were reviewed blind by Claude (Anthropic) and Grok (xAI), with a frozen rubric.

  • Grok's first attempt: 40 out of 40 "OK", every justification field empty, and in its own words "spot checks". It missed an objective error, a multiplicity of 0 where the source says 1. We marked that review invalid, not as "disagreement".
  • Grok's second attempt, with a required quote from the source for every "OK", in four batches of ten: a real review.
  • Agreement: the two reviewers agreed on 35 of 40 items. Each caught something the other missed: Claude was stricter on missing preconditions, Grok caught a claim taken from lines outside the cited range.
  • Result: both reviewers passed 32 of 40 signatures (80%, 95% interval 65–90%). An earlier 6 of 10 had an interval of 31–83%, which told us almost nothing.

The lesson went straight into the method: a review needs proof that the reviewer actually read the source, and planted faulty items that it must catch.

A test registered before it can be contaminated. For the atlas we froze two "needs" from an open learning-theory question before anyone searched the atlas with them in mind. The test pits the atlas against plain grep on the same corpus, with a blind evaluator. My own bet, written in the preregistration: most likely undetermined. We'll see.

Honest limits

  • The method reduces self-deception. It does not produce discoveries.
  • Blind rounds remove my context, not the models' shared training data.
  • The checks come from a specific history. Each one is labelled with its regime, and the skill asks you to rate it useful or not for your problem instead of applying it blindly.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/Freeky7819/research-ledger
cp -r research-ledger/research-ledger ~/.claude/skills/

It also works in Claude.ai (upload the zipped folder) and in Codex (the folder includes agents/openai.yaml). Then just talk to it: "here's an idea…", "evaluate this paper", "this test gave 0.62, what now?", "write a blind-round seed for this".

If a rule fails you, open an issue with the case. That is exactly the kind of "no" the ledger is for.

Disclosure: the skill, the experiments and this post were developed together with AI models (mainly Claude, also GPT, Gemini and Grok). The questions and ideas are mine; most of the code and much of the wording were written with them.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: I Stopped Treating the Reply as the Run
description:
I opened a fresh notebook because a polished reply kept arriving before any process on my side had started. The text looked complete, named a command, and even described a passing check that I had not executed. Why was I ready to copy that sentence into the log as if it were an observation? A chat transcript is not a process table, and it cannot show which binary actually ran.

That gap is the whole job for these notes, not a product tour and not a scoreboard. I wanted one place to ask a model for a patch, and another place to run a narrow command where I could read the exit myself. If those two records disagree, which one deserves the green mark in my notes? I wrote the rule down before I asked for another suggestion, because a fluent paragraph can impersonate a result.

What I tried in the first twelve hours

I started by splitting the work into two witnesses that are not allowed to grade each other. The first witness is a free model session, useful when I want a draft command or a short explanation without opening a paid console. The second witness is a free server session, useful when I need a shell that is not my laptop and not the model's imagination. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I am using those two availability claims only, and I am not treating a marketing page as a measured lab.

I did not record a model name, a quota, a machine size, or a promise that the free option will still look the same next month. Those details change, and inventing them would make these notes lie with a straight face. What I can repeat is the order of operations, which is dull on purpose and hard to fake. Ask, capture, hash the text, run an allowlisted command, then write the exit code beside the hash.

Here is the question I kept asking whenever the reply sounded finished. Did any process outside the chat actually start, and did it finish with a code I can quote? If I cannot answer that, the suggestion stays in a draft folder, even when the wording is clean. A free server is not magic here, because a free shell can still be the wrong tree, the wrong user, or a job that never left the queue.

The notebook I would actually rerun

The artifact below is a small recorder, not a benchmark and not a claim that I timed a vendor. I labeled the sample paths as examples, and I would run them on whatever host I was given rather than trust a pasted success story. You can drop the file on the server, point it at an allowlist, and refuse to print a green line unless the command exits zero. Would I merge a patch because the model said this script already passed? No, I would not, and the script is written to make that laziness slightly harder.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Suggestion ledger. Example workflow, not a recorded benchmark."""

import hashlib
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ALLOW = {
    "py_compile": [sys.executable, "-m", "py_compile"],
    "unit_check": [sys.executable, "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests", "-q"],
}

def stamp(label, text):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    return {
        "label": label,
        "sha256": digest,
        "chars": len(text),
        "at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

def run_allowed(key, extra):
    if key not in ALLOW:
        raise SystemExit(f"refusing unknown job: {key}")
    cmd = ALLOW[key] + list(extra)
    proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=120)
    return {
        "cmd": cmd,
        "code": proc.returncode,
        "stdout_sha256": hashlib.sha256(proc.stdout.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "stderr_sha256": hashlib.sha256(proc.stderr.encode()).hexdigest(),
    }

def main():
    suggestion = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    job = sys.argv[2]
    record = {
        "suggestion": stamp("model_reply", suggestion),
        "run": run_allowed(job, sys.argv[3:]),
    }
    record["agree"] = record["run"]["code"] == 0
    print(json.dumps(record, indent=2))
    return 0 if record["agree"] else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

The commands I actually want in the notes are boring, and that is a feature rather than a lack of ambition. I save the raw reply first, then I compile, then I decide whether a unit discovery is even on the allowlist for this host. A model can propose a piped install, and this recorder will not grow a new key just because the paragraph sounded urgent. Why give a draft the right to invent its own shell history?

mkdir -p notes/day1
# Save the raw completion yourself. Do not let the model write this file.
cp reply.txt notes/day1/reply.txt
python3 ledger.py notes/day1/reply.txt py_compile path/to/changed_module.py
echo "ledger_exit=$?"

I also keep a second command for the case where the server and my laptop do not share a tree. I print the host, the user, and the executable before I trust a zero, because a green code on the wrong machine is just a different story. This check is about identity of the run, not a feeling about how fast the free box answered.

python3 - <<'PY'
import getpass, platform, sys
print(platform.node(), getpass.getuser(), sys.executable)
PY
# Sketch only: replace the alias with the host your panel actually shows.
ssh free-host 'python3 -m py_compile path/to/changed_module.py; echo exit:$?'

I should label that ssh line as a sketch. The host alias free-host is a placeholder, not a hostname I measured, and your free server panel may name the box differently. If the panel does not give you a shell, this branch of the notes simply stops. A free model can still draft the patch, but it cannot substitute for the missing exit code.

What broke when I let the reply grade itself

The first break was social, not technical, and it showed up as soon as the paragraph said the check already passed. I had not started the server job, yet my fingers wanted to write verified next to the suggestion hash. Who was I trying to impress with that word, the future reader or my own impatience? I deleted the word and left the hash alone until ledger_exit existed.

The second break was a mismatched command that still looked related enough to fool a tired note. The reply described unittest, while the only allowlisted job I was willing to run that hour was py_compile, so a clean compile was not the test the paragraph had claimed. A zero from the compiler does not prove the tests, and a model's summary does not prove the compiler ran. I started writing the job key in the same line as the claim, so a later reader can see the gap without guessing.

The third break was environmental, and it is the one I would repeat the warning for. A free server can boot with a different working directory, a different user, or a queue that never dispatched the command I thought I had sent. If the ledger file is missing, I do not infer success from silence, because silence is how a dropped job disguises itself. Did the process start, and did it finish, or did I only receive a sentence about finishing?

A decision table I can reuse tomorrow

I do not want a score that pretends to measure model quality, because I never built that experiment and I will not fake the rows. This table only decides whether my notes may say ran, or must say draft. The columns are evidence I can point at, not feelings about how confident the wording sounded.

What I hold Reply only Server log only Both, and codes match the claim
Note status draft incomplete candidate
May I say verified? no no only for that job key
Next action save hash, do not patch rerun or fix the host read the diff, then decide
Failure I expect fluent false pass wrong tree or no dispatch still review the diff

A candidate is not a merge. It means the command I allowlisted exited in a way that matches the narrow claim, on a host I can name in the note. If the reply promised tests and I only compiled, the row stays incomplete even when the compiler was happy. Would I widen the allowlist mid-session because the model asked nicely? No, that change belongs in a separate note, after I have read the new command.

What I would repeat, and what I would not

I would repeat the capture step, the allowlist, and the refusal to write verified without ledger_exit in the same folder. I would also repeat the host line, because a free server is only useful if I can tell it apart from my laptop and from the chat. The free model access is the part I would keep for drafting, especially when I want another wording of a failing traceback before I open a paid seat. The free server option is the part I would keep for the run, because a suggestion that never meets a shell is still just a suggestion.

I would not repeat any sentence that quotes a quota, a GPU name, or a latency number I did not measure on that day. I would not pipe a model command into a shell, and I would not let the recorder accept arbitrary arguments from the reply text. I would not use this notebook to judge which vendor is best, because two availability switches are not a leaderboard. If your work needs a private dataset, a signed production host, or a change window with an on-call owner, do not rehearse that change on a free shared server just because the reply looked ready.

People who should skip this approach are easy to name, and I would rather name them than pretend the ledger fits every team. Skip it if you cannot read the server log yourself, or if policy forbids sending even a redacted traceback to an outside model. Skip it if the patch touches credentials, production data, or a service you cannot roll back before the next coffee. Skip it if you need a compliance attestation, because a field notebook is not an audit, and a free tier is not a contract I am willing to invent.

Limits I am leaving in the note

This workflow does not prove that the model understood the code, and it does not prove that the server matches production. A timeout of 120 seconds in the example is a guard for the sketch, not a service level I negotiated with anyone. py_compile catches syntax, not behavior, and unittest discover only helps if those tests already exist and already mean something. The hashes tell me whether the text changed, not whether the text was wise.

I also cannot tell you that the free model list or the free server button will remain in the same place, with the same limits, next week. Check the console you actually have, and write down what you see instead of copying these notes as if they were a status page. If the free server never gives you a shell, stop at the draft and run the allowlisted command somewhere you do control. A missing witness is a result, and it should look like a missing witness in the file.

If you already use MonkeyCode, the useful part is ordinary: open the free model path when you need a draft, open the free server path when you need a shell, and keep their outputs in separate files. I would still read the diff myself before I land anything, because agreement on an exit code is not agreement that the change is the one I wanted. The notebook is there so my future self can see what ran, what never started, and what I refused to call done.

title: Revisiting Accent Classification with DistilHuBERT: Speaker-Disjoint Evaluation and Cross-Corpus Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.13440v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent accent classification systems can achieve high accuracy in standard in-corpus evaluations. However, when speakers overlap between the training and test sets, such results may overestimate model robustness compared with real-world deployment scenarios. This study revisits the robustness of DistilHuBERT-based accent classification by using L2-ARCTIC and multiple external English accent datasets. The comparison covers file-level and speaker-disjoint splits, along with balanced external-data training and teacher-student pseudo-labeling. The large performance gap between in-corpus and external evaluations suggests that file-level evaluation substantially overestimates performance, while speaker-disjoint evaluation can provide a more realistic estimate of the generalization to unseen speakers. In this study, models trained on external data alone do not reliably generalize to L2-ARCTIC. Among the tested configurations, balanced external-data training offers the most promising supervised setting. The pseudo-labeling experiments further indicate that confidence-based filtering alone is insufficient under domain mismatch. Overall, this study suggests that robust accent classification evaluation should simultaneously include speaker-disjoint evaluation and cross-corpus testing.

title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.12707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark.
  Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.

title: DEAF: A Benchmark for Diagnostic Evaluation of Acoustic Faithfulness in Audio Language Models
description:
arXiv:2603.18048v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent Audio Multimodal Large Language Models (Audio MLLMs) demonstrate impressive performance on speech benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether these models genuinely process acoustic signals or rely on text-based semantic inference. To systematically study this question, we introduce DEAF (Diagnostic Evaluation of Acoustic Faithfulness), a benchmark of over 2,700 conflict stimuli spanning three acoustic dimensions: emotional prosody, background sounds, and speaker identity. Then, we design a controlled multi-level evaluation framework that progressively increases textual influence, ranging from semantic conflicts in the content to misleading prompts and their combination, allowing us to disentangle content-driven bias from prompt-induced sycophancy. We further introduce diagnostic metrics to quantify model reliance on textual cues over acoustic signals. Our evaluation of seven Audio MLLMs reveals a consistent pattern of text dominance: models are sensitive to acoustic variations, yet predictions are predominantly driven by textual inputs, revealing a gap between high performance on standard speech benchmarks and genuine acoustic understanding.

title: We audited our own agent's ledger: 10% of it was one test that never fails
description:
We audited our own agent's ledger: 10% of it was one test that never fails

We run an open-source AI agent (OpenAmer) that is
supposed to verify itself. Every artifact it produces gets executed and checked; the result
of each gate run is appended as one JSON line to a local ledger:

{"ts": "...", "task": "t...", "goal": "g...", "agent": "a...", "passed": true, "why": "exit=0 OK"}

The why field is the verbatim output of the check — exit code plus error text. Nothing is
self-graded. The repo ships a public snapshot of that file at
docs/EVIDENCE-LEDGER-SNAPSHOT.json,
and the live file on the laptop is memory/si/outcome_ledger.jsonl.

The number we were quoting

Measured just now (2026-10-13, 06:02 UTC), the ledger holds:
rows (gate runs) 1,852
passed 579
failed 1,273
aggregate pass rate 31.3 %
first row → last row 2026-09-28T21:14Z → 2026-10-13T04:47Z
distinct goals / tasks / agents 223 / 833 / 79

31.3 % is not a vanity number, and we have written before about why we publish a failing
pass rate. But "31.3 %" is an average, and averages hide everything. So we grouped the 1,852
rows by goal.

One goal owns 10 % of the ledger and has never failed

goal rows passed pass rate distinct tasks
gX 187 187 100.0 % 1
g629436015 89 19 21.3 % 23
g632120888 84 25 29.8 % 21
g701339560 69 19 27.5 % 35
g632125238 63 0 0.0 % 13
g1118815104 61 1 1.6 % 30
g1424830758 61 1 1.6 % 27
g1509632002 47 1 2.1 % 23

gX is 187 of 1,852 rows — 10.1 % of the whole ledger — recorded by a single agent
(a1) on a single task (tX), every single time with the same why:

exit=0 OK

It has never failed. Not once, in 187 runs going back to 2026-10-04.

That is not a sign of health. It is a sign that the check is too weak to fail. Whatever tX
does, it exits 0 and prints OK, and the ledger faithfully records a pass. A gate that cannot
distinguish "the artifact works" from "the artifact returned zero" contributes exactly one
thing to the ledger: a nicer average.

Strip it out and the honest numbers are:

with gX without gX
rows 1,852 1,665
passed 579 392
pass rate 31.3 % 23.5 %

Four and a half points of our pass rate were one trivial check looping. The goals that
actually do work — the ones with 20+ distinct tasks each — sit between 0.0 % and
29.8 %. One goal ran 63 times and produced zero passing runs.

What the failures actually are

1,273 failures, grouped by the first line of their why field:

signature rows share of failures
exit=1 Traceback (most recent call last): 761 59.8 %
exit=2 + a uv\python\cpython-3.11-windows… path 96 7.5 %
JSON decode errors (raw_decode, decoder.py) 199 15.6 %
regex not found in C:\Users\… 51 4.0 %

The dominant failure mode of a self-improving agent that writes its own verification code is
its own generated code raising an exception. Not the task failing — the checker failing.
The JSON-decode cluster is the same story one layer down: the agent's own scripts printing
something that isn't JSON, then a downstream parser blowing up on it.

We are not proud of these 1,273 rows. We are just not deleting them — a ledger you curate is
not a ledger, it is marketing.

The lesson we wrote down for ourselves

An aggregate pass rate is the wrong headline metric, because it is trivially inflated by
checks that cannot fail. Two rules came out of this audit:

  1. Report per goal, never only in aggregate. A mean over 223 goals tells you nothing about any one of them. The per-goal table above is the first thing we look at now.
  2. Treat "≥ 20 rows, 100 % pass" as a suspect, not a success. Exactly one goal in this ledger matches that pattern. In a healthy population that number should be zero, because real checks fail sometimes and trivial checks get caught.

We have not deleted gX. Deleting it would make the file prettier and less true. What it
needs is a real assertion, and that is a follow-up, not a rewrite of history.

Verify it yourself

  • The format is one JSON object per line: {ts, task, goal, agent, passed, why}; why holds the raw check output. Everything above was computed from the live file with a ~20-line Python script — Counter over goal, passed, and the first 40 characters of why.
  • Public snapshot in the repo: docs/EVIDENCE-LEDGER-SNAPSHOT.json (615 outcomes as of 2026-09-30, with the same field layout and a how_to_verify note).
  • Everything runs CPU-only on one Windows laptop. No GPU, no cluster, no cloud inference for the gate runs.
  • Repo: https://github.com/openamer/openamer (Apache-2.0).

Numbers here are a snapshot. The file grows every day, so the counts you read tomorrow will
differ — that is the point of keeping a ledger instead of a slide.

title: Vercel Sandbox supports forking

title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13194v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.

title: Beyond Pairs: Your Language Model is Secretly Optimizing a Preference Graph
description:
arXiv:2605.08037v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns language models using pairwise preference comparisons, offering a simple and effective alternative to Reinforcement Learning (RL) from human feedback. However, in many practical settings, training data consists of multiple rollouts per prompt, inducing rich preference structure that pairwise DPO fails to exploit. Collapsing such data into independent pairs discards transitivity, introduces redundant or conflicting supervision, and can lead to unstable optimization. We propose Graph Direct Preference Optimization (GraphDPO), a structured generalization of DPO that operates over directed acyclic preference graphs induced by rollout rankings. GraphDPO encodes dominance relations as edges and optimizes a graph-structured Plackett--Luce-inspired objective that aggregates supervision over dominated neighborhoods, propagating the transitive structure of the input preferences while recovering standard DPO as a special case. GraphDPO naturally handles tied and incomparable responses through an equivalence-class construction: responses with identical preference signals form graph layers, incomparable responses share a layer without an edge, and absent edges contribute zero loss, preventing the spurious gradients that strict total-order objectives incur. Under this layered construction, GraphDPO maintains linear per-prompt complexity via efficient log-sum-exp aggregation. We further incorporate optional ground-truth anchoring by inserting verified solutions as dominant nodes and applying an annealed schedule that stabilizes early training while gradually relaxing oracle supervision. Experiments on reasoning and program synthesis tasks demonstrate superior performance, suggesting that graph-structured preference modeling is a scalable and robust alternative to pairwise and listwise alignment objectives.

title: In-Context Learning for System Identification: Probabilistic Formulation, Long-Sequence Handling, and Benchmark Validation
description:
arXiv:2610.13411v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Traditional system identification typically involves two steps: initially, training data is processed to estimate a model of the system of interest; then, the model is used to predict outputs for new input queries. In contrast, recent in-context learning approaches learn a meta model that maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in a zero-shot fashion, bypassing explicit model estimation. This approach leverages a meta model trained offline, on large sets of synthetically generated data, to emulate the behavior of a system identification algorithm. In this work, we advance this meta-learning framework for system identification in three directions. First, we develop a unified probabilistic meta-identification architecture that combines a Transformer-based encoder-decoder with tailored mechanisms for handling long training sequences, enabling calibrated predictions over long horizons. Second, we show how a pre-trained meta model can act as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator for classical system identification, providing task-specific data that regularize parametric models when real data are scarce. Third, we systematically evaluate the framework on standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and on a challenging out-of-distribution scenario, demonstrating competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art methods and strong generalization, including cases where input-only adaptation is sufficient to handle significant distribution shifts.

title: How ElevenLabs Handles Emotion and Prosody in Speech
description:
What Makes a Voice Sound Human‑Like

When we talk about text‑to‑speech, the first thing that comes to mind is the raw audio waveform. But a truly natural voice is more than just a steady stream of sound; it’s a dynamic performance that carries emotion and prosody (the rhythm, stress, and intonation of speech). Developers who want to build immersive chatbots, audiobooks, or voice assistants need to understand how these elements are encoded and how they can be manipulated programmatically.

In this post we’ll dive into the core techniques behind emotion and prosody in modern TTS engines, with a focus on the industry‑leading platform ElevenLabs (https://try.elevenlabs.io/kr07zfuqn1bp). We’ll walk through the architecture, show you how to control prosody via the API, and share practical tips for fine‑tuning voice outputs.

The Building Blocks of Emotional Speech

1. Text Analysis

Before any audio can be produced, the system must parse the text:

  • Syntactic analysis determines sentence structure.
  • Semantic analysis identifies named entities, sentiment, and context.
  • Prosody mapping assigns default pitch, duration, and intensity to each token.

2. Prosody Embedding

Prosody is usually represented as a series of control parameters:
| Parameter | Typical Range | Effect |
|-----------|---------------|--------|
| pitch | 0.5 – 2.0 (relative to baseline) | Raised or lowered intonation |
| duration | 0.5 – 2.0 | Faster or slower speaking rate |
| volume | 0 �� 1 | Soft or loud emphasis |
| stress | 0 – 1 | Focus on specific syllables |

These parameters are fed into a neural synthesis model (often a variant of a Tacotron‑style encoder‑decoder) that generates a spectrogram. A vocoder (e.g., WaveNet, Parallel WaveGAN) then converts the spectrogram into a waveform.

3. Emotion Layer

Emotion is usually injected by conditioning the model on an additional latent vector that represents affective states. The vector can be derived from:

  • Sentiment scores (positive/negative/neutral).
  • Custom emotion embeddings (joy, anger, sadness, etc.).
  • User‑specified emotion tags.

The model learns to modulate pitch, energy, and timbre accordingly.

ElevenLabs’ Approach to Emotion & Prosody

ElevenLabs has built a real‑time, neural TTS engine that exposes fine‑grained prosody controls while keeping the API simple. Their key innovations include:

Feature How It Works
Prosody Tags <pitch=1.2>, <duration=0.9>, <volume=0.8> tags can be inserted inline with the text.
Emotion API A dedicated emotion field lets you pick from a curated list (joy, sadness, anger, fear, neutral).
Voice Cloning The system can learn a custom voice from just a few minutes of audio, automatically capturing its natural prosody patterns.

Because the prosody tags are part of the input text, you can mix static text with dynamic user‑generated content and still preserve natural rhythm.

How to Use the API

Below are three quick examples: a Python client, a JavaScript snippet, and a raw curl command. All use the same base endpoint: https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id}.

Tip: Replace {voice_id} with the ID of the voice you want to use. You can find this in the ElevenLabs dashboard.

1. Python Example 

import requests
import json

API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
VOICE_ID = "your-voice-id"

headers = {
    "Accept": "audio/mpeg",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "xi-api-key": API_KEY
}

payload = {
    "text": "Good morning, <pitch=1.1>everyone! Today we’ll explore <emotion=joy>the wonders of TTS.",
    "voice_settings": {
        "stability": 0.5,   # 0.0 (very stable) – 1.0 (high variability)
        "similarity_boost": 0.75
    }
}

response = requests.post(
    f"https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{VOICE_ID}",
    headers=headers,
    data=json.dumps(payload)
)

with open("output.mp3", "wb") as f:
    f.write(response.content)

2. JavaScript (Node.js) Example 

const fetch = require('node-fetch');

const API_KEY = 'YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY';
const VOICE_ID = 'your-voice-id';

const payload = {
  text: 'Hello, world! <duration=0.8>Let’s talk about <emotion=anger>the future of AI.',
  voice_settings: {
    stability: 0.6,
    similarity_boost: 0.8
  }
};

fetch(`https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/${VOICE_ID}`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Accept': 'audio/mpeg',
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'xi-api-key': API_KEY
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload)
})
  .then(res => res.arrayBuffer())
  .then(buffer => {
    const fs = require('fs');
    fs.writeFileSync('output.mp3', Buffer.from(buffer));
  })
  .catch(console.error);

3. curl Example 

curl -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/your-voice-id" \
     -H "Accept: audio/mpeg" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "xi-api-key: YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" \
     -d '{
           "text": "Hey there! <pitch=0.9>Did you hear about <emotion=sadness>the new update?",
           "voice_settings": {
             "stability": 0.4,
             "similarity_boost": 0.7
           }
         }' \
     --output output.mp3

Fine‑Tuning Prosody for Real‑World Apps

  1. Use Contextual Sentiment

    If your content is dynamic (e.g., user reviews, social media posts), run the text through a sentiment analyzer before generating speech. Map the sentiment score to the emotion field.

  2. Dynamic Pitch Adjustment

    For questions or exclamations, bump the pitch slightly higher. For statements, keep it neutral. A simple heuristic is:

   pitch = 1.0
   if text.endswith('?'):
       pitch = 1.2
   elif text.endswith('!'):
       pitch = 1.3

  1. Tempo Control

    In fast‑paced applications (e.g., news tickers), lower the duration parameter. For storytelling, increase it to give listeners time to absorb details.

  2. Avoid Over‑Tagging

    Too many tags can make the output sound mechanical. Keep the number of tags per sentence to 2–3 maximum.

  3. Voice Cloning for Consistency

    If you’re building a brand voice, clone a professional speaker. The resulting voice will automatically carry its natural prosody, reducing the need for manual tags.

Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them

Pitfall Why It Happens Fix
Mismatched Voice & Text Using a voice trained on a different language or style. Verify the voice’s language and domain before use.
Over‑Smoothing High stability values make speech sound robotic. Lower stability to ~0.3–0.5 for naturalness.
Emotion Overlap Mixing multiple emotion tags in one utterance. Stick to one emotion per sentence or use subtle variations.
Latency Issues Real‑time applications may see delays if the payload is large. Use streaming endpoints (if available) or pre‑generate audio.

Next Steps

You’ve seen how ElevenLabs exposes granular control over prosody and emotion with a clean, developer‑friendly API. Whether you’re building an audiobook, a conversational agent, or a voice‑enabled game, these controls let you craft a voice that feels truly alive.

If you’re ready to experiment, sign up today and get a taste of the power of emotion‑aware TTS. Use the link below to get started and unlock the full potential of your voice‑centric projects.

Try ElevenLabs now: https://try.elevenlabs.io/kr07zfuqn1bp

Happy coding, and may your voices always carry the right emotion!

title: SLX RadioTwin: industrial radio propagation studies with C++ and Qt
description:
Silicon LogiX introduces SLX RadioTwin, a desktop demonstrator for studying radio propagation in a three-dimensional industrial plant. The project brings geometry, antenna configuration, obstacles and robot movement into one environment, making it possible to compare how link conditions change. Version 0.2.1 is available on GitHub with a Windows evaluation package.

For a company integrating wireless sensors, gateways or mobile robots, the questions concern what happens along a mission: where does received power fall? Which obstacles does the radio path cross? What difference does a metal door make? RadioTwin makes these questions explorable and documentable, connecting each result to the assumptions that produced it.

Industrial connectivity also depends on geometry

A plant contains surfaces, volumes and passages that affect propagation. Tanks, machine tools, shelving and walls can change the signal path; a door changing state or a moving receiver introduces different conditions even with the same radio parameters. Studying these variations requires a shared reference between object positions, link configuration and numerical results.

The demonstrator uses a scene with 2,584 meshes in its complete representation: a process area with tanks and pumps, CNC machines, a warehouse, a raised control room, robotic arms, an inspection robot, two gateways and a sliding door. The cutaway view allows users to explore the interior, navigate and select components. The RF engine retains the complete enclosure, including walls and the roof, through 373 meshes dedicated to calculations. Opening up the factory view therefore keeps the obstacles in the radio model.

The robot, door and gateways share the scenario state between the visualization and RF geometry. This consistency makes it possible to relate a change in estimated received power to the configuration actually analyzed, while keeping the demonstration animation distinct from experimental measurements.

An explicit RF model with interpretable results

The solver combines free-space path loss with effective losses associated with the obstacles crossed. Intersections are calculated on the triangles of the RF geometry; a BVH, or bounding volume hierarchy, accelerates the search for possible intersections. Antenna positions, frequency, transmit power, gains, receiver sensitivity and material parameters are configurable.

An optional first-order reflection model uses image sources on six enclosure planes. Each path reports power, length and delay. Powers are summed incoherently: this version does not reconstruct the phase interference of a coherent multipath channel. Results distinguish power in dBm, losses and margins in dB, distances in metres and delays in nanoseconds.

Material coefficients are illustrative assumptions, not values calibrated against a real plant. The model supports comparative studies and checks of software behavior; field accuracy requires surveys and calibration. Diffraction, polarization, antenna patterns, protocol traffic and throughput are not simulated in the published version. The RF model documentation describes equations, units and limitations.

From individual links to scenario comparisons

The interface allows users to observe the link as the robot moves, visualize coverage, identify areas with reduced margin and save configurations for comparison. One example is studying an open door against a closed door while keeping the same planned route and radio parameters.

Coverage is sampled on a 49 × 37 grid at receiver height, with points occupied by solids excluded from the count. The mission profile contains 81 samples along the planned 16-metre corridor. The placement search evaluates up to 15 candidates for gateway A, keeps gateway B fixed and compares the worst value of the best link along the route. This is a comparison between defined candidates; mounting feasibility and site performance require separate verification.

The scenario laboratory in the software. The displayed values belong to an example using illustrative coefficients.

Analyses can be exported as PDF, JSON and CSV, retaining the configuration, geometry identity, units and assumptions. For a technical team, this makes it possible to discuss the same configuration, compare alternatives and retrace the reasoning behind a result. Before export, the application requires an updated analysis when the state has changed.

The technologies: C++, Qt Quick and native GPU rendering

RadioTwin demonstrates a software architecture that separates the interface, scenario management and numerical computation. The C++17 core handles asset import, geometry queries, propagation, coverage and candidate evaluation. The desktop presentation uses Qt Quick and QML, while the 3D viewport is implemented in C++ with QQuickRhiItem and Qt RHI, Qt's interface to the graphics backend.

The renderer groups geometry by material and uses GPU buffers. The Windows distribution has been checked with Direct3D 11. GLB/glTF assets retain geometry, materials and hierarchies; coordinate transformations connect the visual representation to the metric system used by the solver. GPU acceleration applies to rendering: RF calculations in this version run on the CPU.

QtConcurrent runs analyses asynchronously on copies of the scenario. The application checks the parameter version before accepting a result, avoiding the presentation of calculations for an earlier configuration as current. The numerical core is distributed as a DLL with a public API and a versioned ABI, while its implementation remains proprietary. This separation provides a starting point for modules and integrations agreed with the customer.

The build uses CMake, Ninja and the Qt 6.12.0 / MinGW GCC 13.1.0 kit. Checks cover reference equations, radio link-budget accounting, reflections, geometry consistency, persistence and scenario comparison. Public-distribution audits also run through GitHub Actions. These checks verify implementation consistency; RF validation at a plant requires independent measured data.

A concrete basis for tailored industrial tools

The value for companies is the opportunity to evaluate a working application and define a specific need: studying a robot route, comparing permitted antenna positions, documenting a scenario or connecting a model to plant data. This provides a basis for a technical discussion about geometry, devices, available measurements and acceptance criteria.

The custom-development section presents eight proposals, explicitly not implemented in the demonstrator. They cover measurement-based calibration and uncertainty quantification; coherent wideband channels with fading and Doppler; MIMO and beam steering; interference and coexistence; robot missions with radio and navigation constraints; network design with redundancy; CAD/BIM, OPC UA or MQTT integration; and research into programmable RIS surfaces and joint communication and sensing.

Each proposal identifies required data, expected outputs and checks to agree on. The application lets users select modules and prepare a local brief containing objectives and constraints. Extensions can then be defined through a feasibility study, a development scope and a validation plan suited to the industrial case.

Evaluate RadioTwin and discuss a project

The SLX RadioTwin repository contains the frontend, public API, binary SDK, assets and examples. Release 0.2.1 includes a Windows x64 package that runs without installing Qt and without radio hardware. A demonstration video with 3D animations and actual software screens is also available.

The license permits study and business evaluation; production integration and distribution of modifications require an agreement with Silicon LogiX. To assess a custom development, contact us with the type of plant, the wireless devices involved, the behavior to analyze and the data already available. These inputs help define the required model, measurement activities and results to verify.

Originally published at Silicon LogiX.

title: New Platform Needed to Address Shortcomings in Hardware Coding Practice Tools
description:
Introduction

The landscape of hardware coding practice tools is, frankly, a wasteland of missed opportunities. Existing platforms, while functional, are riddled with shortcomings that hinder both learning and innovation. The core issues? Lackluster user interfaces that feel like relics from a bygone era, and feature gaps that leave users scrambling for workarounds. These tools, often built with a one-size-fits-all approach, fail to address the nuanced needs of hardware coding enthusiasts and professionals alike.

The UI Dilemma: Where Usability Goes to Die

Let’s dissect the UI problem. Most hardware coding platforms suffer from inefficient frontend code, leading to unresponsive interfaces under even moderate load. This isn’t just about aesthetics—it’s about functionality. When a user selects a problem, the system should respond instantly, not lag as if it’s processing a decade’s worth of data. The causal chain here is clear: poorly optimized code → increased latency → user frustration → abandonment. Golang, with its concurrency features, offers a solution by enabling parallel processing, ensuring the UI remains snappy even during complex hardware simulations.

Feature Gaps: The Missing Pieces of the Puzzle

Beyond the UI, existing tools lack critical features like modular problem integration and realistic hardware simulations. For instance, simulating a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) scenario requires precise modeling of physical processes—think voltage fluctuations, signal delays, or thermal expansion. Current platforms often simplify these to the point of inaccuracy, leading to user mistrust. Golang’s backend can address this by leveraging its performance capabilities to handle complex simulations without sacrificing speed. However, this requires a modular architecture to seamlessly integrate new problem types, ensuring the platform evolves with user needs.

The Open-Source Imperative: Collaboration or Chaos?

Open-sourcing the platform is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it fosters community contributions and bug fixes. On the other, it introduces risks like security vulnerabilities and inconsistent documentation. For example, an open repository without a continuous integration pipeline could lead to unvetted code merges, potentially exposing user data or breaking core functionalities. The optimal solution? Implement a rigorous CI/CD pipeline to automate testing and deployment, ensuring every contribution meets quality standards. Without this, the platform risks becoming a patchwork of incompatible features.

Scalability: The Achilles’ Heel of Growing Platforms

As the user base grows, so does the strain on the system. Database bottlenecks and backend inefficiencies can lead to performance degradation, turning a promising tool into a frustrating experience. Golang’s concurrency model can mitigate this, but only if paired with a scalable database architecture. For instance, using a distributed database ensures that problem retrieval and user progress tracking remain fast, even under high traffic. Without this, the platform risks becoming unreliable, driving users away.

The Path Forward: A Golang-Powered Solution

The development of a new hardware coding practice tool in Golang isn’t just a nice-to-have—it’s a necessity. By addressing the UI inefficiencies, feature gaps, and scalability challenges of existing platforms, this tool can redefine the learning experience. However, success hinges on leveraging Golang’s strengths while mitigating its limitations. For example, while Golang excels in concurrency, it may struggle with complex hardware simulations. The solution? Use Golang for backend processing and pair it with a specialized simulation engine for hardware-specific tasks.

In conclusion, the current state of hardware coding practice tools is a barrier to innovation. A new platform, built in Golang with a focus on modularity, scalability, and user experience, can bridge this gap. The stakes are high, but the potential rewards—a more skilled hardware coding workforce and a thriving community—make this endeavor not just worthwhile, but essential.

Problem Analysis

Existing hardware coding practice tools suffer from critical flaws that undermine their effectiveness, primarily stemming from poor user interfaces (UI) and missing features. These issues are not merely cosmetic; they directly impact the learning and problem-solving efficiency of users, creating a barrier to innovation in the hardware coding community.

UI Inefficiency: The Root of User Frustration

The UI of current platforms often becomes unresponsive due to inefficient frontend code. This inefficiency leads to increased latency, where user interactions—such as problem selection or submission—are delayed. Mechanically, this occurs because the frontend code fails to optimize resource allocation, causing the browser or application to throttle processing under load. For instance, rendering complex problem descriptions or handling multiple user inputs simultaneously can overwhelm the UI thread, leading to frame rate drops and input lag. This frustration often results in users abandoning the platform, as evidenced by high bounce rates and low session durations in analytics data.

Feature Gaps: Eroding Trust and Utility

Beyond UI issues, existing tools lack realistic hardware simulations and modular problem integration. For example, simulations often fail to account for voltage fluctuations or signal delays, which are critical in hardware design. Physically, these inaccuracies arise because the simulation engines simplify or omit key hardware behaviors to reduce computational complexity. This simplification leads to user mistrust, as practitioners recognize the disparity between simulated and real-world outcomes. Additionally, the inability to integrate new problem types or hardware scenarios limits the platform’s utility, stifling both learning and innovation.

Scalability Bottlenecks: A Hidden Risk

As user bases grow, platforms face scalability challenges due to database bottlenecks and backend inefficiencies. Mechanically, this occurs when the database cannot handle concurrent read/write operations efficiently, leading to query timeouts and data inconsistencies. For instance, a centralized database architecture struggles under high traffic, as each user request competes for the same resources. This results in performance degradation, where problem retrieval times increase exponentially with user load, ultimately crashing the system under peak usage. Such failures not only disrupt user experience but also erode confidence in the platform’s reliability.

Open-Source Risks: Security and Quality Control

While open-sourcing fosters collaboration, it introduces risks such as security vulnerabilities and unvetted code merges. Mechanically, security risks arise when contributors inadvertently introduce injection flaws or unauthenticated access points in the codebase. Without rigorous testing, these vulnerabilities can expose user data or compromise system integrity. Similarly, inconsistent documentation and unvetted merges lead to code fragmentation, where different parts of the platform become incompatible or unstable. This fragmentation slows feature development and increases maintenance overhead, undermining the platform’s long-term viability.

Optimal Solutions: A Hybrid Approach

To address these issues, a hybrid approach leveraging Golang’s concurrency features for backend processing and a specialized simulation engine for hardware-specific tasks is optimal. Golang’s concurrency model enables parallel processing, reducing latency and improving UI responsiveness by offloading heavy computations to background goroutines. However, Golang alone struggles with complex hardware simulations, necessitating a simulation engine that accurately models physical behaviors like voltage drops or signal propagation delays. This hybrid architecture ensures both performance and realism, addressing the core shortcomings of existing tools.

For scalability, a distributed database architecture is essential. By partitioning data across multiple nodes, it mitigates bottlenecks and ensures fast problem retrieval even under high traffic. Mechanically, this works by distributing read/write operations across nodes, reducing contention for resources. However, this solution requires careful tuning of replication strategies and sharding schemes to avoid data inconsistencies or single points of failure.

Finally, a rigorous CI/CD pipeline is critical for open-source contributions. By automating testing and deployment, it ensures that all code merges meet quality and security standards. Mechanically, this pipeline acts as a gatekeeper, blocking merges that fail tests or introduce vulnerabilities, thereby maintaining platform integrity.

Decision Rule

If a hardware coding practice tool exhibits UI unresponsiveness, inaccurate simulations, or scalability issues, use a hybrid Golang-simulation engine architecture with a distributed database and CI/CD pipeline. This combination addresses the root causes of these failures by optimizing performance, ensuring realism, and maintaining quality control.

Proposed Solution: A Golang-Based Hardware Coding Practice Platform

The new platform, built in Golang, is designed to address the critical shortcomings of existing hardware coding practice tools. By leveraging Golang's concurrency features and performance capabilities, the platform ensures a responsive UI and efficient backend processing, even during complex hardware simulations. This section outlines the design, features, and mechanisms that make this tool a game-changer for hardware coding enthusiasts and professionals.

1. Responsive UI Through Concurrency and Modular Architecture

The UI inefficiency in existing tools stems from poorly optimized frontend code, leading to increased latency and user frustration. To combat this, the platform employs Golang's concurrency model, which allows parallel processing of user inputs and simulations. This ensures that the UI remains responsive even under heavy load. For example, when a user submits a solution, the backend processes it asynchronously, preventing the UI thread from being blocked. Additionally, the modular architecture enables seamless integration of new problem types, ensuring the platform evolves without compromising performance.

2. Realistic Hardware Simulations with a Hybrid Approach

Existing tools often simplify hardware simulations, leading to inaccuracies that erode user trust. The new platform adopts a hybrid approach, combining Golang's backend processing with a specialized simulation engine for hardware-specific tasks. This ensures that simulations account for voltage fluctuations, signal delays, and other real-world hardware behaviors. For instance, when simulating a circuit, the engine models how resistors heat up under high current, causing resistance to increase and signal degradation, providing users with a more realistic problem-solving experience.

3. Scalability Through Distributed Database Architecture

Scalability is a common failure point in existing tools, with centralized databases struggling under high traffic. The platform addresses this by implementing a distributed database, partitioning data across nodes to mitigate bottlenecks. This architecture ensures fast problem retrieval and user progress tracking, even as the user base grows. For example, during peak usage, the database replicates and shards data, preventing query timeouts and maintaining performance. However, this approach requires careful tuning of replication and sharding strategies to avoid data inconsistencies.

4. Open-Source Collaboration with Robust CI/CD Pipeline

Open-sourcing the platform introduces risks like security vulnerabilities and unvetted code merges. To mitigate these, a rigorous CI/CD pipeline is implemented, automating testing and deployment. This ensures that all contributions meet quality and security standards. For instance, every code merge triggers automated tests that check for injection flaws and unauthenticated access points, preventing vulnerabilities from entering the codebase. However, maintaining this pipeline requires continuous monitoring and community engagement to address edge cases and emerging threats.

5. User-Centric Features for Enhanced Engagement

The platform incorporates user analytics to provide insights into problem difficulty and engagement levels, guiding content curation. For example, if users consistently struggle with a particular problem type, the platform can dynamically adjust its recommendations to include more practice problems in that area. Additionally, gamification elements, such as leaderboards and achievements, are introduced to enhance motivation. However, these features must be carefully balanced to avoid overloading the UI or distracting users from their learning goals.

Decision Rule: When to Use This Platform

If a hardware coding practice tool exhibits UI unresponsiveness, inaccurate simulations, or scalability issues, implement a hybrid Golang-simulation engine architecture with a distributed database and CI/CD pipeline. This approach addresses the root causes of these failures by leveraging Golang's concurrency for backend efficiency, a specialized engine for realistic simulations, and a scalable database architecture. However, this solution may not be optimal for tools with minimal user interaction or low traffic, where simpler architectures suffice.

Professional Judgment

The proposed platform is a paradigm shift in hardware coding practice tools, addressing both technical and user experience shortcomings. By combining Golang's strengths with a hybrid simulation approach and scalable architecture, it sets a new standard for functionality and reliability. However, its success hinges on continuous community engagement and rigorous quality control to maintain its edge in a rapidly evolving field.

title: Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets
description:
arXiv:2601.13600v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: NLP systems increasingly aggregate claims from retrieved passages, documents, and generated reasoning steps. Yet current factuality methods mostly verify claims individually or compare pairs of claims, leaving open the question of whether the entire aggregated claim set can be retained coherently. This misses a fundamental failure mode: claims may be locally plausible and pairwise compatible while still being jointly inconsistent. We formalize global consistency repair: given an inconsistent natural-language claim set, preserve the largest coherent subset while localizing the compact sources of inconsistency. We introduce QXR, an adaptive diagnosis-and-repair framework that treats an LLM as a noisy set-level consistency judge, localizes minimal conflicting subsets, and repairs the claim set by deleting a small hitting set of claims. Across LLM judges and benchmarks derived from VitaminC, FEVER, and conflicting-evidence RAG, QXR preserves substantially more valid claims than direct all-at-once judging while maintaining high precision. These results suggest that factuality in claim aggregation systems should be treated as a set-level repair problem, not only as local verification.
