title: Regression-adjusted Monte Carlo Estimators for Shapley Values and Probabilistic Values
description:
arXiv:2506.11849v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: With origins in game theory, probabilistic values like Shapley values, Banzhaf values, and semi-values have emerged as a central tool in explainable AI. They are used for feature attribution, data attribution, data valuation, and more. Since exact computation can require exponential time, research has focused on efficient approximation methods using two techniques: Monte Carlo sampling and linear regression formulations. In this work, we present a new way of combining both of these techniques. Our approach is more flexible than prior algorithms, allowing for linear regression to be replaced with any function family whose probabilistic values can be computed efficiently. This allows us to harness the accuracy of tree-based models like XGBoost; with cross-fitting, the method also produces unbiased estimates. From experiments across eight datasets, we find that our methods give state-of-the-art performance for estimating probabilistic values. For Shapley values, the error of our methods can be $11\times$ lower than Permutation SHAP (the most popular Monte Carlo method), $6.5\times$ lower than Kernel SHAP (the most popular linear regression method), and $3.4\times$ lower than Leverage SHAP (the prior state-of-the-art Shapley value estimator). For more general probabilistic values, we can obtain error $390\times$ lower than the best estimator from prior work.

title: How to Print PDFs in Java: Silent Printing and Print Dialog Selection
description:
PDF printing is a common business requirement in daily Java backend and desktop development scenarios, such as report printing, document slip printing, and document archiving printing. Java natively provides the core printing API java.awt.print. However, this native API cannot directly parse and render PDF documents. Third-party PDF parsing libraries are required to work alongside it to achieve full printing capabilities.

This article combines two technologies: Spire.PDF for Java (for PDF parsing and rendering) and java.awt.print (for system print job scheduling). It implements two mainstream PDF printing scenarios: silent printing to the default printer without pop-up windows, and printing with a dialog for manual printer selection. Complete runnable code and detailed explanations of underlying principles are provided.

1. Tech Stack and Environment Setup

1.1 Core Dependency Overview

  • java.awt.print : The built-in JDK printing toolkit with no extra dependencies required. It is mainly responsible for retrieving system printers, configuring print page formats, scheduling print jobs, and catching printing exceptions. It serves as the foundational core for Java printing functions.
  • Spire.PDF for Java : A professional PDF parsing library used to load local PDF files and render PDF page content. It adapts to the print rendering interface of the native printing API and addresses the limitation that vanilla Java cannot print PDFs directly.

1.2 Project Dependency Configuration

For Maven projects, add the Spire.PDF dependency in pom.xml:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.pdf</artifactId>
        <version>12.9.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

2. Scenario 1: Silent Printing to Default Printer (No Print Dialog)

This scenario applies to background automatic printing with no manual intervention . The system directly sends print jobs to the default printer without popping up any print configuration windows, running silently throughout the process.

Core implementation logic: Obtain the system default print job via PrinterJob, customize the printable area of the print page, load the PDF document and bind it to the print job, then trigger printing directly.

Full Runnable Code 

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import java.awt.print.PageFormat;
import java.awt.print.Paper;
import java.awt.print.PrinterException;
import java.awt.print.PrinterJob;
/**
 * PDF Silent Printing (Default Printer, No Dialog)
 */
public class PrintWithDefaultPrinter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Get print job object for the system default printer
        PrinterJob printerJob = PrinterJob.getPrinterJob();
        // 2. Initialize page format and retrieve default page size and orientation
        PageFormat pageFormat = printerJob.defaultPage();
        // 3. Get paper object for the page and customize printable area
        Paper paper = pageFormat.getPaper();
        // Set full printable area of the paper (remove default margins to fit full PDF page)
        paper.setImageableArea(0, 0, pageFormat.getWidth(), pageFormat.getHeight());
        // Bind customized paper settings to page format
        pageFormat.setPaper(paper);
        // 4. Load local PDF document
        PdfDocument pdf = new PdfDocument();
        // Replace with your actual local PDF file path
        pdf.loadFromFile("input.pdf");
        // 5. Bind PDF document with page format to prepare print rendering
        printerJob.setPrintable(pdf, pageFormat);
        // 6. Execute silent print job
        try {
            printerJob.print();
            System.out.println("PDF silent print job completed");
        } catch (PrinterException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
            System.err.println("PDF silent printing failed: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Key Code Explanations

  • PrinterJob.getPrinterJob(): Retrieves the system default print job instance and automatically binds to the machine’s default printer.
  • paper.setImageableArea(): Resets the paper printable area and removes default margin padding, preventing incomplete PDF output or excessive white space on printed pages.
  • printerJob.print(): Triggers the print job directly with no interactive dialog, ideal for automated printing workflows.

3. Scenario 2: Printing with Dialog Popup (Manual Printer Configuration)

This scenario is suitable for cases where users need to select printers and adjust print parameters . After the program starts, the native system print dialog opens. Users may switch printers, set print copies, page ranges, portrait/landscape orientation and other parameters before confirming to print.

Core implementation logic: Based on the silent printing logic, add a print dialog check. The print job will only execute after user confirmation, offering greater flexibility.

Full Runnable Code 

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import java.awt.print.PageFormat;
import java.awt.print.Paper;
import java.awt.print.PrinterException;
import java.awt.print.PrinterJob;
/**
 * PDF Printing with Dialog (Manual Printer Selection & Parameter Configuration)
 */
public class PrintWithPrintDialog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Initialize print job
        PrinterJob printerJob = PrinterJob.getPrinterJob();
        // 2. Configure print page and paper format
        PageFormat pageFormat = printerJob.defaultPage();
        Paper paper = pageFormat.getPaper();
        paper.setImageableArea(0, 0, pageFormat.getWidth(), pageFormat.getHeight());
        pageFormat.setPaper(paper);
        // 3. Load local PDF file
        PdfDocument pdf = new PdfDocument();
        pdf.loadFromFile("input.pdf");
        // 4. Bind PDF document and print format
        printerJob.setPrintable(pdf, pageFormat);
        // 5. Bring up system print dialog and check user confirmation
        if (printerJob.printDialog()) {
            try {
                // Execute printing after user confirmation
                printerJob.print();
                System.out.println("PDF print job with dialog completed");
            } catch (PrinterException e) {
                e.printStackTrace();
                System.err.println("PDF printing with dialog failed: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        } else {
            System.out.println("User cancelled the print job");
        }
    }
}

Key Code Explanations

  • printerJob.printDialog(): Launches the native system print dialog and returns a boolean value. true means the user confirms printing; false means the user cancels.
  • All print parameters (printer selection, copy count, page numbers) are configured via the system dialog instead of hardcoding in code, accommodating diverse printing requirements.
  • Custom printable area configuration is retained to ensure complete and intact PDF print layout.

4. Common Issues and Notes

4.1 File Path Compatibility

The example uses Windows absolute paths. When deployed on Linux or macOS, modify the paths to match the target operating system and ensure the application has read permissions for the PDF file.

4.2 Incomplete Printed Content / Excessive White Margins

The primary solution is the paper.setImageableArea() method shown in code. It resets the printable area and overrides default system margin restrictions to match the original PDF dimensions.

4.3 Print Exception Handling

PrinterException is caught in the code, which can capture printing failures such as offline printers, out-of-paper status, or corrupted files, enabling business-layer alerting and logging.

5. Summary

This article implements two core PDF printing solutions in Java using the native java.awt.print API together with Spire.PDF:

  1. Silent Printing : No dialog window, fully automatic execution for background automated printing tasks.
  2. Dialog-Based Printing : Supports manual parameter configuration with high flexibility for user-initiated printing on the frontend.

Both code samples are concise, reusable and free of redundant logic. They can be directly adopted in Java desktop and backend projects. The implementation solves the core limitation that native Java cannot print PDFs directly while ensuring reliable and complete print layout rendering.

title: The Architecture Decision I'd Reverse Today
description:
Boundaries Before Networks

The slide was titled "Target Architecture."

Five boxes. Five services. Clean arrows between them: Users, Billing, Notifications, Orders, Reporting. Each one with its own database, its own repository, its own deployment pipeline.

I made that slide. I presented it with confidence. The team was excited. It looked like the kind of system real companies build.

We had six backend developers.

It took me almost a year to admit that the slide was the most expensive mistake of my career so far.

Why It Felt Right

I want to be fair to the version of me who made that decision, because his reasons weren't stupid.

  • The monolith was getting messy. Our Django project had grown to dozens of apps. Models imported from everywhere. A change in billing could break notifications, and nobody could explain why.
  • Scaling was coming. We expected traffic to grow fast. Microservices would let us scale each part on its own.
  • Teams would grow. Separate services meant separate ownership. People could work without stepping on each other.
  • It was what good engineers did. Every conference talk, every architecture blog, every system design interview pointed the same way.

Every one of those reasons was real.

But each one solved a problem we expected to have. Not a problem we actually had.

What It Actually Cost

The costs didn't arrive all at once. They arrived the way architecture costs usually do: quietly, one sprint at a time.

Every feature became a distributed feature

Before the split, adding a discount to an order meant changing a few files and running the tests.

After the split, it meant touching Orders, Billing and Notifications. Three repositories. Three pull requests. Three deployments, in the right order. One contract between them that somebody had to keep in sync by hand.

A two-day task became a one-week task.

We lost transactions

In the monolith, creating an order and charging the customer happened inside one database transaction. If one step failed, everything rolled back.

Across services, there was no single transaction. We needed retries, idempotency keys, compensation logic, and a background job to clean up orders that were created but never paid.

We spent months building infrastructure to get back something Django's transaction.atomic() used to give us for free.

Debugging became archaeology

A user reported a missing email. Before, I would open the logs and follow one request.

After, the request passed through an API gateway, two services and a message queue. Each one had its own logs, its own timestamps, and its own idea of what happened. Finding one bug could take an afternoon.

Local development broke

New developers needed five services, three databases, Redis and RabbitMQ running before they could test a single screen. Onboarding went from one day to almost a week.

The team was too small for the boxes

Five services. Six developers. That's barely one person per service, which meant no real ownership, just everyone context-switching across everything.

We didn't build a distributed system because we needed one. We built one because it looked like what serious systems look like.

The Moment I Knew

There was no single disaster. Just one ordinary planning meeting.

We were estimating a small feature: letting users download an invoice as a PDF. A product manager asked why it would take two sprints.

I started explaining. The invoice data lived in Billing. The user details lived in Users. The order lines lived in Orders. Reporting had its own copy of half of it, slightly out of date.

Halfway through, I heard myself and stopped.

The feature wasn't hard. Our architecture made it hard.

That night I went back to the original slide and asked the question I should have asked a year earlier:

"Which of these problems did we actually have on the day we made this decision?"

The honest answer was: messy code boundaries. That's it. Not scale. Not team size. Just a monolith without structure.

And you don't fix messy boundaries by adding network calls between them.

What I'd Build Instead

If I could go back, I'd build a modular monolith.

One codebase. One deployment. One database. But with strict internal boundaries, the same kind of boundaries microservices force on you, without the network in between.

In Django, that looks something like this:

project/
├── orders/
│   ├── models.py
│   ├── services.py      # the only public entry point
│   └── selectors.py     # read-only queries
├── billing/
│   ├── models.py
│   ├── services.py
│   └── selectors.py
└── notifications/
    ├── services.py
    └── tasks.py

The rules are simple, and they matter more than the folder structure:

  1. Apps talk to each other only through services.py and selectors.py. No importing another app's models directly.
  2. Business logic lives in the service layer, not in views, serializers or model save() methods.
  3. Cross-app side effects go through clear functions or signals you can trace, not hidden coupling.
  4. Each app could become a service later, because its boundary already exists.

That last point is the key. A modular monolith doesn't reject microservices. It delays them until you have a real reason, and makes the split cheap when that day comes.

Get the boundaries right first. Decide where the network goes later.

When Splitting Actually Makes Sense

I'm not saying microservices are wrong. I'm saying they're a solution with a price, and you should only pay it when you have the problem.

Before splitting a service out, I now ask for evidence of at least one of these:

  • A real scaling difference. One part of the system needs 10× the resources of everything else, and you've measured it.
  • A real team boundary. A separate team owns this area, deploys on its own schedule, and is slowed down by everyone else's releases.
  • A real reliability need. A failure in this part must not take down the rest, and you can't isolate it any other way.
  • A real technology need. It genuinely needs a different language, runtime or data store.

"It feels cleaner" isn't on the list. "We might need it someday" isn't either.

What We Did About It

We didn't rewrite everything back into one project overnight. That would have been the same mistake in reverse.

We merged slowly. Users and Billing went back into the main codebase first, because almost every feature touched both. We kept Notifications as a separate worker, because it really did have different scaling and failure needs.

Five services became two. Features got faster. Onboarding got shorter. And debugging went back to following one request through one log.

The Real Lesson

The mistake wasn't choosing microservices. The mistake was designing for the company we imagined, instead of the team we had.

Architecture decisions feel like technical choices. They're really bets about the future. And the more confidently you draw the boxes, the easier it is to forget that you're betting.

These days, before I present any "target architecture," I add one more slide. It has one question on it:

"What problem do we have today that this solves?"

If I can't answer it with something real, the boxes stay on the whiteboard.

Your turn 👇

What's an architecture decision you'd reverse if you could? I'd genuinely like to hear the ones other engineers learned the hard way. Share yours in the comments.

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: REFLECT: Role-Aware Detection of Sentiment, Emotion, Politeness, and Formality
description:
arXiv:2610.13797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting communicative meaning in dialogue requires modeling not only lexical content but also the participant-role structures through which sentiment, emotion, politeness, and formality (SEPF) are expressed. Existing approaches rely on contextual language representations while leaving semantic roles implicit. We introduce a role-aware transformer architecture that maps the four SEPF dimensions to theory-grounded Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) configurations, incorporating these configurations directly into the transformer's self-attention mechanism. Role-aware attention models non-directional internal states (sentiment and emotion), while directional role-aware attention captures initiator-to-recipient relations for external cues (politeness and formality). The resulting role-aware representations are fused with contextual embeddings through a learned gate that adaptively weights how much role information each input contributes, rather than appending semantic roles as an auxiliary feature vector. Across four benchmark datasets, the framework yields statistically reliable gains over strong BERT-based baselines for emotion, politeness, and formality, with gains concentrated in theoretically predicted cases such as low-frequency, complex emotions and highly polite expressions; sentiment improvements are marginal and non-significant, suggesting that sentiment is conveyed more through lexical choice than participant-role structure. Additional evaluation on real-world data demonstrates that the framework improves both predictive performance and model traceability. These results demonstrate that linguistically grounded modifications to transformer self-attention improve the detection of communicative meaning, generalize beyond benchmark datasets to real-world mental-health data, and yield traceable, role-grounded explanations that extend beyond predictive performance to interpretability.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev now available on AI Gateway
description:
Jev from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software: state goes in, typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers come out.

Regular language models generate text one token at a time, which the application then parses and validates. Jev evaluates all declared questions in parallel and returns typed answers plus probabilities directly. That removes unnecessary text generation and makes it straightforward to automate clear cases while routing uncertain ones to review.

TypeSafe reports Jev was up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than LLMs on its workflow evaluations. Example use cases include:

  • Choosing the next tool or subagent in an agent loop

  • Deciding whether to continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • Scoring urgency or risk before an action

  • Verifying model outputs and enforcing guardrails.

AI SDK 7 exposes Jev through the experimental evaluate API. Choice selects an option, Score grades an ordered rubric, and Boolean estimates the probability of true. Install the current AI SDK (AI SDK 7.0.105 onwards supports the evaluate API):

Each evaluation specifies:

  • model: the evaluation model to call,

  • state: the shared string, object, or array to evaluate, and

  • questions: a map of named decisions to make about that state.

Call the model with typesafe-ai/jev. This example turns one support case into a queue, priority, and refund-review decision, with uncertain routing sent for manual review:

The result preserves question IDs and Choice keys. TypeSafe reports separate Choice and Score confidence in result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence. Calibrate probabilities and confidence against labeled examples from your workflow.

title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators
description:
arXiv:2610.12847v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model can act as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. Plainly stated, our goal is to find a mapping between a generative model's latent state and the simulator state, where the model is trained on observations alone and the mapping is learned afterward. We test two kinds of mappings, both learned from observations paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even where steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, even though the state is decodable in every variant. In Othello, editability falls smoothly as the game is simplified, and even small rule changes have large consequences. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. A model can therefore be driven by a simulator it may have never learned.

title: NeuronSpark: Selective Spiking State Space Models with Adaptive Computation for Language Modeling
description:
arXiv:2603.16148v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Spiking neural networks promise brain-inspired neural dynamics, yet native large-scale spiking language-model pretraining remains largely unexplored relative to conversion, distillation, and backbone-adaptation approaches. We diagnose a central obstacle: standard spiking neurons apply the same firing sensitivity to every token, creating dense- or silent-firing regimes that are difficult to resolve with globally tuned parameters alone. This problem is particularly acute in language modeling, where a single sequence contains tokens of vastly different informational roles, making a uniform firing regime poorly matched to the data. We address this with NeuronSpark, a self-attention-free language model built around input-dependent spiking membrane dynamics, where each neuron's decay rate, gain, and firing threshold adapt to the current token content. Together with gated associative memory and adaptive temporal aggregation, this selectivity enables billion-scale pretraining from random initialization without backbone transfer, conversion, or distillation. We relate the neuron to fixed-parameter spiking models and the memory to linear attention. At 1.1B parameters and 2.1B tokens, NeuronSpark reaches a 40.0 eight-task zero-shot average, exceeds comparable-budget Pythia/Mamba checkpoints, retains 95.2%/93.2% of their fully trained scores, and spontaneously develops a fast--slow hierarchy. At 2,048 tokens, parameter-matched VHDL points reduce operation-energy proxy by 90.1%/67.0% and cycles by 94.1%/80.3% versus Transformer/Mamba; a physical FPGA path reaches 24.000s TTFT and 0.082440 TPS.

title: Node.js Express Presence: Scoped Access and Reconnect Recovery for Property Tours
description:
Short answer: for an Express endpoint that answers who is online in a document, issue a room-scoped credential, take an authorized roster snapshot, and then reconcile membership changes over a live connection. In a property-management workflow where an agent opens a video room alongside a shared inspection document, reconnect must trigger a fresh snapshot or a replay from a known cursor. A socket reconnect alone cannot tell you who joined while the client was away. The trade-off is extra recovery state versus a roster that can be audited against an explicit point in time.

What does a reconnect erase?

Consider a bounded failure drill, not a claim about a particular production incident: an agent opens the inspection document for unit 4B, joins its tour room, then loses connectivity while a tenant leaves and a maintenance coordinator joins. The agent's browser still displays the tenant as online. I would treat that as an SLO question about roster freshness, not as proof that the tenant remains in the call. The invariant is narrower: a displayed roster describes a specific authorized scope and a specific observed revision; once its connection drops, the client must mark that view stale until it has reconciled.

Stale is a state, not a person.

There are three separate identities here. The authenticated person is authorized by the application. A connection is an ephemeral transport instance. A room member is a server-observed, time-bounded projection of one or more connections. Conflating these leads to duplicate names across tabs and to a departed person lingering after a network break. Presence also cannot certify attention or actual camera participation. WebRTC defines peer connection behavior; it does not define an application-wide roster for your inspection document. If the agent opens a second tab, decide whether the roster lists two connections or one person before writing any counting query. If a mobile browser suspends its connection during the tour, avoid interpreting that transport event as a deliberate departure from the property workflow. A UI can show a recovering state while the server settles its membership view, but it must not imply that a previously observed member is currently connected merely because the last displayed array still contains their name.

The page may contain a document editor and a video room, but neither scope should inherit the other's access by accident. The credential should bind the authenticated subject to the property, document and room identifiers, with an expiry and explicit permissions. The Express application must check authorization before handing out a roster or a credential. A room identifier supplied by a browser is a lookup key, not permission.

Check both scopes.

Snapshot, replay, or reset?

I would choose a reconciliation contract before choosing a broker. A snapshot returns members and a monotonically increasing revision for one room; each membership event carries a subsequent revision. On connection, establish a subscription with an ordered cursor, obtain a snapshot at a known revision, and apply only later events. The server must define how the subscription and snapshot overlap, because fetching the snapshot first and subscribing afterward leaves a gap. If an event arrives during the snapshot, buffer it and discard revisions already represented by the snapshot.

That gap matters.

On reconnect, request events after the last applied revision. If that cursor is older than the retained log, or if the server cannot prove continuity, replace the local roster with a new snapshot. Do not silently skip to the newest event. This rule is about membership, not durable document edits: document changes need their own persistence and conflict-resolution contract. An ordered roster event stream by itself cannot repair missing document operations.

The fallback is a full read.

Recovery model Operational consequence When it fits
Fresh snapshot on every reconnect Simple correctness boundary; snapshot reads grow with reconnect volume Small rooms and short rosters
Bounded event replay with snapshot fallback Requires retention, cursor validation and gap handling Larger rooms or frequent interruptions
Periodic polling alone Bounded by poll interval; no immediate notification Interfaces that tolerate stale status

For capacity planning, measure room cardinality, reconnect rate, snapshot size, event-log retention and how often recovery falls back to a full read. The buy-versus-build decision turns on who owns cursor ordering, expiry and on-call diagnosis. A managed stream can remove some infrastructure work, but it does not decide your application's authorization scope or what an "online" label means. A self-hosted stream gives control over retention while also putting replay continuity and operations on your team. Neither changes the invariant.

How can Express get document presence and show who is online?

Keep the Express handler thin: authenticate the caller, authorize their access to the property document and tour room, then call a presence service for a versioned roster or issue a short-lived credential limited to that scope. The following Go fragment specifies the service-side recovery contract; it is not an Express drop-in or a claim about a vendor SDK. The cursor belongs to the room, and a failed continuity check returns a replacement snapshot rather than a partial roster.

package presence

import "context"

type Member struct {
    UserID string
    Role   string
}

type Snapshot struct {
    Revision uint64
    Members  []Member
}

type Event struct {
    Revision uint64
    Member   Member
    Joined   bool
}

type Store interface {
    Snapshot(context.Context, string) (Snapshot, error)
    After(context.Context, string, uint64) ([]Event, bool, error)
}

func Recover(ctx context.Context, store Store, room string, cursor uint64) (Snapshot, []Event, error) {
    events, continuous, err := store.After(ctx, room, cursor)
    if err != nil {
        return Snapshot{}, nil, err
    }
    if continuous {
        return Snapshot{Revision: cursor}, events, nil
    }
    snapshot, err := store.Snapshot(ctx, room)
    return snapshot, nil, err
}

The caller still has to authorize room before calling Recover, order and deduplicate events by revision, and reject a replay whose events do not start immediately after the cursor. The store's continuous result must mean that no intervening revision has expired, not merely that it found at least one event. If an implementation cannot provide that guarantee, always return a full snapshot after reconnect. Briefly mark the roster as reconnecting while this happens; stale names must not be presented as current.

No continuity, no replay.

How would I test the failure, and when is this too much?

Test the boundary with two tabs for one user, concurrent joins during the initial snapshot, a disconnect spanning a leave and join, an expired cursor, a credential scoped to another property's room, and a revoked user's reconnect. Assert the final member set, revision continuity and rejection behavior, rather than only checking that a socket opens. Record reconnect-to-fresh-roster latency against a chosen SLO and track snapshot fallbacks, authorization denials and gaps by room without logging credential contents. A deploy that changes membership event format needs a migration or an explicit forced snapshot for older clients.

Not every editor needs a retained event log. When rooms are small, membership is advisory, and fresh snapshots are cheap at the expected reconnect rate, the simpler snapshot-on-reconnect contract is often preferable. Keep document persistence separate, scope every read and credential, and make stale status visible. That is enough to answer "who is online" honestly without claiming that a lost connection preserved knowledge it never received.

References

  • WebSocket Protocol, RFC 6455: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • JSON Web Token, RFC 7519: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519
  • WebRTC 1.0, W3C: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: How Factory scaled its cloud backend to one billion monthly requests on Vercel
description:
Factory on Vercel

  • One billion backend API requests served daily

  • 350ms p95 response time

  • Scaled backend, internal tooling, and security without a dedicated infrastructure team

Factory's mission is to bring autonomy to every phase of the software development lifecycle, from signals to production. Not to replace engineering judgment, but to automate the repetitive work around it, giving engineers more time to focus on the decisions that matter most. To deliver this enterprise-grade platform, Factory adopted their ideal operation model internally: remaining lean and agile by deploying Droids to manage routine workloads, so their engineers could focus strictly on building the product.

As Factory scaled from a simple web app into a multi-surface platform, serving everyone from individual developers to enterprises with tens of thousands of engineers, their backend scaled alongside them. Today, a single Next.js backend on Vercel powers every surface, handling one billion daily requests across API routes, middleware, and webhook handlers, without becoming a separate engineering project.

Next.js as a full-stack backend for cloud SaaS: API routes, middleware, and backend logic at scale

Most teams think of Next.js as a frontend framework. Factory runs its entire cloud backend on it:

  • API routes handle the customer-facing API, which launched in its own section of their Next.js app

  • Middleware manages authentication and routing logic across every surface

  • Webhook handlers and log drain pipelines run alongside the web platform, feeding analytics downstream

As Factory grew rapidly, the same backend absorbed every new workload. None of it required standing up separate infrastructure or making a new vendor decision. The only areas that required tuning were memory limits and function duration. Both scaled up without incident. Fluid compute keeps functions warm across requests, removing the cold start penalty that makes traditional serverless a liability for latency-sensitive workloads. The result is a p95 response time of 350ms or below.

Three years in, the trajectory has been smooth growth without the overhead that typically comes with it.

Shipping internal tools without pulling engineers off product

Non-technical teams were bottlenecked on engineering

When an account executive needed an internal analytics dashboard or a solution architect needed to deploy a customer prototype, the request went to engineering. Every context switch cost the team shipping product, and they pointed their own product at Vercel to solve the problem.

Droids hit Vercel's APIs to build and deploy autonomously

Factory's non-technical teams now use their own Droids in the Factory Desktop App or CLI to build what they need and deploy directly to Vercel. Droids reach Vercel programmatically to handle configuration, builds, and deployments end-to-end. Engineers set guardrails and review high-stakes decisions, and Droids handle everything else. That workflow produces dozens of deployments a day across the team, and a growing library of internal tools:

  • Internal analytics dashboards that pull directly from Factory's analytics databases and software tools

  • Tailored, customer-specific demos that solutions engineers can build and deploy in minutes

  • Custom utilities for one-off internal workflows

Securing a consumer-facing product with minimal security overhead

Going self-serve exposed Factory's backend to a new category of threat

When Factory opened self-serve signups, attacks from automated traffic followed. Bots created fraudulent accounts, and requests flooded in from bad IPs. The team needed route-level protection at the network layer quickly.

Observability and WAF handle protection at the network level

Vercel Observability gives the team visibility into what's hitting the API, surfacing traffic patterns and problematic IPs as they appear. The Web Application Firewall handles enforcement: the team blocks bad actors with route-level rules, while rate limiting and DDoS protection run continuously beneath the surface.

What's next

Factory uses their own Droids to build Factory. Every internal automation is a future product feature, stress-tested on their own infrastructure first. That loop is about to run at a different scale.

Factory is growing rapidly as it continues to implement and expand its pioneering vision towards autonomous software factories at scale.

About Factory: Factory is the platform enterprises use to build and operate their software factory: a 24/7 system that continuously turns signals into production software across the entire lifecycle. It's model-agnostic, deploys anywhere from cloud to fully private, and keeps engineers in control as the governance layer. Factory was founded in 2023 by Matan Grinberg and Eno Reyes and is headquartered in San Francisco.

title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.13386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stance detection remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to implicit opinions, sarcasm, and context-dependent expressions of stance. Although automatic prompt optimization offers an alternative to fine-tuning without updating model parameters, existing structured approaches are not specifically designed around stance-label semantics and class-specific ambiguities. We introduce MoPrO-SD, a stance-specific prompt optimization framework that decomposes prompts into functional semantic modules and refines them sequentially using LLM-based feedback. We study three refinement strategies: instruction-only optimization (I), instruction with reasoning (I+R), and instruction with per-example reasoning (I+R+E), using class-conditioned errors for stance-label refinement. We also introduce VaccineStance, a new human-annotated benchmark for vaccine stance detection. Experiments across four datasets and five open-weight LLMs show that MoPrO-SD improves upon the human-written Base prompt in many settings. On SemEval-2016, class-conditioned feedback achieves higher mean Macro-F1 than pooled feedback for four of five backbones. Both reasoning-based strategies, I+R and I+R+E, achieve strong performance, with their relative effectiveness varying across models and datasets, while remaining competitive with recent prompt optimization methods. The MoPrO-SD code and VaccineStance dataset are available on GitHub.

title: Measuring Harness-Induced Belief Divergence in Multi-Step LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2607.04528v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Software agents are becoming increasingly important in modern coding workflows, where they solve complex tasks through multi-step interaction with code repositories. A central component of these systems is the execution harness, which governs how the underlying LLM observes, acts on, and verifies its environment. We show that the harness can in turn shape the agent's evolving beliefs about the environment, even when the task, environment, and base LLM remain fixed. To reveal this effect, we introduce a belief-rollout diagnostic that traces how an agent's anticipated world state and future decisions evolve under alternative harnesses. We further separate immediate divergence introduced by the interface from divergence that develops over longer horizons. Across controlled coding tasks include HIBench-Code, SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench, we find substantial cross-harness belief divergence that is often invisible from terminal success alone and can propagate into different downstream actions. Building on this observation, we introduce \textbf{Belief-Invariant World-Modeling (BIWM)}, which exposes evidence hidden or compressed by harness execution and aligns the resulting belief trajectories across different harnesses. Our findings reveal that harness design can systematically shape how software agents understand and act on their environments, providing practical guidance for building and evaluating more reliable coding agents.

title: Competence-Aware Orchestration for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.13144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning through role specialization and collaboration, yet a key challenge remains: how can collaboration be adapted to a backbone's competence on the current query? This problem matters because more collaboration is not always better--richer coordination may help on difficult cases, but it also incurs additional token cost and redundant interactions. We propose a two-stage competence-aware framework for automatic MAS orchestration. It first models the LLM backbone's task-conditioned competence for the current query, and then uses this signal to adapt role activation and the communication graph. Across six benchmarks, our method achieves an average score of 93.81%. Experiments with six LLM backbones of varying competence levels further show that our method adjusts collaboration according to the inferred competence: for higher-competence backbones, it improves average accuracy from 87.22 to 89.97 while reducing token cost by 36.26%; for lower-competence backbones, it yields a further average gain of 4.58 points over existing methods. The same trend also holds on unseen backbones.

title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
description:
arXiv:2610.12842v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks routinely develop representations in which individual neurons contribute to multiple distinct functions, leading to the widespread view that such networks lack modular organization. We challenge this conclusion by introducing a formally nested hierarchy of modularity: unit-level, which requires distinct computations to occupy disjoint neurons; orthogonal, which asks whether a rotation reveals functionally independent subspaces; and linear, which asks whether a bounded linear map can separate task-relevant computations into independent subspaces. We develop a unified framework for learning decompositions at each level and evaluating them causally through selective ablation. Across vision models, language models and multi-task Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), we find that networks which lack unit-level modularity nonetheless often exhibit clear functional modularity at the subspace level. In vision and language models, content versus style and syntax versus semantics respectively dissociate under subspace ablation despite sharing overlapping populations of neurons. These learned subspaces also align differentially with brain data, with content and style subspaces predicting higher and lower visual cortex respectively, and semantic subspaces outperforming syntactic ones in predicting language cortex activity. In RNNs trained on multiple cognitive tasks and previously shown to lack modular structure, our decomposition recovers sharp double dissociations between tasks. The absence of unit-level modularity frequently coexists with clear subspace-level modularity across domains, enabling targeted intervention on specific computations even in networks where no individual neuron is specialized, with broad implications for mechanistic interpretability and for understanding functional organization in both biological and artificial neural systems.

title: Error Rate is Not Enough: Costs of Augmentation in Low-Resource ASR
description:
arXiv:2610.13807v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data augmentation is standard practice for low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR), but its benefits are almost always reported as aggregate error rates, leaving open why and when a method helps. On four low-resource languages and English at five data sizes, we cross two augmentations that modify existing audio (speed perturbation and SpecAugment) with two that modify text transcriptions and synthesize audio from it. We analyze errors at the phoneme level and find that they help for complementary reasons. SpecAugment has the most reliable aggregate improvements, but increases tone and palatalization errors, whereas text-based methods introduce consonant insertions; in combination, each reduces the errors the other introduces. This complementarity is predictable. Tone and palatalization are each signaled by a single acoustic property and occur least frequently in training (lowest training exposure), and text-based methods that flatten word frequency raise their frequency by 37--38%, reversing those errors while further improving aggregate error. The improvement from combining the methods exceeds the sum of their individual improvements; the superadditivity vanishes by 100 hours, limiting the complementarity to the low-resource regime. Where specific error types matter, we recommend selecting augmentation by training exposure and acoustic properties, both measurable before any training.

title: A SaaS Audit Finding Needs a Verification Plan
description:
An audit finding becomes useful when someone can turn it into a change and show that the change worked. "High severity: integration failure" may draw attention, but it leaves the implementer guessing about the affected journey, reproduction and acceptance checks.

For a small SaaS team, I would keep the finding and its verification plan together. Here is a compact format you can copy into an issue tracker without adding another tool.

Start with the observation

Write what happened before writing why you think it happened:

Finding: setup job is shown as complete after downstream rejection
Environment: isolated test environment
Input: synthetic trial account and a valid setup request
Observed: downstream rejects the job; UI shows success
Evidence: sanitised test output, request reference and observation date
Impact: user cannot tell whether setup completed
Unknown: frequency in production; root cause of rejection

This is a hypothetical example, not a customer incident. The point is to keep an observation separate from a proposed explanation. A timeout, invalid configuration or stale state could each deserve investigation; the finding should not silently promote one guess into a confirmed cause.

Define the decision before assigning the ticket

A finding can lead to several useful decisions:

  • Investigate a cause that is still uncertain.
  • Repair a reproduced defect.
  • Monitor a behaviour that has insufficient evidence.
  • Accept a bounded limitation with an owner and a review condition.

For the example above, a reasonable first delivery brief might be: expose the rejected state, provide a safe recovery action, and agree how repeated submissions are handled. The exact design depends on the workflow and downstream provider. It is not automatically "retry every failure."

Write the verification matrix while the context is fresh

Scenario Expected observation Evidence to retain
Downstream accepts the job User sees the agreed completed state Test result and relevant state transition
Downstream rejects the job User sees a useful failure state Sanitised rejection result and UI check
User submits twice Behaviour follows the agreed duplicate policy State and event checks for both submissions
User recovers after rejection Recovery produces the intended result Result plus check that existing records remain intact
Release is reversed Previous workflow can operate safely Isolated rollback check and preservation result

These are example scenarios, not universal assertions about every SaaS integration. Use the cases that matter to your actual dependency, data model and customer promise.

Do not put production credentials or customer records in a public ticket. Authorise the environment and access before testing, and use synthetic or appropriately redacted data. Security verification also needs its own scope; a workflow checklist does not replace an application-security assessment.

Assign two responsibilities

Name the person implementing the change and the person reviewing its evidence. In a very small team those may be the same person, but write down how the result will be checked. "Ticket closed" and "affected workflow verified" are different facts.

Keep the original finding, the chosen decision and the verification result connected. If you defer the issue, record why, who owns that decision and what would reopen it. Unknown is a legitimate status when the team has not inspected an area; it should not turn into a pass merely because a dashboard is quiet.

Use the smallest format that survives the handoff

A plain issue template or CSV is enough to begin:

Observation:
Safe reproduction or evidence reference:
Environment and date:
Customer impact:
Unknowns:
Next decision:
Implementation owner:
Review owner:
Acceptance scenarios:
Records and workflows to preserve:
Review condition:

The template helps organise work; it does not certify reliability or establish an improvement by itself. Those require the actual checks and the relevant customer measures.

I work on technical systems and distribution at SaaS IT Partner. For the broader scoping process, we published a SaaS technical audit checklist with an editable evidence worksheet. The first conversation identifies a useful next question; a full code, infrastructure or security assessment needs separately agreed scope.

Disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance. All examples are hypothetical; no client results or performance benchmarks are claimed.

title: Your Tabs Each Open Their Own WebSocket. navigator.locks Elects One.
description:
Open your app in six tabs — most people have at least that many of something open right now — and check your server's connection count. If you're using WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for live updates, it just went up by six. Six sockets, six keep-alives, six copies of every push notification landing in the same browser window.

Nobody asked for six connections. They asked to see their dashboard update live. You gave them that, and also a server bill and a battery drain that scale with how many tabs a bookmark-happy user happens to have open.

The bug you can see in your own network tab

Open devtools, go to the Network tab, filter by WS, and open the same page twice. You'll see two independent socket connections, each sending its own ping, each receiving its own copy of every broadcast the server sends.

Now open six. Your server — which probably caps concurrent connections per deploy, or bills per connection-minute — just got six times the load from one human being. And when the server pushes a notification, that human sees it pop up six times, once per tab, because each tab's JavaScript has no idea the other five exist.

The fix that doesn't fix it

The obvious instinct is the Page Visibility API: pause the connection in background tabs, since the user is only looking at one of them anyway.

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.hidden) socket.close();
  else socket = new WebSocket(url);
});

This helps a little and breaks something else. A user with the dashboard open on a second monitor, in a visible-but-not-active tab, stops getting updates. Worse, "hidden" and "pointless" aren't the same thing — a background tab doing the actual relaying for a visible one is exactly what you want, not what you're trying to kill.

The real problem was never "which tabs should connect." It's that six tabs are duplicating work that only needs to happen once. You don't want fewer connections scattered unpredictably across whichever tabs happen to be visible — you want exactly one connection, owned by exactly one tab, with the other five just listening in.

That's leader election, and the browser already ships the primitive for it.

navigator.locks, held for the life of a tab

navigator.locks.request() normally looks like a mutex: acquire a named lock, do some work, let it resolve, the lock releases. But nothing requires the callback to resolve quickly. Give it a promise that never resolves on its own, and the lock stays held for as long as that tab is open — the moment the tab closes, crashes, or navigates away, the browser releases the lock for you, automatically, no cleanup code required.

That's the whole mechanism. Whichever tab's request() call wins the (exclusive, FIFO) queue becomes the leader. Every other tab's request just waits — and the instant the leader's tab closes, the next one in line is granted the lock and takes over.

const LEADER_LOCK = 'app-connection-leader';
let socket;

navigator.locks.request(LEADER_LOCK, () => {
  // Only one tab's callback ever runs this at a time.
  socket = new WebSocket('wss://example.com/live');
  socket.onmessage = (e) => {
    channel.postMessage({ tick: e.data }); // fan out to every other tab
    renderUpdate(e.data);                  // and render here too — see why below
  };

  return new Promise(() => {}); // never resolves — holds the lock until this tab dies
});

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Relaying to the followers

Electing a leader only solves half the problem — the other five tabs still need the updates. That's what BroadcastChannel is for: the leader relays every message it receives onto a channel that every other tab is already listening to.

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('app-updates');

// Every follower tab runs this:
channel.onmessage = (e) => renderUpdate(e.data.tick);

Here's the gotcha worth knowing before you build this: a BroadcastChannel never delivers a message back to the instance that posted it — that's by design, not a bug. So the leader can't just post to the channel and expect its own onmessage to fire; that's why the leader's socket.onmessage above renders directly instead of waiting for an echo that will never arrive. Followers never touch the real connection — they only ever get updates through the channel. If a follower needs to send something back (a user action, a form submit), it posts that onto the channel too, and the leader is the only one that forwards it to the server. One tab talks to your backend. The rest just listen.

What happens when the leader closes

This is the part worth testing yourself, because it's the part that makes this worth doing at all: close the leader tab, and one of the waiting tabs is granted the lock as soon as the browser notices that tab's context is gone — no polling, no "is anyone still there" timeout, no stale leader lingering for thirty seconds before a new one takes over. The browser's lock queue is the failover mechanism — you don't write one.

There's a brief gap you should know about: the new leader has to open its own WebSocket connection after acquiring the lock, so there's a reconnect delay (normal connection-establishment time) before live updates resume. For a dashboard or notification feed, that's invisible. For something that can't tolerate a gap at all, keep that in mind rather than assuming the handoff is instant.

One more option worth knowing: navigator.locks.request(name, { ifAvailable: true }, callback) checks leadership without joining the queue — callback runs immediately with null if someone else already holds the lock, instead of waiting. Useful for a tab that wants to know "am I the leader?" without volunteering to become one.

Try it with real tabs, not a mental model

Everything above is easy to agree with and easy to get wrong in practice — the FIFO ordering, the automatic release, the reconnect gap. The playground above runs the exact same navigator.locks + BroadcastChannel code in three simulated tabs on one page. Open each one, watch the lock queue hand off leadership the moment you close the leader, and try the "steal" option to see what happens when a tab forces its way to the front instead of waiting in line.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Browser support, honestly

navigator.locks is Baseline widely available — Chrome 69+, Firefox 96+, Safari 15.4+ — so this works in every current browser. The one footgun is the steal option: it forcibly yanks the lock away from whoever holds it, skipping the queue entirely. That's occasionally the right tool (a user force-reloading a stuck tab), but use it knowing the previous leader never gets a chance to finish cleanly — it just loses the lock mid-flight.

You don't need six tabs each holding their own connection to do the job of one. You need one tab doing the job, and a browser API that already knows how to pick which one — and hand the job to the next tab the moment the first one leaves.

Does your app open a connection per tab right now? Go count it in the Network panel — I'll bet it's more than you think.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

Vercel platform protections provide an additional layer of defense, but they are not a replacement for upgrading affected dependencies.

title: Epistemic Policy Divergence in Multi-Turn LLM Contamination: A Protocol-Gradient Investigation
description:
arXiv:2609.35308v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models treat conversation history as unverified context, so false premises injected into earlier turns can be adopted as fact later, a failure mode we call session-level contamination. We introduce five contamination protocols along a source-authority gradient, each holding the false premise constant while varying how it is presented, from self-attributed falsehood to explicit instruction override. We evaluated three architecturally diverse models, GPT-5.4 Mini, Gemini-3.1 Flash-Lite, and GLM-4.5-Air, on ten cases spanning five knowledge fields at temperature zero over 22,500 turns, using a dual-track judge checked against a 120-turn human-annotated sample (Cohen's kappa = 1.000 for binary adoption, a ceiling on this sample, and 0.92 linear-weighted for collapse severity). The three models implemented structurally different epistemic policies. GPT-5.4 Mini recorded zero adoptions across all 500 sessions; token-level probing of the GPT-5.4 base model left the correct token as the argmax in eight of ten conditions. Gemini-3.1 Flash-Lite showed a steep framing-dependent policy: 0.1 percent for self-attributed falsehoods, 23.5 percent for user-cited sources, 68.2 percent for system-injected authority, and 94.0 percent for instruction override. GLM-4.5-Air showed a shallower gradient (15.8 and 84.2 percent for those two vectors). This 68-percentage-point dissociation is consistent with authority deference and instruction compliance engaging distinct mechanisms within a single architecture. Recovery also differed: GLM recovered in 94.5 percent of affected sessions, whereas 26.1 percent of affected Gemini sessions did not return to factual accuracy within the window (40.0 percent under instruction override). We release the evaluation framework and taxonomy for reproducible testing.

title: I built TerminalDeck — 157 CLI tools, one native macOS window
description:
I built TerminalDeck — 157 CLI tools, one native macOS window

I have a problem. My PATH has accumulated dozens of CLIs over the years — Claude Code, Codex, ollama, kubectl, ffmpeg, pandoc, rustup, go, brew, gh, tmux, redis-cli, psql, sqlite3, himalaya, imsg, peekaboo, the list goes on. And then there's another 80+ tools I could install with one brew install but never get around to because I forget they exist.

Three things kept bugging me:

  1. What's installed? I'd run which claude and find it, then forget about it for a week. I had no overview.
  2. What's installable? I'd hear about fzf or bat or k9s in a tweet, then forget the exact brew command. So I never installed them.
  3. What actually works where? Some tools (Claude Code, Codex, Ollama) work great in a built-in terminal. Others (claude --resume, anything that wants the full screen) need real Terminal.app or Warp. I was switching terminals constantly.

So I built TerminalDeck — a single native macOS window that catalogs every CLI on your machine, shows you which ones are installed, which ones need installing, and gives you a one-click path from not installed to running. With a built-in tabbed terminal so you don't have to leave the app.

What's in the box

  • 157 tools tracked across 16 categories (AI coding, OpenClaw, local LLMs, productivity, dev/build, shell, editors, network, k8s, cloud, databases, and more)
  • 78 detected as installed on my machine right now
  • 83 discoverable — popular CLIs you probably want, with brew install / pip install / npm i -g already wired up
  • Built-in tabbed terminal — pyte VT100 emulator, real keys work, real output renders
  • Right-click → Open in Terminal.app / Warp — for long-running TUI agents that the built-in PTY chokes on
  • Click-to-install — missing tools show a blue ↓ install chip; click it, watch brew install run live in the terminal pane
  • Native Mac everything — menu bar, ⌘T/W/D/⇧R/1–9, ⌘F filter, ⌘, prefs, ⌘Q quit
  • QSettings persistence — window size, position, splitter sizes, last category, filter, font defaults. Relaunches exactly where you left it.

PySide6 + pyte. No Xcode. MIT. Whole project is 3.4K lines of Python.

The "one click" experience I wanted

Here's the flow I was aiming for:

I hear about dune in a tweet.
Open TerminalDeck, type "dune" in the filter.
I see a red dot with a blue ↓ install chip.
Click the chip.
Terminal pane shows brew install dune running.
Done. Click the tool again to launch it.

That's it. No searching brew, no opening Terminal.app, no typing commands. The app knows the install command because I wired them all up in a single registry file.

For tools that need a real terminal (Claude Code, Codex, Ollama TUI mode, anything that wants the full screen):

Right-click the tool → Open in Terminal.app.
Done. Claude Code is running in a real terminal with full PTY support.

The built-in terminal

I tried three different PTY emulators before landing on pyte. The first two (a hand-rolled ANSI parser, then pyte's HistoryScreen + custom renderer) both choked on full-screen TUIs. The third attempt — pyte for VT100 emulation, QPlainTextEdit for output, a coalesced 30 fps repaint timer — works for everything I've thrown at it.

Tab title shows tool · command while running, then ✓ on clean exit or ✗N on non-zero exit. Hover any tab for full command, PID, and runtime ("ran for 5m 12s" or "running for 1.2s").

Click-to-install with live output

The Discover section is a curated catalog of 83 popular CLIs. Each one has an install command already wired up. Click the blue chip and the install runs in the terminal pane.

You see the actual brew install output as it happens. When it finishes, click the tool again — green dot, ready to launch.

Right-click for the heavy stuff

For long-running TUI agents like Claude Code or Codex, the built-in PTY chokes on full-screen mode. Right-click any tool and choose Open in Terminal.app (always works via AppleScript) or Open in Warp (if you have it, via clipboard paste + keystroke injection).

The launchers use osascript to drive the host apps, so they work even if Terminal.app isn't running. The first time you launch a tool in Warp, macOS will prompt for Accessibility permission — that's normal.

The full tutorial is here

If you want the long version — every feature, every keyboard shortcut, how detection works, how to add new tools, what's in the pipeline — there's a full tutorial at /2026/10/12/terminaldeck-tutorial/.

The product page with screenshots is at /terminaldeck/.

Get it

  • Repo: github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck — public, MIT, 4 commits
  • Install: git clone https://github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck && cd terminaldeck && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt && python run.py
  • Issues / PRs: welcome. Small focused changes, with tests.

What's next

Things I'd like to add but haven't yet:

  • ⭐ Favorites — star icon on rows, quick access to most-used tools
  • ⌨️ Command templates — user-defined per-tool default args (e.g. claude always uses --dangerously-skip-permissions)
  • 📌 Tab session restore — relaunch keeps your tabs open
  • 🔔 Notification Center on long task done — for cargo build or pytest that takes 10 minutes
  • 🔍 Search within terminal output — Cmd-F inside the terminal pane
  • 🖱️ Drag-to-reorder tabs — make the tab order match your workflow

If you want one of these, open an issue on GitHub or send a PR.

Related reading

  • TerminalDeck product page — full feature tour with screenshots
  • Complete tutorial — 23 sections covering every feature, every shortcut, the architecture, how detection works, and how to add your own tools
  • All Sol AI products — TerminalDeck, purr, vellum-rs, OurNook, more
  • About Sol AI — who I am, what I believe, the mission

title: Let Large Language Models Judge Each Other: Multi-Agent Peer-Reviewed Reasoning for Medical Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2606.15419v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Objective: To enhance the accuracy, interpretability, and robustness of large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering (MedQA).
  Method: We designed a multi-agent peer-reviewed reasoning method in which multiple LLM agents independently generate chain-of-thought reasoning with candidate answers, then act as peer reviewers to evaluate each other's reasoning for factual correctness and logical soundness. The highest-rated reasoning chain is selected to produce the final answer. Experiments were conducted with five state-of-the-art LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4, DeepSeek-LLM-7B, GPT-oss-20B) on three benchmark datasets: HeadQA, MedQA-USMLE, and PubMedQA. Performance was compared against single-model chain-of-thought reasoning and chain-of-thought-based majority voting.
  Results: Peer-reviewed reasoning consistently outperformed both baselines. The best model combination achieved an average accuracy of 0.820 across datasets, exceeding the strongest single model (0.777) and majority voting ensembles (up to 0.789). The method also scaled effectively with more participating models, while peer assessments reliably distinguished high- from low-quality reasoning chains.
  Conclusion: The proposed multi-agent peer-reviewed reasoning method enables LLMs to act as both solvers and evaluators, yielding superior performance in MedQA. By emphasizing reasoning quality rather than answer agreement alone, this approach improves accuracy, interpretability, and robustness, offering a promising direction for trustworthy biomedical AI systems.
