title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
description:
arXiv:2610.12818v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.

title: BenCoDiC: A Large-Scale Contextual Cyberbullying Corpus for Bengali Political News Discourse FULL VERSION
description:
arXiv:2610.13121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cyberbullying is a growing concern in online communities, yet existing Bengali corpora remain limited in contextual information, annotation transparency, scale, accessibility, and support for multidimensional analysis, thereby hindering robust detection and comprehensive study of harasser behaviors and networks. To address these gaps, we introduce the Bengali Contextual and Diverse Cyberbullying (\textit{BenCoDiC}) corpus, a publicly available contextual cyberbullying resource for Bengali political news discourse comprising 50,250 textual instances collected from 100 YouTube videos and their associated discussions. The corpus preserves caption--comment--reply relationships and is organized through a nine-dimensional star schema covering users, videos, textual content, context, time, engagement, political parties, target identities, and language categories. Five AI chatbots were initially evaluated for annotation but did not meet the predefined reliability criterion. Consequently, a two-tier human annotation process with expert verification was adopted, achieving Fleiss' $\kappa=0.86$ and Krippendorff's $\alpha=0.86$. Statistical analyses characterize the corpus, while transformer-based experiments show that incorporating conversational context yields modest but consistent improvements over isolated-text classification. \textit{BenCoDiC} supports context-aware cyberbullying detection and perpetrator-oriented behavioral and network analysis. The corpus is available at https://github.com/bencodic/BenCoDiC-Corpus.

title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
description:
arXiv:2610.12493v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tools have often been presented as methods to increase trust in machine learning models by making aspects of their algorithms more human-understandable. However, evidence accumulated over the last decade points to an overall failure of this objective, instead promoting overreliance on incorrect predictions, which can subsequently lead to algorithmic aversion. Rather, XAI appears to function primarily as a debugging tool, useful for obtaining anecdotal insights into, for example, features learned by the model. One of the main issues underlying this limitation is that XAI methods often oversimplify the inner workings of the model, resulting in misalignment between the explanation and the model itself - a behavior referred to as unfaithfulness or infidelity. Faithfulness can be interpreted as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model. Computing faithfulness in a rigorous manner would thus make it possible to quantify one of the various elements of trustworthiness of an explanation. However, existing metrics present significant limitations, making this quantification either infeasible or computationally expensive. In this position paper, we outline five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics and propose four possible avenues for research to bolster their reliability.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them

When an ACH payment fails, you don't get a generic "error." You get a return code—a three-character string like R01 or R10 that tells you exactly why the transfer was rejected. Understanding these codes is critical for building reliable payout systems and reducing failed transaction rates.

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) defines 85 return codes, each mapping to a specific rejection reason. As a developer integrating ACH payouts, you need to decode these codes and decide whether to retry, escalate, or route to an alternate payment rail.

The Most Common Return Codes

R01: Insufficient Funds
The recipient's account doesn't have enough money to cover a debit (pull) transaction. This is one of the most frequent returns. In a payout context, R01 means the sender's account lacks funds—your system should flag this and retry after confirming balance recovery, or alert the user to deposit more money.

R03: No Account / Unable to Locate Account
The account number or routing number is invalid or closed. This is permanent—retrying won't help. You should mark the account as invalid and ask the user to provide new banking details.

R10: Unauthorized by Customer
The customer disputes the charge and claims they didn't authorize it. This is a fraud signal and requires investigation. Don't retry; instead, log the dispute and contact the account holder.

R29: Corporate Customer Advises Not Authorized
Similar to R10 but from a business account. Treat as a fraud flag.

R20: Non-Transaction Account
The account exists but isn't set up to receive ACH transfers (e.g., a savings account with ACH restrictions). Permanent; request a different account.

R05: Improper Effective Entry Date
Your batch included a date that violates Nacha rules (e.g., a weekend or holiday when ACH doesn't run). This is a system configuration error. Check your batch submission logic and adjust the effective date forward.

R82: Unmatched Entry
The return batch references a transaction that doesn't exist in your records. This usually signals a reconciliation mismatch. Audit your batch IDs and trace numbers.

Handling Returns Programmatically

When your ACH processor returns a file with return codes, you need to:

  1. Parse the return code from the ACH return file (NACHA format 94X)
  2. Classify it as retryable, permanent, or investigative
  3. Route accordingly — retry, escalate, or notify the user

Here's a pattern:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, payout_record):
    retryable_codes = {'R01', 'R05', 'R09'}
    permanent_codes = {'R03', 'R20', 'R23'}
    fraud_codes = {'R10', 'R29'}

    if return_code in retryable_codes:
        # Retry after delay (e.g., 2 days for R01)
        payout_record.status = 'PENDING_RETRY'
        payout_record.retry_count += 1
        schedule_retry(payout_record, days=2)

    elif return_code in permanent_codes:
        # Mark account invalid, notify user
        payout_record.status = 'FAILED_PERMANENT'
        notify_user(payout_record, f"Account issue: {return_code}")
        request_new_banking_details(payout_record.user_id)

    elif return_code in fraud_codes:
        # Flag for investigation
        payout_record.status = 'DISPUTED'
        escalate_to_compliance(payout_record)

    else:
        # Log and review
        log_unknown_return(return_code, payout_record)

Timing Matters

ACH returns arrive in batches, typically 1–2 business days after the original transaction was processed. Your reconciliation system must account for this lag. If you're building a dashboard, don't mark a payout as "succeeded" until the return window closes (usually 5 business days).

When to Switch Rails

Some return codes suggest ACH isn't the right tool. For example:

  • R03 (no account) repeatedly? Ask the user for a card instead.
  • R01 (insufficient funds) on a tight deadline? Offer RTP (Real-Time Payments) or Visa Direct as alternatives.

Summary

ACH return codes are your diagnostic toolkit. Invest time in classifying them, automating retries for transient failures, and routing around permanent issues. The Nacha rulebook defines all 85 codes; your job is to map business logic to each one.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: PHRBench: A Behavioral Evaluation of Post-Hallucination Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.10455v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hallucinated information can propagate through multi-stage LLM systems and become part of the context for subsequent reasoning. Existing studies of post-hallucination reasoning (PHR) mainly characterize changes in final outcomes and aggregate reasoning dynamics, leaving how models resolve hallucinated premises at the response level insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce PHRBench, a controlled benchmark for behaviorally structured PHR across four domains and 18 large language models. PHRBench characterizes each reasoning trajectory independently of final-answer correctness through Hallucination Compliance, Hallucination Avoidance, and Heuristic Correction, and defines an insightful trajectory as successful correction that ultimately reaches the correct answer. Across 4820 controlled instances, we find that successful recovery remains relatively rare and is associated with more frequent belief updates along the reasoning trajectory. We further find that properties of the hallucinated prompt contain substantial predictive signal for successful recovery, with a lightweight predictor achieving an AUROC of 0.847. These findings provide a behavioral view of post-hallucination reasoning, characterizing how LLMs resolve erroneous context and when successful recovery is likely to occur.

title: I Built a $6 Menu Translator Cafes Actually Want (Gemma Local, $0 API Cost)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

DineLingo — a local-first menu translator a real restaurant would pay for.

Type a dish in Hinglish like Masala Dosa - crisp rice crepe, aloo masala → get a tourist-ready line + allergen + veg flag, QR-ready for table tents:

Masala Dosa: Crisp rice crepe, aloo masala — crisp rice-lentil crepe with spiced potato filling [veg] — ₹180

Who pays: single-location restaurants with tourist footfall and no English menu. Pitch: “₹499 / $6 one-time for 30 dishes + QR. No monthly SaaS, your recipes never leave your laptop.” That one-time price only works because open weights cost $0 marginal — a closed per-character API would kill the deal.

Problem it solves: owners lose foreign customers daily to “what is Chole Bhature?” Generic translate apps mangle dish names, need internet, and send recipes to a server they don’t control.

Demo

Local demo (2 min, no GPU, zero downloads for phrasebook mode):

pip install -r requirements.txt
python demo.py   # offline CLI — 5 dishes
python app.py    # Gradio UI on http://localhost:7860

Try: Masala Dosa → Spanish → Dosa masala crujiente con relleno de papa especiada (vegetariano, contiene gluten) — Rs180

Video/screenshots: run python app.py, screenshot the Gradio UI + python demo.py output and attach to this post. Live link pending — local-first by design, deploy optional on Render.

Code

AdityaAneNenu / dinelingo

🍽️ DineLingo — Local-First Menu Translator (HF26 Week 2: Side Hustle)

Someone would pay for this: a local restaurant pays once for a QR-ready translated menu instead of per-API-call SaaS that leaks their recipes.

Repo: https://github.com/AdityaAneNenu/dinelingo

Stack: 100% open-source AI — Google Gemma open weights via Hugging Face Transformers. No closed APIs. Demo runs offline with zero downloads.

Why this wins Week 2

  • Real payer: single-location restaurant (tourist footfall, no English menu).
  • Why open > closed: $0 marginal cost per translation, works offline during outages, menu data never leaves laptop, owner can edit phrasebook + fine-tune Gemma later.
  • Partner track: Best Use of Gemma (google/gemma-2-2b-it, local via transformers).

Quickstart (2 min, no GPU, no downloads)

pip install -r requirements.txt
python app.py
# open http://localhost:7860

Upgrade to real Gemma-local (optional, still free)

  2. HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx in .env (see .env.example)
  3. Restart — engine flips from phrasebook-demo →…
View on GitHub

Full repo: https://github.com/AdityaAneNenu/dinelingo

app.py → Gradio UI (name, description, language, price → translated line)
src/translator.py → Gemma conduit + offline phrasebook + allergen/veg rules
data/sample_menu.csv → 5-dish demo menu
demo.py → CLI demo for screenshots
requirements.txt → torch(cpu), transformers, accelerate, gradio

How I Built It

Open-source AI is the core, not a wrapper:

  • Open-weight model: google/gemma-2-2b-it via Hugging Face transformers with device_map=auto, bfloat16 on CUDA / float32 on CPU. Lazy-loaded in try_load_gemma() only when HF_TOKEN is set (accept license at https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-2-2b-it).
  • Local inference: no closed APIs, no server calls in local mode. phrasebook-demo engine runs fully offline on day one; flips to gemma-local automatically when token + torch present.
  • Owner-editable phrasebook: 12 Hinglish → English glosses (paneer tikka, chole bhature, etc.) — this is the fine-tune seed the owner controls.
  • Deterministic safety: allergen + veg flags in code (ALLERGEN_HINTS, detect_veg) so judges see safety beyond LLM vibes.
  • UI: Gradio 6.x, 4 inputs, examples preloaded, provenance line shows Engine: phrasebook-demo|gemma-local | Veg | Allergens.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  1. Cost makes the business work: closed translation API = per-char billing. 30 dishes × re-translates = monthly bleed. Gemma-local = $0 marginal → ₹499 one-time is profitable.
  2. Privacy closes the sale: recipes stay on the owner’s laptop. Real objection: “I don’t want my menu on someone’s server.”
  3. Niche beats generic: generic APIs output “chickpea bread” for Chole Bhature. My phrasebook + future Gemma fine-tune nails house dishes.
  4. Offline survives reality: power/internet cuts kill cloud SaaS. Local still translates and sells.

Open is what makes this a side hustle instead of a SaaS resell.

title: A Second Host Measures Drift. It Does Not Open the Freeze.
description:
A flake freeze is valid only on one host, under one fixture epoch, and against an oracle the patch did not edit. A second machine can measure drift. It cannot open that freeze.

Agent patches fail in ways that look identical on a red CI line. The invariant can be false. The fixture lock can be stale. The owner host can disagree with itself, or a second host can disagree with the first.

Those four outcomes need different records. Collapsing them into one freeze hides the defect the next patch will trip over. The workflow below is a proposal. The snippets are unexecuted specification code, not a report from a live suite, and no pass rate, quota, or hardware figure is claimed.

What must match before a class exists

Treat the run as an equivalence class, not as a test name. Two failures that share a name and differ in their pins are different experiments. Write the pins down before the first replay, and refuse to classify a run that is missing any of them.

The pin set is small.

  • patch_id is the hash of the diff, not the branch name.
  • oracle_hash is the hash of the property module. The patch is not allowed to move it.
  • fixture_epoch is the hash of a manifest that lists every fixture file and that file's own hash.
  • seed is the integer the property checks actually used.
  • host_id names the machine that is allowed to own a freeze later.
  • replay_budget is chosen before the run. A red result does not raise it.

Change one pin and you start a new row. You do not amend the old one.

Build the epoch from bytes, not from directory mtime. A runner can unpack the same files and still change timestamps. Sort relative POSIX paths, write path digest lines, hash that text, and store the digest. If a clock, a temp path, or directory order can change the outcome, put that input in the manifest or stop calling the failure a flake.

Six classes, and only one may freeze

Score the observation with the table below. The freeze column is the policy. The other columns are bookkeeping.

Observation Class Freeze on owner host Next action
Patch changes the oracle hash oracle_tamper No Reject the diff. Restore the oracle file.
Pinned property fails property_fail No Keep the counterexample. Do not replay for a freeze.
Manifest hash differs from the lock fixture_drift No Relock on purpose, or discard the run.
Owner host still inside budget, not a clean pass replay_incomplete No Finish the budget. Do not call host B yet.
Owner host shows both pass and fail after the budget flake_candidate Yes, time-boxed Insert a freeze row bound to that host_id only.
Owner host is stable, other host differs environment No File drift. Do not copy the row into the other ledger.
Owner host is stably red, other host agrees or was not called regression No Treat it as a real failure of the patch.
Owner host is stably green pass No Continue review.

A property failure stays a property failure even if a later run goes green. That green run is a different question, and it does not launder the counterexample into a flake. Stable red on the owner host is a regression when the oracle held. Mixed results after the budget are the only freeze input.

Host B is a measurement, including when host B is a free server rather than another CI runner. Its boolean does not get a vote on the owner ledger.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

MonkeyCode's free model access matters here only as a source of candidate diffs. The free server option matters only as a possible host B. Neither claim adds a model name, a quota, or a performance number to the table, and none of those are required.

A green probe on the free server does not cancel a property failure on the owner host. A red probe does not open the owner host's freeze.

Seven steps

  1. Hash the oracle path. If the diff touches it, emit oracle_tamper and stop.
  2. Build the fixture manifest from the fixture root and compare it with the locked epoch.
  3. Run property checks on the owner host with the stored seed. On failure, emit property_fail and stop.
  4. Run the named regression once on the owner host. A pass skips the freeze path.
  5. On failure, replay on the owner host until the budget is consumed and every outcome is recorded.
  6. Only then, if the class is not already property_fail or fixture_drift, submit the same patch_id, seed, and fixture epoch to host B.
  7. Emit one class from the table. Persist it. Do not edit the class after the ledger write.

Step 6 is deliberately late. An unfinished owner-host run cannot change the table, so calling host B early only spends a seat. If that seat is a free server, keep the probe off until step 5 has a complete vector.

Expiry of a freeze that already exists is a separate policy. This gate only decides whether a new row may be inserted, and on which host.

Classifier

This module is a reviewable proposal. It imports nothing outside the standard library. It encodes the table. It does not discover new invariants.

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

def sha256_file(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    digest.update(path.read_bytes())
    return digest.hexdigest()

def fixture_epoch(root: Path) -> str:
    lines = []
    for path in sorted(p for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file()):
        rel = path.relative_to(root).as_posix()
        lines.append(f"{rel} {sha256_file(path)}")
    payload = ("\n".join(lines)).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

def classify(obs: dict) -> str:
    if obs["oracle_hash"] != obs["oracle_lock"]:
        return "oracle_tamper"
    if obs["fixture_epoch"] != obs["fixture_lock"]:
        return "fixture_drift"
    if not obs["property_passed"]:
        return "property_fail"
    host_a = list(obs["host_a_outcomes"])
    budget = int(obs["replay_budget"])
    if budget < 1 or not host_a or len(host_a) > budget:
        raise ValueError("owner-host outcomes are outside the declared budget")
    distinct = set(host_a)
    host_b = obs.get("host_b_outcome")
    if len(host_a) < budget and distinct != {True}:
        return "replay_incomplete"
    if distinct == {True, False}:
        return "flake_candidate"
    if distinct == {True}:
        return "environment" if host_b is False else "pass"
    if host_b is True:
        return "environment"
    return "regression"

def freeze_allowed(kind: str, host_id: str, owner_host: str) -> bool:
    return kind == "flake_candidate" and host_id == owner_host

freeze_allowed is the policy in one line. Environment drift returns false. A cheaper host does not become the owner by being cheaper. Host B is not consulted inside the mixed-result branch. Instability on the owner host is already enough for flake_candidate, and host B cannot veto that row or inherit it.

Three illustrations use placeholder ids. They are not measured runs.

Owner outcomes [False, False, False], budget 3, property passed, host B True. The class is environment. The owner host is stable. Freezing the test name would block later patches for a failure that did not reproduce on the other host, and it would hide the drift.

Owner outcomes [False, True, False], budget 3, host B False. The class is flake_candidate. A freeze may open, and only for the owner host_id. Host B's failure does not extend that row.

Owner outcomes [False], budget 3. The class is replay_incomplete. One red result is not a class you can freeze. Finish the vector first, and do not call host B on this row yet.

Specification checks

Pair the function with assertions that restate the table. They are part of the proposal. They fail if a later edit lets a second host open the owner ledger.

def test_cross_host_split_is_not_a_freeze():
    kind = classify({
        "oracle_hash": "aa",
        "oracle_lock": "aa",
        "fixture_epoch": "bb",
        "fixture_lock": "bb",
        "property_passed": True,
        "host_a_outcomes": [False, False, False],
        "host_b_outcome": True,
        "replay_budget": 3,
    })
    assert kind == "environment"
    assert freeze_allowed(kind, "ci-a", "ci-a") is False

def test_mixed_owner_host_can_freeze():
    kind = classify({
        "oracle_hash": "aa",
        "oracle_lock": "aa",
        "fixture_epoch": "bb",
        "fixture_lock": "bb",
        "property_passed": True,
        "host_a_outcomes": [False, True, False],
        "host_b_outcome": False,
        "replay_budget": 3,
    })
    assert kind == "flake_candidate"
    assert freeze_allowed(kind, "host-b", "ci-a") is False
    assert freeze_allowed(kind, "ci-a", "ci-a") is True

The host check is the assertion reviewers skip. A flake on ci-a must not be writable by host B, even when both saw a failure. Host identity is part of the key.

A minimal persisted record, again with placeholder values, looks like this.

{
  "patch_id": "example",
  "oracle_hash": "aa",
  "fixture_epoch": "bb",
  "seed": 17,
  "host_id": "ci-a",
  "replay_budget": 3,
  "class": "environment",
  "freeze": false
}

Command order

Check the oracle path before the test runner starts. An assertion inside the test file is too late, because the patch may have weakened that assertion.

git diff --name-only "$BASE"..HEAD -- tests/properties/invariants.py
python -m gate.classify --record runs/patch.json --owner-host ci-a

The first command must print nothing. If it prints the oracle path, emit oracle_tamper and do not start the suite. The second command reads the observation file and prints one class. Exit non-zero for every class other than pass.

Host B gets the same pins and an empty ledger. The flags below belong to the proposed local probe, not to a vendor CLI.

python -m gate.probe \
  --patch-id "$PATCH_ID" \
  --fixture-epoch "$EPOCH" \
  --seed 17 \
  --host-id host-b \
  --ledger none

--ledger none is the useful constraint. Host B may return true or false. It may not append a freeze row. Point --host-id at whatever second machine you already operate. A free server seat can fill that role. It does not become the merge gate.

Keep the agent off the oracle path in two places. Say so in the task instruction, then enforce it with the hash compare. The instruction is not the gate. The hash is.

Limitations

The classifier does not prove the patch is correct. It can only show that the stated properties held and that the named check was stable on one host. Unstated behavior can still be wrong. That is a coverage gap, not a reason to freeze a red name.

A same-host disagreement can still be an unlisted fixture. Wall clocks, temp paths, and directory order will mint false flake_candidate rows if they sit outside the manifest. Widen the manifest before you widen the budget.

The budget in the examples is a policy integer, not a calibrated flake rate. This article does not estimate how often agent patches flake. If you have a measured baseline, use it. If you do not, keep the integer small, and accept that a stable failure costs that many owner-host runs before it becomes regression.

Cross-host comparison here is a boolean. Two hosts can fail in different assertions and look like agreement. Store the exception type and the assertion id if you need a stricter probe. That extension still must not open a freeze by itself.

Who should skip it

Skip the workflow if you cannot name one owner host. A pool of ephemeral runners with no stable id will mark almost every split as environment, and the freeze path will never open. That can be the right policy. Write "no freeze on pooled hosts" instead of pretending the pool is one machine.

Skip it if the suite has no property module the patch is forbidden to edit. Named tests alone cannot separate tamper from regression. Add the oracle before you add host B.

Skip it if you need a vendor quota, a hardware spec, or a published benchmark before a second host is allowed to run. Those are not inputs to the table, and this note does not supply them.

Put the observation JSON in the pull request. If the class is environment, link the two host ids and leave the freeze ledger untouched. If a free MonkeyCode server is already on your bench, use that seat as host B with an empty ledger. The owner host, not the extra seat, still decides whether a freeze exists.

title: Mixture-Greedy for Online Generative Model Selection: Is UCB Necessary in Diversity-Aware Multi-Armed Bandits?
description:
arXiv:2603.21716v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Efficient selection among multiple generative models is increasingly important in modern generative AI, where sampling from suboptimal models is costly. This problem can be viewed as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) task. Under diversity-aware evaluation scores, a non-degenerate mixture of generators can outperform any individual model, distinguishing this MAB setting from classical best-arm identification. Prior approaches incorporate an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) exploration bonus into the mixture objective. However, across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics, we observe that the UCB term consistently slows convergence and reduces sample efficiency. In contrast, a simple Mixture-Greedy strategy without explicit UCB-type optimism converges faster and achieves even better performance, particularly for widely used metrics such as FID and Vendi where tight confidence bounds are difficult to construct. We provide theoretical insight explaining this behavior: under structural conditions, diversity-aware objectives induce implicit exploration by favoring interior mixtures, leading to sampling of all arms and sublinear regret guarantees for diversity-based objectives. These results suggest that in diversity-aware multi-armed bandits, e.g., for generative model selection, exploration can arise intrinsically from the objective's geometry.

title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
description:
arXiv:2610.13672v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.

title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
description:
arXiv:2610.13000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.

title: HAFixAgent: History-Aware Agentic Program Repair
description:
arXiv:2511.01047v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automated program repair (APR) has recently shifted toward large language models and agent-based systems, while prior work shows that repository history can help repair single-line bugs. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of whether, how much, and under what conditions repository history improves agentic APR beyond this setting. We present HAFixAgent, a history-aware program repair agent that injects blame-derived repository context into its repair loop. Across 854 Defects4J (Java) and 501 BugsInPy (Python) bugs, we first show that bug-relevant history is widely available. We then evaluate HAFixAgent across three base models under perfect fault localization. The best history heuristic improves over non-history from +4.4% on Defects4J and +1.1% on BugsInPy with the strongest model to as much as +64.3% with weaker models. HAFixAgent also outperforms RepairAgent by +56.6% and BIRCH-feedback by +47.1% on the strongest model, showing that it is a strong repair agent independent of history. The three history heuristics are complementary: each repairs a different subset of bugs, so their hybrid significantly repairs more bugs than non-history (McNemar's test, p < 0.001), and this advantage persists under realistic spectrum-based fault localization. Individual history heuristics are generally no more expensive than non-history in agent steps or tokens under either localization setting, while the hybrid costs roughly twice a single run in a cascade setting.

title: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
description:
arXiv:2610.12542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is often proposed for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows, yet most studies never run the comparison that could refute it - giving a much simpler method the same search effort. We run that comparison under a controlled protocol. All arms receive an identical budget - the same number of candidate schedules built and evaluated: an MCTS scheduling method, preregistered as the main arm; a randomized-restart list scheduler with no search tree as the control; and a textbook-UCT MCTS arm as a registered follow-up on the same domain. The analysis plan was locked before data collection; an independent checker confirmed all 768 confirmation-stage schedules valid with correct finish times. At the main budget of 2048 evaluated schedules, MCTS is 2.88% worse than the restarts (95% CI [-3.62%,-2.15%]; the 72 of 96 held-out instances with positive baseline-relative headroom). The deficit is not budget starvation: on the separate exploration pool restarts self-improve by 1.85% where MCTS gains 0.24%, and 700 of 720 of MCTS's first results are merely the warm start it was handed. The studied selection rule locks deterministically onto the first-expanded child, keeping its trials correlated while restarts draw gains from the tails; the causal link to makespan remains an inference. A structural map locates where the tree stops paying: restarts win on sparse irregular workflows, no difference is detectable on regular layered ones, and dense ones leave no room to improve. Swapping the rule for textbook UCT removes most of the deficit (-0.26%, 95% CI [-0.71%,+0.23%]) without reversing its sign. Results are confined to a controlled synthetic domain (N in {8,16,32} tasks, 2-8 processors, budgets up to 2048); we make no claim about larger budgets.

title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.12914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
description:
arXiv:2610.13516v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $\tau=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.

title: Wikidata Search Traces: A Dataset for Training Knowledge Graph Search Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.06650v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Wikidata is one of the largest open knowledge bases, yet answering a complex question over it still requires a SPARQL query that names the right entities and properties and chains their relations. Language models offer a natural-language alternative but answer largely from memory, which is least reliable for less prominent entities. We study agents that instead answer by exploring the graph, and argue that two obstacles limit them: the lack of training data recording how a solver explores, and interfaces that add large graph results directly to the model's context. We test three hypotheses: that the difficulty of graph search can be controlled through the structure of a question rather than only through obscure entities or wording; that much of the failure on long-horizon search comes from how retrieved evidence is managed rather than from the model itself; and that, in a suitable environment, open-weight models can match commercial closed ones. We construct multi-hop questions on a frozen Wikidata snapshot by replacing named entities with nested conditions, checking after each expansion that the target remains unique and that every new condition is necessary. We release 10,235 solving traces over single-entity and multi-hop questions, together with the recursive language model (RLM) harness that produced them, in which models batch graph calls, keep results in persistent Python state and interpret selected evidence through sub-calls. On 100 questions, the harness improves both models we ran under both interfaces compared with direct tool calling over the same functions: gpt-6-luna rises from 49 to 61 correct answers, doubling its multi-hop accuracy, and Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model served on a single GPU, from 60 to 74.

title: Remote video support that survives a technician's phone network
description:
Remote visual assistance demos well on office Wi-Fi and fails the first time a technician climbs into a van. I have watched this happen with a working demo and a confused buyer, and the failure is almost never the codec. It is the network underneath it: the phone changes address mid-session, it sits behind a carrier NAT that no direct candidate can reach, and the server does not know its own public address.

This is the write-up I wanted when I started. Symptoms first, because that is what you search for when a field session has gone dark and the customer is waiting.

The whole thing in one line: field video fails in four different layers, and they look identical from the UI.

It works in the office and fails on cellular

ICE finds a path by gathering candidates. A host candidate is the device's own address. An srflx candidate is the address a STUN server saw after NAT. A relay candidate is an address on a TURN server that both sides send to when nothing direct works.

Consumer Wi-Fi is usually cone NAT, so two peers discover each other with STUN alone and the session connects with no infrastructure at all. A phone on cellular is frequently behind a carrier-grade NAT whose mapping is not reusable. The srflx candidate is still gathered, still looks valid, and every packet sent to it is dropped, because the mapping was opened for a different destination.

Symptom: on Wi-Fi the connection establishes in under a second; on cellular it never leaves checking.

What to look at: log the selected candidate pair. If it is never relay when the call fails, you need TURN before you debug anything else.

pc.oniceconnectionstatechange = () => {
  if (pc.iceConnectionState === 'failed') {
    // which pair did we actually end up on?
    pc.getStats().then((s) => s.forEach((r) => {
      if (r.type === 'candidate-pair' && r.state === 'failed') {
        console.log('failed pair', r.localCandidateId, r.remoteCandidateId);
      }
    }));
  }
};

The relay port answers but the allocation is refused

"No video through the relay" has two causes that are indistinguishable from the browser: the UDP port is unreachable, or the port is fine and the relay declined the allocation. Different fixes, so test them separately.

First, a STUN probe against the same host and port as your TURN server. If it returns an srflx candidate, the port is open and something is listening. Then a real allocation with the real credentials. A relay candidate coming back means TURN works and the problem is elsewhere. A refusal with the port open means credentials or the allocation range — usually a 401 in the coturn log, or a relay port range that was never opened even though the control port was.

# coturn: open the control port AND the relay range
listening-port=3478
min-port=49152
max-port=65535

# a cloud VM must be told its own public address
external-ip=203.0.113.10

The relay range is the part people forget. The control port on 3478 answers, the credentials are perfect, and the allocation still fails because the media ports coturn wanted are closed in the security group. This is the trap that makes a TURN config look correct while every cellular session dies.

Video freezes when the technician walks to the van

A WebRTC transport is bound to a 5-tuple: source address, source port, destination address, destination port, protocol. When the phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular it gets a new source address and the 5-tuple the session was using is gone. The old candidate pair cannot be revived. On screen this is a freeze with no error, because the connection object has not given up yet.

The recovery is an ICE restart, which renegotiates connectivity on the existing peer connection instead of tearing the session down. A restart is not always enough after a long outage or a carrier change, so the practical chain is: ICE restart first, full rejoin as fallback, jittered backoff between attempts so a fleet of devices does not hammer the server at once when a tower comes back up.

Do not trust the connection state alone. A connection can read connected while frames have stopped. Watch the frame callbacks instead, and treat a missing frame as frozen even while ICE still says connected:

let last = performance.now();
video.requestVideoFrameCallback(function tick() {
  last = performance.now();
  video.requestVideoFrameCallback(tick);
});
setInterval(() => {
  if (performance.now() - last > 3000) restartChain(); // stalled, not disconnected
}, 1000);

ICE connects but no frame ever decodes

On a cloud VM the network interface usually has a private address and the public address is attached by the provider's NAT. If the server gathers candidates from its own interface it advertises something like 172.16.x.x in SDP, and the remote browser tries a private address it can never reach. ICE can even report connected on a local path while the media never leaves the host.

Tell the server its public address, or force the relay path. In coturn that is external-ip; in a Go server it is a -public-ip flag or an ICE transport policy of relay. If a session connects instantly between two machines on the same office network and fails from outside, check this first.

The tab says connected but nothing arrives

Signaling runs over a WebSocket and reverse proxies reap idle WebSockets, often around 60 seconds. The socket closes, the application does not notice, and the UI keeps saying connected because nothing told it otherwise.

The fix is a protocol-level ping from the server, not a JavaScript heartbeat. Background tabs throttle timers aggressively, so a client timer that fires every 20 seconds in the foreground can fire far less often when the tab is hidden — which is exactly when a technician has put the phone in a pocket.

The check order that saves time

  1. Log the selected candidate pair. Never relay on a cellular failure means you need TURN first.
  2. Probe the relay in two steps: STUN on the control port, then a real allocation. It separates "port unreachable" from "allocation refused".
  3. Confirm the relay media port range is open, not just the control port.
  4. Set the public address explicitly on any host whose interface is private.
  5. Trigger an ICE restart on a freeze and fall back to a full rejoin, with jittered backoff.
  6. Keep the signaling socket alive from the server, not from a client timer.

None of this is exotic once it is written down, and all of it is invisible in a demo on good Wi-Fi. The failure modes only show up in the field, which is where a field-assist product actually runs.

I packaged the working version of all of this — the Go signaling server and SFU, the browser publisher and viewer, the ICE restart and rejoin chain, the diagnostics panel that shows the selected candidate path, the coturn config and the two-probe relay test — as a self-hosted source kit, so you can prove each layer on your own server instead of inferring it from a black box:

https://lowlatencykit.com/field-assist/

The relay test page is free and needs no account, if you just want to check whether your own TURN server allocates:

https://lowlatencykit.com/test/turn/

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
description:
arXiv:2607.09996v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated failure attribution uses LLMs to identify where and why agentic systems fail. As agents become more capable, their failures become subtler, making automated attribution increasingly important. We introduce Who&When Pro, a large-scale benchmark for automated failure attribution in agentic systems. Using a strictly controlled pipeline that injects a failure only after exactly replaying a successful prefix, we construct 12,326 failed trajectories with golden labels across 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks covering various scenarios. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct extensive experiments and analyses, revealing systematic patterns in how models attribute failures across modalities, protocols, and model families, and providing empirical guidance for future automated failure attribution systems.

title: Measuring and Mitigating Solution Mode Collapse in RLVR
description:
arXiv:2610.11064v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A language model (LM) can usually answer the same question in more than one way, but reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is indifferent to which correct answer a model produces. A solution will earn the same reward whether it is the thousandth copy of a familiar answer or one the model has never produced before. Yet, there is potential value in having the model retain multiple correct solutions as it is trained. For instance, multiple modes may give users a choice and provide problem-solving strategies that improve overall model performance. Here, we introduce ModeBench, a benchmark of multi-solution tasks in which the verifier returns both correctness and mode discovered. We then use ModeBench to measure how solution diversity changes under RLVR post-training. We find that RLVR post-training concentrates probability onto fewer correct modes even as accuracy holds or improves, and moreover, that frontier models are already highly concentrated. We then introduce our solution, Re:Max, which stores one verified example per discovered mode in a replay buffer and trains on those stored modes uniformly. A solution found once is, therefore, practiced as often as one found repeatedly. Across three model scales, two RL objectives, and harder task constructions, replay improves both how often a policy succeeds and how many different ways it can succeed.

title: Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance
description:
arXiv:2610.12998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Creativity benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) vary widely in task and metric design. This raises the question of whether they capture a common notion of creativity. We propose that this shared target can be formalized as task-specific performance in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution, which describes how common input-output pairs are relative to a chosen source of text. We ground this proposition in the novelty-quality product formulation and evaluate it empirically across 15 benchmarks and 26 open-weight models, using n-gram absence from the pretraining data as a novelty proxy. Our results show that creativity benchmarks lie further in the tail regions than standard benchmarks. Moreover, on both creativity and standard benchmarks, model rankings from higher-tail subsets of each benchmark align more closely with human creativity judgments in LM-Arena. Building on these findings, we introduce q@Tail($\alpha$), a lower-cost creativity diagnostic that measures mean task quality on the tail fraction of an existing benchmark. Applying it to creativity-promoting methods reveals substantial room to improve LLM creativity through stronger tail performance.

title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
description:
arXiv:2610.13015v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.

title: Teaching neural decoders with language
description:
arXiv:2610.12921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces decode neural activity, yet class-label supervision (CLS) leaves relationships among classes implicit. We propose Language as Supervision (LaS), which aligns neural features with natural-language class descriptions through learned projections and predicts classes using candidate text prototypes. We evaluate seven encoder architectures with independently trained models for visual, motor, and speech decoding from scalp and intracranial recordings. LaS improves speech-decoding accuracy by up to 17.15~pp over matched CLS baselines. Its representations support candidate-set reuse and label-supervised subject and session adaptation, while LaS enables conditional unseen-frequency decoding in steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) responses. Correct class-description correspondence supports this generalization, and dual-sided attribution visualization shows neural and textual contributions to the same class-matching score. These findings suggest that text descriptions can serve as general-purpose references for learning and interpretation in neural decoding.

title: Test the Side Effects of Your LLM Validator with a Fake Model Client
description:
A validator test can pass while the surrounding application does the wrong thing. The warning is correct, but a retry discards useful text. Or the warning is wrong, and the application keeps asking the model to rewrite a sentence that was already acceptable.

At AETHERCORE, we build GenesisCore, which turns calculated astrology data into reports. An audit of a historical implementation reproduced a small but consequential mistake: a string-matching check could confuse the planet responsible for a house with the planet's location. Changing the order of an otherwise equivalent Japanese sentence changed the warning. The Japanese walkthrough covers that detector and its limitations.

The Japanese article examines why the warning appeared. Here, we test what the surrounding application does after receiving it. You can test that before paying for another model call.

Three policies for the same warning

The example below lets you choose between three behaviors:

  • audit: return the original text with its warnings.
  • hold: retain the text for review, but do not deliver it.
  • retry: request another candidate, up to three calls in total.

These are application policies. The validator supplies evidence; the caller decides how much authority it receives. A warning might represent an actual error, a false positive, or an uncertain judgment. This test does not pretend to tell them apart.

The code uses Python's standard-library Mock. Giving it a list through side_effect supplies one predetermined output per call, and call_count records how often the application asks for a candidate.

A complete test without an API key

Save this as validator_policy.py and run python validator_policy.py with Python 3.10 or later. It performs no network requests. All strings and warnings are synthetic. This is a teaching implementation, not a copy of GenesisCore's production runner.

"""Teaching example. Python 3.10+, standard library, no network calls."""
from unittest.mock import Mock


def generate_with_policy(generate, validate, policy, max_calls=3):
    if policy not in {"audit", "hold", "retry"}:
        raise ValueError("unknown policy")
    if max_calls < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_calls must be positive")
    for _ in range(max_calls):
        text = generate()
        if not isinstance(text, str) or not text.strip():
            raise ValueError("nonempty text required")
        warnings = list(validate(text))
        if not warnings or policy == "audit":
            return {"state": "returned", "text": text,
                    "held_text": None, "warnings": warnings}
        if policy == "hold":
            break
    return {"state": "held", "text": None,
            "held_text": text, "warnings": warnings}


def run_tests():
    scenarios = [
        ("retry", [[], [], []], 1, "returned", "candidate 1"),
        ("retry", [["warning"]] * 3, 3, "held", None),
        ("retry", [["warning"], [], []], 2, "returned", "candidate 2"),
        ("audit", [["warning"]] * 3, 1, "returned", "candidate 1"),
        ("hold", [["warning"]] * 3, 1, "held", None),
    ]
    for policy, warnings, calls, state, expected_text in scenarios:
        generate = Mock(side_effect=["candidate 1", "candidate 2", "candidate 3"])
        validate = Mock(side_effect=warnings)
        result = generate_with_policy(generate, validate, policy)
        assert generate.call_count == calls
        assert validate.call_count == calls
        assert result["state"] == state and result["text"] == expected_text
        assert result["warnings"] == warnings[calls - 1]
        assert result["held_text"] == (f"candidate {calls}" if state == "held" else None)

    for raw, limit, expected_calls in [("", 3, 1), ("unused", 0, 0)]:
        generate = Mock(return_value=raw)
        try:
            generate_with_policy(generate, lambda _: [], "audit", limit)
        except ValueError:
            assert generate.call_count == expected_calls
        else:
            raise AssertionError("invalid input was accepted")
    print("7 policy scenarios passed; external model calls: 0")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_tests()

Expected output:

7 policy scenarios passed; external model calls: 0

The tests cover these outcomes:

Situation Policy Calls to the fake generator Text returned to the caller
No warning retry 1 First candidate
Warning persists retry 3 None; held
Warning clears on the second candidate retry 2 Second candidate
Warning persists audit 1 Original candidate plus warnings
Warning persists hold 1 None; original retained for review
Generated text is empty audit 1 Exception
Retry limit is zero retry 0 Exception before generation

The fourth row deserves attention. Audit-only avoids rewriting a possibly correct answer, but it can also return a genuinely wrong one. Holding the answer changes the user experience. Retrying changes the answer and may consume more calls. Each choice has a cost, even when the code behaves exactly as designed.

Why the caller belongs in the test

In the historical GenesisCore runner we inspected, three controlled scenarios produced one, three, and two calls to a fake model client. Persistent validation errors reached a fallback path. Those were control-flow tests against a fixed historical version, not measurements of live model quality, latency, or customer impact.

The example here deliberately holds after the retry limit instead of implementing that fallback. If your application has a fallback, add an assertion for its invocation and for the provenance of the returned text. A correct call count cannot tell you whether the fallback silently replaced useful content.

Similarly, checking only warnings == [] misses several important questions: did the original text survive, did a held result leak into the response, and did a supposedly advisory warning trigger generation? The return object makes those decisions visible with separate text and held_text fields.

Bring one real boundary into the fixture

For your own validator, start with two sentences that mean the same thing but use different word orders. Add an unmistakably incorrect sentence and an expression the detector does not understand. Run those through the real detector, then feed its results into policy tests like these.

Keep the two questions separate: does the detector recognize the problem, and does the application respond appropriately? A fake model answers the second question cheaply and repeatably. It cannot establish a model's factual accuracy.

Which assertion is missing from your current tests: generation count, preservation of the original text, or withholding a flagged response? Pick one you would add first; a concrete failure case is welcome.

This article is by AETHERCORE, the team developing GenesisCore. Our public astrology research is a separate body of work; it is not the repository for the private historical application code discussed here. The complete runnable teaching example is included above.
