title: Separate Captured Commands from Model-Written Troubleshooting Prose
description:
A troubleshooting page stays accurate when a human owns the command transcript and the model owns only the explanation around it. The model may describe intent, order, and reader context inside a file that the registry marks as draftable. It may not invent flags, exit codes, durations, or allowances that the pinned transcript and fact ledger do not already contain. A checker should enforce that split before generated prose is allowed to reach a human review queue.

Why the transcript has to stay human-owned

Generated troubleshooting pages fail in a familiar way when the evidence and the draft occupy the same file. The model can smooth a failed command into a plausible success, or it can add a retry rule that nobody captured in a shell. A later editor may treat that smoothed paragraph as the procedure, because the page looks finished and the original session is gone. A separate transcript makes the captured evidence something a reviewer can diff without rereading the surrounding narrative.

This split is narrower than a ban on generated documentation, and that distinction matters for teams that already draft prose with a model. Explanations still save time when the same captured session must be introduced to readers who did not run the command. Human-owned files stay hash-pinned, and draftable files remain easy to regenerate whenever the captured pin changes. The method does not ask the model to decide which failures are real, which timeouts are acceptable, or which gaps may be filled.

What each side may write

The table is the editorial contract for a single page, not a company-wide style guide you must adopt unchanged. Add a row only when the owner and the source are already known to a person who can update them. Do not add a row because a draft sounded specific or because a missing cell made the page look thin. Empty cells should stay empty until a human records the evidence that belongs in that row.

Block Owner May contain Must not contain
transcript.log Human Captured stdout, stderr, and exit status Edited success lines or hidden failures
facts.yml Human Retryability, owners, and sourced measurements Model-written numbers or undated allowances
narrative.md Model Order, intent, and reader cues New commands, flags, codes, or quotas
review.md Human Accept, reject, or edit notes Unreviewed claims copied into the page

A command belongs in the transcript only after a person runs it in the environment the page claims to describe. A measurement belongs in the ledger only with a source string and a review date that a human can open again later. Narrative text may quote those registered values, but it may not introduce a number the ledger does not list. Publication status remains human-owned even when every sentence in the generated draft is otherwise clean and specific.

Steps to publish one page

  1. Capture each command, its combined output, and its exit status, then store that log on a path a human owns.
  2. Register retryability, support identifiers, and any numeric allowance in the ledger, each with a source you can open without the model.
  3. Mark the narrative file as the only model-writable path, and limit the prompt to explaining the pinned transcript in that file.
  4. Run the checker so a drifted pin or an unregistered number fails the job before anyone spends review time.
  5. Read the narrative against the log, and accept it only after the checker exits zero and the quoted lines still match.
  6. Commit the transcript, the ledger, and the accepted narrative together, then regenerate the narrative whenever either pinned file changes.

The capture script should fail closed when a command exits non-zero, unless the ledger already marks that status as an expected demonstration. Expected failures still belong in the log, because a page that hides the failing session teaches the reader the wrong recovery. Keep the prompt beside the narrative as a build input, not as the procedure that you publish to readers. If the prompt and the narrative disagree, the transcript and the ledger remain the files that win.

Capture script

The capture helper below is an unexecuted fixture, and it assumes a local demo-job binary that you can replace. It records the command line, appends combined output, and writes the exit status even when the first run fails. Remove the status override once you are capturing a procedure that should stop on the first unexpected exit.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
out="docs/retry/transcript.log"
: > "$out"
run() {
  printf '$ %s\n' "$*" | tee -a "$out"
  "$@" >>"$out" 2>&1
  code=$?
  printf 'exit: %s\n' "$code" | tee -a "$out"
  return 0
}
run demo-job --once
run demo-job --once
sha256sum "$out"

Fixtures you can copy

The files in this section are unexecuted tutorial fixtures, not a production incident and not a vendor measurement. Replace every source string and every sample command before you point this pattern at a real documentation page. Dates in the fixtures identify the example, and they are not a claim that any vendor published those values on that day. Treat the exit status and the attempt limit as placeholders that your own ledger must replace.

# docs/retry/facts.yml
page: docs/retry
human_owner: docs-team
pins:
  transcript: docs/retry/transcript.log
  transcript_sha256: "replace-with-real-sha256"
draftable:
  - docs/retry/narrative.md
facts:
  - key: expected_exit
    value: 75
    source: "fixture://exit-codes"
    reviewed: "2026-10-13"
  - key: recovered_exit
    value: 0
    source: "fixture://exit-codes"
    reviewed: "2026-10-13"
  - key: max_attempts
    value: 3
    source: "fixture://retry-policy"
    reviewed: "2026-10-13"

# docs/retry/transcript.log
$ demo-job --once
temporary upstream failure
exit: 75
$ demo-job --once
ok
exit: 0

The first invocation exits 75, which this page treats as a temporary failure.
A second invocation is the expected recovery, and it exits 0 in the pinned log.
The ledger allows at most 3 attempts, so a further failure should stop the procedure.

Run the ownership checker

The Python program below is an unexecuted example intended for a repository branch that you already control. It does not call a model, score prose quality, or connect to an external documentation service. Install PyYAML, replace the placeholder hash with the digest of your transcript, and run the script from the repository root. Until you replace the placeholder hash, the hash comparison stays inactive, so do not treat a green run as proof of pin enforcement.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reject drafts that drift from pins or invent measurements."""

import hashlib
import pathlib
import re
import sys

import yaml

LEDGER = pathlib.Path("docs/retry/facts.yml")
NUMBER = re.compile(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b")

def sha256(path: pathlib.Path) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()

def main() -> int:
    ledger = yaml.safe_load(LEDGER.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    errors = []
    transcript = pathlib.Path(ledger["pins"]["transcript"])
    pinned = ledger["pins"]["transcript_sha256"]
    if pinned != "replace-with-real-sha256" and sha256(transcript) != pinned:
        errors.append(f"transcript hash drift: {transcript}")
    allowed = {str(item["value"]) for item in ledger["facts"]}
    for rel in ledger["draftable"]:
        text = pathlib.Path(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        for match in NUMBER.findall(text):
            if match not in allowed:
                errors.append(f"unregistered number {match} in {rel}")
    if errors:
        print("\n".join(errors))
        return 1
    print("ownership check passed")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

python3 -m pip install pyyaml
sha256sum docs/retry/transcript.log
python3 check_doc_ownership.py

After the happy path passes, append an unregistered duration to the narrative and run the checker a second time. That negative case should exit with status 1, because the added duration is not a registered fact value. Skip that case and a green run on the sample page will not prove that invented durations are blocked. Keep both fixtures in the test directory so a later edit cannot delete the failure mode without a visible diff.

Use a free draft loop without making it the archive

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator describes the project as open source and supplies two availability claims for this draft: free model access and a free server option. Those claims do not include a named model, a fixed quota, a hardware profile, or a permanent time window. Narrower commercial details change, and a human should copy them from current product documentation into the ledger only when a page must state them.

Free model access matters at the narrative step, where the draftable file is generated from the pinned transcript and the allowed numbers. The free server option matters when you want a clean shell in which to recapture the log without using a teammate's laptop. Neither option should become the system of record, because an ephemeral machine can disappear and a regenerated draft can drift. The committed transcript, the ledger, and the review note remain the surface that a later editor should trust.

Write the prompt so that it cannot widen its own write permissions while producing the draft. Provide the transcript, the allowed numbers, and the single output path, and instruct the model to leave gaps instead of guessing. Do not ask it to improve the command, choose a timeout, or complete a missing exit code in the captured log. Those requests remain ownership violations even when the resulting paragraph is grammatically clean and easy to skim.

If the model returns a number you did not register, either update the ledger from a source you control or delete the sentence. Do not publish the allowance as a permanent property of the tool, because availability figures need a current primary source. This draft omits a token count for that reason, and a reviewer should treat any remembered quota as unverified.

Four review checks

Apply the same four checks to every page that adopts the split, and record the answers in the human-owned review note. They are mechanical on purpose, so the reviewer does not have to infer intent from a confident tone. A missing answer is a rejection, not a prompt that invites the model to fill the blank. Attach the checker output to the same note so the next editor can see why the draft was allowed through.

  1. Confirm that the transcript hash matches the ledger, and confirm that a person can still reproduce the session in the named environment.
  2. Confirm that every number in the narrative appears as a fact value, including exits, attempt limits, and any published allowance.
  3. Confirm that the change does not edit the transcript or the ledger inside a commit that was supposed to contain only a model draft.
  4. Confirm that a human accepted the narrative in the review note, with the checker output stored beside that acceptance.

Who should skip this gate

This pattern is a file pin plus a lexical number scan, and it is not proof that the explanation is causally right. A narrative can stay inside the allowlist and still describe the recovery steps in the wrong order. Do not use the gate for security advisories, pricing pages, legal terms, or incident reports whose sentences are themselves commitments. Also skip it when nobody on the team can recapture the transcript, because a stale pin is more dangerous than an obvious gap.

A team that publishes model output without a human reviewer will not receive the intended protection from this script. The script does not judge clarity, safety, or whether the advice should be followed outside the captured environment. The free server option does not replace a durable repository, a named owner, or a fresh reading of current product terms. If the page set is small and almost never changes, the automation may cost more effort than the risk it removes.

In that smaller case, keep the same ownership rule without the script and without a scheduled job. Humans edit the transcript and the ledger, and the model never receives write access to either path. Regenerate the explanation only after those pins change, and discard drafts that arrive with new measurements attached. That manual version is slower, but it preserves the same boundary the checker is meant to automate.

Start with one negative test

Choose one troubleshooting page, pin its transcript, and reject the first draft that introduces an unregistered number. That failure is the useful result, because it shows whether the allowlist matches the way the page is actually written. When a person already maintains the ledger, free model access is enough to rehearse the narrative step before the checker joins the default branch.

title: Hierarchical Experimentalist Agents
description:
arXiv:2606.29315v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to act in the real world and augment human decision-making, yet most systems rely on parametric knowledge acquired through imitation, optionally improved by post-training, retrieval, or search over fixed data. This paradigm struggles in novel domains or on complex queries that require information unavailable from prior knowledge alone; knowing the laws of physics, for example, does not by itself enable reliable reasoning or long-horizon actions in a complex physical system. We argue that agents need active experimentation: the ability to gather targeted query-specific evidence, discover general principles of unseen environments, and convert interaction experience into reusable skills. We introduce Hierarchical Experimentalist Agents (HExA), an in-context, experiment-centric self-improvement framework that (1) iteratively designs and refines query-relevant experiments, (2) incrementally distills experience into reusable and composable skills that accelerate experimentation within and across tasks, and (3) integrates experimental evidence to act or answer queries. HExA can work with any LLM including frontier black-box models, and requires no external supervision, oracle solutions, or offline data. We evaluate HExA on multi-step reasoning, interactive partially observable games, and physics law discovery tasks. To further evaluate when active experimentation is necessary, we introduce Interphyre, a set of hard procedural physics tasks where we enable tool-calling and intervention APIs. Current frontier LLMs including GPT-6 Astra fail in these settings: on the most challenging Interphyre tasks, we show that HExA can enable such models to near 100% success. Moreover, HExA improves token efficiency compared to naive agentic and memory baselines and enables generalization via hierarchical skill transfer from easier to harder tasks.

title: Can Agents Price a Reaction? Evaluating LLMs on Chemical Cost Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2605.07251v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable as tool-using agents, with benchmarks spanning diverse general agentic tasks. Yet rigorous evaluation of scientific tool use remains limited. In chemistry, recent agents can plan syntheses and invoke domain-specific tools, but evaluations often rely on curated demonstrations, expert assessment, or LLM-as-judge scoring rather than exact, judge-free ground truth. We address this gap with chemical procurement cost estimation, a practical task in which an agent must ground chemical identities, retrieve supplier quotes, select valid purchasable packs, normalize quantities, and compute cost from a reaction description. We introduce ChemCost, a benchmark of 1,427 evaluable reactions grounded to a frozen pricing snapshot covering 2,261 chemicals and 230,775 supplier quotes, supporting scalar scoring and stage-level diagnosis of grounding, retrieval, procurement, and arithmetic failures. To evaluate robustness, we further construct controlled noise-injected views that perturb chemical aliases, quantity expressions, missing fields, and input formatting. Experiments with frontier, open-weight, and chemistry-specialized LLM agents show that tool access is necessary but insufficient for solving the task. The strongest agents reach only 50.6% accuracy within 25% relative error on clean inputs and degrade substantially with realistic noise. Stage-level analysis further shows that failures arise from brittle parsing, ineffective evidence integration, invalid pack selection, and non-convergent tool use.

title: LensVLM: Selective Context Expansion for Compressed Visual Representation of Text
description:
arXiv:2605.07019v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) offer the exciting possibility of processing text as rendered images, bypassing the need for tokenizing the text into long token sequences. Since VLM image encoders map fixed-size images to a fixed number of visual tokens, varying rendering resolution provides a fine-grained compression knob. However, accuracy deteriorates quickly as compression increases: characters shrink below the vision encoder's effective resolution, making them indistinguishable. To address this, we propose LensVLM, an inference framework and post-training recipe that enables VLMs to scan compressed images, then selectively expand only the relevant images to their uncompressed form via learned tools. Building on Qwen3.5-9B-Base, LensVLM maintains accuracy comparable to the full-text upper bound at 4.3$\times$ effective compression and outperforms retrieval-based, text- and visual-compression baselines up to 10.1$\times$ effective compression across seven text QA benchmarks. LensVLM also generalizes to multimodal document and code understanding tasks, with the accuracy gain over baselines growing as compression increases. Our analysis validates this approach: training makes visual compression robust to rendering choices, and as compression grows the model increasingly relies on expanded content rather than unreliable visual reading. The analysis also yields practical tool-choice guidance: text expansion is preferable for rendered text, while high-resolution image expansion suits native documents whose layout cues carry task-relevant information.

title: How to Evaluate a Node.js SMS Alert API — SaaS Delivery Status
description:
For a B2B SaaS compliance notice, choose the least complex messaging integration that can produce timely, queryable evidence: an asynchronous delivery feed, a status lookup for repair, and a cancellation result that distinguishes "stopped" from "already sent." Then put a Node.js evidence ledger between that transport and the escalation policy. The key selection criterion is evidence latency, not SDK brevity.

Short answer: callbacks should drive normal state changes, polling should repair stale records, and your scheduler should cancel only against a locally recorded deadline. An accepted send request is evidence of submission. It is not evidence of handset delivery, human receipt, or identity.

Evidence path Pick this when What the team operates Failure you must expose
Callback-led, with polling repair Compliance decisions have a short deadline Authenticated ingress, ledger, repair worker Missing or reordered callbacks
Polling-led Public ingress is prohibited Scheduler, rate controls, ledger Status age between polls
Internal messaging gateway Several teams share retention and escalation policy Gateway, queue, schema, on-call ownership Queue lag and mapping drift
Submission receipt only The workflow needs proof of request, not delivery Adapter and request log No final transport evidence

Can a Node.js SaaS trust its SMS alert API delivery status?

Pick callback-led processing when the next escalation depends on fresh delivery state. A callback can update the ledger as the transport reports a transition; a poller later checks records whose evidence has gone stale. The poller is a repair mechanism. Treating it as a second primary stream makes ordering harder to explain.

Polling-led processing is a defensible choice when network policy rules out inbound requests. Integration looks smaller at first because there is no callback endpoint. The operating burden moves into schedule design: concurrency limits, backoff, jitter, terminal-state detection, and a visible measure of how old each observation is. A polling interval longer than the escalation window cannot support that escalation window.

That is the trade-off.

An internal gateway fits a larger organization that needs one evidence vocabulary across SMS, email, and later channels. It also creates a service to deploy and watch. Use it when shared policy offsets that ownership cost, not because a gateway diagram looks tidy.

Submission-only integration is the smallest option. Its claim is also the smallest: "we asked the transport to send." For some notices that is enough. If a later action depends on delivery or cancellation, it is not.

This table deliberately avoids a vendor score. Country support, sender registration, callback authentication, scheduling, cancellation semantics, data location, and status retention must be verified for the exact US and EU destinations in scope. A broad coverage label cannot answer those narrower questions.

Budget evidence age before choosing an API

Start with a clock. Suppose policy schedules a compliance reminder 10 minutes after an initial notice unless the first notice reaches a terminal state. Reserve 60 seconds for internal queueing and processing, then choose a maximum evidence age that leaves time to make the decision. Those figures are an example policy, not carrier guarantees or universal targets.

The useful signal is evidence_age_seconds: current time minus the time your system last obtained transport evidence. It answers a direct operational question. How stale is the fact on which the next escalation will rely?

Stale is not failed.

Three clocks are easy to mix up:

  1. occurredAt is when the external transition reportedly happened.
  2. observedAt is when your system received or fetched it.
  3. decisionAt is when policy evaluated the record.

Keep all three. A late callback may describe an early event, and overwriting one timestamp with another erases the delay you need to diagnose. Also keep the original external status beside a normalized internal state. Unknown values should enter a quarantine path and increment a mapping-error counter; silently translating them to failed invents evidence. Now picture the 10-minute reminder: the initial submission is observed at 09:00:00, a transport event occurs at 09:00:08, but the callback reaches the ledger at 09:02:40. The occurrence time describes the transport event; the observation time exposes 152 seconds of evidence delay. Policy at 09:09:00 needs both facts to explain why it did, or did not, release the reminder. The numbers make the boundary testable without pretending they describe every network.

SMS status is transport evidence. It does not prove that a person read the notice or that the intended person held the phone. NIST SP 800-63B discusses restrictions and risks around using the public switched telephone network for out-of-band authentication. That makes the boundary crisp: notification delivery and identity proof are separate claims.

Implement the evidence ledger in TypeScript

Use an append-only event shape and derive current state from it. The application supplies a stable notice ID. The adapter translates external vocabulary, while the policy engine sees only the normalized record.

type DeliveryState =
  | "submitted"
  | "scheduled"
  | "sent"
  | "delivered"
  | "failed"
  | "cancelled"
  | "unknown";

type EvidenceEvent = {
  noticeId: string;
  externalMessageId?: string;
  source: "application" | "callback" | "poll";
  state: DeliveryState;
  externalState?: string;
  occurredAt?: string;
  observedAt: string;
  contentDigest: string;
};

type CancelObservation = {
  outcome: "cancelled" | "already_sent" | "not_found" | "unknown";
  observedAt: string;
};

interface MessageTransport {
  submit(input: {
    noticeId: string;
    destination: string;
    body: string;
    sendAt?: Date;
  }): Promise<{ externalMessageId: string; state: DeliveryState }>;
  getState(externalMessageId: string): Promise<{
    state: DeliveryState;
    externalState: string;
    occurredAt?: string;
  }>;
  cancel(externalMessageId: string): Promise<CancelObservation>;
}

Do not make cancellation a boolean. Scheduling and dispatch can race, so false says too little and true can be overread. A recorded outcome lets policy distinguish a notice stopped before dispatch from one that may already be in flight.

Next, make freshness executable. This small function does not guess whether delivery failed. It reports whether the available evidence is old enough to require repair.

type CurrentEvidence = {
  noticeId: string;
  state: DeliveryState;
  observedAt: string;
};

const terminalStates = new Set<DeliveryState>([
  "delivered",
  "failed",
  "cancelled",
]);

function needsRepair(
  record: CurrentEvidence,
  now: Date,
  maximumAgeMs: number,
): boolean {
  if (terminalStates.has(record.state)) return false;

  const observedAtMs = Date.parse(record.observedAt);
  if (!Number.isFinite(observedAtMs)) return true;

  return now.getTime() - observedAtMs >= maximumAgeMs;
}

The repair worker should select nonterminal stale records, add jitter, cap concurrency, and back off after transient errors. Persist the fetched observation before evaluating escalation. If a status lookup returns no usable mapping, preserve unknown; absence is not proof of failure.

There is one serious gap around submission. A process can stop after the remote system accepts a request but before the local ledger records its identifier. Write intent to a transactional outbox first, use a stable logical ID with any documented idempotency mechanism, and reconcile unresolved intents. This recovery path is part of integration effort. Three happy-path method calls are not.

Turn the ledger into alerts, not noise

A diagram in words: the compliance service writes intent to an outbox; a worker submits it; callbacks and status reads append evidence; a projector builds current state; the policy engine evaluates that state; the scheduler either cancels the reminder or releases it. Every arrow needs a durable handoff, an idempotency rule, or both.

Instrument decisions. Count submissions by normalized result, rejected callback authentication, replayed events, unknown status mappings, repair outcomes, and cancellation outcomes. Track evidence age and oldest unresolved notice. Measure callback processing lag separately from provider-reported occurrence time, since the former is the part your service can directly improve.

Alert on policy risk, not a lone failed message. One delivery can fail for an expected destination-specific reason. A sustained rise in stale evidence, a growing oldest-unresolved value, or repeated unknown mappings threatens the decision process itself.

Test that process with a fixed fixture before procurement and before release. Use one immediate notice, one scheduled notice, a cancellation well before its deadline, a cancellation at the dispatch boundary, and a terminal status. Then replay a callback, reverse two callbacks, suppress one callback so polling repairs it, and interrupt the worker after remote acceptance. Nine cases. Each candidate integration should yield an explainable ledger after every case.

This is also where integration effort becomes visible. Record adapter code, ingress authentication, key rotation, replay storage, schema validation, repair load, sandbox constraints, retention behavior, and on-call ownership. Apply hard gates first. A transport whose cancellation outcome cannot support the compliance decision should not pass because its initial setup takes fewer lines.

If email shares the workflow, share the notice ID, content digest, and policy decision record. Do not merge channel claims. DMARC, defined by RFC 7489, provides domain-based email authentication, policy, and reporting; it does not authenticate SMS or prove that an email was read.

Know where the record stops

The ledger proves what the application requested, what transport evidence it observed, and why policy acted. It cannot turn a transport status into proof of human attention. It cannot retract a message after dispatch. It cannot repair vague external state definitions.

This approach is not a fit when submission evidence alone satisfies the requirement; use the smaller request log and avoid operating callback ingress and reconciliation. It is also a poor fit when a team cannot own authenticated inbound traffic or a repair worker. In that case, choose polling-led collection and accept its detection-delay limitation, or move the shared policy into an internal gateway with explicit service ownership. The trade-off is operational surface versus evidence freshness.

Keep the final selection narrow: choose the evidence path that meets the decision deadline with the least operational surface your team can own. Then verify it against the exact destinations, sender rules, cancellation boundary, callback security, and retention needs in the compliance workflow. Fresh, attributable evidence is the deliverable.

Further reading

  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html

title: MultiWorldBench: Do Independently Controlled Views Describe One Shared World?
description:
arXiv:2610.11723v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multiplayer world models must ensure that independently controlled views remain consistent with one shared and persistent world. We introduce MultiWorldBench, a diagnostic Minecraft benchmark containing 495 case configurations across seven task suites and ten capabilities, including independent control, cross-view motion, shared-state synchronization, persistence, structural reasoning, concurrent interaction, and delayed revisit. We evaluate Solaris, Gamma-World, and MineWorld, using Engine GT as a reference. Gamma-World achieves the highest ten-capability average among the generated systems at 21.39, followed by Solaris at 20.88 and MineWorld at 1.89, while Engine GT reaches 91.69. Gamma-World performs better on several control, shared-state, and revisit capabilities, whereas Solaris leads in cross-view motion and race-condition consistency. Nevertheless, all generated systems score at most 8.00 on state persistence and 1.33 on structural consistency, and none succeeds in spatial reasoning or building-identity preservation. Human preferences produce the same overall ranking and show strong alignment with the automatic evaluation, with a mean dimension-level Spearman correlation of 0.96. These results show that plausible individual views do not yet constitute a coherent multiplayer world.

title: A bot-risk score is not an identity: designing order reviews in Shopify
description:
A suspicious order arrives. Two visits share an IP address, an actor report shows several IPs, and the dashboard assigns a risk score. What should the reviewer actually conclude?

I’m Chris, founder of WebDecoy. Two questions on our Shopify launch discussion brought this into focus: what evidence survives a review, and how do you tell missing traffic from missing collection? Here is the distinction we use, including the limits of our current app.

1. Store observations separately from conclusions

Observation What it does not establish by itself
Two requests used the same IP That the same person made them, or that either request was abusive
A correlated actor used multiple IPs The legal identity of a shopper, or fraud on every related order
An IP was classified as a VPN or proxy That the customer intended abuse
A dashboard shows zero detections That collection is healthy, or that no bots visited

Shared Wi-Fi and company networks are straightforward reasons to be careful with IP-based conclusions. Correlation is an investigation aid. It needs supporting session or fingerprint evidence, and a reviewer should inspect the connection to the particular order.

2. A decision log and an evidence snapshot solve different problems

In WebDecoy’s Shopify app, saving a review records the decision, note, staff ID, and timestamp in review history. Updating the current review does not replace those earlier history entries. The UI shows the latest 100 decisions for that order.

That is not a frozen snapshot of all detection evidence. Detection details and the actor’s current cross-IP information can be fetched separately. Looking at them later is not a guarantee that you are seeing precisely what the reviewer saw earlier.

For any review tool, label these views explicitly:

  • Decision history: what a reviewer recorded and when.
  • Order-linked evidence: which detection or session supported the association.
  • Current investigation context: related activity available now.
  • Evidence snapshot: a preserved version of the evidence at decision time, if your tool actually implements one.

WebDecoy currently implements the review history, but not that full evidence snapshot. Do not turn a saved note into a claim of complete historical reproducibility.

3. Keep concurrent reviews from silently overwriting each other

A useful implementation pattern is an optimistic version check. Our review save path validates the submitted version, updates the current decision only when that version still matches, and inserts the history event in the same database transaction.

Conceptually:

begin transaction
  update current review where version = submitted version
  if no row changed: reject as a conflicting review
  append decision + note + reviewer + timestamp
commit

The reviewer receives a reload message when another staff member has changed the record. This protects the review workflow from a lost update. It still does not preserve the entire detection screen: that requires a separate evidence-versioning design.

Keep customer and payment details out of free-text notes. Our review UI asks reviewers to avoid them.

4. Verify collection before interpreting an empty report

WebDecoy’s Setup & health page separates Storefront and Checkout pixel delivery. Each has a last-success timestamp and a last-error timestamp. A missing timestamp appears as Not yet observed.

For storefront collection:

  1. Enable and save the WebDecoy Bot Detection app embed on the published theme.
  2. Open Setup & health and choose Create test.
  3. Open the generated storefront test link, unlocking a password-protected store if needed.
  4. Return and look for Test detection received. Storefront collection verified.

The test verifies the storefront path; it does not verify checkout-pixel delivery. Test detections are labeled and excluded from traffic metrics, order review, and enforcement.

Checkout monitoring is separate. A connected pixel with no events is not proof of failure; event delivery can depend on customer consent. Likewise, the absence of a detection is not proof that every scraper was stopped. A client that neither executes JavaScript nor touches a decoy may not appear in the storefront report.

5. Make the response a deliberate step

In WebDecoy, saving a review records an assessment. Fulfillment actions remain in Shopify. The app’s order-created handler does not independently cancel an order or block checkout. Cancellation requires a separate merchant-configured and enabled Shopify Flow action.

The useful workflow is: verify collection, inspect the order-linked signals, record the reasoning, then choose the response.

See the workflow

Watch the short Shopify demo and setup walkthrough. The demo uses a test store and seeded data, not customer results. WebDecoy is listed on the Shopify App Store.

AI assisted with drafting; implementation claims were checked against the current app code. This is a workflow example, not a fraud-detection accuracy benchmark.

title: Why Java Says 127 == 127 but 128 != 128
description:
Here's a Java puzzle that confused me for days. Look at this code:

Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);

Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(c == d);

Output:

true
false

Same code, one number bigger, opposite result. My first thought was that Java was broken. It's not. It's showing us what happens behind the scenes when Java converts between simple values like int and objects like Integer.

In this post, we'll learn what wrapper classes are, what boxing, unboxing, autoboxing and auto-unboxing mean (and how they differ), and why the puzzle above behaves the way it does. By the end, you'll also know the traps to avoid.

Unless I show a full class, the snippets go inside a main method.

Primitives vs objects

Java has two kinds of data.

Primitives are simple values. There are exactly eight: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean. A primitive holds the value itself, like 10 or true. It has no methods, and it can never be null.

Objects are instances of classes, like String or ArrayList. A variable holds a reference to the object on the heap. Objects have methods, and a reference can be null.

int age = 25;           // the variable holds 25 directly
String name = "Asha";   // the variable holds a reference to an object

Most of the time, primitives are all you need. But sometimes Java insists on an object. That's where wrapper classes come in.

What are wrapper classes?

A wrapper class is an object version of a primitive. It "wraps" the primitive value inside an object. Java gives you one wrapper for each primitive, all in the java.lang package:

  • byte → Byte
  • short → Short
  • int → Integer
  • long → Long
  • float → Float
  • double → Double
  • char → Character
  • boolean → Boolean

Notice that two of them have longer names: int becomes Integer, and char becomes Character. The other six just capitalize the first letter.

Why do we need them?

There are four main reasons:

1. Collections and generics need objects. You can't write List<int>. Generics only work with objects, so you write List<Integer>.

List<int> bad = new ArrayList<>();        // compile error
List<Integer> good = new ArrayList<>();   // works

2. A primitive can't be null, but a wrapper can. Sometimes "no value" is a real answer, like a test score that hasn't been entered yet.

Integer score = null;     // fine: "no score yet"
int plainScore = null;    // compile error

3. Useful methods and constants. Wrappers come with helpers that primitives can't have:

int n = Integer.parseInt("42");
System.out.println(n + 1);
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE);
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(10));
System.out.println(Character.isDigit('7'));
System.out.println(Double.compare(1.5, 2.5));

Output:

43
2147483647
1010
true
-1

4. Some APIs expect Object. Anything that takes an Object (or generic type) needs a wrapper if you want to pass a number.

Wrappers are immutable

Like String, a wrapper object can never change after it's created. Watch what happens when we "change" an Integer:

Integer i = 127;
Integer j = i;
i++;

System.out.println(i + " " + j);

Output:

128 127

i++ didn't modify the object. It created a new Integer holding 128 and pointed i at it. j still points to the old one.

Boxing and unboxing

Now the two key words:

  • Boxing means converting a primitive into its wrapper object (int → Integer).
  • Unboxing means converting a wrapper object back into a primitive (Integer → int).

Think of putting a gift into a box and taking it out again.

            boxing
   int 10  ---------->  Integer object (on the heap)
           <----------
            unboxing

You can do both by hand with methods:

int a = 10;

Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf(a);   // boxing
int b = boxed.intValue();             // unboxing

System.out.println(boxed + " " + b);

Output:

10 10

Every wrapper has its own pair: Double.valueOf(...) and doubleValue(), Boolean.valueOf(...) and booleanValue(), and so on.

(You may see old code write new Integer(10). That constructor is deprecated, because valueOf is better. We'll see why in a moment.)

Autoboxing and auto-unboxing

Doing this by hand every time would be tiring. So since Java 5, the compiler does it for you automatically:

  • Autoboxing is boxing done automatically by the compiler.
  • Auto-unboxing is unboxing done automatically by the compiler. 
Integer x = 10;     // autoboxing: int -> Integer
int y = x;          // auto-unboxing: Integer -> int

So the difference between the pairs is just who does the work:

  • Boxing / unboxing: the general idea, which you can do manually by calling valueOf() or intValue().
  • Autoboxing / auto-unboxing: the compiler does the same thing for you, with no method calls written by you.

Where it happens

Autoboxing and auto-unboxing happen in many everyday places:

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(5);                 // autoboxing: 5 becomes an Integer
int first = nums.get(0);     // auto-unboxing: Integer becomes int
System.out.println(first + 1);

Output:

6

They also happen in arithmetic (Integer a = 5; Integer b = a + 3; unboxes a, adds, then boxes the result), in method arguments, and in return values.

Behind the scenes: the compiler rewrites your code

There's no magic. The compiler simply inserts the method calls we wrote by hand:

Integer x = 10;     // compiler turns this into: Integer x = Integer.valueOf(10);
int y = x;          // compiler turns this into: int y = x.intValue();

This matters, because those hidden calls have a cost, and in one case (null) they can crash your program. We'll see both soon.

The Integer cache: solving the puzzle

Let's go back to the puzzle. First, remember the difference between == and .equals(). For objects, == checks whether two variables point to the same object, not whether the values match.

Now, Integer.valueOf() (which autoboxing uses) has a trick. Small numbers are used all the time, so Java pre-creates and caches the Integer objects for -128 to 127. If your value is in that range, valueOf gives you a shared object. If it's outside, you get a new object. In simplified form:

public static Integer valueOf(int i) {
    if (i >= -128 && i <= 127) {
        return IntegerCache.cache[i + 128];   // shared, pre-made object
    }
    return new Integer(i);                    // a fresh object
}

Here's the picture for our puzzle:

   CACHE (shared objects for -128 ... 127)       REST OF THE HEAP
  +--------------------------------------+      +-------------+
  | ... [126] [127] ...                  |      | Integer 128 |  <- c
  +--------------------------------------+      +-------------+
        ^        ^                              | Integer 128 |  <- d
        |        |                              +-------------+
        a        b
   a and b point to the SAME object          c and d point to DIFFERENT objects
   a == b  -> true                           c == d  -> false

So a == b is true because both point to the same cached 127. And c == d is false because each 128 is a separate object. Let's confirm with equals, and with a mix of wrapper and primitive:

Integer c = 128, d = 128;
int e = 128;

System.out.println(c == d);
System.out.println(c.equals(d));
System.out.println(c == e);

Output:

false
true
true

The last line is true because when you compare a wrapper with a primitive, Java auto-unboxes the wrapper and compares plain numbers. The rule to remember:

  • Wrapper == wrapper compares references (risky).
  • Wrapper == primitive unboxes and compares values.
  • .equals() compares values (safe).

A few facts about the cache:

  • It exists for Byte, Short, Integer and Long (range -128 to 127), for Character (0 to 127) and for Boolean (only true and false).
  • Float and Double have no cache.
  • The upper limit for Integer can be raised with a JVM setting, but never write code that depends on that.
  • This is the reason valueOf is better than new Integer(...). The constructor always creates a new object and skips the cache.

Trap 1: auto-unboxing a null

A wrapper can be null. A primitive can't. So when Java tries to unbox a null, it has nothing to unbox, and your program crashes.

Integer score = null;
int s = score;        // NullPointerException

On recent Java versions, the error looks like this:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because ...

See the method name in the message? intValue(). That's the call the compiler secretly added. The most common real-life version of this bug is with a Map:

Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
stock.put("pen", 10);

int pens = stock.get("pen");
System.out.println(pens);

int pencils = stock.get("pencil");    // get() returns null, then unboxing fails

Output:

10
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null

There's no "pencil" key, so get returns null, and Java tries to unbox it. The fix is to provide a default: stock.getOrDefault("pencil", 0).

Trap 2: the hidden cost of boxing

Every time Java boxes a value outside the cache, it creates a new object. A wrapper object is also bigger than the primitive it holds. An Integer typically takes 16 bytes, while an int takes 4.

Compare how the data is stored:

   int[]          :  [ 10 ][ 20 ][ 30 ]            values sit side by side

   List<Integer>  :  [ ref ][ ref ][ ref ]         references, each pointing to its own object
                        |      |      |
                        v      v      v
                     Integer Integer Integer
                       10      20      30

For a handful of items, you'll never notice. In a big loop, you will:

Long sum = 0L;
for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
    sum += i;
}
System.out.println(sum);

Output:

499999500000

The answer is right, but look at sum += i. Each round, Java unboxes sum, adds i, then boxes the result into a new Long. That's roughly a million short-lived objects. If we simply declare long sum = 0L;, the loop uses plain numbers with no objects at all, and it's much faster. One letter, L vs l, makes a real difference.

Trap 3: overloaded methods and boxing

Here's one that catches even experienced developers. List has two remove methods: remove(int index) and remove(Object o).

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));

list.remove(1);                      // removes the item at INDEX 1
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));    // removes the VALUE 10

System.out.println(list);

Output:

[30]

With list.remove(1), Java sees a plain int, so it picks the index version and removes 20. To remove by value, you have to box it yourself with Integer.valueOf(10), so Java picks the object version.

Trap 4: wrappers don't convert into each other

Widening works for primitives, but not for wrappers:

long a = 5;        // fine: int to long
Long b = 5;        // compile error: int cannot be converted to Long
Long c = 5L;       // fine
Double d = 5;      // compile error
Double e = 5.0;    // fine

Autoboxing only boxes to the matching wrapper. An int boxes to Integer, and nothing else. The same idea applies to equals: Integer.valueOf(1).equals(Long.valueOf(1)) is false, because they're different classes.

Which one should I use?

  • Primitive or wrapper? Default to the primitive (int). Use the wrapper only when you need an object: in collections and generics, when you need null as a valid answer, or when an API demands it.
  • valueOf or new? Always valueOf, or just let autoboxing do it. It uses the cache, and new Integer(...) is deprecated.
  • parseInt or valueOf? Integer.parseInt("42") returns a primitive int. Integer.valueOf("42") returns an Integer object. Use the one that matches what you need.
  • == or equals? For wrappers, use .equals() (or unbox first). For primitives, use ==.
  • Manual or automatic boxing? Let the compiler do it, but stay aware of it. In hot loops and big data structures, check that you aren't boxing millions of times without need.

Common mistakes

  1. Comparing wrappers with ==. It works for small values because of the cache, then fails on 128. Use .equals().
  2. Forgetting that unboxing can throw. Any Integer that might be null is a hidden NullPointerException if you assign it to an int. Check for null first, or use getOrDefault.
  3. Using wrapper types in hot loops. Long sum instead of long sum quietly creates a flood of objects. Use primitives for counters and totals.
  4. Mixing up list.remove(int) and list.remove(Object). Box the value with Integer.valueOf(...) when you want to remove by value.
  5. Expecting wrappers to convert to each other. Long l = 5; and Double d = 5; don't compile. Use 5L and 5.0.
  6. Using new Integer(...). It's deprecated, skips the cache and creates needless objects. Use Integer.valueOf(...) or autoboxing.

Quick recap

  • Primitives hold simple values. Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Character and so on) are their object versions.
  • You need wrappers for collections and generics, for null, for helper methods, and for APIs that expect objects.
  • Boxing turns a primitive into a wrapper. Unboxing turns it back.
  • Autoboxing and auto-unboxing are the same conversions, done automatically by the compiler. It rewrites your code to call valueOf() and intValue().
  • Integer.valueOf() caches values from -128 to 127, which is why 127 == 127 is true and 128 == 128 is false for Integer objects.
  • Wrapper objects are immutable, so "changing" one creates a new object.
  • Watch for null unboxing, boxing in loops, remove overloads and == on wrappers.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: write the Integer a = 127 and Integer c = 128 puzzle yourself and run it. Then change the numbers to -128, -129, 1000 and 100 and predict each result before you run it. After that, create a Map<String, Integer>, read a missing key into an int and see the NullPointerException for yourself. Finally, fix it with getOrDefault.

For a bonus experiment, time the Long sum loop against the long sum loop using System.nanoTime(), and see how big the difference gets with 100 million iterations.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Don't Guess, Just Ask: Evaluating Interactive Requirement Clarification for Repository-Level Software Development
description:
arXiv:2610.13022v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: As LLMs become increasingly capable of implementing software, a critical bottleneck emerges: whether they truly understand what users want. Users often begin with vague intent, leaving important requirements to be clarified through interaction. In repository-level development, misunderstandings can propagate and cause costly rework. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate implementation from complete specifications or underspecified requests, overlooking pre-coding requirement clarification. Prior clarification studies mainly focus on function-level tasks. It therefore remains unclear how well LLMs can transform vague intent into clear requirements through interaction and how this capability affects subsequent code generation.
  We introduce ReqClarifyBench, an interactive requirement clarification benchmark for repository-level software development. It contains 341 tasks spanning game, miniapp, and web development, each with a vague user intent, a human-validated requirement document, and code evaluation artifacts. We employ LLM-based user simulators with diverse personas derived from real-world conversations. We evaluate six LLMs in terms of clarification effectiveness and generated requirement document quality. Results show that stronger clarification effectiveness does not necessarily translate into higher document quality, and performance varies substantially across user personas. We also find that coding-agent harnesses do not further improve requirement document quality compared with their base LLMs. These findings offer insights for building LLM-based end-to-end software development systems.

title: Agentic Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
description:
arXiv:2610.13510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.

title: How to change a primary key that foreign keys already point at
description:
You try to move a table's primary key onto a different column and get:

Msg 3725, Level 16, State 1
The constraint 'PK_Customer' is being referenced by table 'Order', foreign key constraint
'FK_Order_Customer'.
Msg 3727, Level 16, State 1
Could not drop constraint. See previous errors.

A foreign key is a promise that every value in the child column exists exactly once in the parent, and the primary key is what makes that true. Drop the key and the promise has nothing holding it up, so SQL Server refuses while any foreign key still points at it.

The message names one constraint. If three tables point at the key you will see this three times, one drop at a time.

A unique index does not spare you the drop

The intuition is that adding a unique index on the same column gives SQL Server another guarantee to lean on, so the key can then go. It does not work:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UQ_Customer_CustomerCode ON dbo.Customer(CustomerCode);

ALTER TABLE dbo.Customer DROP CONSTRAINT PK_Customer;
-- Msg 3725 again, word for word

The foreign key is bound to the constraint it was created against, not to whatever happens to be unique at the time. So the order of work is fixed:

  1. Script the foreign keys that point at the key, so you can put them back.
  2. Drop those foreign keys.
  3. Drop the primary key.
  4. Add the new primary key.
  5. Recreate the foreign keys.

Step 1 is the one people skip and the only one that cannot be recovered from.

Find what points at the key

The constraints live on the other tables, which is why reading your table's definition does not show them:

SELECT
    fk.name AS foreign_key,
    OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(fk.parent_object_id) + '.' +
    OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id) AS referencing_table
FROM sys.foreign_keys AS fk
WHERE fk.referenced_object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.Customer');

Script them before you drop them

Recreating a foreign key from memory means getting its columns, its name and its referential actions right. Get the ON DELETE CASCADE wrong and you have either a delete that fails forever or one that quietly removes rows nobody asked it to. Generate the statements instead, and keep the output:

SELECT
    'ALTER TABLE ' + QUOTENAME(OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)) + '.' +
    QUOTENAME(OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)) +
    ' ADD CONSTRAINT ' + QUOTENAME(fk.name) + ' FOREIGN KEY (' +
    STUFF((SELECT ', ' + QUOTENAME(pc.name)
           FROM sys.foreign_key_columns fkc
           JOIN sys.columns pc ON pc.object_id = fkc.parent_object_id
                              AND pc.column_id = fkc.parent_column_id
           WHERE fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
           ORDER BY fkc.constraint_column_id
           FOR XML PATH(''), TYPE).value('.', 'nvarchar(max)'), 1, 2, '') +
    ') REFERENCES ' + QUOTENAME(OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(fk.referenced_object_id)) + '.' +
    QUOTENAME(OBJECT_NAME(fk.referenced_object_id)) + ' (' +
    STUFF((SELECT ', ' + QUOTENAME(rc.name)
           FROM sys.foreign_key_columns fkc
           JOIN sys.columns rc ON rc.object_id = fkc.referenced_object_id
                              AND rc.column_id = fkc.referenced_column_id
           WHERE fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
           ORDER BY fkc.constraint_column_id
           FOR XML PATH(''), TYPE).value('.', 'nvarchar(max)'), 1, 2, '') +
    ')' +
    CASE fk.delete_referential_action
        WHEN 1 THEN ' ON DELETE CASCADE'
        WHEN 2 THEN ' ON DELETE SET NULL'
        WHEN 3 THEN ' ON DELETE SET DEFAULT' ELSE '' END +
    CASE fk.update_referential_action
        WHEN 1 THEN ' ON UPDATE CASCADE'
        WHEN 2 THEN ' ON UPDATE SET NULL'
        WHEN 3 THEN ' ON UPDATE SET DEFAULT' ELSE '' END +
    ';' AS recreate_statement
FROM sys.foreign_keys AS fk
WHERE fk.referenced_object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.Customer');

Each row comes back ready to run:

ALTER TABLE [dbo].[Order] ADD CONSTRAINT [FK_Order_Customer]
    FOREIGN KEY ([CustomerCode]) REFERENCES [dbo].[Customer] ([CustomerCode]);

Swapping ADD CONSTRAINT for DROP CONSTRAINT in the same query gives you step 2:

SELECT 'ALTER TABLE ' + QUOTENAME(OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)) + '.' +
       QUOTENAME(OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)) +
       ' DROP CONSTRAINT ' + QUOTENAME(fk.name) + ';' AS drop_statement
FROM sys.foreign_keys AS fk
WHERE fk.referenced_object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.Customer');

Run both before you change anything, and put the recreate output somewhere you will still have it tomorrow. It is the only record of what the keys were.

If the first query returns an error about QUOTED_IDENTIFIER rather than any rows, the tool you are running it in has that option off. SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON; at the top fixes it.

Check the new key's column first

A primary key column must have no duplicates and no empty values. Both failures arrive after the old key is already gone, which is the worst moment to discover them:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerId) AS distinct_values,
       SUM(CASE WHEN CustomerId IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS empty_values
FROM dbo.Customer;

All three numbers have to agree: distinct_values equal to rows_total, and empty_values zero. When they do not, this names the values to fix:

SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS rows_with_this_value
FROM dbo.Customer
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Skip the check and you get one of these. Duplicates:

Msg 1505, Level 16, State 1
The CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement terminated because a duplicate key was found for the object
name 'dbo.Customer' and the index name 'PK_Customer'. The duplicate key value is (AAA).

That says CREATE UNIQUE INDEX even though you wrote ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT, because a key is enforced by an index underneath. Usefully, it names the first duplicate value it found.

An empty value:

Msg 8111, Level 16, State 1
Cannot define PRIMARY KEY constraint on nullable column in table 'Customer'.

The column has to be NOT NULL before it can be in a key, and making it so is its own job once the table has rows.

If the new key has more than one column

A foreign key must name every column of the key it points at, in the key's order. Anything else is refused:

-- the key is (Country, SiteCode); this names one of the two
ALTER TABLE dbo.Asset ADD CONSTRAINT FK_Asset_Site
    FOREIGN KEY (SiteCode) REFERENCES dbo.Site(SiteCode);

Msg 1776, Level 16, State 1
There are no primary or candidate keys in the referenced table 'dbo.Site' that match the
referencing column list in the foreign key 'FK_Asset_Site'.

The same message appears for naming both columns in the wrong order. So widening a key from one column to two means every table pointing at it needs a second column added and filled before its foreign key can go back — which is usually the real size of the job, and worth knowing before you drop anything.

The keys you put back need not point at the primary key

A foreign key can reference any set of columns carrying a unique index, not only the primary key. That is what lets you move the key without rewriting the children:

-- keep the old column unique, so the old relationships are still legal
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UQ_Customer_CustomerCode ON dbo.Customer(CustomerCode);

ALTER TABLE dbo.[Order]  DROP CONSTRAINT FK_Order_Customer;
ALTER TABLE dbo.Customer DROP CONSTRAINT PK_Customer;
ALTER TABLE dbo.Customer ADD  CONSTRAINT PK_Customer PRIMARY KEY (CustomerId);

-- points at the unique index now, and enforces exactly as before
ALTER TABLE dbo.[Order] ADD CONSTRAINT FK_Order_Customer
    FOREIGN KEY (CustomerCode) REFERENCES dbo.Customer(CustomerCode);

The children keep the column they already have, full of values that already match. You still drop and recreate each foreign key, but nothing has to be backfilled and no child table changes shape.

To confirm what a key is actually resting on:

SELECT fk.name AS foreign_key, i.name AS points_at, i.is_primary_key
FROM sys.foreign_keys AS fk
JOIN sys.indexes AS i ON i.object_id = fk.referenced_object_id
                     AND i.index_id = fk.key_index_id;

is_primary_key of 0 means that relationship survives the primary key moving again.

Before you run it

  • Keep the recreate script. A foreign key you forget to put back is not an error. It is a rule that has stopped being enforced, and you find out when bad data turns up months later.
  • Wrap it in one transaction. Half applied, the table has no key and the children have no relationships.
  • Count the keys afterwards against the list you generated at the start. The same query, run again, should return the same rows.

Seeing the whole job before you start

In WoodFireERD, untick PK against the old column and you are asked Change the primary key? before anything changes, with the relationships it affects named. There are two answers: Keep CustomerCode unique, which adds the unique index and keeps every relationship pointing at that column, or Let CustomerCode repeat, which removes them. Tick PK against the new column and the Primary key section lists the key in order, with its Constraint name there to edit.

Pending changes then writes the migration script in the order SQL Server needs — the drops, the key, the keys put back. For anything it cannot do for you, such as filling a new key column that is not an identity, it says so as a step rather than generating a statement that would fail. If you untick a key and change your mind, Restore 1 relationship appears above the editor and puts back what unticking removed.

*Originally published at woodfireerd.com.

title: Knowing Is Not Telling: Identity Ossification in LLM Representations of Trans-border Communities
description:
arXiv:2610.12610v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Ethnic and cultural identities rarely align with political borders, a tension made sharper by migration and long-standing cross-border ties. Communities such as the Sami, the Rohingya, and the Kurds have long lived across more than one state. This tension is especially clear in mainland Southeast Asia, where many communities share history, language, and culture across state lines. We study nine such transborder ethnic communities along China's southwestern border with mainland Southeast Asia, looking at how large language models (LLMs) represent them. We define and study identity ossification: a pattern where LLMs turn a fluid, cross-border ethnic identity into a single, fixed nation-state identity. We introduce the Transborder Identity Ossification Diagnostic Framework (TIODF) that compares direct factual questions with open-ended narrative questions to test whether ossification comes from missing knowledge or from how models frame their answers. We test GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.2 in English and Chinese. Ossification varies substantially across models and query languages. It appears in only 10.1% of GPT-5.1's English answers, but in 62.6% of DeepSeek-V3.2's Chinese answers. Models often still tell a single-nation story even when they answer the factual question correctly. This decoupling suggests that ossification reflects narrative framing rather than simple knowledge absence, which matters for how we test cultural fairness in multilingual AI systems.

title: How to Create AI Product Videos That Convert: A Complete Guide for E-commerce Brands
description:
How to Create AI Product Videos That Convert: A Complete Guide for E-commerce Brands
Introduction
In today's competitive e-commerce market, product images alone are often not enough to capture customer attention.
Consumers want to understand how products look, feel, and work before making a purchase decision. This is why product videos have become one of the most powerful marketing tools for online stores.
However, creating professional product videos traditionally requires:

  • Expensive equipment
  • Professional videographers
  • Complex editing workflows
  • Long production timelines For many small businesses and independent brands, producing high-quality videos consistently is difficult. AI video generators are changing this process. With AI-powered tools, brands can now transform product images, descriptions, and creative ideas into engaging product videos without requiring advanced video production skills. In this guide, we will explain how to create AI product videos that convert and how e-commerce businesses can use AI video technology to grow faster. Why Product Videos Matter for E-commerce
  • Videos Help Customers Understand Products Better Online shoppers cannot physically touch products before purchasing. A product video helps customers see:
  • Product details
  • Size and appearance
  • How the product works
  • Real-world usage scenarios For example, a skincare brand can show:
  • The texture of the product
  • How it is applied
  • Lifestyle scenes
  • Before-and-after effects This creates a stronger shopping experience compared with static images.
  • Videos Increase Customer Engagement Social media platforms such as TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts prioritize video content. Short product videos can help brands:
  • Increase watch time
  • Improve brand awareness
  • Reach new audiences
  • Generate more website traffic A simple product image may be ignored within seconds, while a dynamic video can immediately capture attention. The Challenges of Traditional Product Video Creation Before AI video tools became popular, creating product videos usually required: High Production Costs Professional product videos often require:
  • Cameras
  • Lighting equipment
  • Studio space
  • Models
  • Editors The total cost can easily reach thousands of dollars. Long Production Cycles Traditional workflows often include:
  • Planning
  • Shooting
  • Editing
  • Reviewing
  • Revising A single video may take days or weeks to complete. Difficult Content Scaling E-commerce brands constantly need new content:
  • New products
  • Seasonal campaigns
  • Advertising variations
  • Social media posts Producing enough videos manually is challenging. How AI Video Generators Change Product Video Creation AI video technology allows brands to create professional-looking product videos faster and more efficiently. With AI, businesses can: Turn Product Images Into Videos A single product image can become:
  • A cinematic product showcase
  • A lifestyle advertisement
  • A social media video AI can add:
  • Camera movement
  • Lighting effects
  • Background scenes
  • Product animations Create Multiple Marketing Versions Quickly Instead of producing one expensive video, brands can create multiple versions for testing: Example: Version A:
  • Premium luxury style Version B:
  • Social media trend style Version C:
  • Minimal product showcase This helps marketers discover which creative performs best. Step-by-Step: How to Create AI Product Videos Step 1: Prepare Your Product Assets Start with:
  • High-quality product images
  • Product descriptions
  • Brand style guidelines
  • Target audience information Better input materials usually produce better AI results. Step 2: Choose the Right Video Style Different products require different video approaches. Product Showcase Videos Best for:
  • Electronics
  • Beauty products
  • Fashion items Focus on:
  • Product details
  • Premium visuals
  • Smooth camera movement Lifestyle Videos Best for:
  • Fashion brands
  • Home products
  • Outdoor products Show products in realistic environments. Example: Instead of showing only a coffee machine: "Create a warm morning kitchen scene where someone prepares coffee using this premium coffee maker." Social Media Advertisement Videos Designed for:
  • TikTok
  • Instagram Reels
  • YouTube Shorts Characteristics:
  • Fast pacing
  • Strong opening scenes
  • Eye-catching visuals Step 3: Write Better AI Video Prompts A detailed prompt improves generation quality. A good product video prompt should include: Product Describe the object clearly. Example: "Premium glass skincare serum bottle with elegant packaging" Camera Movement Example: "Slow cinematic camera movement, close-up product rotation" Environment Example: "Luxury beauty studio with soft lighting" Style Example: "High-end commercial advertising style" Step 4: Generate and Optimize After creating the first version: Review:
  • Product accuracy
  • Motion quality
  • Visual consistency
  • Brand style Then improve the prompt and generate new versions. Best AI Product Video Ideas for E-commerce Brands
  • Product Launch Videos Create excitement around new products. Example: "Introducing our new premium wireless headphones with futuristic cinematic visuals."
  • Social Media Ads Short AI videos can be used for:
  • TikTok Ads
  • Instagram Ads
  • Facebook Ads
  • Product Demonstrations Show customers how products work. Examples:
  • Beauty tutorials
  • Electronics demonstrations
  • Fitness equipment usage
  • Seasonal Marketing Campaigns Create videos for:
  • Black Friday
  • Christmas
  • Valentine's Day
  • Summer campaigns Tips to Create Better AI Product Videos Keep the Product Consistent Make sure:
  • Product shape stays accurate
  • Brand colors remain consistent
  • Packaging does not change Focus on the First Few Seconds The opening scene determines whether viewers continue watching. Strong openings include:
  • Product reveal
  • Dramatic camera movement
  • Lifestyle transformation Create Different Versions Do not rely on one video. Test:
  • Different scenes
  • Different angles
  • Different audiences How Vidnix Helps Brands Create AI Product Videos Faster Vidnix enables creators and businesses to transform ideas, images, and product concepts into engaging AI videos. With AI-powered video generation, brands can:
  • Create marketing videos faster
  • Turn images into dynamic content
  • Experiment with multiple creative styles
  • Produce social media-ready videos Whether you are running an online store, building a brand, or managing digital marketing campaigns, AI video tools can help reduce production barriers and create more engaging content. Conclusion AI product videos are becoming an essential tool for modern e-commerce marketing. Instead of spending large budgets on traditional video production, businesses can now use AI video generators to create professional product content faster and more efficiently. By combining high-quality product images, detailed prompts, and the right video style, brands can create videos that attract customers, improve engagement, and increase conversions. The future of e-commerce marketing is becoming more visual, and AI video is helping businesses create better content at scale. FAQ What is an AI product video? An AI product video is a marketing video created using artificial intelligence. AI tools can generate animations, camera movements, backgrounds, and scenes from product images or text descriptions. Can AI create product videos from images? Yes. AI video generators can transform static product images into dynamic videos with motion effects, cinematic camera movements, and realistic scenes. Are AI product videos good for e-commerce? Yes. AI product videos help e-commerce brands showcase products better, increase engagement, and create more advertising content efficiently. How long does it take to create an AI product video? Depending on the complexity, AI video tools can generate product videos within minutes, allowing brands to create and test more marketing content quickly.

title: Vercel applications are protected from Next.js August 2026 security vulnerabilities
description:
Summary

Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action.

Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities

Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities:

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input.

  • CVE-2026-75604 (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components.

After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service.

Impact on Vercel deployments

Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required.

  • Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path.

  • The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected.

Resolution for self-hosted applications

Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version.

For applications running Next.js 16.x:

In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately.

title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.12837v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.
