title: The one test that proves no user can see another user's data
description:
Every multi-tenant app has the same nightmare bug: a route that forgets to check who owns the thing it returns. One missing where owner_id = ? and user B can read user A's projects by changing an id in the URL.

Code review doesn't reliably catch it. Neither do the tests most of us write, because we test the routes we remember, and the leaky one is always the route we forgot.

So I stopped writing per-route authorisation tests and wrote one test that walks every route the API has.

The idea

  1. Collect every route the server registers, automatically.
  2. Make two accounts. Alice creates real data: a project, a file, a secret, an API key.
  3. For every route that takes an id, call it as Mallory using Alice's ids.
  4. Every single one must answer 404 (not 403, which confirms the thing exists). With no session at all, every one must answer 401.
  5. The only exceptions are routes that show something an owner chose to publish, and each exception is written down with its reason.

A route added next month that forgets the owner check fails this test on day one, without anyone remembering to test it.

Collecting the routes

In Fastify there is a hook for exactly this. Register it before your routes:

const routeList: { method: string; url: string }[] = [];
app.addHook('onRoute', (r) => {
  for (const m of [r.method].flat()) {
    if (m !== 'HEAD' && m !== 'OPTIONS') routeList.push({ method: m, url: r.url });
  }
});
app.decorate('routeList', routeList);

In Express 4 you can walk app._router.stack; most frameworks have an equivalent.

The test 

const SHARED: Record<string, string> = {
  'GET /showcase/:id': 'an app its owner shared publicly',
  'GET /shared-chats/:slug': 'a chat its owner published with a link',
};

const withIds = routes.filter((r) => /:|\*/.test(r.url));

// Alice's real ids wherever a route names one of hers.
const fill = (url: string) => url
  .replace(/^\/projects\/:id/, `/projects/${project.id}`)
  .replace(':gid', generation.id)
  .replace(':name', 'ALICE_KEY')
  .replace(/:id/g, randomUUID())
  .replace('*', 'web/secret.ts');

const leaks: string[] = [];
for (const r of withIds) {
  const id = `${r.method} ${r.url}`;
  if (SHARED[id]) continue;
  const url = fill(r.url);
  const res = await app.inject({ method: r.method, url, cookies: mallory.jar, payload: plausibleBody(r.method) });
  if (res.statusCode !== 404) leaks.push(`${id} as another account: ${res.statusCode}`);
  if (res.body.includes('alice only')) leaks.push(`${id} showed Alice's data`);
  const anon = await app.inject({ method: r.method, url, payload: plausibleBody(r.method) });
  if (anon.statusCode !== 401) leaks.push(`${id} with no session: ${anon.statusCode}`);
}
expect(leaks).toEqual([]);

Two details matter more than they look.

Send a plausible body. If a route validates the body before it checks ownership, an empty body gets a 400 and the test learns nothing about the owner check. Give every request a body that would pass validation, so the 404 you get back is the owner check speaking.

Collect leaks, then assert once. A list of every failing route is far more useful than the first failure. On my codebase the list was empty, which brings me to the part most people skip.

Prove the test can fail

An empty list is only good news if the test can actually catch a leak. So I broke one route on purpose: I removed the owner check from the route that lists a project's secrets, and ran the test again.

- "GET /projects/:id/secrets as another account: 200 {"secrets":[{"name":"ALICE_KEY"...

It failed, naming the route and showing the leaked secret names. I put the check back. Now I trust the green.

The lists of "mine"

Routes without an id leak too: /me/projects, /me/exports, /me/api-keys. A second test signs in as Mallory and checks that none of those responses contain Alice's ids, email or names anywhere in the JSON.

What it costs

76 routes with ids, two requests each, about 400 ms with Fastify's inject. It runs with the rest of the test suite before every commit.

I built this for spoe.ai, an AI app builder where people prompt full-stack apps and export the code. When an AI writes a lot of your routes, "we'll remember to test authorisation" stops being a plan. A test that walks every route does not need anyone to remember.

If your app has more than one user, steal the idea. It's an afternoon of work and it closes the most common serious bug in multi-tenant software.

title: The cheapest way to render a 1-minute Blender animation without buying a GPU: six options, with measured numbers
description:
Official JANCTION Render: https://render.janction.jp

Disclosure: this post comes from the team behind JANCTION Render, one of the six options below. The laptop and JANCTION Render numbers are our own measurements. For the other services we describe how they charge and what they ask of you, and link to them instead of quoting prices that change.

Short answer: if waiting costs you nothing, the free routes are your own computer and SheepIt's volunteer farm. If you want the minute back the same day without setting up a machine, you pay for GPU time somewhere. On JANCTION Render, one minute of a simple scene at 1920x1080 and 128 samples comes to about 7,800 GPU-seconds, about 780 JPY (around $5), and a heavier scene such as Blender's Classroom demo to about 1,290 JPY (around $8).

What "one minute" means

At 24 fps, one minute is 1,440 frames. Every option below comes down to how long one frame takes, times 1,440, and who pays for that time. Resolution and Cycles samples move the number more than anything else, so settle them before comparing: denoising with fewer samples often looks the same as many samples without it.

1. Your own computer first (free, slow)

Before paying anyone, make sure Cycles uses the GPU you already have: Edit > Preferences > System > Cycles Render Devices, then Metal on Apple silicon Macs, HIP on recent AMD GPUs, oneAPI on Intel Arc, CUDA or OptiX on NVIDIA, and set Render Properties > Device to GPU Compute. For drafts, EEVEE is much faster than Cycles.

What it costs in time, measured on a simple scene (a rotating cube) on a laptop with a Core Ultra 9 386H: 20.0 seconds per frame on the CPU at 1920x1080 and 128 samples, so about 8 hours for the minute, and 6.6 seconds per frame at 1280x720 and 64 samples, about 2.6 hours. The same laptop's GeForce RTX 5070 Ti took 6.0 and 2.5 seconds per frame: about 2.4 hours and 1 hour. These are single frames multiplied by 1,440; a real scene with more geometry, textures and light bounces takes longer.

2. SheepIt Render Farm (free, you wait)

SheepIt is a free, community-run farm: your frames render on volunteers' computers, and letting your own machine render for others earns points that move your projects up the queue. It costs nothing but waiting. Your .blend is opened on other people's machines, so it suits personal projects better than client work under an NDA. https://www.sheepit-renderfarm.com

3. Google Colab notebooks (free GPU when one is available)

Several open-source notebooks install Blender on a Colab GPU and render a .blend from your Google Drive. It is free when a GPU is available, but free-tier GPUs and session length are not guaranteed, long renders get disconnected, and you set up and watch each run. Read Colab's terms before relying on it.

4. Rent a GPU by the hour (RunPod, Vast.ai and similar)

You start a machine with a GPU, install Blender, upload the file, render, download and stop the machine. You pay for every hour the machine is on, including setup, uploads and the evening you forget to stop it, and everything on it is yours to manage.

5. Commercial render farms (GarageFarm, RebusFarm, Fox Renderfarm and others)

You upload the .blend through their site or plugin and they render on many machines at once, so a minute comes back fast. They charge by node-hour or GHz-hour, show an estimate before you start, and several offer trial credit. For heavy production scenes they are the strongest option; for a short one-off they can be more than you need.

6. A per-second GPU API (JANCTION Render)

JANCTION Render is a cloud GPU render farm for Blender that AI agents call as an MCP server or HTTP API, and that you can also call from a terminal or a script. You send a .blend, a bpy script or a 3D file (glTF / FBX / USD / OBJ), get a preview in seconds, then the frames or an MP4. You pay for the GPU-seconds actually used, 0.1 JPY per GPU-second.

Measured per frame on its GPU (from 24-frame batches, including Blender start-up and scene loading, so a long run comes out a little lower), times 1,440:

  • simple scene, 1280x720, 64 samples: 2.46 GPU-seconds per frame, 3,542 GPU-seconds for the minute, about 354 JPY (about $2.2)
  • simple scene, 1920x1080, 128 samples: 5.39 per frame, 7,762 for the minute, about 776 JPY (about $4.9)
  • Blender's Classroom demo, 1920x1080, 128 samples with denoising: 8.93 per frame, 12,859 for the minute, about 1,286 JPY (about $8.1)

Dollar figures use 158 JPY per USD (ECB reference rate, 2026-10-09); charges are in JPY.

Each new key gets 100 JPY of GPU time with no card, and 400 JPY more after saving a card on a page that charges nothing (once per card), for 14 days. That covers the 720p minute above. After it, previews stay free up to 2 GPU-minutes a day and finals are paid from prepaid credit.

Limits worth knowing before you start: 1920x1080 on free time and up to 3840x2160 on prepaid credit; a job part is at most 240 frames, so the service splits a longer instruction into 240-frame parts and returns each part as its own file, which means a one-minute animation comes back as six MP4s to join; at most 10 GPU-hours per job; files are deleted 24 hours after last use (7 days for keys that have topped up). There are two GPUs, one of them shared with other work, so jobs wait in a queue when they are busy, and https://render.janction.jp/status shows the wait.

From a terminal:

pip install janction-render
janction-render preview minute.blend
janction-render estimate minute.blend --frames 1-240 --size 1920x1080
for s in 1 241 481 721 961 1201; do
  janction-render render minute.blend --frames $s-$((s+239)) --output mp4 --wait
done

The first janction-render command makes a free key, the preview comes back in seconds, the estimate shows the GPU-seconds and the price before anything runs, and each render waits for its MP4 and downloads it.

From an AI agent: add https://render.janction.jp/mcp as a connector in Claude or ChatGPT, or run claude mcp add --transport http janction-render https://render.janction.jp/mcp in Claude Code, then ask for a preview of the scene and the minute.

Side by side

Option Money for the minute Your effort Time until you have it
Own laptop, CPU (simple scene, 1080p, 128 samples) none set and leave about 8 hours
Own laptop, RTX 5070 Ti (same scene) none set and leave about 2.4 hours
SheepIt none (you earn points) upload depends on the queue and your points
Colab notebook none on the free tier set up and watch each run disconnections on long runs
Hourly GPU rental per hour the machine is on run the machine yourself as fast as the GPU you rent
Commercial farm per node-hour or GHz-hour upload through their site or plugin fast, many machines at once
JANCTION Render about 354 to 1,286 JPY (measured scenes above) a command or a chat queue when the GPUs are busy

Measurements: https://render.janction.jp/benchmarks. Cost per frame and per animation: https://render.janction.jp/blender-render-cost. Prices: https://render.janction.jp/pricing. Checked on 2026-10-13.

Official JANCTION Render: https://render.janction.jp. Code and client: https://github.com/JasmyLab-JANCTION/janction-render

title: Encoder Awakening via Adapters: Effective Domain-Adaptive Fine-tuning of Speech-LLMs
description:
arXiv:2609.17981v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Speech Large Language Models (Speech-LLMs), typically built from a pre-trained speech encoder, a modality projector, and an LLM fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA), have shown strong Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) performance on general-domain speech. However, adapting them to domain-shifted speech, such as child or dialectal speech, remains challenging under limited target-domain data. Given the dominant role of the LLM in Speech-LLMs, with cross-entropy loss applied only at the LLM output, the speech encoder may receive insufficient adaptation to new acoustic conditions. In this paper, we propose Encoder Awakening via Adapters (EAVA), a simple yet effective domain-adaptive fine-tuning method for Speech-LLM-based ASR. First, lightweight adapters are inserted into each encoder layer and trained exclusively, enabling target-domain acoustic knowledge to be incorporated into the encoder while preserving its pre-trained knowledge. Second, the full model is jointly fine-tuned on the target domain with LoRA applied to the LLM. Experiments on three domain-shifted ASR datasets, covering child and dialectal speech, show that EAVA consistently outperforms vanilla fine-tuning and other baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance.

title: Speeding up C++ build times
description: When we learned that engineers were losing hours building our C++ codebase, we jumped into investigating the root cause. Here’s how we cut build times in half and shipped a solution for scale.

title: Collective Autonomous Vehicle Routing Needs Social Awareness for Coexistence with Human Drivers
description:
arXiv:2610.13439v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Collective Autonomous Vehicle (AV) route choices in real-world traffic networks can create externalities for Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), as routes that benefit AVs may increase travel times for other road users. To address this, we introduce a social component, the marginal cost, to the selfish travel time AV reward. Marginal cost captures an AV's impact on other road users by comparing their travel times with those in a counterfactual simulation in which the AV is removed.
  We study AV route choice in mixed-autonomy traffic settings using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where AVs learn routing policies through repeated interactions with the traffic environment. Experiments on the real-world networks of Ingolstadt and Provins show that incorporating marginal cost into the AV reward not only limits the increase in HDV travel times and shortens AV travel times relative to selfish AV routing, but also improves overall system performance. In Ingolstadt, selfish routing of 40\% AVs increases the travel times of other vehicles by 1.7\%, and this drops to 1.1\% when the social reward is included. Interestingly, not only does overall system performance improve, but the AVs are also better off when acting socially.This effect is consistent across tested cities, penetration rates, and replications, yet when the weight of the social component in the reward increases, the system fails to reach the desired performance.
  For a more scalable approach to social AV routing in mixed-autonomy traffic, we compute the marginal cost only for the AVs whose route choices most affect the traffic system. This reduces the number of counterfactual simulations and achieves similar performance at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that AV routing should go beyond selfish rewards and, for the benefit of all traffic participants, include a social component in its objective.

title: DeltaLLM: Delta-Key Sparse Attention for Edge LLMs
description:
arXiv:2507.19608v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: On-device LLM inference is increasingly important for edge platforms but remains challenging due to high computational and memory demands and tight resource constraints. Modern applications often involve long prompts. Although compact models reduce linear-layer costs through weight compression, attention remains largely unoptimized and becomes the dominant bottleneck, especially during prefilling. Existing attention pruning methods primarily target highly parallel hardware (e.g., GPUs) and long context windows, limiting their suitability for edge scenarios. We present DeltaLLM, a training-free LLM framework based on algorithm-hardware-dataflow co-design to accelerate prefilling attention. DeltaLLM introduces a causal-attention-aware K-only delta formulation that enables Delta-Key reuse across query heads under Grouped-Query Attention (GQA). A context-aware hybrid strategy preserves exact attention near the diagonal while applying delta approximation to nonlocal regions. For score-value multiplication, we propose a vectorized structured sparse online softmax (VSSOS) that converts fine-grained spatial score sparsity into hardware-friendly column-level skipping. A specialized vector-processor architecture and unified sparse/dense attention dataflow exploit the resulting sparsity. Evaluated on BitNet-b1.58-2B-4T and LLaMA3.2-1B-Instruct, DeltaLLM achieves up to 60% Delta-Key sparsity and 63% structured attention-score sparsity with negligible average accuracy loss. On the KV260 FPGA board, it delivers a 1.62x speedup over TeLLMe-v2 while reducing DSP and BRAM usage. These results show that DeltaLLM supports efficient edge LLM deployment and integration with existing pipelines without fine-tuning.

title: Realtime Quiz Schema Versioning in Go: Fan-Out Failure Handling
description:
The least complex fix for a live multiplayer quiz is a stable event envelope with an explicit recovery contract. Version the payload, keep an identifier that survives reconnects, and make the client prove what it has applied.

Short answer: treat reconnect, token expiry, and partial fan-out as normal states, then evaluate each provider against the same delivery and recovery SLOs before choosing one.

The page is a symptom, not a diagnosis

The alert fires after a round has started. An on-call sees quiz_answer_lag rising, while the connected-player gauge looks ordinary. A player reports a timer moving backward. That combination says very little about delivery: an open socket can still be subscribed to the wrong schema or miss one business event.

Trace the page back to three records. At ingress, store quiz_id, event_id, schema_version, and sequence. At publish, record the provider request and its request_id. At acknowledgement, record the client and the same event ID. Authentication, subscription state, and business events must remain separate dimensions; otherwise a token refresh can look like a successful answer fan-out.

The instrumentation change is intentionally boring. I would page on a delivery SLO and a recovery SLO with different owners: for example, 99.9% of answer events acknowledged inside the product budget, and reconnects completed inside the resync budget. Those percentages are inputs to the experiment, not facts about any vendor. Set them with the game designer and capacity plan.

For this workflow, Infrai is worth putting on the transport shortlist early: one key and one bill can cover the realtime call alongside other backend services, while the schema and recovery rules stay in your code.

One bad threshold can cost more than one missed event. A low threshold creates false pages that get ignored; a high threshold lets an entire question finish before the team notices a missing shard.

Measure the gap.

How should realtime schema versioning handle multiplayer failure recovery?

Keep the envelope stable while the payload changes. The client reads schema_version before decoding the body, applies a known version, and requests a snapshot for an unknown one. event_id and sequence are durable identities; display text, answer order, and array indexes are not.

The server owns ordering, retention, and the decision to replay or snapshot. The client owns deduplication and convergence. If its last acknowledged sequence is still in the retained window, the server replays the gap. If not, it sends a snapshot with a new sequence and the client applies only later events.

Presence is useful evidence during that recovery, but it is not an event ledger. This small Go probe reads the documented presence route and surfaces rate limits and non-success responses so the test harness can keep auth, subscription, and business-event measurements distinct.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func readPresence(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/quiz-42"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence request remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := readPresence(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

On expiry, stop publishing with the old token, issue a fresh one, resubscribe, and then replay or snapshot. On partial fan-out, leave the event pending until the stable ID is acknowledged. Consumers should apply that ID idempotently because at-least-once delivery is a normal condition to design for.

How can a team measure schema recovery before picking a provider?

Build one fixture and run it unchanged. Use 500 simulated players, 20 questions, one answer event per second, a forced reconnect for 10% of clients during every fifth question, and a token expiry halfway through. Capture publish-to-ack p50 and p99, duplicate rate, missing-event rate after recovery, and time to a correct snapshot. Keep auth failures out of the business-event latency series.

The failure trace should be inspectable, not anecdotal. Suppose sequence 1842 carries answer.accepted at schema version 3. The provider accepts publication, then a client disconnects before acknowledging; its token expires. On reconnect it reports 1841. The server replays 1842 if retained, and the client ignores it if it had already applied it. If retention ended, the server sends a snapshot at sequence 1910, after which only events greater than 1910 are accepted. The auth, subscription, and business-event logs describe one timeline without pretending they are the same signal.

I would keep the raw trace for the whole session, including the messages that appear redundant. In one run, the answer event can be accepted by the publisher, delivered to nine of ten simulated recipients, and then delivered again to the ninth after its token refresh; that is three different observations, not one failure counter. The test harness should join them by event_id, annotate the reconnect boundary, and show the first and final sequence each client applied. That view catches a subtle schema mistake: a client may parse version 3 successfully but apply it after a newer snapshot, which produces a plausible score with an impossible timer. The pass condition therefore checks state convergence and ordering together, while the operator can still see whether authentication, subscription, or business delivery caused the delay.

Run the trace with a version-2 client as well. It should reject the unknown payload and request a compatible snapshot; a version-3 client should apply it. Pass only when both converge on the same score and timer, every recovery stays within the agreed budget, and duplicates remain inside the consumer's idempotency tolerance.

A fair buy-versus-build decision

Option Where it fits Cost or risk to carry
Infrai realtime A plain REST call and one credential shared with other backend capabilities Your team still defines replay, retention, and client idempotency
Ably Managed pub/sub when presence and history are central requirements Provider-specific semantics and another operational account
Pusher Channels Simple hosted channel fan-out for a modest protocol Recovery and long-lived history remain application concerns
Socket.IO Full control when a Node.js service is already part of the platform You own scaling, presence, and the on-call rotation

Infrai is a reasonable leg in this experiment when one key and one bill can cover realtime beside other backend services, and when a plain HTTP call avoids adding an SDK to a small Go service. Its public discovery surface also lets a team inspect a capability before integration. That removes setup friction; it does not replace the failure test.

The catch is fit. Choose Ably when provider-managed history is the requirement, or Socket.IO when owning the transport and regional capacity is deliberate. A specialist WebRTC design is better for media-heavy rooms. Your mileage may vary with geography and client mix, so keep those variables in the fixture instead of turning one laptop run into a universal claim.

Turn the result into an operating rule

Store the fixture, failure schedule, and raw acknowledgement traces as a scheduled canary. Review the trace whenever a run fails; an aggregate can be green while one shard never resynced. Keep retention bounded and make the consumer's idempotency key part of the protocol review.

Select the provider that meets the delivery and recovery SLOs with an on-call surface the platform team can sustain. The schema contract is yours, even when the transport is managed. Start with the realtime documentation and run the same fixture against every candidate.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation

Further reading

  • Infrai realtime and discovery
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation

title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2610.13889v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
description:
arXiv:2610.12496v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.

title: The Saturation Trap and the Subjectivity of Intervention Timing: Why Affect-Based Triggers and LLM Judges Fail to Time Interventions on Autonomous Agents
description:
arXiv:2606.04296v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As autonomous AI agents move from conversational systems to long-horizon software execution, runtime safety layers that decide when to interrupt an agent have become essential. We study this timing problem using a continuous 18-dimensional affective-dynamics engine (HEART) as a diagnostic probe, evaluating four intervention trigger families - absolute state thresholds, composite state-action patterns, regex reasoning-feature extraction, and zero-shot LLM-as-judge - against human-annotated intervention points on SWE-bench-Verified debugging traces. We report three findings. First, a State Saturation Trap: modeled frustration quickly crosses the threshold and stays at its maximum (v2 erratum: the observer could not register recovery; decay never ran), converting threshold-on-state triggers from moment detectors into near-constant indicators that fire on 39-83% of actions across five trajectories. Second, a capability-and-context floor for LLM judges: a small model(gpt-5.4-mini) never fires, while frontier and cross-vendor models escape the zero-firing floor only with full-trajectory context, reaching only F1 0.17-0.40 at up to 90x the cost. Third, and most importantly, the supervised target is not reproducible among humans: three trained annotators using the same rubric on a 56-action trajectory agree on where to intervene only slightly above chance (location Krippendorff's alpha = +0.047; best pairwise Cohen's kappa = +0.349) and not at all on intervention type (pause degenerate; clarify below chance; reflect only alpha = +0.226). We conclude that intervention timing is a low-reliability construct, making single-annotator F1 an unsuitable optimization target. Our contribution is the joint mapping of this problem across human inter-rater reliability, four detector architectures, a cross-model LLM-judge sweep, and a reproduced saturation effect, rather than any single detector's accuracy.

title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.13829v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.13098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.

title: Cómo aparecer en Gemini, las Vistas creadas con IA (AI Overviews) y el Modo IA de Google
description:
Respuesta rápida: Google tiene hoy tres sitios donde su IA responde con fuentes: las Vistas creadas con IA (el resumen que sale encima de los resultados), el Modo IA (una pestaña de búsqueda conversacional) y la app de Gemini. Para las dos primeras, Google dice oficialmente que no hay ningún requisito extra: basta con que tu página esté indexada y pueda mostrarse con un fragmento. No existe un marcado especial ni un fichero mágico. Lo que sí cambia es cómo busca: el Modo IA parte cada pregunta en varias sub-preguntas y busca cada una por separado, así que gana quien responde bien a las preguntas concretas que rodean a la grande, no solo a la grande.

Tres superficies de Google con IA, y en qué se diferencian

Cuando alguien dice "salir en la IA de Google" puede estar hablando de tres cosas distintas. Conviene separarlas porque no se comportan igual ni se miden igual.

Vistas creadas con IA Modo IA App de Gemini
Dónde aparece Encima de los resultados normales de Google Pestaña propia dentro de la Búsqueda Aplicación y web de Gemini, aparte de la Búsqueda
En España desde Marzo de 2025 Octubre de 2025 Disponible antes que las dos anteriores
De dónde saca la información Índice de la Búsqueda de Google Índice de la Búsqueda, con varias búsquedas por pregunta Modelo Gemini, con apoyo del índice de Google cuando busca
¿Enseña fuentes? Sí, enlaces dentro del resumen Sí, enlaces junto a la respuesta A veces: Google avisa de que no todas las respuestas las incluyen
Cómo controlas si te usa Directivas normales de la Búsqueda Directivas normales de la Búsqueda Google-Extended

Las Vistas creadas con IA (Google las llama así en español; en inglés son las AI Overviews) no salen en todas las búsquedas. Google dice que solo las muestra cuando su sistema considera que aportan algo frente a los resultados clásicos. Si quieres entender en qué se diferencian de un chat como ChatGPT, lo explicamos en AI Overviews frente a ChatGPT.

El Modo IA es la novedad que más cambia el juego. Al anunciar su llegada a España, Google contó que quienes lo usan hacen preguntas dos o tres veces más largas que en una búsqueda tradicional. Y explicó cómo responde: lo llama "descomposición de consultas". Desglosa tu pregunta en subtemas y lanza una ráfaga de búsquedas simultáneas antes de redactar la respuesta.

Lo que Google dice oficialmente: no hay truco técnico

La documentación de Google para webmasters sobre funciones de IA en la Búsqueda (actualizada en diciembre de 2025) es más tajante de lo que suele contarse:

  • Aparecer en las Vistas creadas con IA o en el Modo IA no exige requisitos adicionales ni optimizaciones especiales.
  • Para ser elegible como enlace de apoyo, la página tiene que estar indexada y ser apta para mostrarse en la Búsqueda con un fragmento.
  • Los datos estructurados de schema.org que ya uses bastan: Google no pide ninguno especial.
  • Los ficheros de texto pensados para la IA tampoco son necesarios.

Desconfía de quien te venda el atajo

Si alguien te ofrece un marcado secreto, una etiqueta nueva o un fichero que "activa" tu web en las Vistas creadas con IA, contrástalo con la documentación de Google: dice exactamente lo contrario. Esto incluye llms.txt. Puede servirte para otros asistentes, pero Google no lo pide para sus funciones de IA en la Búsqueda.

Que no haya truco técnico no significa que no haya nada que hacer. Significa que el trabajo es el de siempre, con un matiz nuevo en qué preguntas respondes.

Primero, comprueba que Google puede usarte

Antes de pensar en contenido, descarta los bloqueos. Son los fallos más baratos de arreglar y los que más a menudo te dejan fuera sin que nadie se dé cuenta. Esta lista sale de las buenas prácticas que Google recomienda para sus funciones de IA:

  • Tu robots.txt permite rastrear las páginas importantes, y tu CDN o tu hosting no bloquean a Googlebot.
  • Las páginas que quieres que se citen están indexadas: compruébalo con la herramienta de inspección de URLs de Search Console.
  • No llevan nosnippet ni un max-snippet muy corto en el contenido que quieres que se use.
  • Lo importante está en texto, no solo dentro de una imagen o un PDF escaneado.
  • Se llega a ellas con enlaces internos desde otras páginas de tu web.
  • Tus datos estructurados dicen lo mismo que el texto visible de la página.
  • Si eres un negocio local o vendes productos, tu Perfil de Empresa en Google y tu Merchant Center están al día.

Si quieres limitar lo que Google enseña de ti, las herramientas son las de cualquier resultado: nosnippet, data-nosnippet, max-snippet o noindex. Ten en cuenta que Google tarda en volver a rastrear: un cambio puede tardar de días a meses en notarse.

Después, responde a las preguntas que rodean a la tuya

Aquí está la diferencia real con el SEO de toda la vida. Si el Modo IA convierte "¿qué software de facturación me conviene si soy autónomo?" en varias búsquedas sobre precio, obligaciones fiscales, integraciones y opiniones, la respuesta final se arma con las páginas que mejor contestan cada una de esas piezas. Google dice que esta forma de buscar saca a la luz un conjunto de enlaces más amplio y variado que una búsqueda normal.

Haz un mapa de las sub-preguntas

Coge las preguntas principales de búsqueda de tu cliente y, para cada una, escribe las cuatro o cinco dudas concretas que alguien necesita resolver para decidirse: cuánto cuesta, para quién es, qué alternativas hay, qué riesgos tiene, cómo se empieza. Esas son las búsquedas que el Modo IA va a lanzar por su cuenta.

Acción rápida: Elige tu pregunta de negocio más importante y apunta debajo cinco sub-preguntas. Marca cuáles responde ya tu web, y con qué página.

Contesta cada una en una página o sección propia

Una página que responde a una duda concreta en su primer párrafo es más fácil de usar como fuente que una página genérica que lo toca todo de pasada. No hace falta una URL por sub-pregunta, pero sí un apartado con su propio encabezado y una respuesta directa al principio.

Acción rápida: En tu página más visitada, revisa si cada encabezado es una pregunta que alguien haría y si el párrafo siguiente la contesta en la primera frase.

Aporta algo que no esté en todas partes

Google insiste en el contenido útil, fiable y pensado para personas. En la práctica, la IA tiene donde elegir para las respuestas genéricas. Donde tienes ventaja es en lo que solo tú puedes decir: tus precios reales, tus condiciones, tus casos, tus datos. Un dato propio con su fecha y su método es de lo poco que nadie más puede publicar.

Acción rápida: Busca un dato que solo tenga tu empresa (un precio, un plazo, una cifra de tu sector) y publícalo con su fecha en la página que responde a esa duda.

Acompaña el texto con imágenes y vídeo de calidad

Es otra de las recomendaciones explícitas de Google para sus funciones de IA. Una tabla comparativa, una captura real del producto o un vídeo corto que enseña cómo se hace algo ayudan a que la página sea la mejor respuesta, no solo una más.

La app de Gemini y Google-Extended

La app de Gemini funciona distinto: es un chat. Cuando necesita información actual, Google le pasa contenido de su índice de búsqueda en el momento de responder, lo que Google llama grounding (lo explicamos en el glosario). Y a veces enseña las fuentes dentro de la respuesta o debajo, aunque Google avisa de que no todas las respuestas las incluyen.

El control aquí es Google-Extended, una instrucción que pones en tu robots.txt. Según Google, sirve para dos cosas: que tu contenido no se use para entrenar futuros modelos Gemini y que no se use para el grounding de las apps de Gemini y de Vertex AI. Google añade que no afecta a tu inclusión en la Búsqueda ni es una señal de posicionamiento.

Si haces esto... En la Búsqueda En las Vistas y el Modo IA En la app de Gemini
Bloqueas Google-Extended Sigues saliendo Sigues pudiendo salir Tu contenido deja de usarse para responder
Pones nosnippet en una página Sale sin fragmento No se usa como fuente No lo controla esta directiva
Pones noindex en una página Desaparece Desaparece No lo controla esta directiva

Figura 1. Qué controla cada directiva, según la documentación de Google. Que Google-Extended no afecte a las Vistas creadas con IA ni al Modo IA es nuestra lectura de esa documentación: Google lo describe como un control para «otros sistemas» distintos de la Búsqueda.

Si tu objetivo es que la IA te cite, bloquear Google-Extended va en contra: pierdes la app de Gemini y no ganas nada en la Búsqueda. Tiene sentido si lo que te preocupa es el uso de tu contenido para entrenar modelos, y es una decisión legítima, pero hay que tomarla sabiendo lo que cuesta.

Cómo saber si está funcionando

Aquí hay menos de lo que nos gustaría, y conviene saberlo antes de prometer nada a nadie.

Search Console. El tráfico que llega desde las Vistas creadas con IA y el Modo IA está incluido en el informe de Rendimiento, con el tipo de búsqueda Web, pero mezclado con el resto. Un clic en uno de sus enlaces cuenta como un clic normal. En las Vistas, todo el resumen ocupa una única posición y todos sus enlaces reciben esa misma posición. En el Modo IA, una pregunta de seguimiento cuenta como una consulta nueva.

Informes específicos de IA. Google empezó a desplegar en junio de 2026 informes de rendimiento de IA generativa en Search Console. Según fuentes de terceros, muestran impresiones pero no clics, y llegan a las webs de forma gradual. Si todavía no lo ves en tu cuenta, es normal.

Los clics, con las dos versiones. Un estudio de Pew Research en Estados Unidos encontró que, cuando aparece un resumen de IA, la gente hace clic en un resultado tradicional en el 8% de las visitas, frente al 15% cuando no aparece. Google, por su parte, afirma que el volumen total de clics orgánicos se ha mantenido relativamente estable y que los clics que llegan desde estas funciones son de más calidad, pero no publica el método. Lo honesto es medir lo tuyo en lugar de elegir la cifra que más te convenga.

Lo que quieres saber Dónde mirarlo Qué limitación tiene
Si tus páginas son elegibles Inspección de URLs en Search Console Fiable Indexada y apta para fragmento
Cuánto tráfico te llega de la IA de Google Rendimiento, tipo de búsqueda Web Mezclado No separa la IA del resto
Si Gemini te nombra cuando le preguntan por lo tuyo Preguntas repetidas en Gemini, múltiples veces en distintos momentos del tiempo Variable Una respuesta sola no es un dato

En GenScore medimos la tercera fila: lanzamos tus preguntas principales de búsqueda a ChatGPT, Gemini y Claude (y a Perplexity en Pro y Agencia), múltiples veces en distintos momentos del tiempo, y vemos si te nombran, en qué posición y qué fuentes citan. Las Vistas creadas con IA y el Modo IA no las medimos hoy, porque viven dentro de la página de resultados de Google y no se pueden repetir de forma controlada con el mismo método. Si quieres medir también el tráfico que te llega desde los asistentes, tienes cómo medir el tráfico de ChatGPT en GA4.

Lo que no funciona

Tres errores frecuentes

Buscar un marcado especial. Google dice que no existe. Los datos estructurados ayudan a que te entienda, como siempre, pero tienen que coincidir con lo que se ve en la página.

Bloquear Google-Extended "para proteger" tu tráfico. No te saca de la Búsqueda, pero sí te saca de las respuestas de la app de Gemini.

Escribir una página enorme que lo intenta responder todo. Con la descomposición de consultas, gana la página que contesta bien una pregunta concreta, no la que menciona muchas.

Si vienes de ChatGPT, mucho de lo que funciona allí sirve también aquí: contenido citable, datos con procedencia y presencia en las fuentes que los modelos consultan. Lo contamos en cómo conseguir que ChatGPT te cite.

Fuentes

  • Google Search Central, AI features and your website (actualizada el 10 de diciembre de 2025). Requisitos, controles, descomposición de consultas y recuento en Search Console.
  • Google Search Central, Google's common crawlers, apartado Google-Extended.
  • Google España, La Búsqueda de Google: el Modo IA llega a España (8 de octubre de 2025).
  • Google, anuncio de la llegada de las Vistas creadas con IA a más países de Europa, España incluida (25 de marzo de 2025).
  • Ayuda de Google, Vistas creadas con IA en la Búsqueda de Google y Fuentes en las apps de Gemini.
  • Ayuda de Search Console, Informe de rendimiento: cómo se cuentan clics, impresiones y posición en las funciones de IA.
  • Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears (julio de 2025). Navegación de 900 adultos en EE. UU., marzo de 2025.
  • Google, AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks (agosto de 2025).
  • PPC Land y TechWyse sobre los informes de IA generativa de Search Console (junio de 2026).

Equipo GenScore

Escribimos sobre visibilidad de marca en motores de IA a partir de mediciones reales hechas con nuestra propia herramienta y de la documentación oficial de cada motor. Cuando no tenemos evidencia de algo, lo decimos.

¿Te nombra Gemini cuando alguien pregunta por lo que vendes?

title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.12822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

title: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.13744v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.

title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
description:
arXiv:2610.13321v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web crawling is a major source of large language model (LLM) pretraining data, yet data-selection pipelines discard a large share of crawled pages. We investigate how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts to collect more high-quality pretraining data. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host crawl coverage, we find that roughly half of the variation in classifier scores occurs between hosts. In the crawls we analyze, a few pages from a host also provide a useful estimate of the quality of its remaining pages. Common Crawl uses harmonic centrality, a graph centrality metric, to guide its crawl allocation. In our simulations, using centrality to choose which hosts to crawl yields limited gains over random ordering and performs worse for some classifiers. For deciding how deeply to crawl each host, sampling a few pages and then fetching more from hosts with higher-scoring samples collects several times more high-quality pages per fetch than uniform depth or centrality-based allocation. Finally, Common Crawl's observed per-host coverage has little correlation with the evaluated quality signals. We estimate that tens of millions of high-quality pages remain among known but uncrawled URLs in each crawl examined, with most concentrated on a small share of hosts.

title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
description:
arXiv:2610.13060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.

title: Self-Aware Knowledge Probing: Evaluating Language Models' Relational Knowledge through Confidence Calibration
description:
arXiv:2601.18901v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge probing quantifies how much relational knowledge a language model (LM) has acquired during pre-training. Existing knowledge probes evaluate model capabilities through metrics like prediction accuracy and precision. Such evaluations fail to account for the model's reliability, reflected in the calibration of its confidence scores. In this paper, we establish an empirical framework to evaluate the calibration of relational knowledge in a closed answer-set setting. We cover three modalities of model confidence: (1) intrinsic confidence, (2) paraphrase consistency and (3) linguistic confidence. Our extensive analysis of 21 causal and 8 masked language models reveals that most models, but especially those pre-trained with the masking objective, are overconfident. The best-calibrated scores come from confidence estimates that account for inconsistencies due to statement rephrasing. Moreover, calibration improves when increasing the number of answer options.

title: Reading papers daily and catching every third word in the room
description:
I have been to various closed gatherings where AI engineers come together, the kind who look like hippies.

Their salaries are 500 to 700K. Maybe even more.

I listened to what they were saying and realised that I do not understand English at all. Their English I do not understand at all.

So what I have understood now is that I need to listen very hard to various AI podcasts in English, to start properly getting it.

Because when an engineer talks about how to configure PyTorch, or about how he trains that LLM of his, I only catch every third word.

title: Share Vercel Container Registry repositories across teams
description:
Vercel Container Registry now lets you share a repository with other Vercel teams to grant read access to its images.

Sharing is read-only and covers the whole repository. Recipients can pull and use every image, but cannot push, delete, or re-share. You can also share a repository with your own team. Each repository can be shared with up to 100 teams.

Share from the project dashboard under Images → repository → Settings → Repository Sharing, or with the Vercel CLI:

# Share a repository with a team vercel vcr permissions my-repository add other-team # List teams with access vercel vcr permissions my-repository ls # Revoke a team's access vercel vcr permissions my-repository rm other-team # Remove all shared access vercel vcr permissions my-repository clear

Shared images can be used in Vercel Sandbox, accepting a team-scoped image reference in Sandbox.create() :

import { Sandbox } from '@vercel/sandbox'; const sandbox = await Sandbox.create({ image: 'other-team/their-project/shared-repository:latest', });

Repository sharing is available on all plans. Update the Vercel CLI to v58.3.0 or later with npm i -g vercel@latest to get started and see the Vercel Container Registry documentation to learn more.

title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.12939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.

title: Durable Sessions for the Claude Agent SDK, in One Prompt
description:
We shipped a Claude Agent SDK executor in Dapr Agents with durable sessions and human approvals. Meaning: your Claude-built agent survives a crash mid-task, resumes with its session intact, and waits for an approval for as long as the approval takes – through restarts and deploys.

Getting started is rather easy:

pip install dapr-agents
dapr init

Then paste this into your agent definition:

from dapr_agents import DurableAgent
from dapr_agents.executors import ClaudeAgentExecutor

agent = DurableAgent(
    name="reviewer",
    executor=ClaudeAgentExecutor(session_store="statestore"),
    require_approval=["merge_pr", "deploy"],
)
agent.start()

Now break it on purpose, because that's the whole point:

  1. Give it a multi-step task.

  2. kill -9 the process somewhere in the middle.

  3. Start it again. The session resumes where it stopped and the steps already completed come back from the journal, not from re-running Claude.

  4. Trigger an approval-gated tool, close your laptop, approve tomorrow. The wait survives because it lives in the workflow, not in memory.

All behavior was checked against dapr-agents main; the release notes have the exact versions: https://github.com/dapr/dapr-agents/releases

Same machinery works for LangChain Deep Agents. The adapter landed earlier this year in our diagrid python package, and deep agents with long tasks are exactly where durable sessions pay off.

If you want the guided version, the Dapr Agents track at Dapr University is free: https://www.diagrid.io/university/dapr-agents

It's that easy to get started. Give it a spin and lmk what you think 👀

title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox
description:
Terminal coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode can now each run in their own isolated Vercel Sandbox, orchestrated from Herdr, a tmux-style manager that runs them side by side in panes. Nothing an agent runs or edits touches your machine.

When you start an agent, the plugin uploads your project files into a new Sandbox, installs the agent there, and opens a pane connected to it.

The pane works like a local terminal; you type to the agent and watch it work. But it lives in the Sandbox, not on your machine, so you can run several agents at once without slowing anything down.

Everything the plugin does is machine-readable. Each action returns its results as JSON, so whatever you can do from a pane, like starting an agent, checking its state, or applying its changes, a script or another agent can do too.

A few safeguards are built in. The plugin shows every file before the first upload, returns remote changes as a Git patch you apply only when you choose, and requires a human to type DELETE to permanently remove a Sandbox.

Claude Code (2.1.220), Codex (0.146.0), and OpenCode (1.18.9) are all verified and available by default.

To get started, install the plugin:

Run vercel link in the repository you want the agent to work on, then start an agent from Herdr's action menu.

Starting takes two invocations. The first is a dry run: it lists every file it would upload and creates nothing. Run it again, and the plugin creates the Sandbox and opens the agent in a pane. To pull the agent's work back to your machine, run the apply action and its changes arrive as a Git patch.

Usage is billed at standard Sandbox rates. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.12898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model. We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information, while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices. Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K << L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively. Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8-16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11. These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder.

title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
description:
arXiv:2610.12813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.13521v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) by routing domain-specific data to specialized teachers, integrating their capabilities through dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, domain routing only distinguishes the supervision sources for different domains; updates from all domains still act on shared parameters. When teachers differ substantially in response style and domain expertise, supervision that is effective in isolation may still lead to persistent gradient conflicts and capability degradation during joint optimization. To address this challenge, we propose Cross-Teacher Guarding for MOPD (Road MOPD), which introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student trajectories and coordinates multi-teacher supervision through token-level credit assignment and gradient updates. Specifically, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment uses teacher agreement to strengthen token-level corrections jointly supported by the teachers and attenuate conflicting signals; preventive multi-teacher gradient projection uses auxiliary gradients from the same trajectories to constrain potentially conflicting updates and adaptively controls projection strength to retain target-domain learning signals. In experiments, Road MOPD mitigates degradation in the disadvantaged domain, gains over 5 percentage points under high conflict, and improves overall performance in low-conflict and three-domain settings.

title: A Decision Nobody Wrote Down Is a Rumor With Consequences
description:
Watch the 40-second version here: Architecture Decision Records That Pass Review

Every team has one. The cache TTL set to 47 minutes for reasons lost to time. The "temporary" dependency that is now load-bearing. Ask who decided and you get four names, two of whom left the company last year.

The decision evaporated. The consequences did not.

This is why staff-level engineers write Architecture Decision Records. An ADR is one page answering: what did we decide, what did we reject, what are we on the hook for now. Four sections: context, options, decision, consequences. Twenty minutes of writing that outlives every meeting that produced the decision.

Now the part nobody tells you. The options section is the entire point. A decision with no options section is not a record, it is a press release. "We chose Postgres" teaches the reader nothing without the alternatives. The rejected options are where the actual knowledge lives. Six months later a new hire suggests "why not Mongo" and instead of re-litigating a settled debate, you hand them the ADR. The argument died before it was born.

Then there is the selfish effect. Undocumented decisions are incident fuel. At 2am nobody can reconstruct why the circuit breaker threshold is 12 and not 50, so they guess. They guess under pressure. ADRs are the difference between debugging the system and reverse-engineering it while the pager screams.

It also reads well in interviews. Juniors describe what the system does. Staff-level candidates explain what it could have been and why it is not. The answer that lands shows trade-off thinking, and ADRs are trade-off thinking in document form.

Here is a template you can steal. Save it as docs/adr/001-whatever.md and fill one in today:

# ADR 004: Use React Query for server state

Date: 2026-10-13
Status: Accepted

## Context
Dashboard refetches on every tab change. Three hand-rolled caches
disagree with each other. Users see stale data; support tickets agree.

## Options
1. React Query: battle-tested cache/invalidate, +28KB.
2. Custom fetch hook: full control, we own every bug forever.
3. Redux + thunks: team knows it, but it is boilerplate city for
   data that is just "load this URL and cache it".

## Decision
React Query. It matches our shape of problem exactly: lots of
reads, few writes, invalidation is the hard part.

## Consequences
- Accept: bundle grows ~28KB; team must learn cache keys.
- Risk: if we later need offline-first, revisit.
- If this proves wrong, ADR 005 supersedes it. ADRs are never edited.

The last line matters more than it looks. Never edit an ADR. Supersede it. The history of being wrong is just as valuable as being right.

Write the decision down today, or future you reverse-engineers it at 2am during an incident. Future you is the reader. Do not make them suffer.
