title: Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.12668v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Language model agents increasingly operate over long interaction streams, requiring online adaptation to distribution shifts through continual learning. However, existing agent harnesses typically either evolve their states only through forward information flow or rely on additional replay or validation data for harness optimization. To address this, we propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that complements forward read and write with backward revision under a strictly online streaming protocol. We ask what information could have been captured differently in the harness state to better inform the current instance in the stream. Specifically, after each instance, we leverage the resulting trajectory as feedback to revise the reflections retrieved for that instance, thereby propagating feedback backward through the textual harness state. Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms strong raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces source-grounded and meaningful revisions, corrects overgeneralized or outdated experience under distribution shifts, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.

title: A Theory of the Mechanics of Information: Generalization Through Measurement of Uncertainty (Learning is Measuring)
description:
arXiv:2510.22809v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Traditional machine learning relies on explicit models and domain assumptions, often limiting flexibility and interpretability. We introduce a "model-free" framework of instance-based learning using surprisal (information theoretic uncertainty) to directly analyze and perform inferences from raw data, eliminating distribution modeling, reducing bias, and enabling efficient updates including direct edits and deletion of training data. By quantifying relevance through uncertainty, the approach enables generalizable inference across tasks including generative inference, causal discovery, anomaly detection, and time series forecasting. Our approach emphasizes traceability, interpretability, and data-driven decision making, offering a unified, human-understandable framework for machine learning, can be adapted to virtually all machine learning tasks, achieving competency across all and state-of-the-art performance on anomaly detection and some supervised tasks. The mathematical foundations create a "physics" of information, which enable these techniques to apply effectively to a wide variety of complex data types, including missing data. Our results suggest that this may be a viable foundation upon which to build scalable machine learning and artificial intelligence that can maintain human understandability of the underlying mechanics.

title: Best Enterprise AI Gateways
description:
TL;DR

  • An enterprise AI gateway sits between your applications (and, increasingly, your agents and employees) and every model provider. It handles routing, failover, budgets, access control, guardrails and audit logs in one place, so you stop rebuilding them in every codebase.
  • Judge an enterprise AI gateway on five things: overhead under real load, governance depth, where it can be deployed, MCP support, and how much of your actual AI traffic it can see.
  • This guide compares the five leading enterprise AI gateways: Bifrost, Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management, Portkey and LiteLLM.
  • Bifrost is the strongest all-round enterprise AI gateway for teams that want a dedicated, self-hostable gateway with MCP governance and, through Bifrost Edge, coverage of AI tools running on employee laptops. The other four each win in a narrower situation, covered below.
  • Two things changed this year and belong in any procurement conversation: Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, and LiteLLM had a PyPI supply chain incident in March.

A couple of years ago, a gateway conversation meant one thing: stop pasting provider keys into config files and get a single invoice. That's still part of the job. But platform teams now get harder questions. Which MCP servers can our agents reach? Who approved them? Why did one team's spend triple in a week? And what is the sales team pasting into the desktop chat app nobody configured?

An enterprise AI gateway is where those answers live, or at least where they should live. The catch is that the category has stretched. Some products are purpose-built LLM gateways, some are classic API gateways with AI policies added on top, and one just got bought by a security vendor. Picking between them on a feature checklist gets you a spreadsheet full of green ticks and no real answer.

Disclosure: Bifrost is built by Maxim AI, which also publishes this blog. Weigh the ranking with that in mind. Each section below says plainly where the alternatives are the better call.

What an enterprise AI gateway actually does

At its core, an AI gateway is a reverse proxy for model traffic. Your apps talk to one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway translates, routes and retries across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

What turns an AI gateway into an enterprise AI gateway is everything around that proxy: identity (SSO and roles), budgets per team or customer, audit trails you can hand to a compliance officer, deployment inside your own network, and policy that applies the same way whether the caller is a service, an autonomous agent or a person. If you want the longer version of that argument, the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide walks through the capability matrix in detail.

What to check before you shortlist an enterprise AI gateway

  • Overhead under load. Every request passes through the gateway, so its processing time is added to every model call. It's invisible on a single chat completion and very visible when an agent chains forty calls.
  • Governance depth. Per-team budgets, rate limits, role-based access and audit logs should be enforced at the infrastructure layer, not left to each app team's good intentions.
  • Where it runs. Regulated teams often need in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment. A gateway that only exists as a hosted service is a non-starter for them.
  • MCP. If agents call tools, the gateway needs to control which servers and tools they can reach, and with whose credentials.
  • Guardrails. PII redaction, secrets detection and prompt injection checks need to run before data reaches a model, with a clear choice between block, redact and log.
  • Coverage. A gateway only governs traffic that reaches it. Ask what happens to the AI tools people install themselves.

Enterprise AI gateways at a glance

If you only have a minute, this is the table to read. Bifrost is the go-to enterprise AI gateway because it covers model calls, MCP tool calls and agent traffic in one gateway, runs entirely inside your own infrastructure, and is the only one here that also reaches the AI tools running on employee laptops, through Bifrost Edge.

Capability Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
Form factor Standalone gateway in Go, single binary Plugins on Kong Gateway or Konnect Policies on Azure API Management Gateway plus hosted platform Python SDK and proxy
Model coverage 10,000+ models, 25+ providers Major hosted and self-hosted providers Azure OpenAI plus other registered backends 1,600+ models 100+ providers
Failover and balancing Weighted routing, retries, fallbacks, adaptive balancing and circuit breakers (Enterprise) Load balancing and semantic routing Backend load balancing Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Routing and fallbacks
Semantic caching Yes (Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) Yes (plugin) Yes (policies with Redis) Select Enterprise plans Yes (Qdrant, Valkey, Redis)
MCP governance Native MCP gateway, tool filtering, per-user OAuth, Code Mode (up to 92.8% fewer input tokens) AI MCP Proxy and OAuth2 plugins MCP servers inside API Management MCP Gateway MCP gateway
Guardrails Content safety, PII and secrets detection, plus AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and more (Enterprise) Prompt guard plugins Content safety policy Built-in guardrails with PII detection Integrations, some need a license
AI on laptops (desktop, browser, coding agents) Yes, with Bifrost Edge Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only
Our verdict Best all-round enterprise choice Best if Kong already runs your APIs Best for Azure-only estates Best managed option, especially for Palo Alto shops Best for Python-first teams

The sections below take each gateway in turn, starting with the one we'd pick.

1. Bifrost

Bifrost is an open-source (Apache 2.0) enterprise AI gateway written in Go. It gives you one OpenAI-compatible interface to 10,000+ models across 25+ providers, and the drop-in setup means moving an existing app over is a single base URL change. It ships as one binary, so it runs on a VM, Kubernetes, private cloud or a fully disconnected network, and most teams are live the same day.

Speed is the headline. Bifrost's published benchmarks show about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In the head-to-head run on AWS EC2 (500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), Bifrost sustained 424 requests per second against 44.84 for LiteLLM, with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds versus 90.72 seconds.

On the governance side, virtual keys carry budgets and rate limits that can be set per key, team, customer or model. In the Enterprise tier, governance runs off the identity provider you already use (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider), with SCIM 2.0 directory sync, fine-grained RBAC and data access control, and reusable access profiles so platform teams set the rules once. Routing combines weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks to another provider, and semantic caching serves stored answers to similar prompts, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2024540241844224013-667'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2024540241844224013&theme=dark" }

The MCP gateway is where it pulls ahead of most of this list. It governs which MCP servers and tools agents can use, with filtering at the client, request and virtual key level, and per-user OAuth so each person connects under their own account. Its Code Mode has the model write a short script to orchestrate tools instead of loading every tool definition into context, which cuts input token use by up to 92.8% across large tool sets. In a 508-tool run, Code Mode took the cost from $377 to $29 with a 100% task pass rate. The full numbers are in the MCP gateway cost and access control write-up.

Then there's Bifrost Edge, which the other gateways here simply don't have an answer for. Edge runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser AI, terminal coding agents and the MCP servers they connect to through your Bifrost gateway, after a one-time SSO sign-in. Only AI traffic is routed, and nothing else on the device is inspected. The same virtual keys, budgets and guardrails apply to tools nobody wired up on purpose, with content safety, PII and secrets detection on requests and responses, plus connections to AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR, Check Point Guard and others. Admins can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally, and a denial is enforced on the device, not just flagged in a dashboard. Rollout goes through the device management you already run: Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud.

For regulated teams, the enterprise tier adds clustering (a peer-to-peer cluster with no leader, so an outage one node sees is acted on by all of them), adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs that can't be altered, secret management through AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment where no prompts or responses leave your infrastructure. Bifrost is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR compliant, and multiple Fortune 500 companies run it in production across financial services, healthcare, technology, pharmaceuticals and defense.

Where to be careful: the enterprise depth (identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail integrations, vault integrations and in-VPC deployment) sits in the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint, so budget for it separately, and it's still offered through early access, so pilot it on a subset of devices before a fleet-wide push.

Best for: Bifrost is built for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require best-in-class performance, scalability, and reliability. It serves as a centralized AI gateway to route, govern, and secure all AI traffic across models and environments with ultra low latency. Bifrost unifies LLM gateway, MCP gateway, and Agents gateway capabilities into a single platform.

Designed for regulated industries and strict enterprise requirements, it supports air-gapped deployments, VPC isolation, and on-prem infrastructure. It provides full control over data, access, and execution, along with robust security, policy enforcement, and governance capabilities.

2. Kong AI Gateway

Kong AI Gateway is what happens when a mature API gateway learns about LLMs. If Kong already fronts your APIs, the pitch writes itself: same control plane, same plugin model, same team on call. The AI layer adds provider routing, token-based rate limiting, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models.

MCP arrived with Gateway 3.12 in October 2025. The AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose existing REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server, with ACLs applied to both tool discovery and tool invocation, and a companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic.

The trade-offs are practical ones. Kong's docs list the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and the OAuth2 plugin was still labelled tech preview there at the time of writing. And if Kong isn't already in your stack, standing up a full API gateway platform just for LLM traffic is a lot of machinery for the job.

Best for: organizations already standardized on Kong that want AI traffic on the control plane they already run.

3. Azure API Management

For Azure-first companies this is the path of least resistance. Microsoft's AI gateway capabilities aren't a separate product, they're a set of policies on top of API Management. A token limit policy enforces per-consumer quotas (and can count prompt tokens up front so oversized requests never reach the backend), a metrics policy sends token usage to Application Insights, and semantic caching runs on Azure Managed Redis or another RediSearch-compatible cache. LLM backends can be load balanced, and Entra ID handles authentication.

MCP support is real too. You can expose APIs as MCP servers and, per the June 2026 release notes, package them into products to control who gets what.

The costs are portability and tier. Capabilities vary by API Management service tier, everything is configured through policy XML, and the whole design assumes you live in Azure. Multi-cloud or on-prem estates will feel the friction.

Best for: Azure-centric enterprises with an existing API Management investment and security teams that already trust Entra and Azure Monitor.

4. Portkey (now Prisma AIRS AI Gateway)

Portkey made its name as the developer-friendly managed gateway: one API for 1,600+ models, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails with PII detection, budgets, RBAC and detailed logs. It added an MCP Gateway in January 2026, the core gateway is open source, and deployment options run from SaaS to private cloud, VPC and fully self-hosted. Enterprise plans bring SAML 2.0 SSO and audit logs.

The big news is ownership. Palo Alto Networks announced it would acquire Portkey and closed the deal on May 29, 2026, and the product now appears as the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. For existing Palo Alto customers that's a neat consolidation, with the gateway sitting next to runtime security and identity tooling. For everyone else it's a fair moment to ask about roadmap and packaging, even though Palo Alto said existing and new Portkey customers will continue to be supported. One more detail: per Portkey's caching docs, semantic caching is limited to select Enterprise plans.

Best for: teams that want a managed, quick-to-adopt gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem.

5. LiteLLM

LiteLLM is where a lot of teams start, for good reason. It's an MIT-licensed Python SDK plus a self-hosted proxy with 100+ providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing and fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching works with Qdrant, Valkey or Redis, though its docs recommend keeping it to single-shot prompts and away from multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations, and Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Two things to weigh. First, performance: in Bifrost's published benchmarks (AWS EC2, 500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), LiteLLM sustained 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds, against 424 requests per second and 1.68 seconds for Bifrost. Second, supply chain hygiene. On March 24, 2026, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published to PyPI carrying credential-stealing malware after attackers got hold of publishing credentials through a compromised CI/CD pipeline, as NetSPI's write-up describes. The bad versions were pulled. It wasn't a flaw in how the gateway works, and it could have hit any popular package. But a gateway holds every provider key you own, so pin versions and mirror packages internally whichever product you choose.

Best for: Python-heavy teams with moderate traffic that value ecosystem breadth and have the capacity to run and harden a self-hosted service.

Also worth a look

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a solid managed option for teams already on Cloudflare, with caching, rate limiting, dynamic routing, guardrails and DLP integration. It runs on Cloudflare's network, though, so it's not an option if you need self-hosted or in-VPC. OpenRouter suits individual developers and small teams who want broad model access under one bill better than it suits governance-heavy enterprise rollouts.

Enterprise controls and deployment compared

This second table covers what security reviews and procurement tend to ask about when they evaluate an enterprise AI gateway: identity, audit, where the gateway runs and how it's licensed. It's where Bifrost's open-source core with an enterprise tier on top makes the most difference for regulated buyers.

Control Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
SSO and roles Okta, Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider, with SCIM 2.0, RBAC and data access control (Enterprise) Kong's existing consumer and identity model Entra ID with Azure RBAC SAML 2.0 SSO and RBAC (Enterprise) Admin UI SSO free for 5 users, license beyond; SCIM with license
Audit trail Signed, tamper-proof audit logs with export to S3, GCS and BigQuery (Enterprise) Kong logging plugins and Konnect analytics Azure Monitor and Application Insights Access rules and audit logs (Enterprise) Audit logs with license
Where it runs Single binary: self-hosted, in-VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, clustered Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Azure SaaS, private cloud, VPC or self-hosted Self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes)
Licensing Apache 2.0 core plus Enterprise tier (14-day free trial); Edge priced per endpoint Open-source core, advanced AI plugins (including MCP) need a license Azure service, capabilities vary by tier Open-source gateway plus enterprise plans MIT plus enterprise license key
Main trade-off Depth sits in the paid tier; Edge needs Enterprise and is in early access Needs Kong in place; MCP OAuth2 in tech preview Azure-centric, policy XML Roadmap now tied to Palo Alto Python overhead and supply chain hygiene

Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team

For teams running enterprise AI workloads with multi-provider routing, agent workflows, regulated industry compliance, or high-throughput applications, the open-source Bifrost enterprise AI gateway addresses requirements that Python-based and lighter managed gateways tend to struggle with at scale. The 11 µs overhead, native MCP gateway, hierarchical virtual key governance, and support for air-gapped and VPC deployments make it the strongest production fit where those factors matter.

LiteLLM fits teams with Python-centric stacks and moderate traffic volumes that prioritize ecosystem familiarity. Kong AI Gateway fits organizations that have standardized on Kong for general API management. Azure API Management fits Azure-first estates where API Management is already approved, and Portkey fits teams that want a managed gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter fit teams with simpler requirements: managed infrastructure, lighter governance needs, or early-stage workloads that have not yet encountered the scale at which a self-hosted, compiled-language gateway becomes necessary. Teams comparing options across this range will find the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide a useful reference before finalizing a decision.

Frequently asked questions

What is an enterprise AI gateway?

It's a control layer between AI consumers (applications, agents and employees) and model providers. It routes and retries requests across models, enforces budgets and access rules, applies guardrails, and records everything for audit, usually through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

How is an enterprise AI gateway different from an API gateway?

A classic API gateway counts requests and checks auth. An AI gateway understands tokens, models and prompts: token-based budgets, failover across model vendors, semantic caching keyed on meaning, and per-model cost attribution. The line is blurrier than it used to be, since Kong and Azure API Management have added AI policies on top of their API gateways, while products like Bifrost treat those capabilities as native.

Should we self-host or use a managed enterprise AI gateway?

Self-hosting keeps prompts, keys and logs inside your own boundary and gives you control, in exchange for running the service. Managed options start faster but send traffic through a vendor's network. Regulated and high-volume teams usually end up self-hosted or in-VPC.

Do enterprise AI gateways support MCP?

All five now offer something. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong uses licensed plugins, Azure API Management exposes and packages MCP servers, Portkey has an MCP Gateway, and LiteLLM added one to its proxy. The differences are in authentication, tool-level access control and token cost, so test those rather than ticking a box.

How much latency does an enterprise AI gateway add?

It depends on the runtime and which features are switched on. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS on a single t3.xlarge, as shown in its published benchmarks. Against model latency measured in seconds, that's noise for a single call, but overhead compounds when agents chain many calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Usually yes, since both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. Bifrost ships drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK, and teams on a LiteLLM proxy can migrate models, keys, teams and users across automatically. The LiteLLM migration guide covers the cutover.

Can an enterprise AI gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only if that traffic reaches it. Standard gateways cover what developers deliberately route through them. Bifrost Edge closes that gap by routing desktop, browser and coding-agent traffic through the gateway so existing policies apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

The core is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to self-host. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail integrations, signed audit logs, vault integrations and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment, with a free 14-day trial. Bifrost Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

The five gateways in this comparison cover different points on the tradeoff curve between operational simplicity and production depth. For teams where AI is a core infrastructure concern, Bifrost provides the performance baseline, governance model, and enterprise deployment options that production requirements demand. To see how Bifrost fits your infrastructure, book a demo with the Bifrost team.

title: Everything hackable will get hacked
description:
Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close.

I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community.

  • Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards.

  • Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today.

The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency.

The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident

This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems.

The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred.

Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today

Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work.

On DeepSec Bench, which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8.

I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox, and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer.

These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface.

The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape.

When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating.

While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit.

Frontier models can help defenders today

Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them.

But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far.

The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. Attackers can also obtain source code, but I think source-code access is a reasonable working signal of defensive intent.

I personally discovered this in March, when I first heard about cyber variants and was also seeing AI code reviews find security issues in my own code. That made me wonder, “If code review can find issues in a diff, can I also run it across an entire codebase?” It turns out the answer was yes. From that experiment, I created deepsec, an open-source security harness for performing security analysis at scale across large codebases.

The temporary defensive advantage

Right now, OpenAI’s Sol 5.6 on XHigh is the best model for cybersecurity defense. It is much smarter than Kimi K3, the best available open-weight model without safeguards against offensive work. As defender, you have the better tool at your disposal, but you have to use it.

A full deepsec review will help you improve the security posture of your codebase by surfacing vulnerability hypotheses for you to investigate. In my experience, it is especially good at finding IDORs, XSS, and SSRF. The Hugging Face incident shows what this kind of application-level research looks like from the other side, since the models kept searching after an SSRF attempt was blocked and eventually found successful routes through file disclosure and template injection.

deepsec is open source and can run entirely in your own infrastructure with inference providers controlled by you. Vercel has no financial gain from you using it. It is really worth trying on your own source code.

Once the run finishes, review every finding yourself and compare the results with what your current security process already catches.

Continuous defense

AI model capabilities will continue to improve, and I expect open-weight models to catch up with Sol’s current performance on application-code vulnerability discovery even as frontier models advance again. We need to prepare for that cycle by continuously improving how we find and fix vulnerabilities as the models progress.

At Vercel, we run full deepsec reviews across mission-critical repositories every quarter and whenever a stronger model becomes available, in addition to automated security reviews on every pull request.

Those full reviews cost tens of thousands of dollars, which we consider a relatively small expense compared with what we spend on our HackerOne program or the opportunity cost of a security incident.

We have connected deepsec output to Vercel software factories for automated vulnerability processing and will share more about this work soon. As these reviews produce more findings, automatically managing them becomes the next frontier.

What Vercel is doing

As an immediate measure, we made the full egress firewall in Vercel Sandbox available on the Hobby plan, giving everyone access to the same network controls.

We are also working to launch a dedicated HackerOne program focused on finding zero-day vulnerabilities in Vercel Sandbox and the egress firewall. We want to redirect offensive model capabilities toward defensive work, so the program will cover AI costs for researchers who use AI Gateway and submit a vulnerability report that is accepted.

We also plan to extend deepsec to use the offensive capabilities of open-weight models and cyber variants of frontier models when triaging the vulnerability hypotheses it identifies.

Defenders can already use stronger models than those broadly available for offensive work. Teams should use that advantage now and continue reviewing their systems as the gap closes.

Takeaways

  • The cybersecurity threat from AI models is real.

  • Everybody can improve their defensive posture with tools like deepsec today.

  • Doing this is urgent, and the practice should continue as models improve.

title: UkrMeme: Multimodal Explainable Persuasion Detection in Ukrainian Memes
description:
arXiv:2610.13783v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.

title: When Should the Teacher Move? Temporal Coupling and Stability in Self On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2606.03532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Self on-policy distillation trains a student policy against a teacher derived from its own parameter history, yet the teacher's update schedule -- which governs the \emph{temporal coupling} between teacher and student -- has not been systematically studied as a stability variable. Through a controlled schedule sweep on Qwen3-8B, we establish that \emph{isolation periods}, defined as complete teacher freezing between updates, are the key structural property enabling stable learning, not teacher age. To characterize these underlying training dynamics, we introduce a diagnostic framework of temporal KL structure, refresh shock, and length-tail risk. This framework further uncovers \emph{state-oblivious collapse}: optimal short-horizon fixed schedules catastrophically fail under long-horizon training because a clock-driven refresh can copy a transiently drifting student into the teacher in a single, irreversible step. This failure mode is invisible under short-horizon evaluation and mechanistically distinct from EMA's chronic contamination. To address this, we propose \emph{Consolidation-Gated Teacher Refresh} (CGTR), which preserves isolation periods while gating each refresh on joint evidence of reward improvement and length-tail safety, ensuring every teacher movement responds to genuine student consolidation rather than a clock signal. With a single shared parameter set and no per-dataset retuning, CGTR achieves \textbf{zero collapse} and the best final score on all four tasks (Chemistry, Biology, Physics, ToolUse), self-regulating its refresh frequency to each task's learning dynamics.

title: Use ACP-compatible harnesses with the AI SDK harness layer
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports any Agent Client Protocol (ACP)-compatible harness with HarnessAgent through the new @ai-sdk/harness-acp package.

Previously, every harness adapter wrapped one specific runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Deep Agents, OpenCode). @ai-sdk/harness-acp wraps the protocol instead. It is a meta adapter: rather than adapting a single harness, it lets you build an adapter for any harness that ships an ACP-compatible package.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

Read the ACP harness documentation to get started.

title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
description:
arXiv:2610.13632v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Custom Environments
description:
Vercel Connect now lets you link a connector to a Custom Environment so deployments there can request provider tokens and receive forwarded webhooks.

Custom Environments appear alongside Production, Preview, and Development when you add or edit a project on a connector in the dashboard.

From the CLI, pass the environment's slug to --environment:

Passing --environment replaces the default environments.

Once linked, a deployment in that environment can request tokens with getToken as usual. If the calling environment isn't on the project link, the request fails with ClientNotEnabledForEnvironmentError.

Trigger destinations can also target a Custom Environment:

Before targeting a Custom Environment with triggers, deploy to it and assign it a verified domain. Vercel Connect forwards events through that domain.

Project links control which deployments can request tokens, and they do not restrict a provider token after it is issued. When environments need provider-level isolation, create a separate connector for each environment and request only the scopes it needs.

Vercel Connect is in beta on all plans. Custom Environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Get started with the Vercel Connect quickstart or read the step-by-step guides.

title: Campo de CPF em React sem dor: máscara, validação em tempo real e acessibilidade
description:
Transparência: sou fundador da CPFHub, citada no final. O componente funciona sem nenhuma API.

O campo de CPF parece trivial até você receber os primeiros tickets: "não consigo colar meu CPF", "o cursor pula para o final", "o teclado do celular abre com letras". Vamos construir um componente React que resolve tudo isso sem biblioteca de máscara.

1. Guarde dígitos, mostre máscara

O estado deve conter apenas dígitos. A máscara é derivada na renderização. Isso elimina a maior parte dos bugs.

const soDigitos = (s) => s.replace(/\D/g, "").slice(0, 11);

function mascararCpf(d) {
  return d
    .replace(/^(\d{3})(\d)/, "$1.$2")
    .replace(/^(\d{3})\.(\d{3})(\d)/, "$1.$2.$3")
    .replace(/\.(\d{3})(\d)/, ".$1-$2");
}

Teste rápido: mascararCpf("52998224725") → "529.982.247-25", e mascararCpf("5299") → "529.9". A máscara progressiva funciona enquanto o usuário digita.

2. Validação dos dígitos 

export function cpfValido(d) {
  if (!/^\d{11}$/.test(d) || /^(\d)\1{10}$/.test(d)) return false;
  for (let t = 9; t < 11; t++) {
    let soma = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < t; i++) soma += Number(d[i]) * (t + 1 - i);
    if (Number(d[t]) !== ((soma * 10) % 11) % 10) return false;
  }
  return true;
}

3. O componente 

import { useId, useState } from "react";

export function CampoCpf({ onValido }) {
  const id = useId();
  const [digitos, setDigitos] = useState("");
  const [tocado, setTocado] = useState(false);

  const completo = digitos.length === 11;
  const valido = completo && cpfValido(digitos);
  const erro = tocado && digitos.length > 0 && (!completo || !valido);

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={id}>CPF</label>
      <input
        id={id}
        name="cpf"
        inputMode="numeric"
        autoComplete="off"
        placeholder="000.000.000-00"
        value={mascararCpf(digitos)}
        onChange={(e) => {
          const d = soDigitos(e.target.value);
          setDigitos(d);
          if (d.length === 11 && cpfValido(d)) onValido?.(d);
        }}
        onBlur={() => setTocado(true)}
        aria-invalid={erro}
        aria-describedby={erro ? `${id}-erro` : undefined}
      />
      {erro && (
        <p id={`${id}-erro`} role="alert">
          {completo ? "CPF inválido. Confira os números." : "O CPF tem 11 dígitos."}
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Decisões que importam:

  • inputMode="numeric" abre o teclado numérico no celular, mas, ao contrário de type="number", mantém o campo como texto (não perde zero à esquerda nem aceita e).
  • Erro só depois do blur. Mostrar "CPF inválido" enquanto a pessoa ainda digita o terceiro número é irritante.
  • Colar funciona porque normalizamos qualquer string com soDigitos, inclusive 529 982 247 25.
  • aria-invalid e aria-describedby fazem o leitor de tela anunciar o erro.

4. E o cursor?

Como a máscara insere caracteres, editar no meio pode empurrar o cursor. Para a maioria dos formulários isso é aceitável, porque as pessoas digitam CPF do início ao fim. Se o seu caso exige edição no meio, calcule quantos dígitos estavam antes do cursor e reposicione em um useLayoutEffect. Ou use uma biblioteca madura como react-imask.

5. React Hook Form + Zod

Em formulários maiores, centralize a regra no schema:

import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  nome: z.string().min(3),
  cpf: z
    .string()
    .transform((s) => s.replace(/\D/g, ""))
    .refine(cpfValido, "CPF inválido"),
});

O transform garante que o backend recebe só dígitos.

6. Nunca confie só no front

Tudo isso é UX. O backend tem que validar de novo, porque qualquer um pode chamar sua API sem passar pelo formulário. E consultar uma API de CPF direto do navegador expõe sua chave: faça a consulta a partir de um endpoint seu (route handler, function, backend).

7. Pré-preenchendo o nome

Um uso comum: quando o CPF fica válido, o front chama o seu backend, que consulta uma API de CPF e devolve o primeiro nome para confirmação ("Você é Maria?"). Isso reduz digitação e erro. Mostre só o necessário e nunca a data de nascimento completa antes de a pessoa confirmar a identidade.

Sobre a CPFHub

Para esse backend, a CPFHub tem GET /cpf/{cpf} (header x-api-key), que retorna nome, gênero e data de nascimento em ~150 ms típicos (não SLA), com 50 créditos grátis por mês. Detalhes na documentação.

title: Copy First, Translate Later: Interpreting Translation Dynamics in Multilingual Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2604.17633v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models exhibit impressive cross-lingual capabilities. However, prior work analyzes this phenomenon through isolated factors and at sparse points during training, limiting our understanding of how cross-lingual generalization emerges--particularly in the early phases of learning. To study the early trajectory of linguistic and translation capabilities, we pretrain a multilingual 1.7B model on nine diverse languages, capturing checkpoints at a much finer granularity. We use word-level translation as a testbed, introducing a novel dataset to trace how translation develops over training through behavioral analyses, model-component analysis, and parameter-based ablations. We find that the model quickly acquires basic linguistic capabilities in parallel with token-level copying, while translation develops in two distinct phases: an initial phase dominated by copying and surface-level similarities, and a second phase in which more generalizing translation mechanisms are developed while copying is refined. Together, these findings provide a fine-grained view of how cross-lingual generalization develops during multilingual pretraining.

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.

title: Estimating Great Expectations Under Autoregressive Language Models with Potentials
description:
arXiv:2610.11399v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many applications of language models hinge not on individual samples but on the expectation of a test functional under the model. Estimating such expectations reliably can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we show how to make estimation more efficient by exploiting the next-token conditional probabilities which are available as a by-product of sampling. We do so through potentials: real-valued functions on prefixes that decompose the test functional additively. We construct an estimator whose variance depends on the chosen potential, and derive conditions under which a potential reduces this variance. We then develop practical potentials for several estimands and applications, and demonstrate substantial variance reductions across several estimands at comparable computational cost.

title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12957v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.

title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
description:
arXiv:2610.13171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Prior work reduces this cost by changing the sampler or the model (e.g., sequential Monte Carlo, approximate lookahead, distillation). We propose Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), which accelerates PowerMH by prefetching future proposals and provably leaves its MH transition kernel unchanged. PreSTO views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions: in each model call, it generates the proposals of a \textit{prefetched subtree} of this tree in one batch, then follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. On LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, the predictive traversal rule is a further $1.25\times$--$1.37\times$ faster than the default breadth-first traversal.

title: Introducing the new v0 API
description:
Today we're introducing the new v0 API: programmatic, headless access to v0's app-building agent. Send a prompt and v0 generates an app, starts a dev server in a Vercel Sandbox, and gives you a preview URL you can embed in your own UI.

Each chat is an isolated workspace for one app, where v0 can read, edit, and run the files. Follow-up messages continue from the current state. v0 verifies the code running in the Sandbox, so it can catch and fix errors in your app in real time.

The new API is now generally available.

How it works

Create a chat from a prompt, stream its work, and render the live preview, all from your own interface. First, install the v0 SDK.

Then, create a chat. Send a prompt, and v0 generates your app.

Send follow-up messages to the same chat to keep building. Each one continues from the current state.

Then embed the app.

A prompt goes in, a running app comes out. v0 operates the Sandbox, dev server, and preview behind it. When you're ready, deploy to Vercel in one API call. v0 manages the whole pipeline.

What this unlocks

The new API lets you run v0's app builder inside your own product or pipeline. This opens use cases like:

  • A white-labeled app builder: Your users describe an app and get one back.

  • Automated app changes: Trigger v0 from a script, CI job, or webhook to generate a new app or update an existing one.

  • A build tool for your agents: An agent hands back a working app instead of a code snippet.

Below, we break down the API primitives behind this workflow.

Start with a chat

Each chat holds the state for one app, and a repo or Vercel project can have many. Keep each chat's ID and send its follow-up messages to that chat. Metadata lets you group chats by customer, workspace, app, or any key you already use.

Learn more about messages.

Stream the trace

Your interface needs to show what happens between sending a request and seeing the updated preview.

Every message includes ordered parts: text, thinking, file reads and edits, searches, bash commands, tool calls, and agent actions. The same object can drive a one-line status, a changed-files view, or the full trace.

Usage is returned with chat and message responses, so you can account for the work when it finishes.

Choose sync, async, or streaming

Chat creation and messages support synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming responses. Use sync when the caller needs the completed response. Use async to queue the work and receive updates via webhook or poll for v0's response later. Stream the request to render v0's work as it happens.

Work from existing code

You can also create a chat from a repository, ZIP archive, or set of files.

Render the dev server preview

Each chat gets a short-lived preview token. Fetch it from a server route and proxy browser requests through it, so your v0 API key never reaches the browser. When a preview is ready, traffic forwards to it; while the Sandbox spins up, requests fall back to a loading route. Point an iframe at your proxy route and cache the preview details until they expire.

Read more about Accessing Previews in the docs.

Bring your own tools and design systems

Turn on specific MCP servers for a chat, or use the defaults.

Design Systems 2.0 saves a design system as a skill. Include it in a request to load its components, tokens, setup, and starter app.

You can pass up to three skills per request, from team or user memory, skills.sh, or the connected repo, or let the agent pull them in for you.

Use v0 from agents

If you're building an agent, give it v0 as a tool. When the agent needs to produce a working app, it calls v0, and gets back a running preview or deployment to hand to the user. Your agent stays in charge of everything else.

There are three ways to connect it:

MCP

Connect the v0 MCP server to an IDE, desktop assistant, or agent runtime that supports MCP.

The first connection starts an OAuth flow. The MCP server exposes tools for creating chats, listing chats, getting chat details, listing and sending messages, resolving pending tasks, and getting preview URLs.

AI SDK

For TypeScript agents built with AI SDK, use @v0-sdk/ai-tools to expose v0's API operations as tools in the agent's own loop.

The agent decides when to create or continue a chat. Your AI SDK run keeps control of the orchestration and final response.

eve

For eve agents, add an OpenAPI connection file. eve turns the allowed operations into tools and attaches the API key at execution time, out of model context.

Connect a Vercel project

Create a Vercel project for the chat, then manage its environment variables, integrations, and settings through the Vercel API. Your apps get Vercel's security and observability by default.

When you're ready to ship, deploy the chat to Vercel.

Migrate your chats

Chats from the previous version of the v0 API don’t run on the new one, so carry them forward. Pick the version you want to keep, download it as a ZIP, and create a new chat from that ZIP. Store the old identifiers in the new chat’s metadata if you need traceability.

The migration guide covers the full mapping. The main changes:

  • Use https://api.v0.dev/v2 for new requests.

  • The chat holds current app state, and messages hold its history.

  • Replace version workflows with chat file workflows, and v0 Project organization with chat metadata.

  • Use vercelProjectId plus the Vercel API for project operations.

  • Render message parts, not only final text.

Get started

Create an API key in v0 settings and install the SDK.

Or, scaffold a full app.

Read the documentation and migration guide.

Use code channels to investigate incidents, write and review code as a team, or manage ongoing work such as dependency upgrades and migrations.

Inside a Vercel Agent code channel:

  • Follow the work: Agent posts relevant deployments, logs, errors, and diffs in the channel as it works.

  • Talk without repeated @Vercel mentions: Agent follows the conversation, recognizes which messages are for it, and continues when the team gives it more work.

  • Review pull requests: Ask Agent for a PR review and it posts its findings in the channel. It can find bugs outside the diff, and explain failing checks and their root causes.

  • Approve every change: Agent is read-only by default and never exceeds the requester's permissions. Before making a change, it drafts a plan and waits for approval. For every action, Vercel records who requested and approved it and what Agent ran.

  • Stop work at any time: The person who created the code channel can cancel an active task.

Vercel Agent in Slack code channels is available in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Add Vercel to Slack, learn about Slack Code, or read the docs.

title: Building a local MCP server inside a Rust desktop app
description:
Your AI assistant can write a state machine in eight seconds but has no idea what assets you own.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game devs, built in Rust and Tauri. It already knows every model, texture, sprite and sound in your library, what bundle it lives in, how it is tagged and what it depends on. Version 0.2.3 adds a built-in MCP server so your assistant can ask.

This is the engineering side: where the server lives, why it talks HTTP, and what it takes to make a local server that can write to your library safe to leave running.

Inside the app, not beside it

The obvious shortcut is a standalone MCP binary that opens the app's SQLite file and reads it directly. We ruled that out for two reasons:

  1. Two processes writing to one SQLite file is how you corrupt a library.
  2. The app would never learn about changes. Ask the assistant to tag forty rocks and the open window keeps showing them untagged until restart.

So the server runs inside AssetHoard and only answers while the app is open. That turned out to be a feature: every change the assistant makes shows up in the UI immediately.

One rule: MCP never touches the database

The MCP module is not allowed to call app commands or SQL. Everything goes through a small internal library API that sits underneath both the UI and the MCP server.

When an assistant moves an asset into a bundle, it runs the same function as a drag and drop. Same validation, same audit log, same undo entry. There is no second code path drifting out of sync with the real one.

It also makes new tools cheap. A tool is a typed argument struct, whose doc comments become the descriptions the model reads, plus a thin method that calls the library API. The interesting logic lives in one place and gets tested once.

Stack: rmcp, streamable HTTP, axum

  • rmcp, the official Rust MCP SDK, with its streamable HTTP transport mounted on axum
  • Database work on blocking worker threads, so a large search never stalls the async runtime
  • Each call recorded in a recent-activity list visible in Settings

We chose HTTP over stdio because the server lives inside an app that is already running. Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf connect to a local endpoint with a header, which is a one-line setup. Claude Desktop only launches stdio servers, so for now it goes through the mcp-remote bridge.

The port is fixed at 47823 by default. It is configurable, but the app never picks another one on its own if it is busy. Auto-switching sounds helpful until every client config you have written silently stops matching. A taken port is a readable error instead.

Making it safe to leave on

A local server that reads your files and writes to your library deserves some paranoia.

  • Off by default. One toggle in Settings, and a toolbar icon whenever it is running.
  • Loopback only. Binds to 127.0.0.1.
  • Bearer token. 48 random hex characters, compared in constant time. Regenerating it disconnects every client.
  • Browsers refused. Any request with an Origin header is rejected, and Host must be a loopback address. Browsers always send Origin; CLI and IDE clients do not. This blocks DNS rebinding, and it is what the MCP spec asks local servers to do.
  • Write tools are a second opt-in. Checked on every call, so switching it off takes effect for already-connected clients.
  • No delete tools for assets or bundles. Exports skip existing files rather than overwrite.
  • Imports ask first. A native prompt shows the path, file count, size and target bundle. No answer within 60 seconds is a no.
  • Everything is undoable. Writes land on the normal undo stack with an MCP: label, e.g. MCP: Moved 1 asset into 'Rocks'.

Small decisions that paid off

Text results, separate thumbnails. Search returns ids, names, types, paths and tags. If the model wants to look, it calls get_thumbnail and gets an image of at most 256px. It can check that the "mossy rock" really is mossy without flooding its context with every result's picture.

Dependencies travel with exports. A model brings its textures, a Godot .tres brings what it references, Unreal assets bring theirs. Assets inside zips or .unitypackage files are extracted first.

Deep links. Every asset, bundle and project returned includes an assethoard:// link, so the assistant can hand you something clickable that jumps straight to the item in the app.

Errors the model can read. Unknown ids or disabled write tools come back as plain error messages rather than protocol failures, so the assistant can explain or try something else.

What it looks like in use

"Find three different barrel models and a wood texture that matches, and copy them into Assets/Props."

The assistant searches, checks thumbnails, picks a set and exports it, textures included. You keep building the level.

"Make a bundle called 'Rocks' under 'Environment', move every rock model into it and tag them 'nature'."

Each step appears live in the app as its own undo entry. If it moves a boulder that was actually a potato, Ctrl+Z.

What is next

The main gap is Claude Desktop needing mcp-remote. A small native shim is on the list.

The full write-up, including more workflows, is on the AssetHoard blog. Setup per client is in the MCP docs and every tool is in the tool reference. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta.

If you have built a local MCP server into a desktop app, I would like to hear how you handled auth and write access.

title: Issue no.13: All systems go
description: When things move fast, foundations matter more than ever.

title: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable supervision for software engineering agents through executable tests, but binary rewards fail to distinguish trajectories with substantially different debugging quality. We investigate whether the current policy can judge its own trajectories and use these judgments to improve task performance without a separately trained reward model. To this end, we introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a reward-refinement method that reuses the policy to compare observable debugging behavior among trajectories from the same task with the same verifier outcome. BSR aggregates pairwise preferences into task-local scores and converts them into bounded auxiliary rewards, introducing reward contrast while preserving the verifier-defined pass/fail ordering. This provides additional supervision from already-collected trajectories without requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live show consistent improvements across the evaluated Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B configurations, supporting using the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.

title: Temporal Evidence Forests for Long-Horizon Multi-Party Conversational Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.12874v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-term memory has been widely adopted in LLM-based agents to support persistent interaction and personalized assistance. Long-term multi-party interactions, however, accumulate substantially more detailed information, with decisions repeatedly updated and states evolving across participants and interaction stages. Temporal structure is therefore crucial for tracing such memories: relevant information often appears densely within short intervals, while transitions among different states are anchored by a strict temporal order. Existing temporally aware memory frameworks primarily store time as metadata or use temporal signals to guide retrieval over preconstructed memory structures, without using temporal structure to both recover locally concentrated evidence and reconstruct its complete event progression. To address these limitations, we propose T-Mem, a temporal-structure-based memory framework that preserves interactions and organizes query-relevant evidence through two temporal mechanisms. Temporal Evidence Discovery exploits the local concentration of related messages to recover overlooked evidence, while Temporal Memory Structuring models state transitions and supporting relations over time and compresses low-information spans within the resulting forest. Evidence Forest Linearization then serializes the structured evidence for answer generation. Experiments on two long-term multi-party memory benchmarks demonstrate that T-Mem consistently outperforms competitive memory frameworks across LLMs, parameter settings, domains, and query types.

title: Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Tactical Decision Making in Heavy-Duty Vehicles
description:
arXiv:2601.18783v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A central difficulty in applying reinforcement learning to real-world applications such as autonomous driving is that conventional scalar reward formulations obtained by aggregating multiple often competing objectives may obscure the structure of their trade-offs. These challenges are particularly relevant to decision-making for heavy-duty vehicles, which requires balancing safety, efficiency, and operational costs under demanding commercial requirements. We present a preference-conditioned multi-objective reinforcement learning framework that explicitly represents these objectives and utilizes Generalized Policy Improvement and Proximal Policy Optimization to learn policies capturing different trade-offs between them. The proposed method approximates the Pareto front across three conflicting objectives: safety, quantified in terms of collisions and successful completion; energy efficiency, quantified using energy cost; and time efficiency, quantified using driver cost. We evaluate the framework in a scalable highway traffic simulation environment tailored for tactical decision making in heavy-duty trucks. It yields smooth and interpretable Pareto fronts, and evaluations across traffic densities and against an analytical baseline show that the learned policies capture meaningful trade-offs. The preference-conditioned policy enables transitions between different driving behaviors without retraining, demonstrating the potential of multi-objective reinforcement learning for adaptive decision making in autonomous heavy-duty vehicles.

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --visibility config or --visibility secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --visibility is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Visibility.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

title: OTel: Open Telco AI Datasets, Benchmarks, and Models
description:
arXiv:2610.07766v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource that releases derived telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, together with 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines spanning 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. Each baseline starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

title: Compliance documents are now available in Team settings
description:
A new Compliance section in Team settings lets you preview and download Vercel's compliance documents directly in the dashboard. These include attestations like SOC 2 Type 2, security policies, and other security documents that are available through the Trust Center.

You can select a single document, an entire attestation, or multiple documents, and download them together as a single zip archive. Every download and preview is watermarked with your user and team information. Some entries link out to external resources instead, such as an auditor's public certificate directory.

The Trust Center remains available for additional security information. Vercel's compliance documents are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the compliance documentation.

description:
When you install a Vercel Marketplace integration from the Vercel CLI, it now also installs that provider's agent skills from skills.sh, so your agents know how to use it:

title: Hobby projects now retain fewer deployments to free up storage
description:
Hobby projects now retain fewer deployments past the 30-day retention window. Hobby teams get 10GB of Deployment Storage. Every deployment you keep uses some of it, and going over the limit can block you from deploying until you free some up. Deployment Retention for Hobby teams now deletes old deployments sooner, so dormant projects stop holding storage that your active projects need.

Each Hobby project now keeps its 3 most recent production deployments, plus its 3 most recent deployments of any type, regardless of age. Preview deployments no longer get their own protection. Your current production deployment is still never deleted, and aliased and active-branch deployments are still protected. See the full list of exceptions in the docs.

If your team is over the 10GB limit, deployments outside those exceptions are now deleted immediately instead of after 30 days.

To stay under the limit, see how to optimize your Deployment Storage usage, or upgrade to Pro, where storage is billed at $0.10 per GB per month.

Read more
