title: Cloudflare’s OHTTP Gateway Refuses to Decrypt Requests That Arrive Through Cloudflare
description:
Cloudflare has opened a closed beta of its OHTTP Gateway, a managed endpoint that decrypts Oblivious HTTP requests for an origin. The design choice drawing attention is a refusal: the Gateway will not decrypt requests arriving from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare, because that would put client identifiers and request contents in the same hands.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: Ling 3.0 Flash is now available on AI Gateway
description:

The model is free to use for the next three weeks, through August 3rd.

Ling 3.0 Flash is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 124B total parameters and about 5.1B active per token. It has a 256K token context window and runs in thinking and non-thinking modes.

Ling 3.0 Flash is built for token-efficient agentic inference at production scale, doing more work within tighter token, latency, and cost budgets across multi-step agent runs. The model targets high-frequency agentic workflows, coding agents, document work, and long-context multi-turn interactions.

To use Ling 3.0 Flash, set model to inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash-free in the AI SDK:

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

title: Microfrontends previews now link across repositories
description:
Microfrontends can now link Preview Deployments across repositories when their Git branch names match exactly.

In a monorepo, projects share the same Git repository, commits, and branches, so Vercel can automatically link their previews. Cross-repository projects have separate commit histories and branches in separate repositories. With this update, Vercel matches Git-connected projects by branch name and links their corresponding previews.

For example, when you preview the new-checkout branch of one project, requests to other projects in the Microfrontends group will use their new-checkout previews when available. This makes it easier to review coordinated changes across repositories in one preview experience.

This feature is enabled by default for new Microfrontends groups. You can manage it in your Microfrontends settings. Learn more about how deployment routing works for Microfrontends.

Read more

title: Export AI Gateway traces with Vercel Drains
description:
AI Gateway now produces an OpenTelemetry trace for every request. Pro and Enterprise teams can send these traces through Vercel Drains to any OTLP/HTTP-compatible endpoint, including native integrations for Braintrust, Dash0, Kubiks, Sentry, and Statsig.

Each trace shows the full request lifecycle, including:

  • Model and provider routing

  • Fallback and retry attempts

  • Token usage and cost

  • Time to first token, request duration, and response status

  • Project, deployment, API key, environment, and custom tag attribution

Trace Drains do not include prompt or completion content. Sampling controls let you choose how much traffic to export to each drain.

AI Gateway traces cost $0.05 per 1,000 traces delivered to each drain, plus the standard Drains rate of $0.50 per GB of data transferred. A request counts once per successful drain delivery, even when AI Gateway makes multiple provider attempts. Failed deliveries do not incur a trace charge.

Set up a Trace Drain from your team's Drains settings or learn more in the AI Gateway documentation.

title: Which AWS Certification Is the Best Choice for Landing a Job in 2026?
description:
Cloud computing continues to power enterprise applications, data platforms, DevOps pipelines, and generative AI solutions. For professionals looking to enter the cloud industry or advance their careers, AWS certifications can help demonstrate relevant technical knowledge.

However, choosing the right certification is not simply about selecting the most advanced exam. The best choice depends on your existing experience, target job role, and the technical skills employers expect.

In 2026, AWS offers certification pathways across cloud architecture, software development, cloud operations, data engineering, machine learning, security, and generative AI.

So, which AWS certification should you choose to improve your chances of landing a job in 2026?

Let's compare the leading options and identify the best pathway for different career goals.

1. AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate

Best overall starting point for many aspiring cloud professionals

The AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate certification is one of the strongest starting points for people who want to build a career in cloud computing.

It validates your ability to design AWS solutions based on requirements involving security, reliability, performance, and cost optimization.

Key topics include:

  • Amazon EC2 and compute services
  • Amazon S3 and storage solutions
  • Amazon VPC and networking fundamentals
  • AWS IAM and security
  • High availability and fault tolerance
  • Database selection and architecture
  • Backup, disaster recovery, and cost optimization

Which jobs can it support?

This certification is relevant to career paths such as:

  • Junior Cloud Engineer
  • Cloud Support Engineer
  • Associate Solutions Architect
  • Cloud Consultant
  • Infrastructure Engineer

It is also valuable for software developers who need to understand how their applications operate in AWS environments.

Why choose it?

Cloud architecture knowledge is useful across many technical roles. Even if you eventually specialize in development, DevOps, or AI, understanding how AWS services fit together provides a solid foundation.

Recommendation: If you are new to AWS and have not yet selected a specialization, start here.

2. AWS Certified Developer – Associate

Best for software developers moving into cloud development

If you already have experience with Java, Python, JavaScript, APIs, or backend development, the AWS Certified Developer – Associate certification may be a more direct fit for your career.

It focuses on developing, deploying, securing, and debugging applications built using AWS services.

Important topics include:

  • AWS Lambda and serverless applications
  • Amazon API Gateway
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • AWS SDKs and API integration
  • IAM permissions and application security
  • Application deployment and troubleshooting
  • Monitoring and debugging with AWS services

Which jobs can it support?

  • AWS Cloud Developer
  • Backend Developer
  • Serverless Application Developer
  • Cloud Application Engineer
  • Software Engineer working with AWS

Why choose it?

Companies need developers who can build applications that use cloud infrastructure effectively. Your existing programming experience can provide an advantage because you are adding AWS capabilities to an established skill set.

For experienced software engineers, this may be a more efficient route than beginning with an infrastructure-focused career path.

Recommendation: Choose Developer – Associate if your goal is to build and maintain cloud-based applications.

3. AWS Certified CloudOps Engineer – Associate

Best for cloud operations and infrastructure management

Previously known as AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate, this certification now reflects the CloudOps Engineer role.

The updated certification focuses on deploying, operating, monitoring, and maintaining AWS workloads.

Key topics include:

  • Monitoring and logging
  • Infrastructure operations
  • Networking and security controls
  • Incident response and troubleshooting
  • Business continuity
  • Performance and cost optimization
  • Automation and infrastructure as code
  • Container operations

Which jobs can it support?

  • Cloud Operations Engineer
  • Cloud Support Engineer
  • Systems Engineer
  • Infrastructure Engineer
  • Site Reliability Engineering support roles

Why choose it?

Organizations need professionals who can keep cloud applications available, secure, and cost-effective after deployment.

This certification is especially relevant if you enjoy troubleshooting, automation, infrastructure management, and operational reliability.

Recommendation: Choose CloudOps Engineer – Associate if you want to specialize in running and maintaining production cloud environments.

4. AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional

Best for experienced cloud engineers targeting advanced architecture roles

The Solutions Architect – Professional certification validates advanced AWS architecture knowledge. It covers complex, large-scale solutions involving multiple services, accounts, environments, and business requirements.

Key areas include:

  • Complex multi-account architectures
  • Large-scale migrations
  • Hybrid cloud environments
  • Resilience and disaster recovery
  • Advanced networking
  • Security and governance
  • Cost and performance optimization
  • Architectural trade-offs

Which jobs can it support?

  • Solutions Architect
  • Senior Cloud Engineer
  • Cloud Consultant
  • Enterprise Cloud Architect
  • Technical Lead for cloud platforms

Why choose it?

Professional-level architecture skills are valuable when organizations need people who can design and evaluate complex cloud solutions.

However, this is not usually the best first certification for someone without practical AWS experience. Build a strong foundation through hands-on work and associate-level learning before attempting it.

Recommendation: Target this certification after gaining substantial experience with AWS services and architecture.

5. AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional

Best for developers targeting production generative AI applications

Generative AI is an important specialization in the AWS certification portfolio in 2026.

The AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional certification validates advanced technical expertise in building and deploying production-ready generative AI solutions using AWS services, including Amazon Bedrock.

Its focus extends beyond prompting an LLM. It addresses the engineering needed to build secure, useful, and production-grade AI applications.

Important areas include:

  • Generative AI application development
  • Foundation model integration
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • Embeddings and knowledge retrieval
  • Tool integration and agentic workflows
  • Security and responsible AI implementation
  • Evaluation and monitoring
  • Performance and cost optimization

Which jobs can it support?

  • Generative AI Developer
  • AI Application Engineer
  • Agentic AI Developer
  • Cloud AI Engineer
  • Backend Engineer specializing in AI applications

Why choose it?

Organizations increasingly need developers who can integrate AI into existing business applications and deliver reliable services rather than just create prototypes.

This certification is particularly relevant for experienced developers who already understand application development and cloud fundamentals.

AWS identifies the target candidate as someone with at least two years of experience building production-grade applications on AWS or with open-source technologies, general AI/ML or data engineering experience, and hands-on generative AI implementation experience.

It is therefore an advanced career target, not necessarily the ideal first AWS certification for a complete beginner.

Recommendation: If you are an experienced developer planning to specialize in generative AI and agentic applications, make this a priority after building the necessary foundations.

6. AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate

Best for professionals pursuing machine learning engineering

Machine learning engineering involves implementing, deploying, and maintaining machine learning solutions in production environments.

The AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate certification is designed for professionals who want to demonstrate practical machine learning engineering skills using AWS services.

Key topics include:

  • Data preparation
  • Machine learning model development
  • Model deployment
  • Model monitoring
  • Operationalizing ML workloads
  • Troubleshooting and optimization
  • Production machine learning pipelines

Which jobs can it support?

  • Machine Learning Engineer
  • MLOps Engineer
  • ML Platform Engineer
  • Data Scientist working with production ML systems
  • Backend Developer transitioning into ML engineering

Important 2026 exam update

AWS has announced an updated version of this certification exam, MLA-C02. Its English-language beta began in September 2026, while the previous English exam, MLA-C01, reached its final testing date on September 28, 2026. The updated exam is therefore the version to watch when planning your preparation.

Always verify the currently available exam version and its registration status before scheduling your test.

Recommendation: Choose this pathway if you want to implement and operate machine learning workloads rather than focus primarily on integrating foundation models into applications.

7. AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate

Best for data engineering and analytics careers

AI and analytics applications depend on reliable data pipelines. Data engineers build the systems that collect, transform, store, and make data available for analysis and machine learning.

The AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate certification validates skills in data engineering using AWS services.

Key topics include:

  • Data ingestion and transformation
  • Data storage and data modeling
  • Data quality and lifecycle management
  • Data pipelines and orchestration
  • Data security and governance
  • Monitoring and troubleshooting data workloads

Which jobs can it support?

  • AWS Data Engineer
  • Cloud Data Engineer
  • Data Platform Engineer
  • Analytics Engineer
  • Data Infrastructure Engineer

Why choose it?

Data engineering is a useful specialization for professionals interested in analytics, machine learning, and enterprise AI infrastructure.

If your long-term goal is to build AI systems, understanding how to prepare and manage data can be an important advantage.

Recommendation: Choose Data Engineer – Associate if you prefer data platforms, pipelines, and large-scale data processing over application development.

8. AWS Certified Security – Specialty

Best for cloud security specialization

Cloud security is essential for organizations operating business-critical applications and sensitive data on AWS.

The AWS Certified Security – Specialty certification validates advanced knowledge of securing AWS workloads and architectures.

Important topics include:

  • Identity and access management
  • Data protection and encryption
  • Infrastructure security
  • Logging and threat detection
  • Incident response
  • Security monitoring and compliance

Which jobs can it support?

  • Cloud Security Engineer
  • AWS Security Specialist
  • Cloud Security Consultant
  • Security Architect
  • Cloud Governance Engineer

This is generally a better target for professionals who already have experience with AWS architecture, networking, and security.

Recommendation: Choose Security – Specialty if you want to build a specialized career protecting cloud infrastructure and applications.

9. AWS Certified AI Practitioner

Best for beginners who want to understand AI on AWS

The AWS Certified AI Practitioner certification validates foundational knowledge of AI, machine learning, and generative AI concepts, including their use cases and responsible implementation.

It covers concepts such as:

  • Artificial intelligence and machine learning fundamentals
  • Generative AI concepts
  • Foundation models
  • Prompt engineering
  • AI use cases and business applications
  • Responsible AI
  • Security and governance considerations

Which jobs can it support?

This is primarily a foundational credential rather than a direct qualification for an advanced AI engineering position.

It can support learning for people exploring cloud AI, technical sales, product management, business analysis, or future AI development training.

Why choose it?

It is useful if you want to understand AI concepts before investing in a more technical specialization.

However, if your immediate goal is a hands-on cloud engineering job, an associate-level technical certification combined with practical projects may provide stronger evidence of implementation skills.

Recommendation: Choose AI Practitioner as a starting point for AI knowledge, not as a substitute for engineering experience.

10. What About AWS Machine Learning – Specialty and Advanced Networking – Specialty?

Certification retirement dates matter when choosing a long-term study plan.

AWS Certified Machine Learning – Specialty reached its final exam date on March 31, 2026. Professionals planning a machine learning certification path should consider the Machine Learning Engineer – Associate credential and the current AWS AI certification options instead.

AWS has also announced the retirement of AWS Certified Advanced Networking – Specialty on December 31, 2026. If you are considering this credential, verify the remaining exam availability and whether it fits your timeline before committing to preparation.

Always use the current AWS certification catalog to confirm exam status, codes, and retirement dates.

Which AWS Certification Is Best for Landing a Job in 2026?

There is no single certification that is best for every candidate. The strongest choice depends on your experience and the role you want.

Your career goal Recommended certification
Starting a career in AWS cloud computing Solutions Architect – Associate
Software development using AWS Developer – Associate
Cloud operations and infrastructure CloudOps Engineer – Associate
Advanced cloud architecture Solutions Architect – Professional
Generative AI and agentic applications Generative AI Developer – Professional
Machine learning engineering Machine Learning Engineer – Associate
Data engineering and analytics Data Engineer – Associate
Cloud security Security – Specialty
Foundational AI knowledge AI Practitioner

For many people entering cloud computing, Solutions Architect – Associate is a strong first choice because its broad coverage helps establish an understanding of AWS services and architectural decisions.

For experienced software developers, Developer – Associate may be the more direct route into AWS application development.

For developers specifically targeting production generative AI and agentic AI applications, Generative AI Developer – Professional is an important advanced credential to consider.

A Practical AWS Certification Roadmap for 2026

Rather than collecting certifications without a clear objective, follow a career-focused progression.

Path A: Cloud Engineer

  1. Learn AWS fundamentals and core services.
  2. Prepare for Solutions Architect – Associate.
  3. Build and deploy cloud projects.
  4. Add CloudOps Engineer – Associate or another role-specific certification.
  5. Progress toward advanced architecture as your experience grows.

Path B: Cloud Application Developer

  1. Strengthen Java or Python programming.
  2. Learn AWS compute, storage, databases, and IAM.
  3. Prepare for Developer – Associate.
  4. Build a serverless or API-driven application.
  5. Add deployment, monitoring, and security capabilities.

Path C: Generative AI and Agentic AI Developer

  1. Build strong programming and application development skills.
  2. Learn AWS fundamentals and cloud security.
  3. Develop applications using foundation models.
  4. Implement RAG, vector search, tool calling, and agent workflows.
  5. Learn evaluation, monitoring, guardrails, and cost optimization.
  6. Prepare for Generative AI Developer – Professional when your experience matches the target level.

Path D: Data and Machine Learning Engineer

  1. Learn data processing and database fundamentals.
  2. Understand data pipelines and data quality.
  3. Choose Data Engineer – Associate or Machine Learning Engineer – Associate according to your target role.
  4. Build production-oriented projects.
  5. Add advanced ML, MLOps, or AI application skills where appropriate.

How to Prepare for an AWS Certification Exam

Regardless of which certification you choose, a structured preparation process can make your learning more effective.

1. Review the official exam guide.

Understand the exam domains, objectives, and expected level of expertise before beginning your preparation.

2. Gain hands-on experience.

Create AWS resources, configure permissions, deploy applications, inspect logs, and troubleshoot failures. Practical work helps connect exam concepts with real engineering problems.

3. Study the services relevant to your target role.

Avoid trying to memorize every AWS service. Focus on the services, design decisions, and operational tasks covered by your chosen exam.

4. Practise with exam-style questions.

Practice tests can help identify knowledge gaps, improve time management, and reveal topics that need further study. Review the reasoning behind each answer instead of memorizing question patterns.

For exam-focused preparation across AWS certification tracks, explore AWS Certification Practice Tests.

5. Build at least one portfolio project.

A certification demonstrates knowledge, but a project shows how you apply it. Build something relevant to your target role and be prepared to explain the architecture, security decisions, trade-offs, and troubleshooting process.

6. Prepare to discuss your work in interviews.

Employers may ask you to explain how you would design a solution, diagnose a failure, secure an application, or reduce infrastructure costs. Practising these scenarios helps you connect certification knowledge with job requirements.

Final Thoughts

The best AWS certification for landing a job in 2026 is the one that aligns with your target role and helps you demonstrate practical, relevant skills.

Choose Solutions Architect – Associate for a broad cloud foundation, Developer – Associate for cloud application development, CloudOps Engineer – Associate for operations, or a specialized data, machine learning, security, or generative AI credential when your career direction is clear.

Most importantly, remember that a certification is a starting point, not a job guarantee. Combine exam preparation with hands-on experience, real projects, troubleshooting skills, and the ability to explain your technical decisions.

A focused certification strategy supported by practical engineering work can help you build a stronger profile for AWS-related opportunities in 2026 and beyond.

title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction
description:
arXiv:2610.12984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.

title: The Depots Sent Whoever They Could Spare to Test Our New System
description:
Last year we replaced the system our depots use to book inbound deliveries from suppliers. The project plan gave the business four weeks of acceptance testing, and each depot was asked to provide two people for those four weeks.

The people who arrived were not the people we had pictured. Of the twenty two testers, nine were agency staff in their first months with us, five were on light duties after injuries, and several more had been released because their own team was quiet that month. They worked carefully through every script we gave them. All three hundred and forty test cases passed, and the depot managers signed off.

The system went live in September and the goods in offices struggled for six weeks. A delivery of mixed pallets could not be split between purchase orders. A haulier bringing three suppliers' goods on one trailer could only be booked against one of them. The rule that lets a regular supplier keep its standing Tuesday slot did not exist. None of this was in the test scripts, because the scripts had been written from the requirements, and the requirements had missed it in the same way. The people who would have found it in an afternoon, goods in supervisors with ten years of exceptions in their heads, had been too busy to release, which is exactly why they were the people we needed.

I do not blame the depot managers. Asked for two people for a month with no cover, they protected their operation, which is what they are paid to do. The cost of releasing their best people would have fallen on them. The cost of not releasing them fell on the project, six weeks later.

Business testing is now costed in the project budget as backfill, so a depot that releases its most experienced supervisor gets agency cover paid for by the project. The sponsor names the testers at the start, by role and experience, and the project cannot enter testing until they are confirmed. At least half of the testing time is unscripted, with testers working through the previous month's real bookings, exceptions included. And sign off comes from the people who did the testing, not only from their manager.

The next system we replaced went live with two defects of any consequence.

Whoever tests a new system sets the standard it goes live at. We had left that choice to whoever happened to be free.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

title: Retractions Revisited: A Replication, Extension, and Mechanistic Evaluation of Linguistic Obfuscation Effects in Fraudulent Science
description:
arXiv:2610.13678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior work suggests fraudulent scientists write their articles with higher rates of linguistic obfuscation than genuine scientists, with a possible mechanism suggesting obfuscation makes research more costly for a reader to analyze. This result has not undergone additional empirical scrutiny in the open science era, nor have other psychological mechanisms been evaluated. The current replication and extension addressed this opportunity by comparing 800 fraudulent and 800 genuine control papers (2013-2025). The results supported the linguistic obfuscation hypothesis, suggesting fraudulent papers were more obfuscated than genuine ones. A parallel mediation model evaluated three competing mechanisms, finding that reality monitoring, as measured through decreased rates of adjectives, best explained the link between fraudulent science and linguistic obfuscation. Cross-validated detection accuracy using obfuscation features (60.7%) and an elastic net of over 100 language dimensions (71.6%) were significantly greater than chance. Implications for scientific fraud and psychology of language research are discussed.

title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.13035v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.

title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM
description:
arXiv:2610.13660v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.

title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
description:
arXiv:2610.12495v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .

title: How Featured's users make 100K media pitches per month on Vercel
description:
Featured on Vercel

  • 3 engineers supporting 3 brands and 100,000+ users on Vercel

  • Migrated 374 Sanity sites from AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Vercel

  • AI SDK and AI Gateway power Featured's chat bot across 17 models

  • Workflow SDK replaced custom long-running job infrastructure

Featured is a co-pilot for public relations (PR) that subject matter experts and PR teams use to find media opportunities. Tell Featured's agents what you know, and it surfaces opportunities across journalist requests, podcasts, awards, and GEO, with no PR background required.

Founder Brett Farmiloe knows from experience how hard and time consuming getting press is. He spent 10 years running Markitors, a digital marketing agency with 500 small business clients. Every client, from an eyelash extension supplier to an equipment financing company, had real expertise to share, but no way to get it in front of journalists. PR, as Farmiloe puts it, "has always been about who has access to what." He founded Featured to change the question from who has access to who has knowledge.

Featured connects one of their users with a journalist or publisher every 6 seconds. Their agents deliver more than 100,000 media pitches per month, and have sent over 100 million Help A Reporter Out (HARO) emails in the past year.

Behind it all is an engineering team of just three people. With a team that lean, there's no time to manage servers or piece together custom integrations. Every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour taken away from building features what will help their customers land more media placements.

The cost of managing infrastructure by hand

Before Vercel, Featured’s infrastructure work pulled the team away from product development. Hosting lived on AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AI features depended on custom provider integrations, and long-running, multi-step jobs ran on separate orchestration infrastructure. Each layer worked, but each one added operational overhead for a three-person team supporting multiple brands.

One platform for compute, AI primitives, and model access

The migration to Vercel started with a forcing function: Featured needed to launch 374 Sanity sites at once, and every Elastic Beanstalk deploy had to be manually spun up, migrated, and then torn down.

When you multiply that process by almost four hundred, the math doesn't work, even when you divide it across a team of three. Vercel collapsed each site launch into to a single-click deploy.

Once the sites were live, the team evaluated Vercel for background jobs and AI tooling, eventually migrating their entire app and the agents that run in it.

Compute without the clusters

Deploys that once meant standing up a new EB instance, migrating the URL, and terminating the old one became a single click. On Vercel, all 374 sites shipped from one platform, and rollouts across all three brands now happen centrally, instead of one cluster at a time. "In hindsight, doing each one of those by hand was kind of crazy," Farmiloe admits.

AI SDK and AI Gateway: one abstraction for every model

AI SDK and AI Gateway handle all of Featured's model traffic through a single abstraction, so their team doesn't have to manage custom rate-limit or API integrations from multiple providers.

Featured routes across 17 models at any given time. Calling a model is one standardized function with a schema, and swapping providers is a configuration change instead of a rewrite. When a new model ships, the team can test it against Featured's use cases right away.

Workflow SDK for long-running backend jobs

After migrating their AI stack, Featured moved long-running jobs from a separate orchestration system onto Workflow SDK. These are the processes that can't live in a request cycle: monitoring the media around the clock, qualifying opportunities, and combining all of those signals to deliver more than 100,000 pitches a month.

Chat became the product

As users kept choosing conversation over navigation, the team made chat Featured's primary interface, and they deliver it through eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework.

eve's useEveAgent hook made the new interface easy to implement. Instead of wiring up an agent by hand, the team got durable sessions, streaming, tool calls, and approval prompts out of the box, with model calls routed through AI Gateway so they can pick the right model per task without managing provider keys.

What would have been a months-long rebuild was a week-long replace and refactor. Now, instead of a dashboard with dozens of buttons, users ask Featured questions, and the team adapts the product to their needs, not the other way around.

What's next

Featured is building toward being the AI layer for public relations, the same way dedicated agent platforms have emerged for legal and finance. The goal is to make it faster and easier for anyone with expertise to share their knowledge and get featured in the media.

The team's advice to other founders building in the agentic era:

  • Know that your data is your moat. For us, access to good information is what lets Featured connect people with the sources that want to publish them.

  • Lean on tested abstractions like Vercel instead of reinventing security and infrastructure by hand.

About Featured: Featured is a co-pilot for public relations that helps people find media opportunities, submit pitches, and get featured in the press. Featured also owns and operates Help A Reporter Out (HARO) and Connectively, journalist request platforms connecting sources with publishers.

title: Efficient Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement via Reinforcement Learning-Based Neural Architecture Search
description:
arXiv:2610.12796v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments but often relies on computationally expensive models unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework to discover compact, efficient AVSE architectures. The search space preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, while a novel reward function jointly optimises speech enhancement performance, measured by SI-SNR improvement, and model compactness. Using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking, the framework evaluates only 35 candidate architectures and identifies a model with 2.9 million parameters, compared with 22 million in the baseline. The proposed architecture achieves a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline, while reducing model size by approximately nine-fold. Evaluation on commercial mobile CPUs demonstrates a 4.3-fold reduction in real-time factor, supporting practical on-device deployment. Compared with random search, RL-NAS achieves 92% higher search efficiency. Architectural analysis reveals that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks and aggressive visual pathway pruning can maintain enhancement performance while substantially reducing computational requirements. These findings demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning-guided architecture search for developing lightweight, efficient and deployable multimodal speech enhancement systems.

title: Conversational versus Dashboard Explainable AI for UAV Intrusion Detection: An Empirical Study of Operator Trust and Reliance
description:
arXiv:2608.10434v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Machine learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) have demonstrated superior performance in securing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. However, the 'black-box' nature of these models, combined with the high dimensionality of multimodal cyber-physical data, poses significant interpretability challenges. Static visualization dashboards may struggle to present complex relationships among multimodal cyber-physical features in a form that is easy for operators to inspect and interpret. To address this, we propose a Conversational XAI interface powered by Large Language Models (LLM) to facilitate on-demand investigation. In a controlled experiment with participants, we systematically evaluated the impact of this conversational interface versus a traditional XAI Dashboard on operator understanding, trust, and reliance during post-incident auditing tasks. Our results suggest that the conversational interface was perceived as more useful than the dashboard, potentially because it helped participants access and synthesize relevant information more easily. However, this benefit was accompanied by a lower level of appropriate self-reliance, indicating a potential risk of over-reliance. One possible interpretation is that the natural-language responses made the AI advice easier to accept, which may have reduced participants' tendency to verify the underlying evidence when the IDS was incorrect. These findings point to a potential trade-off in human-AI collaboration for UAV intrusion auditing: interaction mechanisms that improve perceived usability may also increase the risk of inappropriate reliance. We conclude by discussing design implications for future XAI systems that balance seamless interaction with cognitive forcing functions to foster appropriate reliance.

title: One AGENTS.md to rule Claude Code, Cursor and Codex
description:
If you use more than one AI coding agent, you've probably ended up with three instruction files: a CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, a pile of .cursor/rules for Cursor, and an AGENTS.md for Codex. They start out identical. A month later one still says npm, another says pnpm, and the third forgot that tests live next to the code.

That's how instruction files drift apart. The fix is simple: make AGENTS.md the single source of truth and keep every tool-specific file thin. This post shows the layout, how each tool actually picks up AGENTS.md, and a template you can copy.

The layout 

your-repo/
├── AGENTS.md            # canonical: commands, layout, conventions, definition of done
├── CLAUDE.md            # "@AGENTS.md" + Claude-only notes
├── .claude/
│   ├── settings.json    # permissions + hooks
│   ├── agents/          # subagents
│   └── skills/          # procedures that load on demand
├── .cursor/
│   ├── rules/           # .mdc rules, with the core rule pointing at AGENTS.md
│   └── cli.json         # permissions for the `agent` CLI
├── .cursorignore
└── .codex/
    ├── config.toml      # sandbox + approval defaults
    └── agents/          # custom agents

AGENTS.md holds everything every agent needs. The other files hold only what is specific to one tool: its behaviour, permissions and features.

How each tool picks up AGENTS.md

This is the part people get wrong, because the three tools load it differently.

Codex builds an instruction chain once per run. It starts with the global file (~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md or AGENTS.md), then walks every directory from the project root down to your working directory. In each one it checks AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then any project_doc_fallback_filenames, and takes at most one file per directory. Files closer to your working directory come later, so they win when instructions conflict. The combined chain has a default size cap of 32 KiB, and Codex stops adding files once it reaches it.

Cursor supports AGENTS.md in the root and in subdirectories. Nested files combine with their parents, and the more specific instructions take precedence.

Claude Code has the catch. It reads AGENTS.md directly only when there's no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above. Once you add a CLAUDE.md, put an import at the top so both load:

# CLAUDE.md
@AGENTS.md

A personal, uncommitted CLAUDE.local.md also counts as "a CLAUDE.md exists". So even if you never create a project CLAUDE.md, adding a local one silently stops Claude reading AGENTS.md. Keep the explicit @AGENTS.md import and that can't happen.

The canonical AGENTS.md

Here's a trimmed version of the template I use. Replace the placeholders with your own stack.

# AGENTS.md

## Project snapshot
- What it is: <one sentence>
- Main language / runtime: <TypeScript 5, Node 22>
- Package manager: <pnpm>. Do not use any other package manager.
- Layout:
  - `apps/web/`: frontend
  - `apps/api/`: HTTP API (handlers in `apps/api/src/handlers/`)
  - `packages/db/`: schema + migrations

## Commands
- Install: `<pnpm install>`
- Unit tests (fast, run often): `<pnpm test>`
- Single test file: `<pnpm test -- path/to/file.test.ts>`
- Lint + types: `<pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck>`
- Build: `<pnpm build>`

## Conventions
- Named exports, no default exports.
- Errors: return `{ code, message }` objects from services; never throw raw strings.
- New code needs tests next to it (`*.test.ts`).

## Working agreement
1. Restate the task in one or two lines and list the files you expect to touch before editing.
2. Make the smallest change that solves the task. No drive-by refactors.
3. If requirements are ambiguous, stop and ask. Do not guess on behaviour.
4. Never commit secrets, tokens, or `.env*` files.
5. Do not run `git push`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, force-pushes,
   or destructive DB commands unless explicitly asked.

## Definition of done
- [ ] Lint + types pass
- [ ] Tests pass (and a new test covers the change)
- [ ] Diff is limited to files related to the task
- [ ] Short summary: what changed, why, how it was verified, open risks

## Code Review Rules
- Flag any handler that reads request input without validation.
- Flag SQL built with string concatenation.

Why it's built this way

  • Commands come first because wrong commands cause most wasted agent turns: npm instead of pnpm, or the wrong test runner. The single-file test command also saves tokens, since the agent stops running the whole suite on every iteration.
  • The working agreement turns common failure modes, like silent scope creep and guessing, into explicit rules.
  • The definition of done gives every agent the same exit criteria. Without it you get "Done!" while the tests still fail.
  • ## Code Review Rules is a heading Codex's GitHub code review looks for, so the review guidance comes along for free.

Keep it short. Leave formatting checks to CI, not the rule file. And write instructions the agent can verify: "Run pnpm test before finishing" works better than "test your changes".

The thin files

CLAUDE.md 

# CLAUDE.md: project instructions for Claude Code
<!-- Keep this file under ~200 lines. HTML comments are stripped before Claude sees them. -->

@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code specifics
- Use plan mode before touching more than 3 files.
- For searches that would flood the context, delegate to a subagent
  and ask for a summary with file paths.
- Before calling a task done, run the checks in "Definition of done"
  and paste the command output summary.

## Things that went wrong before
- Do not "fix" failing tests by loosening assertions or adding `.skip`.

Two details: imports are relative to CLAUDE.md and can nest up to four hops. Block-level HTML comments are stripped before injection, so notes for humans cost no context. Run /context to confirm which memory files actually loaded.

.cursor/rules/00-core.mdc

Cursor project rules must be .mdc files in .cursor/rules/. A plain .md file there is ignored. The always-on core rule just points to AGENTS.md and adds a few hard limits:

---
description: "Core working agreement for every Agent chat in this repo"
alwaysApply: true
---

- Follow `AGENTS.md` at the repo root for commands, layout and definition of done.
- Before editing, list the files you plan to change. Keep the diff limited to the task.
- Never read, print, or edit `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key` or credential files.
- Finish every task with: what changed, how you verified it (exact commands), open risks.

Stack-specific rules go in separate .mdc files that attach by globs, so they only cost tokens when a matching file is in context.

.codex/config.toml

Codex instructions come from AGENTS.md. Behaviour (sandbox, approvals, subagents) lives in config.toml:

approval_policy = "on-request"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
web_search = "cached"

[agents]
max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 4

Codex loads a project's .codex/ layers only when you trust the project.

When the agent "ignores" the rules

If an agent ignores your conventions, the cause is almost always that the rule file is too long, vague or contradictory, or wasn't loaded at all. Check before rewriting anything:

  • Claude Code: /context and /memory
  • Codex: /status
  • Cursor: Customize → Rules

Then shorten the file, make the instructions verifiable, and remove conflicts. One canonical file makes that much easier, because there's only one place to fix.

Wrap-up

  • AGENTS.md is canonical. CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules stay thin and point to it.
  • In CLAUDE.md, always add an explicit @AGENTS.md import.
  • Put commands first, use verifiable instructions, and give every agent the same definition of done.
  • Keep tool behaviour (permissions, sandbox, hooks) in each tool's own config, not in the instructions.

Free excerpt: https://lirenplr.gumroad.com/l/zocmzn

This article is adapted from the **AI Coding Agent Workflow Pack: a 37-page guide plus a drop-in template bundle (the full AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, all four Cursor rule types, Codex config, 10 copy-paste workflows and a security checklist). Every file name and flag was checked against the official docs in October 2026. Get it on Gumroad ($24). I post tested agent workflows as @Mars_Peakul on X.

title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
description:
arXiv:2610.13112v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

title: ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments
description:
arXiv:2608.07418v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In medical education, physicians convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through residency: years of training across thousands of encounters, with diverse sources of feedback and progressively greater autonomy. Much of clinical reasoning relies on the patient encounter, a dialogue in which a clinician elicits history, refines diagnostic hypotheses, and decides management under uncertainty. While large language models (LLMs) excel on static medical benchmarks, methods to optimize the full sequence of clinical decisions remain underdeveloped. We present ResidencyRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) method for training clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents through simulated multi-turn clinical encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls per trajectory). ResidencyRL pairs the policy agent with LLM simulators capable of complex, adversarial behaviors, training against a structured reward aligned to diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. On held-out evaluations, the ResidencyRL agent improves diagnostic accuracy by 7.0% under adversarial conditions (88.0% vs. 81.0%) and reduces missed red flag rates by 31%, demonstrating rigorous mitigation of premature closure. Blinded expert clinicians validated these gains, preferring the trained agent in 87.6% of side-by-side comparisons. The procedural competencies transfer to unseen benchmarks: the agent outperforms the base model across all six clinical axes of the AMIE multi-visit benchmark, and shows consistent directional improvements on AgentClinic and CRAFT-MD. Our findings demonstrate that sequential clinical decision-making can be effectively learned through multi-turn RL in simulation, yielding robust, generalizable capabilities, paving the way towards clinical mastery. Prospective validation with real-world workflows remains necessary to establish clinical utility.

title: Efficient Reasoning Exploration via State-Conditioned Latent Steering with Progress Guidance
description:
arXiv:2609.24066v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Best-of-$N$ is a widely used inference strategy for complex reasoning, whose effectiveness depends on whether sampled candidates can cover diverse and high-quality reasoning paths. However, post-trained reasoning models often suffer from \emph{exploration collapse}, where independent rollouts repeatedly follow similar reasoning paths and limit the gains from increasing the rollout budget. Existing methods alleviate this issue by promoting broader exploration, but do not explicitly guide exploration toward continuations that make meaningful progress, resulting in limited exploration efficiency. To address this, we propose \emph{\underline{S}tate-conditioned \underline{P}rogress-guided \underline{S}teering} (SPS), a training-free latent steering framework. Specifically, SPS constructs a state-conditioned Direction Bank containing multiple progress-guided steering vectors for different prefix-state regions. During online inference, SPS retrieves a suitable steering vector based on the current prefix state and applies it at high-uncertainty transitions to guide the next reasoning step toward meaningful progress. Extensive experiments across multiple model scales and benchmarks demonstrate that SPS consistently outperforms strong baselines. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of its key designs and offer valuable insights for future research. The code is available at https://github.com/rattlesnakey/SPS.

title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
description:
arXiv:2610.13755v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response's original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment-backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47-1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state-rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.

title: The Spec Growth Engine: Spec-Anchored, Code-Coupled, Drift-Enforced Architecture for AI-Assisted Software Development
description:
arXiv:2606.27045v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI coding agents dramatically accelerate implementation speed but introduce two structural failure modes that existing spec-driven approaches do not fully solve: (1) context explosion -- the agent must reason over an entire repository at once, degrading output quality as the context window fills; and (2) silent spec-code drift -- code evolves, the specification does not, and the divergence becomes invisible until it is costly to repair.
  We present the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework that addresses both failure modes through a machine-readable spec graph whose nodes carry explicit contract/design separation, a Spine context assembler that scopes agent context to an ownership path, a vertical-slice growth protocol that enforces hardest-first ordering, and a drift gate that makes spec-code divergence a blocking merge condition.
  The design synthesises well-established software engineering principles (Parnas information hiding, C4, ADRs, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, Fitness Functions) into a lean, code-coupled, machine-enforced whole -- without the overhead of heavy-weight frameworks such as RUP or MDA.

title: I built a local Windows SEO audit tool for freelancers (and what it deliberately doesn't do)
description:
I'm a solo developer, and I built VigieWeb, a desktop SEO audit app for Windows aimed at freelancers and small agencies. It's written in Python with Qt (PySide6).

Why a desktop app?

Most SEO tools are monthly subscriptions that live in the cloud. For a freelancer who audits a handful of client sites, that's a recurring cost for an occasional need. I wanted a tool you buy once and run locally.

What it does

  • Audits 1 to 20 pages of a site, with the evidence behind each finding (not just a score)
  • Generates PDF reports in French or English, with white-label support so you can put your own branding on them
  • Builds an action plan and lets you re-audit to show before/after
  • Monitors a site (the app has to be open for this)
  • Compares your site against 1 to 5 competitors
  • Imports Google Search Console data
  • Includes a prospecting helper

What it deliberately doesn't do

  • No guaranteed rankings (nobody can honestly promise that)
  • No rank tracking, no backlink index, no search volume data. Those need big paid data sources, and I'd rather say so than fake it.

Trade-offs I accepted

  • Windows 10/11 64-bit only
  • The installer is large (about 313 MB) because it bundles its own runtime

Pricing

One-time payment, no subscription. It's sold on Whop: https://whop.com/apps-361b/products/vigieweb-pre-audit-et-suivi-commercial/

Disclosure: the promo video was made with AI tools.

I'd love feedback from other freelancers: what's the one thing you'd want in a local audit tool?

title: EchoDistill: Robust Large Audio Language Models via Noisy-to-Clean Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2605.23954v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) remain vulnerable to acoustic noise, which can obscure task-relevant evidence and produce unreliable responses. We propose EchoDistill, a noisy-to-clean self-distillation framework that uses clean audio as privileged information during post-training. A noisy-input student samples candidate responses reflecting its inference-time behavior, while a frozen copy of the same backbone processes the corresponding clean audio. EchoDistill combines masked response-token distillation, task-gated consistency shaping, and teacher-referenced group-relative optimization to align noisy-input generation with clean-conditioned semantics. Only the student is retained at inference time, introducing no additional inference cost. Across three LALM backbones and three audio domains at -10dB, EchoDistill improves average noisy-input accuracy by 1.63 percentage points over the strongest baseline. On Qwen2.5-Omni, it raises noisy-input accuracy from 59.33% to 62.94%, while clean-audio accuracy increases from 76.56% to 77.56%. Replacing matched audio with random, shuffled, or silent inputs reduces accuracy by 3.08-6.42 points, confirming that matched acoustic evidence contributes to its predictions. Additional evaluations show improvements on held-out additive noises and external benchmarks, while revealing that these gains do not reliably extend to non-additive distortions. These results demonstrate robust post-training improvements under severe additive noise without sacrificing clean-audio capability across diverse tasks.

title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
description:
arXiv:2610.13354v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/

title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions
description:
arXiv:2610.13172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment-specific objects. To address this limitation, we introduce RoleWorld, a symbolic world modeling approach which uses reusable prototypes and environment-specific parameter values as functional role abstractions to represent how objects behave in interactions. From interaction trajectories, a teacher LLM extracts role prototypes and executable transition rules defined over role instances, together with a skill that guides the actor LLM to use role information in decision making. In a target world, without the teacher, the actor uses this skill together with its current role assignments and parameter estimates, and actively tests a role instance hypothesis through interaction when its uncertainty affects the current decision. Feedback from each action refines role assignments and estimates parameter values online, with no LLM parameter updates and the transition rules held fixed. Experiments on MARS benchmark show that RoleWorld enables robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior, suggesting that functional role abstractions can serve as an effective component for knowledge transfer in world modeling. Project Page: https://future-item.github.io/RoleWorld.

title: COBALT: Contextual Bandit Learning with Offline Trajectories for Multi-Turn Code Generation
description:
arXiv:2602.03806v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) for multi-turn code generation typically relies on online reinforcement learning (RL), in which models learn from repeatedly generated online rollouts. Although effective, online RL can be costly and unstable. In this paper, we present contextual bandit learning with offline trajectories (COBALT), a simple method that reuses offline multi-turn trajectories to efficiently train LLMs for multi-turn code generation. Building on the observation that multi-turn code generation is a one-step recoverable Markov decision process, COBALT first collects code generation trajectories using a reference LLM and divides them into partial trajectories. Then, during online bandit learning, the LLM is trained to complete each partial trajectory through single-step code generation. On LiveCodeBench, COBALT substantially improves R1-Distill 8B and Qwen3 8B by up to 9.0 and 6.2 absolute Pass@1 points and matches the performance of two multi-turn online RL baselines using GRPO and VeRPO. We also perform a perturbation-based analysis of in-context reward hacking and show that Cobalt can improve robustness to misleading execution feedback. Overall, our results demonstrate that Cobalt is a promising solution for multi-turn code generation. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/cobalt.

title: Branching On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.13481v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories, but a single trajectory realizes only one continuation at each decision, limiting supervision coverage under a finite sampling budget. We propose BranchOPD (Branching On-Policy Distillation), which selects informative decision points using student uncertainty and teacher-student disagreement, resamples student-policy continuations from shared prefixes, and applies token-level teacher supervision to both main trajectories and branches. BranchOPD operates at token-level decisions in mathematics and within-turn decisions in agent tasks. Shared-prefix reuse reduces student-generated token costs by approximately 19% on ALFWorld and 31% on WebShop relative to seven independent trajectories. We also introduce protocol-boundary repair (PBR), which uses targeted supervision under protocol constraints to mitigate repetition and wasted generation. BranchOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD and Multi-Rollout OPD (n=7) across all evaluated benchmarks, with gains over Vanilla OPD of 18.55 percentage points in mean mathematics accuracy over 16 sampled answers (avg@16) and 13.8 points in mean ALFWorld ID/OOD success. Mechanistic analyses and selection ablations show that branching at uncertain decisions expands subsequent behavior coverage and outperforms random selection and turn-initial branching.

title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.12570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost. Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.

title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
description:
arXiv:2610.13811v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.

title: IAD-Unify: Task-Specific Interfaces for Industrial Anomaly Understanding, Segmentation, and Generation
description:
arXiv:2604.12440v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires complementary capabilities: explaining an observed defect, localizing its pixels, and synthesizing a controlled edit. We present IAD-Unify, a unified architecture connecting a multimodal language model (MLLM), dense visual expert, and diffusion editor through task-specific token interfaces. A multi-reference DINOv2 pathway forms a dense anomaly field and compresses its 1,369 cells into 81 structured evidence tokens. Qwen3.5 consumes these tokens for grounded answers and, with 32 task tokens, converts them into a semantic residual over the dense mask. A separate 256-query interface resamples Qwen states into Stable Diffusion's complete cross-attention context, while the editor retains its source latent and hard-mask inputs. The task pathways share one Qwen adaptation without forcing every task through the same visual bottleneck; in particular, evidence tokens are excluded from the generation pathway. Staged optimization initializes dense evidence, aligns it with language, calibrates segmentation, and then pretrains and specializes the diffusion editor while preserving earlier capabilities. We also construct Anomaly Evidence over 54,501 deduplicated industrial images. Its quality-controlled Anomaly Evidence Compiler and Industrial Edit-Pair Compiler produce family-disjoint, validated supervision through independent geometry, semantic-grounding, and edit-consistency checks. This design provides one fixed shared parameter set for understanding, segmentation, and localized generation without conflating their inputs, supervision, or outputs. The resulting model reaches 73.02% MMAD Macro$_7$, the highest listed public segmentation AP average (57.10%) with one reference, and the lowest Controlled masked DINO distance (0.3765), with complementary strengths across reasoning, pixel ranking, and semantic edit fidelity.
