title: AWS now lets customers sign up for AWS and pay invoices using ACH direct debit
description:
Starting today, AWS customers in the United States can use a US bank account to sign up for AWS and pay for their AWS services through ACH direct debit. This feature provides a convenient and secure way to manage AWS payments directly from a USD bank account.

Customers can securely connect a personal or business US bank account and use it to pay AWS invoices. Previously, new AWS customers needed a credit or debit card to complete signing up for an account.

During sign-up, customers can choose Bank Account on the AWS sign-up page, select their bank, and authenticate using their bank's mobile app or online banking credentials. This securely verifies ownership and links their bank account to their AWS account. By default, the account will be used to pay future AWS invoices.

Existing customers can add a bank account from the Payment preferences page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. They choose Add payment method, select Link your bank account, and follow the same bank-selection and authentication flow. Once verified, the bank account is available as a payment method to pay future AWS invoices..

ACH direct debit is available at no additional cost to AWS customers for USD bank accounts. To learn more, see Managing ACH direct debit.

title: Memory Strategies and the Entropy-Reduction Philosophy of Context Engineering
description:
Open-source project: TencentDB Agent Memory

Author: Tencent Cloud Database Team (腾讯云数据库团队)

Why does talking to AI so often feel like hard work?

With an old friend, a glance can be enough. With an AI assistant, the same request may require several paragraphs of explanation.

One useful way to understand this difference is through entropy: uncertainty about what a message means. A friend shares memories with you and can fill in what you leave unsaid. An AI assistant without that context faces many possible interpretations of even a simple phrase.

Context engineering helps bridge that gap. Instead of merely storing conversations, a layered memory system captures the situational information that would otherwise be lost. Drawing on Tencent Cloud's Memory engineering experience, this article explores how to reduce uncertainty before a model acts, moving from repeated clarification toward more precise execution.

1. Entropy reduction in context engineering: from formulas to intuition

1.1 A simple example: “Ask Li to meet us at the usual place”

Imagine that you are busy at work and say to a longtime colleague, without looking up: “Ask Li to come along. We'll meet at the usual place when it's time.”

Your colleague nods and gets on with it. You have not spelled out the details, but your shared history supplies them.

An AI assistant receiving the same request may have to ask several questions, or may make unsupported guesses:

  • Who is Li: the manager in your contacts, someone in the next department, or the intern who joined this week?
  • When is “when it's time”: nine tonight, ten tonight, or tomorrow morning?
  • Where is “the usual place”: a restaurant, a park, or the office lounge?

These are different levels of uncertainty. More plausible interpretations mean higher entropy; a clear, well-grounded interpretation means lower entropy.

In a familiar human relationship, shared memories, the current situation, and established habits resolve references such as “that thing” or “Wang.” Without those signals, the same instruction can represent thousands of combinations.

Context engineering acts as a translation layer: it turns the implicit, ambiguous expressions people naturally use into context a machine can work with.

1.2 Improve the input before changing the model

At a simplified mathematical level, a language-model application can be represented as:

y = f(x)

  • f is the trained model, with its parameters already set.
  • x is everything supplied to it: context in the broad sense.
  • y is the model's response.

For many applications, changing f frequently would be costly and risky. Much of the practical engineering work therefore goes into improving x:

  • The user's current question or instruction.
  • A system prompt defining the model's role and task.
  • Cross-session memory of what happened before.
  • Available tools and instructions for calling them.
  • Retrieved passages from external knowledge bases through RAG.

Selecting, ordering, filtering, and compressing these inputs is context engineering.

The paper Context Engineering 2.0: The Context of Context Engineering frames it as a systematic process for collecting, storing, managing, and using context to bridge the cognitive gap between people and machines.

Can the model understand what you mean when you speak casually? Can it identify the important evidence when a business system supplies a pile of logs? These questions concern how we prepare context as well as the model's capabilities.

1.3 Reduce uncertainty in three steps

The entropy-reduction perspective treats context engineering as a process of making information less ambiguous. Here, entropy refers to informational uncertainty, rather than a literal thermodynamic calculation.

People communicate through emotions, hints, omissions, assumed knowledge, and pauses. We leave many things unsaid because we expect the listener to fill them in. A machine receiving a token sequence cannot reliably reconstruct all of that missing context. Supplying an unfiltered stream of real-world information can leave it with too much noise and too little structure.

The process can be divided into three steps:

  • Collect: capture relevant signals from people and their environment without losing critical clues.
  • Organize and abstract: structure and compress the information, filtering out noise.
  • Use: select the small subset that matters to the current task and supply it to the model.

The earlier formula then becomes:

y = f(g(context))

Here, f is the language model, while g represents context-engineering strategies: knowledge retrieval, tool use, and the memory storage and retrieval methods discussed in this article.

1.4 A formal view of context

The paper describes a world of entities: users, applications, tools, environments, memory modules, and other objects. Each entity e has characterization information, written as Char(e): who a user is, what time it is, or how an application is configured.

For a particular interaction, select the relevant entity set E_rel and combine their characterization information:

C = ⋃ { Char(e) | e ∈ E_rel }

In plain language, the context for a task combines its relevant entities with information describing their current state. Memory supplies a portion of that characterization that is particularly easy to lose and difficult to maintain over time.

1.5 Memory reduces uncertainty about people and time

Context also includes system instructions, tool results, and knowledge-base documents. Memory has a more specific role.

A knowledge base helps a model understand the world. Memory helps it understand a particular person and a particular ongoing task.

Its job is to turn large numbers of fragments about a person, a relationship, or a task into a small amount of ordered, reusable context. Without that history, each conversation starts with substantial uncertainty. With it, the assistant has a basis for interpreting what a short reply such as “Okay” refers to.

2. Memory as intent recognition and selective information supplementation

A powerful language model with no useful persistence can resemble an exceptionally capable colleague who keeps forgetting the conversation. Giving it a notebook helps, but a memory system needs to do more than save a few chat messages.

2.1 From a passive archive to an active context layer

Memory is often imagined as a warehouse: put the user's words in, then look them up later. In a context-engineering pipeline, it is a dynamic layer centered on people and long-running tasks.

It serves two purposes.

Reduce uncertainty about intent. Consider the shopkeeper downstairs who knows a regular customer's usual purchase. Without that history, the customer has to describe the exact product and accessories every time. With it, a nod may be enough. Memory maps an ambiguous signal to an intent grounded in prior interactions.

Supply missing background selectively. When discussing a code change, memory should not insert all 100,000 lines of a project into the prompt. That would contaminate the context. It might instead provide one timely reminder: “This module previously used OAuth 2.0 for authentication; preserve that behavior.”

Restraint matters. Supply the high-value background missing from the current decision; irrelevant additions are noise.

2.2 Five kinds of demand for memory

Requests for memory features can seem scattered. Look more closely, and they reveal five recurring needs.

Keep roles and instructions stable. An agent may lose its assigned persona or forget an initial constraint such as “Respond only in JSON” after many turns. Users want stable role definitions and critical constraints to persist, instead of repeatedly resetting the assistant's identity.

Build personalization and user profiles. In education, an AI tutor should recognize that a student has made the same sign error three times, rather than treating each wrong answer in isolation. In customer service, an assistant might remember a previous purchase and recognize when a replenishment could be useful. Such personalization must be explainable: understanding a user should not feel like intrusive surveillance.

Maintain continuity in long-running tasks. A coding session lasting several hours, or a complex support case, should not feel like starting over each time a new agent or representative takes over. Memory acts as a relay baton, carrying task state through collection, compression, and reuse.

Turn interactions into reusable assets. Enterprise customers see value in conversations, file changes, and other interactions. Recommendation systems extract patterns from structured clickstreams; memory systems must also work with unstructured text. They can use existing information to serve the user while extracting new profile information from the service process, creating a feedback loop.

Remember relationships as well as facts. Remembering “Your name is Bob” is different from remembering that Bob has recently been under pressure at work and may need encouragement. Relationship continuity depends on accumulated understanding of attitudes, emotions, and concerns, rather than isolated factual labels alone.

2.3 Memory's role in the pipeline

Memory reduces uncertainty on the human side of context engineering. It compresses fragments about a person, a relationship, and a task into structured context that can be reused, preparing the model to understand the user before it begins answering.

3. What Claude's chat and coding experiences suggest about memory

Some users find Claude particularly effective with complex context. Alongside the model's reasoning abilities, context-engineering choices provide a useful lens for examining that experience. Chat and coding applications emphasize different forms of memory.

3.1 Chat: continuity around people and conversations

Anthropic's chat search and memory documentation describes memory of professional context, ongoing work, communication preferences, and technical preferences. Project memory can keep one project's context separate from other projects and standalone conversations. Users can manage memory and use incognito chats that do not contribute to it.

Viewed through entropy reduction, conversational memory addresses three questions:

  • Who is speaking, and in what role: student, product manager, developer, or customer?
  • Which ongoing project or topic are we discussing, and what has already been agreed?
  • What style should this answer follow: explanatory prose, a formal proposal, a list, or code?

Project context, summaries, and editable memory provide continuity. Returning after several days to ask “Where did we leave off?” or “Continue in the same style” should not require rebuilding the entire background.

In this setting, memory primarily reduces uncertainty about people and ongoing narrative threads.

3.2 Coding: continuity around repositories and tasks

In Claude Code, the emphasis shifts toward the repository and the work underway.

Persistent instruction files such as CLAUDE.md describe project conventions, structure, boundaries, and quality expectations. Auto memory can retain useful lessons about commands, preferences, and workflows. These serve as project and working-environment context rather than a comprehensive personal profile. See Claude Code's memory documentation.

Coding memory addresses three kinds of uncertainty:

  • Repository structure and boundaries: important modules, dependencies, and generated directories that should not be edited.
  • Task progress: completed refactoring or debugging steps, rejected approaches, and current hypotheses.
  • Constraints: architectural rules, testing requirements, and security or compliance boundaries.

Context isolation also matters. Subagents can work in separate context windows with scoped tools and tasks, returning useful results to the main conversation. This reduces the burden of keeping every tool result and subtask detail in one large context.

3.3 The design lesson

Memory is a scenario-specific design problem:

  • Chatbots need intent memory, maintaining identity and conversational continuity.
  • Coding agents need state memory, maintaining task progress and handling system complexity.

The guiding question is which uncertainty causes the most damage in the current scenario. Is the assistant forgetting who the user is, or misunderstanding code dependencies? Recognizing that difference is more useful than simply increasing the amount stored.

4. “Attention before Attention”: storage and retrieval challenges

Building Tencent Cloud's Memory product has exposed many practical limits to the theoretical picture. Memory engineering involves allocating attention under constraints on compute and latency.

Self-attention determines what the model focuses on within its input. A memory system must first decide which information enters that input at all. This is “Attention before Attention”: a good selection helps the model, while a poor one can make memory itself the largest source of noise.

4.1 Storage: preserve details without losing structure

Personalization creates an incentive to capture user history. But merely storing more information, without a schema, increases uncertainty rather than producing usable memory.

Three failure modes are especially important.

Over-sparsity. A system records every conversational turn as an Event but loses the higher-level task structure. Retrieval then searches thousands of loosely related fragments. Without a coherent context chain, the model cannot reconstruct what happened. Storage needs a schema that retains relationships and task structure.

Over-abstraction. To save tokens and storage, a system compresses a hundred turns into a short conclusion. Intermediate evidence disappears. In coding or teaching, “The user tried this approach and it failed” may matter more than the final outcome. Losing that information causes the assistant to recommend failed approaches again. Summaries should retain the intermediate state needed to continue the task.

Isolated memories. An Event has no Scene ID or Task ID anchoring it to a situation. Retrieval may then bring a coding preference into a cooking conversation, or otherwise mix unrelated contexts. Group fragments into blocks with explicit situational boundaries. Isolation is fundamental to retrieval accuracy.

4.2 Retrieval: relevance, latency, and generalization

Retrieval is where many of the strongest business concerns appear. Practical systems face competing demands for quality, speed, and generalization.

Avoid context contamination. Enterprise users often prefer retrieving less information to retrieving something misleading. Bringing an obsolete price into a new quotation, for example, increases uncertainty and can corrupt the answer. Relevance alone is insufficient; memories must also be unambiguous in their applicability.

Avoid the vector-similarity trap. A strategy overly dependent on similarity to the current query can miss its deeper references. “That old problem again” may refer to a database deadlock discussed last Tuesday. Surface-level similarity does not resolve that reference. Memory needs situational reasoning and, for some questions, multi-hop retrieval.

Handle multi-hop retrieval within a latency budget. Valuable memories can be connected indirectly. Candidate retrieval, reranking, and a small agentic search process all add work. The engineering discussion here uses a 500 ms budget for the responsive retrieval path; fitting these operations into it is an architectural challenge. Deeper agentic searches may take longer.

Return information the model can use. Retrieval should not insert unexplained fragments from an old conversation. Results need concise wording, clear context, and enough background to explain why they matter now.

The goal is to select the few memories that reduce uncertainty in the current decision, within the available time.

4.3 What “Attention before Attention” means

Think of the model's attention as deciding whom to listen to in a room. Memory's attention decides who enters the room.

The source article illustrates the cost of attention using the quadratic O(N²) relationship of standard dense self-attention. A memory system works earlier in the pipeline, screening input before it reaches the model's finite context window.

Its job is to admit useful signals and keep out noise. The 500 ms figure is an engineering budget discussed in this design, rather than a universal latency guarantee for every retrieval operation.

5. Turning layered memory into an engineering architecture

Keeping complete information, retrieving precisely, reasoning deeply, and responding quickly create competing requirements. Adding a vector database alone does not resolve them.

The approach explored in Tencent Cloud's Memory engineering work uses information hierarchy: three storage layers and three retrieval paths, balancing preservation with efficient use.

5.1 Three storage layers: Event, Scene, and Record

The system progressively organizes information rather than simply dumping conversations into storage. Events retain details, MemoryBooks preserve task context, and Records capture dense, reusable information.

Event: the original evidence layer. This layer records who said or did what, and when, in chronological order. It avoids lossy compression of the original content and serves as the source of truth for higher layers. If a summary leaves out an important detail, the system can return to the original evidence.

Scene: the task and situation layer. Events are grouped by task or situation into MemoryBooks. A MemoryBook contains Scenes, such as “March 1, 2025 mathematics lesson: adding and subtracting fractions.” Each Scene links key source passages with intermediate conclusions.

Retrieval can then return both a statement and its situational background: which lesson it came from, or which project discussion established it. That structure helps prevent context from unrelated situations being mixed together.

Record: the long-term information layer. High-value information is extracted across MemoryBooks: user profiles, stable preferences, and important timeline events. Schemas can be customized for the business, such as learning progress in education or brand preferences in commerce.

This turns extensive interaction history into a compact, structured profile that supports intent interpretation at the start of a conversation.

The source architecture also depicts situation recognition, scenario-based extraction and merge policies, and multiple indexes: temporal, semantic, and graph-oriented. Retrieval has both a fast candidate-selection and ranking path and an agentic path that plans, searches, reflects, and constructs an answer.

5.2 Three retrieval paths: from recent context to deeper history

Current conversation: use recent Events. The most recent turns can be supplied directly to the context window. This preserves the immediate exchange and reduces the need to repeat requirements within a short conversation.

Task context: reactivate a MemoryBook. When a task spans turns or days, a Session ID or Task ID identifies its continuing context. The MemoryBook carries progress forward.

An important technique is asynchronous prefetching. Before the next question arrives, the system may use the current situation to load likely relevant material. Entering a student's final-exam review, for example, can trigger retrieval of earlier mistakes. Moving work out of the immediate request path helps meet a tight response budget.

Long-term records: combine a fast path with deeper agentic search. Vector and keyword retrieval can quickly select relevant Records, such as a preferred form of address or a dietary restriction.

More complex requests, such as “What was I doing on this day last year?” or “Summarize my coding style over the past month,” may need several retrieval and reasoning steps. A small internal agent can search iteratively and connect evidence. This path takes longer but addresses questions a single retrieval pass cannot resolve.

5.3 Observations from internal evaluation

The source article reports three outcomes from internal evaluation of this layered approach.

Temporal recall. On time-sensitive questions such as “What was I doing on this day last year?”, the reported accuracy was approximately 45% using the base Qwen3-coder model and 88% after adding layered Memory. These are results reported for that internal evaluation; the article does not supply a public benchmark protocol or sample size, so they should not be generalized into an accuracy guarantee.

Less repetition in long-running work. In coding and teaching scenarios, users needed to repeat requirements and constraints less often. Memory helped preserve the task's structure across sessions spanning multiple days.

More stable personas and continuity. Role drift and breaks between sessions were reduced. Memory acted as persistent support for an agent's assigned role instead of a collection of disconnected fragments.

These observations concern the design and evaluation described in the original article, not a benchmark claim for every deployment of the open-source project linked here.

6. From memory engineering to digital presence

Stepping back from implementation, context engineering raises broader questions about how people and machines share understanding.

6.1 Who will perform entropy reduction?

Context Engineering 2.0 sketches a possible shift in responsibility as machine intelligence develops.

Today, engineers build scaffolding around models: memory systems, knowledge bases, tools, prompts, and storage strategies that filter noise and supply context. In the paper's prospective CE 3.0 and CE 4.0 stages, more capable machines could increasingly perceive, infer, and construct context themselves.

Memory could then become an active part of attention: discovering useful connections in large amounts of history, including connections people have not explicitly identified. This is a proposed direction of development, rather than a feature available in all current systems.

6.2 Digital presence: a structured representation of a person

An ambitious vision for context engineering is “digital presence.” A well-designed memory system can represent aspects of a user's knowledge, habits, decision-making style, and emotional preferences, rather than merely retaining logs.

Such a representation gives an assistant a basis for understanding the user over time. Interactions can feel continuous instead of a series of disconnected computations. The value comes from being understood, rather than from storage alone.

6.3 A question beyond engineering

When designing memory hierarchies and reducing uncertainty for a machine, we are trying to make interactions smoother and more useful. At a longer time scale, we may also be constructing a computational form of self-narrative: a stable representation of “who I am.”

How do we make machines useful while preserving a person's freedom to change, remain open-ended, and resist being reduced to a fixed profile? That may become a central philosophical question for future context engineering.

7. Three questions to ask before building a memory system

7.1 Which uncertainty matters most?

Resources are finite. Identify the main business problem before trying to solve every form of uncertainty at once.

Intent uncertainty. The model struggles with user identity or implicit needs and repeatedly asks for clarification. Optimize for understanding who the user is, their preferences, and what the current message implies. Relevant scenarios include personal assistants, companionship applications, and personalized recommendation agents.

Knowledge uncertainty. Documents, logs, and databases contain extensive information, but retrieval returns noise or fails to locate the useful passage. Optimize for supplying the evidence the current task actually needs. Examples include enterprise search, document question answering, and support knowledge bases.

Process uncertainty. In a long task, the assistant forgets initial constraints or loses track of its progress. Optimize for stable task state and forward movement. Coding assistants, AI tutors, and complex ticket workflows are typical examples.

7.2 Does the architecture address the key engineering questions?

Hierarchy. Distinguish raw Events, task or Scene context, and long-term profiles. A flat store makes retrieval harder to organize; use layered storage and retrieval where the use case calls for it.

Namespaces and isolation. Keep users, projects, and business lines appropriately separated. Preventing cross-user and cross-project contamination is essential to both security and retrieval accuracy.

Storage versus use. Separate frequently needed context from infrequent detail. Core role definitions and critical constraints should be readily available; historical conversation detail belongs in a MemoryBook or another retrievable store until it is needed.

Monitoring and feedback. Capture and correct mistaken memories. When a user identifies an error, the system should use that signal to update the relevant information instead of allowing it to accumulate and be reused.

7.3 Can you explain the business value?

“We are adding vector storage” describes an implementation. “We are reducing uncertainty in this workflow” describes a user benefit:

  • Teachers do not have to repeatedly reconstruct each student's learning history.
  • Support representatives can take over a transferred case without rereading every earlier ticket.
  • Users do not have to restate their identity and requirements every few turns.

Building the underlying system from scratch takes substantial work. Tencent Cloud's Memory product offers a practical reference for the layered approach discussed here: MemoryBooks maintain task continuity, long-term profiles accumulate preferences, and fast retrieval works alongside deeper agentic search.

The aim is to reduce repeated infrastructure work so teams can focus on the value of their applications. For the cloud product discussed in the original article, see the Tencent Cloud Memory documentation.

Open-source project: TencentDB Agent Memory

title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.13058v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.

title: Why I Ended Up Running Python Inside PostgreSQL to Validate XML
description:
Two years ago, a university database assignment led me to do something I hadn't expected: run Python code inside PostgreSQL.

The assignment was straightforward on paper. I needed to accept an XML document, validate it against an XSD schema, and insert the data into relational tables.

I had chosen PostgreSQL for the project. I was already familiar with some of its capabilities, and I wanted to use the assignment to explore the database further.

Things got interesting when I was halfway through the implementation.

PostgreSQL could parse XML, extract values, and turn them into relational data. What I couldn't find was a built-in way to validate a document against an XML Schema Definition (XSD).

Oracle XML DB supported that kind of validation, so switching databases was an option. But I had already invested time in PostgreSQL, and I was curious about whether I could make it work.

That's how I discovered PL/Python.

In this article, I'll walk through the problem, show how I combined PostgreSQL with Python's lxml library, and explain what I learned when I revisited the solution two years later.

This is a practical experiment rather than a recommendation to move XML validation into every database.

The problem: reading XML wasn't enough

Let's start with a simple example.

Suppose an application receives employee records as XML documents. Each document contains information that eventually needs to be stored in a database.

Here's one of our sample records:

<employee>
  <firstName>Ada</firstName>
  <salary>1200.50</salary>
  <hireDate>2024-01-31</hireDate>
</employee>

Nothing particularly complicated here. We have a name, a salary, and a hiring date.

PostgreSQL provides tools for extracting these values, so getting them into relational columns isn't especially difficult.

But receiving a document doesn't mean we should trust its contents.

What if the salary looked like this?

<salary>quite a lot</salary>

As far as XML syntax is concerned, there's nothing wrong with that element. The opening and closing tags match, and the content is valid text.

Our application, however, expects a number.

This is where an XSD comes in.

An XML Schema Definition describes what a document is supposed to look like. It can define required elements, their order, accepted data types, and optional fields.

For our employee document, the rules might say that firstName must be a string, salary must be a decimal, and hireDate must be a date.

Those rules introduce an important distinction:

A document can be well-formed XML without being valid according to an XSD.

That difference was at the heart of my assignment.

Where PostgreSQL stopped short

PostgreSQL has supported XML operations for years.

It includes an xml data type and functions such as XMLPARSE, xpath(), and XMLTABLE. These are useful when you need to inspect XML documents or work with their contents in SQL.

For instance, consider this query:

SELECT xml_is_well_formed_document(
  '<employee>
     <firstName>Ada</firstName>
     <salary>quite a lot</salary>
     <hireDate>2024-01-31</hireDate>
   </employee>'
);

PostgreSQL returns true.

And that's correct. The document is well-formed XML.

The problem is that a successful syntax check tells us nothing about whether quite a lot is an acceptable salary under our schema.

PostgreSQL 18's documentation makes the limitation clear: while the database can parse and process XML, it doesn't provide built-in validation against XML Schema.

I could extract the values and rely on SQL types and constraints to catch certain problems. But that wouldn't be the same as validating the entire document against the rules defined in an XSD.

I needed to add a missing capability without replacing everything PostgreSQL already handled well.

Enter PL/Python

One feature I particularly like about PostgreSQL is its support for procedural languages.

Besides SQL and PL/pgSQL, PostgreSQL can run functions written in other languages, including Python.

The relevant extension is called plpython3u.

Once the appropriate server-side package is installed, the language can be enabled in a database using:

CREATE EXTENSION plpython3u;

This allows a PostgreSQL function to execute Python code inside the database server's process.

That last part matters.

I wasn't trying to build a separate Python service that would communicate with PostgreSQL. The assignment kept the validation logic inside the database, so I needed Python to run there.

The other half of the solution was lxml, a Python library with support for XML Schema validation.

With those two pieces, I could keep the workflow simple:

Incoming XML + XSD
        |
        v
 PL/Python + lxml
        |
   XSD validation
      /     \
    Fail    Pass
     |        |
   Reject  XMLTABLE
              |
              v
          SQL columns
              |
              v
            INSERT

Python would check the document against the schema. PostgreSQL would handle the relational side.

That division of responsibilities gave me what I needed for the assignment without attempting to reimplement PostgreSQL's existing XML features.

Building the XSD validation step

Before looking at the Python code, let's define the rules for our sample employee.

A minimal XSD could look like this:

<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:element name="employee">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:sequence>
        <xs:element name="firstName" type="xs:string"/>
        <xs:element name="salary" type="xs:decimal"/>
        <xs:element name="hireDate" type="xs:date"/>
        <xs:element name="nickname"
                    type="xs:string"
                    minOccurs="0"/>
      </xs:sequence>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>
</xs:schema>

If you haven't worked much with XSD, focus on two attributes.

The type attribute defines the kind of value each element accepts. And minOccurs="0" makes the nickname element optional.

The xs:sequence declaration also specifies the order in which those elements should appear.

Now we need Python to interpret these rules and check an incoming XML document.

The core validation logic is surprisingly small:

from lxml import etree

# Parse the XSD and build a validator.
xsd_root = etree.fromstring(xsd_bytes, parser())
schema = etree.XMLSchema(xsd_root)

# Parse the incoming XML document.
xml_root = etree.fromstring(xml_bytes, parser())

# Validate the document against the schema.
is_valid = schema.validate(xml_root)

This is a simplified excerpt, not a complete standalone function. The actual implementation includes parser configuration, error handling, and input checks.

The important part is how etree.XMLSchema and schema.validate() work together.

First, lxml parses the schema. Then it compiles the schema into a validator. Finally, the validator checks whether the document follows its rules.

If we provide 1200.50 as the salary, the document passes that type check. If we use quite a lot, it fails because the value doesn't match xs:decimal.

And unlike PostgreSQL's well-formedness check, this validation can also detect missing required elements, unexpected elements, and other violations of the schema.

Returning useful errors

My original university implementation raised a PostgreSQL error whenever XSD validation failed.

That worked for rejecting the document, but it wasn't particularly useful for understanding different failure scenarios.

When I reconstructed the experiment, I changed the helper to return structured JSON results.

Instead of exposing only a boolean, the result identifies whether the failure happened while parsing the XML, preparing the XSD, or validating the document against it.

For example, a schema-validation failure can produce a result with the following fields:

{
  "valid": false,
  "stage": "xsd_validation",
  "category": "xsd_invalid"
}

The helper also includes diagnostic details when available.

This makes it easier for the SQL layer to handle a rejected document consistently.

You can inspect the complete implementation in 03-xsd-validation-cases.sql.

Turning validated XML into SQL rows

Once the XML passes validation, we still need to store its data.

I could have written that part in Python too, but PostgreSQL already has a suitable tool: XMLTABLE.

It lets us read values from an XML document and present them as columns in a SQL query.

Here's a small example:

SELECT *
FROM XMLTABLE(
    '/employee'
    PASSING XMLPARSE(
        DOCUMENT '<employee>
                    <firstName>Ada</firstName>
                    <salary>1200.50</salary>
                    <hireDate>2024-01-31</hireDate>
                  </employee>'
    )
    COLUMNS
        first_name text PATH 'firstName',
        salary numeric PATH 'salary',
        hire_date date PATH 'hireDate'
) AS employee;

The query produces a relational row with a name, a numeric salary, and a date.

XMLTABLE does more than select text from the document. It also converts values into the SQL types we specify.

Still, successful SQL type conversion doesn't mean an XML document satisfies its XSD. The schema may impose additional requirements that cannot be inferred from these three columns alone.

That's why I kept schema validation and relational extraction as separate steps.

In the reproducible implementation, a PL/pgSQL function calls the Python validator first:

validation_result :=
    xml_research.validate_xml_xsd_case(
        xml_text, xsd_text
    );

IF COALESCE(
    (validation_result->>'valid')::boolean,
    false
) IS NOT TRUE THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION USING
        ERRCODE = '22023',
        MESSAGE = format(
            'XML rejected during %s: %s',
            validation_result->>'stage',
            validation_result->>'category'
        );
END IF;

This excerpt runs inside a PL/pgSQL function.

If validation fails, the function raises an exception before reaching the INSERT. I chose SQLSTATE 22023 as the error code for these rejections in the experiment.

If validation succeeds, the function uses XMLTABLE to extract the values and insert them into a temporary relational table.

The result is a small processing pipeline in which Python validates the XML contract and PostgreSQL handles the database operations.

Revisiting the implementation two years later

The original assignment was built on PostgreSQL 15.

For this article, I wanted something more useful than a description of an old university project. So I revisited the implementation and created a reproducible experiment using PostgreSQL 18.6.

The repository is available here:

smaje99/postgresql-xml-plpython

It includes the Docker configuration, SQL scripts, synthetic XML fixtures, and validation tests.

You can run the examples locally without configuring PostgreSQL and PL/Python manually on your machine.

Running the experiment

You'll need Docker Engine with the Compose plugin, plus Python 3 to generate a local password.

Start by cloning the repository:

git clone https://github.com/smaje99/postgresql-xml-plpython.git
cd postgresql-xml-plpython
cp .env.example .env

Generate a password:

python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))'

Add the generated value to .env as POSTGRES_PASSWORD, then start the database:

docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps

To run the validation and insertion tests:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps postgres sh -c \
'PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql \
-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
-h postgres \
-U "$POSTGRES_USER" \
-d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
-f /workspace/sql/03-xsd-validation-cases.sql'

The script checks its own expected outcomes and raises an error if a test fails.

The repository's README also covers the other XML experiments, including generating XML from relational tables. That was another part of the original assignment, but the focus here is validating incoming documents before storing their data.

When you're done, use docker compose stop to stop the database while keeping its data volume. The README also explains how to remove the disposable environment.

What the tests showed

The updated experiment includes 17 validation cases.

They cover more than just valid and invalid salaries. I also tested missing required elements, invalid dates, malformed XML, malformed XSD, unexpected elements, and namespace mismatches.

Other cases examine how the parser handles DTD declarations, entities, external schema references, oversized inputs, and deeply nested documents.

In the recorded PostgreSQL 18.6 environment, all 17 cases matched their expected results.

The persistence tests inserted two valid employee documents: one with only the required fields and another with an optional nickname.

The temporary table ended up containing:

first_name | salary  | hire_date  | nickname
-----------+---------+------------+----------
Ada        | 1200.50 | 2024-01-31 | NULL
Ada        | 1200.50 | 2024-01-31 | Countess

The remaining 15 cases were rejected with SQLSTATE 22023, and the tests verified that they added no rows.

Revisiting the old implementation also exposed a small issue in its error handling.

The historical function called plpy.error() when a document failed validation, followed by a return False. But plpy.error() raises an exception, so execution never reaches that return statement.

In the newer experiment, the Python helper returns structured validation information, and the PL/pgSQL wrapper decides whether to raise a SQL exception.

It's a clearer separation, and it makes the behavior easier to test.

But passing a test suite doesn't automatically make the solution production-ready.

What I would worry about in a real system

The biggest consideration is PL/Python itself.

The u in plpython3u stands for untrusted. PostgreSQL does not sandbox this language as a trusted procedural language, and only superusers can create functions written in it.

Running Python inside the database server is powerful, but it also introduces security and operational responsibilities.

You need to think about who owns the functions, who can execute them, which permissions they have, and what happens when a dependency or runtime needs updating.

XML parsing deserves particular care as well.

In the reproducible experiment, the lxml parser is configured to disable entity resolution, DTD loading, network access, and huge-tree mode. The helper rejects external schema directives and enforces explicit limits on input size and nesting depth.

Those restrictions are part of the laboratory's test policy. They shouldn't be treated as universally safe settings or a substitute for a full security review.

There's another architectural question: who gets to decide which XSD is trusted?

In this experiment, both the XML and the XSD are passed to the function. The parser restrictions address certain technical risks, but they don't establish ownership, approval, or versioning rules for schemas.

A real application would need to deal with that separately.

Performance is also an open question. The helper compiles the schema during validation and performs additional parsing checks. I haven't benchmarked the implementation under load, so I can't claim that it scales efficiently or outperforms application-side validation.

The recorded environment used PostgreSQL 18.6, Python 3.11.2, lxml 4.9.2.0, and libxml2 2.9.14. I haven't tested this implementation across every PostgreSQL release or verified its deployment on managed PostgreSQL services.

These limitations don't invalidate the experiment. They define what it actually demonstrates.

Would I still choose PL/Python today?

I enjoyed working on this solution because it pushed me to explore PostgreSQL beyond the features I already knew.

For the original assignment, it made sense. I needed to keep the validation workflow inside the database, and PL/Python let me add XSD validation while continuing to use PostgreSQL's SQL/XML features.

But if I were designing a production system that receives XML from external users or services today, I wouldn't automatically put the validator inside PostgreSQL.

I'd first look at the application's boundaries.

Where should a document be accepted or rejected? Who owns the schema? How should validation errors reach the client? And what would placing Python inside the database mean for deployment, security, and maintenance?

Validating XML in the application before it reaches the database is another reasonable option. Whether that approach is preferable depends on the system's requirements and constraints.

That's the question I want to explore in the follow-up article: Do we really need PL/Python to process XML in PostgreSQL?

For now, this experiment taught me something valuable.

Knowing that a database can do something is useful. Understanding when it should do it is an entirely different engineering decision.

And sometimes, exploring a limitation is what helps you understand a tool better.

Source code and further reading

The reproducible experiment is published under the GPL-3.0-only license.

  • Source code on GitHub
  • XSD validation and persistence implementation
  • PostgreSQL 18 XML data type documentation
  • PostgreSQL XML functions and XMLTABLE
  • PostgreSQL PL/Python documentation
  • Oracle XML DB schema validation

This is an educational experiment, not a production-ready XML validation service.

title: Experience Makes Skillful: Enabling Generalizable Medical Agent Reasoning via Self-Evolving Skill Memory
description:
arXiv:2606.09365v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Medical agent systems are increasingly expected to support interactive clinical decision making rather than only static question answering. In such settings, effective agents must reuse prior experience across evolving cases, yet existing memory mechanisms often retain raw historical traces that are redundant, noisy, and difficult to govern. More importantly, they rarely distinguish which memories are truly useful for future reasoning. This limits their ability to accumulate compact and reliable experience for long-horizon clinical reasoning. To close this gap, we propose SkeMex, a post-deployment self-evolution framework that improves medical agents through a skill-based memory without updating model weights. SkeMex distills informative interaction trajectories into structured skills that encode reusable procedural knowledge, and organizes them into a multi-branch repository spanning general, task-specific, and action-level experience. To determine which memories should be reused and retained, SkeMex estimates context-dependent utility from environment feedback and uses it to guide value-aware retrieval and repository governance. A closed-loop ``Read--Write--Assess--Govern" lifecycle further supports continual evolution by writing new skills, updating utilities, promoting useful memories, and removing harmful entries. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that SkeMex consistently outperforms representative memory-based agents in both offline and online settings. It also generalizes across model backbones and supports transferable skill memory. All data and code will be released publicly.

title: SEEDS: Preview-Guided Evidence Admission for Search Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12932v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Search agents extend large reasoning models with multi-round access to external knowledge, yet most existing systems largely conflate retrieving evidence with consuming it. Retrieved documents are commonly incorporated according to fixed or rank-based policies, despite the fact that evidence utility is conditioned on the agent's current reasoning state. Consequently, a lower-ranked candidate may be critical for the current step, while a higher-ranked candidate may provide redundant, irrelevant, or misleading information. We formulate this overlooked problem as evidence admission, which asks, at each search step, which retrieved candidates should be allowed to enter the agent's evolving reasoning context. To enable such selective control, we introduce SEEDS (Selective Evidence Entry During Search), a preview-guided evidence admission framework for search agents. SEEDS first exposes lightweight previews of retrieved candidates and then lets the agent jointly determine which candidates and how many should be fully inspected, conditioned on its current reasoning state. Unlike fixed or adaptive prefix policies, SEEDS can select arbitrary subsets with flexible cardinality, and it can be instantiated directly with an existing reasoning agent or further optimized through learning. Across nine knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks under both local corpus and live web search, SEEDS consistently improves search effectiveness while substantially reducing full-evidence consumption. Experimental analyses show that SEEDS more effectively selects useful candidates beyond the corresponding retrieval prefix. These results establish evidence admission as a complementary dimension of agentic search, separating what information is retrieved from what information is ultimately allowed to shape reasoning.

title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
description:
arXiv:2610.12881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.

title: Freeze Refund Outcomes, Then Extract One Predicate
description:
Mixed refund gates should stay intact until tests pin every current decision. The smallest safe change is one extracted predicate, not a rewrite. This walkthrough shows that order with a frozen ten-row table.

Why the mix fails review

Legacy checkout code often hides refund policy inside a router. Age checks, payment state, and shipment flags share one return path. A reviewer cannot see which input changed the outcome.

That mix blocks a clean split during review. A helper move can flip a borderline order without a failing test. Characterization tests record today's behavior before any extraction.

What this pass will not do

This pass will not invent a new refund policy. It will not merge age, payment, and shipment into one helper. It will not treat a model draft as proof.

The sample below is a proposed fixture, not a production log. It uses ten labeled orders and one pure function. No network call, clock read, or database lookup belongs in it.

Step 1: Freeze observed decisions

Start from observed outputs, not from the policy you wish existed. Each row names inputs and the current string result. Keep the table in the repository beside the test.

row age_days paid shipped partial result
1 0 yes no no allow_full
2 14 yes no no allow_full
3 15 yes no no deny_age
4 10 no no no deny_unpaid
5 3 yes yes no deny_shipped
6 3 yes yes yes allow_partial
7 20 yes yes yes deny_age
8 7 yes no yes allow_full
9 14 yes yes yes allow_partial
10 1 no yes yes deny_unpaid

Row 2 and row 3 lock the age edge. Day fourteen still allows a full refund here. Day fifteen denies for age before shipment matters.

Row 6 and row 9 allow a partial refund inside the window. Row 7 denies for age even when the shipment is partial. Row 10 shows unpaid status beating every later flag.

Treat these ten rows as the contract for this pass. If a later edit changes a row, the split is not safe yet. Stop and restore the prior mapping before you continue.

Step 2: Pin the public function

Put the messy function and the rows in one test module. The test should call the public function only. Do not assert on private helpers that do not exist yet.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OrderView:
    age_days: int
    paid: bool
    shipped: bool
    partial: bool

def refund_gate(order: OrderView) -> str:
    if not order.paid:
        return "deny_unpaid"
    if order.age_days > 14:
        return "deny_age"
    if order.shipped and order.partial:
        return "allow_partial"
    if order.shipped:
        return "deny_shipped"
    return "allow_full"

CASES = [
    (0, True, False, False, "allow_full"),
    (14, True, False, False, "allow_full"),
    (15, True, False, False, "deny_age"),
    (10, False, False, False, "deny_unpaid"),
    (3, True, True, False, "deny_shipped"),
    (3, True, True, True, "allow_partial"),
    (20, True, True, True, "deny_age"),
    (7, True, False, True, "allow_full"),
    (14, True, True, True, "allow_partial"),
    (1, False, True, True, "deny_unpaid"),
]

def test_refund_gate_matches_frozen_rows():
    for age, paid, shipped, partial, expected in CASES:
        order = OrderView(age, paid, shipped, partial)
        assert refund_gate(order) == expected

The function above is the legacy shape, left intact on purpose. Unpaid orders lose before the age check runs. Shipped partial orders stay allowed only inside the window.

The current precedence is unpaid, then age, then partial, then shipped. A split must not reorder those four checks. Reordering is a behavior change even when names stay stable.

This code is an unexecuted example for the workflow. Run it in a scratch repository before you trust it. Do not paste it over a live billing module.

Step 3: Run the pin on one file

Run one file before you open a broader suite. A green pin means the table matches this function. A red pin means the table is wrong, not that policy should change.

python -m pytest tests/test_refund_gate.py -q --tb=short

Record that command and the pass count in the pull request. This example expects ten assertions inside one test. Do not treat that count as a benchmark for other repos.

Add a tiny runner if pytest is not installed yet. The runner prints each mismatched row and a nonzero status. Keep it beside the function, and treat it as unexecuted until you run it.

def pin_rows() -> int:
    failed = 0
    for index, row in enumerate(CASES, start=1):
        age, paid, shipped, partial, expected = row
        actual = refund_gate(OrderView(age, paid, shipped, partial))
        if actual != expected:
            print(f"row {index}: expected {expected}, got {actual}")
            failed += 1
    print(f"pinned_rows={len(CASES)} failed={failed}")
    return 1 if failed else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(pin_rows())

python refund_pin.py

Read the printed row number before you edit code. A failure on row 3 is an age-edge miss. A failure on row 10 is an unpaid-order miss.

Step 4: Ask for one predicate only

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode's free model access can draft the extraction prompt and the diff. Use that draft only after the ten rows are green locally.

The free server option can rerun the same file away from the laptop. Do not ask the model to invent new refund policy. Paste the frozen cases and forbid extra status strings.

Task: extract is_partial_refundable from refund_gate.
Keep every CASES row returning the same string.
Do not add statuses, logs, clocks, or I/O.
Return one function plus the updated call site.

Require a diff that moves one predicate and leaves one public entry. That prompt is a proposal, not a measured product claim. If the draft changes any row, reject it.

Free access does not remove the need to read the diff. No model name, quota, or hardware note belongs in this review. Those limits were not supplied for this article.

Check the current product terms before you rely on availability. Availability can change, so treat it as a convenience only. The pin still has to pass on a machine you control.

Step 5: Apply the smallest diff

The safe split is the partial-shipment predicate only. Age and payment checks stay inline until their own pins exist. One branch per change keeps the review small.

def is_partial_refundable(order: OrderView) -> bool:
    return order.shipped and order.partial

def refund_gate(order: OrderView) -> str:
    if not order.paid:
        return "deny_unpaid"
    if order.age_days > 14:
        return "deny_age"
    if is_partial_refundable(order):
        return "allow_partial"
    if order.shipped:
        return "deny_shipped"
    return "allow_full"

Notice the boolean does not choose the status string. The caller still owns the mapping from flag to result. That limit stops a helper from growing a second policy.

Refuse a draft that also extracts the age check. Two moves in one commit hide the failing row. Land the partial predicate, rerun the pin, and stop.

Step 6: Re-run the same ten rows

Repeat the identical pytest command after the move. Compare status strings, not just the process exit code. Ten matches mean this split held for the fixture.

python -m pytest tests/test_refund_gate.py -q --tb=line
git diff --stat -- refund_gate.py tests/test_refund_gate.py

Any mismatch means revert that commit before more edits. Do not fix forward by editing the expected column. The column is the contract you just promised to hold.

If you use the free server option, copy the same two files only. Do not point it at secrets, live orders, or a writable production tree. A remote green run confirms the fixture, not your billing system.

How to read the matrix

signal action stop rule
local pin red fix the table or the fixture no model edit yet
local pin green request one predicate extraction no policy rewrite
draft changes a row discard the draft restore the prior function
draft keeps all rows apply that diff only do not stack a second split
remote rerun red treat it as environment drift do not merge
remote rerun green open review with the command log still read the diff

The matrix is the artifact to keep beside the code. It tells the next editor when a model draft is eligible. It also states when a remote run is evidence and when it is not.

Use the matrix in the pull request description. Quote the signal you observed, not a general claim of safety. A green remote job without the local pin is not enough.

What these rows cover

Ten rows cover the branches in this toy function. They do not cover currency, tax, or chargeback state. A real order object needs more columns before a similar split.

The age boundary is inclusive at day fourteen. It becomes a deny on the next day. Row 7 checks that age still wins after a partial shipment.

No timing data appears here because none was measured. Do not quote a speedup, a quota, or a hardware spec from this text. Operator notes confirm free model access and a free server option, not their limits.

No run from 13 October 2026 is claimed in this text. The fixture is a proposal you must execute yourself. Product limits, if any, belong in the current vendor terms.

Limitations you should keep

Characterization tests preserve behavior, including bugs you already ship. If deny_age is wrong for partial orders, the pin will protect that mistake. Change policy only in a later commit with a written reason.

The fixture ignores time zones and windows stored in config. Age days arrive already computed by an upstream job. Splitting that source needs a separate table later.

A model can rename a status while keeping tests green. That happens if you edit the expected column in the same diff. Review the diff for string changes, not only for a passing command.

One extracted function is the cap for this pass. A second helper needs a new row that fails before the move. Without that failing row, you are only guessing.

Who should skip this flow

Skip this flow when the refund rule is not pure. Hidden reads of wallets, feature flags, or profiles will not show up here. Pin those inputs first, or do not extract yet.

Skip it when legal or finance must change the outcome this week. A characterization pin is the wrong tool for an intentional policy break. Write the new expected column in a separate approved change.

Skip the remote rerun if the repository holds production credentials. A free server is not a reason to upload secrets for convenience. Keep the sample self-contained and easy to delete.

Skip the model draft if nobody can review Python diffs. The ten-row pin does not replace a human reader. An unread extraction is still an unread extraction.

Review checklist before merge

  1. Confirm the test file has the same ten tuples as the table.
  2. Confirm unpaid checks still run before age checks.
  3. Confirm only is_partial_refundable was added in this commit.
  4. Confirm no new status string appears in the diff.
  5. Attach the local pytest line and, if used, the remote command.

That list is the merge gate for this split. A green badge without those five checks is incomplete. The next split starts by adding rows, not by trusting this pin.

If the ten rows are already green, draft only the one-predicate diff. Review that diff yourself before you merge it. Leave the policy strings untouched until a later separate change.

title: FORTE: A Production Framework for Feature Evaluation and Deprecation in Industrial Recommender Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.13806v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Production recommender systems have feature-lifecycle asymmetry: adding new features must produce gains on some metric, while feature removal must not regress any metric. In practice, feature deprecation is hard to prioritize as a feature can fail to be removed if it interacts with other features, its importance changes daily, it cannot be evaluated before production models change or data drift occurs, it is in contention for A/B test space with other launches, it causes regressions in an online A/B test, or it is consumed by multiple models that need to coordinate its deprecation. We present FORTE, a model-agnostic production framework for discovering, validating, and removing features. Its efficient perturbation implementation allows daily feature evaluation. To account for interactions, it evaluates candidate feature sets constructed from all the low-rank features through grouped ablation and its offline results are sufficiently predictive of online A/B tests to allow deprecations to proceed to online testing with confidence. Lineage tracing identifies all downstream consumer models to realize the full savings of removing a feature from the training set. We validate FORTE over 2 large-scale recommender systems and find that it identifies deprecable feature sets which do not cause online regressions, while the impact on efficiency depends on model characteristics. On a search-relevance model, FORTE resulted in 3 nested candidate sets of 32, 48, and 59 features. Online guardrails rejected the largest treatment. The 48-feature set was selected for deprecation, removing 43.3% of the model's features. On a large ranking model, FORTE identified 8 candidates for removal. Retraining and A/B testing confirmed no regression. Its launch reduced the trainable parameters by 29.9%, improved serving throughput by 19.8-25.5%, and reduced annual training costs by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing
description:
arXiv:2610.13236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.

title: Exa joins the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace

Exa is now available on the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace as a native integration. Exa's neural search engine grounds models in current information.

Exa search on AI Gateway

The tool takes the same controls as the Exa API, so you can set how many results come back, focus a search on a category such as news or research papers, restrict it to a country, and include or exclude domains.

title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.13399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.

title: Extend eve agents with installable extensions
description:
You can now package tools, connections, skills, instructions, and hooks into extensions that any eve agent can import. Extensions can be published to package registries, then installed, versioned, and upgraded like any other project dependency.

A browser-use extension might ship tools for navigating a site, a memory extension can capture context with hooks and recall it with tools, and a self-improvement extension pairs hooks with dynamic instructions.

Scaffold a new extension with a single command:

When the extension is ready, running eve extension build generates the publishable package.

To use an extension, install the package and import it from a file in agent/extensions/:

The filename sets the namespace, so the extension's search tool runs in the agent as crm__search.

Extensions allow you to:

title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.13078v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

title: Measuring Artifact Reliance in Machine-Generated Text Detectors
description:
arXiv:2610.13583v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detectors of machine-generated text score almost perfectly on scientific-literature benchmarks, implying we can reliably distinguish with these detectors human and machine-generated documents. We looked at ten scientific-document subsets from six popular resources, and on several of them that apparent ease is a side effect of how the documents were put together. A logistic regression using 27 superficial features reached 0.833-0.997 macro-F1, and on the three arXiv subsets it outperformed every detector we evaluate with F1-scores 0.951-0.997. The strongest cue to the detector is the PDF extraction artifact: human texts retain their original line breaks, whereas generated texts are extracted as a single block of prose. This cue, together with three other formatting features, tell the classes apart at 0.996 AUC. To distinguish benchmarks that contain such a signal from detectors that rely on one, we introduce format counterfactuals: just re-wrapping a machine-written abstract without changing a single word reverses 20-27% of a public detector's correct decisions. Normalizing formatting before training reduces the generalization gap from 0.32 to 0.22. On format-clean benchmarks, it also raises out-of-domain macro-F1 from 0.33 to 0.65 for detectors trained on artifact-containing subsets.

title: A Fake AWS Terraform Provider Was Smuggling Malware Inside .woff Font Files
description:
Zscaler's ThreatLabz published a campaign on October 8, 2026 built around a Terraform provider named terraform-provider-awsbeta_v1.0.0 — a Go binary that looks and behaves like a real AWS provider, complete with a working provider scaffold, while a malicious package inside it runs the moment Terraform loads the plugin. The malware itself, once unpacked, isn't especially novel as backdoors go. Where it hid before that point is the part worth studying.

Where it actually hid

The payloads were disguised as .woff web font files — HiraginoSans-Bold.woff, NotoSansCJK-Regular.woff, MalgunGothic-Italic.woff, named and extensioned to look exactly like what a normal build pipeline downloads without a second glance. Each file contains real decoy font data, followed by a marker (@@ENDFONT@@) and an AES-256-CBC-encrypted executable. The loader strips the decoy content, decrypts the payload, and runs it using whichever of Python, Node.js, Perl, or OpenSSL happens to already be installed on the victim's machine — no need to bring its own interpreter when developer workstations already have four to choose from.

Delivery used a dynamic DNS host, a GitHub repository, and a Vercel-hosted site, in that fallback order. None of those platforms were compromised; the attackers just used ordinary accounts on infrastructure that blends in. A request for a .woff file from a GitHub raw URL or a Vercel subdomain is exactly the kind of traffic a CI pipeline generates all day, which is precisely why it was chosen.

What actually runs once it's unpacked

The primary payload is FLATROOF, a Rust-based cross-platform backdoor with platform-specific persistence — a Linux service, a macOS shell logout hook, or a Windows registry Run key, depending on where it landed. Its Python-based stealer components go after Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox credential and cookie databases, shell and command history, running processes, and — on Windows specifically — Windows Credential Manager entries and browser-extension data for MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, and Rabby. On macOS it collects Safari history and the login.keychain-db file directly.

A second backdoor, ROOFDECK, handles command-and-control discovery in a way built to survive takedowns: it reads an encrypted server address from a Pastebin paste, and if that lookup fails, falls back to querying Nostr profile metadata for the current address instead. Killing one channel doesn't kill the backdoor — it just makes it check the other one.

Why Terraform specifically is a good place to hide this

A Terraform provider executes as a plugin directly on whatever machine runs terraform init, plan, or apply — a developer's laptop, or more consequentially, a CI/CD runner. Both routinely hold cloud credentials, API tokens, git repository access, and infrastructure deployment permissions that go well beyond what a typical employee endpoint carries. A malicious provider doesn't need a separate privilege-escalation step. It simply inherits whatever the person or pipeline invoking it already has standing access to — which, for a DevOps engineer's machine, is usually quite a lot.

This is close to the same shape as the npm malware campaign that rode in on a routine dependency bump: a trusted package manager executing attacker code automatically, during a step nobody treats as a security decision, inside an environment that already has more access than the task in front of it needs.

What I'd actually check

Pin provider sources and versions explicitly, and verify checksums rather than trusting whatever terraform init happens to resolve from the registry that day:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "= 5.XX.X"  # pin the exact version, don't float on a range
    }
  }
}

Run Terraform commands inside something disposable, not on a daily-driver laptop that's also logged into a personal browser profile and a crypto wallet extension. The stealer components in this specific campaign go after exactly those two things, and a machine that's never held either has nothing in it worth exfiltrating.

Treat CI/CD runners with the same suspicion as developer laptops, not less — short-lived credentials, least-privilege IAM roles scoped to what that specific pipeline actually needs, and runners that don't carry state or secrets forward between unrelated jobs. A privileged pipeline running an unverified provider is a worse outcome than a single compromised laptop, not a better one.

The rule

A plugin that executes automatically the moment a trusted tool loads it is a privilege-escalation vector by default — whether it's an npm postinstall script, a VS Code extension, or a Terraform provider. The defense doesn't change across ecosystems: assume the code runs, and control what's reachable from wherever it runs before that happens, not after you find out it already did.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud — disposable VMs with no browser sessions, no saved wallets, and nothing of standing value sitting around for exactly this class of malware to go looking for. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.
