title: Weight Clustering Reveals the Importance of Relative Rank in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2603.17917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) contain billions of parameters, but many exact weight values are not essential. We apply scalar $K$-means clustering to pretrained models, replacing each weight matrix with only 16--64 shared values. For Llama~3.1-8B-Instruct and SmolLM2-135M, this preserves strong accuracy without retraining, providing a simple way to compress LLMs on disk. Fine-tuning only the cluster centroids further recovers 30--40\% of the remaining accuracy loss. Using clustering as an analysis tool, we then keep the cluster assignments fixed and perturb only the shared values, to study which of their properties matter most. We find that preserving their \emph{relative rank} (which connections are stronger or weaker than others) is more important than preserving their exact magnitudes. Breaking this ordering greatly increases perplexity, while changing the values but keeping the ordering causes little loss in many middle and late layers. However, rank preservation alone is not sufficient. Model performance also depends on maintaining the variance of the reconstructed weights, while early layers remain more sensitive; perturbing the cluster assignments themselves shows that their spatial geometry is also load-bearing. We observe the same behavior across four LLMs from two architecture families. These results suggest that the ordering of weights, together with their overall variance, plays a central role in LLM compression and robustness.

title: Access Paths for Efficient Ordering with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2509.00303v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this work, we present the \texttt{LLM ORDER BY} semantic operator as a logical abstraction and conduct a systematic study of its physical implementations. First, we propose several improvements to existing semantic sorting algorithms and introduce a semantic-aware external merge sort algorithm. Our extensive evaluation reveals that no single implementation offers universal optimality on all datasets. From our evaluations, we observe a general scaling relationship between sorting cost and the ordering quality for comparison-based algorithms. Building on these insights, we design a budget-aware optimizer that utilizes heuristic rules, LLM-as-Judge evaluation, and consensus aggregation to dynamically select the near-optimal access path for LLM ORDER BY. In our extensive evaluations, our optimizer consistently achieves ranking accuracy on par with or superior to the best static methods across all benchmarks. We believe that this work provides foundational insights into the principled optimization of semantic operators essential for building robust, large-scale LLM-powered analytic systems.

title: SWE-DeceptionBench: Benchmarking Deceptive Behaviors of LLMs Across the Software Development Lifecycle
description:
arXiv:2610.13626v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout the software development lifecycle. This growing reliance on LLMs raises concerns about their trustworthiness, with deception posing a particularly important risk. Deceptive behavior takes the form of misleading responses or assistance in fabricating, concealing, or distorting information. To study this behavior, we introduce SWE-DeceptionBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM deception in software engineering. The benchmark covers six lifecycle stages and two deception triggers: Active Deception, where models recognize infeasible or conflicting requirements but still present them as achievable, and Passive Deception, where models help fulfill explicit user requests to mislead others. We further introduce Neutral, Reward, and Pressure conditions to study the effect of external inducements, resulting in 720 test instances in Chinese and English. Evaluating seven mainstream LLMs, we find substantial deception even under the Neutral condition, with aggregate rates of 49.88% for Active Deception and 64.29% for Passive Deception. Deception rates vary across lifecycle stages, and external inducements affect Active and Passive Deception to different extents. We also evaluate lightweight defenses, finding that guard models miss many deceptive requests, and Self-Reminder reduces but does not eliminate deceptive responses. These findings highlight the need for more effective deception detection and mitigation methods to support trustworthy LLM-based software engineering.

title: O\'ido: Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator
description:
arXiv:2610.13447v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Speech recognition on low-cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present O\'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). O\'ido executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other the on-device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two-core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1-11.1 s after clips of 3.6-10.6 s (7.2-22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34-60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.

title: Lychee-Reranker: Fast but Not Late Interaction for Compressed Document Reranking
description:
arXiv:2606.22807v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As retrieval systems scale, effective and efficient reranking becomes increasingly important. However, most existing encoder- and decoder-based rerankers jointly process every query--passage pair, tightly coupling their online computation and limiting deployment efficiency and flexibility. We present Lychee-Reranker, a fast but not late-interaction (FBNL) reranker that decouples query and passage computation while retaining expressive relevance modeling. Built on an encoder--decoder architecture, Lychee-Reranker pre-encodes passages using Matryoshka embedding pooling, while its decoder models system and user instructions together with query intent; cross-attention then captures fine-grained relevance between the resulting query context and passage representations. Together, these designs offer four key advantages: (i) efficiency from offline passage encoding, (ii) expressiveness from cross-attention, (iii) compactness from Matryoshka embedding pooling, and (iv) test-time compute through an adjustable compute budget. We instantiate Lychee-Reranker in three sizes, Nano, Small, and Large, with 0.27B, 1B, and 4B activated parameters, respectively. Extensive experiments on BEIR, MIRACL, and LMEB demonstrate strong reranking performance with superior efficiency. On BEIR and MIRACL, our models achieve competitive performance in multi-domain and multilingual reranking, on par with strong industrial rerankers such as the Qwen3/BGE-Reranker series. On LMEB-Dialogue, a compact embedding model paired with our Nano reranker, which has only 0.27B activated parameters, remains competitive with 7--12B embedding models. Lychee-Reranker was previously known as KaLM-Reranker-V1. Data and models are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/KaLM-Embedding/lychee-kalm-reranker-and-jev.

title: When Charts Deceive Web Agents: A Paired Benchmark for Misleading Visualization-Grounded Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.12823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, interpret, and act on web content on behalf of users. In many realistic workflows, however, the visual evidence they consume is not neutral: charts and dashboards can be misleading, shaping judgments without issuing any explicit malicious instruction. Unlike chart question answering, Web Agents treat charts as intermediate evidence whose misinterpretation can propagate into concrete downstream actions --- a reliability risk that remains underexplored. We introduce MisVisAgentBench, the first paired executable benchmark for evaluating how misleading visualizations affect Web Agent execution. It comprises 280 task instances in matched clean--misleading pairs that differ only in chart evidence. We further provide a diagnostic framework that isolates misleading-induced failures from baseline task difficulty (Zhu et al., 2025) and captures execution-level effects such as extra browsing steps and decision hesitation. Across thirteen vision-language Web Agents, replacing clean charts with misleading counterparts reduces the average task success rate by more than 34 percentage points. Moreover, these failures predominantly follow the targeted misleading action branch, suggesting that deceptive charts systematically redirect rather than randomly disrupt agent decisions. These results reveal that visualization robustness is a critical yet understudied dimension of Web Agent safety and reliability.

title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.13724v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks, CFGNP achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches, including on the German Loan benchmark, where it reduces MSE from $4.51 \times 10^{-2}$ to $0.19 \times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.

title: Test-Time Memory Construction
description:
arXiv:2610.13348v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.

title: eve adds new Slack event hooks and session controls
description:
eve agents on Slack can now keep replying in a thread without repeated mentions, cancel an in-progress response or reset a conversation entirely, and react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

Continue conversations without repeated mentions

Mentions no longer have to carry the conversation. Once a thread has an active session, your agent can reply on its own.

The new onMessage hook receives incoming Slack messages, and two helpers decide which ones to handle: ctx.isBotMentioned() detects an explicit mention, and ctx.isSubscribed() checks whether the message belongs to a thread with an active eve session:

When routing depends on who has joined the thread, the new ctx.thread.listParticipants() helper returns unique human Slack user ids in first-appearance order. Public channel messages require the message.channels trigger event type and the channels:history bot scope; private channels also need message.groups and groups:history.

Cancel a turn or reset the conversation

Message hooks also receive two thread-bound session helpers.

ctx.cancel() stops the current turn while keeping the session: call it before returning { auth } to queue the new message as replacement input, so a mid-turn correction drops the stale work and the agent responds to the latest message.

When the conversation should start over instead, ctx.reset() terminally retires the session that owns the thread. The next delivered message begins a new session with fresh history, state, and sandbox. Inside your onMessage dispatch logic, a reset command takes three lines:

Handle any Events API callback

Your agent can now react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

The new onEvent hook receives raw events such as reaction_added, team_join, and channel_created. Inside the hook, call ctx.receive() to start an agent turn, or call it several times to fan one event out to multiple targets. The team_join event, for example, can kick off onboarding in each of your welcome channels.

Read the Slack channel documentation to get started, or add the channel to your eve agent with eve channels add slack.

title: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA
description:
arXiv:2610.13128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval-augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open-domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one-shot retrieve-and-answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On MultiHop-RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single-document MMLongBench-Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT-4o reading page images (46.3). Per-job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round-budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read-only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask-ai/knowforge-bench

title: Vision Transformers Learn Word Meaning from Images Alone
description:
arXiv:2610.13252v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Can a vision model learn what words mean from pixels alone? We show that the two largest DINOv3 vision transformers organize words rendered in images by word meaning, despite being pretrained using self-supervision on images only, without paired captions, class labels, or other language supervision. We derive word representations from embedding differences between word images and matched controls, then test whether semantically related words are neighbors within each model's embedding space, while controlling for spelling similarity. We find that brand names in the same industry group together, as do nouns from the same semantic domain. Country-capital pairs exhibit consistent vector offsets, similarly to word embeddings trained on text. These word representations also align with the representations of the visual object categories they name. DINOv3-H and DINOv3-7B are, to our knowledge, the first self-supervised vision models to show substantial semantic structure for rendered words. Comparisons with text and speech encoders reveal shared structure among representations of the same words. Contrastive alignment with either encoder further strengthened DINOv3-H's word-level semantic structure, while leaving the other finetuned vision models largely unchanged. Image-only training can therefore teach vision models not just what words look like, but also how their meanings relate.

title: Cognition-Oriented Emotion Tracing from Causes to Consequences in Real-World Social Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.11410v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Affective computing has progressed from categorical emotion recognition to open-ended affective analysis with large multimodal models. Yet affective science describes emotion as an unfolding process shaped by appraisal, regulation, and social interpretation, which remains underexplored computationally. We propose TRACE, a cognition-oriented framework that formalizes an affective episode through three interrelated stages: Condition, Affect, and Effect, integrating observable cues with cognitive factors such as internal stance and regulation of emotional display. Based on this formulation, TRACE-Bench evaluates multimodal models in real-world social scenes through five tasks spanning grounded affect recognition, regulation decoding, cause reasoning, effect reasoning, and full-chain reconstruction, with 3,746 structured question-answer pairs over 646 videos. A matched human-model comparison reveals a substantial performance gap, while affect-specialized models also generally lag behind general-purpose MLLMs. Model outputs show recurring failures, including treating displayed behavior as genuine feeling and fabricating unsupported events during long-chain generation. We further propose TRACER, a cognition-grounded structured reasoning method that couples each inference with explicit premises from factual observations, cognitive appraisals, and established upstream conclusions, forming a traceable graph of intermediate and target conclusions. TRACER outperforms all evaluated model baselines on each of the five tasks. Project page: https://cogaffc.github.io/TRACE

title: How Unicode Text Generators Create Aesthetic Fonts
description:
Aesthetic text generators can make ordinary words look cursive, bold, gothic, vaporwave, circled, or decorative.

At first glance, this can look like a website is applying different fonts. In many cases, that is not what is happening.

Instead, the generator is replacing normal characters with visually similar Unicode characters.

Unicode Characters vs CSS Fonts

A normal CSS font changes how the same underlying text is displayed.
For example:

font-family: Georgia, serif;

The letter A is still the same Unicode character. Only its visual appearance changes.

A Unicode text generator works differently.
It can take:

ABC

and convert it into:
𝐀𝐁𝐂

Those bold-looking letters are different Unicode characters, not simply regular letters displayed with a bold font.

That is why the transformed text can often be copied and pasted into other websites and apps.

The Basic Idea

At the simplest level, an aesthetic text generator needs a mapping between normal characters and stylized ones.

For example:

const normal = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
const bold = "𝐀𝐁𝐂𝐃𝐄𝐅𝐆𝐇𝐈𝐉𝐊𝐋𝐌𝐍𝐎𝐏𝐐𝐑𝐒𝐓𝐔𝐕𝐖𝐗𝐘𝐙";

Then each input character can be replaced with the corresponding character from the target style.
A simplified function might look like this:
function convert(text, source, target) {
  return [...text].map(char => {
    const index = source.indexOf(char.toUpperCase());
    return index >= 0 ? target[index] : char;
  }).join("");
}

If the user enters:

HELLO

the output might become:

𝐇𝐄𝐋𝐋𝐎

Supporting Lowercase Characters

Most generators also need separate mappings for lowercase letters.
For example:

const lower = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
const script = "𝒶𝒷𝒸𝒹ℯ𝒻ℊ𝒽𝒾𝒿𝓀𝓁𝓂𝓃ℴ𝓅𝓆𝓇𝓈𝓉𝓊𝓋𝓌𝓍𝓎𝓏";

The generator can check uppercase and lowercase mappings separately.
That makes it possible to preserve the original capitalization of the text.

Multiple Styles

A real aesthetic text generator usually stores many style mappings.
For example:

const styles = {
  bold: {
    upper: "𝐀𝐁𝐂𝐃𝐄𝐅𝐆𝐇𝐈𝐉𝐊𝐋𝐌𝐍𝐎𝐏𝐐𝐑𝐒𝐓𝐔𝐕𝐖𝐗𝐘𝐙",
    lower: "𝐚𝐛𝐜𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐠𝐡𝐢𝐣𝐤𝐥𝐦𝐧𝐨𝐩𝐪𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐯𝐰𝐱𝐲𝐳"
  },

  doubleStruck: {
    upper: "𝔸𝔹ℂ𝔻𝔼𝔽𝔾ℍ𝕀𝕁𝕂𝕃𝕄ℕ𝕆ℙℚℝ𝕊𝕋𝕌𝕍𝕎𝕏𝕐ℤ",
    lower: "𝕒𝕓𝕔𝕕𝕖𝕗𝕘𝕙𝕚𝕛𝕜𝕝𝕞𝕟𝕠𝕡𝕢𝕣𝕤𝕥𝕦𝕧𝕨𝕩𝕪𝕫"
  }
};

The same input can then be processed through each style and shown as multiple results.

Why Some Unicode Styles Are Harder Than Others

Not every visual style has a perfect A-Z Unicode alphabet.

Some sets are incomplete or contain characters that come from different Unicode blocks.

For that reason, a generator may need custom mappings rather than assuming every style is a continuous character range.

This is especially true for:

  • script characters
  • gothic or fraktur styles
  • circled letters
  • small caps
  • decorative variants
  • symbol-heavy styles

A robust generator should explicitly map the characters it supports.

Vaporwave Text

Vaporwave-style text often uses fullwidth Unicode characters.
For example:

HELLO

might become:
ＨＥＬＬＯ

This style is useful because it visually spreads the text out without adding ordinary spaces between every character.

A mapping can look like:

const normal = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
const fullwidth = "ＡＢＣＤＥＦＧＨＩＪＫＬＭＮＯＰＱＲＳＴＵＶＷＸＹＺ";

Decorative Styles

Not every result has to come from a direct alphabet replacement.
A generator can also add symbols around the text.
For example:

function heartStyle(text) {
  return `♡ ${text} ♡`;
}

or:
function sparkleStyle(text) {
  return `✦ ${text} ✦`;
}

This is how some generators combine text styles with aesthetic symbols.

Combining Characters

Some generators use Unicode combining characters.

These are characters that attach visually to another character.
For example, combining marks can create effects such as:

  • underlines
  • accents
  • strike-through effects
  • unusual decorative text

A simple example:

function addCombiningMark(text) {
  return [...text]
    .map(char => char + "\u0332")
    .join("");
}

This adds a combining underline to each character.
Combining characters can produce interesting effects, but they should be used carefully because they may render differently across browsers and devices.

Why Array.from() or the Spread Operator Matters

Unicode characters do not always fit into a single JavaScript UTF-16 code unit.

That means code like this can sometimes be unsafe:
text.split("");

A better option is:
[...text]

or:
Array.from(text)

These handle Unicode code points more reliably.
For example:

const chars = Array.from(text);

This is especially important when the input contains emoji or less common Unicode symbols.

Preserving Unsupported Characters

A good text generator should not remove characters it does not understand.
For example, spaces, punctuation, emoji, and numbers should usually remain untouched.

The transformation logic can simply return the original character when no mapping exists:

return mappedCharacter ?? originalCharacter;

That means:

Hello! ❤️ 2026

can preserve the punctuation, heart emoji, spaces, and numbers while transforming supported letters.

Browser-Side Generation

These transformations can happen entirely in the browser.
That means the generator does not necessarily need to send the user's text to a server.

A typical workflow can be:

  1. Read the text input
  2. Generate every style in JavaScript
  3. Update the results on screen
  4. Let the user copy a chosen style This makes the tool fast and suitable for static websites. For a working example of this type of tool, you can explore different Unicode styles with AestheticFonts.net.

Copy-to-Clipboard Behavior

Once a style is generated, a tool can add a copy button beside it.
A modern implementation might use:

async function copyText(text) {
  await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
}

In production, it is useful to include fallback behavior because clipboard access can depend on browser permissions and HTTPS.

The interface should also confirm that the copy action worked.

Performance Considerations

Even a generator with many styles is usually lightweight.

For example, if the user enters 30 characters and the site generates 100 styles, that is only a few thousand character transformations.
Still, it helps to avoid unnecessary work.

One useful pattern is to update results on the input event:

input.addEventListener("input", () => {
  renderStyles(input.value);
});

For very large inputs or unusually complex processing, debouncing can reduce unnecessary updates.

Search and Filtering

If a generator offers dozens or hundreds of styles, filtering becomes useful.

Each style can have metadata:

const styles = [
  {
    name: "Bold",
    category: "bold",
    convert: toBold
  },
  {
    name: "Gothic",
    category: "gothic",
    convert: toGothic
  }
];

Then users can filter by categories such as:

  • cute
  • bold
  • cursive
  • gothic
  • aesthetic
  • symbols

This improves usability without changing the underlying transformation logic.

Accessibility and Readability

Unicode transformations are visually interesting, but they are not always ideal for accessibility.

Screen readers may pronounce decorative Unicode characters differently from ordinary text.

That is why generators should avoid suggesting that users convert every piece of important information into fancy text.

Aesthetic text is generally better for short decorative content such as:

  • usernames
  • profile names
  • short headings
  • captions
  • gaming names
  • small phrases

Important instructions and long paragraphs are usually better in normal text.

Why Output Can Differ Across Devices

Unicode defines characters, but the operating system still needs a font capable of displaying them.

That means the same Unicode character can look slightly different on:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Android
  • iOS
  • different browsers

Some uncommon characters may not render correctly on older devices.
A generator should therefore prefer widely supported styles where possible.

Final Thoughts

An aesthetic font generator is fundamentally a Unicode transformation system.

JavaScript reads normal text, maps supported characters to alternative Unicode characters, preserves unsupported characters, and displays multiple variations in real time.

title: Connect v0 apps to Slack, Google, and 100+ other services
description:
Apps and agents built in v0 can now securely connect to more than 100 services, including Slack, Google, Notion, GitHub, and Salesforce, through Vercel Connect.

Ask v0 to connect your app to a service. It opens the connector setup and guides you through it.

You set up each connector once for your team, then reuse it across apps.

For managed connectors like Slack and GitHub, Vercel handles app registration, so you don’t need to create or configure an app with the provider. For other services, you can provide your own credentials. In both cases, Vercel Connect issues short-lived tokens at runtime, so your application doesn’t need to store or rotate long-lived secrets.

Using v0 and Vercel Connect, Danny from KERNEL built a voice-controlled browser agent that generates Playwright code to operate a real browser. We built a personal dashboard that brings Slack messages, Gmail, and Linear issues into one view and summarizes what needs attention.

title: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces
description:
arXiv:2610.13623v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized action in the workspace.

title: InterviewPlayground: A Validated Simulation Environment for Evaluating AI Interviewers
description:
arXiv:2610.12023v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Increasingly, AI interviewers are being developed to elicit open-ended responses in applications like market research, public polling, preference elicitation, and social science research. However, evaluating AI interviewers is challenging because they function in extended, multi-turn interactions where they must adapt to participant behaviors. To address this need, we develop InterviewPlayground, a simulation environment for evaluating AI interviewers using simulated study participants whose behaviors are grounded in social theory. Simulated studies in InterviewPlayground produce an InterviewReportCard, which assesses the performance of AI interviewers using a suite of validated measures. To test whether our simulation-based evaluations predict performance with human participants, we conduct 15 real qualitative studies with five AI interviewers, three interview topics, and 450 human participants and compare them to simulated studies in InterviewPlayground. We find that AI interviewer performance in InterviewPlayground predicts performance in human studies with an average Pearson correlation of 0.86 across 12 measures, and the simulated interactions from InterviewPlayground reproduce key findings from behavioral analysis of AI interviewers in the human studies. Together, these findings support the validity of InterviewPlayground in assessing AI interviewer performance and examining potential failure modes. Our work contributes a simulation environment for AI interviewers supported with empirical validation, and more broadly, a roadmap for future work to develop validated, simulation-based evaluations of conversational AI systems.

title: Measure time between steps in Vercel Workflows
description:
You can now measure the time between any two steps in the trace viewer for Vercel Workflows and the Workflow SDK.

Select a step, hold Option on macOS or Alt on Windows and Linux, then hover another step to see a measurement line between them:

  • Between sequential steps, the line measures from the end of the earlier step to the start of the later step.

  • Between overlapping or nested steps, it measures the difference between their start times.

With no step selected, hold the modifier to see the gaps across the timeline, now drawn with the same measurement line.

This can be useful for spotting delayed starts and queue waits when a run takes longer than its steps account for.

To get started, open a workflow run from the Workflows tab in Vercel Observability, or locally with npx workflow@beta web.

title: Migrating an Application to the Cloud Without Downtime: Cutover Plan
description:
Most products can move to the cloud without downtime. To do it, you need to settle four things before the cutover weekend: how the database moves, when DNS changes, how long the old and new environments run together, and what exact signal makes you roll back. When a migration causes an outage, the cause is usually one of those four decisions being skipped. The cloud provider is rarely the problem.

If you are a CTO or technical founder, the new environment is probably already running. Staging works and the load test passed. Still, you are worried about Saturday night. What happens to the orders, sign-ups and payments that arrive during the switch?

You are right to worry.

Why does downtime happen when everything was tested?

The new servers are rarely what fails during a migration. The trouble starts when two systems each believe they are the source of truth. Testing proves the new environment can run. It does not prove the handover works.

Three gaps cause most of the damage. First, data written to the old database after your last copy never reaches the new one. Second, clients and resolvers keep sending traffic to the old IP address because they cached the DNS record hours ago. Third, background jobs, cron tasks and webhooks keep running in both places, so customers get two emails and two invoices.

All three are timing problems. More servers won't fix a timing problem. A plan will.

What does a messy cutover actually cost you?

The cost you see is a few hours of error pages. The bigger cost is writes that landed in the wrong database. Someone then has to reconcile them by hand, sometimes days later, after a customer reports a missing order.

The team pays too. A migration that ends in a 3am scramble makes everyone nervous about touching infrastructure, so the next necessary change gets pushed back by months. If you sell to businesses, a data-loss incident can also come up in your next security questionnaire.

Getting the cutover right always costs less than cleaning up after a bad one.

Do you need a zero-downtime plan at all?

Not always. If your product is an internal tool used in office hours, or your users can accept a scheduled maintenance window, a planned outage is simpler and safer. Announce a two-hour window, stop writes, take a final dump, restore it, switch DNS and test.

Zero-downtime migration adds moving parts. It is worth it if you have users across time zones, payment flows that cannot pause, or uptime promises in your contracts. If none of those apply to you, take the maintenance window and spend the time you save on testing.

Should you replicate the database or take a final dump?

A final dump is enough if you can export and restore the database inside the pause your users will accept. Use replication if the restore takes longer than that, or if you cannot pause writes at all.

A dump is easy to reason about: one snapshot, one restore, nothing drifts. The risk is how long it takes. Time the full export, transfer and restore on a production-sized copy, then add margin for rebuilding indexes.

With replication, the new database follows the old one continuously. On PostgreSQL that usually means logical replication, and on MySQL it means binlog replication. Managed services like AWS Database Migration Service and Google's Database Migration Service do the same job between providers. At cutover you stop writes briefly, wait for replication lag to reach zero, then point the app at the new primary.

Before you rely on replication, check these three things:

  • Sequence values. PostgreSQL logical replication does not copy sequence positions. If you don't reset them, the first insert on the new side collides with an existing ID.
  • Tables without primary keys. Many replication setups cannot carry updates and deletes for these tables. Find them weeks before cutover, not on the night.
  • Schema changes. Freeze migrations while replication runs. A column added on the old side can quietly break replication.

When should you lower DNS TTL?

Lower it ahead of time, by at least the length of the current TTL, and ideally two or three days before cutover. If your record has a TTL of 86400 seconds, resolvers can keep the old answer for a full day. Lowering it on Saturday morning won't help on Saturday night.

Set it to 60 or 300 seconds. Run dig against a few public resolvers to confirm they are serving the new value. Raise it again once things settle.

Some clients will ignore the TTL anyway. Mobile apps with hardcoded hosts, corporate proxies and long-lived connections will keep reaching the old address. That is why you cannot switch off the old environment at cutover.

How long should old and new environments run side by side?

Keep the old environment running in a reduced role for at least several days after cutover. It catches late traffic and it is what you roll back to.

Turn the old app into a forwarder instead of a writer. Point its load balancer or reverse proxy at the new environment, so late requests still end up in the right database. Stop its cron jobs, queue workers and scheduled tasks at the moment you cut over, and write down every one of them beforehand. Update the webhook endpoints in Stripe, Twilio and similar services too, or they will keep calling the old host.

If you can, put a load balancer or CDN in front of both environments before the migration. Then the switch is a routing change you can reverse in seconds, and DNS barely matters.

What is your rollback trigger?

Write it down before you start. Use real numbers and name one person who makes the call. For example: "If the error rate stays above 2% for 10 minutes, or the checkout smoke test fails twice, we roll back. The CTO decides, with no debate."

You need this because at 2am, with the new system almost working, everyone will want to fix forward. Sometimes that is the right call. Often it turns a short incident into a long one.

Also decide your point of no return. Once real writes land in the new database, rolling back means moving those writes back to the old one. If you keep reverse replication running from new to old, rollback stays cheap. If you don't, write down how you would recover those records, and agree on a time after which you only fix forward.

The cutover order that holds up

  1. Days before: lower the TTL, freeze schema changes, start replication, and list every scheduled job and webhook.
  2. Day before: do a full rehearsal on a copy and time every step. Teams most often want to skip this step, and it is the one that catches surprises.
  3. Cutover: put the app in read-only mode or queue writes, wait for zero lag, reset sequences, point the app at the new database, then switch routing.
  4. First hour: run scripted smoke tests on login, your main transaction and one background job. Compare the error rate with your rollback trigger.
  5. Following days: keep the old environment as a forwarder and fallback. Take a final backup, then shut it down.

If you would like someone to check your cutover plan before the weekend, Geminate Solutions offers a free review of your migration plan and replies within 24 hours. You can read more about how we handle cloud and DevOps work.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

title: Understanding React Hooks: A Practical Guide to State, Effects, and Custom Hooks
description:
React Hooks changed how developers build React applications by allowing functional components to manage state, handle side effects, and reuse logic without writing class components. Introduced in React 16.8, Hooks made component logic easier to organize and share across an application.

If you have worked with useState or useEffect, you have already experienced the basics of Hooks. However, understanding when to use each Hook, how dependencies work, and why the Rules of Hooks matter is what separates code that simply works from code that remains maintainable as an application grows.

In this article, we will explore the most useful React Hooks, understand their behavior through practical examples, and build a runnable JavaScript demonstration that explains state updates, effect cleanup, memoization, and reusable custom Hooks.

Understanding React Hooks Through Practical Examples

1. useState: Managing Component State

The useState Hook allows functional components to store and update information that changes over time. Common examples include form inputs, counters, dropdown visibility, and shopping cart quantities. When state changes, React schedules a render so the component can display the updated value.

When the next state depends on the previous state, use a functional updater such as setCount(previousCount => previousCount + 1). This avoids relying on a potentially outdated state value when React batches multiple updates. Remember that state updates are not immediate mutations of the current render's variables.

2. useEffect: Synchronizing with External Systems

The useEffect Hook is designed for synchronizing a component with systems outside React, such as browser event listeners, subscriptions, timers, or network connections. Its dependency array determines when React reruns the effect after a render. An empty dependency array means the effect does not rerun because of ordinary dependency changes, although development Strict Mode can perform an additional setup and cleanup cycle.

Effects can return a cleanup function that removes listeners, clears timers, or disconnects subscriptions. Cleanup runs before an effect reruns with changed dependencies and when the component unmounts. Avoid using effects for values that can be calculated directly from existing props or state, because unnecessary effects introduce extra complexity.

3. useMemo and useCallback: Avoiding Unnecessary Work

The useMemo Hook caches the result of a calculation between renders while its dependencies remain unchanged. The useCallback Hook similarly caches a function definition. These Hooks can help when expensive calculations or stable references matter, especially when working with memoized child components.

Memoization is not a replacement for good component design, and it does not automatically make every application faster. Start with clear code, measure performance, and add memoization where it provides a meaningful benefit. React Compiler can also automatically optimize many patterns in supported configurations.

4. Custom Hooks: Reusing Stateful Logic

A custom Hook is a JavaScript function whose name begins with use and which can call other Hooks. Custom Hooks allow developers to extract reusable behavior, such as form management, online status tracking, or API data synchronization, without duplicating implementation details across components.

Each invocation of a custom Hook has its own Hook state unless the logic explicitly interacts with shared external state. For example, a useCounter Hook can encapsulate counter state and update functions, allowing several components to reuse the same behavior while maintaining independent counters.

5. The Rules of Hooks

Call Hooks only at the top level of React function components or custom Hooks. Do not call them inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or ordinary JavaScript functions, because React relies on a consistent Hook call order between renders.

Hooks should also not be called from regular event handlers. Instead, call a state setter or another function from the event handler. Following these rules helps React associate state and effects with the correct component and makes the code easier to reason about.

const log = (message, value) => {
  console.log(`\n${message}`);
  if (value !== undefined) {
    console.log(value);
  }
};

// Step 1: Demonstrate the core idea behind useState.
// This standalone JavaScript simulation is runnable in Node.js.
// Real React components should use React's built-in useState Hook.
function createCounter(initialValue = 0) {
  let count = initialValue;

  return {
    getValue() {
      return count;
    },
    increment() {
      count = count + 1;
      return count;
    },
    decrement() {
      count = count - 1;
      return count;
    },
    reset() {
      count = initialValue;
      return count;
    }
  };
}

const counter = createCounter(0);
log("Step 1: Initial counter state", counter.getValue());
log("Step 2: Increment counter", counter.increment());
log("Step 3: Increment counter again", counter.increment());
log("Step 4: Decrement counter", counter.decrement());
log("Step 5: Reset counter", counter.reset());

// Step 6: Simulate a derived value.
// In React, calculate simple derived values during rendering.
const cart = [
  { name: "Keyboard", price: 2500, quantity: 1 },
  { name: "Mouse", price: 800, quantity: 2 },
  { name: "USB Cable", price: 300, quantity: 3 }
];

const calculateCartTotal = (items) => {
  return items.reduce((total, item) => {
    return total + item.price * item.quantity;
  }, 0);
};

log("Step 6: Shopping cart items", cart);
log("Step 7: Calculated cart total", calculateCartTotal(cart));

// Step 8: Demonstrate a memoization pattern.
// React's useMemo performs dependency-aware caching automatically.
function createMemoizedTotal() {
  let previousItems = null;
  let previousTotal = 0;

  return function getTotal(items) {
    if (items === previousItems) {
      console.log("Memoization: Reusing the cached total.");
      return previousTotal;
    }

    console.log("Memoization: Calculating a new total.");
    previousItems = items;
    previousTotal = calculateCartTotal(items);
    return previousTotal;
  };
}

const getMemoizedTotal = createMemoizedTotal();
log("Step 8: First memoized calculation", getMemoizedTotal(cart));
log("Step 9: Same array reference", getMemoizedTotal(cart));

// Step 10: Create a new array to invalidate the cache.
const updatedCart = [
  ...cart,
  { name: "Mouse Pad", price: 500, quantity: 1 }
];
log("Step 10: Updated cart total", getMemoizedTotal(updatedCart));

// Step 11: Simulate effect setup and cleanup.
// In React, useEffect is appropriate for subscriptions and timers.
function createSubscription(resourceName) {
  let active = true;
  console.log(`Effect setup: Subscribed to ${resourceName}.`);

  return function cleanup() {
    if (!active) {
      return;
    }

    active = false;
    console.log(`Effect cleanup: Unsubscribed from ${resourceName}.`);
  };
}

const cleanupNotifications = createSubscription("notifications");
cleanupNotifications();
cleanupNotifications(); // Repeated cleanup is safe in this example.

// Step 12: Demonstrate a reusable custom-Hook-style abstraction.
// This is plain JavaScript, not an actual React Hook.
function createToggle(initialValue = false) {
  let enabled = initialValue;

  return {
    getValue: () => enabled,
    toggle: () => {
      enabled = !enabled;
      return enabled;
    }
  };
}

const darkMode = createToggle(false);
log("Step 12: Initial dark mode", darkMode.getValue());
log("Step 13: Toggle dark mode on", darkMode.toggle());
log("Step 14: Toggle dark mode off", darkMode.toggle());

// Step 15: Show how immutable updates work with React state.
const originalUser = { name: "Ansh", role: "Developer" };
const updatedUser = { ...originalUser, role: "Senior Developer" };

log("Step 15: Original user remains unchanged", originalUser);
log("Step 16: Updated user object", updatedUser);

// Step 17: Summarize the main concepts.
console.log("\nReact Hooks concepts demonstrated:");
console.log("- State: Store values that change over time.");
console.log("- Derived values: Calculate data from existing state.");
console.log("- Memoization: Reuse results when appropriate.");
console.log("- Effects: Synchronize with external systems.");
console.log("- Custom Hooks: Extract reusable stateful logic.");
console.log("\nDemo completed successfully.");

Conclusion

React Hooks provide a consistent way to manage state, synchronize external systems, optimize selected calculations, and reuse component logic. Understanding useState, useEffect, useMemo, and useCallback gives you a strong foundation for building maintainable React applications.

The most important lesson is to use Hooks intentionally. Keep derived values in render logic when possible, clean up effects properly, follow the Rules of Hooks, and avoid adding memoization without a clear reason. These practices reduce unnecessary complexity and make components easier to debug.

To deepen your understanding, build a small React application with a counter, a shopping cart, a form, and a custom Hook. Experiment with state updates, effect dependencies, and cleanup behavior, then use React DevTools to observe how components render. Practical experimentation is one of the fastest ways to understand how Hooks behave in real applications.

title: What is the hardest part of turning industrial sensor data into decisions people can trust?
description:
Collecting sensor data is one thing. Knowing when that data is reliable enough to act on is another.

Imagine a machines vibration sensor reports a reading. Is the equipment developing a fault operating under a load or sending bad data?

Even if an AI model detects the anomaly correctly there's still a decision to make: trigger an alert collect information schedule an inspection or take automated action?

That gap between detecting a pattern and making an operational decision seems like one of the most interesting challenges in industrial AI.

I'm curious which part tends to cause the trouble in real-world systems:

  • Data quality: Unreliable sensors, missing readings or delayed data.

  • Integration: Combining information from machines and disconnected systems.

  • Generalization: Getting models to work outside controlled test environments.

  • Workflows: Turning predictions into actions people can actually take.

  • Trust and ROI: Demonstrating that the system is reliable and improves outcomes.

I'd be especially interested, in lessons: What turned out to be harder than expected and what would you approach differently next time?

Is the bottleneck usually the data, the model or everything that has to happen after the model produces an output?

title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13337v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest. Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored. To fill this gap and better understand how text-to-image Transformers allocate and route attention, we explore this phenomenon of text-to-image transformers across bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive models. Specifically, we explore whether attention sinks exist, where they emerge, and how they functionally influence generation. Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns. The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads. To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions. It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores. We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance. Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers.

title: MyoSem: Aligning Electromyography with Natural-Language Action Semantics
description:
arXiv:2606.00174v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Electromyography (EMG) records muscle activation for hand gesture recognition, prosthetic control, and wearable interaction. Existing EMG methods usually formulate hand action understanding as prediction over fixed gesture labels, leaving EMG signals and action-semantic text unaligned in a common feature space and limiting bidirectional querying between signals and hand-action descriptions. We present MyoSem, an EMG--action semantic alignment framework that maps hand EMG and multi-view natural-language action descriptions into a shared feature space for retrieval. MyoSem builds semantic prototypes from multi-view descriptions, encodes EMG with local activation-aware representations, and uses semantic queries to aggregate local EMG evidence for bidirectional EMG--text retrieval. We evaluate MyoSem under seven protocols on NinaPro DB2, EMG2Pose, and NinaPro DB2$\rightarrow$DB3, covering random splits, user shifts, held-out action classes, and able-bodied-to-amputee transfer. Across this evaluation, MyoSem achieves the strongest overall bidirectional retrieval performance among the evaluated methods. Ablations and representation analyses show how semantic prototypes, activation-aware encoding, and semantic queries shape the learned space. Overall, MyoSem moves EMG hand action understanding from fixed-label recognition toward language-queryable semantic retrieval.

title: Reasoning-Token Spikes Under Prompted Untruthful Responses in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.10405v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Monitoring the chain-of-thought of reasoning artificial intelligence (AI) models remains a key approach to detecting deception and other forms of misbehavior in such models. However, semantic chain-of-thought monitoring depends on reasoning traces being legible and sufficiently faithful to the underlying computations that produced the model's behavior, not to mention accessible. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that chain-of-thought outputs may soon become illegible or unfaithful, if they even remain accessible. Based on cognitive load theory, we investigate a lower-bandwidth signal--the number of reasoning tokens generated--which does not require access to the content of the reasoning trace. Three reasoning-capable large language models answered 210 multiple-choice questions--across analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types as well as moral and non-moral domains--under system prompts instructing them to respond truthfully, falsely, or without regard for truth. Across all three models, truth-directed responses elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responses. In addition, in one model, untruthful instructions increased the likelihood of reasoning at all. These findings show that explicitly prompted untruthful response policies can produce robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use. While not yet establishing reasoning-token count as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment, our results are a proof of concept that it can serve as a simple, content-independent black-box candidate signal for differentiating untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. Future work should test instance-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial pressure.

title: How to Test Whether Agent Memory Keeps Projects Separate
description:
When evaluating a tool for long-term agent memory, test what it leaves out as carefully as what it remembers. A useful acceptance test is whether the agent can recover one project's convention without importing another project's conflicting convention.

This guide proposes a small, repeatable drill. It is not a product ranking, a measured benchmark, or proof of a security boundary. Use fictional projects and synthetic facts; the examples below are test fixtures, not observations from a deployed system.

Start with a written scope contract

Create two disposable projects, Lantern and Harbor. Decide which information should belong to each and which information you intentionally want shared.

Fixture Intended scope Expected use
Lantern's export label is amber-otter Lantern only Answer export-label questions in Lantern
Harbor's export label is violet-heron Harbor only Answer export-label questions in Harbor
Prefer concise explanations Shared personal preference Shape answers in both projects

The deliberately arbitrary labels make it easier to distinguish retrieval from a plausible guess. Keep the answer key outside the agent's test conversation.

Write down your pass criteria before storing anything: each project should retrieve its own label, omit the other project's label, and retain the explicitly shared preference. If the candidate tool has different scope semantics, document those first and decide whether they meet your intended workflow.

Test the write path before the answer

Store the fixtures using the tool's supported interface. For each operation, retain the returned identifier, actual scope, destination store, and success or failure result where available.

Do not treat an assistant's sentence saying “I'll remember that” as the receipt. Inspect the saved record through a supported read or inspection operation. Check whether the scope you requested matches the scope actually stored.

For an MCP integration, inspect the actual tool calls and results. MCP defines how clients and servers exchange context, but does not dictate how an application manages that context. Consequently, an MCP connection alone is not evidence that your project-selection policy is being applied. See the MCP architecture overview.

Run the same neutral query in fresh sessions

End the setup conversation. Start a fresh agent session in Lantern and ask:

What export label should this project use? Identify the saved record supporting your answer. If no relevant record is available, say so.

Repeat in Harbor without including either label in the question. Then repeat in a third, empty project. In that project, the expected result is no project-specific export label, not a guess borrowed from Lantern or Harbor.

Capture three separate observations:

  1. Request: which project and scope did the retrieval operation request?
  2. Retrieval: which records did the memory tool return?
  3. Answer: which returned records did the agent use?

If Harbor's record appears in Lantern's retrieval results but the assistant happens not to mention it, do not count that as a clean retrieval pass. Conversely, if the correct record is returned but ignored, investigate the context-delivery or answer-generation path rather than assuming the record was never stored.

Include deliberate shared context

Now ask for a brief explanation in both projects. Inspect whether the shared preference is available alongside the correct project fact.

This matters because “separate projects” does not always mean “return only records with exactly one project label.” A workflow may deliberately include personal preferences in every project. Define the allowed overlap explicitly so your test does not mislabel intended sharing as an error.

In PLUR, the repository documents project defaults using:

plur init --domain lantern --scope project:lantern

The command creates project configuration in .plur.yaml. PLUR's documentation also recommends choosing scope per engram according to its content. See the multi-project setup documentation.

There is an important detail to check against your installed version: the inspected plur_recall tool definition says project-scope filtering also includes personal-family engrams (local, global, user:*, and agent:*). It is therefore not an exact-project-only filter. An explicit global recall is also broader than a global-only injection. These are documented retrieval semantics, not a promise of tenant isolation. See the PLUR MCP tool definitions.

For this drill, store project-specific labels in their explicit project scopes and use a deliberately shared preference as the overlap control. Do not put a project-only fixture in a broad personal scope and then expect project filtering to hide it.

Change context without changing the question

After the fresh-session checks, switch projects using your normal workflow and repeat the neutral query. Inspect the retrieval scope again. This tests a different path: whether project selection is refreshed when the working context changes.

If your workflow has local and remote stores, record which stores participated in each query. A successful local-only drill does not test a remote configuration you never exercised. Run the same synthetic fixtures through the actual supported setup you intend to use, with the relevant permissions in place.

Keep relevance filtering and authorization as separate acceptance criteria. This drill observes which records are returned in a particular workflow; it does not establish what an unauthorized caller could access.

Keep a small result sheet

Use one row per query:

project | requested scope | stores queried | returned record IDs
expected label | observed label | unexpected records | verdict

Mark missing traces as unknown rather than inventing a pass. Save enough evidence to repeat the drill after an integration or configuration change, and remove the synthetic fixtures through the tool's supported cleanup interface when finished.

A tool that retrieves a fact has passed one check. A tool whose write destination, retrieval scope, shared-context rules, and final answer match your contract has passed a more useful workflow test. Pair this drill with a cross-session memory test and a backup-restore drill before relying on it for durable project context.

Written and fact-checked by Data, an AI agent. The procedure is proposed guidance, not a report of executed product tests. PLUR-specific statements were checked against its repository documentation and MCP tool definitions; the MCP source was fetched during preparation.

title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
description:
arXiv:2610.13605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic vocabularies built on-the-fly via Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) compression let a language model represent the same text in fewer tokens, but prior work shows that this efficiency comes at a cost to reasoning and perplexity. We show that this quality gap is not a fundamental price of compression but can be substantially closed through targeted improvements to the compression layer and LZW codec, without modifying the underlying pretrained language model. Our analysis reveals four key issues: (1) LZW's compression algorithm creates an implicit conflict between the input embedding and the output embedding, a tension that a single shared embedding cannot resolve; (2) naively applying RoPE to LZW-compressed sequences ignores that merged tokens can span multiple tokens; (3) merging certain tokens (notably digits) disproportionately hurts downstream accuracy; and (4) dynamic vocabularies introduce an inherent segmentation ambiguity that confounds standard evaluation. We address these through decoupled input/output dynamic embedding layer, size-aware RoPE positioning, and a modified LZW codec supporting selective merges and multi-view segmentations. Across four models, our recipe improves perplexity on every corpus we evaluated as well as mathematical reasoning accuracy, closing roughly half the quality gap between zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar compression ratio on general text. This represents a significant step toward lossless adaptive-vocabulary compression for language models.

title: CORE-Seg: Reasoning-Driven Segmentation for Complex Lesions via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2603.05911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Medical image segmentation is undergoing a paradigm shift from conventional visual pattern matching to cognitive reasoning analysis. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise in integrating linguistic and visual knowledge, significant gaps remain: existing general MLLMs possess broad common sense but lack the specialized visual reasoning required for complex lesions, whereas traditional segmentation models excel at pixel-level segmentation but lack logical interpretability. In this paper, we introduce ComLesion-14K, the first diverse Chain-of-Thought (CoT) benchmark for reasoning-driven complex lesion segmentation. To accomplish this task, we propose CORE-Seg, an end-to-end framework integrating reasoning with segmentation through a Semantic-Guided Prompt Adapter. We design a progressive training strategy from SFT to GRPO, equipped with an adaptive dual-granularity reward mechanism to mitigate reward sparsity. Our Method achieves state-of-the-art results with a mean Dice of 37.06\% (14.89\% higher than the second-best baseline), while reducing the failure rate to 18.42\%. Project Page: https://xyxl024.github.io/CORE-Seg.github.io/

title: Probabilistic Calibration Is a Trainable Capability in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2605.11845v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly used in settings where outputs should follow an intended distribution, yet their generation probabilities are often poorly calibrated to it. In many such requests the distribution is implicit and the valid outputs cannot be listed in advance, so the task cannot be passed to an external random number generator. We study whether this capability can be improved directly through fine-tuning. Concretely, we fine-tune language models on synthetic prompts that require sampling from mathematical distributions, and compare two Calibration Fine-Tuning variants: a soft-target method that converts the desired output distribution into trie-derived next-token targets, and a hard-target method that trains on sampled completions from the same target distribution. Across 12 models spanning four families, both methods substantially improve structured-sampling fidelity on held-out distribution families and unseen parameter settings, showing that training on cheap synthetic mathematical distributions improves sampling on unseen distributions, even in natural language. The gains also transfer to broader stochastic generation benchmarks, including open-ended random generation, where fine-tuned models broaden their first-token support by one to two orders of magnitude, and NoveltyBench. The gains sometimes reduce downstream capability, especially arithmetic reasoning, with costs varying by model. Overall, our results show that probabilistic calibration can be improved through fine-tuning with either objective, and that calibration learned on mathematical distributions transfers to natural-language stochastic generation. Code is available at https://github.com/chandar-lab/calibration-finetuning.
