title: Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases
description:
arXiv:2610.13370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the standard architecture for frontier LLMs. The multiple parallel experts in each transformer block theoretically enable expert specialization according to categories such as domains, languages, or modalities during pretraining. However, when data is imbalanced across categories, minority categories can become concentrated in a small fraction of the expert pool or spread inefficiently across them, effectively limiting their available capacity. In this work, we demonstrate that category-conditioned expert-selection biases can preferentially route tokens from different categories toward specialized expert pools. By applying biases based on input category, we provide a simple way to induce soft category-aligned specialization. This intervention encourages categories toward distinct expert subsets while retaining cross-category sharing when useful. More importantly, it enables the over-allocation of expert capacity to categories that would otherwise be disadvantaged by data scarcity. We observe performance improvements across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters. At our smallest and largest model scales, these gains are equivalent to allocating 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens, respectively. Overall, our results show that expert biases can serve as a lightweight control for category-level expert allocation, making room for low-resource categories while retaining standard MoE inference.

title: jpomop: open code to convert Japanese DPC inpatient data to OMOP
description:
Japan has a standard format for some inpatient data called DPC. Many people in the OHDSI world use the OMOP Common Data Model. I could not find public code that connects the two, so I started writing it. The project is called jpomop, and the code is on GitHub: https://github.com/kojikojikojikoji/jpomop

I am a Japanese data scientist, and I live in London.

Why DPC data matters

DPC is used to classify acute inpatient stays and help set hospital payments in Japan. Hospitals in the system send standard files about each stay to the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW). The ministry publishes the file layout every year in a long manual. The FY2026 edition has 244 pages (MHLW, PDF).

The scale is large. The MHLW summary of the FY2024 discharged patient survey lists 1,767 DPC hospitals in the analysed data (MHLW, PDF). Other hospitals also take part in the survey. Every hospital in the survey makes its files from the same manual for that year.

jpomop reads two of those files. Form 1 (様式1) holds details about the patient and stay, with diagnoses coded in ICD-10. The EF file (入院EF統合ファイル) records billed services by day, including drugs and procedures, and ward information.

Why OMOP

The OMOP CDM is an open community standard for observational health data. The OHDSI CDM Working Group manages it (OHDSI).

In Europe, EHDEN says it has a network of over 100 data partners mapped to the OMOP CDM (EHDEN). In England, the NHS Research Secure Data Environment Network agreed in 2023 to adopt the OMOP CDM (HDR UK).

OMOP is used in many places where I would like Japanese data to be usable. Putting DPC data into OMOP tables is a first step toward using OHDSI tools and study code. Whether a study works also depends on the mappings and on what DPC records.

What was missing

I looked for open code that turns DPC files into OMOP tables. I did not find any. There is an open ETL for Japanese EHR tables from the Rinchu-net standard data tables (GitHub). Its source list does not include DPC files.

I wanted something anyone could run without real patient data. I wrote the converter from the public specification and tested it with synthetic data and the worked examples in the manual.

What jpomop does

This is the quick start from the README:

pip install -e .
jpomop synth --n 100 --out synth/
jpomop validate --yoshiki1 synth/yoshiki1.txt --ef synth/ef.txt
jpomop convert --yoshiki1 synth/yoshiki1.txt --ef synth/ef.txt --out cdm.duckdb
jpomop report --cdm cdm.duckdb

synth makes fake data for 100 patients. validate checks the files against the parts of the FY2026 specification that jpomop supports and lists the problems it finds. convert writes the CDM tables to DuckDB. report summarises the result.

The validation step can be useful on its own. It does not need OMOP or a vocabulary. A hospital that does not use OMOP could still use it to check the supported fields in its DPC files. I have not tried this on real files yet.

This table shows which OMOP tables jpomop writes from each input:

DPC CDM table
Form 1, whole-stay form person, visit_occurrence, observation_period
EF, ward code for each day visit_detail
Form 1, non-suspected diagnoses (ICD-10) condition_occurrence
EF, codes that start with 6 drug_exposure
EF, codes that start with 1 procedure_occurrence
Form 1, discharge outcome 6 or 7 death

That makes eight CDM tables. Patient IDs are hashed.

The manual tells hospitals to set the ward code for each service date, not the ward at discharge (page 193). jpomop makes one visit_detail row for each run of days on the same ward. The ward code is each hospital's own code.

The specification lives in YAML files. Each field has a name, a length, a type and the page number in the manual. I did not copy the manual's text.

The tricky parts

Suspected diagnoses. Japanese claims data often carry diagnoses marked as "suspected". In Form 1, this is the modifier code 8002. jpomop leaves these out of condition_occurrence and counts them. I made this choice to avoid treating them as confirmed diagnoses.

Dates. Form 1 has no date for each diagnosis, so jpomop uses the admission date as the condition start date. This matters for studies of when a condition began: admission may not be the start date. The EF file has a date for each service, so jpomop uses the recorded service dates for drugs and procedures.

Form types. Form 1 has several form types for one stay. jpomop uses the form for the whole stay. It uses the day-90 interim form only when a stay has no whole-stay form yet. Ward-group forms and readmission forms are counted but not converted. In the manual, a ward-group form covers part of a stay (page 42). A readmission form joins two stays, and each of those stays also has its own form (page 125). So their days are already in the forms that jpomop uses. I have not checked this on real files.

Diagnosis codes. DPC writes ICD-10 without a dot, and sometimes with a fifth character. jpomop tries the most specific Athena code first and then shorter ones. For example, S7200 becomes S72.00, then S72.0, then S72.

Drug mapping. The EF file uses receipt codes for drugs. jpomop looks up each code in the public drug master to get the NHI drug price code. Then it looks up that code in the table by Kimura et al. (2025), which maps Japanese drugs to RxNorm concepts (dataset, CC BY 4.0; paper). The table has 12,178 rows for oral and injectable drugs. It does not cover every drug. In the October 2026 drug master, 11,956 of 19,222 items have a concept ID in the table. That is 62% of the items, not of real drug use. I have not checked these concept IDs against Athena yet. Drugs that patients bring from home are left out.

Masters are not included. The code masters come from the Japanese body that reviews and pays health insurance claims. Its website terms prohibit using or reproducing its documents without permission. So the repository does not include them. Users download the masters, the Athena vocabularies and the Kimura table themselves. Then jpomop vocab build joins them on the user's own machine. Without a vocabulary, diagnosis and drug concept IDs are 0, and the original codes stay in the source value columns.

The repository has a PROVENANCE.md file. It lists every document used, with its version, URL, retrieval date and SHA-256 hash.

Status and honest limits

jpomop is early. The current version number is 0.0.1. Here is what is true today:

  • It reads and checks both files and writes eight CDM tables.
  • 44 tests pass. Some of them rebuild the worked examples in the FY2026 manual.
  • I have tested it only with synthetic data and those manual examples.
  • I have not run it on real hospital data.
  • I have not measured mapping rates with a full Athena vocabulary.
  • Procedures keep their DPC code as the source value. Their concept ID is 0 for now.
  • It targets CDM v5.4. The OHDSI site now lists v5.5 as the current version.

Synthetic data shows that the code works on the cases I made. It does not show that it works on real hospital files. Errors such as double counting or wrong joins between Form 1 and EF may not show up until the code is tested on real data.

I plan to release v0.1 at the end of November 2026.

How you can help

I am looking for two kinds of people.

If you work with DPC data in Japan, I would like you to run jpomop inside your own environment. You do not need to share any data. Counts and error messages are enough. If my reading of the manual is wrong, I want to know.

If you work with OHDSI tools, I would like your view on the mapping choices. How should suspected diagnoses be handled? Is the admission date a fair start date for conditions? What would make Japanese inpatient data useful in your network studies?

Issues and pull requests are open on GitHub: https://github.com/kojikojikojikoji/jpomop

The code is under Apache-2.0. Mapping tables made by the project are under CC BY 4.0. This does not cover the masters, the Athena vocabularies or the Kimura table. They keep their own terms.

title: CNN-Transformer with Sigmoid Label for High-Resolution Sub-Degree DOA Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.13433v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This paper addresses the grid quantization error of deep-learning (DL)-based direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation. Classification- based DOA methods discretize the continuous angular space into a grid, so that with a peak-based read-out, the accuracy and resolution are limited by the grid step and by the width of the label peak. To address this issue, we propose a sigmoid label that encodes the sources' DOAs as the sum of angle-shifted monotonic sigmoid functions. Differentiating the output of a CNN-Transformer network trained with the sigmoid label produces sharp spectral peaks at the source DOAs. Combined with a moderately refined grid step of 0.25 degrees, the CNN-Transformer with the proposed sigmoid label attains sub-degree accuracy and a 1-degree resolution, breaking the limit of the grid quantization error. Under the unified CNN-Transformer backbone, we compare the proposed Sigmoid label with the Gaussian label, the 0-1 hard label, and the binary cross-entropy (BCE) baseline. Numerical results demonstrate that the Sigmoid label attains the highest accuracy and superior resolution compared to other labels.

title: VIDRAFT's VKORE: An NPU Acceleration Software Layer That Unlocks Both Inference *and* Training on Non-GPU Hardware
description:
VIDRAFT's VKORE: An NPU Acceleration Software Layer That Unlocks Both Inference and Training on Non-GPU Hardware

TL;DR: VIDRAFT has released VKORE, a software acceleration layer for NPUs that — analogous to CUDA for NVIDIA GPUs — dramatically improves inference throughput and, for the first time on these chips, enables transformer model training without any hardware changes. Paired with a top-ranked judge model and a recursive self-improvement (RSI) engine hitting perfect scores on public math benchmarks, VKORE is designed to let data centers run a full inference-by-day / training-by-night loop entirely on NPU silicon. Developers in ML infrastructure and LLMOps should pay attention.

What it is

VKORE is a software acceleration stack built by VIDRAFT (비드래프트), a Korean Pre-AGI AI startup, targeting Neural Processing Units (NPUs) — the class of inference-optimized accelerators that are increasingly common in data centers alongside traditional GPUs.

The core pitch: NPUs have historically been considered inference-only devices. Manufacturers themselves have positioned them that way. VKORE challenges that assumption by operating purely at the software layer — no chip swap required — to unlock:

  • High-throughput inference with dramatically lower latency per request
  • Transformer model training (specifically LoRA fine-tuning, as tested), which was previously impractical or effectively impossible on NPUs at competitive speeds

VKORE is positioned as the NPU equivalent of what CUDA is to NVIDIA GPUs: a foundational software layer that exposes and maximizes the hardware's computational potential for AI workloads.

How it works

At a conceptual level, VKORE introduces an optimized software execution layer between the ML framework and the NPU hardware. The idea is analogous to a custom kernel/runtime that schedules and batches operations in a way that the default NPU drivers do not.

Without VKORE, running a server CPU on a LoRA training task that takes ~1 hour on an NVIDIA B200 GPU requires roughly 320 hours — and a naively-driven NPU performs worse than that CPU baseline. VKORE restructures how operations are dispatched to the NPU, recovering massive efficiency gains without modifying the underlying silicon.

The intended operational pattern VIDRAFT describes is a day/night inference-training loop:

  • Daytime: The NPU cluster serves live inference traffic
  • Nighttime: VKORE enables the same NPU cluster to train on that day's accumulated judge logs and feedback signals

This cyclical architecture is designed to reduce dependence on additional GPU procurement and to support hybrid data center environments where GPUs and NPUs coexist.

VKORE also serves as the execution platform for two other VIDRAFT AI components:

  • Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5, a judge/decision model
  • An RSI (Recursive Self-Improvement) reasoning engine

Benchmarks & results

All figures below are sourced directly from the AI타임스 report:

VKORE inference & training gains (same NPU, VKORE vs. baseline NPU):

  • Single-request response latency: 3.8× faster
  • Server-level concurrent throughput: 4.1× higher
  • LoRA transformer training: successfully completed (previously impractical on NPU)

Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5 (judge model) — S1MB global benchmark:

  • Ranked #1 out of 152 models in the S1MB public benchmark
  • Outscored the official JEV reference model by 9.72 points
  • In 137 head-to-head benchmark comparisons: won 97 out of 137
  • Notable rankings of competitors in the same benchmark: Perplexity (#2), Cloudflare (#17), Meta (#27)

Darwin-27B-ZTC uses a zero-token-cost (ZTC) inference design: it completes a judgment via a single forward pass without generating output tokens, making it highly power-efficient for high-frequency operations like response quality scoring and task routing (where millions of calls per day are typical in production LLM systems).

RSI reasoning engine — math benchmarks:

  • AIME 2026: 100% (perfect score)
  • HMMT 2026: 100% (perfect score) — reported as the first perfect score on a certified math leaderboard
  • GPQA Diamond (science reasoning): #1 among models with fewer than 500B parameters

VIDRAFT has stated that full performance results will be released as a research paper.

How to try it

VKORE, Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5, and the RSI engine are not yet publicly available via Hugging Face, GitHub, or a public API as of this report. VIDRAFT has announced the technology and indicated a forthcoming paper, but no public access channel has been disclosed.

Developers interested in access or early partnerships should monitor VIDRAFT's official channels. The company is participating in a government-backed AI foundation model program (under MSIT/NIPA) as part of the NAVER Cloud consortium, which may influence future release timelines.

FAQ

Q: Is VKORE hardware-specific, or can it work on any NPU?
A: The source does not specify supported NPU vendors or chip families. VIDRAFT's CEO stated the goal is to run workloads on domestic (Korean) NPUs, but no supported hardware list has been publicly released. Check VIDRAFT's forthcoming paper for details.

Q: Darwin-27B-ZTC uses a single forward pass — how does that work for judgment tasks?
A: Rather than generating a chain of tokens to arrive at a verdict, Darwin-27B-ZTC is designed as a classification/scoring model that outputs a judgment signal directly from one forward pass. This is architecturally similar to reward models or cross-encoders used in RLHF pipelines, but optimized specifically for high-throughput, low-latency decision-making in production LLM routing and quality-evaluation scenarios.

Q: When will the VKORE paper be available?
A: VIDRAFT has confirmed a paper is planned but no publication date or venue has been announced. The AI타임스 article from October 13, 2026 is the primary public source at this time.

Originally reported by AI타임스 (2026-10-13) — source article.

title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation
description:
arXiv:2610.12977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) of social media platforms commonly retrieves items by autoregressively decoding discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) with finite-width beam search. This work examines how this output interface constrains whether held-out targets enter finite returned lists, while distinguishing catalog-wide scoreability from empirical top-K support. We introduce two continuous-query paradigms: CQG-Single generates one retrieval query in a single pass, and CQG-AR autoregressively generates continuous residual updates, retaining step-wise decoding while removing the SID item-token vocabulary, code lookup, and discrete beam expansion. These designs thereby eliminate the SID-specific reachability constraint induced by finite-beam decoding and avoid the technical challenge of aligning a discrete SID vocabulary with the pretrained backbone's vector space. Both methods make every encoded item directly scoreable through dense or approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Under a unified protocol with valid-prefix constrained decoding, CQG-Single exceeds the TIGER-style baseline in all seven runs while using 55.3% as many trainable parameters. CQG-AR remains comparable on ML-1M and is numerically stronger on Beauty and Sports datasets. A controlled depth ablation further shows that additional continuous refinement does not monotonically improve shallow accuracy. These findings motivate decoupling output representation, autoregressive modeling, and retrieval budget when evaluating generative recommendation systems.

title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
description:
arXiv:2610.13008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.

title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.13737v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.

title: EdTech Has Three Users, Not One. Model That Before You Build
description:
Most apps have one user type with a settings screen. EdTech has three, and they're adversarial by design: the learner must not see the grading tools, the educator must not need IT to reset a roster, and the admin needs to provision hundreds of accounts without touching a database.

If those three roles arrive in the data model after the first screens are built, you get authorization checks sprayed across controllers, a permissions bug in every sprint, and a rewrite somewhere around the first district contract. It's the same class of mistake as retrofitting multi-tenancy, and it costs about the same.

Here are nine firms with public edtech delivery history, judged on that.

What to verify before shortlisting

  • Ask how they'd model the three roles. A good answer talks about a permission model separate from the role label, because a teacher at one school and a department head at another need different scopes with the same title. A weak answer talks about screens.
  • Ask what happens with no connectivity. Not "can you add offline." Ask what syncs, what conflicts, and who wins. K-12, rural, and international deployments make this a launch requirement, not a phase two.
  • Ask how they test WCAG. Automated axe scans plus manual keyboard and screen reader passes is a real answer. "We follow best practices" is not, and district procurement will find out before you do.
  • Ask for one shipped AI feature. Named, with what the model does. "Recommends the next lesson from the last five wrong answers" is a feature. "AI-powered personalization" is a homepage.
  • Ask about the back-to-school window. Bug-fix SLAs in late August are a different commitment than the rest of the year, and a partner who has shipped in this vertical knows it without being told.

1.Vention

Stack: broad enterprise, Unity for interactive builds
Best for: large funded edtech needing enterprise-scale capacity

New York, 2002, 3,000+ engineers, six figures and up.

Technical note: built a Unity-based interactive kiosk for Cranbrook Institute of Science, a 3D aquatic ecosystem explorer with 73 models, delivered in 3 months. No public edtech-specific case study beyond that, so the general enterprise record is what you're buying.

2. N-iX

Stack: microservices, enterprise backends
Best for: scaling edtech SaaS that needs a dedicated pod

Ukraine with EU delivery centers, 2002, 2,500+ engineers, typically $150k+.

Technical note: the most concrete performance result on this list. Modernized WBS TRAINING's legacy LMS into microservices and took page response from 5+ minutes to under 0.5 seconds, with a 30% overall lift. That's a real re-architecture, not a reskin. The $150k floor rules out seed stage.

3. ScienceSoft

Stack: .NET, Java, Python, mobile
Best for: institutions with formal procurement requirements

McKinney TX, 1989, 700+ people, enterprise tier.

Technical note: shipped language-learning apps across 8 languages with text-to-speech under a 40MB footprint, which reached #1 education app in 10+ countries. That binary size discipline matters more than it sounds for schools distributing on old devices. Enterprise process means longer timelines.

4. Simform

Stack: cloud-native, Azure OpenAI, AWS
Best for: products where the scaling story is the hard part

California with India delivery, 2010, 700+ people, $50 to $150/hr.

Technical note: built a GenAI research platform for a psychology association over 50,000+ studies, reporting 50% faster research and 99% uptime. Architecture-first positioning, which means pedagogy and teacher workflow are not their center of gravity. Ask for explicit edtech references.

5. Netguru

Stack: React, Rails
Best for: founders who need the UX to carry the product

Poland, 2008, 700+ people, $50 to $99/hr.

Technical note: built Babbel's B2B admin dashboard, including team license management for corporate accounts like Hyundai and Paramount. Seat provisioning and license reassignment is exactly the admin-role work most agencies underestimate. Design-forward positioning can undersell backend complexity, so push on permissions and sync.

6. Miquido

Stack: Golang, React, mobile, ML tooling
Best for: mobile-first products heavy on media

Poland, 2011, 250+ people, mid-tier.

Technical note: built Brainly's Content Tool in Golang and React in 3 months, after which 50% of questions were answered within 24 hours and users saved about 3 hours a week. That's a throughput result on a moderation-style workflow, which is a genuinely hard queueing problem.

7. Cleveroad

Stack: custom web and iOS
Best for: mid-size European teams wanting LMS breadth

Estonia with Ukraine delivery, 2011, 200+ people, $25 to $49/hr, the lowest band here.

Technical note: replaced Crossfader's WordPress setup with a custom web and iOS build for 5,000+ users, including an offline iOS mode and a subscription revenue feature. The offline mode is the detail worth asking about, since most agencies on this list have not shipped one. Broad portfolio, so confirm end-to-end ownership.

8. Geniusee

Stack: MediaSoup SFU, Fabric.js, Node ecosystem
Best for: seed-stage founders wanting a senior-heavy team

Estonia and Ukraine, 2016, 150+ people, mid-tier.

Technical note: the most interesting stack detail on the list. Built an AI-enabled virtual classroom for K-12 tutoring on a MediaSoup SFU with a Fabric.js collaborative whiteboard. Running your own SFU rather than buying Twilio or Agora is a real latency-versus-ops tradeoff, and they made it deliberately. Case studies lean SaaS-adjacent, so confirm education-native depth.

9. Brocoders

Stack: Node.js, React, React Native, AWS
Best for: MVP-to-scaling edtech founders wanting shipped vertical proof

Estonia, 2011, 60 to 70 people at roughly 60% senior, $80k+ typical MVP floor.

Technical note: five named edtech builds across four segments, which is the part worth checking. 99math for gamified elementary math. Kiddom for K-12 digital curriculum. Kedzoh for mobile corporate training, which took Startup Chile, Brazil, and French Tech Ticket awards. Casers for higher-ed talent acquisition. HeyPractice, an AI-powered sales and marketing training platform on Node.js and React with AWS CI/CD and GDPR compliance built in rather than added. Roles, offline behavior, and accessibility get decided in a paid discovery phase instead of a fixed feature-list quote. In-house DevOps, and bcboilerplates.com covers auth and RBAC scaffolding so sprint one goes into the domain. Brocoders. Not an edtech-only shop, unlike ScienceSoft or Cleveroad.

Modeling the three roles properly

The mistake is making role an enum on the user. The fix is separating identity from scoped membership:

user            → a person, one account, one login
organization    → district, school, or company
membership      → user × org × role, scoped
   (a user can be a teacher in one school and a parent in another)
course / cohort → the unit work is assigned against
enrollment      → membership × cohort, with its own capabilities

permission check = can(membership, action, resource)
   never  if (user.role === 'teacher')

Two rules make this hold up. Permissions are checked against a resource, not a page, so "can view grades" is always "can view grades for this cohort." And the check lives in one policy layer that every route and every background job calls, because a report generator that skips the check is the same leak as a controller that does.

Roster provisioning deserves its own thought. Schools arrive with CSVs, Clever, ClassLink, or an LTI 1.3 launch from an existing LMS, and each of those creates users differently. Decide early which are in scope; retrofitting LTI into an auth flow built for email signup is a rewrite of the session layer.

For offline: the learner app is the one that needs it, and the conflict cases are narrow. Answers submitted offline are append-only and replay with a client-generated op_id. Progress is a counter that merges rather than overwrites. Content is cached with a version, and an assignment changed by the teacher mid-session surfaces as a visible update rather than a silent swap.

Cost bands

MVP timelines run 8 to 16 weeks, driven mostly by how many roles ship in v1 and whether offline is in scope.

Pre-build checklist

  • Role model as scoped memberships, not a user enum, from migration 001
  • One policy layer every route and every background job calls
  • Roster provisioning decided: CSV, Clever, ClassLink, or LTI 1.3, chosen before the auth flow is written
  • Offline scope named per role, with conflict rules written down
  • Idempotency: op_id on submitted work, so replay never double-counts
  • WCAG: automated axe in CI plus a manual keyboard and screen reader pass before any district demo
  • Content versioning so a mid-session curriculum change doesn't corrupt a learner's attempt
  • Data handling: FERPA or GDPR scoped early, including what leaves the region
  • Support model: bug-fix SLA that names the back-to-school window explicitly
  • Ownership: repo, infrastructure, deployment scripts, and a documented exit path

If you're scoping an edtech build

Write down what each of the three roles sees and does before you talk to anyone. It takes an afternoon and it changes which of these nine is the right size for the job. Happy to work through it with you, including telling you plainly if the segment isn't ours. brocoders.com

title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
description:
arXiv:2610.12855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR.

title: winnow-args: yet another args parser
description:
winnow-args is a command line parser for Rust, built on winnow.

Why another one

There are plenty of great crates already, why adding one more given that you have clap, bpaf and usage?

All of them are quite good for different purposes:

  • clap is pretty much the standard, quite user-friendly, but bit slow and not as flexible as you want once you need to parse something more than the usual --long, -l options.
  • bpaf is way more flexible, but not built for speed.
  • usage-rs has a very interesting approach to get the best performance while having as many features as clap.

Sadly the 3 do not have at the same time the flexibility and speed I need.

Speed on the cli?

In brush, every builtin is a small command line: set -eu, declare -x NAME=value, printf -v var '%s' x.

A script runs thousands of them, so the parser runs thousands of times in one process, and a parser that builds its
description of the command at each call is paid for at each call.

Builtins also have to support patterns that are not so common, e.g: set +x turns off what set -x turns on.

I'm using brush extensively in my portage rewrite to parse ebuilds, anything that gets me a bit of speed is welcome.

How can a cli be annoyingly irregular?

One of the most annoying and yet widely used cli syntax is the one used by the GNU linker and thus supported by lld, mold and wild.

Since I started looking at supporting more special pattern I decided to tackle also that. Sadly the mold author prefers the current bespoke solution at least so far.

Here few examples on how irregular it can be:

ld -shared -o out.so --as-needed -lc a.o -z now
  • long options with one dash: -shared
  • short options with arguments: -o and -z
  • flags whose order matters: --as-needed applies to the libraries after it.

And it can get even more complex.

winnow-args

Under the hood it leverages winnow zero-copy combinators over a slice of &OsStr, that maps neatly with the native BStr provided.

To make it easier to use a derive is provided in a fashion similar to the other crates.

  • A struct is a command line.
  • A field in the struct is a flag or a positional, its doc comment is its help.
  • Enums can be used to express possible values or subcommands.

Here some examples:

mini-mise

This example uses subcommands, aliases, dynamic custom values, examples, runtime completion support and colored help.

use winnow_args::color::{Color, Paint, Palette, Theme};
use winnow_args::complete::{Candidate, Shell};
use winnow_args::{Args, Subcommand, ValueEnum, report_with};

/// Install and run development tools
#[derive(Args, Debug)]
#[arg(
    name = "tool",
    version,
    default_subcommand = "use",
    example("tool use -g node@22", header = "Install a tool for every project"),
    example = "tool ls --json"
)]
struct Cli {
    /// Show more (repeat for more)
    #[arg(short, long, count, global)]
    verbose: u8,
    /// When to use color
    #[arg(long, global, default = "auto")]
    color: When,
    #[arg(subcommand)]
    command: Command,
}

#[derive(ValueEnum, Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum When {
    Auto,
    Always,
    Never,
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Debug)]
enum Command {
    /// Install a tool and add it to the project
    #[arg(alias = "u", example = "tool use node@22 python@3.13")]
    Use {
        /// Use the global config instead of the project's
        #[arg(short, long)]
        global: bool,
        /// How many downloads run at once
        #[arg(short, long, default = "4", env = "TOOL_JOBS")]
        jobs: u32,
        /// What to install, as `name@version`
        #[arg(positional, required, complete = tools)]
        tools: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// List installed tools
    Ls {
        /// Print JSON
        #[arg(long)]
        json: bool,
    },
    /// Remove a tool
    #[arg(alias = "rm")]
    Remove {
        /// The tool to remove, as `name@version`
        #[arg(positional, complete = tools)]
        tool: String,
        /// Remove it even if a project uses it
        #[arg(short, long, warning = "Projects that pin it will stop working.")]
        force: bool,
    },
    /// Print a completion script
    Completion {
        #[arg(positional)]
        shell: Shell,
    },
}

/// What a shell offers for a tool, given what is typed of it.
fn tools(typed: &str) -> Vec<Candidate> {
    ["node@20", "node@22", "python@3.13", "ruby@3.4", "zig@0.15"]
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|tool| tool.starts_with(typed))
        .map(|tool| Candidate {
            value: tool.to_owned(),
            help: "",
        })
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<_> = std::env::args_os().skip(1).collect();
    if let Some(answer) = Cli::completion_request(&args) {
        print!("{answer}");
        return;
    }
    let cli = match Cli::parse_from(&args) {
        Ok(cli) => cli,
        // Help and version end up here too: `report_with` prints and says how to exit. The theme() implementation is further below.
        Err(error) => std::process::exit(report_with(&error, "tool", &theme())),
    };
    if let Command::Completion { shell } = cli.command {
        print!("{}", Cli::completion_script(shell));
        return;
    }
    println!("{cli:#?}");
}

Help, from the doc comments

-h is the summary and --help the whole text. A subcommand's page lists the global flags it
inherits, a flag can carry a warning, and the examples are declared, not pasted into a string.

Palettes and themes

Help and errors are painted from a palette, and the terminal says how deep it goes: no color in a pipe or under NO_COLOR, the 16 basic colors, 256, or 24 bits.

A theme is a palette for each depth.
The default one, on a 16-color and on a 256-color terminal:

With NO_COLOR=1, or in a pipe:

A program brings its own with a few lines. Here one palette for 24-bit terminals, and clap's look for people who are used to it:

/// The paints of help and errors: `TOOL_THEME` picks one.
fn theme() -> Theme {
    const fn rgb(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) -> Paint {
        Paint::fg(Color::Rgb(r, g, b))
    }
    // On a 24-bit terminal only; the others keep the default palettes.
    const SUNSET: Palette = Palette {
        header: rgb(255, 158, 100).bold(),
        flag: rgb(224, 175, 104).bold(),
        command: rgb(224, 175, 104).bold(),
        placeholder: rgb(187, 154, 247),
        default: rgb(247, 118, 142),
        choice: rgb(247, 118, 142),
        ..Palette::DEFAULT_256
    };
    match std::env::var("TOOL_THEME").as_deref() {
        // clap's own look: bold and underline, color only in errors.
        Ok("clap") => Theme {
            ansi16: Palette::CLAP,
            ansi256: None,
            truecolor: None,
        },
        Ok("sunset") => Theme {
            truecolor: Some(SUNSET),
            ..Theme::DEFAULT
        },
        _ => Theme::DEFAULT,
    }
}

Extended error reporting

Completion that asks the program

tool completion fish prints a short script that calls the program back, so the shell always offers what this build of the program takes.

Flags come with their descriptions, a value with its choices, and complete = tools above hands the question to a function of yours.

bash, zsh, fish, elvish and PowerShell are supported.

Exotic syntaxes

  • -eu +x is three fields of type Option<bool>, each declared #[arg(short = 'e', plus = 'e')].

The linker's flags are an enum, and the struct holds them in the order they were given.

Under the hood

The derive produces the following:

  • the parser
  • the help as static data
  • optionally a toml description.

At run time the words go through a small lexer, the generated parser binds each to its field, FromArg turns a word into a
value, and a last step applies the environment, the defaults and the rules between fields.

Help, the tips in errors and completion all read the same static data, and only when needed.

The toml descriptions are needed by the documentation builders. They read the files the derive writes on request and they do not depend on running the code generated for the target architecture.

Key features

  • The parser is generated at compile time. The derive writes a match over the flags of your struct. Nothing is assebled when the program starts, so a program with two hundred subcommands starts parsing as fast as one with two.
  • Words are borrowed. Nothing is copied or re-split, and the bytes need not be UTF-8 until a field's type asks for text.
  • Mistakes in the declaration are compile errors. A conflicts("nme") that names no field, two flags with the same letter, a positional after a list that takes every word: the build fails.
  • Help is data. The prose sits in read-only memory until --help asks for it, and a feature leaves it out of the binary altogether if it is not needed.

Everything is a winnow parser, so you can build your own by combining the basic parsers together manually.

Performance

winnow-args is built essentially for speed first, comfort as close second.

The repository has two benchmarks used to make sure adding features won't cause slow downs.

It compares with the other argument parsers I normally use:

a small CLI mise's 211 commands
winnow-args 187 ns 327 ns
usage 7 516 ns 767 ns
clap 4 15.0 µs 757 µs
bpaf 0.9 14.8 µs 2.65 ms

The same command lines are written once per framework in the repository's benchmarks/.

A program that parses once will not feel the difference with clap on a small command line. A shell does, and so does a tool with as many subcommands as mise.

Implemented features

A good deal of features are already implemented, but some found on more mature parsers are still missing.

winnow-args usage clap
Flags, values, positionals, subcommands, global flags, flatten ✓ ✓ ✓
Conflicts, requirements, groups ✓ ✓ ✓
Help from doc comments ✓ ✓ ✓
Completion scripts ✓ ✓ ~
Parser generated at compile time, words borrowed ✓ ✓ –
Combinators, without a macro ✓ – ~
+x options, as a shell builtin takes ✓ – –
Long options with one dash, -z keywords, as GNU ld takes ✓ – –
Flags kept in command-line order ✓ ~ ~
Flag constraints checked at compile time ✓ – –
Help prose left out of the binary by a feature ✓ ~ –
A CLI built at runtime, external subcommands – ✓ ✓
Conditional requirements (required_if) – ✓ ✓
Man pages, markdown ~ ✓ ~
"Did you mean" suggestions ✓ ✓ ✓

winnow-args-man and winnow-args-markdown render one page per command.

They do not run the program to build it:

  • when WINNOW_ARGS_SPEC set, the derives write a description of each type while cargo check or cargo build expands them.
  • the pages are built from those files.

So man pages can be built correctly even when cross compiling.

In closing

With version 0.3.0 winnow-args graduated from being a quick experiment to see how far I could push the parsing performance and now it can be used to deal with the quirks of complex CLIs.

Some features that I didn't need to support brush and portage-cli em are still missing and I have plans to add a more flexible generator based on minijinja, but I welcome you to try it and possibly provide feedback and pull requests to improve it further.

title: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning
description:
arXiv:2610.13536v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When a language model is distilled from a teacher that shares its base parameters, the student can inherit behavioural traits of the teacher---including misalignment---even from data that is semantically unrelated to the trait (Cloud et al., 2026). All existing defences require knowing the trait. We remove this requirement and prove that a subliminally transferred trait can be recovered from the parameter updates alone, without supervision, by exploiting a single asymmetry: the trait is expressed consistently across diverse datasets generated by the teacher, whereas task-specific and shared capabilities vary. The resulting estimator returns a weight-space direction that can be amplified to discover and interpret the trait or projected out to suppress it. Applied to the subliminal-learning benchmarks of (Cloud et al., 2026), our method recovers the transmitted animal-preference traits without any trait labels and suppresses their expression with almost no impact to task performance.

title: AI Gateway adds unified fast mode support
description:
AI Gateway has a unified fast mode abstraction, now in beta.

You can now request fast mode the same way for every model on AI Gateway. Set speed to fast, and the gateway serves the fast tier when it's available and falls back to standard speed when it isn't.

Fast mode trades a higher per-token cost for lower latency or higher throughput. You get it wherever it is available, without pinning a provider or wiring anything up yourself.

Requesting fast mode

Set speed to fast under providerOptions.gateway to upgrade the model to its fast serving path when one is routable:

You can also address a fast variant directly with its fast slug, such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-fast, which is the same as setting speed: 'fast' on the base model.

Use the speed option when you want to stay on the base model ID and fall back to standard speed. Use a fast slug when you want to name the fast variant directly, for example in a gateway.models fallback list. The speed option works across every AI Gateway API format.

Fast mode is available for a growing set of models. Find them in the models list with a lightning bolt next to the slug. Requesting fast mode on a model with no fast tier has no effect, and the request runs at standard speed. Fast variants of models are usually more expensive than the base model: check pricing for more details.

Using fast mode in coding agents

In Claude Code, toggle fast mode with /fast for Anthropic Opus models after setup. For other agents, select a fast slug in your model configuration, such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-fast.

For more information about fast mode, read the documentation.

title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: MiniMax H3 now available on AI Gateway
description:
MiniMax H3 is now available on AI Gateway.

H3 generates 2K video from a text prompt, a starting image, a pair of first and last frames, or reference material.

title: Vercel WAF for Blob is now generally available
description:
Vercel WAF for Blob is now generally available and supported for production use on all plans. If you protected a store during the beta, nothing has changed: your rules and setup carry over exactly as they are.

Vercel WAF protects a Blob store with custom rules, the same kind you use to guard your deployments. Rules that match on properties like IP address, country, and path can deny, challenge, or rate limit requests to your stored objects. This requires no changes to your code, your blob URLs, or how you use @vercel/blob.

Rules are evaluated at Vercel's edge, so a denied request is turned away before any data transfer occurs. Unwanted traffic to AI-generated media, user uploads, or paid downloads never reaches your store and never generates a bill.

To enable protection, open your Blob store's Settings tab, and in the Firewall section select Protect your store, then Enable firewall. This connects the store to a dedicated team-wide project where your Blob firewall rules live, shared by every store you protect.

Read the Blob security documentation to protect a store.

title: Semantic Views: Certified Reuse of LLM Labels Across Semantic Queries
description:
arXiv:2610.12768v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Semantic query engines evaluate natural-language filters with a large language model, and every evaluation is a costly oracle call. Optimizers that reduce these calls face a dilemma: cascades that trust a cheap proxy miss their precision and recall targets on many queries, methods with finite-sample guarantees save little, and all of them discard the oracle's labels when the query ends. We present SemViews, a certified semantic filter that orders tuples by signals that cost no oracle calls (the labels that earlier queries left behind as semantic views, a local embedding, and a helper model's score), refines that order with labels it must pay for anyway, and certifies its answer with fresh stratified oracle samples. The answer meets user precision and recall targets with probability at least $1-\delta$ for every workload and every catalog, so a stale or misleading view can cost oracle calls but never accuracy. On four workloads replayed against 725,000 recorded oracle labels, SemViews meets both targets on 99.63% of queries and saves 28%-45% of the oracle calls, whereas the only prior method in our study with the same guarantee needs 1.32x-1.71x as many calls. When a question returns in different words, views cut its calls by a further 27%-36%, with both targets met on at least 99.8% of such queries; similarity caches and entailment-based reuse meet them on only 17%-47%.

title: RepoDNA v1.3.2: A Dedicated Documentation Website and Reliability Improvements
description:
RepoDNA v1.3.2: A Dedicated Documentation Website and Reliability Improvements

Tags: opensource, rust, devtools, webdev

RepoDNA v1.3.2 is now available!

This release introduces a dedicated documentation website and improves several parts of the project's error handling, GitHub Actions downloads, and documentation workflow.

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence and code archaeology tool. It helps developers explore code structure, architecture, dependencies, Git history, quality signals, and project evolution.

The goal is to make a repository easier to understand—not just easier to browse.

A documentation website of its own

The documentation now has a dedicated home:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/docs/

The site brings together the project's guides, changelog, roadmap, policies, examples, benchmarks, and fixtures.

It includes:

  • Search across documentation sections.
  • A sidebar that follows the documentation index.
  • Previous and next page navigation.
  • Copy buttons for code examples.
  • Light and dark themes.
  • Responsive layouts for phones.
  • Print-friendly pages.
  • Links between related guides and repository files.

The documentation is published alongside the web version, making the guides easier to discover and navigate.

Better error handling

The repodna-wasm component now reports missing files and folders more clearly.

Previously, some invalid inputs could surface low-level Node.js errors or be treated as the wrong kind of input. The improved behavior explains what is missing and clarifies when commands such as report or card require an analysis file.

More reliable GitHub Actions downloads

Temporary failures from GitHub's servers could cause downloads to fail after only a short period.

The GitHub Action now retries download attempts for up to two minutes and provides a more accurate error when a download actually fails.

The guide for the action has also been updated to include the security-only profile in its supported profile options.

Documentation checks

The development and documentation workflows now check for broken links and anchors. This helps catch navigation problems before changes are released.

The project also updates documentation destinations and support links across the relevant application and repository pages.

Why this release matters

Documentation is part of the developer experience. It should be easy to search, navigate, read on a small screen, and use while working through real development problems.

Likewise, errors should explain what went wrong, and automation should distinguish temporary infrastructure failures from genuinely missing files.

Those improvements make the project easier to explore and maintain.

Try RepoDNA

Release notes:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.3.2

Documentation:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/docs/

Web version:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

Source code:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA

RepoDNA remains focused on local-first analysis and evidence-backed findings, with optional AI explanations rather than AI as a requirement.

Feedback, testing, contributions, and ideas for future releases are welcome.

title: ZenGen: Social Mind for LLMs
description:
arXiv:2607.23740v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As large language models move from isolated task solving toward long-term service in human environments, they require social intelligence: the ability to infer mental states, track social relations, reason over norms, and adapt behavior under context. This report presents ZenGen, an integrated framework for measuring, internalizing, and grounding social intelligence. For measurement, we introduce SoMBench, a psychology-grounded benchmark spanning 3 primary dimensions, 17 secondary dimensions, and 71 task paradigms. It controls question format, narrative perspective, and context length across 284 shared scenarios and 3,481 expert-verified instances. Evaluation of 20 representative LLMs reveals substantial headroom: the best model achieves only 72.08% overall accuracy, and none of the 17 secondary dimensions reaches the 90% near-ceiling band. For internalization, we develop ZenGen, a diagnosis-driven training recipe combining supervised fine-tuning, on-policy distillation, and rubric-based reinforcement learning. Across five social-cognition benchmarks, ZenGen consistently outperforms its base models, with ZenGen-27B-Stage2 achieving the best average score and ZenGen-32B-Stage2 remaining competitive with DeepSeek-V4-Pro. For deployment-time grounding, we build Actio, a harness-controlled inference architecture that routes four typed supports into reasoning: PRISM for procedural guidance, Starling for runtime mental-state representation, SAGE for reusable experience, and gated RAG for external social and normative knowledge. Across five base models and three benchmarks, the full harness improves 14 of 15 model-benchmark pairs and is best or tied for best in 8, demonstrating the effectiveness of typed runtime support. Together, these results show that socially intelligent LLMs require coordinated advances in evaluation, parametric internalization, and deployment-time grounding.

title: When LLMs Sit Above Diagnostic Tools: Unrealized Complementarity in Industrial Fault Diagnosis
description:
arXiv:2610.05031v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as integration layers above specialized tools, but a stronger component does not necessarily produce a stronger combined system. Across five diagnostic datasets (bearing vibration, process monitoring, semiconductor equipment), we study whether an LLM can reliably use external diagnostic information; paired repeat calls separate advice effects from output instability. In all five, conflicting external information overturned initially correct LLM judgments. Among the four datasets with direct integration comparisons, none showed a consistent advantage for implicit LLM integration over the stronger standalone source. On a Tennessee Eastman confirmation set whose protocol was fixed before evaluation, unaided accuracy was 64.67%, implicit LLM-specialist integration 77.43%, and the specialist alone 83.33%. Specialist information improved the LLM by 12.8 points (95% interval 9.7 to 15.9), yet the integrated output stayed 5.9 points below the specialist (95% interval -12.0 to -0.7). A two-source selector oracle reached 92.76%, indicating complementarity that the integrated output did not fully realize. The integrated output missed 140 of 295 specialist corrections (47.5%) but lost 15 of 99 initially correct LLM judgments (15.2%). The deficit remained under prompt and specialist sensitivity analyses. Among CWRU cases solved under both evidence presentations, task-aligned physical evidence yielded lower estimates of susceptibility to incorrect advice in six of seven models (five intervals excluding zero); higher reasoning effort gave no reliable reduction in five models, and a separate four-model TEP analysis gave no clear evidence that it resolves the integration problem. Source quality and integration quality should be evaluated separately: an integration layer should be compared with its stronger standalone component, not only with the unaided LLM.

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

Read more

title: ReasoningShield: Safety Detection over Reasoning Traces of Large Reasoning Models
description:
arXiv:2505.17244v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) leverage explicit reasoning traces, known as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, to decompose complex problems into intermediate steps before deriving final answers. However, these reasoning traces introduce unique safety challenges: harmful content can be embedded in intermediate steps even when final answers appear benign. Our study reveals that existing state-of-the-art moderation tools experience significant performance degradation on CoT moderation, with F1 scores dropping by up to 35.2% compared to traditional answer moderation. To address these challenges, we present ReasoningShield, a comprehensive benchmark and a suite of strong lightweight models for CoT safety moderation. Our benchmark includes 9.2K annotated (Query, CoT) pairs with structured stepwise risk analysis, consisting of a 7K-sample training set and a 2.2K human-annotated test set, spanning 10 risk categories, 3 safety levels, and 8 LRMs with diverse reasoning paradigms. To further demonstrate the utility of the benchmark, we develop lightweight models with 1B/3B parameters using a two-stage training strategy. Our models achieve 91.8% F1 on our benchmark, substantially outperforming leading tools such as LlamaGuard-4 by 35.6% and commercial models such as GPT-4o by 15.8%, while generalizing effectively across diverse reasoning paradigms and unseen scenarios. Resources are publicly available: Project Page: https://cosmosyi.github.io/ReasoningShield/, Code: https://github.com/CosmosYi/ReasoningShield, Models: https://huggingface.co/ReasoningShield/models, and Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReasoningShield/ReasoningShield-Dataset.

title: Exporting a paginated task feed without losing provenance
description:
A JSON endpoint is easy to download. A complete, attributable snapshot takes a little more care.

I maintain Instinct Tasks, an independent, unofficial guide. Its public /api/tasks endpoint returns an envelope containing protocolVersion, snapshot, items, nextCursor and checkpoint. In the October 10 export, the first response contained 20 items. Treating that response as the whole library would have missed most of the 128 records.

The export therefore follows nextCursor until it is empty. Every response must have the same snapshot identifier. If that identifier changes, the export should stop and be investigated or restarted rather than silently mixing versions.

There are three useful integrity checks after pagination:

  • Task IDs are unique across the collected responses.
  • Each task URL belongs to the expected guide domain.
  • Each record retains its source URLs and evidence type.

The first check catches duplicate pages. The second catches a wrong-domain export. The third preserves the distinction between a community report and an example published by the product maker. None of these checks proves that the underlying task works; they verify the structure and provenance of the export.

Here is a small local inspection of the completed snapshot:

import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

snapshot = json.loads(Path("tasks.json").read_text())
tasks = snapshot["items"]
assert len(tasks) == len({task["taskId"] for task in tasks})
print(Counter(task["evidenceType"] for task in tasks))
for task in tasks:
    print(task["title"], task["url"], task["sources"])

For this export, the evidence labels were 124 user reports and four official examples. They are counts of published records, not trial results or adoption statistics.

The snapshot also records its retrieval time, original endpoint and snapshot ID. A checksum in the README identifies the exact file. That makes it possible to discuss a fixed version even as the website changes.

The resulting reference repository is https://github.com/1021ju/instinct-tasks. It contains published metadata, not private tasks or execution logs. Source links are retained, and no blanket open-source license is asserted for third-party materials. The guide is not affiliated with Instinct and has not independently reproduced the source examples.

title: Validando e consultando CPF em Go: pacote enxuto, context e testes table-driven
description:
Transparência: sou fundador da CPFHub, uma das APIs citadas no final. O pacote de validação é independente.

Go é ótimo para serviços de backend que recebem cadastro em alto volume. Vamos escrever um pacote cpf pequeno, sem dependências, e um cliente HTTP que respeita context, timeout e limites de taxa.

1. O pacote 

package cpf

import "strings"

// Normalize remove tudo que não for dígito ASCII.
func Normalize(s string) string {
    var b strings.Builder
    for _, r := range s {
        if r >= '0' && r <= '9' {
            b.WriteRune(r)
        }
    }
    return b.String()
}

// Valid confere tamanho, sequência repetida e dígitos verificadores.
func Valid(s string) bool {
    c := Normalize(s)
    if len(c) != 11 || strings.Count(c, c[:1]) == 11 {
        return false
    }
    for t := 9; t < 11; t++ {
        sum := 0
        for i := 0; i < t; i++ {
            sum += int(c[i]-'0') * (t + 1 - i)
        }
        if int(c[t]-'0') != sum*10%11%10 {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

// Format aplica a máscara 000.000.000-00.
func Format(s string) string {
    c := Normalize(s)
    if len(c) != 11 {
        return s
    }
    return c[:3] + "." + c[3:6] + "." + c[6:9] + "-" + c[9:]
}

2. Testes table-driven 

func TestValid(t *testing.T) {
    cases := []struct {
        in   string
        want bool
    }{
        {"529.982.247-25", true},
        {"52998224725", true},
        {"11111111111", false},
        {"52998224724", false},
        {"", false},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        if got := Valid(c.in); got != c.want {
            t.Errorf("Valid(%q) = %v, want %v", c.in, got, c.want)
        }
    }
}

Vale adicionar um fuzz test (go test -fuzz) garantindo que Valid nunca entra em pânico com entrada arbitrária.

3. Cliente HTTP

Depois que o DV passa, uma API externa confirma se o CPF existe. Um cliente idiomático:

type Data struct {
    CPF       string `json:"cpf"`
    Name      string `json:"name"`
    Gender    string `json:"gender"`
    BirthDate string `json:"birthDate"`
}

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("cpf não encontrado")

type RateLimitError struct{ RetryAfter string }

func (e RateLimitError) Error() string { return "limite por minuto; retry-after " + e.RetryAfter }

type Client struct {
    HTTP   *http.Client
    APIKey string
}

func (c *Client) Lookup(ctx context.Context, raw string) (*Data, error) {
    n := cpf.Normalize(raw)
    if !cpf.Valid(n) {
        return nil, errors.New("cpf inválido")
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.cpfhub.io/cpf/"+n, nil)
    req.Header.Set("x-api-key", c.APIKey)

    res, err := c.HTTP.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()

    switch res.StatusCode {
    case http.StatusOK:
        var body struct {
            Success bool `json:"success"`
            Data    Data `json:"data"`
        }
        if err := json.NewDecoder(res.Body).Decode(&body); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return &body.Data, nil
    case http.StatusNotFound:
        return nil, ErrNotFound
    case http.StatusTooManyRequests:
        return nil, RateLimitError{res.Header.Get("Retry-After")}
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d", res.StatusCode)
    }
}

Uso:

c := &Client{HTTP: &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, APIKey: os.Getenv("CPFHUB_API_KEY")}
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
defer cancel()
d, err := c.Lookup(ctx, "529.982.247-25")
switch {
case errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound):
    // trate como resultado normal
case err != nil:
    var rl RateLimitError
    if errors.As(err, &rl) { /* reagende */ }
}

4. Controlando a taxa do seu lado

Toda API tem limite por minuto. Em vez de descobrir isso tomando 429, limite antes com golang.org/x/time/rate:

lim := rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(2*time.Second), 1) // 30/min
for _, doc := range docs {
    if err := lim.Wait(ctx); err != nil { break }
    go process(doc)
}

Para listas grandes, prefira um endpoint de lote se o provedor tiver: uma requisição em vez de milhares.

5. Dicas

  • Nunca logue o CPF completo; use Format com mascaramento (***.982.247-**) nos logs.
  • Use errors.Is/As em vez de comparar strings de erro.
  • Não reutilize http.DefaultClient: ele não tem timeout.

Sobre a CPFHub

O cliente acima já está apontado para a CPFHub: GET /cpf/{cpf} com x-api-key, ~150 ms típicos (não SLA), 404 sem custo, e um POST /cpf/bulk para listas de até 10.000 CPFs. O plano gratuito tem 50 créditos por mês. Mais na documentação.
