title: First-Order In-Context Shapley: Scalable Data Auditing for LLM Alignment and Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2607.22766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Post-training alignment of Large Language Models is increasingly bottlenecked by data quality: preference and instruction-tuning corpora accumulate label noise, safety inversions, and inter-annotator contradictions that deduplication misses and full-corpus LLM judging cannot afford. While Data Shapley offers a principled valuation framework, exact computation requires intractable retraining, and embedding surrogates like KNN-Shapley fail to separate high- from low-utility demonstrations ($\rho = 0.0003$ with generative utility). We introduce an inference-only valuation pipeline that computes the first-order term of an in-context cooperative game over semantic $k$-NN neighborhoods in $O(k)$ forward passes without parameter updates, correlating positively with multi-shot Monte-Carlo in-context Shapley on 100% of targets at 19x less compute. Projecting pairwise log-likelihood shifts onto a directed influence graph characterizes each record via three signals: outgoing Exemplifying Advantage, incoming Exemplified Advantage, and a topological One-of-a-Kind Score protecting rare prompts. Pre-filtering restricts LLM twin arbitration to 1%-5% of records while achieving 4.5x enrichment in confirmed errors on HelpSteer2 and 2.2x on Anthropic HH-RLHF, catching contradictions that zero-shot likelihood and margin filters miss. During DPO training, confirmed contradictions oppose the update far more often than clean records (56.7% vs. 37.0% in LoRA gradients) and stay below chance in reward accuracy. Finally, auditing the HH-RLHF benchmark exposes label errors where aligned models disagree with human labels 73%-83% of the time, and retraining DPO after repairing or filtering flagged records improves reward accuracy by +0.5%-0.6% overall and +3.1%-3.5% on repaired inversions, even without LLM arbitration.

title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.13277v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
description:
arXiv:2610.13790v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.

title: People Making Conversation: Evaluating How Naturally Speech Models Converse
description:
arXiv:2610.12802v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A conversational speech model has to decide, at every pause, whether to speak. Existing evaluations test boundary detection, policy adherence, or aggregate statistics, not this decision. We place real-time speech systems at 427 pauses and 482 turn ends from 176 unscripted conversations in Seamless Interaction, give each the conversation so far, and score what it generates against what the person did: whether and how soon it speaks at a pause; its latency, length, and wording at a turn end; and whether it can answer a question about the preceding 30 to 120 seconds. Across six systems, the hosted APIs (GPT Realtime, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Grok Voice) respond at almost every pause whichever endpointer they use; only their latency, about 1 to 4 s with silence-based endpointers and about 8 s with semantic turn detection, decides whether the words land inside the pause. The full-duplex models (PersonaPlex, Moshi) are the only systems that regularly stay silent and the only ones that interrupt within a human reaction time. Hosted systems reply longer than the person. Given the history as text, hosted systems recall 41 to 60% of conversation facts under a Claude Opus 5.5 judge and 19 to 26% under a strict word matcher; hearing it as audio, full-duplex models recall 17 to 22% and 12 to 15%. We release the labels, points, harness, and every output.

title: The Alignment Veto: How Safety Training Suppresses Cultural Knowledge in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2510.13154v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: What happens inside a language model when alignment training conflicts with a cultural value it encodes? Across 16 MENA countries, 26 models, and 1.53M human survey responses, we show the answer is suppression, not erasure: at the moment of refusal, a model's internal logit distribution correlates with human survey data more strongly than its freely generated answers. We call this the alignment veto. We distinguish suppression failures (accurate internal distributions blocked at output) from representational bias failures (the encoding itself diverges from human values), and show the two require different interventions. The gate is inequitable: the safety tax reaches 37.6%, with a 19.8% alignment-quality gap between best- and worst-served nations, and native-language prompting widens rather than closes it. Sparse autoencoder analysis corroborated by comparisons across alignment stages identifies a candidate DPO-stage feature mediating suppression in Tulu-3-8B. The gate is real, its costs are unequal, and deciding what it should protect is not a technical question.

title: I tested 4 'uncensored' AI image generators against their own written policies
description:
Most "uncensored AI generator" content does one of two things: runs a prompt and reports whether it worked, or quotes a policy page and stops there. Neither one tells you the one thing that matters, whether a platform's written rules predict what it will draw.

So this is an audit, not just a test. Four tools, three identical prompts, one revision. For each tool, I'm pairing the test result against that tool's own published policy, and flagging every place the two didn't line up. If you typed "ai image generator no restrictions" into a search bar, or you're hunting for the best uncensored AI image generator specifically, the mismatches here tell you more than either the test or the policy alone. Read it as a map of which platform works as an AI image generator with fewer restrictions for your actual use case, not a search for the one tool with none at all.

Disclosure: this is a paid collaboration with PixAI. I ran every test myself and every judgment is mine.

The setup

Tools: PixAI with Tsubaki.3, SeaArt with Z Image Turbo, Tensor.Art with Krea-2-Turbo, NovelAI with V5 Full.

Date: October 2026. Plans: free plan or free trial on all four.

Settings: one image per prompt, default settings, PixAI's Prompt Helper off. Test 1 ran at 2:3 portrait, Tests 2 and 3 ran landscape.

Revision method: PixAI let me click the image and type the change directly. Tensor.Art and NovelAI had no prompt-based edit, so those two used image-to-image with the first image as the source.

Three prompts, run word for word on every tool:

  1. A hotel suite fashion editorial (new image), then a revision asking for a more daring pose and outfit.
  2. A monster hunter after a fight, with blood, a gun and a cigarette (new image).
  3. A kitchen fire with trigger words like "Bloody" and "knife" baked into the prompt (new image).

Each one stresses a different kind of filter: revealing clothing, violence and weapons, and keyword triggers that simple filters flag on sight regardless of context.

Audit: PixAI

What the policy says: 18 minimum age, NSFW tag system required for mature content, firm bans on sexualized minors, realistic explicit images and extremism. Sensitive content stays visible only to you. PixAI doesn't publish which tags count as sensitive; an AI moderator makes the first call, with human review on appeal.

What the test showed: the strongest Test 1 result of the four, keeping the satin bodysuit, sheer stockings, heels, pose, skyline, armchair and champagne intact. On the revision, it was also the only tool to change the pose with high quality, getting the seated position, the over-the-shoulder look and the moonlight. Test 2 was excellent, shadows and blood and the half-submerged creature reading as one coherent scene. Test 3 had strong fire and composition, but background faces came apart, with the photographer and a staff member both missing or poorly drawn eyes.


Left to right PixAI, SeaArt


Test 2- Left to right PixAI, SeaArt


PixAI the shadows, blood and creature hold together as one scene.


PixAI strong fire and lighting. Look at the photographer's face.

Where policy and result matched, and where they didn't: the policy says sensitive content stays private by default, and nothing in testing contradicted that since I never tested publishing.

The missing piece shows up elsewhere. Policy doesn't name which tags are sensitive, and in practice that made the revision prompt an interesting case: phrases like "no nudity or sexual activity," written into my own prompt as a safety clarification, didn't trigger any warning on PixAI the way the same phrases did on Tensor.Art.

That's not a contradiction, just an unlisted threshold working differently than you'd guess from the policy text alone.

The real mismatch is quality-based rather than policy-based: PixAI's own documented strength is anime fashion and character work, and the test confirmed that, but it also confirmed a known weak point with multiple background figures in one wide scene, which the policy page says nothing about since it's a capability limit, not a rule.

Audit: SeaArt

What the policy says: minimum age 12, with parental consent where needed. Written rule bans any image that isn't "G-rated," the strictest standard on paper of all four tools. Firmly bars pornographic and obscene material, along with content depicting public figures. Public images may be reused for promotion.

What the test showed: a good pass on Test 1, with brighter, flatter lighting than requested. On the revision, SeaArt did change the pose, placing her on the ledge with crossed legs, though the lamp stayed lit and the sheer panels went missing. Test 2 was a good pass with extra creatures drawn and a brighter station than the mood called for. Test 3 gave a dramatic fire with clear reactions, though the knife and towel were hard to spot.


SeaArt extra creatures and a brighter station.


SeaArt the fire fills the frame and pulls attention from the photographer.

Where policy and result didn't line up: this is the sharpest mismatch in the whole test. "G-rated" is the strictest written bar of any of the four platforms, and a fitted satin bodysuit with a plunging neckline and high-cut sides doesn't read as G-rated by any normal definition of the term. SeaArt generated it anyway, with no warning.

Either the written policy is aspirational rather than enforced at the filter level, or SeaArt's internal definition of "G-rated" is looser than the plain reading of its own terms. I can't tell which from one test, and SeaArt's policy page doesn't clarify it either.

Audit: Tensor.Art

What the policy says: no stated minimum age on the policy page itself, an omission that stands out on its own. Bars explicit content and nudity outright, firmly bans child sexual content, real celebrities and extreme violence. The platform states it's moving toward a fully safe-for-work model.

What the test showed: close behind PixAI on Test 1, with the best atmosphere of the four, though it added long sleeves nobody asked for. On the revision, Tensor.Art was the only tool in the entire test to show a policy warning: a red pop-up reading "nudity, sexual activity is not permitted" appeared when I pasted the prompt. It generated the image anyway, and she stayed standing, so the actual pose change never happened. Test 2 was excellent, dark horror mood, though it dropped the specified braided ponytail. Test 3 was the best of the four: every requested object in frame, every face complete.


Tensor.Art, NovelAI. All four kept the plunging bodysuit. Look for the long sleeves on Tensor.Art and NovelAI.


Tensor.Art's warning pop-up on the revision prompt.


Tensor.Art muted colours and a strong mood, but no braided ponytail.


Tensor.Art every requested object is in the frame, and every face is finished.

Where policy and result lined up exactly: the stated move toward a fully safe-for-work model predicts exactly what happened. My own prompt contained the phrases "no nudity or sexual activity" and "intimate areas," written as safety clarification, not as a request for anything explicit.

The filter flagged those words regardless of the actual content they were attached to, which is consistent with a keyword-level filter tuned conservatively ahead of a policy shift that's already in progress. This is the one case in the whole audit where the policy's stated direction and the test's observed behavior point the same way.

Audit: NovelAI

What the policy says: minimum age 18. Terms list no specific content categories. Reselling the service or sharing accounts is banned. Its Explore gallery is reviewed by hand under a strict "No NSFW" rule, and it rejects image-to-image and inpainting results from that gallery specifically.

What the test showed: a good pass on Test 1, brighter and flatter than requested, with added long sleeves. On the revision, NovelAI kept her standing, so the pose change didn't happen, and it turned the bodysuit into heavy lace, further than the subtle sheer panels the prompt asked for. Test 2 was a good pass, every character detail kept, though the station looked too clean for a scene set right after a fight. Test 3 dropped the photographer entirely, removing the actual point of the scene, while giving the tallest flames of the four.


Test 2-Tensor.Art, NovelAI. Only PixAI and SeaArt changed the pose. Look at PixAI's legs and the shoe near the floor


NovelAI every character detail kept, in a clean, bright station.


Anime illustration, cozy evening restaurant kitchen during a sudden kitchen accident

Where policy and result didn't line up: the terms listing no content categories reads, on its face, like the least restrictive policy of the four. The generation step backed that up, since nothing was refused. But the Explore gallery's hand-reviewed "No NSFW" rule and its rejection of image-to-image results specifically means the generation-time policy and the publishing-time policy are two different systems with two different standards, and the terms page doesn't flag that split anywhere. A tool can read as permissive at the point where you type a prompt and strict at the point where you try to share the result, and NovelAI is the cleanest example of that split in this set of four.

The pattern across all four

PixAI SeaArt Tensor.Art NovelAI
Written policy strictness Moderate, unlisted thresholds Strictest on paper (G-rated) Moderate, shifting stricter Loosest on paper
Matched test behavior Mostly, with one unlisted threshold No, generated a non-G-rated scene freely Yes, flagged safety language as written No, generation and publishing rules diverge
Revision handled well Best quality, anatomy errors Pose changed, details dropped Pose ignored, warning shown anyway Pose ignored, outfit overcorrected
Biggest capability shortfall Multiple background faces Flat lighting discipline None observed in this test Dropping a named figure entirely

No tool refused a single prompt across nine generations and one revision. That by itself tells you content-level refusal isn't really the differentiator between these four platforms anymore. The differentiator is whether what the policy claims predicts what shows up on screen, and on that measure, Tensor.Art is the only one of the four where the written rule and the tested behavior matched.

What this means if you're choosing one

If style quality and a direct text edit matter most, PixAI is the strongest of the four on both counts, and the policy gaps that showed up here were about unlisted thresholds, not contradictions. The Tsubaki.3 prompt guide covers how to write prompts in the style tested here. Watch background faces in crowded scenes specifically, since that's the one area the policy can't warn you about.

If you need several people drawn correctly in one frame, Tensor.Art earned that in testing, and its policy was also the most internally consistent of the four.

If free daily volume matters more than any of the above, Tensor.Art and SeaArt both gave noticeably larger free allowances than PixAI or NovelAI in this round. PixAI's free credits guide lists ways to add to the daily total if you want to stay on that platform anyway.

If keeping generations private matters most, NovelAI doesn't publish anything by default, though its generation-time leniency and its publishing-time strictness are two separate policies, not one.

If your actual question is about a specific kind of content, none of this audit answers it. Read each platform's current policy page directly, since every one of them can and does change independently of anything tested here.

FAQ

Does "uncensored" mean no content rules? No. All four platforms have published terms, and none of this testing changes what's legal where you live. "Uncensored" in practice means a platform filters less aggressively on a specific set of prompts, nothing more universal than that.

Is any of the four free and fully unlimited? No. Three give a free daily allowance and stop there. NovelAI's $25 Opus plan is unlimited only on older models at standard sizes, which excludes both the model and the revision method used in this test.

Can a policy's wording predict what a tool will generate? Sometimes. Tensor.Art's stated direction toward safe-for-work matched its test behavior closely. SeaArt's and NovelAI's written policies predicted the test results the least accurately of the four.

Nine generations, one revision, four different policy pages, and only one tool where the written rule and the tested behavior agreed. Run your own version of this audit before you commit to a platform based on its policy page alone, because the page and the product aren't always telling you the same thing.

title: One-Step Text Generation by Seq-Drifting
description:
arXiv:2610.12879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but still require multiple sampling steps to produce high-quality text. In this paper, we investigate whether a model can learn to generate an entire sequence in a single forward pass. We propose Seq-Drifting, a framework that applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations and directly learns a map from Gaussian noise to text. Unlike existing DLMs that derive the supervision at each position directly from the observed token in a training sequence, Seq-Drifting builds a drift field whose position-wise targets adapt to the current generated context. At each position, attraction guides each output toward a set of contextually plausible token representations, while repulsion discourages collapse across samples and repetition within sequences. The generator learns from this drift field during training and produces all tokens jointly in one pass at inference. Empirically, Seq-Drifting achieves a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and performs competitively in both unconditional and conditional generation. Experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning further demonstrate the applicability of the framework beyond open-ended generation. These results suggest that drifting over token sequences offers a promising path toward effective one-step text generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jyliu-ai/Seq-Drifting.

title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
description:
arXiv:2610.13840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.12602v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.

title: Node.js Cron Cleanup: Expired User Sessions, Token Ranges, and Public Endpoint Retries
description:
Short answer: for a Node.js cron cleanup of old user sessions and expired tokens in an edtech reservation system, let cron call a public HTTPS trigger, enqueue bounded cleanup jobs, and let an idempotent worker delete rows and tokens. The cron request is a signal, not the janitor.

That boundary matters when a student holds a seat for 20 minutes and then closes the tab. The reservation, session, and one-time token have different owners and different retry consequences. I want the database transaction to decide what is stale; I want the scheduler to decide when to look; and I want the worker to decide how much work fits in one attempt.

The decision record: three invariants and two failure edges

The first invariant is a cutoff, not a wall-clock guess. At 12:00 UTC, calculate expires_at <= 11:40 UTC for a 20-minute hold, then claim a bounded range of reservation IDs. A later retry must select the same logical work without reviving a reservation that has already been paid for.

The second invariant is idempotency. A standard queue is at-least-once, so the consumer may see the same range twice. Delete with a predicate such as status = 'held' AND expires_at <= cutoff, and make the state transition conditional. A duplicate delivery then becomes a no-op. FIFO deduplication is only a five-minute window; it is not a substitute for this database rule.

The third invariant is a failure boundary: cron has a 900-second execution ceiling and only calls a public http_url; it does not run your application code. A cleanup that might run longer must enqueue per-tenant or per-ID-range jobs. Keep the public endpoint thin, authenticate it with a secret that is separate from the user session, and return after the publish succeeds.

Infrai fits this handoff when you want the cron trigger and queue publish to share one plain REST API: a Node.js endpoint can call it over HTTPS without installing an SDK, and one key, one bill cover the trigger and queue handoff even when the worker runs in another language. It is a useful integration boundary, not a replacement for your database policy. Infrai gives one key and one bill for the scheduling and queue calls. The platform also exposes one consistent API across many backend capabilities, which keeps a later handoff from creating another integration. The concrete platform trade-off is one key, one wallet, one bill across the backend surface; its live discovery lists 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so a later storage or observability handoff can keep the same convention instead of adding another credential.

Small details become operational details.

The long tail is where this design earns its keep. Imagine three campuses closing enrollment at once: one has a clock skew, one has a burst of abandoned holds, and one is replaying a delivery after a database failover. The scheduler should still emit a bounded request, the queue should still carry a compact range rather than thousands of row IDs, and the SQL predicate should still refuse a reservation whose status changed to paid. The worker log needs tenant, range, cutoff, affected-row count, and correlation ID. Those fields let support answer “why did this seat reopen?” without reading a scheduler output buffer. They also make a replay safe: the same message can be consumed again after a process crash, and the conditional update simply finds fewer eligible rows. This is the difference between a timer that happens to call an endpoint and a retention policy that can be explained six weeks later. Cron expressions are conventional; an L extension is not available. A paused cron does not replay missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Run output history keeps only the first 4 KB, so the endpoint should emit a request ID and the application should keep the detailed log in Postgres or your log system.

How should Node.js cron cleanup handle expired sessions, tokens, and queue consumers?

The application can be Node.js even though this sample uses Python, because the important contract is HTTP plus a database transaction. The public trigger finds a cutoff, publishes one message per bounded range, and records the run. The worker consumes a message, performs the conditional update, and acknowledges only after the transaction commits.

Here is the critical path in deliberately plain Python. The first helper shows the two verified Infrai routes; the rest is application and database code. The publish_cleanup_ranges function is the application handler behind the public webhook; consume_once represents the worker loop. The message carries a deterministic id, so a retry cannot create a second logical cleanup task.

import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from hashlib import sha256

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

def infrai_request(method, path, payload):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ[\"INFRAI_API_KEY\"]}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(method, BASE_URL + path, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=30)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            delay = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(delay) if delay else 2 ** attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit did not clear")

def configure_cleanup(schedule, public_url, queue_name):
    requests.post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/create", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ[\"INFRAI_API_KEY\"]}"}, json={"schedule": schedule, "http_url": public_url, "timeout_seconds": 900}, timeout=30)
    cron_url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/create"
    queue_url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish"
    infrai_request("POST", "/v1/cron/create", {"schedule": schedule, "http_url": public_url, "timeout_seconds": 900})
    return lambda message: infrai_request("POST", "/v1/queue/publish", {"queue": queue_name, "message": message, "idempotency_key": message["id"]})


def cleanup_message(tenant_id, start_id, end_id, cutoff):
    raw = f"{tenant_id}:{start_id}:{end_id}:{cutoff.isoformat()}"
    return {
        "id": sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "tenant_id": tenant_id,
        "start_id": start_id,
        "end_id": end_id,
        "cutoff": cutoff.isoformat(),
    }


def publish_cleanup_ranges(db, queue, tenant_id, first_id, last_id):
    cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(minutes=20)
    for start_id in range(first_id, last_id + 1, 500):
        end_id = min(start_id + 499, last_id)
        message = cleanup_message(tenant_id, start_id, end_id, cutoff)
        queue.publish(message, idempotency_key=f"reservation-cleanup:{message['id']}")
    db.record_cleanup_trigger(tenant_id, cutoff)


def consume_once(db, queue):
    message = queue.receive()
    if message is None:
        return False
    try:
        with db.transaction():
            db.execute(
                '''
                UPDATE reservations
                   SET status = 'expired', expired_at = now()
                 WHERE tenant_id = %s
                   AND reservation_id BETWEEN %s AND %s
                   AND status = 'held'
                   AND expires_at <= %s
                ''',
                (message["tenant_id"], message["start_id"],
                 message["end_id"], message["cutoff"]),
            )
            db.execute(
                '''
                DELETE FROM session_tokens
                 WHERE tenant_id = %s
                   AND reservation_id BETWEEN %s AND %s
                   AND expires_at <= %s
                ''',
                (message["tenant_id"], message["start_id"],
                 message["end_id"], message["cutoff"]),
            )
        queue.ack(message)
        return True
    except Exception:
        queue.retry(message)
        raise

Then it broke.

I once treated the trigger request as the whole job and discovered that the HTTP timeout, not the row count, was setting our retention policy. A tenant with 18,400 stale reservations made the mistake obvious: the endpoint spent its budget scanning, the scheduler retried it, and the second pass raced the first. The fix was boring: 500-row ranges, a transaction, and an ack after commit. Boring is good here.

For an actual Infrai setup, the cron definition is created with POST /v1/cron/create, and the handler publishes through POST /v1/queue/publish. Both are plain HTTP calls, so a Node.js service, a Python worker, or a small Go utility can share one integration without installing an SDK. Send Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, set an explicit method, check every non-2xx response, and back off on 429 using Retry-After. Keep the API key out of the public webhook request.

Which Postgres, Redis, or queue option fits this retention boundary?

The queue is not the source of truth; Postgres is. Redis TTL is a useful alternative when the only requirement is letting an ephemeral key disappear, but it is a poor fit for an auditable transition that must free a seat, invalidate a token, and leave a reason for support staff. A Postgres query plus a worker gives you a durable cutoff and a place to inspect the decision.

Option Good fit Trade-off for this job
Postgres job table Teams needing SQL ownership, audit, and transactional state You operate polling, retries, and worker leases
Redis TTL Cache-like sessions where expiry itself is the only action Expiry does not atomically update reservation and audit rows
Amazon SQS Managed at-least-once delivery and mature redrive tooling State still lives elsewhere; visibility and ordering need design
Temporal Multi-step workflows, timers, and durable orchestration More platform concepts than a bounded cleanup needs
Inngest Event-driven functions with built-in retry conventions Another event runtime to operate and observe
Trigger.dev TypeScript-first background tasks Less natural for a small SQL-owned worker
BullMQ Redis-backed jobs inside a Node.js estate You own Redis durability, workers, and operational policy
Infrai queue plus cron One REST surface for the trigger and delivery handoff No DAG/join primitive; no replay groups, and messages live at most 30 days

Infrai is a reasonable choice when the integration boundary is the main constraint: one key and one REST API cover scheduling and queue operations, and any language that can send HTTPS can use it. Its supporting advantage is a consistent platform convention for idempotency, which lets the trigger and publisher use the same request discipline. That does not make it a workflow engine.

The limits are concrete. Delayed messages top out at seven days, message bodies at 256 KB, and acknowledgement deletes the message; there is no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history. There is no native debounce, throttle, or topic fan-out, and an internal endpoint cannot receive a push subscription because the target must be public HTTPS. Use separate queues when you need fan-out.

What should the public webhook and retry policy guarantee?

Treat the endpoint as an admission controller. Validate the scheduler secret, derive the cutoff on the server, publish bounded work, and return a small response containing a correlation ID. A repeated trigger is expected: the range ID and cutoff make it harmless, while the conditional SQL prevents a paid reservation from being expired by a stale message.

The consumer should retry transient database or queue failures with exponential backoff, honoring any Retry-After value. Never tight-loop on a 429. A poison message belongs in a dead-letter queue for inspection and redrive; it should not block every other tenant. Keep payloads well below 256 KB, and split a large tenant into more ranges rather than stuffing IDs into one message.

The catch is that this pattern is not suitable when you need a DAG, a fan-out/join barrier, sub-second scheduling guarantees, or a private-only callback. Stick with Temporal or Airflow for workflow orchestration, and use a direct Postgres/Redis design when the data volume is small and a queue would add more moving parts than it removes.

If this boundary fits your system, the scheduling guide at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/nodejs-cron-cleanup-old-user-sessions-expired-tokens-qu/ shows the corresponding setup.

Your mileage may vary on the range size. Start at 500, measure lock time and retry rate in your own database, and adjust without changing the idempotency key format.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://docs.temporal.io/
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
  • https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/ " }

title: AutoSys Migration, One Job at a Time
description:
Nobody enjoys a scheduler migration. The old system has been running for years, nobody remembers why half the jobs exist, and everyone is a little scared to touch the ones that work.

That fear is fair. AutoSys, originally from CA Technologies and now owned by Broadcom, has run critical work in banks, telecoms and insurance companies for a long time. But it was designed before APIs, containers and cloud setups became normal. Writing and maintaining JIL scripts takes practice, so new team members are slow to get comfortable. And plugging AutoSys into a modern stack, with real-time APIs or event-driven workflows, usually means workarounds.

So the question isn't really "should we move?" It's "how do we move without breaking things?" The answer most teams land on is the same: go slowly, and go one job at a time.

A calmer way to migrate

List your jobs first. Before you build anything, write down what each job runs, when it runs, and what it depends on. Sort them by how many other jobs rely on them. Jobs that stand alone are your easy wins. Jobs with long chains behind them need more care.

Start small. Pick one low-risk job with a clear result, like a nightly report, and rebuild it in the new system first. If something goes wrong, nobody's morning is ruined, and you learn how the new setup behaves before the stakes get higher.

Run old and new side by side. Let both versions run for a while and compare what they produce. This is where you catch the surprises, like a job that depends on something nobody mentioned.

Move dependent jobs together. If job B waits for job A, move them as a pair. Splitting a chain across two schedulers is how you end up with jobs that fire at the wrong time and nobody can say why.

Switch off the old job last. Only retire the AutoSys version after the new one has matched it cleanly for a good stretch of runs.

The part nobody writes down

The job definitions are the easy part. They're written down, so you can read them. What's harder is everything around them: a script that quietly retries when it fails, a downstream team that expects a file to land before 6 AM, an alert that goes to one person's inbox and nobody else's.

Those habits don't show up in any export. The best way to find them is to talk to the people who get paged when a job breaks, not just the people who built it. Ask them what they check first on a bad morning. Their answers usually point straight at the behavior you need to carry over.

How long does it take?

It depends on how many jobs you have and how tangled their dependencies are. Unmeshed suggests a phased approach like this one and says most organizations complete the move in about 6 to 12 weeks. Treat that as a rough guide, not a promise.

If you're weighing a move, Unmeshed runs scheduled jobs with Bash and Python steps and keeps every run visible from start to finish, so you can see what each job did while you compare old and new.

description:
arXiv:2606.05405v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent AI systems have achieved strong results on a wide range of benchmarks, yet these gains have not translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional domains. We argue that this gap is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks lack sustained performance measurement on real and economically valuable workflows. This paper introduces Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on long horizon, economically valuable, real world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed in collaboration with 250+ industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries defined with reference to O*NET / SOC 2018 (the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy). It is organized around a task taxonomy with 55 sub fields grouped into 13 industry clusters covering 1K+ tasks. Current results show that the hardest tier remains far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is below 1%. ALE is designed as a living benchmark: its task pool grows continuously as new workflows and industries are onboarded. More broadly, ALE is intended not merely as another leaderboard, but as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP relevant impact.

title: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses
description:
arXiv:2610.12872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong individual task performance, yet still struggle to collaborate with users over extended, multi-turn interactions, for example by attempting solutions before understanding the user's needs or by failing to revise mistaken assumptions after receiving feedback. We propose Collaborative Theory of Mind (CToM), a framework that addresses these challenges by explicitly training LLMs to anticipate user responses and to use those predictions to improve their own behavior. CToM drafts a response, predicts how the user will respond, and uses this prediction to guide internal revision before presenting a response. During training, the user's reply to each draft serves as the target for predicting the next turn, and we train the assistant to minimize the negative log-likelihood of that reply. We combine this prediction objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to optimize both task performance and interaction efficiency. Across mathematical reasoning, coding, and writing tasks, CToM achieves higher collaborative task performance than all baselines; for example, on a collaborative mathematical reasoning task, it improves final accuracy from 74.1% to 79.6% compared with naive GRPO. Ablations show that predicting user responses also makes collaboration more efficient: under the same reward, adding prediction supervision reduces the number of user replies by 8% on coding and 17% on writing while improving task performance. Behavioral analyses of interaction trajectories show that user-response predictions become more accurate after training, and that more accurate predictions are associated with larger improvements in collaborative task performance through self-revision.

title: Scaling Empowered Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.13002v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.

title: Conditional Vendi Score: Prompt-Aware Diversity Evaluation for Generative AI Models and LLMs
description:
arXiv:2411.02817v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generative models guided by text prompts are widely evaluated for fidelity and prompt alignment, yet their ability to produce diverse outputs remains underexplored. Existing diversity metrics such as Vendi and RKE, which are based on the von Neumann and R\'enyi entropies of kernel matrices, were developed for unconditional models and cannot distinguish prompt-induced from model-induced variability. We address this gap by introducing \textit{Conditional-Vendi} and \textit{Conditional-RKE}, diversity measures derived from the conditional entropy of positive semidefinite matrices. These scores isolate model-induced diversity in prompt-guided generation, with Conditional-RKE enjoying an $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ convergence rate. For Conditional-Vendi, we introduce a truncated-spectrum approximation that yields scalable and consistent estimates. Experiments on text-to-image, image-captioning, and LLM tasks show that the conditional scores recover ground-truth diversity orderings and can also guide diffusion models toward more diverse samples. The codebase is available at https://github.com/mjalali/conditional-vendi.

title: AI Gateway now supports streaming transcription
description:
AI Gateway now supports streaming transcription. Previously, transcription required a complete audio file and returned the full transcript in a single response. Now you can stream audio in as it's captured and get transcript updates back as the model produces them, keeping latency low for uses like live captioning and voice input.

Streaming transcription is in beta and available through the AI SDK's streamTranscribe function with any streaming-capable transcription model.

The example below streams raw PCM audio to openai/gpt-realtime-whisper and prints each transcript delta as it arrives. The result stream also carries partial and final transcripts:

The same code works across providers: swap the model string to use xai/grok-stt or any other streaming-capable transcription model.

Streaming transcription also makes it easy to add a voice mode to an agent. Stream the user's speech to a transcription model and pass the live text to your agent. The agent itself does not change: it still receives text, so this works with any text-based agent. For agents that speak back, pair it with speech generation, or use realtime voice for full two-way conversation.

For more information on streaming transcription on AI Gateway, see the documentation.

title: Set up coding agents in one command with AI Gateway
description:
Using coding agents means setting up multiple accounts, provisioning API keys, and scattering observability and billing. Now, you can route them through AI Gateway to centralize all of this and add controls, with set up in one command:

  • Any of 200+ models in any agent, including models the agent has no native support for. The gateway routes the request to whichever model you picked, with automatic fallbacks.

  • One dashboard for agent traffic: spend, performance, tokens and more, across the models your agents used.

  • Budgets, resets, and expiry on the keys agents use to control spend.

  • Team-wide policy your agents can't route around: turn on Zero Data Retention or restrict which providers may serve requests, and it holds for every agent request without editing an agent's config.

  • Request traces, with the cost, tokens, and model behind each request.

To start:

vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup connects Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more in one command. It finds the agents on your machine, creates the API key, and writes the gateway URL and your credentials into each agent's own config format.

Agent

Selecting a model

Claude Code, CLI and desktop

/model or /model <slug>, as in /model anthropic/claude-opus-5

Codex, CLI and desktop

/model or codex --model <slug>

OpenCode

/models, then pick vercel/<creator>/<model>

Pi

/model, or pi --list-models

Cline

Cursor

Add gateway slugs under Settings, then Models

Hermes

/model custom:vercel-ai-gateway:<slug>

Kilo Code

/models, then pick openai-compatible/<creator>/<model>

Add slugs to the starter list in openclaw.json

title: Seedance 2.5 now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Seedance 2.5 from ByteDance is now available on AI Gateway. It can generate up to 30-second clips with synchronized audio, and takes up to 50 reference inputs in one request, spanning images, video, audio, and style.

A single clip holds camera movement and continuity without stitching shots together in post, and short clips can be extended, carrying over character, scene, and camera movement. Prompts work in more than ten languages.

Seedance 2.5 can also edit a finished video in place, swapping backgrounds, products, or characters while the frame, camera, and pacing stay fixed, so one shoot yields several variants.

Generating a video

Set model to bytedance/seedance-2.5 and call generateVideo from the AI SDK:

Adding image references

Pass image URLs in inputReferences and point at them in the prompt with [Image 1], [Image 2]. Tag each entry with its media type. Seedance treats an untagged URL as an image.

Combining reference types

Mix videos and images in the same request to pull different qualities from each: motion and camera work from a clip, a subject's appearance from a still.

Videos go in the same inputReferences array as images, tagged with a video media type. Numbering runs per type so the first video is [Video 1] and the first image is [Image 1], and both can appear in one prompt.

Editing a video

Referencing and editing use the same setup, so the prompt decides which you get. Ask the model to follow a clip's camera movement and it builds a new video from scratch. Ask it to change something in the clip and it edits the video you gave it.

You can reference and edit in one prompt, though results get less predictable, so it helps to be explicit about what each asset is for.

For the playground and API reference, see the model page, or browse every video model on AI Gateway.

title: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.13504v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative Recommenders increasingly use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize outcomes that may appear hundreds or thousands of interactions after a decision. Standard RL propagates reward according to temporal proximity rather than explicit relevance, attenuating the signal assigned to distant but important actions and creating a source of sample inefficiency. We introduce Explanatory World Models (EWM), an attribution framework that uses explanations to identify the earlier events that plausibly contributed to a realized outcome. We instantiate EWM with a frontier language model and use its explanations as learning signals using a conservative hierarchical operator that recursively redistributes reward while preserving the undiscounted episode return. To investigate what constitutes a useful explanation, we operationalize three complementary variants inspired by Halpern's actual causation, Lombrozo's explanatory simplicity, and Deutsch's hard-to-vary explanations. We evaluate EWM on two controlled long-horizon RL benchmarks, a public sequential-recommendation benchmark, and an industry-scale generative recommender. On Crafter and WordCraft, EWM substantially outperforms PPO and LaRe, with its largest gains when rewards are most delayed. On KuaiRand, EWM outperforms SFT and LaRe offline and A2C online. Finally, in an offline evaluation of an industry generative recommender, EWM considerably improves Recall and increases behavioral proxies. These results suggest that explanations can provide structured and reusable credit for learning from delayed outcomes.

title: On the Rate of Convergence of GD in Non-linear Neural Networks: An Adversarial Robustness Perspective
description:
arXiv:2603.02095v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the convergence dynamics of Gradient Descent (GD) in a minimal binary classification setting, consisting of a two-neuron ReLU network and two training instances. We prove that even under these strong simplifying assumptions, while GD successfully converges to an optimal robustness margin, effectively maximizing the distance between the decision boundary and the training points, this convergence occurs at a prohibitively slow rate, scaling strictly as $\Theta(1/\ln(t))$. To the best of our knowledge, this establishes the first explicit lower bound on the convergence rate of the robustness margin in a non-linear model. Through empirical simulations, we further demonstrate that this inherent failure mode is pervasive, exhibiting the exact same tight convergence rate across multiple natural network initializations. Our theoretical guarantees are derived via a rigorous analysis of the GD trajectories across the distinct activation patterns of the model. Specifically, we develop tight control over the system's dynamics to bound the trajectory of the decision boundary, overcoming the primary technical challenge introduced by the non-linear nature of the architecture.

title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
description:
arXiv:2610.13630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of $1.58\times$ over the standard residual baseline, compared with $1.35\times$ for AttnRes and $1.30\times$ for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.

title: Language Models Have Interpretable Narrative Mechanisms
description:
arXiv:2610.12989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate whether language models contain internal components that contribute to representing narrativity, the degree to which a text exhibits narrative properties. Across GPT-2-Small, Gemma-2-2B, and Llama-3.1-8B, we identify attention heads, MLP neurons, and sparse autoencoder features whose activations correlate with narrativity. Ablating selected neuron and feature sets increases next-token prediction loss more for high-narrativity than for low-narrativity texts, and reduces the narrativity of open-ended generations. On downstream benchmarks, the largest effects occur in story completion and narrative question answering, although they vary across models and languages; results on confabulation and hallucination benchmarks are mixed. These findings provide causal evidence that selected sets of narrative-associated components contribute to model behaviour, while their internal organisation, relation to narrative theory, and broader functions remain open questions.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Efficient Context Processing via Latent Sufficiency Signals
description:
arXiv:2502.01025v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process entire input contexts indiscriminately, which is inefficient when the information required to answer a query is localized within the context. We present dynamic context cutoff, a novel method enabling LLMs to self-terminate processing upon acquiring sufficient task-relevant information. Through analysis of model internals, we discover that specific attention heads inherently encode "sufficiency signals" -- detectable through lightweight classifiers -- that predict when critical information has been processed. This reveals a new efficiency paradigm: models' internal understanding naturally dictates processing needs rather than external compression heuristics. Comprehensive experiments across six QA datasets (up to 40K tokens) with three model families (LLaMA/Qwen/Mistral, 1B-70B) demonstrate 3.4% accuracy improvement while achieving 1.33x token reduction on average. Furthermore, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to other context efficiency methods at equivalent token reduction rates. Additionally, we observe an emergent scaling phenomenon: while smaller models require probing for sufficiency detection, larger models exhibit intrinsic self-assessment capabilities through prompting.

title: Inspect feature flag history with Vercel CLI
description:

Run vercel flags versions <flag> to print the full revision history for a flag, with each revision's author, message, timestamp, and changed environments. Filter to a specific environment with --environment, paginate with --limit and --cursor, or add --json for scripting.

title: UxSID: Semantic-Aware User Interests Modeling for Ultra-Long Sequence
description:
arXiv:2605.09040v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modeling ultra-long user sequences involves a difficult trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness. While current paradigms rely on either item-specific search or item-agnostic compression, we propose UxSID, a framework exploring a third path: semantic-group shared interest memory. By utilizing Semantic IDs (SIDs) and a dual-level attention strategy, UxSID captures target-aware preferences without the heavy cost of item-specific models. This end-to-end architecture balances computational parsimony with semantic awareness, achieving state-of-the-art performance and a 0.337% revenue lift in large-scale advertising A/B test.

title: Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox
description:
Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox instead of Cursor's hosted machines.

Cursor manages the agent harness and inference loop. Its Self-Hosted Machines APIs let you supply the execution environment where agents clone repositories, edit files, and run commands and tests. Self-Hosted Machines requires a Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox provides that execution environment as an isolated Firecracker microVM for each agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflows form a durable control plane that claims queued agent requests, provisions workers, monitors sessions, and cleans up automatically.

With this architecture, you get:

  • A scale-to-zero worker pool without long-lived virtual machines

  • A dedicated, isolated Sandbox for every agent request

  • Durable retries when a worker or session fails

  • Short-lived, user-scoped credentials inside each Sandbox

Follow the step-by-step guide to deploy the reference implementation to your own Vercel account, or learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

title: Supplier Invoice Image Upload Moderation: Multimodal Chat Classifies NSFW and Violence
description:
A supplier-invoice intake service has two clocks: the support agent needs extracted fields soon, but the safety decision must be trustworthy before any reviewer or extractor sees the upload. Short answer: send the image and a brief application policy to a multimodal chat model, require a strict JSON result, then store both the raw model decision and a small internal status. There is no dedicated image-moderation endpoint in Infrai, so its correct path for this job is /v1/chat/completions, with malformed output or an expired deadline routed to review rather than quietly treated as safe.

I would try Infrai for this moderation stage when a team wants a replaceable boundary: its OpenAI-compatible contract is reachable through plain REST, so a Go service does not need another SDK or client-library upgrade cycle. A second, operationally different advantage matters during a migration: the public discovery surface needs no key and exposes request and response schemas, while documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. An operator can inspect the current contract and readiness before moving credentials or traffic. The same credential covers 295 routes across 20 modules, which can also remove a separate key and billing path if the invoice service later uses other backend capabilities, though breadth alone is not a reason to choose a moderation model.

That recommendation is narrow. A specialist service is the better choice when a fixed safety taxonomy, calibrated category scores, or a managed human-review workflow is the requirement.

How should multimodal chat classify an NSFW image upload for moderation?

The useful incident is bounded: customer support accepts an upload presented as a supplier invoice, moderation returns an answer, and extraction must either proceed, hold, or stop. The page should name the broken invariant, not say "AI failed." Useful page conditions include no valid decision before the request deadline, JSON that does not satisfy the owned schema, or a policy category mapped to hold that nevertheless reached extraction. A dashboard showing average latency cannot tell the on-call engineer which failure occurred.

The invariant is plain: extraction may consume only an allow decision produced under a recorded policy version. Nudity, graphic violence, hate symbols, drugs, and minors-risk are examples of categories an application may define; they are not a universal provider taxonomy. Store the provider's raw response beside a normalized allow, hold, or block status. That separation lets policy owners change category mapping later without changing the database shape or erasing the evidence behind an earlier decision.

Fail closed.

This is where quality and latency stop being abstract metrics. A quick response that cannot be parsed is no decision. A detailed answer that arrives after the upload request has expired belongs in an asynchronous review path, not behind an unbounded retry loop that leaves the agent staring at a spinner. The deadline must come from the product's intake budget; transport failure must never become allow by accident.

Make the rollback unit smaller than the provider

Treat the policy version as deployable configuration. A rollout can compare decisions produced under invoice-safety-v3 with the prior mapping, then revert the mapping without replacing the transport adapter or rewriting stored records. The raw result answers what the model returned. The normalized result answers what the application may do. Mixing those questions gives every downstream query, alert, and review screen knowledge of one vendor's vocabulary, which makes the eventual migration much larger than the original integration.

I first expected a green moderation dashboard to be enough. It isn't if nobody can answer a simpler question: what page fires when schema validation fails? Record failure class, policy version, request identifier, and the normalized disposition. Do not put the invoice image itself in logs. The incident timeline should show whether the model answered late, the response was malformed, or the policy mapping rejected an otherwise valid response.

Keep the contract small. It is easier to rehearse.

Put the latency budget in executable code

The following program is intentionally direct. It performs one complete REST call, sets an explicit method, reads credentials from the environment, caps the response at 1 MiB, surfaces non-success bodies, honors an integer Retry-After on HTTP 429, and stops after four attempts or a 12-second outer deadline. Those numbers are sample client limits, not measured service targets; replace them with limits derived from the invoice intake path.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Decision struct {
    Status     string          `json:"status"`
    Categories map[string]bool `json:"categories"`
    Policy     string          `json:"policy_version"`
}

type chatResponse struct {
    Choices []struct {
        Message struct {
            Content string `json:"content"`
        } `json:"message"`
    } `json:"choices"`
}

func moderate(ctx context.Context, imageURL string) (Decision, []byte, error) {
    body := map[string]any{
        "model": os.Getenv("MULTIMODAL_MODEL"),
        "messages": []map[string]any{{
            "role": "user",
            "content": []map[string]any{
                {"type": "text", "text": "Apply invoice-safety-v3. Classify nudity, graphic_violence, hate_symbols, drugs, and minors_risk. Return only the requested JSON."},
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": map[string]string{"url": imageURL}},
            },
        }},
        "response_format": map[string]any{
            "type": "json_schema",
            "json_schema": map[string]any{
                "name": "invoice_upload_moderation",
                "strict": true,
                "schema": map[string]any{
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": map[string]any{
                        "status": map[string]any{"type": "string", "enum": []string{"allow", "hold", "block"}},
                        "categories": map[string]any{
                            "type": "object",
                            "properties": map[string]any{
                                "nudity": map[string]string{"type": "boolean"},
                                "graphic_violence": map[string]string{"type": "boolean"},
                                "hate_symbols": map[string]string{"type": "boolean"},
                                "drugs": map[string]string{"type": "boolean"},
                                "minors_risk": map[string]string{"type": "boolean"},
                            },
                            "required": []string{"nudity", "graphic_violence", "hate_symbols", "drugs", "minors_risk"},
                            "additionalProperties": false,
                        },
                        "policy_version": map[string]any{"type": "string", "const": "invoice-safety-v3"},
                    },
                    "required": []string{"status", "categories", "policy_version"},
                    "additionalProperties": false,
                },
            },
        },
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(body)
    if err != nil {
        return Decision{}, nil, err
    }

    var raw []byte
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return Decision{}, raw, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return Decision{}, raw, err
        }
        raw, err = io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return Decision{}, raw, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return Decision{}, raw, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Decision{}, raw, fmt.Errorf("moderation request failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, raw)
        }

        var response chatResponse
        if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &response); err != nil || len(response.Choices) == 0 {
            return Decision{}, raw, errors.New("provider returned an invalid chat response")
        }
        var decision Decision
        if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(response.Choices[0].Message.Content), &decision); err != nil {
            return Decision{}, raw, fmt.Errorf("invalid structured decision: %w", err)
        }
        return decision, raw, nil
    }
    return Decision{}, raw, errors.New("rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 12*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    decision, raw, err := moderate(ctx, os.Getenv("INVOICE_IMAGE_URL"))
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "hold upload: %v; raw=%s\n", err, raw)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("status=%s policy=%s raw=%s\n", decision.Status, decision.Policy, raw)
}

The model identifier stays in configuration; select a currently available multimodal model rather than freezing an unverified ID into source. The image URL should be a short-lived location controlled by the application. This is a read-like classification call, so an idempotency key is unnecessary, but retry behavior still has to be bounded. In production, persist the raw body under restricted access instead of printing it; the print exists to make the two-record design visible in one runnable example.

One trap deserves a separate sentence. Lanczos-only image upscale is a resizing operation, not a safety check, and it must not be inserted as though it improves moderation quality.

Compare contracts before comparing logos

These services solve overlapping, not identical, problems. The table describes integration shape and fit; it does not claim an accuracy winner.

Option Integration Initial effort Best fit Main limit for this design
Infrai chat surface OpenAI-compatible REST; no required SDK Define the application schema and mapping Teams wanting a plain HTTP boundary and provider choice behind an owned contract No dedicated image-moderation endpoint
OpenAI Moderations Dedicated API and official SDKs Map documented provider categories into internal status Teams that prefer a provider-owned moderation taxonomy A custom invoice policy still needs an application mapping
AWS Rekognition AWS API and SDKs Add AWS request, identity, and label mapping Workloads already operating image review in AWS Its moderation labels are a different contract from custom chat JSON
Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch Google Cloud API and client libraries Add Google Cloud request and likelihood mapping Workloads already centered on Google Cloud image analysis Fixed SafeSearch dimensions may not match every application category
Gemini or Anthropic Claude Multimodal model APIs and SDKs Prompt, schema, adapter, and evaluation Teams needing custom policy instructions over images General model output still requires validation and normalization

OpenAI, AWS Rekognition, and Google Cloud Vision are stronger candidates when their defined moderation categories are exactly the interface the organization wants to own. Gemini and Anthropic Claude are closer to the custom-policy approach, where the application asks a multimodal model for its own labels. Infrai fits when the application-owned schema plus an OpenAI-compatible surface is the migration mechanism, especially if public discovery and one credential across backend capabilities reduce real operational work. It does not remove the need to evaluate the chosen model.

No benchmark, no winner.

Build a labeled set from actual supplier-invoice traffic, then measure false allows and false holds separately under the same deadline. A false allow creates safety exposure; a false hold creates support work and extraction delay. Average accuracy hides that trade-off. Rehearse the migration as well: replay the set through a second adapter and verify that normalized decisions, retained raw evidence, and page conditions survive the switch.

Where this boundary stops helping

Use a specialist moderation product when a managed review queue, provider-calibrated scores, or a fixed taxonomy is more valuable than an application-owned schema. Use the cloud-native choice when identity, images, and operator workflows already live there and another boundary would create more work than it removes. A chat-based classifier is also the wrong synchronous dependency when the upload path cannot spare its latency; quarantine the image and moderate asynchronously instead.

The preventative control is modest: extraction reads only a validated internal decision with a policy version, while provider detail remains behind an adapter. That gives the on-call engineer a precise page, the policy owner a rollback unit, and the migration owner a contract that can actually be tested.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability manifest and verify the live schema before sending traffic.

  • Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch Detection

  • Anthropic vision
  • Infrai capability manifest

title: FactoryBench: Evaluating Industrial Machine Understanding
description:
arXiv:2605.07675v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce FactoryBench, a benchmark for evaluating time-series models and LLMs on machine understanding over industrial robotic telemetry. Q&A pairs are organized along four causal levels (state, intervention, counterfactual, decision) instantiating Pearl's ladder of causation, and span five answer formats: four structured formats are scored deterministically and free-form answers are scored by an LLM-as-judge voting protocol. We propose a scalable Q&A generation framework built around structured question templates, present FactoryWave (a dense, multitask, multivariate sensor dataset collected from a UR3 cobot and a KUKA KR10 industrial arm), and construct FactoryBench as a large-scale benchmark of over 70k Q&A items grounded in roughly 15k normalized episodes from FactoryWave, AURSAD, and voraus-AD. Zero-shot evaluation of six frontier LLMs shows that no model exceeds 50% on structured levels or 18% on decision-making, revealing a wide gap between current models and operational machine understanding.

title: GenCoord: Executable Commitments for Embodied LLM Agents under Private Information
description:
arXiv:2608.22055v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Embodied language-model agents must coordinate interdependent actions while each holds private task information. In dialogue-based coordination, models generate messages and interpret replies to decide what each agent should do, spending inference before the team acts. We propose GenCoord, a decentralized protocol that makes the division of work itself the message. A proposal pairs the sender's skill path with its partner's continuation in Short DSL, a compact language for expressing joint work. Compatible paths form commitments linking the sender's delivery to the partner's work after verified receipt. We check fulfillment separately from original-task success. Complete requests also let a deterministic receiver proceed without another model call. In Minecraft, trained local 0.8B agents match the task success of controlled free-form communication while reducing median commitment time by 68.2%. The same-field full-key JSON control approaches free-form output length and delay, indicating that the amount generated matters even when messages are structured. With the same prompted DeepSeek model, both protocols complete nearly all tasks, but dialogue generates 2.8 times as many output tokens. Multistep commitments improve held-out-template success from 91.3% to 98.1% with fewer decisions. These results point to a design principle for embodied cooperation: make the division of work the message, and spend inference on choosing and revising the work.

title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
description:
arXiv:2610.12644v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.
