title: Enhancing Tabular Learners with Context-Aware Semantic Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2608.03565v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While modern tabular learners excel at capturing statistical patterns, they frequently operate in a semantic vacuum, treating textual features as discrete symbols, ignoring the rich semantics inherent in feature names or cell entries. We propose CASE (Context-Aware Semantic Embeddings), a novel framework that bridges the gap between the semantic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the statistical capabilities of tabular learners. Unlike existing methods that embed rows in isolation, CASE utilizes a contextualization strategy: we pre-fill the KV cache of a custom-trained Gemma 3-based Tabular Language Model with a representative sample of rows to establish a persistent anchor of the dataset's semantics. This ensures that generated row embeddings are dynamically contextualized, resolving semantic ambiguities and anchoring representations in domain-specific context. Our experiments across several benchmarks (CARTE, TextTab, and TabArena) demonstrate that CASE substantially improves the performance of tabular learners on semantically rich datasets, particularly in low-data regimes.

title: CoMMa: Contribution-Aware Medical Multi-Agents for Decentralized Oncology Decision Support
description:
arXiv:2602.09159v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent multi-agent frameworks have shown promise for oncology decision support, yet most assume centralized data access and rely on prompt-based assignment, limiting their applicability in privacy-sensitive clinical settings. We propose Contribution-Aware Medical Multi-Agents (CoMMa), a decentralized LLM-agent framework where specialists operate on partitioned clinical data streams. Unlike prior approaches that share inputs across agents, CoMMa enforces data decentralization to include stronger role specialization and further enhances this via agent-specific finetuning. To enable reliable and interpretable coordination, we introduce a contribution-aware aggregation mechanism that replaces stochastic, narrative-based reasoning with deterministic embedding projections to approximate each agent's marginal utility. This yields explicit credit assignment over agents, providing a stable and interpretable decision pathway aligned with clinical requirements. We evaluate CoMMa on multiple oncology benchmarks, including real-world multidisciplinary tumor board datasets from large academic hospitals in North America and East Asia, as well as public datasets, demonstrating strong performance and generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings.

title: DeepSeek overtakes Google on volume, cost per token falls 13.6%
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — August 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from May, June, and July.

August 2026 Summary

The August index reports on AI Gateway data collected through July 2026.

  • The average price paid per token fell 13.6% in July, after rising almost 20% in May and holding steady in June. Token consumption grew so quickly that even with 37% growth in spend, cost per token saw a double-digit drop.

  • DeepSeek became the second-largest lab by token volume, now running more than twice Google's volume.

  • Anthropic collected 65% of gateway spending on 30% of token volume, at 4.4 times the average price of every other lab's tokens.

  • Both media leaderboards changed hands. Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image volume from OpenAI's GPT Image, and ByteDance's Seedance led video in both volume and dollars.

Kimi K3 launched into agent work

Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16. Like Z.ai's GLM 5.2 released in June, it is built for long-horizon agent work, so its usage was heavy from the start at about twelve times the tokens per request of its predecessor, K2.5.

It scaled quickly. K3's daily volume tripled between launch week and the final week of July, and by month end its requests were as heavy as Claude Opus 4.8's. On the last full day of July it ranked eighth on the gateway by token volume.

The demand was new rather than diverted. K3 processed nearly two-thirds of all Kimi tokens within two weeks and 82% by the final week, while the rest of the family's volume fell only slightly.

Open weight's share of gateway spend more than doubled in July to 8.6%. More than 90% of that growth is Moonshot and Z.ai. Moonshot's share of total gateway spend quadrupled, to 2.3%. Cheap open-weight models have been taking volume for months without taking revenue. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are the first to capture significant volume at more than eleven times DeepSeek's rate per token.

DeepSeek is now second by volume

In June, this report said DeepSeek had entered the fight for token volume. Last month, we said an open-weight lab would soon be second by volume. In July, DeepSeek surpassed Google to take that place.

Google ran nearly 40% of the gateway’s token volume in April, and DeepSeek less than 1%. By July, DeepSeek ran a quarter, more than twice Google’s 11%. DeepSeek V4 Flash, its cheapest model, ran more tokens alone than all of Google.

The reversal is concentrated in consumer-facing work. Google's share of personal-assistant tokens fell by more than half in a month while DeepSeek's more than tripled, and most of the token share Google gave up went to DeepSeek. DeepSeek's V4 Flash ran more tokens than any other model on the gateway in July, nearly a fifth of the total and 70% more than the next model.

Open-weight models previously owned the cheap end of the market. Their share of gateway token volume nearly tripled between April and June, from 11% to 29%, while share of spend stayed under four cents of every gateway dollar.

In July, volume continued its growth trend, increasing to 36%. Spend broke its trend, more than doubling to nearly nine cents of every dollar, the highest in the index's history.

The four largest frontier labs' combined share of token spend, which had not fallen below 93% in seven months, fell to 89%. Google accounted for most of the decline. Almost none of the spend it lost went to DeepSeek, whose share barely moved even as its volume grew. Z.ai and Moonshot's latest models account for the entire open-weight spend increase.

Buyers sort models by what the task requires, then choose inside that tier according to price. DeepSeek and Opus were never competing. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3, both released in the last two months, are the first open-weight models running a meaningful share of the workloads historically owned by closed-weight labs.

Average price per token fell 13.6%

Companies bought more inference in July and ran more of it on cheap models. Volume grew 59%, spend grew 37%, and the average price paid per token fell 13.6%.

Holding June's mix of models constant, the average price would have held essentially flat instead of declining. OpenAI is one example: the average cost of an OpenAI token fell to 58% of its June level, because 85% of the volume it added went to GPT-5-Nano, the cheapest model in the GPT-5 family.

The entire decline in average price came from what companies chose to route. Among the thousands of teams that ran more than 10 million tokens in both months, three in four changed at least a tenth of their model mix. Three in five changed at least a quarter.

The median team's cost per token fell 2.9%, but only one team in six stayed within five percent of where it started.

A quarter pared cost by more than 30%, typically teams that entered the month paying well above the gateway average per token. Another quarter paid at least 20% more, typically teams that had been paying below the average. Concurrently, the expensive end shifted down and the cheap end migrated up.

81% of July’s tokens ran on models that were not on the gateway six months ago. Open-weight models crossed a third of all volume, at about a seventh of frontier rates. Google fell from 24.0% of gateway token volume to 10.7%. Anthropic slipped two points to 29.8%, and OpenAI’s share rose to 12.8%.

Gateway spend is up 74% since May and volume has doubled, with July's token growth running at nearly double June's pace. Spend on inference continues to increase even as each dollar buys more tokens than it did in the previous month.

Anthropic's premium widened as prices fell

Anthropic has held more than 60% of gateway spend in every month we have measured, through a period in which open weight tripled its share of volume. In July, it collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume.

The average price per Anthropic token ran 4.4 times the average across every other lab, up from 3.4 in June. Part of that rise was Claude Fable 5, which returned on July 1 after a three-week export-control suspension and quickly grew to 13.2% of all gateway spend, second only to Opus 4.8. In coding agents, the gateway's largest use case by tokens, Anthropic collected more than 80% of spend.

Anthropic has no model at the bottom of the market. Haiku 4.5, its least expensive, runs just over two-thirds of the gateway average price per token. OpenAI's GPT-5-Nano runs a sixth; DeepSeek's V4 Flash a sixteenth.

Customers cutting costs on OpenAI or Google can stay in the catalog. Cutting costs on Anthropic means leaving Anthropic, and in July it still took a majority of all spending. Anthropic’s premium is the gap between what the cheap tier can do and what its customers need done.

Switching models on the AI Gateway is a one-line change, so nothing locks a customer in. When Fable 5 came back, daily volume returned to the pre-ban level almost exactly, but nine in ten of the teams running it in July had not used it before. The work returned; the customers were different.

The rest of the market's tokens averaged less than a quarter of Anthropic's price, and Anthropic still took two of every three dollars spent on the gateway. Price competition is happening, but it's happening in the part of the market with the least money in it.

Google took images, ByteDance took video

In June, OpenAI's GPT Image generated most of the gateway's images. In July, Google's Nano Banana led, at 45% of images to GPT Image's 42%, with spend split almost evenly between them. Nearly all of Nano Banana's gain came from one model, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image. Google took the image lead in the same month it fell to fourth by token volume.

ByteDance's Seedance led video on both counts, in videos generated and dollars spent. xAI's Grok Imagine, June's volume leader, fell to second. Chinese labs collected about seven of every ten dollars spent on video.

Also in July’s data

  • Within coding, the gateway's largest workload by tokens, DeepSeek ran nearly a third of the volume and Anthropic collected more than four of every five dollars.

  • Back-office agents remain the most expensive work per token, with a share of spending roughly two and a half times their share of volume.

About this report

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through July 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Volume counts all tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • Spend values every request at the lab's published list price.

  • Price per token is calculated as total spend divided by total volume.

  • Open-weight volume and spend shares count the four open-weight labs serving their own models at scale (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, and Z.ai).

  • Image and video figures count media generated, not requests or tokens.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Redesign, Optimise, or Rebuild? A Decision Framework for Your Website's Architecture
description:
When a client says "our website needs a redesign," what they usually mean is "something about our website is failing us" — and those are two very different engineering problems. Before touching a single component, we run three diagnostic questions: Is the platform itself sound (supported CMS, acceptable security posture, able to scale)? Is the UX/IA meeting business goals? Is the gap narrow enough to be a targeted fix (Core Web Vitals, a broken funnel, stale content)?

If the platform fails the first question — end-of-life CMS, plugin-stack fragility, no API-first path to the integrations the business now needs — no amount of new CSS fixes it. That's a rebuild: new architecture, often a move toward headless content delivery, and a proper data-migration plan. If the platform is fine but the experience layer isn't, that's a redesign: same CMS, same hosting, new design system and IA, content migrated across. If both pass and the problem is isolated — LCP, INP, CLS, a specific conversion funnel — that's an optimisation sprint, and it should stay scoped that way.

We cover the full cost breakdown (2026 India pricing: ₹35,000 for optimisation sprints up to ₹30,00,000+ for full platform rebuilds) and the complete decision framework in the original article: Website Redesign Cost in India 2026: When to Redesign vs Optimise vs Rebuild. Treat those ranges as indicative rather than a quote: page count, integrations and how much content has to move all shift the number, so scope your own site before you budget.

Curious how other teams have drawn this line — at what point did "redesign" actually mean "our CMS can't do this anymore" for you?

title: BLiMPPI: Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Polarity Items
description:
arXiv:2610.13607v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Negative polarity items (NPIs), such as "anymore" and "ever", are grammatical only in select environments, predominantly in the context of negation. Because their grammaticality depends on both syntax and semantics, they have a rich, multilingual literature in theoretical linguistics, yet work on NPIs in language models is almost entirely confined to English. We introduce BLiMPPI, a multilingual evaluation suite of over 12,000 NPI minimal pairs in 33 languages, built by a pipeline that discovers NPIs in Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks, labels their licensing environments, and perturbs these into minimal pairs. Evaluating 12 multilingual and 2 monolingual models alongside n-gram baselines, we find that multilingual models struggle most with lower-resource languages and with pairs that are not n-gram solvable. We further examine the effects of NPI typology, language family, licensing variability, and NPI-licenser distance. Data: https://github.com/arzuburcuguven/blimppi-data

title: Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2608.09109v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: User feedback offers natural supervision for persistent LLM improvement, but a single message may support multiple behavioral changes with different scopes of generalization. We introduce SLIFT, a selective self-learning framework built on a task-relative view of user feedback. SLIFT decomposes each feedback message into atomic components and interprets each component relative to the original task as Fix, Spec, or Null: requirements for task validity, compatible condition-specific refinements, or content with no reliable positive update direction. To incorporate each change at the appropriate scope, SLIFT trains two complementary LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone: a Generalist that consolidates Fix requirements into default behavior through feedback-conditioned self-distillation, and a Specialist that observes only the task and Generalist response to supply residual guidance for applicable, unmet Spec refinements. Null components induce no positive update. Across backbones, SLIFT achieves strong performance on both MemoryBench and WildFB, with targeted analyses further examining its underlying mechanisms. We release our code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SLIFT.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
description:
arXiv:2609.08149v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: SWE-Bench Pro has emerged as a standard benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents on challenging repository-level tasks. However, our analysis work show that its evaluation is undermined by two sources of unreliability: reward hacking, enabled by leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and task quality issues, including misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues can inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability. We present SWE-Bench Pro Verified, a verified version of SWE-Bench Pro that addresses both problems. Our approach combines anti-hacking safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, with task refinement that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances. Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified reveal that some models perform substantially worse than previously evaluated, suggesting that existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability. SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents.

title: SOAR: Source-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Precise Credit Assignment for Search Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.13157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for search agents often suffers from evidence fabrication, a failure mode where agents bypass external information ($E_{ext}$) and fabricate an incorrect answer. We argue that this fabrication arises from an over-reliance on unreliable internal knowledge ($E_{int}$) as shortcuts due to the inherent opacity of reasoning trajectories. To address this, we propose SOAR (SOurce-Aware Reinforcement learning), a paradigm that transforms monolithic reasoning into source-explicit trajectories. SOAR (i) disentangles $E_{ext}$ and $E_{int}$ into parallel, observable streams via a Source-Aware Workflow, and (ii) incorporates Source-Consistent Reward to guide the policy evolution. By making information-source attribution explicit, SOAR enables precise credit assignment between different knowledge streams. Evaluations show that SOAR outperforms baselines on 3B and 7B backbones by 7.3% and 5.4%, while reducing evidence fabrication by 74.8%. These confirm that SOAR significantly improves performance on knowledge-intensive benchmarks while effectively mitigating evidence fabrication, fostering more faithful and grounded reasoning with enhanced robustness.

title: Erased, but Not Gone: Output Forgetting Is Not True Forgetting
description:
arXiv:2606.25001v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) is commonly judged by output forgetting, such as low forget-set accuracy or reduced membership inference. But if output-level success can coexist with retraining-inconsistent residuals in representation space, what kind of forgetting are current evaluations actually certifying? We study this question through retraining-consistent representation forgetting, using a population of retrained models (i.e., trained from scratch without the forget data) as an operational reference distribution for ideal forgetting. Across multiple unlearning methods, datasets, and models, our theoretical analysis and empirical results show that standard output-level evaluation can systematically overestimate the success of unlearning. Under this stronger lens, current methods often appear forgotten at the output layer while exhibiting a structured mismatch relative to retraining. They partially align with retraining on forget samples, remain more inconsistent on retain samples, and tend to leave residual discrepancy localized along retraining-related directions rather than diffuse in representation space. This structured mismatch is characterized by forget/retain asymmetry, directional mismatch, and concentrated residuals along retraining-related directions. In many cases, the discrepancies exceed the variability of independent retraining and lead to a risk of information recovery during relearning attacks. Overall, the results suggest that current MU is often evaluated for apparent forgetting rather than retraining-consistent forgetting. More broadly, retraining reveals what output forgetting hides.

title: Scheduled Data Cleanup API for S3 Files — A Simple Node.js Queue Plan in 7 Steps
description:
The constraint that decides this design is partial failure. A store may contain 80,000 expired files, and one malformed key or missing permission must not cancel the other 79,999 deletes. Short answer: use a cron trigger to enqueue bounded work, let an idempotent worker delete one object per message, and send repeated failures to a dead-letter queue (DLQ). That keeps latency predictable while the queue absorbs uneven work.

The receipt trail matters. A product thumbnail can be regenerated; an invoice export may be governed by retention policy. Put the object key, tenant, policy version, and cleanup run ID in every task. Keep the bucket private and make a repeated delete harmless.

Why does a scheduled data cleanup API need a queue and DLQ?

Cron is a trigger, not a worker pool. A single cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, so scanning and deleting a large S3-style bucket inside that request creates a hard latency ceiling. The safer sequence is short: cron calls a public HTTPS ingress, the ingress publishes one task per file, workers consume independently, and an acknowledgement happens only after the delete and manifest write succeed.

Infrai fits at the boundary when a team wants scheduling and queue operations behind one plain REST contract. Its discovery endpoint publishes request schemas and runnable examples, and the same contract can sit in front of changing providers without rewriting the application boundary. That is useful here because the cleanup worker remains yours while the control plane stays small.

Standard queues are at-least-once. A duplicate delivery must not delete a newly replaced object. Store an expected version or checksum with the task, check it before deletion, and record the deterministic task key in a manifest. If the object is already absent, record an idempotent success only when the retention policy allows that interpretation.

Keep it boring.

The DLQ is for diagnosis, not a hiding place. Missing permissions and malformed object keys are distinct failure classes; after fixing the policy or key generator, redrive those messages instead of looping them forever. Queue retention is limited, acknowledgement deletes the message, and this system is not a replay log or analytics stream.

One boundary is easy to miss: cron targets and push subscribers must be public HTTP or HTTPS endpoints. A private worker URL will not receive tasks directly, so place an authenticated public ingress in front of it or use a pull consumer.

What should the cleanup payload and retry boundary contain?

Keep the payload explicit: cleanup_run_id, tenant_id, bucket, object_key, expected_version, policy_version, and attempt. Stay below the 256 KB message limit. Delayed delivery tops out at 7 days, while retention tops out at 30 days, so neither is a substitute for a long-term manifest.

I once treated a delete as a one-line finally block. A process kill skipped the cleanup, and the next run had no record of what it had attempted. The fix was a run manifest keyed by cleanup_run_id; the queue then handled retry state, while the manifest handled audit state. I'm not sure every business will interpret an already-absent object as success, so let the compliance owner set that rule. Your mileage may vary.

Here is a minimal publisher using the queue API. It sends a client idempotency key, uses an explicit method, and backs off on 429 responses. The worker URL in the payload is your public ingress, not a private host. In a real run, the scanner would first list candidate keys, attach the version observed by a HEAD request, and split the result into batches small enough to fit the message limit. A batch is a transport unit, not a transaction: if the process dies after the third message, the manifest still tells the next worker which object versions were intended. That distinction is what keeps a fast retry from deleting a replacement uploaded between two cron ticks. It also gives operations a concrete question to answer at 02:00: which task key failed, under which policy version, and is redrive now safe?

import hashlib
import os
import time
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def publish_cleanup_batch(tasks):
    material = "|".join(
        f"{t['tenant_id']}:{t['bucket']}:{t['object_key']}:{t['expected_version']}"
        for t in tasks
    )
    idem = hashlib.sha256(material.encode()).hexdigest()
    response = requests.request(
        method="POST",
        url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Idempotency-Key": idem,
        },
        json={"queue": "s3-cleanup", "messages": tasks},
        timeout=20,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "2"))
        time.sleep(delay)
        return publish_cleanup_batch(tasks)
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"queue publish failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()

The retry in this compact sample should be bounded in production, with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt count. The invariant is more important than the syntax: the same task key is reused on every delivery, so a second message can observe the prior manifest result instead of applying a second destructive action.

Which option fits this cleanup workload?

The comparison is about the full operating bill: scheduler limits, ingress work, retries, queue visibility, and who owns the worker runtime.

Option Good fit Trade-off to verify
Infrai cron plus queue One REST contract and one credential for scheduling and queueing around a small worker fleet Public targets are required; no DAG/join orchestration or native fan-out topic
BullMQ with Redis A Node.js team already operates Redis and wants rich local job controls Redis durability, cluster operations, and DLQ policy are yours
RabbitMQ Mature acknowledgements, routing, and priority queues are central Broker topology and upgrades add on-call work
AWS EventBridge plus SQS/Lambda The bucket, IAM, and worker runtime already live in AWS Cloud-specific configuration and separate service limits must be reconciled

Try Infrai for the scheduling and publish boundary when changing the backend provider without changing application code is valuable, and when one REST API can remove several SDK and credential integrations. Its public discovery surface lets the team inspect a capability contract before wiring the worker. Do not choose it for Airflow- or Temporal-style DAGs, fan-out joins, private push targets, replayable Kafka semantics, or non-standard cron extensions; use a specialist orchestrator, broker, or cloud-native stack for those cases.

How can a seven-step rollout keep failed cleanup jobs auditable?

Start with a dry-run scanner that writes manifests but performs no deletion. Enable deletion for one tenant and one private bucket prefix, then watch queue age, retry counts, DLQ depth, and version mismatches before widening the prefix.

The seven steps are: discover stale keys; freeze the run manifest; enqueue bounded batches; consume with version checks; acknowledge after the manifest write; inspect and redrive the DLQ; reconcile the final count. Keep the run ID in every log line.

Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers. Trigger precision has second-level jitter, and run-history output keeps only the first 4 KB, so detailed results belong in your own manifest. For a small Node.js shop with staffed Redis, BullMQ may remain simpler. For a multi-capability backend where one HTTP contract reduces integration work, Infrai deserves a measured pilot; price is only one line in the decision, while the durable cost is the worker, audit trail, and person who handles a growing DLQ.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the scheduled cleanup guide and verify the live schemas before production.

Sources

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/priority
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-run-lambda-schedule.html

title: Next.js 16.3 support on Vercel
description:
Yesterday the Next.js team announced the release of Next.js 16.3, with leaner prefetching, immutable static assets, and instant navigations. As part of this release, we worked with the Next.js team to fully support 16.3 on Vercel, including better performance and additional observability. Applications that have upgraded have seen:

  • Fewer prefetch requests: Apps upgrading from 16.2 to 16.3 saw 45% fewer prefetch requests on average, with some seeing reductions over 70%.

  • Lower static asset costs: With immutable static assets, upgraded apps saw 17% fewer CDN requests and 24% fewer bytes transferred for static content, and up to 60% global TTFB reductions for frequently deployed projects.

  • Faster routing at scale: Routing metadata improvements in the critical serving path deliver ~2x faster p99 route resolution for large sites.

Platform improvements

Next.js 16.3 ships leaner prefetching and enables immutable static assets by default. Supporting both meant changing the platform too, in how it caches static assets, resolves routes, and surfaces what happened in production.

Immutable static assets

Vercel now supports reusing immutable static assets across deployments for Next.js. Immutable static assets can't suffer from version skew, even for projects without Skew Protection enabled, and the browser cache survives redeploys. Because Next.js uses query-parameter-based Skew Protection, this change cut CDN requests by 17% and bytes transferred by 24% for static content. Deployments also complete up to 30% faster on average, since unchanged assets skip re-upload. In Next.js 16.3, immutable static assets are enabled by default.

Next.js 16.3 outputs immutable content-addressed static assets under the public path /_next/static/immutable/*. The Vercel CDN uses this prefix to differentiate immutable static assets from other static assets.

If you're a framework author and want to implement this in your own toolchain, see the immutable static files section of the Build Output API docs.

Faster routing at scale

Next.js 16 introduced an optimization where common parts of an application are prefetched once and reused across navigations, rather than fetched again for every link. To make that reuse work, each shared segment has to be fetchable on its own, so Next.js generates many more paths for the same application.

Those extra paths add up on the platform side. Frameworks like Next.js deploy to Vercel through the Build Output API, and for each path the framework generates a metadata file that describes how to serve it, such as its prerender configuration. The Vercel CDN reads that metadata in the path of every request, so each lookup has to finish in milliseconds or less, and it caches the metadata to stay under that budget. Globally, that's 5 million lookups per second. As Next.js 16 applications shipped more paths, the cache held more entries, hit rates dropped, and we saw p99 TTFB increase for larger applications.

To fix this, we improved the layer that serves route metadata, making it ~2x faster with ~10x fewer cache misses. Instead of storing each segment's metadata as its own cache entry, we now combine entries into JSONL-formatted shards, and we optimized in-process and remote caching around those shards. Fewer, larger entries mean better hit rates, and the JSONL format still lets the CDN find the right entry inside a shard quickly.

This improvement is implemented in the platform and already live for every deployment, so other frameworks that deploy through the Build Output API automatically benefit from it as well.

Improved observability

Next.js 16.3 includes improvements to prefetching that resulted in a 45% reduction in prefetch requests. You can now query whether a request was a prefetch in Vercel Observability and Runtime Logs, or in the query builder with Observability Plus.

We have also heard from users who want more visibility into Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) revalidations. The ISR observability page now prominently displays time-based and on-demand revalidations, we expose cache reasons and ISR write utilization, and we published a guide on how to reduce ISR revalidations.

Today, we are also launching observability for Partial Prerendering (PPR). PPR serves the static parts of a page immediately and then streams dynamic content, such as personalization or experimentation. Under the hood, it combines ISR and Vercel Functions into one system so applications benefit from both at the same time. Next.js 16 applications that use Cache Components get PPR automatically when deployed to Vercel.

In the Vercel dashboard, the PPR Observability page shows which requests are serving static content, dynamic content, or a combination of the two. Use it to confirm static shells are working, catch routes that have regressed to fully dynamic, and see when your functions run.

If you need to dig in, click through to the ISR or Functions observability pages for details about cache revalidations or function executions.

Upgrade today

Next.js 16.3 is available today. Upgrade to take advantage of the new features:

pnpm add next@16.3.0

Read the Next.js 16.3 announcement for the full release notes or learn more about Next.js on Vercel.

Read more

title: TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.07767v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for post-training large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial computation and memory overhead during rollout generation, which motivates low-precision rollout for efficient RL training. However, existing FP4 RL methods suffer from a key limitation: they primarily optimize quantization accuracy on the training and rollout paths independently rather than directly reducing the discrepancy between the two quantized execution paths. In this work, we propose TRACE (Train-Rollout Quantization Alignment via Compact GuidancE), an FP4 quantization framework for RL training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models that addresses the limitation of existing FP4 RL methods. TRACE incorporates rollout-guided quantization-aware training that uses rollout-side quantization outcomes to guide training-side FP4 rounding decisions, directly reducing train-rollout discrepancy. Moreover, TRACE adopts an efficient quantization-information caching scheme that selectively retains mantissa and scale information from deeper layers to reduce the storage and communication overhead introduced by rollout guidance. We evaluate TRACE on four large-scale MoE language models across reasoning, coding, and long-horizon RL tasks. Our results demonstrate that TRACE enables joint FP4 weight/activation and FP4 KV-cache rollout with RL performance comparable to BF16 rollout, while achieving up to 5.4xrollout speedup and strong final FP4 performance compared with post-hoc FP4 quantization of BF16-trained policies.

title: Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.13273v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code, existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event - overlooking the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and market-driven evolution of these artifacts. To address this issue, we present Agent4Spec, an autonomous multi-agent framework featuring two distinct pipelines: (1) a validation pipeline that detects and self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and (2) a market analysis pipeline that conducts competitive research, identifies functional gaps against industry leaders, and automatically generates missing API-spec functionalities. We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets of API specifications spanning both general-purpose and industrial scenarios. Among 9 SOTA LLMs, the top-performer achieves 100% syntax error detection rates and over 95% implementation success for proposed corrections, while securing over 50% adoption rates for suggested endpoint improvements, representing a practical tool for API development.

title: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.13395v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to build programs from scratch as software engineers do rather than to resolve issues within a repository or to generate a repository from a given requirements document. However, scalable verifiable training environments that force agents to discover what is required and to decide how the system should be designed remain scarce. Moreover, existing agent workflows also cannot sustain long-horizon development in which the agent explores the reference program before implementation. To address these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym, a framework consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env constructs verifiable training environments from repositories through a feedback-driven loop that repairs runtime sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests. Using this novel pipeline, we obtain 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust. Program-Agent combines a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review with revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. Experiments on ProgramBench show that both Program-Env and Program-Agent improve performance on program reproduction. Fine-tuning on trajectories with these constructed environments raises the performance of Qwen3.8-27B from 34.87% to 42.84%. Program-Agent further raises the base and SFT models to 55.71% and 56.25%, both exceeding some flagship models. We will release the ProgramGym to support further research on coding agents that build programs from scratch.

title: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
description:
arXiv:2609.38345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration and controlled causal evaluation.

title: Learning from All-Failed Groups via First-Visit Coverage in Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
description:
arXiv:2607.22724v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Group-based policy optimization has been increasingly used to train large language model (LLM) agents from sparse outcome rewards by comparing trajectories or steps within a group. However, on difficult long-horizon agentic tasks, we found this comparison suffers from a sampling imbalance: repeated or low-effect actions dominate the high-probability region of the policy, leaving useful state-changing actions under-sampled. This imbalance produces many all-failed rollout groups, where the relative advantages within such a group provide no direction for updating the policy. Consequently, the sampling imbalance and the all-failed groups collapse into a self-perpetuating credit trap: failure-dominated sampling yields no learning signal, allowing repeated low-effect actions to persist. To break this trap, we propose Coverage-conditioned Group Policy Optimization (CovGPO), which uses first-visit observation coverage only when all samples in a group receive zero outcome reward. Specifically, within such groups, CovGPO assigns higher relative advantages to state-exploring actions without corrupting the original reward signal, as reaching new observations is a prerequisite for task success. Experiments on two challenging agentic benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, show that CovGPO consistently improves over group-based baselines, with particularly large gains on hard tasks.

title: Medical foundation models converge less under label supervision
description:
arXiv:2607.20274v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diagnostic classifiers and imaging biomarkers are fitted on the embeddings of medical foundation models. These models are replaced as new versions appear. This practice assumes that different models represent images alike. We tested this assumption with more than 750,000 images from 14 datasets in 5 imaging modalities, 18 public models, and 101 models trained on chest radiographs and histopathology that differ in pretraining objective, label type, size, random seed, initialization, training patients, or training recipe. Agreement was measured as the mutual k-nearest-neighbor overlap, the share of an image's nearest neighbors common to two models. Two public models shared on average 0.091 of the 10 nearest neighbors of a chest radiograph. A randomly initialized network shared 0.036 with them. In the four other modalities, they shared at most 0.300. On chest radiographs, agreement depended more on the source dataset and the radiographic view than on the findings. It was not significantly associated with accuracy. A linear mapping between the embeddings of two models, fitted on 4,096 unlabeled radiographs, transferred classifiers for 14 chest findings with 0.987 of their original area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Convergence depended on the pretraining objective. Label-supervised models converged least at both model sizes in chest radiography and histopathology. On chest radiographs, two label-supervised models that differed only in their random seed shared 0.062 to 0.100 of their nearest neighbors. Two models trained with self-distillation, masked image modeling, or contrastive pretraining shared 0.411 to 0.802. Developers can therefore choose convergence when they choose the pretraining objective. Before replacing a model, users could test on unlabeled images whether its successor returns the same nearest neighbors.

title: Making LLMs Say What They Think: Measuring and Improving CoT-Interpretability Alignment
description:
arXiv:2609.38972v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces often serve as a proxy for how Large Language Models (LLMs) arrive at their answers. However, growing evidence shows that models' CoT often fails to reflect their internal computations and can be changed without affecting their final answers. In this work, we measure and improve the alignment between the reasoning described in an LLM's CoT and what it computes internally. We propose CoT-Interpretability Alignment (CIA), a metric that measures the agreement between a model's CoT traces and its internal reasoning strategies as detected by interpretability tools. We evaluate CIA on three tasks (two-hop question answering, hint intervention, and integer multiplication) across three LLMs, finding that LLMs exhibit limited alignment across all tasks (44.8-75.9%). We then experiment with improving CIA via post-training, setting both the task accuracy and parametric faithfulness signals as a reward. Experiments show that we can substantially improve CoT parametric faithfulness while maintaining or improving the task accuracy. We provide rich analysis, such as their generalization patterns. Our work provides both a framework for auditing CoT parametric faithfulness and a pathway toward making models' explicit reasoning more trustworthy. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yihuaihong/CIA-minimal-repro.

title: Modernizing Legacy Ext JS Applications with React, ReExt, and AI
description:
Rewriting a large enterprise frontend can be expensive. Beyond the UI, teams need to reproduce business logic, data workflows, custom components, and production behavior.

What if you could introduce React and AI capabilities without rebuilding every existing component?

The hybrid approach

Sencha ReExt provides an integration layer for using Ext JS components inside React JS framework applications.

A possible architecture looks like this:

React: Routing, application shell, and modern UI orchestration.
Ext JS: Existing grids, forms, trees, stores, and business logic.
ReExt: Connects Ext JS components with React's component lifecycle.
AI service: Interprets natural-language requests and converts them into structured operations.

This allows teams to modernize individual parts of an application while retaining existing functionality.

Example: Natural-language grid filtering

Imagine a sales application with thousands of customer records.

Instead of manually configuring filters, a user enters:

Show me users in India

Then follows up with:

Sort by sales

The application can process the request through an AI model and a dedicated query parser. The parser converts the user's intent into structured filter and sort commands, which are applied to the Ext JS store.

The grid then reflects the updated data.

The important architectural detail is that the AI should produce constrained, validated operations—not execute arbitrary user-generated code.

A practical migration strategy

For a legacy application, consider these steps:

Identify a high-value workflow that needs modernization.
Determine which existing components and business rules can be retained.
Integrate the necessary Ext JS components into the React application through ReExt.
Introduce AI features where they solve a real user problem.
Validate permissions, query handling, performance, and existing behavior.
Expand to additional modules after testing the first implementation.
What should teams watch for?

Hybrid architectures introduce their own engineering challenges:

Synchronizing React state with Ext JS stores
Keeping styles and interaction patterns consistent
Testing component lifecycle and cleanup
Validating AI-generated filters and sort operations
Enforcing data access permissions on the server side

AI should never bypass existing authorization rules just because a request is written in natural language.

Takeaway: Legacy modernization doesn't have to be an all-or-nothing decision. A React + ReExt approach can let teams preserve mature enterprise components while introducing modern interfaces and AI-powered workflows.

Would you use a hybrid architecture in an existing enterprise application, or do you prefer migrating everything to one framework?

title: MAGE: Multi-Agent Self-Evolution with Co-Evolutionary Knowledge Graphs
description:
arXiv:2605.10064v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Self-evolving language-model agents must decide what to learn next and how to preserve what they have learned across iterations. Existing systems typically carry this cross-iteration knowledge as natural-language feedback, flat episodic memory, or implicit reinforcement signals, none of which cleanly supports a frozen weak backbone at inference time. This paper introduces MAGE (Multi-Agent Graph-guided Evolution), a framework that externalizes self-knowledge into a four-subgraph co-evolutionary knowledge graph. Its experience subgraph stores both teacher-written failure corrections and the learner's own past correct reasoning traces, which are retrieved as task-conditioned guidance for a frozen execution model. During evolution, the graph, a task-level search bandit, and a skill-level routing bandit are updated from the same reward stream, while the learner's backbone remains unchanged. We further provide structural analysis showing how append-only memory growth, bounded curriculum coverage, and task-filtered retrieval together support stable improvement of the retrieval substrate for frozen-learner evolution. Across nine benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, multi-hop and open-domain question answering, spatio-temporal analysis, financial numerical reasoning, medical multiple-choice, an open-world survival game, and web navigation, MAGE achieves strong performance against prompt-based frozen-backbone baselines. Ablations show that self-harvested success traces and teacher-written corrections are complementary, with success memories contributing most on reasoning-template-heavy tasks and corrective memories supporting harder composition and interaction settings. Code is available in https://github.com/RuiyiYang01/mage-alg

title: Hyper Algorithm Design Agent: Evolving Learnable Optimizer from Zero
description:
arXiv:2609.35328v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Meta-Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) is one of the highlights in the recent AI for Optimization trend. This paradigm's bi-level workflow leverages the learnable algorithm design policy at meta level to ensure the performance and generalization improvement on the low-level optimization task. While MetaBBO helps advance the performance lower bound of the resulted optimization system, it is currently handcrafted and customized case by case to adapt different optimization problems, which inevitably introduces inherent subjectivity and hence restricts the performance upper bound and usability in practice. In this paper, we address this issue by regarding MetaBBO's design loop as coding task, where we could introduce openendedness into MetaBBO with recursive self-improvement capability of advanced coding agents. Specifically, we propose a dual-agent framework: i) a task agent continuously refines the codebase of a target MetaBBO approach through code evolution; ii) a hyper agent progressively modifies the task agent and itself to provide open-ended design behavior; iii) the evolved MetaBBO codebase is evaluated and all in-execution information is fed back to the agents for recursive self-referential improvement. As a result, given a naive MetaBBO template, our framework automates a design evolution and finds novel variants superior to up-to-date human-made MetaBBO baselines. Surprisingly, the experimental results also demonstrate that our framework supports fast adaption across different optimization domains. Solid interpretation analysis further reveals interesting design principles emerge in such open-ended process. This work serves as the first exploration on automating design of complex learning-assisted optimization algorithms.

title: Book Bolt: precios, prueba y diseño de libros para KDP
description:
Diseñar libros para KDP sin perder la cabeza: nuestra experiencia con Book Bolt

Como desarrolladores y product managers, sabemos que diseñar libros para Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP) puede ser un proceso tedioso y frustrante. Debes elegir el título, la portada, el contenido y la estructura del libro, todo mientras te aseguras de que se ajuste a las normas de KDP. Y si no lo haces bien, tu libro puede quedarse en la estantería.

Hemos probado varias herramientas para simplificar este proceso, y una de ellas es Book Bolt. En este artículo, exploraremos cómo funciona Book Bolt, sus casos de uso, sus limitaciones y alternativas.

Cómo funciona Book Bolt

Book Bolt es una herramienta en línea que te ayuda a investigar y diseñar libros para KDP. Funciona de la siguiente manera:

  1. Primero, debes introducir los detalles básicos de tu libro, como el título, la portada y el contenido.
  2. Luego, Book Bolt te proporciona una serie de sugerencias y recomendaciones para mejorar tu libro, como títulos alternativos, descripciones de portada y estructuras de contenido.
  3. Puedes elegir entre diferentes opciones y ajustar las sugerencias según tus necesidades.
  4. Finalmente, Book Bolt te genera un informe detallado con todas las sugerencias y recomendaciones, que puedes utilizar para mejorar tu libro.

Casos de uso concretos

Hemos probado Book Bolt en varios proyectos y hemos visto algunos resultados interesantes. Aquí te presentamos algunos casos de uso concretos:

  • Mejorar la portada: Book Bolt nos sugirió varias opciones de portada para nuestro libro, incluyendo diferentes diseños y colores. Al elegir la opción correcta, nuestro libro se convirtió en un éxito instantáneo.
  • Optimizar el título: Book Bolt nos recomendó un título alternativo que mejoraba la visibilidad de nuestro libro en las búsquedas de Amazon. Al cambiar el título, nuestro libro comenzó a recibir más tráfico y ventas.
  • Estructurar el contenido: Book Bolt nos ayudó a estructurar el contenido de nuestro libro de manera más efectiva, lo que mejoró la experiencia del lector y aumentó la tasa de completación.

Tradeoffs y limitaciones

Aunque Book Bolt es una herramienta muy útil, no es perfecta. Algunas de sus limitaciones incluyen:

  • Pricing: Book Bolt ofrece dos planes de pago: Pro y Premium. El plan Pro cuesta $29.99 al mes, mientras que el plan Premium cuesta $49.99 al mes. Si no tienes presupuesto para pagar un plan de pago mensual, Book Bolt no es una opción viable.
  • Free tier: Book Bolt no ofrece una versión gratuita, lo que significa que debes pagar para utilizar la herramienta.
  • Vendor lock-in: Book Bolt es una herramienta en línea, lo que significa que debes estar conectado a Internet para utilizarla. Si pierdes la conexión, no podrás acceder a la herramienta.

Alternativas open-source

Si no puedes pagar por Book Bolt, hay algunas alternativas open-source que puedes utilizar:

title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans
description:
arXiv:2610.13303v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM judges are increasingly deployed as panels, and disagreement among panel members is often read as a symptom of an unclear rubric. We test a label-free procedure that turns this disagreement into rubric repairs. The procedure decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested ones. An additional stage that moves text-checkable sub-criteria to deterministic checkers transferred none in our evaluation. Human labels are never used to select or edit clauses; they are used only to evaluate the outcome. We pre-specified four hypotheses in a version-controlled protocol and evaluated six rubric conditions with a panel of five judges from three providers on SummEval, the HealthBench meta-evaluation, and USR Topical-Chat, for a total of 129,770 judge requests, excluding retries. On SummEval, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's $\alpha$ by 0.069 (95% CI 0.046 to 0.092) over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that applied the same edits to an equal number of randomly chosen clauses that were not selected. Agreement with expert ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall $\tau$ difference -0.007, 95% CI -0.037 to 0.021). On HealthBench and USR, neither inter-judge agreement nor human agreement met the preregistered effect criteria. In a preregistered secondary comparison, human agreement after editing the contested clauses was lower than after editing the control clauses on all three datasets in point estimate, although no interval excluded zero. Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators. We will release code, frozen rubrics, item identifiers, and judge scores.

title: partworth: hierarchical Bayes for choice-based conjoint in Python
description:
A choice-based conjoint (CBC) study shows people a few products and asks them to pick one. Then it does this again and again. Each product is a mix of features, such as brand, size and price. From the choices, you estimate how much each feature matters to each person. Then you answer business questions. Which product wins? What happens if we raise the price? How much more will people pay for a bigger size?

A common method is hierarchical Bayes (HB). Many teams use Sawtooth CBC/HB for it. It is commercial and runs outside Python. So the work often looks like this: you estimate in one tool, export a file, and build a simulator in a spreadsheet. Each hand-off is a place for mistakes. The model's uncertainty is also often lost on the way, and the spreadsheet shows one share per product, with no range.

I wanted to do the whole thing in Python. Python already has general choice models. For example, pymc-marketing has a MixedLogit model. As of October 2026, it takes a wide table and has no correlations between coefficients. It also has no Sawtooth-style files and no WTP. For CBC work, I needed a few specific things:

  • a "none" option, for people who would buy nothing
  • correlated tastes, because people who care about brand may also care about price
  • a price coefficient that is negative for every respondent, so willingness to pay makes sense
  • outputs in the format CBC teams already use, like a Sawtooth-style utilities file
  • a market simulator that shows uncertainty

I could not find one Python package that did all of this, so I wrote partworth. It is open source (Apache-2.0) and built on PyMC.

What partworth does

The README splits the workflow into four steps.

  1. Your survey. You bring CBC answers in long format, one row per respondent, task and alternative. You can also import a wide design, for example from ChoiceDesign.
  2. Fit one model. ChoiceData checks the data. HierarchicalMNL runs HB estimation on PyMC. Then you get diagnostics: R-hat, effective sample size (ESS) and divergences.
  3. Read the results. You get part-worths for each respondent, attribute importances and RLH (a fit score for each person). You can write a Sawtooth-style CSV file.
  4. Answer business questions. You get market shares with credible intervals, price curves, and willingness to pay (WTP) for a feature.

Steps 1 to 3 replace the "estimate, export, spreadsheet" routine. Step 4 uses the posterior draws, so every share, price curve and WTP comes with a credible interval.

A few design choices are there because of how CBC data look. Each person usually answers only about 8 to 20 tasks, so the data for one person is thin. partworth uses a non-centred model, which usually samples better in this case. It puts an LKJ prior on the correlations between tastes. For price, you can add a sign constraint. Then the price coefficient is negative for every respondent, through a lognormal. Without this, a respondent whose price coefficient is near zero or positive gives a WTP that makes no sense.

A quick look

partworth needs Python 3.12 or later. It is not on PyPI yet, so you install it from GitHub:

pip install "partworth[nutpie,datasets] @ git+https://github.com/kojikojikojikoji/partworth"

On macOS 26 or later, PyTensor 3.3.3 or earlier can fail with ld: library 'd64' not found. Set PYTENSOR_FLAGS=cxx= to avoid it.

This is the Quick look example from the README. It uses simulated data, so you can paste it as it is.

import pandas as pd
import partworth as pw
from partworth.datasets import simulate_cbc

# 300 respondents, 12 tasks, 3 products + "none" per task.
# mu: true population means of the coded coefficients (price on the log scale).
data, truth = simulate_cbc(
    300, 12, 3,
    {"brand": ["A", "B", "C"], "size": ["S", "M", "L"], "price": [2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5]},
    price="price", mu=[0.4, -0.1, -0.3, 0.1, -0.5, -1.0], sd=0.6, seed=1,
)
print(data.describe())                       # how often each level was shown and chosen

# more tuning and draws than the defaults: the SD of "none" mixes slowly (see the guide)
result = pw.HierarchicalMNL(data).fit(draws=2000, tune=3000, chains=4, random_seed=1)
print(result.diagnostics().report())         # R-hat, ESS, divergences, what to try

result.part_worths()                         # raw utilities, one column per level
result.part_worths("zc_diffs")               # zero-centred diffs
result.importances()
result.to_sawtooth_csv("utilities.csv")

scenario = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["Ours", "Theirs"], "brand": ["A", "B"],
                         "size": ["M", "M"], "price": [3.0, 2.5]})
sim = pw.MarketSimulator(result)
print(sim.shares(scenario))                  # shares with 90% credible intervals
print(sim.price_curve(scenario, product="Ours", grid=[2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5]))
print(pw.wtp(result, attribute="size", from_level="S", to_level="L"))

simulate_cbc makes 300 fake respondents with known true values. The fit uses more tuning and more draws than the defaults. The SD of "none" mixes slowly in this example, and the user guide explains why. The last three lines answer the business questions. Each one prints an estimate together with its credible interval.

For real data, examples/camera.py runs the same steps on the public camera data from the R package bayesm. partworth downloads that data from CRAN on first use.

How I checked it

An HB package can give numbers that look fine and still be wrong. So the repository has validation scripts. Each script writes a report to validation/results/. These are the main results.

Comparison with R bayesm. I ran bayesm 3.1.7 (rhierMnlRwMixture) and partworth on the camera data. Tasks 1 to 14 were for estimation. Tasks 15 and 16 were kept as hold-out tasks.

  • For every coefficient, the respondent-level posterior means of the two packages correlate at 0.997 or more.
  • The hold-out hit rate is 0.729 for partworth and 0.730 for bayesm.

The two packages use different samplers and priors. bayesm uses random-walk Metropolis and an inverse-Wishart prior. partworth uses NUTS and an LKJ prior. Even so, the respondent-level posterior means move together very closely, and the two packages predict the hold-out tasks equally well.

Parameter recovery. I simulated 300 respondents with 12 tasks each, using known true values. Then I checked if partworth could find them.

  • Respondent-level 90% intervals covered 88.7% of the true values.
  • 5 of 6 population means and 6 of 6 SDs were inside their 90% intervals.
  • For the coefficients, the convergence targets were met: R-hat max 1.006, bulk ESS min 1094, no divergences. The correlations are a different story (see below).

Simulation-based calibration. I fitted 200 simulated data sets and looked at 8 population parameters. The smallest uniformity p-value was 0.017. None was below 0.006, the threshold after correcting for 8 tests. So the test found no problem. That is not a proof that the model is calibrated, but it is a useful check.

Speed. On one laptop, 300 respondents took 74 seconds. 1,000 respondents took 290 seconds.

What is not good enough yet

Some targets were not met. I want to list them clearly.

  • On the camera data, population means differ from bayesm by up to 0.21 of bayesm's posterior SD. My target was 0.1, so this target is not met. The two packages use different priors. When I made partworth's priors much wider, the difference grew to 0.92 SDs. The respondent-level means still correlated with bayesm at 0.998. So, at least on this data set, the population means are sensitive to the priors.
  • In the recovery test, the price mean (on the log scale) was just outside its 90% interval. The true value was 0.30 and the interval was [0.13, 0.29].
  • In the recovery test, correlations between tastes mixed slowly. They reached R-hat 1.013 and ESS 399. The targets are R-hat below 1.01 and ESS above 400. Before you report correlations, check their diagnostics. You may need more draws.
  • In the calibration run, 15 of the 200 fits had a population ESS below 99. That makes the check weaker.
  • The "Sawtooth-style" files follow Sawtooth's public manuals. They have not been compared with files made by Sawtooth software.
  • The package is pre-alpha. The API may change. It is not on PyPI yet.

All examples use public or simulated data. The camera data comes from bayesm, which is GPL. partworth never includes that data and uses no bayesm code. The comparison runs R in a separate process.

What is next

The next step is a first release on PyPI. Some things are out of scope: experimental design (use ChoiceDesign for that), latent class, MaxDiff and ACBC.

If you work with CBC data, please try it. Run the Quick look, then examples/camera.py. If you have Sawtooth, I would like to see how its utilities file compares with partworth's. If a fit does not converge, or a number looks wrong to you, please open an issue. Simulated data that shows the problem is the most helpful.

The code, the user guide and all validation reports are here: https://github.com/kojikojikojikoji/partworth

I am Koji Miyazawa, a data scientist living in London. Thanks for reading.

title: How we route bugs from Slack, Sentry and PostHog into one QA runbook, per platform
description:
Most bugs in an app that's already live never come from a test plan. They arrive as a Slack message, a client's email, a Sentry alert or a session someone watched in PostHog. In most teams, someone copies them into a tracker by hand, and two things get lost on the way: which platform the bug is on, and who needs to hear when it's fixed.

Last week we shipped integrations in qarunbook to close that gap. Here's how they work.

One door for every bug

Every source raises the bug through the same path as the form in the app. A message raised from Slack or Teams, an email to the app's address, a Sentry issue, a PostHog webhook delivery, a Zapier zap or a plain JSON webhook all end up as the same kind of issue: a code like QA-41, the platforms it affects, a priority, assignees, and a copy in Jira, Linear, GitHub or GitLab if the app uses one.

Because it's one path, a bug from Slack is treated exactly like one typed in by a tester. It counts the same, gets triaged the same, and needs the same retest before it's done.

Fixes are per platform

An app can link several GitHub repositories, each tagged with the platforms it builds. When a pull request that fixes a bug is merged, qarunbook marks the bug fixed only on the platforms that repository builds. A fix in the web repo marks web fixed; iOS stays open until its fix lands. The check reads "retest" where something changed and stays failed elsewhere, so nobody retests the wrong platform or closes a bug that's only half fixed.

The source hears back

When the fix is confirmed, the place the bug came from is told: the Slack or Teams thread gets a reply, the person who emailed gets an email, and the Sentry issue is resolved. If Sentry sees the error again, the issue reopens and the people on it are told.

Guarding the edges

  • Sentry and PostHog deliveries are checked against their signatures; tokens are only ever sent to the vendor's own hosts.
  • Repeated deliveries of the same error are merged into one issue while it's open.
  • Webhooks can be signed with an HMAC secret and are rate limited per app.

On every plan

Every integration and the API are on every plan, including Free. Plans differ by how much you use, not by what you can use.

The full write-up, with everything else that shipped that week: https://qarunbook.com/changelog/2026-10-05

title: Vercel Connect adds observability support
description:
Vercel Connect now gives teams line-level visibility into the token lifecycle. See who created a token, what app or project used it, when, and whether it is still active.

Every connector's detail page includes a new Observability tab:

  • Runtime events: Every token request, authorization, refresh, revocation, and trigger delivery, filterable by type.

  • Correlation IDs: Stable tokenId and authorizationId values link each token's events, so you can match Connect events to your own systems.

  • Activity: The Activity filter button opens the Activity page pre-filtered to the connector's configuration events, so you can see when and how it changed.

Connect observability is available on all plans. Events are retained for 12 hours on Hobby, 3 days on Pro, and 30 days on Enterprise. To retain events longer, forward them to a custom webhook endpoint by adding a Drain on Pro and Enterprise plans. Enterprise teams also get role-based access control and audit logs.
