title: CSS only game: Point and click puzzle cube
description:
Introduction

Recently I wanted to experiment more with 3D objects in CSS. So, I started with setting up a “simple” 3D object in CSS: a cube.
After fiddling around I managed to create said cube, and proceeded to stack 3 on top of them to create a 3D rotating snowman: https://codepen.io/jvp/pen/XJrPXjx
This gave me the idea to take it a step further: how far CSS could go in building not just a 3D object, but an actual interactive game?

Starting from a simple cube, I ended up building a layered point-and-click puzzle box powered entirely by CSS: state management, animations, and even puzzle progression logic.

In this article, I’ll walk through the key techniques that make this work:

  • building a 3D cube
  • reading input values in CSS
  • and sequencing game logic without JavaScript

If you want to see the full code and/or go straight to the result you can view the game at https://codepen.io/jvp/full/RNPbPNw. I will not explain every line of code in this article but instead will pick the parts that are worth explaining how the entire thing works and behaves.

Disclaimer
Currently, this CSS-only game only works in Chrome because it uses style container queries which are not yet supported in other browsers.
If you open the game in another browser, you will see a dialog that will provide a link to an older version of the game where range sliders have an oninput change listener to set the input's value to a data-value property with JavaScript.

Setting up a cube in CSS

To create a CSS cube we need to set our HTML with a container element and 6 faces of the cube:

<div class="cube-container">
  <div class="cube-face front"></div>
  <div class="cube-face back"></div>
  <div class="cube-face right"></div>
  <div class="cube-face left"></div>
  <div class="cube-face top"></div>
  <div class="cube-face bottom"></div>
</div>

Then we add some CSS, first for the container:

.cube-container {
  --cube-size: 200px;
  --half-size: calc(var(--cube-size) / 2);
  width: var(--cube-size);
  height: var(--cube-size);
  margin: var(--half-size);
  transform-style: preserve-3d;
  position: relative;
  transform: rotateX(var(--rotate-x, -15deg)) rotateY(var(--rotate-y, -45deg));
}

Transform-style: preserve-3d is necessary to make the 3D perspective work.
As for transform property itself, a rotate3d value exists but I found that to be quite confusing. Instead, we are using rotateX to rotate the cube on the vertical axis (yes, this is counterintuitive) and rotateY for the horizontal axis.
Right now the --rotate-x and --rotate-y vars have default values of -15deg and -45deg, but we’ll properly set these vars later.

Next is the CSS for the faces:

.cube-face {
  position: absolute;
  width: inherit;
  height: inherit;

  &.front { transform: translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.back { transform: translateZ(calc(-1 * var(--half-size))) rotateY(180deg); }
  &.right { transform: rotateY(90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.left { transform: rotateY(-90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.top { transform: rotateX(90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.bottom { transform: rotateX(-90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
}

With this CSS applied, the cube will look something like this:

And this is where code for CSS cubes get a bit more counterintuitive, at least to my opinion. TranslateZ will move the element along the Z axis, or in other words: depth. Each face starts from the “center” of the cube.
So, for the front face we need move it forwards on the Z axis, half a cube size.
For the back face, we need to move it backwards using translateZ with a negative half-size value. But after it has been moved back, we will be looking at the backside of the element. We flip it on its horizontal axis by then applying rotateY(180deg) so that we can look at the front-side of this face.
For the right and left sides, we define rotateY first to let the face turn to the correct side and then apply the depth with translateZ to move it outwards. The same approach Is used for the top and bottom sides.

As you can see when comparing the back and the right/left style definitions, determining the order of your transformations has an impact on how the 3d aspect is applied and it can become hard to visualize the outcome of your styling beforehand. The best approach is to just try out stuff in your browser’s devtools, so you get instant feedback of your changes.

At this point, we have made a 3D cube out of CSS and HTML that still has a static rotation value.
In the next step we will apply controls for our game so that we can rotate and zoom our cube using sliders.

Adding range sliders as game controls — and reading their values in CSS.

In this game there are multiple range sliders that control the game in different ways. For example, for zoom and for rotating the cube horizontally/vertically. But there are also range sliders for individual puzzles.
Usually, you can’t read the values of range sliders in CSS, you’d need JS for that. But by applying a combination of cool CSS features we can actually use the values of the sliders in CSS.

In a nutshell: we will leverage view-timeline on range sliders to keep track of the range slider thumb’s position, then update a CSS var using a keyframe animation based on that position, then can use that CSS var in/on other elements.

We’ll look at a range slider which is the easiest to explain so that we can understand how the technique works.
The zoom slider allows us to zoom in/out a bit on the cube:

<div class="slider-container zoom-slider">
  <div class="thumb-track">
    <input type="range" min="0" max="5" value="2" class="slider">
  </div>
</div>

The HTML part is straightforward: a range slider with a min, max and value attribute. Its parent is a div with class “thumb-track” which we’ll get into later.

The CSS part contains a lot more stuff to go over, so we’ll dissect that step by step:

@property --zoom-value {
  syntax: "<integer>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: 2;
}

input[type="range"] {
  overflow: hidden;
  animation: --zoom-anim linear both;
  animation-timeline: --zoom-timeline;
  animation-range: entry 100% exit 0%;
  timeline-scope: --zoom-timeline;
}

input[type="range"]::-webkit-zoom-thumb {
  view-timeline: --zoom-timeline inline;
}

@keyframes --zoom-anim {
  from { --zoom-val: 5 }
  to { --zoom-val:  0 }
}
  1. --zoom-value registration using @property.
    • By using @property to register the CSS var as an integer, we tell the browser how to interpolate its value.
    • Without this, the browser will handle the var as a string, making it impossible to use the var's value in animations.
  2. view-timeline: --zoom-timeline
    • Defined on the webkit-zoom-thumb pseudo selector, turns the thumb's position within a scroll container into a named progress timeline.
    • As we move the thumb to the right using our mouse, the thumb "scrolls" and we can track its progress as it goes from 0% to 100%.
    • inline means that we work on the x/horizontal axis. block would mean that we would work on a y/vertical axis.
  3. overflow: hidden
    • Will make sure that the "viewport" of the scroll container is bound to the input's size.
  4. animation-timeline: --zoom-timeline
    • Means that the animation is driven by the timeline/scroll position, instead of regular keyframe animations that are based on seconds.
  5. timeline-scope: --zoom-timeline
    • By default, a view-timeline is only usable by the children of the element that defined the timeline (in our case the thumb).
    • By defining timeline-scope on the input, it can grab the --zoom-timeline from the thumb and apply it on itself (the input) instead.
  6. animation-fill-mode: both
    • Timeline-driven animations only apply their keyframe values (on --zoom-value) while the element is within the animation-range. Outside that range (at start or end), the --zoom-value property resets back to its initial value.
    • By applying the value both, we make sure that the property's value holds at either the start or end values when at the edges of the range.
  7. animation-range: entry 100% exit 0
    • This feels wrong, but by default, scroll/view-timelines are designed for elements entering the viewport from the bottom and move to the top, or from right to left.
    • "0%" is the moment the element starts to enter the view, and "100%" is when it exits/leaves.
    • Since our slider thumb starts on the left (the "entry" side), we map the start of the animation to entry 100% so that moving right (towards the "exit") progresses the value forward.
    • This flips the timeline logic to compensate for the earlier mentioned default direction of the view timeline.
  8. animation: --zoom-anim
    • This keyframe animation follows the same logic as the "inverted" animation-range.
    • At the end (from) of the timeline animation, update --zoom-value to be 5.
    • At the start (to) of the timeline animation, update --zoom-value to be 0.
    • Any timeline progress (when you drag the thumb) between end and start will be interpolated to values like 1, 2, 3 or 4.

That’s a lot of information, but it takes some time to explain it and to wrap your head around this solution.
But, now that we can update our CSS var, it’s time to use it!

.container .game-holder {
  scale: calc(0.8 + var(--zoom-val) * 0.18);
}

body {
  --rotate-x: calc((var(--ver-val) - 90) * 1deg);
  --rotate-y: calc(var(--hor-val) * 1deg);
}

Based on the zoom slider’s value, the scaling of our cube will be somewhere between 0.8 and 1.8.
On the body, we define the --rotate-y and --rotate-x CSS vars (for the horizontal and vertical sliders) based on the --ver-val and --hor-val custom properties that were created in a similar manner like --zoom-val.
In the previous chapter we already used these rotate vars on the .cube-container for rotation, so now that we added the sliders, we can scale and rotate our cube in real time!

At this point, we have implemented a technique based on view-timeline to read and store the value of input range sliders without any JavaScript.
This isn’t just used for rotation and zooming of the cube, it’s also used as a game mechanic in a few puzzles.

Adding visuals, a puzzle element, an inventory and a dialog

With the basics in place, we can start adding textures to our cube and incorporate puzzle elements to it.
For this game I decided to build multiple layers of the cube. So, there’s an outer / 1st layer where we start and once that layer is solved, we go deeper into the cube to the 2nd layer and finally into the 3rd layer.
For the aesthetics, I decided to go with a copper steampunk style. Given the fact that we’re dealing with a puzzle cube, steampunk gears would also fit perfectly. I made use of Bing’s free AI image generator and asked it to generate 6 faces of a cube in this aesthetic and named 6 different animal faces that should be on each face of the cube. The result was a beautiful image with a great steampunk aesthetic; we’re off to a great start!

As one could expect with AI though (it’s never perfect), there were 2 bears in it, and the wolf and fox looked a bit similar. I decided to put the bear and wolf faces at the top and bottom of the cube so they were less prominent.
The bear with the goggles gave a great opportunity to put a red gemstone in one of the goggles that the player could inspect and collect. Putting the bear with the goggles on the back of the cube meant that it would only become visible once the player rotates the cube. This way the player is taught to look around the cube for clues to solve puzzles.
I mapped each face from the image to each face of the cube, gave the cube an extra layer-1 class and added a inside the right face for the gem, which, based on the starting point of view (POV) for the game, was at the back of the cube.

<div class="cube-container cube-layer-1">
  ...
  <div class="cube-face right">
    <label for="gem-red-dialog" class="gem-red-get gem-label"></label>
  </div>
  ...
</div>

At the start of the HTML, I added a checkbox with id gem-red-dialog, to which the aforementioned label points to with it’s for attribute.

<input type="checkbox" id="gem-red-dialog" />

After clicking the label, the input for the dialog will become checked. Using the label + checkbox combination is one way of doing state management without JS, and it’s probably the most robust one as it will result in a clear boolean value after clicking on the label.

Now that the red gem is clickable, we will hook into it and do two things:

  • Display a dialog describing the item that was picked up.
  • Add some UI for an inventory so we can display the collected red gem.

The dialog element is a simple div container that’s hidden by default and has disabled pointer events.

<div class="dialog gem-red">
  <div class="item gem-red"></div>
  <h1>Garnet</h1>
  <p>An expensive looking gemstone.</p>
  <p>Looks like it could fit into something.</p>
  <label for="gem-red-get" class="close"></label>
</div>

Once the checkbox is checked, it animates in:

.dialog {
  ...
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
}

#gem-red-dialog:checked ~ .dialog.gem-red {
  pointer-events: all;
  animation: dialogIn 0.6s cubic-bezier(.4, 0, .2, 1) forwards;
}

@keyframes dialogIn {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translate(-50%, -40%); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translate(-50%, -50%); }
}

The inventory is positioned at the bottom left of the screen. Each item (which is just another label that will target another checkbox) is hidden by default and will only be shown when the checkbox for getting that item has been checked.

<div class="inventory">
  <label for="gem-red-use" class="gem-red-use"></label>
  <label for="gem-blue-use" class="gem-blue-use"></label>
  <label for="glass-use" class="glass"></label>
</div>

When the player picks up the gem and closes the dialog, another checkbox (#gem-red-get) gets checked which in turn will show the item in the inventory.

<div class="dialog gem-red">
  ...
  <label for="gem-red-get" class="close"></label>
</div>

#gem-red-get:checked ~ .inventory .gem-red-use {
  display: block;
}

Puzzles from the cube’s 2nd layer – and container queries

As the red gem is collected the 1st layer opens up, revealing the 2nd layer of the cube.

Once the 2nd layer is focused into view, we are automatically facing the first face of the second cube which has a steampunk metal tree on it. Let’s call this the front face of the 2nd layer for orientation purposes.
At the base of the tree, there are two pipes running off to the left and right, hinting that the other faces are connected and could power/feed the tree somehow.

Electric box/lever puzzle

If we look at the face to the left, we see a face where the pipe goes into an electric box.
This puzzle (constructed by using multiple elements/layers) also has three range sliders rotated at 90 degrees, with the numbers 1 through 10 written alongside.
When the range sliders are adjusted to match this combination, the electric box opens and reveals a lever that you can pull down:

Wheel puzzle

On the back face we find a large wheel with a rotating handle attached to it, the handle is actually just another range slider. By default a range slider is never curved, but the illusion here of a curved range slider is created by rotating the range slider with its own value as you drag it. Around the edge of the wheel are various steampunk-themed icons. The goal is to find the tree icon (the same one from the front face) and align the handle with it.
Once solved, a compartment with the item Aether monocle is revealed.

9 buttons puzzle

The right face contains a large circular glass with a 3×3 grid of nine buttons beside it. For this puzzle the player needs to press the correct buttons.

To know which buttons need to be pressed, the player should use the Aether monocle from their inventory to see the solution.
Once the correct buttons are checked and the rest are left unchecked, the puzzle has been solved and the glass lights up with blue electricity.

Container queries

To read the values of these puzzles and respond to them, @container style queries are used for most of these 2nd layer’s puzzles.
Why container queries? We need a way to combine and manage separate pieces of state:

  • checkbox values (state of HTML elements)
  • range slider values (CSS variables)
  • triggering a transition that only fires when all conditions are met.

We achieve this by using :has() selectors and @container style() queries together, leveraging the strengths of each:

  • The :has() selector is perfect for checking DOM states (like :checked on checkboxes). By chaining :has() and :not() selectors, we can verify the exact combination of checked and unchecked boxes for the 9-buttons puzzle. If the pattern is correct, the --checkboxes-solved variable is updated to 1.
  • Container style queries act as a rule engine: While :has() is great for DOM states, it cannot read CSS variables and thus cannot check the exact numeric value of a range slider. Container style queries solve this. They allow us to treat CSS variables as a state and react to them declaratively.

By combining both techniques, we can check to see whether both required puzzles are solved before we proceed.

body
  :has(#n-1:not(:checked))
  :has(#n-2:checked)
  :has(#n-3:checked)
  :has(#n-4:checked)
  :has(#n-5:not(:checked))
  :has(#n-6:not(:checked))
  :has(#n-7:not(:checked))
  :has(#n-8:checked)
  :has(#n-9:checked)
{
  --checkboxes-solved: 1;
}

// A value of 2 for --lever-val means that the electric box lever was pulled down (in other words: solved)
@container style(--checkboxes-solved: 1) and style(--lever-val: 2) {
  // Styling here to transition the game to the 3rd layer
}

Once both the “9 buttons” and “electric box” puzzles have been solved, all controls are locked and fade out, then the cube automatically rotates back to the front face to show an animation where green leaves grow on the metallic tree.

Once the leaves animation is done, the blue gem fades in on one of the branches. Clicking it opens another dialog and adds the gem to the inventory.
Closing the dialog will open up the 2nd layer’s cube and show the 3rd and final layer, the layer with the dark crystal.

At this point we have used the same range slider technique as actual game mechanics, and leveraged container style queries to check whether we have the right values for CSS vars to continue.
By now we have tackled all the advanced CSS logic. However, for our 3rd layer we have one final trick using simple HTML form elements and CSS.

The final puzzle

The 3rd layer is the core of the cube, a dark floating crystal that slowly hovers up and down. The crystal projects an entire map of stars in our room. These stars slowly fade in and out, but the player with a keen eye will notice that a star on the left side and a star on the right side blink in a different pattern. These two stars are the key to solving this final puzzle.

The 2 new arrow buttons on the left and right sides of the screen are disabled by default, but both buttons contain gray slots in the middle.
By placing the gems from the inventory in each button, the buttons become active, allowing the player to rotate the dark crystal.

In this section we will implement a way for the user to click the left and right buttons in a certain pattern in order to solve this last puzzle.
We will cover the following challenges:

  1. How do we implement a click-pattern in HTML/CSS without JavaScript?
  2. How do we know whether the player has clicked the correct or incorrect button?
  3. How do we keep track of the number of clicks that are done for this pattern?
  4. How do we reset the pattern if an incorrect answer was selected and the player needs to start over?

Luckily, we have a robust set of old HTML elements that allow us to do just that: a radio button group.

<div class="layer-3-controls">
  <div class="radios">
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step1" name="layer-3" value="1" checked />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step1b" name="layer-3" value="1b" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step2" name="layer-3" value="2" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step3" name="layer-3" value="3" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step3b" name="layer-3" value="3b" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step4" name="layer-3" value="4" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step5" name="layer-3" value="5" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-step6" name="layer-3" value="6" />
    <input type="radio" id="layer-3-solved" name="layer-3" value="solved" />
  </div>

  <div class="step n1">
    <div class="progress">step 1</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step2"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step1b"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n1b">
    <div class="progress">step 1b</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step2"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step1"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n2">
    <div class="progress">step 2</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step3"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step1"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n3">
    <div class="progress">step 3</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step3b"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step4"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n3b">
    <div class="progress">step 3b</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step3"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step4"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n4">
    <div class="progress">step 4</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step2"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step5"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n5">
    <div class="progress">step 5</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step6"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-step1"></label>
  </div>
  <div class="step n6">
    <div class="progress">step 6</div>
    <label class="left" for="layer-3-step3"></label>
    <label class="right" for="layer-3-solved"></label>
  </div>
</div>

.step {
  display: none;
}

.radios:has(#layer-3-step1:checked) ~ .step.n1 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step1b:checked) ~ .step.n1b { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step2:checked) ~ .step.n2 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step3:checked) ~ .step.n3 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step3b:checked) ~ .step.n3b { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step4:checked) ~ .step.n4 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step5:checked) ~ .step.n5 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-step6:checked) ~ .step.n6 { display: block; }
.radios:has(#layer-3-solved:checked) ~ .step.solved { display: block; }

I’m not going to lie, setting this up is where my brain started to hurt.
To simplify things, let’s ignore the 1b/3b steps for now.

The idea is fairly straightforward:

  • There are 6 step containers, and we only show 1 step at a time.
    • Only the active step has display: block, while the others have display: none.
  • All steps have position: absolute and are all placed in the same position.
  • Each step has a left and right button that target a different radio input.
    • One button is the correct answer for that current step and will take you further into the pattern, the other button is the incorrect answer.
  • By clicking the correct button (and thus checking the next radio input in the radio input group) the next step becomes visible.
    • Since these steps are instantly swapped with display: block/none, the player does not notice that a new step with new buttons is being shown.
  • By clicking the incorrect button, you are either taken back to step 1, or an earlier step.
  • If you click the final correct button, the layer-3-solved radio input will be checked and we finish the game.
  • In case you haven't seen this puzzle in action yet and have not seen the pattern of the blinking left/right stars, the correct pattern is left, left, right, right, left, right.

This is an elegant solution to keep track of a click pattern without needing any JavaScript, and this is probably my favorite part of code for this game.

If we look at the dark crystal while we click on the left or right buttons, we can see that the crystal will rotate clockwise (left) or counterclockwise (right). At first, I did not have the 1b and 3b steps, but the downside was that the rotating of the crystal didn’t make much sense without these extra steps.
If you are on step 1 and you would click on the right button (the incorrect answer), it wouldn’t make much sense to target the same step 1 radio input to prevent progression as nothing visually would change. We need to give the player visual feedback that something happened, and the impression that clicking on the right button will rotate the crystal just like normal. At this point the player still needs to find out that there actually is a pattern that needs to be solved.

Hence why I introduced the 1b step. If you are on step 1 and click on the right button, then the crystal will rotate to the right and step 1b becomes active. Clicking on the right button while in step 1b (still the incorrect answer) will activate step 1 again and the process/pattern has successfully been reset, thus creating a perfect infinite loop if the player keeps clicking on the right button while having a visual indication that something is still happening.
The same reasoning has been used for step 3b to keep the impression that rotating continues “like normal” even when the incorrect button has been clicked.

What makes this setup even better is that an incorrect answer will never break the puzzle/sequence, it just resets you to an earlier step and there is no finite amount of tries.
This means that no matter when you start following the pattern of the blinking stars, as long as you follow their pattern, you'll eventually solve the puzzle.

Once the final radio button (#layer-3-solved) is checked, the controls disappear and the crystal starts spinning rapidly with a flickering light effect. The same six animal faces from the 1st layer appear as constellations and begin counterrotating around the crystal. After a few seconds a white radial flash scales from the center and the final “win screen” dialog is shown, congratulating the player on its keen observation skills:

Outro

Phew, that was quite a lot to cover. As mentioned in the intro I did not/could not cover every little piece of code in this article, but you are more than welcome to check out the source at https://codepen.io/jvp/full/RNPbPNw to take a deep dive. There’s more nifty pieces of code like the growth of the leaves to take a look at.

The techniques that we discussed and the combination of them is indeed powerful, but this obviously comes with tradeoffs:

  • Browser support (currently limited due to techniques used on the range sliders - Chrome only)
  • Complexity and maintainability (state is distributed across CSS selectors, which can become hard debug)
  • Accessibility (interactions rely heavily on visuals and hidden inputs)
  • Maintainability (adding new puzzles increases selector complexity quickly)

In a real-world application this obviously is not a recommended setup, but as an experiment this shows how far CSS can be pushed as a state system.
Individually though, these techniques themselves can be very powerful tools for styling your site.

Thank you for reading and hopefully this has been an enjoyable and informative read about the wonders and (lack of) limitations of CSS. There are so many cool things we can do if we think creatively with the HTML and CSS tools that we have at our disposal.

Did you create any cool CSS-only showcases yourself? I’d love to see them in the comments!

title: GeopoliticalQA: Benchmarking Retrieval and Generation over Intelligence Reports
description:
arXiv:2610.12617v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports constitute a rich source of expert knowledge and have increasing value in the current political climate, but their heterogeneity and analytical complexity pose challenges for retrieval-augmented question answering. We introduce a benchmark for grounded question answering over 415 open-source geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports, comprising 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions. We propose a document-aware generation pipeline that profiles reports before generating questions and validate dataset quality through expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Using the benchmark, we evaluate 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs for RAG. We find that models perform similarly on document-level retrieval, while at the harder chunk level retrieval quality is not driven by embedding-model scale: bge-m3, a mid-size open encoder matches an order of magnitude larger ones and outperforms commercial embedding APIs. In contrast, answer generation remains challenging even given the gold evidence, particularly for inferential and risk-oriented questions.

title: Do Prompt Optimizers Break Requirements They Are Not Scored On? A Preregistered Study
description:
arXiv:2610.13287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prompt optimizers rewrite a prompt to raise one target metric, but prompts also state requirements the metric does not score, such as an output format, citations, or abstention. In a preregistered study, we run GEPA, MIPROv2, and TextGrad on HotpotQA, SQuAD 2.0, and IFEval and count per-item violations of unscored requirements with deterministic checks. By the preregistered criterion, all three optimizers produce regressions, substantially on HotpotQA, where net regression in citation validity reaches 10.7 to 41.6 points while exact match rises by 21 to 34 points. A post-hoc decomposition changes this reading. The optimized prompts elicit reasoning before the required JSON object, and under the 200-token output cap used throughout, 13.9% to 47.0% of responses end before any answer appears. Among parseable outputs, net regression is within 3 points of zero. With a 1,024-token cap, extraction failures disappear, content regression stays below 1 point, and exact match rises further. Two simple gates fail the preregistered criterion. The side effect is narrower than hypothesized: optimized prompts are more accurate and break an explicit output contract, and a lenient target metric does not show the cost.

title: Convex Optimization of Spiking Neural Networks with Global and Approximation Guarantees
description:
arXiv:2605.08022v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have been proposed as energy-efficient alternatives to deep neural networks. Their training is non-convex and involves a non-differentiable spike function, so existing methods offer no guarantee of reaching a global optimum. We address this issue by formulating SNN optimization as an equivalent convex optimization problem. Specifically, we show that the weight-decay-regularized training problem for a class of threshold RNNs, including leaky integrate-and-fire SNNs, has zero duality gap and the same optimal value as a convex program. Since the resulting convex programs can have exponentially many variables in the amount of data, we introduce a practical randomized surrogate and establish a high-probability guarantee on its approximation quality. Empirically, the best convex variant outperforms surrogate-gradient training on addition and first-last-XOR, matches its performance on sequential MNIST, and trails a reservoir baseline on base-3 and base-5 addition.

title: DeepsecBench: evaluating model performance in finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities
description:
Last week, OpenAI evaluated two models on an exploit benchmark within an isolated sandbox. Guardrails were reduced for testing, and the models found a vulnerability in their environment, accessed the internet, and reached Hugging Face's production database.

No human directed the action, but the breach is a clear example of how much more capable malicious attackers are when equipped with powerful AI models. But defenders have the same tools, and a clear advantage: knowledge of their own codebase. Hacks are initiated from the outside, so the single best defense is finding vulnerabilities from the inside before attackers do.

Today we're releasing DeepsecBench, a benchmark that evaluates how well different models find cybersecurity vulnerabilities in application code. For each model the report includes recall, precision, cost, and total time, and combines recall and precision into a single benchmark score. Here is a sample of model performance from the leaderboard:

We built deepsec to make scanning as easy as possible. Now you can use the benchmark report to build a security scanning program that fits your budget and the complexity of your codebase, choosing the right mix of models to run and how often to run them.

How the benchmark works

DeepsecBench runs on an open-source codebase at a commit state just before a large number of vulnerabilities were fixed. We selected 50 entry-point files and built a golden set of 231 human-judged findings. Each model's score is a recall-weighted F2 (Score = 100 × 5PR/(4P+R)), weighting recall (R) twice as much as precision (P), because missed vulnerabilities will go unfixed, while false positives don't make your codebase less secure.

Findings beyond the golden set are classified by a judge model as real or false, and count for or against the model in the precision measure (recall measures only the 231 known findings).

The benchmark is run three times and the data published in the report is the median of the three runs.

The construction of the benchmark stays secret. We don't disclose the repository, the commit, the files, or the findings, so there is nothing for models to train against. A model reciting memorized fixes would score near-total recall. Instead, the best run finds 30.7%, and 20 of the 25 runs come in under 20%.

The cost of capable analysis is falling

When we introduced deepsec, thorough scanning on production codebases required using the most capable models, and they were expensive to run. Frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic still score highest, but open-weight models and more efficient reasoning options are closing that gap, making comprehensive scanning far more cost-efficient.

Today, higher price does not buy proportionally more. Kimi K3, from Moonshot AI, ranks eighth at a score of 17.56 for $12.38 on the high setting, half the top score for about a fifth of the cost. Grok 4.5 set to high delivers near-Kimi performance for less than half the cost, scoring 15.58 for only $5.60. GPT-5.6 Sol set to medium offers the best score-to-cost balance of the top-performing models, taking fifth place with a score of 25.10 at a cost of $17.95.

You can interact with and download these charts on the DeepsecBench page.

Anthropic's most capable model, Fable 5, is absent because it declines security work, including defensive tasks. We will add security-enabled versions to the benchmark when they are made available.

The costs reported in the benchmark cover 50 files. A production codebase can run on the order of 100 times that, pricing a full pass at roughly $1,200 for a Kimi K3 sweep, or over $5,000 for the top-scoring frontier model from OpenAI.

Building a scanning program across multiple models

Because security scanning is recurring work, the question is which model to use for which task, and when. For example, frontier models can be used for periodic deep audits, while cheaper models like Kimi K3 or Grok 4.5 run scans at a higher cadence. Turning GPT-5.6 Sol's reasoning down from xhigh to medium moves it from 35.58 in 3 hours, 39 minutes to 25.10 in just over 30 minutes, fast enough for reviewing new features before they are pushed to production.

A startup might scan every merge with Grok 4.5 and save more expensive audits for milestone releases. A large enterprise might run frontier audits on its critical services, the same model at lower reasoning on key pull requests, and a continuous Kimi-class or Grok sweep across the rest of the codebase.

To implement scheduled reviews, follow Run recurring security reviews with deepsec on Vercel. The guide shows how to configure models and schedules for individual repositories, preserve progress across long-running reviews, and deliver findings to GitHub and Slack.

Running the benchmark on one endpoint

Security scans are spiky workloads that consume a large number of tokens in a short time window, and that burst capacity is hard to buy from any single provider directly. Every DeepsecBench run goes through AI Gateway. The gateway gives us a single endpoint to reach each model. During runs, routing, retries, and failover happen automatically, without any per-provider keys or rate limits to manage.

The same routing we use for the benchmark can run your security scanning program. Pass provider/model to deepsec, and one AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY in your environment covers every model on the board (or on a linked Vercel project, access AI Gateway via OIDC).

Find your vulnerabilities first

Attackers can use AI models, but they act from the outside. Defenders can see their entire system: the source, the architecture, the history. That visibility makes the same models more powerful in your hands than in theirs, because a model that can read the source finds what an attacker can only probe for. The advantage is real, but it only counts if you use it first.

We will continue to update DeepsecBench with new models as they are released and measured.

title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.13527v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multimodal language models (MLLMs) exhibit promising spatial reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms supporting them remain poorly understood. We uncover S-Space, a linear representation subspace in which object-token representations encode continuous coordinates along horizontal, vertical, and distance axes. Although we identify these axes by differentiating spatial-answer scores with respect to object-token activations, S-Space is intrinsic rather than induced by specific data or prompts, remaining readable under non-spatial questions. We show that S-Space functions as an internal spatial workspace of MLLMs. Perception encodes object locations into it, forming spatial representations that can be directly read out to support accurate spatial judgments. Internal reasoning transforms it for changing viewpoints. Verbal responses selectively access it, evidenced by causal interventions that alter spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses. Case studies further show that S-Space assigns locations to unseen entities and the observer, and connects physical directions with abstract linguistic meanings, suggesting both the capabilities and limitations of large-scale language training. Finally, we use S-Space as a diagnostic tool for spatial reasoning failures. Direction-word readouts reveal systematic coupling between cardinal and image-relative reference frames. More importantly, a perception-computation decomposition exposes a key bottleneck: MLLMs can form capable spatial representations, yet fall short in the spatial transformations required to reason reliably across viewpoint changes.

title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
description:
arXiv:2610.12596v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

title: Your Discrete Graph Diffusion Model is Secretly Memorizing
description:
arXiv:2610.13786v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Discrete graph diffusion models (GDMs) corrupt the graph structure by adding noise independently to nodes and edges under a Markovian noise model. In the unconditional setting without node features, an equivariant denoiser trained on a single graph is able to generate novel graphs and sample-level metrics such as edge overlap and WL kernel similarity find no evidence of memorization. In this work, we challenge this view and show for the first time that graph diffusion models indeed exhibit memorization. Analyzing the reverse diffusion trajectories of GDMs trained on two-block stochastic block models (SBMs), we find a strong train-data bias: the model recovers a corrupted training graph almost perfectly compared to a held-out test graph. We term this conditional memorization, as it surfaces only when the reverse trajectory is conditioned on a corrupted training graph and is not apparent during inference. It coincides with a growing generalization gap, where the training loss improves as the loss on held-out graphs degrades, and it cannot be mitigated by early stopping. The onset of memorization always precedes the emergence of community structure in the generated graphs, thus every checkpoint earlier produces structureless graphs. This behavior holds across all node sizes we test.

title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.13732v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

title: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.12916v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $\tau$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.

title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
description:
arXiv:2610.13823v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per-query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO-Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

title: API Benchmark Scores Do Not Reliably Transfer to Chatbot Interfaces
description:
arXiv:2609.08861v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Benchmark scores are a central currency in model releases: they inform purchasing decisions, shape public trust, and influence policy. Yet, a key assumption underlying benchmark scores is that the model performance measured through APIs faithfully reflects the behavior of deployed systems.
  We challenge this assumption by auditing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across seven systems and nine benchmarks spanning general capability, social bias, and sycophancy. We find systematic API--interface differences in both accuracy and consistency. On average, API evaluations score 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test--retest agreement than corresponding interface evaluations. For ChatGPT, the performance difference between API and interface access rivals the API-only difference between GPT 5.3 and GPT 5.4. Put differently, switching access surfaces can degrade performance as much as downgrading a full model version.
  We further test whether exposed API controls can reproduce interface behavior by varying system prompts, sampling parameters, and reasoning settings. These controls shift behavior in some cases but do not reliably eliminate the gap. Our findings document a context-validity gap: measurements obtained through APIs do not necessarily generalize to corresponding deployed interfaces, complicating the use of API evaluations as proxies for deployed systems.

title: Machine Learning and Time-Series Foundation Models for Day-Ahead Electricity Forecasting in a University Building
description:
arXiv:2610.12638v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Day-ahead electricity forecasts can help building operators schedule heating, ventilation, and other services around anticipated demand. Choosing a forecasting model also requires balancing accuracy with its forecast-time inputs, local training, and computational requirements.
  We benchmark statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural-network, and pretrained TimesFM models for a university building. We use chronological validation and evaluate all configurations on the same 57 test days, comparing accuracy across workdays, weekends, and holidays alongside local fitting and forecasting time. Weather covariates use retrospective observations.
  TimesFM 3.0 with covariates achieves the lowest overall errors, reducing mean absolute error by approximately 43\% relative to weekly seasonal-naive forecasting. XGBoost remains competitive, although paired daily comparisons do not establish a clear mean-absolute-error advantage for TimesFM. TimesFM also performs strongly using only past electricity consumption. Adding covariates improves its holiday forecasts but slightly worsens workday and weekend forecasts, leaving overall mean absolute error almost unchanged. TimesFM requires no building-specific weight training, while XGBoost offers rapid local fitting and inference. The evaluated LSTM takes longer to fit without outperforming either approach.
  An exploratory historical evaluation reveals seasonal variation, while a separate weather-source comparison produces only small changes in the selected TimesFM configuration's accuracy. These results support pretrained TimesFM as a strong initial forecasting baseline for this building, with XGBoost as a competitive locally fitted alternative. Covariates are particularly useful when improved holiday forecasts justify the additional input preparation.

title: "Nvidia B200 Chips, Rented by API: 31 of 33 Jobs Came Up Ready"
description:
We rented Nvidia B200 GPUs through a single API call, 33 times, and measured what happened. Every job in this run was a B200. Here are the results.

What we ran

Kilawatt Cloud is an orchestration layer that routes GPU jobs across multiple suppliers. In this run we sent 38 B200 requests to the API. The router launched 33 of them: 30 five-minute jobs and 3 one-hour jobs. Across those 33 jobs we launched 39 cards.

The headline numbers

  1. 31 of 33 launched jobs came up ready (94%). The two that did not were refunded automatically.

  2. 37 of 39 cards came up ready.

  3. 25 of the 31 ready jobs were ready in under 60 seconds.

By supplier

  1. RunPod: 13 launched, 13 ready. Median time to ready was 8 seconds. The slowest was 14 seconds.

  2. Vast.ai: 20 launched, 18 ready. Median time to ready was 44 seconds. The slowest was 316 seconds.

The one-hour test

The RunPod one-hour job ran the full hour. We checked its health 87 times and all 87 checks passed. It logged 0 XID errors, 0 uncorrectable ECC errors, and a peak GPU temperature of 34C.

Both Vast.ai one-hour jobs stopped about 15 to 16 minutes in. That was at the supplier account level, not a hardware fault. We are not counting them as host failures.

What did not launch

Five requests for four cards at once could not be placed. RunPod had no machine available, and the Vast.ai quote for four cards failed our pricing check. Nothing was charged for those requests, and the router skipped them instead of forcing a bad launch.

What this does and does not show

This is a small run on one GPU type. It measures how fast and how reliably the router gets a B200 to ready. It does not yet measure what happens when a host dies mid-job. That is the next test we are building: checkpoint-aware jobs that resume on a second supplier. We will publish the timings we measure, whatever they are.

Read the full report

The full report, with charts and the job-by-job breakdown, is on our Super Intelligence page:

kilawattcloud.dev/super-intelligence

Open the latest entry, "Nvidia B200 Chips, Rented by API: 31 of 33 Jobs Came Up Ready", to read or download the PDF. We publish each test run there, including the ones that do not go perfectly.

Questions about the method or the raw numbers are welcome in the comments.

title: Learning to Report Unsafe Tasks in a Multi-Agent Game
description:
arXiv:2610.09002v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When a team of agents shares a reward for completed tasks, reporting and stopping unsafe work reduces the team's reward. Random audits that penalize silence can make universal reporting optimal without ensuring that a silent team learns to report. We study this problem in a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting. When a task's k witnesses share a policy and draw actions independently, the derivative of expected reward with respect to the shared silence probability at universal silence counts its benefit k times, while the comparison between universal reporting and silence counts it once. A fully shared policy can therefore be locally attracted to silence even when reporting is optimal. For any grouping into shared policies, we give an audit condition sufficient for exact policy-gradient updates to reach universal reporting and, outside boundary cases, necessary from near universal silence. In a balanced family, meeting the condition with prescribed margins costs k times as much for a fully shared policy as for one policy per role. We test these predictions with PPO on 24 witness graphs, starting from learned silence. Witness groups, which place co-witnesses in separate networks, reduce unsafe task completion by 33.59 percentage points relative to shuffled groups of the same sizes under the same audits (95% graph-bootstrap interval: 21.03-45.13). Only 9 of 48 witness-group runs achieve below 1% unsafe completion while retaining at least 90% legitimate completion. At the same audit budget, a fully shared network meets both thresholds in 0/48 runs with independent action draws and 48/48 with a common draw. On 24 further graphs with witness groups fixed, audits allocated by the condition reduce unsafe completion by 42.22 points relative to audits maximizing a static coalition deterrence ratio at the same budget.

title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.12659v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.

title: MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2607.21552v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can behave very differently depending on whether the same underlying problem is presented textually or visually. This inconsistency suggests that different views expose different reasoning paths and failure modes that standard multimodal post-training does not fully exploit. To study and exploit this phenomenon, we construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined image+text views of the same problems, together with splits for training and evaluating view dependent reasoning behaviors. We then develop Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization (MIRROR), a reinforcement learning approach that derives a cross-view self-distillation signal from the model's own modality-dependent capabilities. For each problem, MIRROR evaluates the model under all views, selects the best-performing view as a teacher, and trains the remaining views using a GRPO task-reward objective augmented with a reverse-KL regularizer toward that teacher. Across reasoning benchmarks that evaluate on multimodal mathematics problems, MIRROR improves over standard RL and yields more accurate and consistent behavior across different input modality representations.

title: SQL Injection: The Bug That Refuses to Die
description:
SQL injection is older than some of the engineers shipping it today. It was written up publicly back in 1998. It is still sitting on the OWASP Top Ten. Let that sink in. We have had more than two decades to kill this bug, and it is still in production, right now, inside apps people trust with their money.

I have a penetration-testing background. SQL injection is often the first thing I reach for on a login form, not because I am clever, but because it still works far too often.

Let me explain the concept, because once you see it you cannot unsee it.

Your query is a sentence, and user input is a word in it

A database query is just a command written in a language called SQL. "Give me the user whose email matches this." Simple enough.

The trouble starts when a developer builds that command by gluing strings together. They take the sentence, cut a hole where the user's input goes, and paste whatever the user typed straight into the hole.

Here is the mental model. The database does not know where your trusted sentence ends and the user's untrusted input begins. To the database, it is all one string. One command. So if an attacker types something that reads like SQL instead of reading like a name, the database happily treats it as part of the command.

That is the whole trick. Input that was meant to be data gets executed as code. The user stopped answering your question and started giving the database new orders.

I will not hand you a working payload. You do not need one to understand the danger. Just picture a login box where the "password" field quietly rewrites the question from "is this password correct" into "log me in no matter what." Same mechanism. Different sentence.

Why it refuses to die

Because string concatenation feels natural. You need a dynamic query, you have a variable, you add them together. It reads fine. It passes a code review from someone who is tired. It works perfectly in testing, because testers type names, not commands.

It also hides in the boring corners. An old reporting endpoint. A search filter someone bolted on during a Friday rush. A legacy service nobody wants to touch. The shiny new parts of your stack are usually fine. The ten-year-old admin panel is where I go hunting.

The fix is boring, and boring is good

Parameterized queries. Also called prepared statements. This is the one that matters.

Instead of gluing input into the sentence, you send the command and the data separately. You tell the database, "here is the query, and here are the values, and the values are values, do not read them as commands." The database keeps the two apart. The hole is sealed. Input can never cross back into code.

In practice:

  • Use parameterized queries or prepared statements everywhere. No exceptions for "just this one small query."
  • Let a mature ORM build your queries for you. They parameterize by default.
  • Never concatenate user input into a query string. Not for ids. Not for sort order. Not ever.
  • Apply least privilege to the database account, so one mistake stays contained.

ORMs help, until you hand them a loaded gun

Here is the part people miss. An ORM protects you right up until you drop into its raw-query escape hatch and start concatenating again. Most ORMs have one. Most teams use it. That raw string is exactly where the injection sneaks back in.

So the rule holds even inside your safe framework. Pass values as parameters. If you find yourself building a query by adding strings together, stop, no matter which tool you are in.

SQL injection is not a hard problem anymore. The fix has existed for as long as the bug has. We keep shipping it because we keep taking the shortcut. Write the parameterized query. It costs you three extra seconds, and it is the difference between a database and a crime scene.

I am Ksatria Bintang Samudra, an AI-native full-stack engineer with a penetration-testing background and a deep interest in digital forensics, open to remote work worldwide. More of what I build at ksatriabintangsamudra.com.

title: Claim-Gated Source-Risk Auditing for Generative Search
description:
arXiv:2609.29145v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A generative search answer can cite a supported passage yet omit a source relationship that changes its interpretation. We specify a claim-gated audit of the query-source-answer tuple. An omission is resolved only when relationship evidence, answer adoption, materiality, and disclosure are all observed; incomplete evidence remains unresolved rather than being treated as independence. The specification separates this endpoint from citation support and review priority, and binds decisions to versioned evidence spans. A reference checker makes the record contract executable. On an exhaustive synthetic suite, it reproduces all 81 three-state predicate combinations and rejects 192 deliberately malformed records. Common-guard baselines and predicate ablations isolate endpoint logic from missing-evidence handling, while controlled transitions check support separation and evidence removal. These are finite contract-conformance results, not detector accuracy or evidence of improved user outcomes. We define the independent annotation, held-out evaluation, and paired utility tests still required to establish semantic validity and deployment benefit.

title: Understanding Transformer-based Vision Models through Inversion
description:
arXiv:2412.06534v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning. In computer vision, one promising yet only preliminarily explored approach is feature inversion via inverse networks, which reconstructs images from intermediate representations using trained inverse networks. In this study, we revisit feature inversion via inverse networks, introducing a novel, modular variant that enables a computationally more efficient application of the technique while, in some cases, producing semantically more coherent image reconstructions. We apply our method to large-scale transformer-based vision models, specifically Detection Transformer, Vision Transformer, Swin Transformer, and Data-Efficient Image Transformer, analyzing the resulting reconstructions across network depth. Our main analysis compares Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, which exhibit the most informative differences among the evaluated architectures. At the same time, results for Swin Transformer and Data-Efficient Image Transformer support the broader applicability of our framework. Our findings reveal gradual representational changes across transformer layers as a shared characteristic of Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, as well as systematic differences in how they preserve contextual shape and fine-grained image details, and in their robustness to color perturbations. These findings deepen understanding of transformer-based vision models and demonstrate the utility of modular feature inversion as an interpretability tool.

title: Towards a Measure Theory of Semantic Information
description:
arXiv:2508.00525v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A classic account of the quantification of semantic information is that of Bar-Hiller and Carnap. Their account proposes an inverse relation between the informativeness of a statement and its probability. However, their approach assigns the maximum informativeness to a contradiction: which Floridi refers to as the Bar-Hillel-Carnap paradox. He developed a novel theory founded on a distance metric and parabolic relation, designed to remove this paradox. Unfortunately is approach does not succeed in that aim.
  In this paper I critique Floridi's theory of strongly semantic information on its own terms and show where it succeeds and fails. I then present a new approach based on the unit circle (a relation that has been the basis of theories from basic trigonometry to quantum theory). This is used, by analogy with von Neumann's quantum probability to construct a measure space for informativeness that meets all the requirements stipulated by Floridi and removes the paradox. In addition, while contradictions and tautologies have zero informativeness, it is found that messages which are contradictory to each other are equally informative. The utility of this is explained by means of an example.
