title: KubeSense: A Private, Local-First AI DevOps Assistant
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend

What I Built

I built KubeSense, a high-density, terminal-based Kubernetes monitoring dashboard.
I built this for my junior batchmate, who is an aspiring DevOps engineer. During one of his internships, he expressed how constant pod monitoring is cumbersome and he wanted something that is terminal native so that he does not have to switch windows while working unlike heavy web-based UIs like Lens or Rancher. He wished something lightweight that stays in the CLI but is smart enough to highlight exactly what matters and filters out the unnecessary jargon. KubeSense solves this by bringing real-time metrics and AI-driven log anomaly detection directly to their terminal window.

Demo

Code

The project is publicly available at: https://github.com/Joydeep2005Banik/KubeSense

How I Built It

KubeSense is built entirely in Python, utilizing a decoupled architecture driven by a central PodMonitor engine. Here is a high-level look at the architecture:

graph TD
    subgraph UI Layer
        A[Terminal UI]
    end
    subgraph Core Logic
        B[Monitor Engine]
    end
    subgraph Data Sources
        C[K8s API]
        D[SSH Fallback]
    end
    subgraph AI Processing
        E[Log Optimizer]
        F[LLM Providers]
    end

    B <-->|State Updates| A
    B -->|Fetch Metrics| C
    B -->|Fallback| D
    B -->|Raw Logs| E
    E -->|Clean Context| F
    F -->|Alerts| A

Here is a breakdown of the core systems:

1. Reactive Terminal UI (Textual)

I used the Textual framework to build the dashboard. Instead of relying on heavy "while-true" redraw loops, the UI uses Textual's event-driven reactive properties. When the Monitor Engine pushes new metrics, only the changed widgets redraw, ensuring a lightning-fast, zero-overhead experience without screen tearing.

flowchart LR
    A[Monitor Engine] -->|Sends updated<br/>Metrics Object| B(Reactive Variable)
    B -->|Triggers Auto-Update| C[UI Node / Widget]
    C -->|Only redraws changed region| D[Terminal Display]

2. Resilient Metric Collection & SSH Fallback

The tool primarily connects to the cluster using the official kubernetes Python client to fetch live status and log streams. However, if the cluster's K8s Metrics Server goes down, KubeSense intelligently engages a graceful fallback mechanism to connect directly to the underlying cluster nodes via asyncssh.

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Monitor
    participant K as K8s Metrics API
    participant S as SSH Fallback
    participant N as Node Shell

    M->>K: Fetch Pod CPU/Mem
    alt Metrics Server Unavailable
        K-->>M: HTTP 404 / Error
        M->>S: Engage Fallback (asyncssh)
        S->>N: Connect to Node via SSH
        N-->>S: Execute `top` & parse usage
        S-->>M: Return hardware metrics
    else Success
        K-->>M: Standard API Metrics
    end

3. Log Optimization Pipeline

Logs can be incredibly noisy and expensive to process. Before any logs touch the AI, they pass through a custom LogOptimizer:

flowchart LR
    A[Raw Log Stream] --> B{Severity Filter}
    B -- Keep WARNING+ --> C[Deduplication]
    C -->|Collapse repeated| D[PII Scrubbing]
    D -->|Mask IPs/UUIDs| E[Optimized Payload]

This ensures the context window remains small, protecting privacy and saving tokens.

4. Multi-Provider AI Engine (Local-First)

For the AI core, I implemented an abstract factory pattern to handle the anomaly detection. While it supports BYOK for cloud providers like Groq or OpenAI, the default engine runs entirely locally via Ollama.

flowchart TD
    A[Optimized Payload] --> B{AI Factory Config}
    B -->|groq| C[GroqProvider<br/>Cloud API]
    B -->|openai| D[OpenAIProvider<br/>Cloud API]
    B -->|ollama| E[OllamaProvider<br/>Local/Air-gapped]
    B -->|mock| F[MockProvider<br/>Heuristics Fallback]

    C & D & E & F --> G[JSON Enforcement & Parser]
    G --> H[Anomaly Alerts to UI]

Key Features

  • Smart Log Filtering & Deduplication: Aggressively filters noise (INFO, DEBUG), deduplicates repeated errors, and scrubs PII before any AI processing.
  • BYOK (Bring Your Own Key): While local open-weight models via Ollama are the default, you can easily plug in an API key for Groq or OpenAI via config.yaml or environment variables if you prefer cloud inference.
  • SSH Fallback: Automatically drops to a direct SSH connection to scrape node hardware via top if the Kubernetes Metrics Server isn't available.

As KubeSense streams the optimized container logs, it passes these batches to an open-weight model running locally. The model analyzes the logs in the background, strictly returning structured JSON, and alerts to warnings, hidden errors, or unusual patterns before they escalate without adding any overhead to the cluster itself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Deploying open-weight models locally resolves critical architectural and operational limitations associated with closed APIs:

1. Data Sovereignty & Air-Gapped Execution

Kubernetes logs frequently leak sensitive infrastructure data, internal IP schemas, and environment variables. Streaming these logs to a third-party server via a closed API introduces unacceptable security risks and compliance violations (e.g., SOC2/HIPAA). By running inference locally via Ollama, KubeSense ensures complete data sovereignty. The tool can operate entirely offline, making AI-driven log analysis viable for strict, air-gapped environments.

2. O(1) Inference Costs

Streaming high-volume log data through a token-metered API creates unbounded operational costs. Local inference with open-weight models reduces the marginal cost of analysis to zero, making continuous 24/7 log processing financially viable.

3. Hardware-Specific Model Tuning

Closed ecosystems abstract away model selection. An open architecture allows users to define the exact AI engine based on their hardware constraints. Systems with limited VRAM can deploy highly efficient models like Google's Gemma (gemma:2b), while robust systems can load higher-parameter models (e.g., llama3.1:8b) for complex log reasoning.

4. Deterministic Availability

Cloud AI APIs introduce network latency and are subject to HTTP 429 Too Many Requests rate limits. When triaging a production cluster outage, network dependency and API throttling are unacceptable. Local open-weight models guarantee deterministic availability and consistent latency independent of external network conditions.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma (Using Google's Gemma open-weight model via Ollama for local log anomaly detection)

Let's Chat! 💬

If you have any questions about how the architecture works, why I chose Textual, or how to set up Ollama for your own cluster monitoring, please drop a comment below! I'd love to discuss why I think lightweight, terminal-native tools are often far more effective than heavy dashboards, and hear your thoughts on local AI for DevOps.

title: MemReread: Enhancing Agentic Long-Context Reasoning via Memory-Guided Rereading
description:
arXiv:2605.10268v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-context reasoning tasks have motivated agent-memory approaches that process document chunks sequentially while maintaining a dynamically updated memory, avoiding the quadratic complexity of standard attention. Existing methods often rely on retrieval to recover information discarded during memory overwriting, but remain vulnerable to evidence loss during memory formation and interference from invalid queries. To overcome these limitations, we propose MemReread. Built upon streaming reading, it circumvents intermediate retrieval, triggering question decomposition and targeted rereading when the final memory is insufficient. By recovering indirect evidence that may have been prematurely discarded, MemReread enables non-linear reasoning while preserving the logical flow of document comprehension. We further introduce a reinforcement learning framework that improves length extrapolation and adaptively determines the number of rereading passes according to task complexity, enabling flexible control of computational overhead. Our MemReread-4B outperforms strong baselines on long-context reasoning tasks (e.g., +1.6pp v.s. DeepSeek-V4-Pro on 2WikiMultiHopQA) while maintaining linear time complexity with respect to context length.

title: 7 Checks Before Launching an E-commerce Website
description:
A storefront can look finished before it is ready to accept real orders.

The product pages work. The cart updates. A test payment succeeds.

But what happens when two customers buy the last item, a payment notification arrives twice, or the shipping service stops responding?

For developers and business owners planning an online store, these are useful questions to answer before launch.

Here are seven checks to include in your e-commerce launch review.

1. Calculate prices on the server

The browser can display a price, but it should not decide what the customer pays.

When creating a checkout session, the backend should:

  • Load current product and variant prices.
  • Validate quantities.
  • Apply eligible discounts.
  • Calculate delivery charges and applicable taxes.

Do not accept a total from the frontend as authoritative.

Try this: Modify the price in a checkout request. The server should calculate the correct amount independently or reject the request.

2. Verify payments and handle duplicate notifications

A customer reaching a success page is not enough evidence to mark an order as paid.

Use the payment provider's supported server-side verification flow. For webhook integrations, verify signatures and match the payment to the expected order, amount and currency.

Design for repeated notifications too. Stripe's webhook documentation explains that duplicate events can occur and that event delivery order is not guaranteed.

Processing the same successful payment again should not:

  • Create another order.
  • Reduce stock twice.
  • Trigger a second shipment.

This is the practical purpose of idempotency: repeating an operation does not repeat its business effect.

Try this: Replay a valid payment event. Check that the order and fulfilment records remain consistent.

3. Decide how inventory is reserved

Checking stock when an item enters the cart is not enough.

Imagine two customers checking out while only one unit remains. If both requests read the same stock value before either updates it, both may appear valid.

Choose an inventory policy explicitly:

  • When is stock reserved?
  • When does the reservation expire?
  • What happens if payment completes after expiry?
  • When is reserved stock released after a failed payment?

Use atomic conditional updates or appropriate database transactions to enforce that policy. A separate “read stock, then subtract” sequence can race.

Try this: Send simultaneous checkout requests for the last available unit.

4. Check who can access each order

Authentication answers: “Who is this user?”

Authorisation answers: “Can this user access this particular order?”

Every order-detail, invoice, cancellation and refund endpoint needs the appropriate server-side permission checks.

Hiding buttons in the interface does not protect the API.

The OWASP Authorisation Cheat Sheet recommends denying access by default and validating permissions on every request.

Try this: Sign in as Customer A and request Customer B's order. Repeat the check for endpoints that modify the order.

5. Plan for delivery-service failures

Payment, order processing and shipment creation are separate steps.

If the shipping provider times out after payment succeeds, retain the paid order and show its actual fulfilment status.

Record the failed shipment attempt so it can be retried or reviewed.

Before retrying, consider whether the provider created the shipment but its response was lost. Use provider-supported idempotency or reconcile with existing shipments to avoid duplicates.

Your team should be able to identify:

  • Orders awaiting shipment creation.
  • Failed shipment attempts.
  • Orders requiring manual review.

Try this: Simulate a shipping timeout and verify that the team can identify and recover the affected order.

6. Test the complete mobile journey

Review more than the homepage.

On a real phone, go through the entire shopping journey:

  1. Open a product page.
  2. Select a size, colour or other variant.
  3. Add the product to the cart.
  4. Change the quantity.
  5. Enter a delivery address.
  6. Apply a coupon.
  7. Complete payment.
  8. Return to the order page.

Check whether validation messages are understandable, form fields have labels, and the cart survives recoverable errors.

Try this: Complete checkout on a small screen using a slower connection.

7. Make failures traceable

When a customer asks, “I paid, but where is my order?”, support needs a way to investigate.

Connect order records, payment references and shipment references.

Record useful status changes and failures without logging secrets or unnecessary personal data.

Give the team a clear recovery process for:

  • Paid orders awaiting confirmation.
  • Unsuccessful shipment attempts.
  • Refunds needing attention.

Try this: Pick a failed test order and see whether another team member can explain what happened.

Your pre-launch checklist

Before accepting real orders, check that:

  • [ ] Prices and discounts are validated on the server.
  • [ ] Payments are verified through the provider's supported flow.
  • [ ] Repeated payment events do not repeat business actions.
  • [ ] Inventory updates handle concurrent purchases.
  • [ ] Customers can access only the orders they are permitted to access.
  • [ ] Shipment failures have a recovery path.
  • [ ] Mobile checkout has been tested.
  • [ ] Support can trace failed transactions.

A successful test purchase is a useful milestone. Testing failures, permissions and recovery gives you more evidence that the store is ready for everyday use.

Which edge case would you add to this checklist? Share it in the comments.

About the author

I'm Anandhu R S, a full-stack developer and founder of Kode Company, based in Trivandrum, Kerala.

We provide web development, e-commerce development, CRM, SaaS and custom software services for businesses.

title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
description:
arXiv:2610.13075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.

title: Vercel Sandbox now runs on Vercel Managed Images
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel Managed Images (VMI), a set of versioned, open-source base images you can use as-is or extend. The source for every image lives in the public vercel/sandbox repository.

Managed images replace Sandbox runtimes, which are now deprecated. Starting with version 3 of the Sandbox SDK, new sandboxes default to vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. It ships with Node.js, Python, common coding agents and standard utilities, so most users never build a custom image or install packages at boot.

The universal image switches our default operating system from Amazon Linux to Ubuntu, a lighter and more widely used system across the industry.

Secure by default

Every managed image gets a nightly release. Rolling tags such as latest and the major-version tags pick up operating system and dependency updates automatically, including security patches and new releases of Node.js, Python, and the preinstalled coding agents.

Within each release, dependencies are pinned to specific versions wherever possible, so a given image version stays consistent.

If you need a fully immutable, reproducible environment, pin to an image digest (SHA). Digest-pinned images opt out of automatic updates.

Choose a managed image from the catalog

Each managed image targets a different starting point:

  • vercel/sandbox/universal:latest is the new default, a rolling release on Ubuntu 26.04 with Node.js 24, Python 3.14 with uv, the opencode, claude-code, codex, and pi coding agents, and utilities including git, vim, nano, tmux, ripgrep, jq, and fzf.

  • vercel/sandbox/node:22, node:24, and node:26 provide Node.js versions on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/python:3.14 provides Python on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/ubuntu:latest provides base Ubuntu 26.04 with no extra tooling.

  • vercel/sandbox/arch:latest provides Arch Linux, regularly updated, with no Node.js or Python preinstalled. Its large package repository makes it useful for agents that install tools on the fly.

Reference an image and migrate from runtimes

Sandboxes can use an image from any repository in your project, a repository which has been shared with your team or any public repository.

Images are addressed by their full path, team-slug/project/repo:tag, for example vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. The SDK types the image property so built-in images autocomplete while any string is still accepted. The previous runtime property is deprecated, not removed, so existing code keeps working.

Amazon Linux runtimes are not part of the managed image catalog, so teams that need AL2023 can stay on runtime. Managed images run as the default ubuntu or arch user with passwordless sudo, rather than the vercel-sandbox user.

Open an issue or a pull request to improve them, and read the Vercel Sandbox images documentation to get started.

title: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.12794v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-guided evolutionary optimization has successfully improved prompts, programs, and even entire AI systems. Most optimization methods select a candidate from the search frontier, then mutate it in one LLM pass based only on its failures. This focus on the frontier can stall on production AI systems, where isolated failures reveal little about complex, hidden interactions. We introduce CoCoEvolve (Cortex Code Evolve), an evolutionary optimizer built around what we call meta-reflection, wherein an agentic mutator (Cortex Code) selectively retrieves evidence from the entire evolutionary history and probes the live system before verifying and proposing mutations. We apply CoCoEvolve to optimize three classes of production AI systems: data agents, LLM-powered data pipelines, and data engineering workflows. On DABStep, CoCoEvolve tops the public leaderboard, reaching 92.8% held-out hard accuracy compared to 78.4% for Meta-Harness and 30.4% for GEPA under matched conditions. Across six LLM data pipeline workloads, it outperforms every evaluated baseline. On data-eng-bench, CoCoEvolve lifts test-set solve rate from 59.1% to 77.4%, past the best baseline of 73.6%. It also has 11 percentage points higher accuracy than GEPA on HotpotQA while remaining competitive with specialized optimizers on established mathematical and systems benchmarks. Matched ablations confirm that each component of CoCoEvolve contributes to these gains, demonstrating the value of meta-reflection for optimizing production AI systems.

title: Forecasting Corpus-Sampling Disagreement in Masked Text Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.12987v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: If a second text corpus were collected from the same population, how much would a predictor's outputs change? We study this question for masked-text reconstruction using a smoothed predictor built from nearby token-pair counts and evaluated over the full 50,257-token GPT-2 vocabulary. Treating each source document as one observation, we derive a first-order formula for the expected disagreement between predictors fitted to two independent corpora. The formula accounts for variable document length, random context counts, and correlations across token offsets, and it can be evaluated from a separate reference corpus without access to either target corpus. On TinyStories, WikiText-103, and CNN/DailyMail, growing each corpus from 512 to 2,048 chunks of 64 tokens lowers disagreement by only 5--40\%, far short of the 75\% implied by $1/n$ scaling. The forecast tracks this slow decline, which we trace to smoothing of rarely seen contexts. Forecast accuracy depends less on how these correlations are modeled than on the size of the reference corpus: small references systematically underpredict disagreement. A source-split jackknife that uses only reference data reduces this calibration error by 57--59\%. After this correction, a simpler smoothed-multinomial approximation is most accurate when the reference corpus is smaller than the target corpus, and a nonlinear source bootstrap is most accurate when it is larger. Finally, small masked diffusion language models trained on the same corpora show that the count-based forecasts partly identify which inputs are most sensitive to the corpus, but miss the neural models' much faster decline in disagreement.

title: Training FLUX.2 and Kolors LoRAs on a space dataset
description:

In short: A space-themed image generation project: a dataset of 1,964 image-caption pairs from NASA, Wallhaven and LAION-Aesthetics, auto-captioned with JoyCaption, and LoRA adapters trained on FLUX.2-klein (9B) and Kolors. The dataset has 3,300+ downloads on Hugging Face.

The dataset

Kiffusion is 1,964 image-caption pairs of space and sci-fi imagery, collected from NASA, Wallhaven and LAION-Aesthetics. Every image was captioned automatically with JoyCaption, so the captions describe composition and lighting in the detail a diffusion model needs, instead of relying on short alt text.

The LoRAs

SpaceVision is the set of LoRA adapters trained on that dataset, using SimpleTuner and Diffusers:

  • FLUX.2-klein (9B), a 38 MB adapter
  • Kolors, a 46.6 MB adapter

A LoRA trains a small set of extra weights instead of the whole model, so the adapters stay small enough to download and swap in seconds.

title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
description:
arXiv:2610.12995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.

title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.13113v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

title: How AI Writing Assistance Distorts Perceptions of AI Users and Their Opinions
description:
arXiv:2604.22503v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hundreds of millions of people use AI for writing assistance. We asked how AI distorts perceptions of AI users and their opinions. Writers (N=2,939) wrote political opinion paragraphs with and without AI assistance. Separate readers (N=11,091) blindly evaluated these paragraphs and made inferences about the writers. With AI, writers seemed more opinionated, competent, positive, and demographically privileged. Writers objected to many of these distortions yet preferred AI-assisted text even when made aware of them. Reward models trained on our data mitigated objectionable distortions but reduced user acceptance. Additional readers (N=8,798) trusted AI-assisted writers more and were more persuaded by AI writing when AI was more distortive. Overall, distortions from AI writing assistance are pervasive, persistent under human oversight, and likely to have consequential effects on human behaviours and attitudes.

title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
description:
arXiv:2610.12536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.

title: IT Support Ticketing System for Organized Technical Assistance
description:
Explore how an IT support ticketing system helps businesses record technical issues, assign requests to the right specialists, track progress, and improve internal IT support.

Introduction
Technical problems can affect employee productivity and disrupt business operations. Issues involving computers, software, connectivity, and user access require a reliable process for reporting and resolution.

An IT support ticketing system helps organizations record these problems, assign responsibility, and monitor progress through a centralized platform.

How an IT Support Ticketing System Works

When an employee reports a technical issue, the system creates a ticket containing the relevant information. Support staff can categorize the request, assign it to a technician, set a priority, and update its status as work progresses.

This process gives employees a clear way to report problems and allows IT managers to monitor outstanding requests.

Benefits of Helpdesk Ticketing Software

Helpdesk ticketing software can reduce the need to coordinate requests through separate email conversations or spreadsheets. Centralized ticket records help teams find previous information, review troubleshooting steps, and maintain communication histories.

Automated notifications can also help agents follow up on requests and keep users informed about progress.

Combining IT Ticketing Software With Service Desk Processes

IT ticketing software can support broader IT service desk software workflows by recording incidents and service requests in a consistent format.

Organizations may establish different processes for urgent incidents, routine assistance, and access requests. Clear categories and escalation procedures help technicians prioritize their work more effectively.

Improving IT Support Performance

Reporting can help managers identify common technical problems, understand workload distribution, and evaluate support processes. Reviewing recurring incidents may reveal opportunities for improved documentation, system maintenance, or employee training.

Businesses should select an IT support ticketing system that matches their team size, technical environment, security requirements, and budget.

Conclusion

An IT support ticketing system helps organizations manage technical requests through clear processes and centralized records. By combining ticket tracking, communication, and reporting, IT teams can improve coordination and provide more organized support to employees.

title: LLM API Outages in 2026: OpenAI and Claude Overlapped for 36 Minutes in 90 Days
description:
If your product calls a hosted model, its worst days are partly your provider's worst days. The only public record of those days is a status page, and every provider runs its own, with its own rules for what gets declared. Most of the numbers people pass around are also old: an IsDown report from December 2025, which Vercel still cites in its AI gateway guide, counted 22 OpenAI incidents and roughly 182.7 hours of incident time in one month.

So we collected fresh data: every incident posted on 12 LLM provider status pages between July 14 and October 11, 2026. OpenAI's model APIs spent 72.7 hours with an incident open. Anthropic's Claude API spent 76.5. The two were in an incident at the same time for only 36 minutes, and both times the two sides were broken in different ways. The full write-up, with the per-provider tables and a free CSV of all 459 incidents, is on DevToolLab.

The Short Version

  • OpenAI posted 109 incidents across all its products in the window. Twenty touched its model APIs, which had an incident open 3.4% of the 2,160 hours.
  • Anthropic posted 82. Sixty touched the Claude API, open 3.5% of the time. Its median API incident ran 51 minutes; OpenAI's ran 124.
  • The two APIs overlapped twice, on July 21 and October 6, for 36 minutes total.
  • Fireworks AI listed 210 API incidents, Google's Gemini API page listed 2, and Together AI listed zero. Those numbers say more about posting habits than uptime.
  • 49% of OpenAI and Anthropic API incidents started on a weekday between 9 AM and 5 PM Eastern, which is only 24% of the week.

How the Incidents Were Counted

The window is July 14, 2026 at 00:00 UTC through October 12 at 00:00 UTC, and every page was read on October 12. Ninety days is not arbitrary: OpenAI's page runs on incident.io, which keeps 90 days of history, and so do Groq, Cohere, Perplexity and Fireworks AI. Anthropic and Cerebras use Atlassian Statuspage, and Google posts Gemini API status on Google AI Studio. xAI's and Mistral's pages answered our scripts with Cloudflare bot checks, so they are missing.

An incident counts as an API incident only if the provider attached it to a model API component: OpenAI's APIs group without the dashboard Login component, Anthropic's Claude API (api.anthropic.com), and Google's API and Multimodal Live API components. Four incidents with no component were classified from their text. ChatGPT, claude.ai, Claude Code, Codex, billing and support incidents are in the totals but not in the API numbers.

Hours run from the provider's reported start to the update that restored the API component. A reopened incident uses its first resolution, and overlapping incidents from the same provider are merged so an hour is never counted twice. Error spikes nobody declared do not exist in this data.

OpenAI vs Anthropic vs Gemini

Provider All incidents API incidents API hours Median Longest Page's own uptime
OpenAI 109 20 72.7 124 min 20.6 h, Responses API latency, Aug 31 99.95%
Anthropic 82 60 76.5 51 min 6.0 h, multiple models, Aug 5 99.54%
Gemini API 4 2 48.0 2.8 h and 45.2 h 45.2 h, Batch API, Sep 14 bars, no number

OpenAI and Anthropic finished within 4 hours of each other, by opposite routes. Anthropic usually puts the affected model in the title ("Elevated errors on Claude Sonnet 5"), and it logged three times as many API incidents as OpenAI, each one shorter. OpenAI logs fewer and keeps them open: "Elevated latency in the Responses API" ran 20.6 hours starting the evening of August 31, and "Errors processing large PDFs in the Responses API" ran 12.8 hours on October 6.

Severity tilts the other way. Anthropic marked the Claude API as a major outage 3 times and a partial outage 23 times, including a 2.5-hour "Elevated errors across all models" on July 29. OpenAI's API components peaked at partial outage, 3 times, and 15 of its 20 API incidents were labeled degraded performance. Anthropic's volume also dropped month over month: 31 API incidents in the last 18 days of July, then 17, 8, and 4 in the first 11 days of October. OpenAI went 8, 3, 7, 2.

Do not compare the uptime percentages. On October 12, OpenAI showed 99.95% for its APIs group and Claude's page showed 99.54% for the Claude API, even though their incident hours were nearly identical. Different status-page software computes those numbers over different component lists. Compare timelines instead. If you want to see what a percentage means in minutes per month, the Uptime SLA Calculator does the conversion.

The Two Overlaps

On July 21, 2026, between 9:04 and 9:22 AM ET, an OpenAI image generation incident had spread to its Images API while Anthropic was reporting elevated errors on Claude Haiku 4.5. On October 6, between 8:24 and 8:43 AM ET, OpenAI's Responses API was choking on large PDFs while Anthropic reported elevated errors for Claude Opus 5.5.

That is the whole list. According to the providers' own pages, a plain text request had a working provider to fail over to for every minute of the 90 days.

Gemini's overlaps look bigger, 230 minutes with OpenAI and 146 with Anthropic, but each one involves either the 45.2-hour Batch API delay that started September 14 or a voice-cloning failure on October 1. Neither affects a real-time text call.

Incident Counts Mostly Measure Posting Policy

The smaller providers make the point clearly:

Provider API incidents API hours What the count reflects
Fireworks AI 210 181.8 207 are automated single-model "Service Degradation" alerts, median 12 min
DeepSeek 29 13.5 short API alerts, median 14 min, titled in Chinese and English
OpenRouter 3 4.4 includes a 4-minute burst of 429s on its Anthropic and OpenAI routes
Cerebras 3 5.0 one 5.0-hour disruption on September 25
Perplexity 2 1.7 most of its 8 incidents cover its Computer product
Groq 1 6.1 one model, minimax-m2.7, October 10
Cohere 1 4.4 one multi-endpoint disruption, September 1
Together AI 0 0 nothing posted, though its monitors show 99.061% to 100% per model
Vertex AI 0 0 the public feed had 7 incidents total, none for Vertex AI

Fireworks AI posted 52 times as many incidents as the Gemini API page, which does not make it 52 times less reliable. Together AI posted nothing while its own Better Stack monitors show Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B at 99.061% over 90 days. A raw count rewards whoever posts least. Google's page is also candid about priority: "Free-tier requests use sheddable capacity, while billed-tier requests are protected by critical priority."

Incidents Cluster in the US Workday

Out of 80 OpenAI and Anthropic API incidents, 39 started Monday through Friday between 9 AM and 5 PM Eastern. Those 40 hours are 24% of a 168-hour week but caught 49% of incidents. Part of that is just when engineers are around to declare something. Either way, that is when your fallback should be tested.

What It Means for Your Fallback

A retry loop with exponential backoff buys you seconds. It will not outlast a 51-minute median incident, let alone a 124-minute one. Run your own schedule through the Exponential Backoff Calculator and the gap is obvious. Past the retry budget, the request needs a different destination.

Fail over to another provider, not just another model. On July 29, Anthropic's outage hit every model for 2.5 hours, so falling back from Opus to Sonnet would have failed too, while OpenAI would have answered. Route by feature as well: every overlap involved images, PDFs, batch or voice on at least one side. Those workloads deserve their own fallback, their own health check, and a deadline on batch jobs so a 45-hour delay does not go unnoticed.

You can skip writing the failover yourself. Vercel AI Gateway tries a models array in providerOptions.gateway in order, OpenRouter has a models parameter that does the same, and LiteLLM takes a fallbacks list per model. The original post links a full comparison of LLM gateways.

Monitoring What the Status Page Leaves Out

Your own 500s may come from short spikes nobody ever declares. Upptime (MIT, 17,178 stars on October 12, 2026) runs checks from GitHub Actions every 5 minutes, which is the tightest schedule Actions allows, opens an issue when a check fails, closes it on recovery, and publishes a status page on GitHub Pages. A config for both APIs, with keys stored as repository secrets:

secrets:
  - OPENAI_API_KEY
  - ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

sites:
  - name: OpenAI API
    url: https://api.openai.com/v1/models
    headers:
      - "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"
    maxResponseTime: 5000
  - name: Claude API
    url: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models
    headers:
      - "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
      - "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01"
    maxResponseTime: 5000

Listing models costs no tokens, but it only proves the API responds. To catch the per-model failures Anthropic tends to post, switch an entry to method: POST and send a one-token request to the model you actually use.

Rerun the Numbers

Each CSV row is one incident: UTC times, API impact windows, severity, components, our classification note and a link to the original post. The original article includes a short Python script that merges each provider's windows and finds the overlaps. On the published file it prints:

OpenAI               72.7 h with an API incident open
Anthropic            76.5 h with an API incident open
Google Gemini API    48.0 h with an API incident open
OpenAI + Anthropic: 36 min at the same time
OpenAI + Google Gemini API: 230 min at the same time
Anthropic + Google Gemini API: 146 min at the same time

If you would classify an incident differently, open it from the url column, empty its api_windows_utc cell and run the script again.

What to Do With It

  • Single provider, no fallback: expect 73 to 77 hours per 90 days with an API incident open, roughly 3.5% of the time. Add a second provider before you spend time tuning retries.
  • Already on a gateway: pair OpenAI with Anthropic. Their 36 minutes of overlap means each covers the other for text.
  • Batch, PDF, image or voice: that is where both overlaps landed. Give each one a separate fallback and a deadline check.
  • Choosing a vendor: skip incident counts and uptime percentages, and compare hours on the components you call.

Wrapping Up

Three months of status pages put OpenAI and Anthropic about 4 hours apart, each with an API incident open around 3.5% of the time, and never broken on the same kind of request at once. Incident counts mostly reflect how a provider writes its status page. The fix for an LLM outage is a second provider behind a gateway plus a check you run yourself, not a longer retry loop. The full dataset and analysis are free to rerun and cite.

title: H2Table: Hierarchical Hypergraph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Complex Table Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2609.01216v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tables are ubiquitous across diverse domains, yet reasoning over them remains a significant challenge for modern large language models (LLMs). Current approaches typically linearize tables into sequences, inherently overlooking their intrinsic two-dimensional and hierarchical structure. To address this, we propose H2Table (Hierarchical Hypergraph-Enhanced Table Reasoning), a novel framework that represents complex tables as hierarchical nested hypergraphs. To process this representation, we design a tailored hypergraph encoder to facilitate message passing between hyperedges (headers) and nodes (cells), thereby perceiving the semantic entailment relationships between them within complex tables. Furthermore, we introduce a set of learnable query vectors acting as a lightweight bridge to extract representative structural embeddings from the encoder into the LLM. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively handles complex table question answering tasks with hierarchical nested headers. Notably, on the HiTab dataset, H2Table achieves an average improvement of 22.88% over state-of-the-art baselines on highly complex tables with a nesting depth of four. Our code is available at: https://github.com/lila120/h2table.

title: Evolving Creatives with Clicks: CTR-Driven Advertising image Editing via Attribute Disentanglement and Preference Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.13066v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The optimization objective for e-commerce advertising creatives has shifted from aesthetic quality to online business metrics like click-through rate (CTR). Recent methods generate appealing ad images from product images by constructing CTR-based reward signals and refining prompt generation via Reinforcement Learning. Such paradigms equally penalize all attributes within an underperforming image, even though some are actually beneficial to clicks. In this work, we propose Evolving Creatives with Clicks (ECC), which reformulates creative optimization as fine-grained editing rather than generation from scratch. ECC selectively refines attributes that hurt CTR while preserving those that contribute positively. Specifically, faced with a rich attribute space across massive images, ECC first identifies 28 attributes significantly correlated with CTR via ANOVA and Random Forest regression. Based on attribute contrasts between images with disparate CTRs, we instruction-tune a prompt model to generate editing suggestions, then refine it with real click preferences since reference-derived suggestions are not uniformly beneficial. Furthermore, we introduce Consistent Preference Optimization (CPO) as ECC's preference optimization strategy, which enforces consistency across semantically equivalent shuffled suggestions to mitigate DPO overfitting and improve preference generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ECC significantly improves the CTR of ad images, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a substantial margin. The complete data pipeline, including attribute extraction and analysis, the resulting dataset, and source code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Recording what the Firestore emulator sends to Cloud Functions, and replaying it in Rust
description:
hidane is a reimplementation of the Cloud Firestore emulator as a single Rust binary: no JDK, the same gRPC, REST and WebChannel wire protocols, and it runs under firebase-tools with hidane exec -- firebase emulators:start. Its rule is that every claim of compatibility has a test behind it: scripts record how the official emulator answers, and hidane's test suite replays every recording.

Until now, one thing was missing under emulators:start: Firestore-triggered Cloud Functions. Since 0.2.3 hidane accepted the Functions emulator's trigger registrations, so functions loaded, but no event ever reached them. 0.4.0 delivers those events. This post is about how.

How the two emulators talk

When you run firebase emulators:start with Firestore and Functions, firebase-tools starts the Firestore emulator with --functions_emulator <host:port>. The Functions emulator then registers each Firestore trigger with the Firestore emulator. After a commit, the Firestore emulator sends an event for each document the commit changed to every trigger that watches it, as POST /functions/projects/{p}/triggers/{key} on the Functions emulator.

None of this is a documented API. It is a conversation between two local processes, and the only reliable description of it is what the official emulator actually sends.

Recording it from the outside

hidane treats the official emulator as a black box: its jar is never decompiled, and everything below was observed on the wire (docs/clean-room describes the policy).

tools/oracle/function_events.py starts the official emulator (v1.22.0, the version firebase-tools pins) three times, under an English locale:

  1. with --functions_emulator pointing at a small server of the script's own, which records every request it receives and answers 200, or 500, 404 or a late answer depending on the trigger's key;
  2. without the flag;
  3. with the flag pointing at a port nothing listens on.

Against each, it registers triggers the way firebase-tools does, writes over REST, gRPC Commit and the Write stream, and records for every step: the answer, every request the Functions emulator received (in order, every header, the body as sent), and the WARNING lines the emulator printed.

What it sends

v1 triggers (providers/cloud.firestore/eventTypes/document.*) get a compact JSON body:

{"data":{"value":…,"oldValue":…,"updateMask":{}},
 "context":{"eventId":…,"timestamp":…,"eventType":…,
            "resource":{"name":…,"service":"firestore.googleapis.com"}}}

A few details only a recording shows: the v1 triggers of one change share the same eventId; updateMask is always empty; the timestamp is the commit time; and v1 triggers only ever see the (default) database.

v2 triggers (google.cloud.firestore.document.v1.*, including withAuthContext) get a binary-mode CloudEvent. The attributes travel as ce-* headers (ce-type, ce-source, ce-id, ce-subject, ce-time, ce-database, ce-document, and so on), and the body is a google.events.cloud.firestore.v1.DocumentEventData protobuf, base64-encoded, which firebase-tools decodes. For withAuthContext, the emulator sends ce-authtype: unknown and the same placeholder ce-authid whoever wrote.

The order: a Java HashMap

Ordering looked simple at first: all v1 events of a commit, then the v2 ones, document by document in the order the writes name them. But when several triggers watch the same document, they did not come in registration order, nor alphabetically.

They come in the iteration order of a Java HashMap sized for the project's triggers of that version. The model was fitted on 116 observations, and hidane reproduces it in presized_hash_order:

pub fn presized_hash_order<S: AsRef<str>>(keys: &[S]) -> Vec<usize> {
    // `(int) Math.ceil(n / 0.75)`, then `tableSizeFor`.
    let wanted = (keys.len() * 4).div_ceil(3).max(1);
    let capacity = u32::try_from(wanted.next_power_of_two()).unwrap_or(1 << 30);
    let mut ordered: Vec<(usize, u32)> = keys
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .map(|(i, key)| (i, spread(string_hash(key.as_ref())) & (capacity - 1)))
        .collect();
    ordered.sort_by_key(|&(i, bucket)| (bucket, i));
    ordered.into_iter().map(|(i, _)| i).collect()
}

string_hash is Java's String.hashCode (base 31 over UTF-16 code units), spread folds the high half into the low one, and the table is the smallest power of two that holds n / 0.75 entries. Keys come out by bucket, and by insertion within a bucket. Functions that depend on the order in which their siblings fire are fragile, but a test suite that passes on the official emulator should not start failing because the order changed.

Timing and failures

Events go out after the commit, from one background queue, so a write never waits for a function. Each event waits for the answer to the previous one, for up to 20 seconds. hidane does the same, one event at a time from a task of its own.

When delivery fails (an error status, a refused connection, a timeout), the official emulator logs a WARNING and does not retry, for example Unsuccessful HTTP response when publishing event for … or Failed to publish event to {host}: Connection refused. Without --functions_emulator, every event is a WARNING that the Functions emulator host/port is not configured. hidane prints the same wording.

Batches, transactions, :batchWrite, gRPC Commit, the Write stream, deleted paths and cleared databases send events; imports and POST /reset do not.

Replaying it

crates/hidane/tests/function_events.rs replays the 133 steps of the three runs against hidane and compares the status of each answer, every request the Functions emulator receives (v1 bodies byte for byte, v2 bodies decoded, with times and IDs compared as labels), and every WARNING.

Recording also turned up something unrelated: Java prints the smallest double as 4.9E-324, and hidane printed 5.0E-324, over REST and WebChannel too. That is fixed now.

What hidane does not copy

Matching the official emulator is the goal, but not its bugs. Each of these is listed in docs/parity-exceptions.md:

  • A v2 event's ce-source (a function's event.source) names the project twice: //firestore.googleapis.com/projects/projects/{p}/databases/{d}. hidane names it once, as production does.
  • A write that changes nothing sends v2 updated and written events, and deleting a missing document sends v2 created and written; v1 triggers get neither. hidane sends no event for either, as production does.
  • POST /reset makes the official emulator forget every registered trigger, so functions stop firing, silently, until they reload. hidane keeps them.
  • A v2 trigger registered without a database makes every write to the project answer 500. hidane has it watch (default).

End to end

Recordings check the wire; the last check is whether functions actually receive the same data. tools/oracle/functions/ is a functions project (firebase-functions 6.6.0) with v1 onCreate / onUpdate / onDelete / onWrite, v2 onDocumentCreated / Updated / Deleted / Written, onDocumentWrittenWithAuthContext, a subcollection and a named database. It runs under firebase emulators:exec --only functions,firestore (firebase-tools 15.33.0), once with the official emulator and once under hidane exec.

The same 37 events reach the same functions with the same data. The official run has 6 more, the v2 events for the no-op write and the missing delete, and projects/projects/ in event.source; both transcripts are in results/functions-triggers-*.json.

Also in 0.4.0

  • A commit's problems are reported in the official emulator's order.
  • The Go, Python and Java server SDKs are verified against both emulators: documents, queries, aggregations, vector search, transactions and listeners.
  • A weekly CI job starts the official emulator, re-records a set of recordings and fails if one differs from the committed fixture.
  • The parity table now counts 20,224 recorded answers that the test suite replays.

Try it 

curl -fsSL https://hidane.dev/install.sh | sh   # or Homebrew, npm, cargo, pub, Docker
hidane exec -- firebase emulators:start

Other ways to install:

brew install hidane-dev/tap/hidane
npm install --save-dev hidane
cargo binstall hidane
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/hidane-dev/hidane
  • Website: https://hidane.dev
  • GitHub: https://github.com/hidane-dev/hidane
  • Release notes: https://github.com/hidane-dev/hidane/releases/tag/v0.4.0

hidane is also listed on DevHunt this week: https://devhunt.org/tool/hidane

If your tests get a different answer from hidane than from the official emulator, please open an issue with the Parity gap template. That is the most useful feedback.

title: Supabase Data API exposure changes on 30 October: grant tables explicitly
description:
On a project with the new default, a table you just created is invisible to the Data API until someone grants it. Your app gets an error where it used to get rows, while the table sits in your database looking fine. Supabase announced the change on 28 April 2026, and it reaches every existing project on 30 October 2026.

This post covers the exposure change only: what changed, the dates, the grants to add, and how to check them before the 30th. For the policy side, see the row-level security production checklist.

What changed

Until now, a new table in the public schema was reachable through the Data API as soon as it existed. The Supabase changelog states the new rule in one line: "New tables in the public schema will no longer be exposed to the Data API automatically." A new table now needs an explicit Postgres grant before the Data API can see it.

The changelog gives three dates:

  • 28 April 2026: the new setting is available for new projects, at project creation.
  • 30 May 2026: it becomes the default for new projects, rolled out over a few weeks.
  • 30 October 2026: it is applied to all existing projects.

Existing tables are not touched. The changelog says they "keep their current grants and stay reachable." The change matters most for tables you create from now on, and for any project that moves to the new default.

If your app only uses a direct Postgres connection, such as an ORM, psql or a server with a connection string, the changelog says it is unaffected. The change is about the Data API, which supabase-js and the other client libraries call over HTTP.

Why a table goes missing

The Data API docs put the rule plainly: "A table isn't reachable through the Data API unless you have granted a role privileges on it." A missing grant returns a 42501 error from PostgREST.

On existing projects today, new tables in public get select, insert, update and delete for anon, authenticated and service_role by default. The docs say Supabase is "changing the platform default to revoke these automatic grants so that exposure becomes opt-in." That default is the thing you need to plan around.

1. Find the tables the Data API can reach

Run this in the SQL Editor. It is our query, not Supabase's, so check the output against your own schema:

select table_name, grantee, privilege_type
from information_schema.role_table_grants
where table_schema = 'public'
  and grantee in ('anon', 'authenticated', 'service_role')
order by table_name, grantee;

A table your app needs that is missing from the output has no grants, so it stays unreachable until you add them. Also open the Security Advisor. The changelog says it will flag affected tables before the date, and that owners and admins will be emailed.

2. Grant each role the minimum

The docs recommend the smallest grant that works: read-only for anonymous clients, full access for signed-in users with RLS still applied, and full access for the service role only where server code reaches the table through the Data API.

-- Read-only access for anonymous clients
grant select on table public.your_table to anon;

-- Full access for signed-in users; RLS still applies
grant select, insert, update, delete on table public.your_table to authenticated;

-- Full access for server-side code using the service role
grant select, insert, update, delete on table public.your_table to service_role;

Our rule is no write grant to anon unless anonymous writes are the point of the table.

3. Turn on row level security

The docs say tables created through the Supabase Dashboard have RLS on by default. Tables created in the SQL Editor or with another tool do not, so enable it yourself:

alter table public.your_table enable row level security;

The docs warn that "Tables and views exposed through the Data API without RLS can be accessed by any role with matching grants." A grant lets a role in, and RLS decides which rows it sees. The docs also note that RLS does not apply to functions, so grant EXECUTE only to the roles that need it.

4. Choose grant-per-table or opt in early

You have two routes. The first is the grant in step 2, table by table. The second is to revoke the defaults, so every new table starts closed. The docs give the statements:

alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke select, insert, update, delete on tables from anon, authenticated, service_role;

alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke execute on functions from anon, authenticated, service_role;

alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke usage, select on sequences from anon, authenticated, service_role;

alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke execute on functions from public;

The changelog says running the revoke statements the dashboard runs at project creation adopts the new behavior on an existing project today. The docs list the statements above, but we could not confirm they match the dashboard's exactly, so compare them before you run anything. Opting in is optional before the 30th. Our reading is that default privileges apply to objects created after you run them, so tables that already exist keep their grants. Run the statements on a staging project first. After that, every new table needs its grants in the same migration that creates it, or your app will not see it.

5. Test each role

Call your own endpoints three ways: with the anon key, with a signed-in user's token, and with the service role key from server code. Each request should return what that role is meant to see.

Our reading of the two errors you will meet: a 42501 on a table the app needs means a grant is missing. An empty result from a table you expected rows from usually points to a policy that filters every row, not to the grant.

Work backward from 30 October

Give yourself at least a week. Run the query in step 1 and list the tables your app reads and writes. Put the grants and the RLS policies into a migration, and test that migration on staging with all three roles. Run the opt-in statements on staging, then on production, and check the Security Advisor the next day.

What we could not confirm

  • The docs do not say whether the default has already taken effect on a given project. Check your project's Data API settings and the tables it exposes, rather than relying on the date alone.
  • The changelog gives the dates but no per-project migration steps. The Security Advisor and the emails are the only signals it names.
  • We have not run these steps against a live Supabase project. Test the SQL on staging before you run it on production.

Sources

  • Supabase changelog, "Breaking change: tables not exposed to Data and GraphQL API automatically," 28 April 2026: https://supabase.com/changelog/45329-breaking-change-tables-not-exposed-to-data-and-graphql-api-automatically
  • Supabase Data API docs, the securing your API page: the grant, RLS and default-privilege statements above. Named here, not linked.
  • OTF posts for the policy side: Row-level security production checklist and Supabase Row Level Security for mobile data.

title: OARelatedWork: A Large-Scale Dataset of Related Work Sections with Full-texts from Open Access Sources
description:
arXiv:2405.01930v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This paper introduces OARelatedWork: a dataset for related work generation from open-access sources. It is the first large-scale multi-document summarization dataset for related work generation, containing whole related work sections and full texts of cited papers. Its validation and test splits are constructed so that every source paper is available in full text, enabling controlled evaluation of full-text related work generation. The dataset includes 94 450 papers from multiple domains. With OARelatedWork, we aim to shift the field from generating parts of related work sections from abstracts only to generating entire related work sections from all available content. We (i) benchmark a wide spectrum of models, highlighting that synthesizing massive full-text contexts remains challenge for tested cost-effective Large Language Models (LLMs): under our statement-level judge, GPT-4o-mini's evidence-grounded True rate drops from 92.9% with abstracts to 83.8% with full texts. We (ii) empirically analyze human writing behavior through a human evaluation over 40 papers and 408 factual statements, revealing that authors frequently introduce abstractive claims ungrounded in localized source texts; consequently, tested LLMs actually surpass human baselines in strict, evidence-grounded factuality. Finally, we (iii) conduct a fine-grained meta-evaluation, revealing that standard reference-based metrics are inadequate for evaluating such long-form structured outputs, and introduce a robust statement-level evaluation framework to address this gap.

title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.12975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).

title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.13132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation.
  In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.

title: Physics-guided surrogate learning enables zero-shot control of turbulent wings
description:
arXiv:2604.09434v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Turbulent boundary layers over aerodynamic surfaces are a major source of aircraft drag, yet their control remains challenging due to multiscale dynamics and spatial variability, particularly under adverse pressure gradients. Reinforcement learning has outperformed state-of-the-art strategies in canonical flows, but its application to realistic geometries is limited by computational cost and transferability. Here we show that these limitations can be overcome by exploiting local structures of wall-bounded turbulence. Policies are trained in turbulent channel flows matched to wing boundary-layer statistics and deployed directly onto a NACA4412 wing section at $Re_c=2\times10^5$ without additional training on the wing, constituting zero-shot deployment. The transferred policies reduce total drag by 11.1\%, while state-of-the-art opposition control reduces it by 8.9\%. With the actuation cost taken into account, the corresponding net-energy savings are 10.9\% and 8.8\%, respectively. Surrogate training provides an estimated improvement of four orders of magnitude in exploration efficiency over direct on-wing training, enabling scalable flow control.

title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.12954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.
